f-w-de-klerk: Frederik Willem de Klerk was born on 18 March 1936 in Mayfair, a suburb of Johannesburg, into an influential Afrikaner family with long ties to the National Party. His father Jan de Klerk was a senator, president of the senate for seven years, acting state president and a cabinet member for fifteen years. His aunt's husband, J. G. Strijdom, was a former prime minister, and his brother Willem later left the party to found the liberal Democratic Party. De Klerk studied at Potchefstroom University from 1954 to 1958, took degrees in arts and law, and was initiated into the Broederbond. He set up a law partnership in Vereeniging in 1962. In 1972 he was elected to the House of Assembly.

As a minister in the government of P. W. Botha, de Klerk supported and enforced apartheid. After Botha resigned as party leader, de Klerk defeated Barend du Plessis, 69 votes to 61, and was elected leader of the National Party on 2 February 1989. Botha resigned the presidency on 14 August 1989, and de Klerk was elected State President on 20 September. ANC leaders and Desmond Tutu doubted that he would differ from his predecessors, but he allowed a protest march of about 30,000 people in Cape Town to proceed, saying the door to a new South Africa was open.

His presidency was dominated by negotiations between his government and the ANC. In a whites-only referendum on 17 March 1992 more than two thirds voted to continue negotiating an end to apartheid. State security forces committed widespread human rights abuses and encouraged violence between Xhosa and Zulu people, though de Klerk later denied sanctioning such actions. Mandela distrusted de Klerk's role, particularly regarding the so-called third force, and the question was never clarified. In 1993 de Klerk publicly apologised for apartheid's harmful effects. After the 1994 election he served as one of two deputy presidents, and he opposed the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, preferring a blanket amnesty. In May 1996 the National Party withdrew from the coalition.

De Klerk retired from active politics in 1997 and lectured internationally. His autobiography The Last Trek appeared in 1999. He died on 11 November 2021 at his home in Cape Town, a few months after a diagnosis of mesothelioma. Afterwards the F. W. de Klerk Foundation released a video in which he apologised without qualification for the harm caused by apartheid. He was a controversial figure. Anti-apartheid activists criticised him for offering only a qualified apology and for ignoring abuses by the security forces, while supporters of apartheid held that he had betrayed the Afrikaner minority. He himself said that his views had changed completely, as in a conversion.
fa-ngum: Fa Ngum was born in 1316 in Muang Sua, a Lao principality on the site of present-day Luang Prabang. His grandfather, the ruler of Muang Sua, banished him and his father to the Khmer kingdom of Angkor in the 1320s, by one account because of the father's indiscretion with one of the grandfather's wives. Another tradition says the boy was sent away because he was born with thirty-three teeth, an omen that threatened his grandfather's kingdom. He was brought up by the religious scholar Maha Pasaman and married a Khmer princess.

With the support of the Khmer king Jayavarman IX, Fa Ngum returned with an army to win control of his homeland. Between 1352 and 1354 he took Muang Sing, Chiang Hung, Chiang Saen, Chiang Mai, Pak Ou and Pak Beng, and in 1353 Vientiane, Xiang Khouang and Luang Phrabang. He defeated his uncle in battle near Xiang Dong Xiang Thong and became undisputed master of the land. His conquests also reached western Nghệ An, the valleys between the Red River and the Black River in Vietnam, and present-day Isan in Thailand.

He named the kingdom Lan Xang Hôm Khao, the land of a million elephants and a white parasol: the elephant stood for military power, since most battles were fought with elephants, and the white parasol for royalty, above all a Buddhist king. He made Xiang Dong Xiang Thong, later renamed Luang Prabang, his capital, and legitimised his rule by enshrining the Prabang image of the Buddha as protector of the kingdom.

Fa Ngum is credited with bringing Khmer culture and Singhalese Buddhism to the region; in keeping with his Khmer wife's wishes he made Theravada Buddhism the state religion, and his tutor Maha Pasaman brought sacred texts and the Phra Bang. The kingdom passed to his son Oun Huan, called Samsenethai after a census that counted 300,000 Tai subjects. Samsenethai set up an administration based on the muang, with governors for each, that lasted until it was abolished by the Communist government in 1975.
fabre-geffrard: Geffrard was born in L'Anse-à-Veau in southern Haiti. His father, General Nicolas Geffrard, a veteran of the Haitian Revolution who had helped draft the 1806 Constitution, died before his son was born, and the boy was adopted by Colonel Fabre, a close associate of his father, who had him educated in Aux Cayes. He was the first head of state of Haiti to be born after independence.

He joined the army at fifteen in his father's former unit, the 13th Regiment, and rose steadily. After the fall of President Jean-Pierre Boyer in 1843 he gained a command in Jacmel in 1845, but President Jean-Baptiste Riché saw him as a rival and removed him. Tried before a military court presided over by Faustin Soulouque, he was pardoned. Once Soulouque had made himself emperor, he gave Geffrard command against the Dominicans, and after a victory at La Tabarra created him Duke of Tabara in 1852.

Sworn in on 18 January 1859, Geffrard called himself a conservative liberal and restored a constitution close to that of 1846, with a life presidency and the power to dissolve congress. He replaced the export duty known as the royal fifth with port duties, signed a treaty of trade and navigation with the United States on 3 November 1864, let individuals buy up to fifteen acres of state land and ordered a mineral survey. He also suppressed Vodou, ordering altars and drums destroyed; the Affaire de Bizoton of 1864 ended in public executions.

Schooling grew quickly. Agricultural schools were decreed for each arrondissement, the first girls' schools in Haitian history were opened, lycées were founded in five cities, and a law school and a naval academy were created. By 1864 Geffrard reported 210 schools and 14,600 pupils.

His rule was challenged from the start. In September 1859 conspirators linked to his interior minister, Guerrier Prophète, shot dead his daughter Cora at his mother's house, hoping to lure him there; seventeen were sentenced to death. In 1865 Sylvain Salnave seized Cap-Haïtien. The city was retaken after British warships bombarded it in October, but about half of it burned, and the foreign role cost Geffrard much of his standing before Salnave overthrew him in 1867.
fabrizio-ruffo: Ruffo was born on 16 September 1744 at San Lucido in Calabria Citra, then part of the Kingdom of Naples, the son of Litterio Ruffo, duke of Baranello, and Giustiniana, of the Roman Colonna family. He owed his education to his uncle, Cardinal Tommaso Ruffo, dean of the College of Cardinals, and won the favour of Giovanni Angelo Braschi, who became Pope Pius VI in 1775.

The pope made him one of the chierici di camera, the papal civil and financial service, and later treasurer-general, a post that carried the ministry of war. Pietro Colletta called him corrupt, a charge since dismissed as part of a hostile tradition; he was widely seen as a reformer, and by restricting landowners' feudal powers he made enemies. Removed from the treasurership in 1791, he was made a cardinal, though he never became a priest.

When French troops advanced on Naples in December 1798, Ruffo fled to Palermo with the royal family. Named the King's General Official, he landed in Calabria on 8 February and raised the army of the faith with Michele Pezza, known as Fra Diavolo, and other brigand leaders, enlisting 25,000 farmers on his fiefs of Scilla and Bagnara. The army took Crotone and moved through Basilicata and Apulia, and with Admiral Ushakov's Russian fleet behind him he reached Naples by June 1799.

Possibly exceeding his authority, Ruffo promised the republicans immunity and obtained their surrender. Rear-Admiral Horatio Nelson, sent by King Ferdinand, called the pact infamous and revoked it. Former Admiral Francesco Caracciolo was executed on 30 June, and of the prisoners handed to Bourbon justice 124 were put to death. Ruffo seems to have lost the king's favour by his leniency, and he gave up the vicar-generalship granted him on 25 January 1800.

Ruffo later served Ferdinand as ambassador in Paris, attended Napoleon's marriage to Marie Louise of Austria on 2 April 1810 and received the Cross of the Legion of Honour. Recalled to Rome by Pope Pius VII in 1815, he was Camerlengo from 1819 to 1820 and took part in the conclave of 1823 that elected Pope Leo XII. He died in Naples on 13 December 1827 and was buried in the basilica of San Domenico Maggiore. His campaign divided nineteenth-century historians.
faccetta-nera: The march is sung by an Italian Blackshirt soldier during the invasion of Ethiopia in the Second Italo-Ethiopian War. He tells a beautiful young enslaved Abyssinian girl that she will be freed from slavery and ruled by a new regime, and invites her to parade with the fascist Blackshirts in Rome, where she is promised a new and better life. The song is said to have been inspired by a young Abyssinian girl whom Italian troops found at the beginning of the invasion. Slavery in Ethiopia is its main theme, in keeping with the propaganda that presented the war as one of liberation.

During the invasion the song was hugely popular in Italy and stirred national fervour. Its implicitly erotic content soon embarrassed the Fascist government. Under the occupation, Ethiopian women lived with Italian men in a system of concubinage known as madamismo, but from May 1936 the regime passed laws forbidding cohabitation and marriage between Italians and the native peoples of the Italian colonial empire, which culminated in the Italian racial laws of 1938. The authorities considered banning the song, and they removed every picture postcard showing Abyssinian women from the shop windows of Rome.

The song has since been heard in films. Martin Scorsese used it among the many Italian songs of Mean Streets (1973), and it is heard prominently in Francesco Rosi's Christ Stopped at Eboli, in a scene where Blackshirts prepare to leave for Ethiopia.
factory-acts: The first act, the Health and Morals of Apprentices Act 1802, was introduced by Sir Robert Peel after concerns raised by the medical men of Manchester, first voiced in 1784 over an outbreak of putrid fever at a mill at Radcliffe owned by Peel. It dealt mainly with apprentices and left free children unregulated. The Cotton Mills and Factories Act 1819, a watered-down version of a draft by Robert Owen, limited children aged 9–16 in cotton mills to 12 hours a day, but enforcement rested with local magistrates and by 1825 there had been only two prosecutions.

Reformers pressed for more. Michael Thomas Sadler's bill of 1832 would have cut children's hours to ten a day across the textile industries, with the backing of Short Time Committees in Yorkshire and Lancashire. Outside Parliament the Tory Richard Oastler campaigned for a ten-hour day, and in the Commons Anthony Ashley-Cooper, later 7th Earl of Shaftesbury, led the Ten-Hour Movement.

The Labour of Children, etc., in Factories Act 1833, known as Althorp's Act, barred those under 18 from night work and limited children aged 9–12 to 48 hours a week, allowing millowners to work relays of children so that adults could work a 15-hour day. In 1835 the inspectors reported that the education clauses were impracticable and relays difficult, and there were too few of them to oversee all 4,000 factories.

The Factory Act 1844 extended the twelve-hour day and ban on night work for young persons to women of all ages. Under Lord John Russell's Whig government, whose cabinet held no collective view, the Ten Hour Bill passed as the Factories Act 1847, limiting the week of women and those under 18 in most textile mills to 63 hours from 1 July 1847 and 58 hours from 1 May 1848. Acts of 1850 and 1853 remedied its defects, among them the false relay system of split shifts.

The ten-hour day had none of the dire consequences its opponents predicted, and from the 1860s acts brought bleaching, dyeing, lace work, calendaring and finishing under similar rules. In the Lords debate on the bill of 1874, Shaftesbury noted that employment in textile mills had grown from 354,684 in 1835 to 880,920 in 1871 while accidents had halved. The Factory and Workshop Act 1878 consolidated 16 earlier acts, later acts raised the minimum working age to 11 in 1891 and to 12 in 1901, and the Factories Act 1961 consolidated the acts of 1937 and 1959.
fadluya: Fadluya, whose full name was Amir Abu'l-Abbas Fadl, was the son of Ali ibn Hasan ibn Ayyub of the Ramani clan of the Shabankara, Kurds from Syria who had migrated to Fars. The Shabankara held the mountain region of Kuhgiluya and kept a large measure of independence, and Fadluya is counted the founder of the Shabankara dynasty of Fars, which lasted, with interruptions, until 1355.

His father sent him to Saheb-e Adel, vizier of the Buyid ruler Abu Kalijar, asking for a court post for his son. Fadluya rose under the vizier's patronage to the rank of sepahsalar. He was alienated when Abu Kalijar decided to take the Shabankara territories for himself.

When the Seljuk prince Qavurt invaded Fars in 1053, Fadluya turned to Qavurt's brother Alp Arslan and offered an annual tribute of 27 million dirhams in return for being left as ruler of Fars. Alp Arslan accepted. Fadluya's main capital was Goshnabad, or Joshnabad, a town somewhere north-east of Fasa, and he also resided at times at Darabgerd and Shiraz.

Under Alp Arslan as sultan he rebelled, stopped sending the tribute, proclaimed himself independent and took up a defensive position in the fortress of Khvorsha near Jahrom. The sultan's vizier Nizam al-Mulk took the fortress after 16 days. Fadluya surrendered, offered reparations and was forgiven and restored to his position.

He rebelled a second time, and Nizam al-Mulk was again sent against him. An attempt to settle matters peacefully failed, and Fadluya shut himself up in a fortress. The siege was short: the defenders surrendered for lack of water, and Fadluya, trying to flee, was captured and brought before Alp Arslan.
failaka-island: Failaka lies in the northern Persian Gulf, 20 kilometres off the coast of Kuwait City and about 50 kilometres south-east of the point where the Tigris and Euphrates empty into the Gulf. For thousands of years it was a strategic prize in the trade that passed up and down the Gulf. The name Failaka is thought to derive from the Greek phylakion, meaning outpost. Its village of Al-Zawr, on the north-west side, was the longest continuously inhabited place in Kuwait until the Gulf War.

Mesopotamian traders from Ur settled the island around 2000 BCE, and its buildings of that time resemble those found in Iraq. Sumerian cuneiform texts found on the island name it Agarum, the land of the god Enzak, and it became a hub of the Dilmun civilization. A seal of about 1650 BCE preserves the name of a king's daughter, and the title servant of Inzak of Akarum was the king's title in Dilmun. Failaka was later under the Kassite dynasty of Babylon, and in the Neo-Babylonian period Nebuchadnezzar II had a palace and temple there, while Nabonidus had a governor.

After an apparent abandonment of about seven centuries, the bay of Kuwait was resettled in the Achaemenid period. In 324 BCE Alexander the Great sent expeditions to explore the Gulf, and the island was named Ikaros, because, according to Strabo and Arrian, it resembled the Aegean island of that name. Remains include a large Hellenistic fort and two Greek temples; Strabo wrote of a temple of Apollo and an oracle of Artemis. Later a commercial station of the kingdom of Characene existed there. Nestorian Christian farms, villages and two large churches of the fifth and sixth centuries flourished until the ninth century.

A Danish team under Geoffrey Bibby excavated four tells between 1958 and 1963 and found about 50 cylinder seals and about 400 stamp seals, most of the stamp seals of Dilmun type. French, Italian, Polish, Slovak and Greek teams have worked there since, as have groups from the United States and Georgia.

Before the Iraqi invasion of 1990 the island had over two thousand residents and several schools. During 1990 and 1991 the invading Iraqis expelled all its residents to the mainland and mined the beaches. After the war the island was cleared of mines, though it remains under some military use. Many old homes still stood empty, and a resort has made it a holiday destination for visitors from Kuwait City.
faisal-bin-shamlan: Faisal Othman bin Shamlan was educated at the Ghayl ba-Wazeer School in Hadhramaut, then on a scholarship at the Bakht al-Ridha Institute in Sudan, and studied civil engineering at Kingston University in London. As a young activist he was a mild Islamic nationalist, one of a group of intellectuals from Hadhramaut and elsewhere in Yemen who pioneered a moderate Islamic movement, while keeping an independent place at the centre of politics.

He belonged to the coalition that overthrew the Qu'aiti Sultanate in Hadhramaut on 17 September 1967 and ran the province from day to day before independence on 30 November. In the first cabinet of the People's Republic of South Yemen, under Qahtan Al-Shaabi, he was Minister of Public Works and Transport, one of only two ministers from outside the National Liberation Front; with Mohammad Abdul Qader Bafaqeeh he inventoried and preserved the contents of the sultans' palaces. He headed the Public Corporation for Electric Power from 1969 and the Aden Oil Refinery from 1977, and sat in the Supreme People's Council from 1971 to 1990.

After unification in 1990 he led an independent bloc in the Council of Representatives, co-founded the Yemeni Free Forum and kept his seat in 1993 and 1997. He became Minister of Oil and Mineral Resources in October 1994 on condition that he could reform the ministry, resigned in March 1995, and was replaced in June. He resigned from parliament in 2003.

On 2 July 2006 the Joint Meeting Parties, a coalition of Islah, the Yemen Socialist Party and smaller parties, named him their candidate for the presidential election of 20 September 2006, in which he received about 22% of the vote according to official results. He died of cancer in Aden on 1 January 2010.
faisal-i-of-iraq: Faisal was born in Mecca on 20 May 1885, the third son of Hussein bin Ali, the Grand Sharif of Mecca, and grew up in Constantinople. In 1913 he was elected to the Ottoman parliament as representative of Jeddah. When the Ottoman Empire entered the war in December 1914, his father sent him to Constantinople, and on the way he met members of the Arab secret societies al-Fatat and Al-'Ahd. He joined al-Fatat. On 23 October 1916 he met Captain T. E. Lawrence, and from 1916 to 1918 he headed the Northern Army of the Great Arab Revolt against the Ottomans, with British assistance.

British and Arab forces took Damascus in October 1918, and Faisal helped set up an Arab government there. In 1919 he led the Arab delegation to the Paris Peace Conference, and on 4 January 1919 he signed an agreement with the Zionist leader Chaim Weizmann, which he accepted only conditionally. On 8 March 1920 the Syrian National Congress proclaimed him king of the Arab Kingdom of Syria. After the San Remo conference gave France the Mandate for Syria and Lebanon, the French defeated his forces at the Battle of Maysalun on 24 July 1920 and expelled him from Syria.

At the Cairo Conference in March 1921 the British chose Faisal to rule their Mandate of Iraq, partly on the advice of Lawrence. A plebiscite reported 96 per cent in favour, and he was made king on 23 August 1921, though few Iraqis knew him and the Shia majority was at first lukewarm. He encouraged pan-Arab nationalism and sought unity between Sunni and Shia, though equating Iraqi patriotism with being Arab marginalised the Kurds. In 1932 Iraq became independent and entered the League of Nations. Faisal died of a heart attack in Bern on 8 September 1933, aged 48, and was succeeded by his eldest son Ghazi.
faisal-ibn-turki-al-saud: Faisal was born in 1785, the son of Imam Turki bin Abdullah. He was among the members of the Al Saud taken to Cairo after Ibrahim Pasha, son of Muhammad Ali, captured Diriyah in May 1819, and he returned to Riyadh in 1827-1828. In 1830 he was sent on campaign to Al Hasa in the east. While he was away, his father was assassinated in 1834 by Mishari bin Abdul Rahman, a second cousin. Faisal hurried back, his troops stormed the castle and killed Mishari, and the town pledged allegiance to him.

His refusal to pay tribute to the Egyptian forces in the Hejaz brought an expedition into Najd. The Egyptian governor Khurshid Pasha backed a rival from the senior line of the family, Khalid bin Saud, and Faisal fled to the princes of the Bani Tamim. In December 1838 he tried to come to terms with Khurshid Pasha but was taken to Cairo with his brother Jiluwi, his sons Abdullah and Muhammad and a cousin. Released in 1843, after the Egyptian troops had left Najd, he returned to Riyadh and easily defeated his third cousin Abdullah bin Thunayan, who had seized power from Khalid.

In his second reign he accepted Ottoman supremacy and was named governor of Najd. He subdued opposing tribes and took control of Al-Ahsa, Qatif and Saihat, whose revenues, levied as zakat, funded his treasury. His attempts on Bahrain failed, partly because of British opposition to Saudi expansion in the Gulf. In June 1851 Qatari forces under Mohammed bin Thani and his son Jassim bin Mohammed defeated his army in the Battle of Mesaimeer, and an agreement of 25 July 1851 gave him an annual payment from Ali bin Khalifa of Bahrain in return for leaving Qatar alone.

In the 1850s and 1860s his moves against Oman, Bahrain and the Trucial States were halted by British forces. Faisal drew his income from zakat, import duties, pilgrim fees, a fifth of the spoils of raids, fines, his own domains and tribute from Bahrain and Muscat. In his last years he grew frail and blind, and his heir Abdullah was the effective ruler. He died in Riyadh in December 1865 after a long illness. His four sons, Abdullah, Saud, Muhammad and Abdul Rahman, born of two mothers, fell into the infighting that eventually destroyed the state. One of his daughters married Abdullah bin Rashid of Ha'il.
faisal-ii-of-iraq: Faisal was the only son of King Ghazi of Iraq and Queen Aliya, a daughter of 'Ali bin Hussein, King of the Hejaz. His father was killed in a car crash when Faisal was three, and he came to the throne on 4 April 1939, with Prince 'Abd al-Ilah as regent. In April 1941 a military coup aimed at aligning Iraq with the Axis powers briefly deposed the regent. It led to the Anglo-Iraqi War, and a combined Allied force restored 'Abd al-Ilah. During the Second World War Faisal lived for a time with his mother in Berkshire and attended Harrow School with Prince Hussein, the future King of Jordan, with whom he formed a close friendship.

Faisal came of age on 2 May 1953, the same day Hussein was enthroned in Jordan. He relied at first on 'Abd al-Ilah and on the veteran politician Nuri al-Sa'id. The Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of 1948 and the Baghdad Pact of 1955, which kept Britain involved in Iraqi affairs, met large protests that left hundreds of demonstrators dead. Oil revenues grew in the 1950s after negotiations with the Iraq Petroleum Company in 1952, and a Development Board received a share of them. It drew up plans for a Greater Baghdad, and architects including Walter Gropius and Le Corbusier were invited to design buildings there.

Opposition widened. There were uprisings in Najaf and Hayy in 1956, and in February 1957 a Front of National Union brought together the National Democrats, Independents, Communists and the Ba'ath Party, while a Supreme Committee of Free Officers formed in the army. After Egypt and Syria formed the United Arab Republic on 1 February 1958, Iraq and Jordan declared the Arab Hashemite Union on 14 February, with Faisal as head of state.

In July 1958 Iraqi army units under Colonel Abdul-Karim Qasim, sent towards Jordan during the Lebanon crisis, marched on Baghdad instead and carried out a coup on 14 July. Faisal ordered the Royal Guard to offer no resistance. At the Rihab Palace the king, 'Abd al-Ilah and other members of the family were gathered and, according to the account given, fired on as they crossed the kitchen garden. Faisal was shot in the head and neck, and only Princess Hiyam survived. The 14 July Revolution ended the thirty-seven-year-old Hashemite monarchy and Iraq became a republic. Faisal was later reburied in a marble tomb next to his father in the Royal Cemetery in Baghdad.
faizabad: Faizabad lies on the southern bank of the river Saryu, about 6.5 kilometres from Ayodhya and 130 kilometres east of Lucknow, the state capital of Uttar Pradesh. It has a monsoon-influenced humid subtropical climate, with more than 85 percent of its annual rainfall of about 1,100 millimetres falling between June and September. Its twin city Ayodhya was the headquarters of the province before Faizabad grew up beside it.

According to the Imperial Gazetteer of India, Saadat Khan built a hunting lodge four miles west of Ayodhya in 1730, after he was appointed governor of Oudh. Gardens were laid out and shops sprang up nearby, and the name Faizabad was first applied in the time of his successor Safdar Jang. Shuja-ud-daula, the third nawab, lived chiefly at Lucknow early in his reign, but after his defeat at Buxar in 1764 he made Faizabad his residence, strengthened its defences and laid out a large town. He died early in 1775 and before the year ended his successor Asaf-ud-daula moved permanently to Lucknow, after relations with his mother had soured.

The city declined but remained the home of Asaf-ud-daula's grandmother and mother, the Nawab Begam and Bahu Begam, whose treatment was the subject of charges against Warren Hastings. Bahu Begam, who had married Shuja-ud-daula in 1743, is credited with most of the Muslim buildings of Faizabad, and after her death the city fell further into decay. Oudh was annexed by the British in 1856, and Faizabad was a centre of one of the battles of the Mutiny of 1857. Local self-government for Ayodhya and Faizabad was introduced in 1865, with the two administered jointly as a municipality. The revolutionary Ashfaqulla Khan was hanged in Faizabad jail on 19 December 1927 for his part in the Kakori train robbery of 9 August 1925.

Monuments of the nawabs survive, among them the Gulab Bari, the garden tomb of Shuja-ud-daula, and the mausoleum of Bahu Begam, built at a cost of three lakh rupees by her chief adviser Darab Ali Khan and regarded as one of the finest buildings of its kind in Awadh. Tradition holds that Guptar Ghat on the Saryu is where Rama left the earth. Before November 2018 the city was the headquarters of Faizabad district and division. Both were then renamed Ayodhya, and the city is administered by the Ayodhya Municipal Corporation. The census of 2011 counted 165,228 people in the Faizabad municipal council.
faizullah-khan: Faizullah Khan was the second son of Nawab Ali Mohammed Khan and succeeded his elder brother, Nawab Saadullah Khan, as chief of the Rohillas. He fought alongside Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat and was granted Shikohabad for his service. In 1774, when the armies of the Vizier Shuja-ud-Daula and the East India Company invaded Rohilkhand and many Rohilla chiefs were killed, he escaped with his treasure to the hills, gathered the survivors and was widely accepted as his father's heir.

After a month's siege in the forest of Lal Dang both sides sought peace, and a treaty mediated by Colonel Champion let him choose the land for his state. He agreed to cut his army from 20,000 to 5,000, to correspond only with the Company or Awadh, and to raise up to 3,000 troops when Awadh went to war. With Awadh reduced to a British puppet after Shuja-ud-Daula's death, he sought ratification from Calcutta; Warren Hastings had it ratified in 1778 through Nathaniel Middleton, after taking one lakh rupees for the Company.

Rampur's cavalry became valuable to the British against raids by Sikhs, Gujars and outlaw Rohillas, and in 1779 he sent 2,000 horse to help the British against the French in South India. Short of funds in the early 1780s, the Company pressed him for more horse than the treaty required, and by the Treaty of Chunar of 1781 Hastings agreed to Awadh's annexation of Rampur. The Court of Directors judged this illegitimate in February 1783, but Faizullah still paid 15 lakh rupees after demands brought by William Palmer.

Balancing refusals with concessions, Faizullah kept Rampur at peace for some 20 years until his death on 17 July 1794. He was a Sunni, but his eldest son, Muhammad Ali Khan, took up the Shia creed under the influence of Nawab Asaf ud Daula of Awadh, and Rampur became one of the important Shia princely states. He had 18 children by four wives.
fakhr-al-din-ii: Fakhr al-Din was the eldest son of Qurqumaz ibn Yunus of the Ma'n dynasty, a Druze family of Arab stock settled in the Chouf of southern Mount Lebanon since before the Ottoman conquest of 1516. Unlike his predecessors he cooperated with the Ottomans. When the general Murad Pasha arrived at Sidon as governor of Damascus in September 1593, Fakhr al-Din received him with costly gifts and was made sanjak-bey of Sidon-Beirut that December; Safed followed in 1602. Contemporaries describe him as small, with an olive complexion and black eyes.

In 1606 he joined the Kurdish rebel Ali Janbulad of Aleppo against Yusuf Sayfa, yet kept his post. His alliance with the Medici grand dukes of Tuscany, his garrisoning of the fortresses of Shaqif Arnun and Subayba and his outlawed sekban mercenaries alarmed the imperial government, and after Murad Pasha's death in 1611 the grand vizier Nasuh Pasha turned against him. An imperial expedition followed in 1613, and Fakhr al-Din fled to Livorno and Florence; Pope Paul V opposed military aid for him, fearing a naval war with the Ottomans.

Returning in 1618, he recovered his domains, attacked the Sayfas, taking their stronghold of Hisn Akkar on 4 February 1619, and in 1623 defeated the governor of Damascus at the Battle of Anjar. He then held the Beqaa, fortresses across central Syria and, in practice, Tripoli. His wealth came mainly from tax farms whose price stayed fixed as their value rose, but also, by the account of the traveller Sandys, from extortion and counterfeit Dutch coins. He spent it on fortifications, government houses in Sidon, Beirut and Deir al-Qamar, caravanserais, mills and bridges, and on the mulberry groves that began Mount Lebanon's silk trade.

Murad IV grew alarmed at his presence in northern Syria, and after victories over the Safavids freed Ottoman troops, Fakhr al-Din surrendered during a siege of his Chouf hideout in 1633. He was executed in Constantinople on 13 April 1635. The union he had forged between the Druze Chouf and the Maronite Keserwan outlasted him: in 1697 his grandnephew Ahmad ibn Mulhim received the tax farm of these districts, which under the Shihabs became the Lebanese emirate. Druze and Maronite historians alike credit him with a decisive part in Lebanon's history, while the Sunni establishment of Damascus regarded him as a tyrant and rebel.
fakhruddin-mubarak-shah: According to some historians Fakhruddin, also known simply as Fakhra, was born into a Bengali Muslim family in a village in the east of Noakhali, in present-day Bangladesh. The exact place is uncertain, but it is thought to lie in Kabirhat Upazila. He served as silahdar, or chief armour-bearer, under Bahram Khan, the governor of Sonargaon appointed by the Delhi sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq.

After Bahram Khan's death Fakhruddin declared himself an independent ruler with his capital at Sonargaon, founding the Mubarak Shahi dynasty. Qadar Khan, the governor of Lakhnauti, sent a large army against him. Fakhruddin fled the field and lost Sonargaon, but when Qadar Khan's army fell out over the sharing of the spoils he regained the city and had Qadar Khan executed. His servant Mukhlis, whom he placed over Lakhnauti, was defeated by Qadar Khan's war minister, Alauddin Ali Shah.

Fakhruddin went on to take Comilla and Noakhali and to extend his territory north into Sylhet and south into Chittagong, the principal port of Bengal, which he conquered in 1340, the first Muslim ruler to do so. He won a naval action against Sultan Alauddin Ali Shah of Lakhnauti. Under him Sonargaon became a major regional power. He sponsored a trunk road and raised embankments as well as mosques and tombs, and the administrative division of Mubarakabad is said to have been named after him.

Ibn Battuta, who visited his capital in 1346, described him as a distinguished sovereign who loved strangers, above all fakirs and Sufis. Ikhtiyaruddin Ghazi Shah, who according to the historian Jadunath Sarkar was most probably his son, succeeded him and ruled the sultanate from Sonargaon until 1352.
fakir-azizuddin: Aziz ud-Din came from a Sayyid family, the eldest son of Hakīm Ghulām Mohy-ud-Dīn. His two brothers, Nūr ud-Dīn and Imām ud-Dīn, both held senior military posts in the Sikh Empire. Trained as a physician, he was first known by the title Hakīm; later he took the title Fakir, meaning beggar, as a mark of humility, and it appears in British correspondence after 1826.

He first came to Ranjit Singh as a physician. The Maharaja was impressed by his medical skill and his command of Arabic, Persian and English, and granted him a jagir and a place at court. His first major task was to help in the negotiations with the British that led to the Treaty of Amritsar of 1809. From 1810 to 1838 he carried out a long series of diplomatic missions and served as interpreter, trusted completely by the Maharaja, who rewarded him with honours and further jagirs.

He stayed in the empire's service after Ranjit Singh's death. In December 1839 he represented Maharaja Kharak Singh on a mission to the Governor-General, Lord Auckland, and in 1842, for Maharaja Sher Singh, he welcomed the new Governor-General, Lord Ellenborough, at Firozpur. Through these years he kept carefully apart from the factional intrigues that overtook the court.
Grieved by the course events had taken and by the deaths of two of his sons, Aziz ud-Din died in Lahore on 3 December 1845, aged 65. He was one of many non-Sikhs who served at Ranjit Singh's court.
falaki-shirvani: Of Persian descent, Falaki was born in 1107 in Shamakhi, the capital of the Shirvanshahs. He calls himself Muhammad Falaki in his poems; Falaki, his pen name, means astronomer, and since Khaqani said he was aware of the mysteries of the nine spheres he may have been a professional astronomer, though this could be wordplay. Some biographical collections give him other names, such as Abu'l-Nizam Jalalu'd-Din or Najmu'd-Din. He was a student of Khaqani although older than him.

Later biographers such as Dawlatshah Samarqandi tell that both were pupils of the poet Abu'l-Ala Ganjavi, who gave Khaqani his daughter in marriage and Falaki only 20,000 dirhams; the Iranologist Anna Livia Beelaert does not think the story real. Falaki's wife died soon after bearing their daughter, and his other relatives also died.

Of his Persian divan, 1,512 verses survive. Hadi Hasan published a collection of them in 1929 from an anthology in Munich and quotations in other works, and an enlarged edition in 1958 using a manuscript from Madras. Manuchihr III is the only ruler in the poems, which praise his victory over the Alans and Kipchaks, his seizure of parts of Arran, his building of Kardinan and Sa'dun and his restoration of the Bakilani dam.

Falaki is the first known Shirvani poet of habsiyat, prison poetry, and helped shape the genre's vocabulary of gham (sorrow), mihnat (affliction) and ranj (suffering). He claimed to surpass its founder, the Ghaznavid poet Masud Sa'd Salman, and set himself beside Abu Nuwas and Abu Tammam. The historian Rebecca Gould judges his impact much smaller than Masud's but important to the genre's spread.

Rivals' libel had him imprisoned in the fortress of Shabaran; freed, he wrote that confinement had left him a mere skeleton. Khaqani called his death premature, and Hadi Hasan placed it in Shirvan in about 1155; since the poems do not mention Manuchihr III's death, Francois de Blois dismissed a date of 1181/82. He was buried in Shamakhi, according to Taqi Kashi, and Khaqani wrote a eulogy for him. Salman Savaji and Ismat Bukhara'i later copied his style.
falange-espanola-de-las-jons: The party grew out of a small movement under attack. During and after the 1933 election campaign members of both the Falange and the JONS were killed: on 9 February 1934 Matías Montero was murdered while selling Falangist newspapers, and by June 1934 ten were dead, killed mainly by Socialists, who feared that a fascist movement would crush them as had happened in Germany and Italy. The merged party was first led by a triumvirate of Ramiro Ledesma, Julio Ruiz de Alda and José Antonio Primo de Rivera, with Raimundo Fernández-Cuesta as General Secretary, and it drew intellectuals such as Rafael Sánchez Mazas, Ernesto Giménez Caballero and Dionisio Ridruejo.

The historian Martin Blinkhorn distinguishes four strands in the early party: the monarchist conservatism of Francisco Moreno Herrera, marquis of Eliseda, the authoritarian Catholicism of Onésimo Redondo, the radical national syndicalism of Ledesma and the elitist regenerationism of Primo de Rivera. Eliseda, a financial backer, left in November 1934 over the party's view of church and state, and Ledesma was expelled in January 1935. From 1935 the Italian Fascist regime paid the party 50,000 lire a month. Probably never more than ten thousand members strong, the Falange was shunned by other right-wing parties in the 1936 election and ran candidates in 19 of 60 districts.

Under the Popular Front government sixty-seven Falangists were killed, and the Falange killed sixty-four leftists, mostly socialists and communists; on 16 April 1936 Falangists fired submachine guns at workers in central Madrid, killing three. Persecuted by the government, the party adopted cells of three members and joined the conspiracy against the Second Spanish Republic. In the Civil War it grew from several thousand members to several hundred thousand, while 60% of its pre-war members lost their lives. With Primo de Rivera in prison, Manuel Hedilla, a former mechanic, led the party until the merger of 1937.

The Twenty-Seven Points, drafted mainly by Ledesma, called for vertical syndicates uniting workers and employers by industry, land reform for the peasants, the nationalisation of credit and a ban on strikes and lockouts, and condemned what the party called usurious, financial and speculative capitalism. They also called for the abolition of political parties and a nationalist dictatorship. The militia, the Primera Línea, had a training manual for guerrilla warfare, and the Sección Femenina, led by José Antonio's sister Pilar Primo de Rivera, kept the party alive underground in the spring of 1936. Its emblem was the yoke and arrows and its anthem Cara al Sol.
falklands-war: The war was a major episode in a long dispute over sovereignty. Argentina claims the islands as its own territory and described its action as the reclamation of that territory, while the British government regarded it as an invasion of a territory that had been a Crown colony since 1841. The Falkland Islanders, who have lived on the islands since the early 19th century, are mostly descendants of British settlers and strongly favoured British sovereignty. In 1965 the United Nations called on both states to settle the dispute, and talks made little progress, since the islanders refused to consider Argentine sovereignty. Argentina in 1981 was in economic stagnation and widespread unrest against the military junta that had governed since 1976.

On 2 April 1982 Argentine forces made amphibious landings, known as Operation Rosario, on the Falkland Islands. The garrison of 68 marines and 11 naval hydrographers, with 23 volunteers, offered a brief but fierce defence organised by the Governor, Sir Rex Hunt. South Georgia was invaded the next day. On 5 April the British government sent a naval task force, eventually of 127 ships, and by early May the Argentine garrison numbered around 13,000. United Nations Security Council Resolution 502 demanded the withdrawal of Argentine troops, and shuttle diplomacy by the United States Secretary of State Alexander Haig failed. Neither state formally declared war.

British forces retook South Georgia in April. On 2 May a British submarine sank the Argentine cruiser ARA General Belgrano, and on 4 May an Exocet missile struck the destroyer HMS Sheffield. British troops landed at San Carlos Water on 21 May, where Argentine air attacks gave the bay the name Bomb Alley. After the battle of Goose Green on 27 and 28 May, in which 961 Argentine personnel were taken prisoner, the British attacked the high ground round Stanley on the night of 11 June, with the hardest fighting at Mount Longdon. A ceasefire came on 14 June, when General Mario Menéndez surrendered to Major General Jeremy Moore.

In all, 649 Argentine and 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders were killed in 74 days. Patriotic feeling ran high in Argentina, but the defeat prompted large protests against the ruling military government, hastening its fall and the return of democracy. In Britain the Conservative government was re-elected with an increased majority the following year. Diplomatic relations between the two states were restored in 1989, with no change in either position on sovereignty. Britain built a permanent military complex at Mount Pleasant, opened in 1985, and the islands remain a self-governing British Overseas Territory.
fall-of-constantinople: Constantinople had been an imperial capital since 330 and had been captured only once in eleven centuries, in the Sack of Constantinople during the Fourth Crusade in 1204. The Nicaeans retook it in 1261 and restored the Byzantine Empire under the Palaiologos dynasty. Between 1346 and 1349 the Black Death killed almost half the inhabitants. By 1453 the city was a series of walled villages separated by fields, encircled by the fifth-century Theodosian walls.

Mehmed II succeeded his father in 1451 at the age of 19, and many European courts expected little of him. In early 1452 he began building the fortress of Rumeli Hisarı on the European shore of the Bosphorus, which with the older Anadolu Hisarı controlled sea traffic. Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos asked Western Europe for help, but union of the eastern and western churches, agreed at the Council of Florence in 1439, met strong resistance in the city.

The Byzantines stretched a chain across the mouth of the Golden Horn and repaired the land walls. The defenders numbered under 8,000 in all. George Sphrantzes recorded 4,773 Greeks and 200 foreigners, with up to three thousand Genoese, Venetians and others who came to help, to guard a perimeter of twelve miles. The siege began on 6 April 1453. Mehmed's cannons fired on the walls for weeks, but their slow rate of fire let the Byzantines repair most of the damage after each shot.

On 28 May processions were held and the emperor attended a last Vespers in the Hagia Sophia. The final assault came on 29 May, after a siege of 53 days. The walls had protected the city for 800 years, but Ottoman infantry with the support of cannons and bombards overcame them.

Mehmed promised his soldiers three days of plunder, but later sources say he rode into the city on the first day and halted the looting. By 2 June he found the city largely deserted and half in ruins. Mehmed let Christians who had escaped capture or been ransomed return to their homes, and made Constantinople the Ottoman capital in place of Adrianople. He called himself Kayser-i Rum, Caesar of the Romans.

The fall ended the Roman Empire, which had lasted nearly 1,500 years, and many modern historians treat it as the end of the medieval period. Byzantine scholars who migrated to Italy are considered by many to have been key to the revival of Greek and Roman studies behind Renaissance humanism. The name Istanbul became official only in 1930.
fall-of-nineveh: The Neo-Assyrian Empire, which emerged in the 10th century BCE, had by the reign of Ashurbanipal controlled or held in vassalage lands from the Caucasus to Egypt, Arabia and central Iran. After his death in 631 BCE bitter wars of succession weakened it, and from 625 BCE its hold on the Near East began to fade. By their own records the Assyrians had been brutal rulers, and they had made many enemies. The Chaldeans, with Babylonian help, took control of much of Babylonia, founding the Neo-Babylonian Empire under Nabopolassar, while the Medes under King Cyaxares rebuilt their army after an early defeat.

Nineveh was a political capital, the home of a great library of Akkadian tablets and the recipient of tribute from across the Near East. The surviving accounts were all written by its enemies: a Babylonian chronicle, Herodotus, the Hebrew tradition attributed to Nahum and Egyptian records.

The Fall of Nineveh Chronicle describes a 12-year struggle. In 616 BCE the Babylonians defeated the Assyrian army and sacked towns upriver; the Assyrians drove them back to Takritain but were beaten there. The Babylonians then allied with the Medes and Scythians, and in 614 BCE the Medes sacked Assur. In 612 BCE the Babylonians joined Cyaxares before Nineveh, besieged it from May for three months and in August broke through, plundering and burning the city, with the Medes the decisive force. King Sin-shar-ishkun was killed. Diodorus records that the Tigris flooded the city, and one theory holds that the attackers diverted the Khosr River to breach the walls.

Sin-shar-ishkun's brother Ashur-uballit II fought his way out and set up a last capital at Harran. The Babylonians and their allies campaigned against him for several more years, once against an Egyptian-Assyrian army, and his fate is unknown: he may have died at the Fall of Harran in 609 BCE or at Carchemish in 605 BCE. Babylon became the imperial centre of Mesopotamia for the first time in over a thousand years. Archaeology shows Nineveh was largely depopulated in the following centuries, and the burning of its palace may have helped preserve its clay texts. A garbled memory of the fall gave rise to the legend of King Sardanapalus.
fall-of-singapore: Singapore was the foremost British military base and economic port in South-East Asia. After the Anglo-Japanese alliance lapsed in 1923 Britain built a naval base there, a key part of its interwar defence planning for the region, though financial constraints hampered construction. In November 1940 the German raider Atlantis captured the British steamer Automedon, whose papers described the weakness of the Singapore base, and the Germans passed copies to the Japanese. The Japanese had also broken the British Army's codes.

The Japanese 25th Army invaded Malaya from Indochina on 8 December 1941, almost simultaneously with the attack on Pearl Harbor. Conventional British thinking held that the Japanese were inferior and the jungle impassable, and the Japanese repeatedly outflanked hastily established defensive lines. Their general Tomoyuki Yamashita advanced with about 30,000 men down the Malayan peninsula.

Lieutenant-General Arthur Percival commanded 85,000 Allied troops at Singapore, many of them under-strength and inexperienced. The British destroyed the causeway across the Johor Strait, which delayed the attack for over a week. After a bombardment of 88,000 shells, the first Japanese wave crossed shortly before 20:30 on 8 February 1942. The main weight, about 13,000 men, fell on the 22nd Australian Brigade, which had about 3,000 men and no significant reserve. Percival had expected a crossing in the north and did not reinforce the brigade until the morning of 9 February.

On 14 February the Japanese broke through towards the Alexandra Barracks Hospital, where they killed soldiers, doctors and nurses. By 15 February about a million civilians were crammed into 1 per cent of the island, the water system was badly damaged and ammunition was nearly gone. After a conference at Fort Canning at 09:30 all agreed that no counter-attack was possible. For the second time Yamashita demanded unconditional surrender, and on the afternoon of 15 February Percival capitulated.

About 80,000 British, Indian, Australian and local troops became prisoners of war, joining the 50,000 taken in Malaya, and many died of neglect, abuse or forced labour. About 40,000 Indian soldiers, mostly conscripts, joined the Indian National Army and fought with the Japanese in the Burma campaign. The Japanese renamed the city Syonan-to and murdered thousands of civilians, mostly ethnic Chinese, in the Sook Ching massacre.

Winston Churchill called it the worst disaster and largest capitulation in British history. Together with the fall of Hong Kong and the sinking of Prince of Wales and Repulse two months earlier, it severely undermined British prestige in Asia, which contributed to the end of British colonial rule in the region after the war. The Australian prime minister John Curtin said the fall of Singapore opened the Battle for Australia. Singapore has marked Total Defence Day on 15 February since 1998.
fall-of-tenochtitlan: In April 1519 Hernán Cortés landed at San Juan de Ulúa with 508 soldiers, 100 sailors and 14 small cannons, leading an expedition whose mandate the Governor of Cuba, Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, had already revoked. Moctezuma cooperated with the Spaniards for reasons that remain uncertain. While Cortés was away, Pedro de Alvarado, left in command with 80 soldiers, tortured priests and nobles at the time of the festival of Toxcatl in early May, and after the attack on the festival the Mexica turned against both Moctezuma and the Spanish.

The Spanish fled the city on La Noche Triste, the Night of Sorrows, along the western causeway to Tlacopan, and narrowly escaped destruction before winning the Battle of Otumba on the way to Tlaxcala. The Tlaxcalans rejected Aztec offers of peace and kept their alliance with Cortés.

Smallpox broke out in Tenochtitlan in late October 1520 and lasted sixty days. The new ruler Cuitláhuac died of it after eighty days, and Cuauhtémoc, son of King Ahuitzotl, took the throne in February 1521. Cortés meanwhile had thirteen brigantines built in Tlaxcala by his shipbuilder Martín López and gathered reinforcements, many of them from the failed ventures of Francisco de Garay, the Governor of Jamaica.

Forces under Alvarado and Olid first cut the aqueduct from Chapultepec, while Cortés's ships overturned many of the canoes sent against them on the lake. Lakeside towns such as Iztapalapa and Mixquic made peace with the Spaniards. The fighting moved street by street to the Tlatelolco marketplace, where the Mexica sacrificed 70 Spanish prisoners at the altar of Huitzilopochtli. Cuauhtémoc finally opened talks, and the city surrendered on 13 August 1521 (Julian date).

Between 100,000 and 240,000 people were killed in the campaign, warriors and civilians together, and as many as 40,000 bodies lay in the canals after the siege. Almost all of the Aztec nobility died. The Tlaxcalans, who for a century had been forced to hand over young people for sacrifice in Tenochtitlan, went on killing and looting after the surrender; one source puts the dead of Ixtapalapa alone at 6,000.

Cortés had Cuauhtémoc and the lord of Tacuba tortured to learn where the lost gold lay. Cuauhtémoc remained the nominal ruler under Spanish control until he was hanged for treason in 1525 during an expedition to Guatemala. The conquest was a critical stage in the Spanish colonization of the Americas.
fall-of-the-berlin-wall: The Wall consisted of two concrete walls 4 metres tall, 155 kilometres long, with a mined corridor between them guarded from 302 watchtowers by 1989; guards were authorised to shoot people crossing it. In 1989 the Iron Curtain began to open elsewhere. Hungary opened its border with Austria at the Pan-European Picnic on 19 August, and tens of thousands of East Germans left through it. On 30 September the West German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher told refugees in the West German embassy in Prague that they could leave for West Germany. Erich Honecker stepped down as party leader on 18 October in favour of Egon Krenz, whose promises of reform did not end the protests.

On 9 November 1989 the Politburo's decision to let East Germans cross the border directly was passed to Günter Schabowski, the party spokesman, in a note he had not been briefed on. At a press conference that began at 18:00 he read it out, and when a reporter asked when it took effect he answered, as far as he knew, immediately, without delay. West German television carried the news that evening, and crowds gathered at the six checkpoints between East and West Berlin. Guards first tried to stamp the passports of the most insistent, then found that nobody would take responsibility for ordering lethal force.

At 22:45, or 23:30 by another account, Harald Jäger, commander of the Bornholmer Straße crossing, let people through with little or no checking. West Berliners greeted them with flowers and champagne and climbed onto the Wall. People nicknamed Mauerspechte, wallpeckers, began chipping off pieces that night, and the East German government soon announced ten new crossings, among them Potsdamer Platz and Bernauer Straße. The Brandenburg Gate opened on 22 December, when Chancellor Helmut Kohl was greeted by Prime Minister Hans Modrow.

East German border troops began the official demolition on 13 June 1990, and about 1.7 million tonnes of rubble came from it; six sections were kept as a memorial. Free elections in spring 1990 favoured reunification, and Germany was reunified on 3 October 1990. Margaret Thatcher and François Mitterrand had both feared a united Germany. The date 9 November also marks the 1918 declaration of the Weimar Republic and the Kristallnacht pogroms of 1938, which is why 3 October was chosen as German Unity Day. The historian Mary Elise Sarotte called the fall of the Wall an accident, a semicomical and bureaucratic mistake.
fall-of-the-western-roman-empire: Under Trajan (r. 98–117) the Roman Empire stretched from Armenia to the Atlantic, with large numbers of trained and supplied soldiers and a civil administration based in thriving cities. Historians trace its weakening through the Antonine Plague, which ended a long period of expansion, and the Crisis of the Third Century, when climate change, renewed disease and political instability brought the imperial system close to collapse.

In 376 a large migration of Goths and other peoples, fleeing from the Huns, entered the Empire, and Roman forces could not exterminate, expel or subjugate them. At the Battle of Adrianople on 9 August 378 the eastern emperor Valens lost much of his army and his own life. When Theodosius I died in 395 he left a collapsing field army, and the Empire was divided between the warring ministers of his two sons.

The crossing of the Rhine in 405 or 406 brought Germanic and Alan peoples, perhaps some 30,000 warriors and 100,000 people in all, into Gaul. Roman forces fought each other in the name of the emperor Honorius and rival claimants. The general Stilicho was killed in 408 after taking sanctuary in a church. Under Valentinian III the general Aetius stabilised parts of Gaul and Hispania, relying heavily on Hunnic troops, while the Huns under Attila extracted vast sums from the Eastern Empire until 450.

In 454 Valentinian stabbed Aetius to death, and he was himself murdered a year later by the dead general's supporters. In 455 a Vandal fleet entered Rome and plundered it for two weeks. Ricimer, a commander of the army of Italy, was effective ruler of Italy from 461. A great Eastern expedition against the Vandals in 468 ended when Genseric's fireships destroyed most of the Roman fleet at Cape Bon, and the Vandals kept the Diocese of Africa.

The end is dated by convention to 4 September 476, but the convention has many qualifications. In Roman constitutional theory the Empire was still united under one emperor. Julius Nepos, who still claimed to be emperor of the West, controlled Dalmatia until he was murdered in 480, and Syagrius ruled the Domain of Soissons until his murder in 486.

Historians have long argued over causes. Alexander Demandt counted 210 theories, and modern scholarship stresses climate, disease, the army, the economy, religious change and pressure from invading peoples. Henri Pirenne held that Roman culture and legitimacy continued long after 476. Many scholars now speak of a cultural transformation, a period of late antiquity, rather than a simple fall.
false-waldemar: The legitimate Waldemar, Margrave of Brandenburg-Stendal, was buried in 1319, and with this supposed extinction of the Brandenburg House of Ascania, the Wittelsbach Emperor Louis the Bavarian gave the March of Brandenburg to his own son Louis in 1320. The man who later claimed Waldemar's name was elderly when he appeared. Contemporaries and chroniclers said he was a Jacob Rehbuck, possibly a journeyman miller, and Thomas Carlyle wrote that he might have served the real Waldemar and learned his manners. These were rumours, and his true identity remains unknown.

In the summer of 1348 he presented himself to Otto, Archbishop of Magdeburg, as a returning pilgrim and as the old margrave, claiming that the burial of 1319 had been staged while he went on pilgrimage to the Holy Land. He quickly won adherents, above all among the rivals of the Wittelsbach royals, posing as the representative of the old Ascanian house against the foreign and unpopular Bavaria, and within weeks much of the March accepted him. Charles IV, then on the defensive, invested him with the Margraviate of Brandenburg on 2 October 1348. Only a few towns held on to the Wittelsbach, among them Treuenbrietzen, which took its prefix treu-, faithful, from this time.

In April 1350 he was exposed as a cheat, and Charles deposed him under an agreement with the Wittelsbach, the Treaty of Eltville. He then kept an Ascanian court at Anhalt-Dessau, where he was treated with courtly honour for the rest of his life, and died of natural causes in 1356. Carlyle called him a new goblin in the dance round Louis the Bavarian. Willibald Alexis made him the subject of the novel Der falsche Woldemar in 1842, and Horst Bosetzky of Der letzte Askanier in 1997.
falun-mine: Falun Mine (Falu Gruva) operated for a millennium, from the 10th century to 1992. No written account fixes when mining began; archaeological and geological studies indicate, with considerable uncertainty, that it started around the year 1000. Objects of the 10th century contain its copper, and the mine was certainly working by 1080. At first local farmers gathered the ore, smelted it and used the metal for household needs. Around the reign of Magnus III, king of Sweden from 1275 to 1290, nobles and merchants from Lübeck took over, and the first written document, of 1288, records that the Bishop of Västerås acquired a 12.5 percent interest in exchange for an estate.

By the middle of the 14th century the mine had become a vital national resource. King Magnus IV visited the area and drafted a charter, in 1347, that secured the sovereign's financial interest. Under it free miners held shares in proportion to the smelters they owned, a structure regarded as a precursor of the joint stock company. Output peaked in the 17th century, with over 3,000 tonnes of copper in 1650, and the Privy Council called the mine the nation's treasury and stronghold. It helped fund Sweden's wars in its great power era, and Sweden held a virtual monopoly on copper throughout the century.

The main method was fire-setting: fires lit at the end of the day heated the rock, which cracked when it cooled and was broken loose with wedges and sledge hammers, so that the miners advanced about 1 metre a month. The ore was roasted in open hearths, producing a thick, poisonous smoke, and then smelted; the cycle was repeated until crude copper resulted. The process changed little for seven centuries. On Midsummer's Eve 1687, after decades of intensive digging, a large part of the mine collapsed; no one was killed, because the miners did not work on that day. Carl Linnaeus described the mine as one of the great wonders of Sweden but as horrible as hell itself.

Copper output fell to less than 2,000 tonnes by 1665 and barely 1,000 tonnes a year between 1710 and 1720. The mining company turned to iron and timber and began producing Falu red paint in earnest. Gold was found in 1881, leading to a short-lived gold rush and a total of 5 tonnes. The last shot was fired on 8 December 1992. Chemists found new elements in its minerals, among them selenium, isolated in 1817 by Jöns Jakob Berzelius and Johan Gottlieb Gahn. The mine is now a museum, owned by the Stora Kopparberget foundation, and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001, together with the town of Falun, its 17th-century miners' cottages and the surrounding Bergsmansbygden.
fan-li: Fan Li lived in the Spring and Autumn period and was a political and military adviser to King Goujian of Yue. He and Goujian were once held hostage together by the state of Wu, and after three years of captivity they returned to Yue, where Fan Li helped the king carry out reforms that streamlined its administration. These prepared the way for the destruction of Wu in 473 BCE.

Later tradition credits him with a scheme to weaken King Fuchai of Wu through his love of women. In this account Fan Li chose two women, Xi Shi and Zheng Dan, who were trained in singing, dancing and court manners and sent to Wu with three aims: to draw Fuchai away from affairs of state, to lead him into costly wars abroad, and to set him against his loyal minister Wu Zixu.

After the victory Fan Li resigned. He is said to have written from Qi, in present-day Shandong, to his colleague Wen Zhong, advising him to leave Goujian's service too. Another tradition has him retire with Xi Shi, one of the Four Beauties of ancient China, to a fishing boat on Lake Tai, living in the manner of a Taoist immortal. His success in business was long remembered, and after his death he was worshipped as Cai Shen, the God of Wealth. Dingtao in Shandong is said to take its name from him, and the Song dynasty chancellor Fan Zhongyan was among his descendants.

His writings are lost and are known only through quotations in a compilation by Cai Mo (281–356); his theories of business were summarised by Ma Zong under the Tang dynasty. Works attributed to him include treatises on managing a business and its risks, the Yangyu Jing or Fish-Breeding Classic, an early text on fish farming, and a Bingfa on military strategy, distinct from the Art of War of Sunzi.
fan-noli: Fan Noli was born in 1882 in the village of İbriktepe in the Ottoman vilayet of Adrianople, which Orthodox Albanians from southern Albania had settled. He was educated in Greek schools and wandered around the Mediterranean, living in Athens, Alexandria and Odessa and working as an actor and translator. Through the Albanian expatriate movement he became an ardent supporter of Albanian nationalism and moved to the United States in 1906, where he worked in a lumber mill in Buffalo and then in Boston. He studied at Harvard from 1908 and took his degree in 1912.

Albanian Orthodox immigrants in Boston belonged to the Greek Orthodox Church, whose leaders opposed Albanian nationalism. When a young Albanian, Kristaq Dishnica, was refused burial, Noli and other émigrés began work on an independent Albanian Orthodox Church, an episode known as the Hudson Incident. He was ordained a priest in 1908 and had the liturgy translated into Tosk Albanian. In April 1912 he and Faik Konica led the diaspora organisation Vatra. His diplomacy in the United States and Geneva won the support of President Woodrow Wilson and, in 1920, Albania's membership of the League of Nations.

He entered the Albanian Parliament in 1921 for the liberal People's Party, and in 1922 a congress at Berat consecrated him Bishop of Korçë and primate of the new church. After the assassination of the politician Avni Rustemi, Noli's funeral speech helped bring on an uprising that forced Ahmet Zogu to flee in March 1924. Noli became prime minister and regent on 16 June 1924, but his Twenty Point Program proved unpopular, and supporters of Zogu overthrew him on Christmas Eve. He fled to Italy under sentence of death and founded a committee in Vienna to oppose Zogu.

Noli returned to the United States in 1932 and later studied Byzantine music and wrote on Skanderbeg, Shakespeare and Beethoven. He took a doctorate in history at Boston University in 1945, translated works of world literature into Albanian and published an English New Testament in 1961. He died on 13 March 1965 and is buried in Forest Hills Cemetery in Boston. The Albanian Orthodox Archdiocese in America that he founded later joined the Orthodox Church in America, and he appeared on Albania's 100 lekë banknote of 1996.
fan-zhongyan: Fan Zhongyan was born in Wu County, Su Prefecture. His father Fan Yong died the year after his birth, and when he was about four or five his mother, Lady Xie, remarried Zhu Wenhan, an official, so that he was called Zhu Yue. In his late teens and early twenties he travelled and studied with Confucian scholars and with Taoist and Buddhist sages. In 1011 he began study at the Yingtianfu Academy, one of the Six Great Academies, where anecdotes say he lived on scarce food and took no help from his family. In 1015 he passed the imperial examination as a jinshi, resumed his Fan surname and received his mother again to provide for her.

In the early 1020s he held regional posts, including magistrate of Xinghua County. From 1025, with his friend Teng Zongliang, he built dykes along the coastal counties, and locals named the 150 kilometre dyke Mr. Fan Dyke. In 1036, as prefect of Kaifeng, he took Ouyang Xiu as a disciple and condemned the grand councilor Lü Yijian for favouritism in promotions. The quarrel ended in his exile, and began factional controversies that troubled the empire. In 1040, facing the revolt of the Tangut leader Li Yuanhao, he went to Shaanxi with Han Qi, reorganised the troops and built a deep defence on fortified settlements; his methods helped bring peace negotiations in 1042.

As vice chancellor under Emperor Renzong he launched the Qingli reforms with Fu Bi, Ouyang Xiu and Han Qi. In autumn 1043 he and Fu Bi presented a ten-point proposal on the civil examinations, higher pay for minor local officials to discourage corruption, and selection of officials on merit. Conservatives opposed it, Fan and Ouyang Xiu were charged with forming a faction, and Renzong rescinded the reforms in 1045. Fan served at Dengzhou and Hangzhou from 1046 to 1050; at Hangzhou he ended a famine with a work relief programme on public works. His reforms later inspired Wang Anshi.

Fan favoured the classical prose movement and held that writing should serve political discourse and social reform. His collection consists mostly of letters, memoranda and policy critiques, and he is better remembered for his ci poems than his shi poetry. His essay On Yueyang Tower of 1046, written at Teng Zongliang's invitation without a visit to the tower, holds the line that scholar-officials should be the first to worry the worries of all-under-Heaven and the last to enjoy its joys. He also founded a charitable estate for his clan, which became an institution of social welfare. He died in June 1052 at the age of 64 and was posthumously titled Wenzheng.
fangataufa: Fangataufa, also written Fangatafoa, is a coral atoll in the eastern part of the Tuamotu Archipelago in French Polynesia. It is a coral outgrowth of a seamount that rises about 3,600 metres from the seafloor and was formed between 33.4 and 34.7 million years ago by the Pitcairn hotspot. The atoll is about 9.5 kilometres long and wide, with a lagoon of 45 square kilometres. It lies 37 kilometres south of Moruroa, 240 kilometres south-west of the Gambier Islands and 1,190 kilometres south-east of Tahiti. Administratively it belongs to the commune of Tureia.

The first recorded European to arrive was Frederick William Beechey in 1826, who named it Cockburn Island in honour of George Cockburn. In 1963 France chose the atoll as a nuclear test site to replace Reggane and In Ecker in the Algerian Sahara, and with Moruroa it was formally ceded to France by the Territorial Assembly in 1964. The first test, Rigel, an atmospheric explosion, took place on 24 September 1966. On 24 August 1968 Canopus became France's first two-stage thermonuclear test, and the last atmospheric test, Orion, took place on 2 August 1970.

After criticism from Pacific countries France moved to underground testing; the first such test, Achille, was carried out on 5 June 1975. Testing then moved exclusively to Moruroa until 1988, when growing safety concerns about the stability of that atoll brought some tests back to Fangataufa.

The final test, Xouthos, was on 27 January 1996. In all, 4 atmospheric and 10 underground explosions were carried out on the atoll. Infrastructure built for the tests included a dredged channel into the lagoon, two quays and an airfield.

Fangataufa is permanently uninhabited and serves as a wildlife sanctuary for various species of birds. It is classified as a Common Military Zone, and entry is prohibited without authorization. Radiological monitoring has been carried out there since 1998 by military personnel and the Atomic Energy Commission.

In 2006 an inquiry by the French Polynesian government found that the French government had misled the local population about the effects of atmospheric testing, and the Assembly of French Polynesia adopted a report concluding that the tests had a major impact on health, the environment, society and the economy. In 2008 France agreed to compensate military personnel involved. In 2012 Senator Richard Tuheiava's bill to return the atolls passed the French Senate but was not debated by the National Assembly.
fannie-lou-hamer: Fannie Lou Hamer was born Fannie Lou Townsend on 6 October 1917 in Montgomery County, Mississippi, the last of the 20 children of Lou Ella and James Lee Townsend. In 1919 the family moved to Ruleville to work as sharecroppers on W. D. Marlow's plantation. From the age of six she picked cotton, and at 12 she left school to help support her aging parents. In 1944, after the plantation owner discovered that she could read, she was made the plantation's time and record keeper. The next year she married Perry Hamer, a tractor driver on the plantation, and they stayed there for 18 years.

On 31 August 1962 Hamer and 17 others tried to register to vote and failed a literacy test. She took the test again and passed it on 10 January 1963, but her county also required two poll tax receipts, which she later paid for and obtained. After her first attempt she was fired, and on 10 September 1962 she was shot at 15 times in a drive-by shooting; no one was injured. In early 1963 she became a field secretary of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee for voter registration and welfare programs.

On 9 June 1963 she was arrested at Winona, Mississippi, with fellow activists returning from a workshop. In the county jail police ordered two inmates to beat her with a baton, and she was almost killed.

In 1964 she co-founded the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party. At the Democratic National Convention that summer its members stood as Mississippi's official delegation. Hamer's televised testimony to the Credentials Committee was interrupted by an impromptu press conference by President Lyndon B. Johnson, but most major networks broadcast it in full that evening. The party rejected a compromise offering two seats, and it was seated at the 1968 convention. She ran for the U.S. House in 1964 and for the Mississippi State Senate in 1971, and in 1969 she began the Freedom Farm Cooperative, an attempt to redistribute economic power among Black farmers.

Hamer published her autobiography in 1967 with the help of Julius Lester and Mary Varela. In 1970 she led legal action against the government of Sunflower County for continued illegal segregation, and in 1972 she was elected a national party delegate. She also co-founded the National Women's Political Caucus. She died on 14 March 1977, aged 59, in Mound Bayou, Mississippi, and Andrew Young delivered the eulogy at her memorial service. She was inducted into the National Women's Hall of Fame in 1993, and in January 2025 President Joe Biden posthumously awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
fano: Fano is a coastal city of the province of Pesaro and Urbino in the Marche, twelve kilometres south-east of Pesaro, at the point where the Via Flaminia reaches the Adriatic Sea. Its ancient name, Fanum Fortunae, means Temple of Fortune, after a prominent local sanctuary dedicated to the goddess Fortuna. The remains of a monumental podium beneath the medieval convent of Saint Augustine are identified as that temple.

The settlement is first mentioned in 49 BCE, when Julius Caesar held it along with Pisaurum and Ancona. Augustus established a colony there and built a wall, parts of which remain, and in 2 CE he built an arch at the entrance to the town. In January 271 the Roman army won the Battle of Fano on the banks of the Metauro river, just inland. The Ostrogoths under Vitiges destroyed the town in 538. The Byzantines rebuilt it, and it became the capital of the maritime Pentapolis, the Five Cities, which also included Rimini, Pesaro, Senigallia and Ancona. In 754 the Frankish kings donated it to the Holy See.

The Malatesta became lords of the city in 1356 with Galeotto I Malatesta, nominally only a vicar of the popes. Pandolfo III resided in the city and was buried in the church of San Francesco in a tomb designed by Leon Battista Alberti. In 1463 papal troops under Federico III da Montefeltro besieged Roberto, son of Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta, in the castle, and his peace treaty ended Malatesta rule in Fano. The siege ordered by Pope Pius II destroyed the upper storey of the Roman arch. The city was later part of the short-lived state of Cesare Borgia and then of the della Rovere duchy.

Fano had about 59,000 inhabitants in 2021. Its Arch of Augustus still stands, and the cathedral, begun in the twelfth century on the site of one burned in 1111, was restored in the 1920s. The church of Santa Maria Nuova holds two works by Perugino. A week-long festival, Fano dei Cesari, ends each summer with a parade in Roman costume and chariot races.
farabundo-marti: Farabundo Martí was born on 5 May 1893 in Teotepeque, El Salvador, the sixth of fourteen children of Pedro Martí and Socorro Rodríguez. His father had changed the family surname from Martír out of admiration for the Cuban nationalist José Martí. According to the biography by Jorge Arias Gómez, the young Martí repeatedly pointed out to his parents the gap between his relatively wealthy family and the peasant workers around them, in food, clothes and shoes.

He was educated at the Saint Cecilia Salesian School in Santa Tecla and enrolled at the University of El Salvador in San Salvador, but left his course in political science and jurisprudence to take up political activity. Miguel Mármol described him in his testimonio as an intellectual but a proletarian-like young man.

In 1920 Martí was arrested with other students for a protest against the ruling Meléndez-Quiñónez dynasty and sent into exile, living in Guatemala and later Mexico until he returned in 1925. Invited to a conference of the Anti-Imperialist League of the Americas in New York City, he was arrested on arrival and released, and he worked for a limited time with Augusto César Sandino, the two men differing in their approaches to change.

Martí took part in founding the Communist Party of Central America and served as a representative of the International Red Aid, a communist alternative to the Red Cross. In December 1930, during the depths of the economic depression, he was exiled again, as his popularity among peasants and workers grew and rumours spread of a presidential candidacy.

After Arturo Araujo was elected president in March 1931, Martí returned and, with Alfonso Luna and Mario Zapata and as interim general secretary of the party, helped prepare a revolt of indigenous farmers. The uprising, fed by collapsing coffee prices, was directed against Maximiliano Hernández Martínez, who had toppled the elected government weeks earlier. The army crushed it within ten days, and an estimated 30,000 civilians were killed on Hernández Martínez's orders in what became known as La Matanza, the Slaughter. Martí was shot after a court-martial, and many came to regard him as a martyr.
farabundo-marti-national-liberation-fron: The Communist Party of El Salvador (PCES) was founded in 1930. In 1970 its general secretary Cayetano Carpio left it, convinced that elections could not transform the country, and founded the Farabundo Martí Popular Liberation Forces (FPL), calling for a prolonged popular war against the military dictatorship that had ruled since 1931.

Other groups followed, among them the People's Revolutionary Army, the National Resistance Armed Forces and, in 1979, the Armed Liberation Forces of the PCES. The FMLN was established on 10 October 1980 by the merger of the guerrilla groups, the PRTC joining in December, and in 1981 it allied with the Revolutionary Democratic Front.

The FMLN launched its first major offensive on 10 January 1981 with 43 attacks. It held 82 towns and villages by 17 January, but the government's counteroffensive prevailed and by 26 January the offensive had failed to spark the national uprising it sought.

A second offensive on 28 March 1982 failed to stop the election of a Constitutional Assembly. In 1983 Carpio, who rejected negotiation, had his rival Mélida Anaya Montes killed in Managua and took his own life days later. The war ended with the Chapultepec Peace Accords, under which the FMLN demobilised.

The Legislative Assembly legalised the FMLN on 30 June 1992 and it was registered as a party on 14 December. In the first postwar election, in 1994, its candidate Zamora reached the second round and lost to ARENA's Armando Calderón Sol with 31.7 per cent, and the party became the second largest in the Assembly. For about three decades it shared the national stage with the right-wing ARENA.

It lost its first three presidential elections, then won in 2009 with the journalist Mauricio Funes and in 2014 with Salvador Sánchez Cerén, a former guerrilla commander. It lost the next two, and after the 2024 election it held no seats in the Legislative Assembly.
