In the civil war the member groups ranged from Marxism-Leninism and a Maoist current to social democratic positions, and the front was inspired by the Cuban Revolution and liberation theology. Between 1988 and 1991 it abandoned Marxism-Leninism and embraced democratic socialism. Catholic clergy had a prominent part, and some priests became guerrillas. The Sandinista National Liberation Front, which took power in Nicaragua in 1979, was a source of inspiration and support. The party has belonged to the São Paulo Forum, to COPPPAL and to the Parliamentary Group of the Left in the Central American Parliament, and several splinter parties have broken from it.
faramurz: Abu Mansur Faramurz was the eldest son of Muhammad ibn Rustam Dushmanziyar. In 1037 his father strengthened the defences of Isfahan against the plundering Turkmen nomads from Khorasan. In 1041, after the Seljuqs defeated the Ghaznavids at the Battle of Dandanaqan, they became neighbours of the Kakuyids, and their leader Tughril made Ray his capital. Faramurz seems to have been present with the Seljuqs at Dandanaqan.

When Faramurz succeeded his father in Isfahan, his younger brother Garshasp I took power in Hamadan as his vassal. A third brother, Abu Harb, rebelled and called on the Buyids of Fars for help, but Faramurz defeated him. Tughril sought to secure his allegiance, yet neither Faramurz nor Garshasp was willing to go over to the Seljuqs. In 1044 Faramurz took several towns in Kirman from the Buyid Abu Kalijar, who soon struck back.

When Tughril came to Isfahan, Faramurz submitted to him. Around 1045–46, after Tughril had returned to Khorasan, Faramurz declared himself independent of Seljuq rule and submitted to the Buyids instead, which forced Tughril back to Isfahan, where he defeated the Kakuyids and made Faramurz his vassal once more. In 1050 Tughril laid siege to Isfahan. Its people defended the city for a year before they surrendered; its walls were razed, and Tughril made it his capital.

Yazd and Abarkuh, given to Faramurz in compensation, had already been under Kakuyid control. Although he had lost almost all his power, he was highly respected at the Seljuq court, which twice awarded him the title Shams al-Mulk, Sun of royalty, in 1061 and 1063. In this period he went with Tughril and the Seljuq vizier Al-Kunduri to Baghdad to arrange the sultan's wedding to the daughter of the Abbasid caliph Al-Qa'im. Nothing more is known of him after that. He was succeeded by his son Ali ibn Faramurz, who later married one of the daughters of Chaghri Beg.
faras: Faras lay in Lower Nubia, on the border between modern Egypt and Sudan at the Wadi Halfa Salient, upriver from Abu Simbel. In Greek it was called Pakhoras, and in Old Nubian Pakhōras. The site was flooded by Lake Nasser in the 1960s and is now permanently underwater.

The town dates back to the A-Group period. It was a major centre in the Meroitic period, with a major temple, and under ancient Egyptian control of Nubia it became an Egyptian administrative centre where Egyptian cultural influence was strong. The city reached its height in the Christian period of Nubia as the capital of Silko, basiliskos of Nobadia. After Nobadia was absorbed into Makuria it remained the leading centre of the north and the seat of Nobadia's eparch. A nearby citadel, the site now known as Qasr el-Wizz, housed a major church and monastery, probably named after a local saint, Apa Dios or Apa Dioskoros.

In the turbulent later years of Christian Nubia the town seems to have declined, and the administrative centre moved to the more easily defended Silmi, now Qasr Ibrim. A British expedition from the University of Oxford under F.Ll. Griffith worked at the site in 1909–1912 and uncovered Meroitic and Christian cemeteries and Egyptian temples. During UNESCO's Nubian Salvage Campaign the Polish Centre of Mediterranean Archaeology, founded by Kazimierz Michałowski, excavated from 1960 to 1964 and found a Christian cathedral beneath a hill.

The cathedral was founded by Bishop Aetios in 620 and rebuilt twice, by Paulos at the beginning of the 8th century and by Petros I at the end of the 10th. Sand had filled it completely, which preserved its structure and decoration. A major pottery workshop was also found, and a List of Bishops of Faras made it possible to date each episcopate and, through them, some of the paintings.

The paintings, in tempera on dry plaster, show archangels, chiefly Michael, monarchs and bishops of Faras, saints, the Virgin Mary and Biblical scenes, and they are the best surviving examples of Christian Nubian art. Of the 169 uncovered, 120 were taken down from the walls; they are shown in the Polish National Museum in Warsaw and the Sudan National Museum in Khartoum.
farewell-of-slavianka: The march was written by the composer Vasily Agapkin in honour of Slavic women who saw their husbands off to the First Balkan War, and it was first played in Tambov in late 1912. The Zimmerman Production Association published it around that year, and it was released as a gramophone single in Kiev in the summer of 1915. Because it was first published in 1912, the composition has passed into the public domain in the United States and many other places.

The melody grew popular in Russia and neighbouring countries during the First World War, when departing soldiers were accompanied by it. It was also an unofficial anthem of Admiral Kolchak's White Army. Its earliest known performance by communist troops was in 1918, and it was one of four marching tunes played at the parade on Red Square on 7 November 1941, after which the soldiers went straight to the Battle of Moscow. Some sources say it was banned before it was used in the 1957 film The Cranes Are Flying, but it was performed earlier, often under Agapkin himself. Its earliest known Soviet publication was in 1929.

Many writers have set new words to the melody. The Red Guards adapted it in the Finnish Civil War as Vapaa Venäjä, and in German-occupied Poland the resistance sang a version, Rozszumiały się wierzby płaczące, based on words by Roman Ślęzak. Haim Hefer wrote a Hebrew version for the Palmach in 1945, and the poet and tank officer Ion Degen used the tune for a poem written in December 1944. Official Soviet words were first written by A. Fedotov, and Vladimir Lazarev wrote another set in 1984. The tune also serves as the anthem of Tambov Oblast, with words of 2002, and the party Yabloko unsuccessfully lobbied in the 1990s for it to become the Russian national anthem.
farhud: In the 1930s the position of Iraq's Jews worsened. Arab nationalism had earlier counted them as fellow Arabs, but this changed with the conflict in Mandatory Palestine and Nazi propaganda aimed at the Arab world. In September 1934 tens of Jews were dismissed from the ministry of economics and communications, and unofficial quotas limited their entry to the civil service and to schools and colleges. Between 1932 and 1941 the German embassy under Fritz Grobba supported antisemitic and fascist movements. By 1941 about 150,000 Jews lived in Iraq, and they were widely viewed as pro-British.

On 1 April 1941 a group of pro-Axis officers known as the Golden Square, led by Rashid Ali al-Gaylani, overthrew the regent, Abd al-Ilah, in a coup with significant popular support. Fighting with British forces followed, and on 30 May the British column Kingcol reached Baghdad. In the days before the violence, Jewish houses were reportedly marked with red palm prints, and false rumours spread that Jews had signalled the Royal Air Force by radio.

The pogrom took place on 1 and 2 June 1941, during the Jewish festival of Shavuot. Iraqi government and British sources say it began when a Jewish delegation going to meet the regent was attacked on Al Khurr Bridge, while the scholar Zvi Yehuda argues that anti-Jewish preaching at a mosque set it off. Violence spread through the Al Rusafa and Abu Sifyan districts, shops were burned, a synagogue was destroyed and police joined in on the second day. Some Muslim neighbours sheltered Jews. Order returned on the afternoon of 2 June, when Prime Minister Jamil Al Midfai imposed a curfew and had violators shot. Many sources give about 180 Jews killed, others nearly 200.

On 7 June the restored government set up a committee of inquiry, and military courts sentenced a number of men to death, among them the minister Yunis al-Sabawi and army officers and policemen. Historians disagree on its significance. Some see it as the turning point for Iraq's Jews, while others place that between 1948 and 1951, noting that many who left after the Farhud returned and that permanent emigration did not accelerate until 1950-1951. Orit Bashkin writes that the community strove for integration before and after the event. The United Nations held the first International Farhud Day on 1 June 2015.
fariburz-i: Fakhr al-Din Fariburz ibn Sallar succeeded his father Sallar on 20 February 1063, having already governed most of the kingdom in his father's last years. Within weeks the Shaddadid ruler of Arran, Abu'l-Aswar Shavur I, invaded, probably because Fariburz sheltered a prince Shavur had deposed. After four invasions Fariburz made peace in 1064, paying 40,000 dinars for the return of the fortress of Quylamiyan.

From 1065 he fought the townspeople of Derbent (al-Bab), whose chiefs had killed his cousin, the emir Mansur ibn Abd al-Malik. He defeated them, executed many of their leaders and in 1066 installed his son Afridun as governor of the city. The struggle with Derbent's chiefs, who sought to govern the city themselves, continued through his reign.

The Oghuz Turks raided Shirvan from 1066, and the warlord Qara-tegin besieged the capital, Yazidiyya (Shamakhi), with Fariburz's uncle Mamlan ibn Yazid, a rival claimant. Fariburz paid 6,000 dinars to Savtegin, chamberlain of the Seljuq sultan Alp Arslan, and Mamlan was killed on the night of 24 February 1067. Fariburz then undertook to pay a yearly tribute of 30,000 dinars for protection. When Alp Arslan entered the South Caucasus late in 1067, Fariburz submitted with gifts and in 1068 joined his campaign against Bagrat IV of Georgia.

Under Malik-Shah I, Fariburz surrendered Derbent to Savtegin, now holding it as an iqta', and became a vassal paying an annual tax; the sources give the tribute variously as 70,000, later 40,000, or 100,000 dinars. His coins trace his standing: early issues give him the royal style al-malik al-adil, later ones of debased silver name Malik-Shah and give him no title, and the last, struck after 1094, name no sultan and call him al-Malik Fariburz again. No source records his death; coins and an inscription of 1096 naming his son Manuchihr II as Shirvanshah place it between 1094 and 1096.

At its widest his realm reached from Mughan to Kumuk and Alania. The poet Masud ibn Namdar credits him with taking the Mughan steppe and with seizing Arran and appointing an official over Ganja, and he sought to subdue the Ghumiq of southern Dagestan. His vizier, Baha al-Din Muhammad of the Kakuyid house, was with him a patron of men of letters. Sara Ashurbeyli judged that the Seljuqs, though they subjected Shirvan, could not end the Shirvanshah's power.
farinata-degli-uberti: His name was Manente degli Uberti, and he belonged to one of the most ancient and prominent noble families of Florence. He led the Ghibelline faction of the city from 1239. After the death of Emperor Frederick II in 1250 the Guelphs regained power in Florence and secured the exile of Farinata and his supporters, who took refuge in Siena, a Ghibelline stronghold. There he allied himself with Frederick's illegitimate son, Manfred of Sicily, who was seeking allies to secure his hold on the throne of Sicily.

In September 1260 the Ghibelline forces defeated the Guelphs at the Battle of Montaperti and took Florence. The leading Guelph families were banished and the government was restructured to ensure Ghibelline rule. Farinata's allies wanted Florence never again to threaten them and, following the example of Roman ruthlessness towards Carthage, voted to raze the city. Farinata alone stood against them, declaring himself a Florentine first and a Ghibelline second and vowing to defend his city with his own sword. The Ghibellines instead destroyed the city's defences and the homes of the leading Guelphs, pulling down 103 palaces, 580 houses and 85 towers.

Farinata died in Florence on 11 November 1264. When the Guelphs returned in 1266 they destroyed every building of the Uberti clan, on what is now the Piazza della Signoria, and decreed that nothing should ever be built on that ground, which is why the Palazzo Vecchio, begun in the 1290s, stands to one side of the square.

In 1283 his body and that of his wife, Adaleta, were exhumed from Santa Reparata and tried for heresy by the Franciscan-led Inquisition, which found them guilty and subjected their remains to a posthumous execution. According to Boccaccio, the Inquisition found that he held with Epicurus that the soul dies with the body. Dante Alighieri placed him in Canto X of the Inferno among those who denied the immortality of the soul, entombed in fiery coffins within the city of Dis.
faroe-islands: The Faroe Islands are a group of 18 major islands, with 779 islands, islets and skerries in all, about 655 kilometres off the coast of Northern Europe, roughly halfway between Iceland and Norway. They cover 1,393 square kilometres. The islands are rugged and rocky, the coasts are mostly cliffs, and the highest point is Slættaratindur in northern Eysturoy, at 882 metres.

They consist of a succession of mostly basaltic lava about six kilometres thick, erupted in the Paleogene during the opening of the North Atlantic. The name Føroyar derives from the Old Norse Færeyjar. The most widely held theory, first attested in Færeyinga saga, reads it as sheep islands, from fær and eyjar, though others have proposed Old Irish or other origins.

Archaeological studies from 2021 found burnt grains of domesticated barley and peat ash dated between the mid-fourth and the late eighth centuries, and sheep DNA in lake sediments dating to the year 500. Because Scandinavians did not begin using sails until about 750, the study concluded that these earlier settlers more likely came from Scotland or Ireland. Færeyinga saga and Dicuil date the Norse settlement to the early 9th century, and Grímur Kamban is recorded as the first permanent settler.

The islands were first governed as an independent commonwealth under the Løgting, and they came under Norwegian rule in the early 11th century after Sigmundur Brestisson introduced Christianity. They came under de facto Danish rule after 1523. After the introduction of Lutheranism in 1538 the Faroese language was banned in public institutions and disappeared from writing for more than three centuries. The Treaty of Kiel ceded the islands to Denmark in 1814, and the Løgting was abolished in 1816 and reinstated in 1851. A referendum in 1946 produced a narrow majority for independence, which King Christian X annulled, and home rule was granted in 1948.

The Faroe Islands are an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark. The capital is Tórshavn and the official language is Faroese, which is partially mutually intelligible with Icelandic. They are self-governing apart from defence, policing, justice and currency. The Løgting claims to be one of the oldest continuously running parliaments in the world.

Fishing accounts for around 90 per cent of exports. The islands did not join the European Economic Community in 1973, which left them in control of their own fishing waters. Faroese folk songs, the kvæði, were handed down orally and accompanied the medieval chain dance.
farouk-of-egypt: Farouk was born at the Abdeen Palace in Cairo on 11 February 1920, the eldest child of Sultan Fuad I, later King Fuad I, and his second wife Nazli Sabri. His family had Albanian, Circassian, Turkish, French, Greek and Egyptian ancestry. Fuad I died on 28 April 1936, and the sixteen-year-old Farouk left England to return as king, reaching Alexandria on 6 May 1936, where large crowds greeted him.

A regency council governed until 29 June 1937, when Farouk turned 17 by the Islamic lunar calendar and was counted as 18. He was crowned in Cairo on 29 July 1937. He cultivated an image as a pious king and courted the Muslim Brotherhood as a counterweight to the Wafd Party of Nahas Pasha, whose government he dismissed in the autumn of 1937. Egypt stayed neutral in the Second World War, though under British pressure he broke relations with Germany in September 1939.

Egypt ended the war as a creditor of Britain, yet wealth was very unevenly spread: the kingdom had 500 millionaires while most peasants lived in great poverty, and a cholera epidemic in 1947 killed 80,000 people. Farouk's popularity declined. British troops left the Nile valley in 1946 but kept their base on the Suez Canal. In May 1948 Farouk overruled Prime Minister Mahmoud El Nokrashy Pasha, who had warned that the army was not ready, and took Egypt into war with Israel, fearing that the Muslim Brotherhood would otherwise gain strength.

On 17 October 1951 Parliament cancelled the Anglo-Egyptian Treaty of 1936, and guerrilla attacks on the Suez base followed. On 25 January 1952 British forces besieged the police station at Ismailia, and 43 policemen and 3 soldiers were killed. The next day, 26 January 1952, known as Black Saturday, rioters burned much of downtown Cairo; 26 people died. Farouk dismissed Nahas and then changed prime ministers repeatedly over the following six months.

Farouk was overthrown in July 1952 and forced to abdicate in favour of his six-month-old son Ahmed Fuad, who reigned formally as Fuad II until the monarchy was abolished in June 1953. Farouk settled first in Naples and then in Rome. In October 1952 he was indicted for treason in Egypt, though no extradition request was made. He died in exile in Italy on 18 March 1965. His wealth and lavish way of life made him known abroad as a playboy king, and the corruption of his government was widely condemned in Egypt.
farrukh-yasar: Farrukh Yasar was the last independent ruler of Shirvan. Breaking with his ancestors' alliance with the Timurids, he turned to Uzun Hasan of the Aq Qoyunlu and married his daughter Gawhar-Sultan Khanum to Uzun Hasan's son Yaqub; the later Aq Qoyunlu sultans Baysunghur and Murad were his grandsons. On 31 January 1468 the forces of Shirvan and the Aq Qoyunlu together defeated the Timurid ruler Abu Sa'id Mirza. He also sought ties with Mehmed the Conqueror, sending an envoy and his merchant Khawja Yar Ahmad to Istanbul with gold.

In 1465 his envoy Hasan Shirvani went to Moscow, and Ivan III of Russia answered with an embassy under Vasily Papin, accompanied by merchants including Afanasy Nikitin, to seek trade and a pact against the Golden Horde. In 1488 Shaykh Haydar, marching through Shirvan towards Derbent on the pretext of a war against the Circassians, besieged Shamakhi, took the capital and burned it. Unable to defend it, Farrukh Yasar called on his son-in-law Sultan Yaqub. On 9 July 1488 the Aq Qoyunlu under Suleiman Bey and the Shirvan forces led by the shah himself defeated the Qizilbash; Haydar was wounded by an arrow, captured and beheaded, and his head was sent to Yaqub.

After Yaqub died in 1490, Farrukh Yasar backed his grandson Baysunghur, who fled to Shirvan when he was deposed in 1492 and was later killed in battle between Barda and Ganja; Baysunghur's brother Murad also took refuge in Shirvan until 1497. That year the ruler of Shaki, Shah Husain, rebelled with the shah's youngest son, the future Ibrahim II Shaykhshah, and raided Gabala for eight days; Farrukh Yasar crushed the revolt but pardoned them.

Haydar's son Ismail, freed in 1492 by the Aq Qoyunlu sultan Rustam, set out to avenge his father and in 1499 began his march on Shirvan. At the Battle of Jabani near Shamakhi the Shirvan army was destroyed and Farrukh Yasar was captured and beheaded; Ismail took Shamakhi and moved on to Baku. Many sources remember him as a merciful ruler, and he patronised the building of the Tuba Shahi Mosque and the Juma Mosque in Derbent. His descendants ruled Shirvan under Safavid suzerainty until 1538, when Tahmasp I appointed its first Safavid governor.
farrukhan-the-great: Little is written about the Dabuyids. They are known mainly from the local histories of Ibn Isfandiyar (early 13th century) and Zahir al-Din Mar'ashi (died after 1489), with brief mentions by al-Tabari, Ibn al-Athir and the geographers Ibn al-Faqih and Ibn Khurdadbih. Both local historians trace the family to the Sasanian royal house through Jamasp. Their rule over Gilan, Daylam and the mountains of Tabaristan was nominal: local chiefs and the Qarinvandid and Bavandid dynasties held real power there, and the Dabuyids ruled directly only Ruyan and the valleys of Tabaristan as far as Tammisha.

Farrukhan bore the titles ispahbadh, Padashwargarshah and Gilgilan. He first agreed to pay tribute to the Turks to stop their raids, then fortified the passes into Tabaristan and stopped paying after two years; when they invaded, he defeated them in a night attack. A revolt of his Daylamite subjects drove him to the castle of Firuz-Khusra at Amul, and the besiegers withdrew when he had clay shaped like loaves of bread set on the walls to look well provisioned.

When the Arab governor of Iraq and Khurasan, Yazid ibn al-Muhallab, invaded, he at first defeated Farrukhan and took Dihistan and Gurgan. Farrukhan then raised the Daylamites and Gilites, defeated the Arabs and stirred Gurgan to revolt; its Arab garrison was massacred, including fifty members of Yazid's family. After the treaty that followed, the caliph Umar II had Yazid dismissed and imprisoned.

Ibn Isfandiyar tells that Farrukhan ordered a man named Bav to build a city at a place called Ohar, but Bav was bribed to build it elsewhere and was hanged; the city, Sari, took the name of Farrukhan's son Saruya. Beside it Farrukhan built a palace called Shahr-e Espahbodan. He is the first Dabuyid whose coins are known, half-weight imitations of those of Khosrow II with Middle Persian legends and a winged crown referring to Verethragna, the god of victory, a pattern his successors and the later Abbasid governors kept. He died in 728 and was succeeded by his son Dadhburzmihr.
farrukhi-sistani: Abu'l-Hasan Ali ibn Julugh Farrukhi Sistani was born around 1000 in Sistan, a region across the border of eastern Iran and present-day southern Afghanistan, then under Saffarid rule. His father Julugh, whose origins are unclear, was a high-ranking military slave (ghulam) of the Saffarid king Khalaf ibn Ahmad. Farrukhi grew up in a Muslim, Persian-speaking setting. In 1003 the Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud abolished the Saffarid dynasty and made Sistan a province of his empire.

According to the tadhkirahs, the biographical collections of poets, Farrukhi was gifted in poetry and the lute from an early age. He first served a landowner (dehqan) in Sistan, but finding the pay too low he went to Transoxiana and in the autumn of 1016 entered the service of the Muhtajid prince Abu'l-Muzaffar Fakhr al-Dawla Ahmad ibn Muhammad, ruler of Chaghaniyan as a Ghaznavid vassal, for whom he wrote a poem at the Mehregan festival. Hardly a year later he moved to Ghazni and joined Mahmud's court, where he won fame and wealth as panegyrist to Mahmud, to his son Mas'ud I and to many viziers and princes.

He never lived in Sistan again but kept in touch with relatives and friends there. In 1027 he praised the vizier Hasanak for improving conditions in the province, which had been in chaos since Mahmud's conquest; many Sistanis, though, resented the Ghaznavids and their heavy taxes.

Farrukhi's surviving work is chiefly his divan of about 9,000 couplets. His poems mark court occasions: the Iranian festivals of Mihragan, Nowruz and Sadeh, the Islamic Eid al-Fitr, and Mahmud's raid on the temple of Somnath in Gujarat in 1026. The Encyclopedia Iranica calls him one of the most successful court poets in the history of Persian literature. A document in the Bankipore Library names him as author of an epic, the Shahriyarnameh, a claim not yet confirmed. He died at Ghazni.
farrukhsiyar: Farrukhsiyar was born in Aurangabad on the Deccan Plateau to a Kashmiri mother, Sahiba Niswan, the second son of Azim-ush-Shan and a great-grandson of Aurangzeb. He spent his early years governing Dhaka, the capital of the province of Bengal. In 1712 Azim-ush-Shan was defeated by an alliance that placed Farrukhsiyar's uncle Jahandar Shah on the throne. The prince considered suicide but was dissuaded by his friends from Bengal, and he sought revenge for his father's death, joined by Husain Ali Khan, the governor of Bengal, and his brother Abdullah Khan, the governor of Allahabad.

On 10 January 1713 Farrukhsiyar's forces met Jahandar Shah's at Samugarh, 14 kilometres east of Agra. Jahandar Shah was defeated and imprisoned, and Farrukhsiyar proclaimed himself emperor the next day. Abdullah Khan demanded the post of wazir and Farrukhsiyar finally gave in, while his brother Husain Ali Khan became commander-in-chief. Because the Sayyid brothers controlled the strongest part of the army, they became the real rulers of the empire, and Farrukhsiyar was emperor in little more than name.

His government fought several campaigns. In 1714 Husain Ali Khan forced Ajit Singh of Marwar to submit, and Ajit Singh gave a daughter in marriage to the emperor. Jai Singh II besieged the Jat leader Churaman at Thun, and Churaman accepted Mughal authority in 1718. After a siege at Gurdaspur the Sikh leader Banda Singh Bahadur surrendered, and on 19 June 1716 he and his followers were executed in Delhi. In 1717 Farrukhsiyar issued a farman allowing the British East India Company to trade in Bengal duty-free, which its officials misused for private trade and which angered the nawab of Bengal.

Farrukhsiyar's advisers Mir Jumla III and Khan Dauran told him that the Sayyids were unfit for office, and the two sides struggled for years. In February 1719 Husain Ali Khan entered Delhi with a large army, including Maratha horsemen led by Balaji Vishwanath, and Abdullah Khan seized the palace. Farrukhsiyar was captured, blinded and eventually killed in prison, and the Sayyids crowned Prince Rafi-ud-darjat in his place. He was known afterwards as Shahid-i-marhum, the martyr received with mercy. The town of Farrukhnagar near Delhi and Farrukhabad in Uttar Pradesh are named after him.
fascism: The historian Zeev Sternhell traced the ideological roots of fascism to the 1880s, to a fin de siècle revolt against materialism, rationalism, positivism, bourgeois society and democracy. The word comes from the Italian fascio, a bundle of sticks, ultimately from the Latin fasces, the bundle of rods tied round an axe that was an ancient Roman symbol of a magistrate's authority and suggested strength through unity. Fascists saw the First World War as a revolution in war, society, the state and technology.

When the war began in August 1914 the Italian left split. Benito Mussolini, expelled as chief editor of the Socialist Party's newspaper Avanti! for his anti-German stance, joined the interventionist cause, and members of his Fasces of Revolutionary Action first used the term fascism in 1915. In 1919 he founded the Italian Fasces of Combat in Milan, which became the National Fascist Party two years later.

Definition has been a long and complex debate. Historian Ian Kershaw wrote that defining fascism is like trying to nail jelly to the wall. One school, including Stanley G. Payne, Roger Griffin and Roger Eatwell, understands it as a movement based on the myth of national rebirth, and Griffin identifies palingenetic ultranationalism as its core. Scholars place it on the far right, as opposed to communism, socialism and parliamentary liberalism.

Fascism promotes a totalitarian state. Mussolini's The Doctrine of Fascism (1932), partly ghostwritten by the philosopher Giovanni Gentile, states that outside the state no human or spiritual values can exist. It treats violence as a means of national rejuvenation, and most fascist parties created their own militias, such as the Blackshirts and the Nazi Party's Sturmabteilung.

Named prime minister, Mussolini had to form a coalition government, which at first pursued economically liberal policies under the finance minister Alberto De Stefani. The Great Depression brought social unrest, and fascist propaganda blamed minorities and scapegoats. During World War II the Axis Powers in Europe, led by Nazi Germany, took part in the Holocaust, the extermination of millions of Jews, Poles, Roma, Sinti and others. In 1943 Mussolini was removed and arrested on the order of King Victor Emmanuel III, then rescued by German forces to lead the Italian Social Republic until 1945.

Anti-fascist movements began in the 1920s. After the defeat of the Axis the Nuremberg Trials convicted several Nazi leaders, and fascism has been almost universally condemned. George Orwell wrote in 1944 that the word had become almost meaningless.
fascist-italy: The Kingdom of Italy was governed by the National Fascist Party from 1922 to 1943, with Benito Mussolini as prime minister turning the country into a totalitarian dictatorship. The regime crushed political opposition, while promoting economic modernisation, traditional social values and a rapprochement with the Catholic Church. The historian Stanley G. Payne distinguishes six phases. The first, from 1922 to 1925, was nominally a continuation of the parliamentary system, though with a legally organised executive dictatorship, and the second, from 1925 to 1929, was the construction of the Fascist dictatorship proper. In 1929 Mussolini and the papacy reached an agreement that ended a standoff between the Church and the Italian state going back to 1860.

In its first years the regime pacified Libya, bombed and occupied Corfu in 1923, and made Albania a protectorate in 1925. The fourth phase, from 1935 to 1940, was marked by an aggressive foreign policy: the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, launched from Eritrea and Somaliland, which brought League of Nations sanctions, growing economic autarky, the invasion of Albania and the Pact of Steel. In 1938 the regime passed racial laws that stripped Jews of their Italian citizenship, barred them from professional positions and forbade marriages between Italians and Jews or Africans. Mussolini had until then denied antisemitism in Italy, and Italo Balbo opposed the laws.

Italy was a leading member of the Axis in the Second World War and fought at first with some success. After the German-Italian defeat in Africa and the Allied landings in Sicily, King Victor Emmanuel III overthrew and arrested Mussolini, and the new government signed an armistice with the Allies in September 1943. Germany seized the north and rescued Mussolini, setting up the Italian Social Republic, a puppet state, and Italian resistance groups fought German and Republic forces until 1945.

The regime set out to become a one-party state, and the Doctrine of Fascism of 1935 declared a totalitarian state. Mussolini created the Blackshirt militia in 1923 and the secret police OVRA in 1927, which terrorised opponents, in some cases with forced doses of castor oil. The state took control of textbooks in 1929, and in 1933 university teachers had to belong to the party.

The Opera Nazionale Dopolavoro, founded in 1925, organised leisure for adults and by 1936 had reached an estimated 80 per cent of salaried workers. The Fascists promised corporatism, with unions and employers grouped into professional corporations. Mussolini was captured and killed by the resistance on 28 April 1945. In 1946 Italians voted in a referendum to abandon the monarchy and form the Italian Republic.
fashoda: Kodok, also written Kothok, lies in Fashoda County of Upper Nile State, in the Greater Upper Nile region of South Sudan, and is the capital of Shilluk country. In Shilluk belief and tradition it is the mediating city of the Shilluk King, where each new king is crowned. Believers hold that the spirits of Juok (God), of Nyikango, founder of the kingdom and spiritual leader of the Shilluk religion, of the deceased kings and of the living king meet there for the kingdom's spiritual healing. For long it was kept hidden as a forbidden city of the king.

An Egyptian military post was set up at Fashoda in 1865, and the place became a trading station of some importance, the slave trade included. It fell to the Mahdists between 1883 and 1884. In 1898 British plans for a block of influence from southern Africa to Egypt met French ambitions to expand eastward from West Africa along the Sahel, and the standoff at Fashoda brought the two countries to the brink of war. Its outcome gave rise to the Fashoda syndrome in French foreign policy. After the Entente Cordiale of 1904 the British renamed the town Kodok, hoping to erase the memory of the incident.

From 1898 the British administration assigned the town to the Church Mission Society, while the Catholic Verona Fathers received the land west of the Nile and the Presbyterian Church (USA) the east. A Catholic mission opened in Kodok in January 1933, and the town also became a Presbyterian centre. Its population was about 9,100 in 1955. In 1964, during the First Sudanese Civil War, the army sent from Khartoum carried out a massacre there. Kodok suffered a serious famine in the 1990s, when Operation Lifeline Sudan was among the relief efforts, and refugees returned in 2004 and 2005 as the Second Sudanese Civil War ended.

The people of Kodok live mainly from subsistence farming, growing millet as their staple and raising cattle. Since the mid-1990s they have also sold gum arabic, taken from Acacia seyal, to traders from the north.
fatali-khan-khoyski: Fatali Khan Khoyski was born on 7 December 1875 (O.S. 25 November 1875) in Nukha, now Shaki, into the noble family of Iskandar Khan Khoyski, a colonel in the Russian Army. His great-grandfather Jafar Qoli, the Khan of Khoy, sided with Russia in the Russo-Persian war of 1804 to 1813 and was rewarded by Tsar Alexander I with the Khanate of Shaki. Khoyski graduated from the Ganja Classical Gymnasium in 1893, where he learned Russian, Greek, Latin, French and German, and from the Law Faculty of Moscow University in 1901, and worked as a court lawyer in Ganja, Sukhumi, Batumi and Kutaisi.

Elected to the Second State Duma from Elizavetpol Governorate, he criticised Russian colonial policy in Azerbaijan and the Caucasus in a speech on 2 February 1907. After the February Revolution of 1917 he joined the committee of the Muslim National Councils and was elected chairman of the Baku City Duma, regarded as the chief rival of the Baku Soviet. At the Musavat summit of October 1917 he spoke for Azerbaijan's autonomy, and in December he was elected to the Transcaucasian Sejm and named Minister of Justice of the Transcaucasian Democratic Federative Republic.

When the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic was proclaimed on 28 May 1918 he formed its first cabinet and on 30 May sent a radiogram announcing independence to the world's political centres. His governments worked for an alliance with the Turkish government, helped remove the Centrocaspian Dictatorship from Baku and set up diplomatic ties; he sought recognition of independence at the Paris Peace Conference. Under them Turkish was made the official language, education was nationalised, the first steps toward a national army were taken, a multi-party system and the manat currency were introduced, and Azerbaijan State University was founded.

In January 1920 Georgy Chicherin repeatedly asked Khoyski to open a front against Anton Denikin; he refused, saying the republic would not meddle in Russia's internal affairs. He moved his family to Tbilisi before the Red Army entered Baku on 28 April 1920.

On 19 June 1920 Aram Yerganian shot him in Tiflis near Erivansky Square, as part of Operation Nemesis organised by the Armenian Revolutionary Federation, which said he had played a major role in the September 1918 massacre of Armenians in Baku. He was buried in Tiflis next to Mirza Fatali Akhundzade, in a ceremony arranged by the Persian consulate.
fatawa-i-alamgiri: The work is also known as Al-Fatawa al-Hindiyyah, the Fatwa of India. To compile it, Emperor Aurangzeb gathered 500 experts in Islamic jurisprudence, 300 from South Asia, 100 from Iraq and 100 from the Hejaz, working in Delhi and Lahore under the chairmanship of Shaikh Nizam Burhanpuri. The compilation took eight years, from 1664 to 1672. It applied Hanafi law creatively, restricted the discretion of jurists to issue their own fatwas, and allowed the emperor to issue farmans that overruled them. Burton Stein saw in it a return of the ulama to the prominence in government they had lost under Akbar.

Drawing on the Qur'an and on hadith collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, it set out rulings on personal and family law, inheritance, gifts, slavery, war, property, relations between religions, contracts, taxation and the economy. It treated people differently according to their religion. It confirmed the right of Muslims to own slaves, denied slaves inheritance and the right to testify, and set hudud punishments for zina, stoning or flogging according to the status of the accused. It also formalised the office of the muhtasib, or censor, enforced by officials called kotwal. Originally in 30 volumes, it is now printed in six.

Jamal Malik argues that it hardened social ranks among Muslims, exempting nobles such as Sayyids from physical punishment while commoners could be arrested and beaten. Mona Siddiqui notes that, despite its name, it is not a collection of fatwas of Aurangzeb's time but a compendium of earlier Hanafi statements.

When power in India passed to the British, the colonial authorities kept local laws, and the Fatawa, written in Arabic, became a reference text for enforcing sharia from the 18th to the early 20th century. English-speaking judges depended on Muslim legal specialists, and rulings in similar cases varied. In the second half of the 19th century its inconsistencies and its Hanafi Sunni basis, which Shia Muslims and Hindus did not accept, led officials to frame separate laws for Muslims and non-Muslims, most of which independent India kept after 1947. Neil Baillie's Digest of Mohummudan Law of 1865 drew on it, and Muhammad Naimuddin published a Bengali translation in 1892.
fatehpur-sikri: The city takes its name from the village of Sikri, which occupied the site before. Excavations at Birchhabili Tila show a settlement from the 6th century CE and Jain temples of the 9th to 11th centuries. The Sikarwar Rajputs controlled the area from the 7th to the 16th century, until the Battle of Khanwa in 1527. Babur loved the place, called it Shukri, and laid out a garden there after defeating Rana Sangha.

Akbar had no surviving heir until 1569, when his son, later known as Jahangir, was born at Sikri. The Chishti saint Sheikh Salim had predicted the birth, and Akbar began a religious compound in his honour. After Jahangir's second birthday he started on a walled city and imperial palace. The city became known as Fatehpur Sikri, the City of Victory, after his Gujarat campaign of 1573. He left it in 1585 for a campaign in Punjab, and it was completely abandoned by 1610. The usual explanation is the failure of the water supply, though Akbar's loss of interest may also have played a part. After occupying Agra in 1803 the East India Company set up an administrative centre there, which remained until 1850.

The palace city stands on a rocky ridge about 3 kilometres long and 1 kilometre wide, enclosed by a wall some 6 kilometres long on three sides, with a lake on the fourth. Its architecture is modelled on Timurid forms, with Gujarati influences, and reflects both Hindu and Muslim domestic building of the time. Its continuous pattern of gardens and services leads archaeologists to conclude that it was built mainly to provide leisure and luxury for its residents.

The Jama Masjid was finished by 1571 to 1572, and the Buland Darwaza was added about five years later as a victory arch for the Gujarat campaign. The white marble tomb of Salim Chishti stands in the mosque's courtyard. The Diwan-i-Khas is known for its carved central pillar, and the Ibadat Khana, built in 1575, is where tradition says the foundations of Akbar's new syncretic faith, Din-e-Ilahi, were laid.

Because of its importance as a Mughal capital and its outstanding architecture, Fatehpur Sikri was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986. The state of preservation of its original spaces allows archaeologists to reconstruct scenes of Mughal court life. The town lies in the Agra District of Uttar Pradesh, about 37 kilometres from Agra.
fath-ali-khan-afshar: Fath-Ali Khan belonged to the Arashlu branch of the Afshar tribe, part of the Afshars who had lived in Urmia since the Safavid era. The modern historian P. Oberling called him the best known of the Afshar governors of Urmia. The Urmia Afshars took a large part in the wars that followed the death of Nader Shah, and with wide local support Fath-Ali Khan had brought the whole province of Azerbaijan under his control by 1749.

He served as deputy and general of Azad Khan Afghan, a Ghilzai Pashtun from Kabul who had his base at Urmia, and he was one of four contenders for supremacy in Iran, with Azad Khan, Karim Khan Zand and the Qajar chieftain Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar. In 1753, after Azad Khan had taken Isfahan, Fath-Ali Khan devastated Qumishah and led an attack into the town that killed Karim Khan's half-brother Eskandar Khan Zand and forced the Zands to withdraw.

In 1754 he attacked a Zand army weakened by a harsh winter, and in September he repelled Karim Khan's small force at Kazerun. Soon afterwards his Afshar troops were ambushed at the narrow Kamarej pass by Zand, Dashtestani and Khesht musketeers and fled to Shiraz, which Azad Khan had to abandon ten days later. The next spring Fath-Ali Khan was defeated by Mohammad Khan Zand. When Urmia surrendered to the Qajars in June 1757 and Azad Khan fled to Baghdad, he was persuaded to join the Qajars.

In 1760 he defended Tabriz so well that Karim Khan's lightly equipped army could not take it, and that summer he was among the former allies who defeated Azad Khan's attempt to return to Azerbaijan. In 1761 he besieged Shusha in Karabakh, lifting the siege when its ruler Panah Ali Khan gave him his son Ibrahim Khalil Khan as a hostage. In the summer of 1762 Karim Khan defeated him at the Battle of Qara Chaman. Fath-Ali Khan fled to Urmia, whose fall in February 1763 ended his confederation and left Karim Khan master of all Iran except Afsharid Khorasan.
fath-ali-shah-qajar: Fath-Ali Shah was born on 5 August 1772 at Damghan, where his father, Hossein Qoli Khan Qajar, was governor. Until his coronation he was known mainly as Baba Khan. His father was killed by the Kuklan Turkmens in 1777, and his uncle Agha Mohammad Khan, who married his mother, became his guardian. After Agha Mohammad Khan took the throne at Tehran on 21 March 1786, Baba Khan was named his heir and vice-regent. He was governor of Fars when his uncle was assassinated in 1797.

Baba Khan ascended the throne at Shiraz on 28 July 1797 and held his official coronation at Tehran on 19 March 1798. His coins bore his own name rather than a Shia Imam's, a sign of full sovereignty. The reign saw a revival of Persian arts and an elaborate court with rigid etiquette, with portraiture and oil painting reaching a height unknown under earlier Islamic dynasties thanks to his patronage. He also had rock reliefs carved beside those of the Sasanian Empire, presenting himself as heir to ancient Persia.

Russia took control of Georgia, which Iran had ruled intermittently since 1555, and in 1804 the shah went to war, under pressure from the Shia clergy. Russian artillery gave the advantage, and Britain and France both failed to support Iran. After the fall of Lankaran on 1 January 1813 he accepted the Treaty of Gulistan, which gave Russia Georgia and most khanates of the Caucasus. In 1826 he tried to recover them, and his son Abbas Mirza regained much ground at first. But Ivan Paskevich captured Erivan on 1 October 1827, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828 gave Russia the khanates of Erivan and Nakhchivan, imposed a payment of 10 million in gold and provided for the resettlement of Armenians from Iran.

When the crown prince Abbas Mirza died on 25 October 1833, Fath-Ali Shah named his grandson Mohammed Mirza as heir. He died a year later and was buried in the shrine of Fatima Masumeh at Qom. Iranians often see him as a weak ruler because of the two treaties. Others stress that he turned a largely Turkic tribal khanship into a centralised monarchy on the old imperial model. He is recognisable in all of his 25 known portraits by his black beard, which reached below his waist, and he was survived by fifty-seven sons and forty-six daughters.
fatherland-front-austria: After the First World War three camps shaped the Austrian First Republic: the Social Democrats, the Christian Social Party and the German nationalists. Chancellor Ignaz Seipel, a proponent of Catholic social teaching, advocated a corporate state above the parliamentary system, drawing on the encyclicals Rerum novarum of 1891 and Quadragesimo anno of 1931. On 10 May 1932 Engelbert Dollfuss became chancellor with a narrow majority, and he used a constitutional crisis in March 1933 to suspend the National Council and rule by decree. On 20 May 1933 he founded the Fatherland Front, merging his Christian Social Party, the Heimwehr forces and other right-wing groups, to gather all loyal Austrians under one banner.

On 30 May 1933 the government banned the paramilitary Republikanischer Schutzbund, and the Communist and Nazi parties were prohibited shortly after. The Schutzbund revolted from 12 February 1934 in the Austrian Civil War against the Heimwehr and the army, and was crushed in a few days; the Social Democratic Party was then dissolved. On 1 May a rump session recast the constitution as authoritarian and corporatist and renamed the country the Federal State of Austria, with the Front as the only legal political organisation. Dollfuss was assassinated in the Nazi July Putsch on 25 July 1934. Kurt Schuschnigg became chancellor and took over the Front in 1936.

On 12 February 1938 Hitler summoned Schuschnigg to the Berghof and demanded the readmission of the Nazi Party. Schuschnigg announced a referendum on independence and agreed to lift the ban on the Social Democrats and their unions in return for support, but he was forced to resign on 11 March 1938. Austria was annexed the next day, and the Front was banned two days after that.

The Front held a monopoly in politics, with civilian and military divisions. Its symbol was the crutch cross, and its greeting was Österreich! or Front heil!. Membership was obligatory for officials, and by the end of 1937 it had 3 million members among 6.5 million Austrians, but it never became a mass movement. It was backed by the Catholic Church, the bureaucracy, police, military, most of the rural population and a significant part of Vienna's Jewish community. Historians dispute its character: many call it Austrofascism, while conservative authors stress its defence of independence against Nazism. After 1945 former members such as Julius Raab and Leopold Figl founded the Austrian People's Party.
fatherland-front-bulgaria: The Fatherland Front brought together the Zveno movement, the communist Bulgarian Workers Party, a wing of the Bulgarian Agrarian National Union and the Bulgarian Social Democratic Workers Party. Its members held widely different ideologies and had united only against the pro-German militarist dictatorship then ruling Bulgaria. Professional associations and trade unions could also join the front while keeping their own organisations.

The coup of 9 September 1944 followed the Soviet Union's declaration of war on Bulgaria, and the new government at once declared war on Germany and the other Axis powers. It was headed by Kimon Georgiev of Zveno and signed a ceasefire with the Soviet Union on 28 October 1944. In the summer of 1945 most of the Agrarian Union, led by Nikola Petkov, and most of the Social Democrats left the front and formed a large opposition, which after the 1946 Grand National Assembly election held 99 of the 465 seats.

The front won a large majority in the national elections of 18 November 1945. Bulgaria became a People's Republic on 15 September 1946 after a referendum, and in November 1946 Georgiev resigned as prime minister in favour of the communist leader Georgi Dimitrov. In 1948 and 1949 all the remaining parties of the front except the pro-communist wing of the Agrarian Union dissolved themselves and merged into the Communist Party.

From 1947 the Fatherland Front was in effect the only legal political organisation in Bulgaria, a broad popular front under the control of the communists. At every election from 1949 to 1986 voters were offered a single list from the front, which official figures showed approved by well over 99 per cent. Its National Council was chaired by Georgi Dimitrov until 1949, then by Valko Chervenkov, Encho Staykov, Boyan Bulgaranov, Georgi Traikov, Pencho Kubadinski from 1974 to 1989, and finally Zhivko Zhivkov.
fatima: Fatima was born in Mecca to Khadija, the first of the Prophet Muhammad's wives. The mainstream Sunni view is that she was born in 605, five years before the first Quranic revelations, while Twelver sources report about 612 or 615. She is commonly called al-Zahra, the radiant, which the Shia take to refer to her creation from light, and hadith collections including Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim call her mistress of the women of paradise.

She married Muhammad's cousin Ali in Medina around 1 or 2 AH (623–5 CE), possibly after the Battle of Badr. Some companions, including Abu Bakr and Umar, had asked for her hand and been refused, since Muhammad said he was waiting for the moment fixed by destiny. When Muhammad put Ali's proposal to her she remained silent, which was understood as agreement, and on this report a woman's consent has always been needed in Islamic law.

Fatima was severely bereaved when Muhammad died in 11 AH, 632 CE. According to Shia tradition she contested Abu Bakr's succession and held that Ali was the rightful successor, and the village of Fadak near Medina was at issue between them, the Shia holding that Muhammad had given his share of it to her. She died within six months of her father. Sunnis believe she died of grief, while Shia Islam holds that injuries in a raid by Umar on her house caused a miscarriage and her death shortly after. According to the Sunni al-Tabari her dying wish was that Abu Bakr should not attend her funeral, and Ali buried her secretly at night, hiding the grave.

She was survived by her sons Hasan and Husayn, the second and third Shia imams, and her daughters Zaynab and Umm Kulthum. Her descendants bear the titles sayyid or sharif and are respected by Muslims. The Fatimid dynasty, which ruled in North Africa from 909 to 1171, claimed descent from her through the Isma'ili imam Muhammad ibn Isma'il, though the claim has been challenged. She is not named in the Quran, but commentaries link several verses to her, and Shia Islam limits the Ahl al-Bayt, the people of the house, to Muhammad, Fatima, Ali, Hasan and Husayn. She has been compared to Mary, mother of Jesus, especially in Shia Islam.
fatima-al-fihri: Little is known of Fatima's life beyond what the 14th-century historian Ibn Abi Zar' recorded in The Garden of Pages, which forms the basis of the traditional narrative. She is said to have been born in Kairouan, in present-day Tunisia, possibly around 800, the daughter of a wealthy merchant, Muhammad al-Fihri al-Qayrawani. He came to Fez with his wife, his sister and his daughter as part of a larger migration of families from Kairouan in the early Idrisid period. When he died, Fatima inherited his wealth. She was also known as Umm al-Banin, the Mother of the Sons.

According to Ibn Abi Zar', Fatima took no part in commerce and wished to devote her inheritance to a pious act. She bought a property in the centre of Fez at high cost and laid the foundations of the al-Qarawiyyin mosque on the first day of Ramadan in the year 245 of the Islamic calendar, 859 CE. The materials are said to have been quarried on the site, so that no doubt could fall on their source. Fatima fasted until the work was finished, then went in and prayed to thank God. The same tradition says her sister Maryam founded the mosque of the Andalusians in the district across the river at about the same time.

The mosque became the most important congregational mosque in Fez and one of the foremost intellectual centres of Islamic North Africa. Its teaching later became the University of al-Qarawiyyin, which took that form in 1963.

Fatima is said to have died around 880. Since she is first mentioned many centuries after her death, some modern historians doubt her existence. Roger Le Tourneau and Jonathan Bloom see the symmetry of two sisters founding the two great mosques of Fez as too neat, and Bloom notes that no part of the present mosque is older than the tenth century. A foundation inscription found under plaster in the 20th century names Dawud ibn Idris as founder in 877 CE. Chafik Benchekroun argues it is the original inscription and that Fatima may be a figure of legend. Ian D. Morris finds no evidence that she founded the library or the university.
fatimid-caliphate: The Fatimids led Isma'ilism, a revolutionary Shi'a movement that was at once political and religious, philosophical and social, and that originally proclaimed the arrival of an Islamic messiah. They traced their descent from Fatima, the daughter of Muhammad, and her husband Ali, and called themselves simply the Alid dynasty. The origins of the movement are obscure before the late ninth century. Its founder, Abdallah al-Mahdi Billah, was Arab in origin, but its first army was made up of Kutama Berbers from Little Kabylia.

Ifriqiya was then held by the Aghlabids, an Arab dynasty that ruled nominally for the Abbasids. In 893 the missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i settled among the Kutama, and over two years he won most of the tribes by persuasion or coercion and set up an Isma'ili theocratic state at Tazrut, near Mila. Between 902 and 909 his forces conquered Aghlabid Ifriqiya, and al-Mahdi was accepted as imam and first caliph in 909.

For much of the tenth century the Fatimids rivalled the Umayyads of Córdoba for control of the western Maghreb. Their capitals were first al-Mahdiyya, on a peninsula on the coast of modern Tunisia, then al-Mansuriyya near Kairouan. In 969 the general Jawhar invaded Egypt, which the Ikhshidids held, and founded al-Qahira, Cairo, several miles north-east of Fustat. The caliphate's centre moved there in 973, and Egypt became the political, cultural and religious centre of the empire.

After the reigns of al-'Aziz and al-Hakim, the long reign of al-Mustansir left the caliph aloof from affairs and the viziers more powerful. Factionalism in the army led to a civil war in the 1060s, followed by a revival under the vizier Badr al-Jamali. The Seljuk Turks pressed into Syria in the 1070s and the Crusaders arrived in the Levant in 1097. In 1171 Saladin abolished the dynasty and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. After al-Mustansir his sons Nizar and al-Musta'li both claimed the imamate, splitting the Isma'ilis into Nizari and Musta'li branches.

Fatimid society was highly pluralistic. Isma'ili Shi'ism was the religion of the state and the court, but most Muslims stayed Sunni, a large part of the population remained Christian, and Jews were a smaller minority. Non-Muslims were dhimmis and paid the jizya, and scholars generally agree that Fatimid rule was tolerant and inclusive. Its leaders made little headway in persuading the population to adopt their beliefs.

The army began with Kutama Berbers. From the reign of al-'Aziz Turkish freedmen, Daylamis, Kurds and Black infantry bought as slaves in Nubia joined it, and the Kutama lost their privileged place. Fatimid art is known for lively figurative motifs, angular floriated Kufic script, lustre ceramics and carved rock crystal. The mosque of al-Azhar in Cairo still stands.
fatimid-conquest-of-egypt: The Fatimids came to power in Ifriqiya in 909 and, as imams claiming descent from Fatima, saw themselves as the rightful leaders of the whole Muslim world against the Abbasids. Their early invasions of Egypt failed. By the 960s the Abbasid caliphs had become pawns of the Buyids, while the Ikhshidid regime in Egypt faced Makurian raids from the south, the Lawata Berbers around Alexandria, Qarmatian and Bedouin attacks in Syria and a severe famine. Fatimid agents worked openly in Fustat, and many of the local elite came to welcome a Fatimid takeover as an end to the insecurity.

The death of Abu al-Misk Kafur in April 968, without an heir, paralysed the regime. A power-sharing pact under al-Ikhshid's 11-year-old grandson soon broke down, and early in 969 the regent al-Hasan ibn Ubayd Allah returned to Palestine, leaving Egypt effectively without government. Caliph al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah had prepared for years; the 15th-century historian al-Maqrizi put the cost at 24 million gold dinars, a figure historians do not take literally.

The army, which Arab sources put at over a hundred thousand men, left Raqqada on 6 February 969 under Jawhar, to whom al-Mu'izz gave full powers. In May it entered the Nile Delta and occupied Alexandria without resistance. A delegation from Fustat sought guarantees, and Jawhar issued a writ of safe-conduct, the amān, promising to respect the rights of the notables and people and to take up the jihād against the Byzantines. The Ikhshidid soldiers tried to bar his crossing of the Nile between 29 June and 3 July and were overcome. Pro-Fatimid agents took control of Fustat, Jawhar entered on 6 July, and the Friday prayer was read in the name of al-Mu'izz on 9 July.

Jawhar governed Egypt as viceroy for four years, disarming the Ikhshidid troops and confiscating their property, quelling rebellions and beginning a new capital. An advance into Syria ended in disaster: Ja'far ibn Fallah was defeated and killed by the Qarmatians in August 971, and their invasion was fought off just north of the new city. Al-Mu'izz set out from Ifriqiya with his court, his treasure and the coffins of his ancestors, and on 10 June 973 he crossed the Nile and went straight to his capital, named al-Qāhira al-Muʿizzīya, which became Cairo. It remained the seat of the Fatimid Caliphate until Saladin abolished the regime in 1171.
fatwa: A fatwa is a legal ruling on a point of Islamic law given by a qualified jurist, or faqih, in answer to a question from a private person, a judge or a government. The jurist who issues it is a mufti, and the act is called ifta. The word comes from an Arabic root with meanings that include youth, newness and clarification. The practice has roots in the Quran, which on several occasions tells Muhammad how to answer questions from his followers, in two cases with verbal forms of the root f-t-y.

After Muhammad's death in 632 the community turned to his Companions for guidance, and then to the generation of Successors, and the question-and-answer format took its definitive form with the development of the classical theory of Islamic law.

Fatwas are issued in reply to a query and may range from a yes or no answer to a book-length treatise. Queries were supposed to concern real situations and to leave out names of places and people. A fatwa is nonbinding, unless issued by a government judge in an Islamic state, whereas a court decision is binding. It may deal with rituals, ethics, doctrine and sometimes philosophy, and it applies to every case fitting the premises of the question, while a judgment applies only to its own case. The classical institution resembles the jus respondendi of Roman law and the responsa of Jewish law.

Fatwas played three roles in the classical legal system: they informed Muslims about ritual and ethics, advised courts on finer points of law, and developed substantive law, since author-jurists collected the fatwas of prominent muftis in books. Manuals called adab al-mufti required a mufti to be an adult Muslim of good character and sound mind, trained as a jurist. A student normally studied for several years with recognised scholars, and a teacher certified readiness to issue fatwas with an ijaza. Over the centuries Sunni muftis were gradually incorporated into state bureaucracies, while Shia jurists in Iran asserted autonomous authority from the early modern era.

Public and political fatwas were issued to take a stand on doctrinal controversies, to legitimise government policies or to express grievances, and during European colonialism they helped mobilise resistance. In the modern era codified state laws and Western-style legal education displaced muftis from elaborating the law applied in courts, and fatwas increasingly advise the public on ritual and everyday life.
faustin-soulouque: Faustin-Élie Soulouque was born on 15 August 1782 at Petit-Goâve in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the son of Marie-Catherine Soulouque, a creole of Mandinka descent. He was freed by the emancipation decree of 1793 issued by the civil commissioner Léger-Félicité Sonthonax, and in 1803, when France tried to restore slavery, he joined the revolutionary army as a private. After independence he was commissioned a lieutenant in 1806, served in the Horse Guards under President Alexandre Pétion and rose over four decades to lieutenant general and commander of the presidential guard under Jean-Baptiste Riché.

After Riché's death the Boyerist ruling class picked Soulouque, then in his sixties, thinking him dull and easily led; he took the oath as president on 2 March 1847. He soon turned on his backers, raised a private militia, the Zinglins, and attacked opponents, above all the mixed-race mulattoes, who were massacred in Port-au-Prince on 16 April 1848. An open follower of Vodou, he kept manbos and bokors at his residence and gave the religion semi-official standing. On 26 August 1849 the legislature proclaimed him emperor, and on 18 April 1852 he and Empress Adélina were crowned in a lavish ceremony modelled on Napoleon's. He created a nobility of princes, dukes, counts and barons, and orders of chivalry.

His foreign policy turned on the Dominican Republic, independent since 1844. His invasion of 1849 broke at Ocoa, a second in 1850 was halted by British, French and American diplomacy, and in 1855 his army of 30,000 fled after heavy losses at Santomé, Cambronal and Sabana Larga. He also clashed with the United States over Navassa Island, withdrawing his warships for a share of the guano revenue.

In December 1858 General Fabre Geffrard defeated his army, and the republic was restored. Soulouque abdicated on 15 January 1859 and left on a British warship for Kingston, Jamaica. He later returned to Haiti and died on 3 August 1867. He was the last Haitian head of state who had fought in the revolution, been born before independence, been a slave and styled himself a monarch. The scholar Murdo J. MacLeod judged him intelligent, pragmatic and a ruthless but able politician.
fausto-sozzini: Fausto Sozzini was born in Siena on 5 December 1539, the only son of Alessandro Sozzini, who died in 1541. He had no regular education and grew up at home, reading widely; his uncle Celso Sozzini, a nominal Catholic, gave him early stimulus. His grandfather's will in 1556 left him a quarter of the family estates, and the next year he entered the Accademia degli Intronati, preferring sonnets to the law. After coming of age in 1561 he went to Lyon, and in his Brevis explicatio of 1562 he already attributed to Christ an official, not an essential, deity, an antitrinitarian position.

Late in 1563 he returned to Italy and conformed to the Catholic Church. For twelve years he served Isabella de' Medici, daughter of Cosimo I de' Medici. He left Italy at the end of 1575, and an agreement with the grand duke Francesco, reported by Samuel Przypkowski, let him keep the income of his property if he published nothing under his own name. At Basel he finished De Jesu Christo servatore in 1578, which brought him to the notice of Giorgio Biandrata, the court physician in Poland and Transylvania.

In November 1578 Sozzini reached Kolozsvár to argue with the bishop Ferenc Dávid, who had renounced the worship of Christ; Dávid was tried and died in prison at Déva, while Sozzini had returned to Poland. From 1579 he lived in Poland. His views on baptism at first excluded him from the antitrinitarian Ecclesia Minor, but he gradually gained a leading influence in its synods. In 1598 a mob expelled him from Kraków, wrecked his house and beat him, and he died at Luslawice on 4 March 1604.

Sozzini systematised the antitrinitarian beliefs of his uncle Lelio Sozzini into a coherent doctrine called Socinianism, developed among the Polish Brethren and embraced by the Unitarian Church of Transylvania. His treatise on the authority of scripture, written in the 1580s, influenced Remonstrant thinkers such as Simon Episcopius, who drew on it to treat scripture as historical text. He held that the work of Christ operates upon man alone, and that war and the taking of human life were unlawful for a Christian. His proposals for dealing with religious offenders were comparatively mild, though he had not grasped a complete theory of toleration.
faxian: Faxian was born in Shanxi in the 4th century, under the Later Zhao dynasty of the Sixteen Kingdoms period, and his birth surname was Gong. Three of his elder brothers died young, and his father, fearing the same fate for him, had him ordained as a novice monk at the age of three. The name Faxian, which he adopted later, means Splendor of Dharma.

In 399, at about the age of 60, he set out from Chang'an, the capital of the Buddhist Later Qin dynasty, with four companions to find sacred Buddhist texts. Five more pilgrims joined them at Zhangye. He is said to have walked the whole way from China across icy desert and rugged mountain passes, making him one of the earliest attested pilgrims to India.

Faxian entered the Indian subcontinent from the northwest and reached Pataliputra. His visit fell in the reign of Chandragupta II. He spent ten years in India, visiting the major sites linked to the life of the Buddha, among them Kapilvastu, Bodh Gaya, Benares, Shravasti and Kushinagar, as well as well-known monasteries and centres of learning. He learned Sanskrit and collected Indian literature at Pataliputra, Oddiyana and Taxila.

He left India about 409 from the port of Tamralipti. After two years in Sri Lanka, a violent storm drove his ship onto an island, probably Java. Five months later he took another ship for southern China, but it was blown off course and landed him at Mount Lao, in what is now Shandong, about 30 kilometres east of Qingdao. He returned in 412 and settled in what is now Nanjing, where he spent the rest of his life translating and editing the scriptures he had brought back.

Faxian's major work is his account of the journey, the Foguoji, known in English as A Record of the Buddhist Kingdoms, written around 414. It is an independent record of the society and culture of the places he visited, especially India, and of early Buddhism. He notes that cities of Central Asia such as Khotan were Buddhist, with clergy reading Indian manuscripts, and describes a Buddhist community at Taxila amid a generally non-Buddhist population.

He calls the cities of Magadha the largest of the Middle Kingdom, with inhabitants rich and prosperous, and describes an annual procession of images and charitable houses where the poor and sick received food, medicine and care. His translations of the Sanskrit texts he brought back are an important means of dating texts, named individuals and Buddhist traditions. Jean-Pierre Abel-Rémusat published a French translation in 1836, and James Legge's English version appeared in 1886.
fayzabad-badakhshan: Fayzabad stands on the right bank of the Kokcha River, near where the river leaves a gorge and before it reaches a large open plain, at an altitude of 1,254 metres. Historically it connected Kabul with Kashgar in Xinjiang, China, and it is the main commercial and administrative centre of the Pamir region. Its bazaars trade cotton cloth, salt, sugar, tea, indigo and cutlery. Barley, wheat and rice are grown around it, and gold is panned and salt mined nearby. Before the 21st century the town was relatively isolated from the rest of Afghanistan for lack of paved roads.

Until 1680 the town was called Jauz Gun because of the many walnut farms in the area (jauz means walnut). It was renamed Faizabad, roughly the abode of divine bounty, blessing and charity, when the robe of the Prophet Muhammad was delivered there. Tradition holds that Muhammad Shaykh Ziya and Shaykh Niyaz brought it after Wais Qaran had carried it to Balkh. The city then replaced Munjan as the capital of Badakhshan. The relic was removed to Kandahar by Ahmad Shah Durrani in 1768, who established the Kirka Sharif there. Seven historical forts, several now in ruins, were built in and around the city to defend it and the road in and out.

In 1821 Mohammad Murad Beg destroyed the city and its inhabitants were removed to Kunduz. After Emir Abdur Rahman Khan annexed it in 1888 the town regained its former importance and became a considerable place of trade. In 1979 it became a base of Afghan mujahideen resisting the Soviet invasion, and Soviet forces took it in 1980 and made it one of their bases in Afghanistan.

Fayzabad is the capital of Badakhshan Province, with an estimated population of 85,477, mostly Tajiks, with Pashtun, Pamiri, Uzbek, Hazara and Turkmen communities. Eleven languages are spoken there, among them Dari, Pashto, Wakhi, Shughni and Uzbek. It is home to Badakhshan University and serves as the gateway to the Wakhan National Park in Wakhan District.
fayzulla-khodzhayev: Fayzulla Xoʻjayev (Fayzulla Ubaydulloyevich Xoʻjayev) was born in 1896 into a family of wealthy traders in the city of Bukhara, then part of the Emirate of Bukhara. His father sent him to Moscow in 1907, where he came to see the gap between European society and technology and the tradition-bound ways of his homeland. His father died in 1912. In 1916 he joined the Jadid movement of reformers and, with his father's fortune, founded the Young Bukharan Party.

In March 1918, after the Bolsheviks had established Soviet rule in Kokand, he led an attempt to form a Young Bukharan government with the Emir as a figurehead. For a few days it seemed to succeed, but in his later account he admitted that he and his fellow revolutionaries had been gullible and had underestimated the clergy and the forces loyal to the old regime. Thousands of Young Bukharan supporters were killed in the reaction. He escaped to Tashkent and was sentenced to death in his absence, returning only after the Red Army overthrew the Emir's administration on 2 September 1920.

After joining the Russian Communist Party in mid-1920, Xoʻjayev was appointed Chairman of the Council of People's Nazirs of the Bukharan People's Soviet Republic in September 1920. A Basmachi attempt on his life failed on 7 July 1922. Moscow temporarily recognised the republic as independent and sent an ambassador and advisers. The Soviet diplomat Alexander Barmine remembered him as small, wiry and full of energy, called the Lenin of the Uzbeks.

When Soviet Central Asia was reorganised, Xoʻjayev became Chair of the Revolutionary Committee of the Uzbek SSR on 5 December 1924 and Chair of its Council of People's Commissars on 17 February 1925. He opposed Joseph Stalin's heavy-handed control, particularly the cotton monoculture. From 1929 his influence was eclipsed by Akmal Ikramov, the First Secretary of the Uzbek party, and he was never elected to the Central Committee of the Soviet party.

In June 1937 Xoʻjayev was absent from the Uzbek party's Seventh Congress, was removed from office on 27 June and was arrested by 9 July. In March 1938 he and Ikramov were arraigned at the Trial of the Twenty-One in Moscow, each accusing the other of lying. He confessed to membership of a secret pan-Turkic society, Milli Ittikhad, and to opposing the division of Turkestan and the cotton policy. He was sentenced to death, executed on 13 March 1938 and buried at Kommunarka. He was rehabilitated officially in 1966 and remains a controversial figure in Uzbekistan, with few monuments; his father's house in Bukhara is a museum styled as the House of a Wealthy Local Merchant.
feargus-oconnor: O'Connor was born on 18 July 1796 at Connorville house in west County Cork, into a prominent Protestant family. His father, Roger O'Connor, and his uncle Arthur O'Connor were active in the United Irishmen, and his elder brother Francis became a general in Simón Bolívar's army. He studied law at Trinity College, Dublin, without taking a degree and was called to the Irish bar about 1820; his father disinherited him for taking the oath of allegiance this required. His first known speech, in 1822 at Enniskeen, denounced landlords and the Protestant clergy.

Elected for County Cork as a Repeal candidate, O'Connor entered Parliament as a follower of Daniel O'Connell but broke with him over his yielding to the Whigs. Unseated in 1835 for lacking the property qualification, he turned to the working men of the north of England, denouncing the Poor Law Amendment Act of 1834 and calling for manhood suffrage at huge meetings. The Northern Star, first published on 18 November 1837, soon became the most widely bought provincial newspaper in Britain, and his weekly front-page letter was often read aloud at meetings.

Leaders of the London Working Men's Association such as William Lovett disliked his confrontational style. O'Connor was no insurrectionist but favoured intimidating the authorities through monster meetings and mass petitions. After the petition of 1839 was rejected and the Newport Rising followed, in which he took no part, he was sentenced in May 1840 to 18 months in York Castle.

His Land Plan, set out in A Practical Work on the Management of Small Farms, settled working families on plots of two to four acres; £112,100 was subscribed, six estates were bought, and the first, Heronsgate, renamed O'Connorsville, opened in May 1847. A House of Commons inquiry reported in June 1848 that the company could not meet its shareholders' expectations and that its books had been imperfectly kept.

Under strain, O'Connor drank heavily, and in 1849 the Commons rejected the Charter by 222 votes to 17. He quarrelled with Ernest Jones, Julian Harney and Thomas Clark, and after the assaults of June 1852 he was kept in Dr Thomas Harrington Tuke's asylum in Chiswick until 1854. He died at Notting Hill Gate on 30 August 1855 and was buried at Kensal Green. Early historians of Chartism blamed his egotism for much of its failure, but Dorothy Thompson called him the movement's most well-loved man, and more recent historians have judged him more favourably.
february-revolution: The revolution took place when Russia still used the Julian calendar, which is why it is called the February Revolution although its events fell in March by the Gregorian calendar. Historians disagree about its main causes. Liberal historians stress the turmoil of the First World War, Marxists the inevitability of change, and revisionists land disputes after the end of serfdom. Long-term causes included the failure of Imperial Russia to modernise its structures while keeping loyalty to the autocracy, and the Revolution of 1905.

By early 1917 the Russian army had suffered about 9.15 million casualties, including some 1.7 million killed, and desertion ran at around 34,000 a month. The authority of Nicholas II was further weakened by the assassination of Rasputin on 30 December 1916 and by a rapid turnover of ministers.

Workers at the Putilov Factory went on strike on 18 February Old Style (3 March New Style). On 23 February Old Style (8 March) they were joined by women marking International Women's Day and protesting against food rationing. By the next day nearly 200,000 protesters were in the streets, and by 25 February some 250,000 were on strike and nearly all industrial enterprises in Petrograd had shut down.

Many soldiers of the garrison, largely draftees of low morale, joined the crowds, and on 27 February Old Style most of it sided with the revolutionaries. Duma members formed a Provisional Committee, and the socialist parties re-established the Petrograd Soviet. The committee took control of the railway telegraph and forbade trains to travel within 265 kilometres of Petrograd, which made it very hard for loyal troops to reach the capital. Nicholas II, stranded on his train at Pskov, was forced to abdicate on the advice of his generals. Over 1,300 people were killed.

A Provisional Government, at first under Georgy Lvov, replaced the Council of Ministers. Its manifesto promised civil and political rights and a Constituent Assembly but did not address the war or land. It shared authority with the Petrograd Soviet in an arrangement known as dual power; the Soviet had more practical power because it controlled the workers and soldiers.

After the July Days, in which the government killed hundreds of protesters, Alexander Kerensky became head of the government. He could not resolve food shortages and mass unemployment and kept Russia in the war. These failures led to the October Revolution by the Bolsheviks, and the collapse of authority contributed to the Russian Civil War and the formation of the Soviet Union.
fecamp-abbey: Around 658 Waningus, a Merovingian count, founded a nunnery at Fécamp, which the Vikings destroyed in 841; a second convent he founded in 660, near the site of the Precious Relic, was destroyed in 842. In the 990s Richard I of Normandy, who was born at Fécamp, the main ducal residence, began to rebuild the monastery as his burial place. In 1001 Richard II invited William of Volpiano to renew its life under the Cluniac Benedictine rule as part of a wider strengthening of Norman monasticism, and William's successor, John of Fécamp, was also influential.

The abbey answered to no Norman bishop, only to the Pope, and it played a part in the Norman conquest of England. Edward the Confessor granted it the royal minster church of Steyning, with its manors and port, in gratitude to his Norman protectors during his exile; King Cnut had already given it land around Rye, Winchelsea and Hastings. In 1052 Godwin, Earl of Wessex, expelled the monks from Steyning, and his son Harold kept it. William the Conqueror swore on a knife to recover it, gained a ship from the abbey, and after his victory at Hastings returned Steyning, which the abbey held until the 15th century. The abbey also gave William Remigius de Fécamp, the first Bishop of Lincoln.

The abbey church of the Holy Trinity was built between 1175 and 1220 of cream-coloured Caen stone, and under the Plantagenets the scriptorium produced many illuminated manuscripts. Henry II of England had Richard I and Richard II reburied in the church's southern transept in 1162, and William of Volpiano lies in one of the northern chapels.
