When French, Danish and Norwegian researchers opened the dukes' lead boxes in February 2016, radiocarbon dating showed that neither skeleton could be theirs: one dated from the third century BCE, the other from the eighth century CE. The abbey is known as the first producer of bénédictine, a herbal liqueur based on brandy.
federal-charter-of-1291: The Federal Charter, or Letter of Alliance, known in German as the Bundesbrief, records an Eternal Alliance of the League of the Three Forest Cantons, a union of Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden in what is now central Switzerland. It is written in Latin and refers to an earlier pact that is lost or was never written down. It is one of a series of alliances from which the Old Swiss Confederacy emerged.

It was probably meant to ensure legal certainty after the death of Rudolf I of Habsburg on 15 July 1291. The parties are called conspirati and coniurati, traditionally translated in German as Eidgenossen and in English as confederates.

The first two paragraphs commit all three communities to the joint defence of the three valleys. The rest of the Charter concerns judicial matters. It calls for arbitration in conflicts, rejects foreign judges, sets the death penalty for murderers and exile for arsonists, and commands obedience to judges and their verdicts.

Its authenticity was once disputed as a supposed modern forgery, but historians now agree that it is a product of the 14th century. In 1991 the parchment was radiocarbon dated at ETH to between 1252 and 1312 with a probability of 85 per cent, or alternatively to between 1352 and 1385 with a probability of 15 per cent. It is therefore not a forgery tied to the founding of the federal state in 1848 and is better seen against Chapter 15 of the Golden Bull of 1356, in which Charles IV outlawed leagues and conspiracies such as the city alliances. At the time agreements were mostly verbal, and documents drawn up later might have their contents or dates changed to suit current purposes.

The Charter became important in Swiss historiography only in the late 19th century. Before then the foundation of the Confederacy was traditionally dated to 1307, following Aegidius Tschudi, the year inscribed on the Tell Monument commissioned in 1895. The idea of 1291 as the founding date was first put forward in a report of the Federal Department of Home Affairs of 21 November 1889, for a combined celebration in 1891. A national holiday on 1 August was suggested in 1899 and made official only in 1994.
A Federal Charter Archive designed by Joseph Beeler was opened in Schwyz in 1936, and is now the Museum of the Swiss Charters of Confederation, where the Charter is exhibited.
federal-convention-german-confederation: The German Confederation and its diet were created by the Congress of Vienna in 1815, after the defeat of Napoleon, to give Germany a new constitutional structure following the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire eight years before. Because the princes of the German states wished to keep their sovereignty, the confederation was a loose union of independent monarchies that also included four free cities. Its founding act, the German Federal Act of 8 June 1815, was part of the treaty of the Congress of Vienna, and the convention met once a week from 5 November 1816.

The convention had two bodies, an inner council and a plenary session. Its members were not elected but appointed by the state governments or princes. The inner council had 17 curias: one seat each for the 11 larger states, five for the 24 smaller states and one for the four free cities. It set the legislative agenda and decided which matters went to the plenary, which had 69 seats distributed roughly by size and dealt above all with constitutional changes. Both bodies came to require unanimous consent, the inner council from 1822.

Decisions of the convention bound the member states, but each state carried them out itself and kept full sovereignty over customs, police and the military. Until 1848 and again after 1851 the convention was the main instrument of the reactionary forces of Germany against democracy, liberalism and nationalism. In 1835/36, for example, it decreed rules of censorship that banned the works of Heinrich Heine and other authors in every state of the confederation.

The March Revolution of 1848 brought a rival in the National Assembly, which met in Frankfurt from 18 May 1848 and on 29 June elected Archduke John of Austria Regent of the Provisional Central Power. At noon on 12 July the convention handed its responsibilities to the Regent and dissolved itself. After the Punctuation of Olmütz of 30 November 1850 forced Prussia to drop its plans, the old diet reopened in the Thurn and Taxis Palace on 30 May 1851. It was dissolved for good after the Austro-Prussian War, under the Peace of Prague of 23 August 1866.
federal-republic-of-central-america: Spain conquered Central America in the 16th century, and in 1568 the region became the Captaincy General of Guatemala. After Napoleon overthrew Ferdinand VII in 1808, some criollo leaders wanted greater autonomy, and rebellions in San Salvador in November 1811 and 1814, in Nicaragua in December 1811 and in Guatemala in 1813 were defeated by loyalist forces. The captaincy declared independence from Spain in September 1821 and was annexed by the First Mexican Empire in January 1822. It regained independence on 1 July 1823 as the United Provinces of Central America, renamed the Federal Republic of Central America when its constitution, modelled on that of the United States, was adopted on 22 November 1824.

The republic had five states, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua, with a Federal District from 1835 to 1839. Guatemala City was the capital until 1834, then San Salvador. Elections were indirect, in three rounds, and voting was compulsory. In the first presidential election, on 21 April 1825, no candidate won a majority, and the Federal Congress chose the liberal Manuel José Arce by 22 votes to 5. Arce then aligned with conservatives, and from 1827 to 1829 civil war divided his supporters from the liberals. Francisco Morazán led the liberals to victory, captured Guatemala City in April 1828 and was elected president in 1830. His government imprisoned or exiled many conservatives, confiscated property and expelled clergy who had backed them.

A second civil war ran from 1838 to 1840. Nicaragua seceded on 30 April 1838, Honduras on 26 October and Costa Rica on 15 November. On 17 April 1839 Guatemalan President Rafael Carrera decreed the republic dissolved, which the Federal Congress accepted on 14 July, and El Salvador declared independence on 30 January 1841. Historians have blamed the instability on the federal system and on economic troubles: exports were insufficient, the government could not repay foreign loans or collect taxes, and when Arce took office the treasury held 600 pesos.

In 1824 the population was 1,287,491, of whom 65 percent were indigenous and over half lived in Guatemala, which gave it the largest share of seats in the Federal Congress. Catholicism was the official religion, and public worship of others was allowed only from May 1832. Central American writers and politicians have since called for reunification, and attempts in the 19th and 20th centuries lasted at most a few months. All five states belong to the Central American Integration System.
federal-treaty: When the troops of the coalition against Napoleon entered Switzerland in 1813, the Act of Mediation imposed in 1803 lost its force. Ten of the nineteen cantons repealed it and founded a Confederate Convention in Zürich, and from February 1814 a new constitution was negotiated. Meanwhile reaction spread. The Bernese bourgeoisie seized power, abolished the sovereignty of Vaud and Aargau and annexed them back to Bern, the bourgeoisie also took power in Solothurn, Fribourg and Lucerne, and Schwyz, Nidwalden, Uri and Zug convened an Anti-Diet. By March 1814 the country stood on the brink of civil war.

During the Long Diet, from 6 April 1814 to 31 August 1815, envoys of the great powers insisted on the survival of the new cantons and threatened a forced mediation. A draft shaped under the influence of Ioannis Kapodistrias, Stratford Canning, Claude Marie Gustave de Damas and August Ernst von Steigentesch strengthened the military powers of the Confederacy, which the reactionary cantons, Bern above all, rejected. With a separate alliance and civil war again in prospect, the powers considered partitioning Switzerland, and the Diet came to terms. The treaty was adopted on 9 September 1814.

The treaty had 15 articles. It guaranteed the equal freedom of the cantons and mentioned civil rights only in the prohibition of subjects, the Untertanenverbot. Federal authority, much weaker than under the Act of Mediation, lay with the Diet, which met in turn at Zürich, Bern and Lucerne. The only competence of the Confederacy was common security through the army, and there was no longer a Swiss Landammann. Territorial disputes between cantons were to be settled by an arbitration court of the Congress of Vienna.

The treaty left open the question of a separate alliance, or Sonderbund, among cantons. That question led in 1847 to the Sonderbund War and in 1848 to the replacement of the Federal Treaty by the Federal Constitution, after the treaty had served for more than three decades as the constitution of the Restoration.
federal-war: The war arose from the Conservative Party's hold on government posts and land ownership and its refusal of reform, which drove the Liberals, known as the Federalists, to seek greater autonomy for the provinces. Social problems inherited from the struggle for independence, tensions among economic and political groups and a succession of armed risings in the countryside added to the strain. The immediate contest was for power between the conservative government of President Julián Castro, who had ousted José Tadeo Monagas in March 1858, and the liberal opposition led by Ezequiel Zamora.

On 20 February 1859 Lieutenant Colonel Tirso Salaverría occupied the military base at Coro and proclaimed a federation, the abolition of the death penalty, universal suffrage and political pluralism, and fighting broke out across the country. Zamora won the first major battle, at Santa Inés on 10 December 1859, and secured the Llanos, but he was killed by a sniper on 10 January 1860 while besieging San Carlos, and the siege was abandoned.

His brother-in-law, General Juan Crisóstomo Falcón, took command. On 17 February 1860 government troops under General León de Febres Cordero defeated the Federalists at Coplé, though they withdrew in good order. Falcón turned to guerrilla warfare and sought help in Colombia, Haiti and the Caribbean, returning in July 1861. Peace talks in December 1861 failed, and in 1862 the Federalists won at Pureche, El Corubo, Mapararí and Buchivacoa. Weakened by thousands of desertions, the government agreed to negotiate after the Federalists surrounded Coro in April 1863.

On 22 May 1863 President José Antonio Páez and Falcón signed the Treaty of Coche, named after an estate near Caracas, and Falcón became president on 15 June 1863. Around a hundred thousand people had died in the fighting or of hunger and disease, in a country of just over a million, making it the bloodiest civil war in Venezuela since independence. The death penalty was abolished and the central government's army reduced, while fires had cut farming in the plains and foreign trade declined.
federalism: The words federalism and confederalism share a root in the Latin foedus, meaning treaty, pact or covenant. Until the late eighteenth century they meant much the same thing, a simple league among sovereign states based on a treaty. The first forms of federalism were alliances between tribes or city states in ancient times, such as the Delian League. The Achaean League of Hellenistic Greece is considered an early ancestor, since cities then banded together even at the cost of surrendering part of their sovereignty. Johannes Althusius is considered the father of modern federalism, along with Montesquieu, and in the modern era it was first adopted by a union of states of the Old Swiss Confederacy from the mid-14th century.

Federalism combines a general level of government with a regional level of sub-unit governments, such as states, provinces or cantons, and divides the powers of governing between them. It differs from confederalism, where the central government is subordinate to the regional states, and from the unitary state, where the regional level is subordinate to the centre. James Madison called the new United States Constitution neither a national nor a federal constitution, but a composition of both, and in the nineteenth century federalism in the United States came to mean this new compound form alone.

In a federation the division of power is usually set out in the constitution, and the right of the component states to self-government is entrenched. Foreign policy and defence are almost always federal powers. An upper house often represents the component states, as in the Senate of the United States and Australia and the German Bundesrat. Constitutional amendment often requires the consent of the states.

Proponents have argued that the checks and the sharing of power in a federation reduce threats from within and abroad and allow a state to be both large and diverse. The word has opposite senses on two continents. In the United States the Federalists of the founding era wanted a stronger central government, while in Europe federalists favour a common government above the nations, an idea that grew out of post-war Europe and Winston Churchill's speech in Zürich in 1946. Anarchists such as Pierre-Joseph Proudhon envisaged a stateless federalism built from the bottom up.
federated-states-of-micronesia: The Federated States of Micronesia consists of around 607 islands spread across the western Pacific just north of the equator, with a combined land area of about 702 square kilometres. It includes most of the Caroline Islands, excluding Palau. Each of the four states, Yap, Chuuk (called Truk until January 1990), Pohnpei (Ponape until November 1984) and Kosrae (formerly Kusaie), is centred on one or more main volcanic islands, and all but Kosrae include numerous outlying atolls. The climate is warm, humid and rainy all year round.

The ancestors of the Micronesians settled more than four thousand years ago. A decentralised chieftain-based system eventually evolved into a more centralised economic and religious culture centred on Yap. On Pohnpei, Nan Madol, a series of small artificial islands linked by canals and often called the Venice of the Pacific, was the ceremonial and political seat of the Saudeleur dynasty, which united the island's estimated 25,000 people from about 500 CE until the centralised system collapsed around 1500.

The Portuguese and then the Spanish reached the Carolines in the sixteenth century, and Spain incorporated the archipelago into the Spanish East Indies. When Germany began extending its influence in the 1870s, Pope Leo XIII was asked in the Carolines Question of 1885 to decide between the two powers, and he confirmed Spanish authority while giving Germany free access. After its defeat in the Spanish–American War, Spain sold the archipelago to Germany in 1899. Japan captured it in the First World War and administered it under a League of Nations mandate.

In February 1944 the United States Navy attacked the Japanese base at Truk Lagoon in Operation Hailstone, sinking numerous ships and destroying hundreds of aircraft. In 1947 the islands became part of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, administered by the United States. On 10 May 1979 four districts ratified a constitution, and the Compact of Free Association with the United States entered into force on 3 November 1986. The United Nations ended the trusteeship in 1990.

The capital is Palikir on Pohnpei, and the largest city is Weno in the Chuuk Lagoon. English is the official language of the federation, and 17 other languages are spoken. Yap is known for its stone money, large calcite disks called Rai stones, and Nan Madol is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
federation-of-rhodesia-and-nyasaland: In 1929 the Hilton Young Commission concluded that the interests of Nyasaland and Northern Rhodesia lay with each other and with the self-governing colony of Southern Rhodesia. In 1938 the Bledisloe Commission stopped short of recommending federation and advised an inter-territorial council instead; the Central African Council, with consultative powers only, was set up in 1945.

In 1950 the British government decided to examine closer union again, and conferences followed in 1951. They were arduous, because Southern Rhodesia and the northern territories had very different traditions in their treatment of black Africans. Sir Andrew Cohen of the Colonial Office was one of the central architects of the agreement. The Southern Rhodesian prime minister, Sir Godfrey Huggins, preferred a unitary state, but Britain opposed it because Southern Rhodesia's large European population would then dominate the franchise. In a referendum on 9 April 1953 a little more than 25,000 white Southern Rhodesians voted for federation and nearly 15,000 against; a majority of black Africans in all three territories were resolutely against it.

The Federation was established on 1 August 1953 with a Governor-General as the Queen's representative. It had a unicameral Federal Assembly, which included an African Affairs Board to safeguard African interests, and a Supreme Court inaugurated in 1955. Huggins, created Viscount Malvern in 1955, was prime minister until 1956 and was followed by Sir Roy Welensky of Northern Rhodesia. The Federation's economy grew, and the Kariba hydro-electric station was announced in 1955, but the average income of a European remained about ten times that of an African in the cash economy. The European population of Southern Rhodesia rose from 135,000 before federation to 223,000 by its end.

African opposition grew. Hastings Banda returned to Nyasaland in July 1958 and Kenneth Kaunda became leader of the Zambian African National Congress in October; the Congress was banned in March 1959 and Kaunda imprisoned for nine months. After unrest in Nyasaland in early 1959 the authorities declared a state of emergency and arrested Banda and other leaders. A commission led by Viscount Monckton was appointed to advise on the future of the Federation, and by 1962 Britain and the federal government had agreed that Nyasaland might secede; Northern Rhodesia was given the same status a year later.

The Victoria Falls Conference met in 1963, partly to save the Federation and partly to dissolve it, which was done formally on 31 December 1963. Its assets went to the territorial governments, and Southern Rhodesia received the great majority of them, including those of the federal army. Nyasaland became independent as Malawi in July 1964 under Banda, and Northern Rhodesia as Zambia in October under Kaunda. On 11 November 1965 the government of Prime Minister Ian Smith proclaimed Southern Rhodesia's unilateral independence from the United Kingdom.
federico-da-montefeltro: Federico was born on 7 June 1422 at the Castello di Petroia in Gubbio. Guidantonio da Montefeltro, lord of Urbino, Gubbio and Casteldurante, acknowledged him as his illegitimate son, and Pope Martin V legitimised him two years later. Persistent rumours held that he was in fact Guidantonio's grandson, born to the illegitimate daughter Aura and passed off as his own; Pope Pius II recorded the rumour in Federico's lifetime. After the Peace of Ferrara in 1433 he lived as a hostage in Venice and Mantua. In 1437 Emperor Sigismund knighted him, and he married Gentile Brancaleoni. At sixteen he began a career as a condottiero under Niccolò Piccinino.

On 22 July 1444 his half-brother Oddantonio, recently made Duke of Urbino by Pope Eugene IV, was assassinated in a conspiracy. Federico's part in the plot has never been firmly established, and he seized the city. Since he never fought for free, he served Francesco I Sforza, Florence and later the papacy. In 1450 he lost his right eye in a joust. Pope Pius II made him Gonfaloniere of the Holy Roman Church, and in 1462 he defeated Sigismondo Pandolfo Malatesta at the Cesano river. In 1474 Pope Sixtus IV gave him the title of Duke of Urbino and married his nephew Giovanni Della Rovere to Federico's daughter Giovanna.

Federico then fought against Florence, and in 1478 he was involved in the Pazzi conspiracy and attacked the territory of Lorenzo de' Medici. He commissioned a great library, perhaps the largest in Italy after the Vatican's, with a team of scribes, and assembled a humanistic court in the Ducal Palace, designed by Luciano Laurana and Francesco di Giorgio Martini. His interests were the classics, especially history and philosophy.

His second wife Battista Sforza died of pneumonia at the age of 25 after the birth of their seventh child, and he spent much of his time afterwards in the palace at Urbino. In 1482 he was called to command the army of Ercole I of Ferrara against Venice, but was struck by fever and died at Ferrara on 10 September. His son Guidobaldo, who married Elisabetta Gonzaga, died in 1508, and the duchy then passed through Giovanna to the Della Rovere family. Commentators note his care for his soldiers, which explains their loyalty. Edward IV of England made him a Knight of the Garter.
federico-ii-gonzaga-duke-of-mantua: Federico was the son of Francesco II Gonzaga, Marquess of Mantua, and Isabella d'Este. Because of the turbulent politics of the time, he spent three years from the age of ten as a hostage in Rome under Pope Julius II, and from 1515 to 1517 he was the hostage of King Francis I of France, to ensure Gonzaga help in Italy. In these situations he served as a diplomatic representative of his family and gained courtly experience. In Rome he was tutored by Ausonio and acquired a taste for festivals and parties.

On 3 April 1519 Federico succeeded his father as Marquis of Mantua, at first under the regency of his mother and his uncles Sigismondo and Giovanni Gonzaga. He received imperial investiture from Charles V on 7 April 1521. In July 1521 Pope Leo X named him Captain General of the Church, and he fought the French at Parma in 1521 and at Piacenza in 1522.

His marriages served his wish to gain Montferrat. He signed a contract with Maria Palaeologina, heir to the marquisate, but in 1528 Pope Clement VII voided it in exchange for two prisoners. He then contracted to marry Julia of Aragon, and in 1530 was granted the ducal title. When Boniface, Marquis of Montferrat, died after a fall from a horse, Federico paid Charles 50,000 ducats to annul the Aragon contract and pressed the pope to restore the earlier agreement. After Maria's death he married her sister Margaret on 3 October 1531. When the last legitimate male Palaiologos heir died, Montferrat passed to the Gonzaga, who held it until the 18th century.

Like his parents, Federico was a patron of the arts, and his years in Rome left him an admirer of Roman art. He sent agents to Rome and Venice to buy works, and in 1527, during the sack of Rome, wrote to the imperial commander Fabrizio Maramaldo asking whether looted statues or busts were for sale. He acquired several works by Correggio, bought and commissioned paintings from Titian, and had his portrait painted by Titian and by Raphael. Giulio Romano spent sixteen years as his court artist. A notarial contract of 1535 shows Flemish paintings entering Italy through his court.

Federico suffered long from syphilis, like his father, and died in 1540 at his villa at Marmirolo. His son Francesco briefly held the title of duke before dying in his teens, and the second son, Guglielmo, became the third duke and Duke of Montferrat and continued the line.
federico-ponce-vaides: Juan Federico Ponce Vaides was born on 27 March 1889 into a wealthy upper-class family in Cobán, Alta Verapaz, the son of Mariano Ponce Contreras and Victoria Vaides Arrivillaga. Under the government of Manuel Estrada Cabrera he took part in the National Campaign of 1906 against Honduras and El Salvador, and he afterwards served as commander and political leader in several departments. After Cabrera's fall in 1920 his brother was executed during a popular uprising.

Jorge Ubico, dictator of Guatemala since 1931, was forced to resign on 1 July 1944 by a popular pro-democracy movement and named three generals, Ponce Vaides, Eduardo Villagran Ariza and Buenaventura Pineda, to a junta to succeed him. On 3 July Ponce Vaides forced the Guatemalan congress at gunpoint to appoint him interim president. He pledged free elections while suppressing the protests: freedom of the press was suspended, arbitrary detentions continued and memorial services for slain revolutionaries were prohibited.

Protest spread to the countryside, the police were used to intimidate the indigenous population ahead of the election, and progressive officers began to plot a coup. After Alejandro Cordova, editor of the opposition newspaper El Imparcial, was assassinated on 1 October 1944, the plotters reached out to the protest leaders. Ponce Vaides tried to exploit Ladino fears, paying thousands of Indigenous peasants to march in Guatemala City in his support and promising them land if they backed Ubico's Liberal party.

On 19 October a small group of officers led by Francisco Javier Arana and Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán launched a coup from within the army, joined the next day by other army factions and civilians. The fighting went against them at first, but unionists and students swelled their ranks, the police and loyal troops were subdued, and Ponce Vaides surrendered unconditionally.

Ponce Vaides and Ubico were allowed to leave the country safely. A new three-man junta of Árbenz, Arana and Jorge Toriello promised free elections to the presidency, the congress and a constituent assembly. The presidential election was won by Juan José Arévalo, whose social and economic reforms began the Guatemalan Revolution. Ponce Vaides died on 29 January 1956.
federico-tinoco-granados: José Federico Alberto de Jesús Tinoco Granados was born on 21 November 1868 in San José, Costa Rica. On 5 June 1898 he married María de las Mercedes Elodia Fernández Le Cappellain in San José; the couple had no children. After a career in the army he was appointed Minister of War and Navy in the cabinet of President Alfredo González Flores, the post from which he moved against the government.

On 27 January 1917 Tinoco and his brother José Joaquín seized power. The new regime at first had wide support in Costa Rica, but it became a repressive military dictatorship that tried to crush all opposition and allowed only one party. Tinoco declared war on the German Empire in May 1918, during World War I, yet the United States still withheld recognition. Without US financial support his government printed more money, which brought inflation and financial chaos.

Popular opposition, which had begun on 13 June 1919, quickly came to a head, and by early August his brother had been assassinated. On 13 August 1919 Tinoco resigned in favour of Juan Bautista Quirós and left for exile in Europe. His government was the last military dictatorship in Costa Rican history.

Tinoco died in Paris on 7 September 1931, but the dispute over the legitimacy of his government outlived him. Because of it Costa Rica was not a party to the Treaty of Versailles, and so never ended the state of war with Germany that Tinoco had declared. Costa Rica issued a new declaration of war on Germany on 11 December 1941, although technically it had been at war since 1918, and the state of war ended only after World War II, when Costa Rica was included in the Potsdam Agreement.
federsee: The lake lies just north of Bad Buchau and is ringed by the town and the villages of Moosburg, Alleshausen, Seekirch, Tiefenbach and Oggelshausen. The surrounding moorland, partly overgrown with reeds, covers 33 square kilometres and is fed by groundwater. The lake itself is shallow, no more than 2 metres deep at its deepest point. Federsee means feather lake, and its outline resembles a feather, though locally some trace the name to the feathers found on its surface; the most probable origin is the Celtic word pheder, meaning marsh, which would describe the lake and its landscape.

Around 265 bird species live near the lake, 107 of which breed there, among them about 200 breeding pairs of whinchats and 18 of marsh harriers, both endangered. The lake and its surroundings are a Special Protection Area under the European Union's directives on wild birds and habitats, and part of the Natura 2000 network.

Because belts of reed and bog enclose the lake, it cannot be reached directly on foot. A wooden boardwalk about 1.5 kilometres long runs from near the Federsee Museum, which displays the Stone Age and Bronze Age finds of the basin, through the reeds to an observation platform and a boat rental at open water, and other piers lead into the protected area. Tiefenbach is the village closest to the water, and when the lake freezes in winter it is possible to walk across the ice from Tiefenbach to Bad Buchau.
feidlimid-mac-crimthainn: Feidlimid belonged to the Cenél Fíngin sept of the Eóganacht Chaisil branch of the Eóganachta and took the kingship of Munster in 820. He was counted among the Céli Dé and as abbot of Cork and Clonfert. In 823, together with Bishop Artrí mac Conchobar of Armagh, he had the Law of St. Patrick established in Munster and sacked the monastery of Gailline of the Britons in modern County Offaly. In 827 he held the first of several royal meetings with Conchobar mac Donnchada of the Southern Uí Néill, King of Tara.

His campaigns struck at kingdoms and churches alike. In 830 he probably burned Fore Abbey and destroyed the Uí Briúin in southern Galway, and in 831 and 832 he led an army of Leinster and Munster into East Meath as far as Slane and burned Clonmacnoise. In 833 he burned it again, together with the Clann Cholmáin monastery of Durrow. In 836 he took the oratory of Kildare against Forindam, abbot of Armagh, and imprisoned him with the congregation of Patrick, and in 837 he took the abbacy of Cork.

After a great royal meeting in 838 with Niall Caille mac Áeda, King of the Northern Uí Néill, the Annals of Inisfallen, which probably follow Munster tradition, report that Feidlimid became full king of Ireland that day and occupied the abbot's chair of Clonfert. In 840, probably the height of his power, he ravaged Mide and Brega and rested at Tara, where he seized Gormlaith, daughter of Murchad, king of Laigin.

In 841 Niall Caille defeated him at Magh-Ochtar in Kildare, apparently by surprise; a verse tells how Feidlimid's crozier was abandoned in the blackthorns and taken by Niall by right of victory. He seems never to have recovered and died in 847.

The Annals of Ulster give no cause of death, but most other sources blame St. Kieran, patron saint of Clonmacnoise, avenging the plunder of his monastery. The Annals of Clonmacnoise tell that the saint appeared to the king in his bed and struck him in the belly with his staff, bringing on the illness that killed him. The same annals add that, for all his love of plunder, some numbered him among the scribes and anchorites of Ireland.
felice-baciocchi: Felice Pasquale Baciocchi was born on 18 May 1762 in Ajaccio, the son of Francis, into a noble but poor Corsican family. He became a second lieutenant in the French army in 1778, a lieutenant in 1788 and a captain in 1794. Around 5 May 1797 he married Elisa Maria Bonaparte, Napoleon's younger sister, in Marseille.

In November 1800 Baciocchi was appointed secretary to the ambassador to the Spanish royal court and moved to Madrid, while his wife remained in France. He was promoted colonel in 1802, brigadier general in 1804 and major general in 1809, was made a senator in 1804 and an imperial prince in 1805, and received the Grand Eagle of the Legion of Honour on 6 March 1805.

Thanks to his brother-in-law's conquests he became Prince of Lucca and Piombino by right of his wife, jure uxoris, but the sovereign power was exercised by Elisa. He accepted her infidelities with equanimity and was content with a role between that of an aide-de-camp and a prince consort. An avid amateur violinist, he studied for ten years with the virtuoso Niccolò Paganini while living in Lucca and Florence, during which time Elisa and Paganini were having a romantic affair.
After the collapse of Napoleon's empire Baciocchi retired from public life with Elisa, who died in 1820. He spent his last years in Bologna and died there on 27 April 1841.

The couple had five children, of whom only two reached adulthood. Elisa Napoléone Baciocchi (1806–1869) married Philippe, Comte Camerata-Passionei de Mazzoleni, and had one son, Charles Félix Jean-Baptiste Camerata-Passionei di Mazzoleni. Frédéric Napoléon Baciocchi lived from 1813 to 1833. Felix Napoléon, Napoléon and Jérôme Charles died as infants.
felipe-guaman-poma-de-ayala: Guaman Poma came from a noble family of the Yarowilca dynasty of Guánuco in the northern Peruvian cordillera, which was Indigenous but not Inca. He spoke several Quechua and Aru dialects fluently and probably learned Spanish as a child or adolescent, though without a perfect grasp of its grammar. In his manuscript of 1615 he called himself eighty years old, from which many deduce a birth around 1535, but the figure may be a metaphor for old age, and other references suggest 1550 or soon after. He spent most of his life in or near Huamanga.

He served as an interpreter for the priest Cristóbal de Albornoz and in the late 1580s and early 1590s assisted Friar Martín de Murúa. From the late 1590s he sued to recover land and title in the Chupas valley, lost, and in 1600 was stripped of all his property and banished from Huamanga.

Between 1600 and 1615 he wrote the Primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno, a 1,189-page work in Spanish with passages in Quechua, addressed to King Philip III of Spain. It is the longest sustained critique of Spanish colonial rule by an Indigenous subject of the period. It argued that the Spanish were foreign settlers in Peru: it is our country, he wrote, because God has given it to us. Of its pages, 398 are full-page drawings, and it includes a world map in the medieval European style with Cusco at the centre.

He proposed a good government drawing on Inca social and economic structures, European technology and Christian theology, and asked the king to appoint Indians to authority. He rejected Spanish rule but not the Spanish king, whom he saw as God's representative and believed would not have allowed injustices had he known of them. The king never received the book.

A Getty Research Institute project of 2007 and 2008 proved that Murúa's Historia general del Piru includes illustrations by Guaman Poma, one of a team of artists. In his own work he attacked Murúa, drawing the friar striking an Indigenous woman at a loom. The manuscript has been in the Danish Royal Library since at least the early 1660s, and came to public notice in 1908 when the German scholar Richard Pietschmann found it. A critical transcription by John Murra and Rolena Adorno appeared in 1980, and a digital facsimile online in 2001.
felipe-santiago-salaverry: Felipe Santiago Salaverry del Solar was born in Lima and studied at the College of San Carlos there. When José de San Martín arrived in Peru in 1820, Salaverry left college against his father's wishes, made his way to Huaura Province and volunteered for the general's forces, who enlisted him as a cadet of the battalion of Numancia. He led the Peruvian cavalry at the battles of Junin and Ayacucho, which helped secure the independence of Peru, and after the republic was founded he rose rapidly, becoming General Inspector of the Peruvian Army at twenty-eight.

When the garrison of Callao revolted against President Luis Orbegoso in January 1835 and declared for La Fuente, Salaverry defeated the insurgents and was made governor of the fortress. On 23 February he rose in arms against the government himself. Orbegoso abandoned Lima, and Salaverry occupied the capital and proclaimed himself Supreme Chief of the Republic on 25 February. Within a few months he held the south, while Orbegoso withdrew with a small force to the northern provinces.

A decree of Salaverry made the import of slaves from other Latin American countries legal again; the line that no slave should enter Peru without becoming free was taken out of the constitution in 1839. Orbegoso meanwhile concluded a treaty with Andrés Santa Cruz, leader of Bolivia, giving him a third of Peru, and the Bolivian army soon invaded.

Salaverry fell back on Arequipa and won the Battle of Uchumayo on 4 February 1836, but three days later his forces were routed at Socabaya, a district of the city. He wandered for several days trying to reach the Peruvian Navy at Islay before General Miller captured him and delivered him to Santa Cruz, who ordered the execution of Salaverry and his general staff. He was shot at Arequipa. The field jacket he wore at his execution is shown at the Peruvian Museum of Gold at Monterrico.
felix-and-regula: According to the legend, Felix and his sister Regula belonged to the Theban Legion under Saint Maurice, stationed at Agaunum in the Valais. When the legion refused to sacrifice to Emperor Maximian and was ordered to be executed, the siblings fled by way of Glarus to Zürich, then called Turicum, where they were caught, tried and beheaded with their servant Exuperantius.

The legend tells that after their beheading they stood up, picked up their own heads, walked forty paces uphill and prayed before lying down in death, and that they were buried where they lay, on the hill where the Grossmünster now stands. The story was said to have been revealed in a dream to a monk named Florentius in the 8th century.

In the 9th century a small monastery stood on the spot, outside the settlement on the left bank of the Limmat. The Grossmünster was built over the graves from about 1100, and the Wasserkirche on the place of execution. From the 13th century the saints appeared on the city's seals and coins. On their feast day, 11 September, their relics were carried in procession between the Grossmünster and the Fraumünster, whose communities competed for them, and the pilgrims they drew made Zürich the most important pilgrimage site in the bishopric of Konstanz.

The feast became the national holiday of the early modern Republic of Zürich, and the Knabenschiessen shooting competition, begun in 1889, grew from it. Felix and Regula are saints of both the Roman Catholic and the Coptic Orthodox churches.

When Huldrych Zwingli dissolved the monasteries in 1524, the graves were opened, and the accounts of what followed differ. The Protestant theologian Heinrich Bullinger wrote that the graves held only a few bone fragments, which were buried in the common graveyard. Catholics held that a man of Uri rescued the relics and carried them to Andermatt, where two skulls are still shown; the remaining relics returned to Zürich in 1950, to the new Catholic church of St. Felix und Regula.

Radiocarbon dating found one skull medieval and the other made of fragments of two skulls, one medieval and one possibly Roman. Many modern historians regard the Theban Legion as fictitious, while others hold that evidence places it in Switzerland at the time.
felix-dzerzhinsky: Felix Edmundovich Dzerzhinsky was born on 11 September 1877 on the Ozhyemblovo estate near Ivyanets, in the Minsk Governorate of Russian Poland, now Belarus, to Polish parents of old noble descent. His father, a teacher, died of tuberculosis in 1882. He attended the Vilnius Gymnasium from 1887 and was expelled shortly before graduating for revolutionary activity. In 1895 he had joined a Marxist group, and he later helped found the Social Democracy of the Kingdom of Poland and Lithuania, which took the position of Rosa Luxemburg on the right of nations to self-determination.

He was arrested for the first time in 1897 and served almost a year in Kaunas prison. Exiled to Siberia several times, he escaped every time, and he worked for his party in Berlin, where he met Luxemburg. After the failed Revolution of 1905 he was jailed again. The police found him at the end of 1912, and he spent four and a half years in prison, where Russian guards beat him, disfiguring his jaw and mouth. The February Revolution of 1917 freed him from Butyrka prison.

He joined the Bolsheviks, entered the Central Committee in July 1917 and took part in the October Revolution. On 20 December 1917 the Council of People's Commissars established the Cheka, with Dzerzhinsky as its director. It became notorious for mass summary executions, and tens of thousands of political opponents and saboteurs were shot without trial in prison basements and public places during the Red Terror. Dzerzhinsky said, We represent in ourselves organized terror. In 1922 the Cheka became the GPU and in 1923 the OGPU, with Dzerzhinsky still at its head.

Dzerzhinsky died of a heart attack on 20 July 1926, immediately after a two-hour speech denouncing the United Opposition of Leon Trotsky, Grigory Zinoviev and Lev Kamenev. He was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis and succeeded at the OGPU by Vyacheslav Menzhinsky. Chekists remembered him as a hero of the revolution, and many places in the Soviet Union were named after him, while critics saw him as a symbol of repression and brutality. The iron statue sculpted by Yevgeny Vuchetich in 1958 stood on Lubyanka Square near the KGB headquarters, known as Iron Felix. The Moscow Soviet had it removed in August 1991 after the failed coup attempt.
felix-eboue: Adolphe Sylvestre Félix Éboué was born on 26 December 1884 in Cayenne, French Guiana, the grandson of slaves and the fourth of five brothers. His father, Yves Urbain Éboué, was a gold prospector, and his mother, Marie Josephine Aurélie Léveillé, a shop owner born in Roura, raised her sons in the Guiana Créole tradition. A scholarship took him to secondary school in Bordeaux, where he captained the school football team on trips to Belgium and England. In 1908 he graduated in administrative law from the École nationale de la France d'Outre-Mer in Paris.

Éboué served for twenty years as a colonial administrator in Oubangui-Chari, and then in Martinique. A Socialist and a Freemason, he was made acting governor of Guadeloupe in 1936 under the Popular Front government, the first man of black African descent appointed to so senior a post anywhere in the French colonies. Soon in conflict with the local elite, he left after two years and arrived in Fort Lamy as Governor of Chad on 4 January 1939. His acceptance of de Gaulle's authority in August 1940 gave the Free French movement a territorial base from which to exercise sovereignty and organise military forces.

As governor of French Equatorial Africa from 1940 to 1944 he published The New Indigenous Policy for French Equatorial Africa, which called for respect for African traditions, support for traditional leaders, the development of existing social structures and better working conditions. It served as a basis for the Brazzaville Conference of French colonial governors in 1944. He classed 200 educated Africans as notable évolués and reduced their taxes, and he placed some Gabonese civil servants in positions of authority.

Éboué married Eugénie Tell, and in 1946 their daughter Ginette married Léopold Sédar Senghor, the poet and later president of independent Senegal. He died of a stroke in Cairo on 17 May 1944, and in 1949 his remains were reburied in the Panthéon in Paris, which made him the first black French man so honoured. He had received the Cross of the Liberation in 1941. A square in Paris, Place Félix-Éboué, and the Métro station Daumesnil Félix-Éboué bear his name, and in 2012 the main airport of Cayenne was renamed in his honour.
felix-gouin: Félix Gouin was born on 5 October 1884 at Peypin in the Bouches-du-Rhône, the son of school teachers. He studied law in Aix-en-Provence and became a member of the French Section of the Workers' International, the SFIO. In 1940 he was among the minority of parliamentarians who refused to grant full powers to Marshal Philippe Pétain. During the war he sat on the central committee that reconstituted the Human Rights League and co-founded the Brutus Network, a Socialist Resistance group.

In 1946 Gouin succeeded Charles de Gaulle as head of the French Provisional Government. His government, which held office from 26 January to 24 June 1946, included Francisque Gay and Maurice Thorez as vice presidents of the council, Georges Bidault as foreign minister and Ambroise Croizat as minister of labour and social security. Its tenure is arguably most notable for the first compulsory, amply funded retirement and workers' compensation laws in France's history. The 40-hour week and overtime pay were re-established, and works councils, the comités d'entreprise, were extended to firms with 50 workers.

In April 1946 the French Parliament adopted a statute abolishing the colonial legal status of France's four oldest colonies: Réunion, Guyane, Martinique and Guadeloupe. His time in office also saw a significant extension of the state's role in the economy, with electricity, gas, coal and the nine main insurance groups nationalised.
Gouin died on 25 October 1977. He was made a Grand Croix of the Légion d'honneur and received the Grand Decoration of Honour in Silver with Sash for Services to the Republic of Austria.
felix-houphouet-boigny: According to his official biography Houphouët-Boigny was probably born on 18 October 1905 in Yamoussoukro, into a family of hereditary chiefs of the Baoulé people; unofficial accounts place his birth up to seven years earlier. After the village chief Kouassi N'Go was murdered in 1910, he was named his successor, and his stepfather ruled as regent. In 1925 he began work as a doctor's aide at a hospital in Abidjan. At Abengourou he saw the mistreatment of African cocoa farmers by colonists, and in 1932 he led a movement of farmers against the large white landowners.

As chef de canton of Akouè he took charge of the family plantation and became one of Africa's richest farmers. On 3 September 1944 he founded the African Agricultural Union, which demanded better working conditions and the abolition of forced labour. Elected to the French National Assembly in 1945, he proposed a bill to abolish forced labour, adopted on 11 April 1946 as the Loi Houphouët-Boigny. In October 1946 he helped found the African Democratic Rally at Bamako and became its president. From 1956 he was a minister in the French government, the first African in so senior a post.

He became head of the government of Ivory Coast on 1 May 1959 and was elected unopposed president on 27 November 1960, after independence on 7 August 1960. The constitution he drafted gave great power to the executive. He kept the closest links with France, a policy he called Françafrique, and severed relations with the Soviet Union in 1969, restoring them in February 1986. His liberal economic laws of 1959 encouraged foreign investors, and the economy grew by 11 to 12 percent a year from 1960 to 1965.

From 1978 the fall in world prices of coffee and cocoa brought a serious decline. Houphouët-Boigny delayed naming a successor, and by 1990 Prime Minister Alassane Ouattara was running the country while the president was in hospital in France. He died of prostate cancer on 7 December 1993 and left no written will. A contest between Henri Konan Bédié, president of the National Assembly, and Ouattara followed, and Ouattara resigned as prime minister on 9 December. In 1989 he had created a peace prize sponsored by UNESCO. He also moved the capital from Abidjan to Yamoussoukro and built the Basilica of Our Lady of Peace there.
felix-manz: Felix Manz, also written Mantz, was born in Zürich, in the Old Swiss Confederacy, where his father was a canon of the Grossmünster church. Records of his education are scant, but there is evidence that he received a liberal education and had a thorough knowledge of Hebrew, Greek and Latin. He became a follower of Huldrych Zwingli after the reformer came to Zürich in 1519, and when Conrad Grebel joined the circle in 1521 the two men became friends.

Manz and Grebel came to question the mass, the ties between church and state, and the baptism of infants. After the Second Disputation of Zürich in 1523 they grew dissatisfied, believing that Zwingli had compromised his plans for reform with the city council. Several parents in their circle refused to have their children baptised. A public disputation with Zwingli was held on 17 January 1525, and the council declared Zwingli the victor.

On 18 January the council ordered the brethren to stop arguing and to have their children baptised within eight days. Three days later they gathered at the home of Manz and his mother, where the first baptisms of the Swiss Brethren took place, completing the break with Zwingli and the council. Manz used his languages to translate texts into the speech of the people and worked as an evangelist. He was arrested several times between 1525 and 1527, and was finally taken while preaching with George Blaurock in the Grüningen region and held in the Wellenburg prison in Zürich.

On 7 March 1526 the Zürich council had made adult rebaptism punishable by drowning, and Manz was the first to die under that edict. Zwingli and the council accused him of obstinately refusing to recede from his error. As he was led from the Wellenburg to a boat he preached to the crowd, while his mother and brother urged him to stand firm. His hands were bound behind his knees with a pole between them. His property was confiscated and he was buried in the St. Jakobs cemetery.

Manz left an eighteen-stanza hymn of praise, preserved in the Ausbund, a 16th-century hymn book still used by the Amish, and was apparently the author of the Protestation und Schutzschrift, a defence of Anabaptism presented to the Zürich council. The Amish, Baptist, Mennonite and Bruderhof churches are all influenced in varying degrees by him and the other Anabaptists of the Reformation era.
felix-maria-calleja: Calleja was born on 1 November 1753 in Medina del Campo, Spain. As a captain he accompanied the Count of Revillagigedo to New Spain in 1789, when the count became viceroy, and went on to command an infantry brigade in the intendancy of San Luis Potosí. Under Viceroy Miguel José de Azanza he fought with severity and cruelty to subdue the Indians of the area, and he also fought Anglo-American filibusters encroaching on Texas. Ignacio Allende, later a leader of the independence movement, served under him.

After Miguel Hidalgo's Grito de Dolores of 16 September 1810 and the insurgent victory at Monte de las Cruces on 30 October, Viceroy Francisco Javier Venegas ordered Calleja, now a brigadier commanding a cavalry division, to the capital's aid. He routed the insurgents at San Jerónimo Aculco on 7 November 1810 and retook Guanajuato on 25 November. At the Bridge of Calderón the insurgents were near victory when a grenade ignited a munitions wagon in their camp. His 4,000 troops became the core of the royalist Army of the Center.

After an unsuccessful 72-day siege of José María Morelos at Cuautla, Calleja withdrew to Mexico City. Named viceroy on 28 January 1813, he took office on 4 March and found the treasury empty, with more than two million pesos owed to the troops. He confiscated the property of the abolished Inquisition, raised a loan of two million pesos from merchants, farmed out the alcabala, reorganised the treasury and restored commerce and the post, building a well-equipped and paid army.

He exiled many insurgents to Cuba and later to the Philippines. The capture and execution of Morelos on 22 December 1815 seemed to end the insurrection, but it revived with the revolt of Vicente Guerrero in the south, and Calleja's rule grew more dictatorial. Liberal royalists blamed his brutal methods, and his tolerance of his commanders' abuses, for causing more rebellion; their complaints reached the Spanish court, and he was relieved on 20 September 1816.

In Spain he was made Conde de Calderón, received the grand crosses of Isabel the Catholic and San Hermenegildo, and became military commander in Andalucía and governor of Cádiz, charged with organising an expeditionary army for America. Taken prisoner by Rafael Riego, whose uprising against Ferdinand VII began the Liberal Restoration of 1820, he was held on Mallorca until it collapsed, then restored to his rank. He died on 24 July 1828 in Valencia, where he was commander.
felix-mendelssohn: Jakob Ludwig Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy was born on 3 February 1809 in Hamburg, then an independent city-state. His father, the banker Abraham Mendelssohn, was the son of the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn; his mother was Lea Salomon of the Itzig family. Felix was the second of four children. He was raised largely without religion until, on 21 March 1816, the children were baptised in a private ceremony in the family's Berlin apartment into the Reformed Protestant church. The family used the surname Mendelssohn Bartholdy from 1812.

He began piano lessons with his mother at six and was taught in Paris by Marie Bigot at seven. In Berlin he studied piano with Ludwig Berger and, from at least May 1819, counterpoint and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter, together with his sister Fanny, who showed similar talent. His great-aunt Sarah Levy, a patron of the Berliner Singakademie, had gathered a collection of Bach family manuscripts, and the study of Baroque music shaped his tastes.

Mendelssohn enjoyed early success in Germany and revived interest in the music of Johann Sebastian Bach, notably with his performance of the St Matthew Passion in 1829. In the same year he made his London debut as a conductor, where his use of a baton was a novelty. He travelled widely in Europe as composer, conductor and soloist, and his ten visits to Britain, during which many of his major works were first performed, form an important part of his adult career.

His success at the Lower Rhine music festival of 1836 led to his first paid professional post, as director at Düsseldorf. At Leipzig he led the Gewandhaus Orchestra, playing the older masters and also music by Robert Schumann and Hector Berlioz. He founded the Leipzig Conservatory, where he taught classes in composition and ensemble playing. He married Cécile Charlotte Sophie Jeanrenaud on 28 March 1837, and they had five children. He died on 4 November 1847.

His compositions include symphonies, concertos, piano, organ and chamber music, the String Octet, the oratorios St. Paul and Elijah, the Hebrides Overture and the Songs Without Words for solo piano. His tastes were essentially conservative, which set him apart from Franz Liszt, Richard Wagner and Berlioz. Heinrich Heine thought his work marked by strict seriousness and a lack of naïveté, and Wagner attacked him in an anti-Jewish pamphlet. After a long period of denigration, owing to changing tastes and antisemitism, his music was re-evaluated from the mid-20th century. He was also an editor of Baroque scores, keeping close to the composers' intentions.
felix-of-aquitaine: Felix held the rank of patrician in the Frankish kingdom of the Merovingians and had his seat at Toulouse. The tenth-century Miracula sancti Martialis lemovicensis describes him as a noble patrician from the town of Toulouse who had obtained authority over all the cities up to the Pyrenees and over the people of the Wascones, that is, the Basques, whom it calls iniquitous. He was probably the first ruler of the Duchy of Aquitaine, which grew out of the old kingdom of Charibert II in the decades after Charibert's death in 632 and Dagobert I's subjection of the Basques.

Felix was probably a supporter of King Chlothar III and his majordomo, Ebroin, and his patriciate falls in the years when Chlothar's appointee Erembert was bishop of Toulouse. After Chlothar's death in 673 Erembert retired, and Chlothar's brother Childeric II took the throne and deposed Ebroin. A regional synod held at Bordeaux under Childeric, while Felix was still in power, points to continued Frankish sovereignty or suzerainty over Aquitaine and Gascony; a break with the Merovingians appears to have followed Childeric's death in 675.

The synod at Bordeaux was presided over by a certain Lupus, whom the Miracula describes as coming to Felix. Lupus is often considered Felix's protégé, entrusted with Gascony, who eventually succeeded him over all Aquitaine. Yet Lupus was an opponent of Ebroin, and so he may instead have been an enemy of Felix who usurped authority in Gascony. Later he held southern Aquitaine and was trying to assert his rule in the north when he died. Felix stands at the head of the list of semi-independent rulers of Aquitaine that runs through the Middle Ages, yet historians describe him as mysterious and obscure.
felix-of-burgundy: Felix was born and ordained in the Frankish kingdom of Burgundy, though his name does not allow historians to settle his nationality. Almost all that is known of him comes from Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed in about 731, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. The historian Peter Hunter Blair suggested that he may have been linked to the Irish missionary work in Francia centred on Columbanus and Luxeuil Abbey, and N. J. Higham notes suggestions that he came from Luxeuil, Châlons or the area around Autun.

Judith McClure and Roger Collins have noted that Felix, already a consecrated bishop, may have become a political fugitive before reaching England. A bishop named Felix held the see of Châlons in 626 or 627 but was deprived of it after the death of the Frankish king Chlothar II in 629. Ties between Francia and East Anglia were close at the time, as the Frankish workmanship of the grave goods at Sutton Hoo suggests.

Felix went to Archbishop Honorius in Canterbury, who sent him to preach to the East Angles. His arrival seems to have coincided with the accession of King Sigeberht, who had become a devout Christian in exile, and the historian Marios Costambeys suggests that the new reign may have been why Honorius sent him. A local tradition holds that Felix landed at Babingley in Norfolk and founded its church in 631.

His see of Dommoc is widely thought to have been Dunwich in Suffolk, a town since destroyed by coastal erosion, while Richard Hoggett has argued for Walton Castle near Felixstowe, the site of a Roman fort. The teachers of his school may have come from the kingdom of Kent. The Liber Eliensis credits him with founding Soham Abbey and a church at Reedham, and during his years as bishop the Irish monk Fursey founded a monastery at Cnobheresburg, probably Burgh Castle.

Felix died on 8 March 647 or 648, probably in the reign of Anna of East Anglia, and Thomas, a Fenman, became the second bishop of the East Angles. According to William of Malmesbury his relics were moved from Dommoc to Soham, whose church the Vikings later destroyed, and were afterwards found and buried at Ramsey Abbey. Venerated as a saint before the Schism of 1054, he is commemorated on 8 March, six English churches are dedicated to him, and he is one of the patron saints of the Catholic Diocese of East Anglia.
felix-zu-schwarzenberg: Felix Ludwig Johann Friedrich, Prince of Schwarzenberg, was born on 2 October 1800 at Český Krumlov Castle in Bohemia, the second son of Prince Joseph of Schwarzenberg. The House of Schwarzenberg was one of the most influential Bohemian noble families, and his uncle Prince Karl Philipp of Schwarzenberg commanded the Austrian armies in the last phases of the Napoleonic Wars. After a short military interlude he entered the diplomatic service as a protégé of State Chancellor Klemens von Metternich and served in embassies at Saint Petersburg, London, Paris, Turin and Naples.

When the revolutions of 1848 broke out, he joined Field Marshal Joseph Radetzky in Lombardy–Venetia against King Charles Albert of Sardinia. As Radetzky's adviser, and as brother-in-law of Prince Alfred of Windisch-Grätz, he was appointed minister-president, the sixth within a year, and foreign minister on 21 November 1848. His first step was to replace the incapacitated Emperor Ferdinand I with his nephew Francis Joseph, and Ferdinand abdicated at Olomouc on 2 December.

Determined, in the light of Metternich's fate, not merely to fight revolution but to overcome it, he formed a government of conservatives and liberals. He undermined the Frankfurt Parliament by recalling the Austrian delegates and pre-empted the Kremsier Parliament with the March Constitution of 1849, which made the Habsburg Empire a unitary, centralised state.

With the new emperor he called in the Russian army to help suppress the Hungarian revolt, which left Austria free to thwart the drive of Prussia to dominate Germany. He imposed the Punctation of Olmütz on Prussia, forcing it to give up for the moment its plan to unify Germany under its own leadership.

Schwarzenberg suffered a stroke in Vienna on 5 April 1852 and died in office. He had won substantial respect in Europe as an able statesman, and some called him the Austrian Bismarck, though he was not much trusted, even by his emperor. A remark attributed to him, that Austria would shock the world by the depth of her ingratitude, was bitterly remembered in the Crimean War; the historian Edward Crankshaw considers it apocryphal. Historians have generally seen his sudden death as a grave setback to Austria. In 2011 Budapest revoked the honorary citizenship it had given him.
felou-falls: At the falls the Sénégal River drops 13 metres down an irregular series of rocky steps. The river is formed 82 kilometres upstream, near Bafoulabé, where the Bakoye and the Bafing meet; both rise in the Fouta Djallon highlands of Guinea, which receive heavy rain from June to October during the West African Monsoon. Between 1903 and 1980 most of the water reaching Félou came from the Bafing, and the flow was highly seasonal, highest in September and almost nil from January to June, with large differences from year to year.

Since the Manantali Dam was completed on the Bafing in 1987, about 200 kilometres upstream, the largest floods below it have been reduced and a flow of between 150 and 200 cubic metres a second is kept up in the dry season.

The falls were the furthest point up the river from Saint Louis that boats could reach, and because of the seasonal water level they could get there only for a few months after the rains. French forces used the river in their conquest of the Sudan in the 19th century. In 1855 Louis Faidherbe, the French governor of Sénégal, built a fort at the village of Médine, 3 kilometres downstream of the falls, to strengthen French control of the river and serve as a base for expansion into the interior.

In the 1920s the colonial government built a weir and a small run-of-the-river hydroelectric plant at the falls, which used about one per cent of the river's water to drive a 600-kilowatt generator and was updated in 1992.

In 2009 work began on the Félou Hydroelectric Plant, a 62.3-megawatt run-of-the-river plant replacing the one built in the 1920s. Little use is made of the river for goods and passengers, and studies have looked at cutting a navigable channel 905 kilometres long between Ambidédi in Mali and Saint-Louis in Senegal, which would give landlocked Mali a direct route to the Atlantic.
feminism: Feminist movements originated in late 18th-century Europe. Mary Wollstonecraft is seen by many as a founder of feminism because of her book A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), in which she argues that class and private property are the basis of discrimination against women, and that women as much as men needed equal rights.

The word came later. Charles Fourier is credited with coining féminisme in 1837, but no trace of the word has been found in his works. It first appeared in France in 1871, in a medical thesis by Ferdinand-Valère Faneau de la Cour, and Alexandre Dumas fils coined féministe in 1872 for men who supported women's rights; both uses were very negative. The Oxford English Dictionary dates its first appearance in English in this meaning to 1895.

Feminism is a range of movements and ideologies that aim to establish the political, economic, personal and social equality of the sexes. It holds that modern societies are patriarchal and that women are treated unjustly in them. Since the 19th century, first-wave liberal feminism, which sought political and legal equality through reforms within a liberal democratic framework, was contrasted with labour-based proletarian women's movements that developed into socialist and Marxist feminism. Since the 1960s both have been contrasted with radical feminism, which arose from the radical wing of second-wave feminism.

Feminist theory emerged from the movements and draws on anthropology, sociology, economics, literary criticism, psychoanalysis and philosophy to understand gender inequality. In the 1970s French feminists such as Hélène Cixous developed the concept of écriture féminine, or female writing.

Many scholars consider feminist campaigns a main force behind changes in women's rights, particularly in the West, where they are near-universally credited with women's suffrage, reproductive rights and the right to enter into contracts and own property. At the International Conference of Socialist Women in Stuttgart in 1907, suffrage was described as a tool of class struggle. In 1918 Constance Markievicz became the first woman elected to the British House of Commons, but in line with Sinn Féin policy she did not take her seat. In the United States the National Organization for Women began in 1966 to seek equality, including through the Equal Rights Amendment, which did not pass.
fen-river: The Fen rises in the Guancen Mountains of Ningwu County in north-east Shanxi, flows south-east into the basin of Taiyuan and then south through the central valley of Shanxi, before turning west to join the Yellow River west of Hejin. It drains 39,417 km2, 25.3% of the province, and one-seventh of its course lies within Taiyuan prefecture. The cities on or near it, from north to south, are Taiyuan, Linfen, Houma and Hejin; Fenyang, though named after the river, lies more than 20 km to the west of it.

The Fen is usually identified with the Ji River, which Sima Qian and others placed beside the home of the Yellow Emperor. The Discourses of the States calls the Ji the home of the Yellow Emperor's clan before he fought the clan of Yandi, the Flame Emperor, and Ji was also the surname of the Zhou royal family. Pulleyblank argues, however, that the Ji River may be a later invention, since there seems to be no record of it outside the myth.

The lower Fen lay in the core area of ancient China, the Central Plain, and held the capital of the state of Jin near present-day Houma. Its valley opened routes of communication to the Wei River valley on either side of the Yellow River. Known in Shanxi as the mother river of the people, the Fen made its fertile valley the economic centre of the province.

Dams built upstream once reduced the river at Taiyuan to a trickle and left its bed dry. From 1949 reservoirs were built on the Fen and on tributaries such as the Wenyu and Hui rivers, supplying industrial water to Taiyuan and other cities and enlarging the irrigated land of the Taiyuan and Linfen basins. Before the 1950s floods covered 133,400 hectares of the valley, and 66,700 hectares were saline-alkali soil, much of which has since been reclaimed.

The No. 1 Fen River Reservoir, built in 1960, is the largest artificial reservoir in Shanxi, with a capacity of 720 million cubic metres, and a second was built in 2000 about 50 kilometres downstream. In the 1990s Taiyuan built removable structures across the river to hold water for landscaping, forming the 6-kilometre Fen River Park.
feng-ba: Feng Ba's grandfather Feng He, a Han Chinese, settled in Shangdang Commandery, and his father Feng An served the Western Yan emperor Murong Yong as a general. When Later Yan destroyed Western Yan in 394 the household was moved to Helong, also called Longcheng, where Feng Ba grew up under strong Xianbei influence, as his Xianbei nickname Qizhifa suggests. Unlike his three younger brothers, who ignored social restraints, he was thought careful and diligent. He became a general under Murong Bao and a close friend of Murong Bao's adoptive son Murong Yun.

In 407 he and his brother Feng Sufu offended the emperor Murong Xi and hid in the countryside, then rose inside Longcheng while the emperor was away burying his wife, and persuaded Murong Yun, who soon took back his original name Gao Yun, to lead them. Gao Yun made Feng Ba prime minister, and the government was effectively in his hands.

Feng Ba made Feng Sufu prime minister and gave high posts to his kinsmen and allies. He and Feng Sufu were regarded as diligent, frugal and intelligent, and Northern Yan was thought well governed. In 410 his cousin Feng Wani and Feng Ruchen rebelled; Feng Hong defeated them and executed them after their surrender. In 411 Feng Ba married his daughter Princess Lelang to the Rouran khan Yujiulü Hulü, and in 414 he brought back 5,000 households of his clan from Changle.

He refused the submission demanded by the Northern Wei envoy Huniuyu Shimen, imprisoning but sparing him, and allied instead with Helian Bobo of Xia. In 415 he executed three brothers of the general Sun Hu for complaining and then poisoned Sun Hu himself. In 418 the Northern Wei emperor Mingyuan besieged Helong; Feng Ba held the city, but the Wei carried off some 10,000 households.

Seriously ill in 430, Feng Ba transferred his authority to his crown prince Feng Yi, but his favourite, Consort Song, wanted the throne for her own son Feng Shouju and cut him off from the court with orders issued in his name. Her official Hu Fu warned Feng Hong, who seized the palace; Feng Ba died of the shock, and Feng Hong took the throne and killed all his sons. Historians disagree whether Gao Yun or Feng Ba should count as the first ruler of Northern Yan.
feng-dao: Feng Dao was born in 882, under Emperor Xizong of the late Tang, to a family of farmers and scholars from Jingcheng in modern Cangzhou, Hebei. He was said to be studious and capable in writing, and willing to endure hard labour and poverty to support his parents. He first served the warlord Liu Shouguang at Youzhou, in modern Beijing, and by 911 was a military adviser to Liu's new state of Yan. When he urged Liu not to attack Yiwu, Liu imprisoned him, sparing his life only after others interceded.

Feng fled to Jin, where the chief eunuch Zhang Chengye recommended him, and the prince Li Cunxu entrusted him with drafting military orders. Around 919, when the prince angrily ordered him to draft a declaration against the adviser Guo Chongtao, Feng refused to write and persuaded him that the quarrel would only encourage his enemies. He lived frugally on campaign, sharing his salary with his staff and returning women whom officers offered him to their families. After Li Cunxu founded the Later Tang in 923 as Emperor Zhuangzong, Feng became an imperial scholar, and during his mourning for his father he gave away his wealth in a famine.

In 938 the Later Jin emperor Gaozu sent him to the Khitan court, where Emperor Taizong considered keeping him but let him return. After Taizong took Kaifeng in 946 and the next year proclaimed the Liao dynasty, Feng submitted and was consulted on important matters; it was believed that his reply that only the emperor could save the people helped keep Taizong from mass executions of his new Han Chinese subjects. Later he advised Guo Wei to reward the imperial guards lavishly before marching against the rebel Li Shouzhen, and under the Later Zhou he helped persuade Emperor Taizu to pardon the soldiers of the rebel Murong Yanchao.

Feng Dao died on 21 May 954 and received the posthumous title Wenyi Prince of Ying. For the classics he printed he used the text that the Tang chancellor Zheng Tan had ordered carved in stone at Chang'an, and the finished blocks were presented to Emperor Taizu of Later Zhou. Scholars compare his work to that of Johannes Gutenberg in Europe. The historians Ouyang Xiu and Sima Guang praised his virtues but condemned him for serving one dynasty after another.
feng-hong: Feng Hong's birth date is unknown, and nothing is recorded of him before 407, when his brothers Feng Ba and Feng Sufu overthrew the Later Yan emperor Murong Xi and raised Gao Yun to the throne. Late that year Gao Yun made Feng Hong a major general, and he was created Duke of Ji. In 410 he and Zhang Xing put down the revolt of his kinsmen Feng Wani and Feng Ruchen and executed them after they surrendered, after which Feng Ba made him Duke of Zhongshan. By 430 he was Feng Ba's prime minister, and he took the throne that year with the title Heavenly King.

Northern Wei attacked Northern Yan again and again, above all after it annexed Xia in 431 and no longer had a major rival in the west. In 432 the emperor Taiwu besieged Helong, ten commanderies surrendered, and he withdrew two months later with 30,000 households. Feng Hong refused advice to become a Wei vassal, saying the enmity was so deep that he would be killed even if he surrendered. In 431 he had passed over his eldest son Feng Chong and in 432 made Feng Wangren, son of Princess Murong, crown prince; early in 433 Feng Chong and two of his brothers went over to Northern Wei.

In 434 Feng Hong offered submission and a daughter to Taiwu, but would not send Feng Wangren to Pingcheng as a hostage, and executed the official Liu Zi for warning him of the danger. He submitted as a vassal to Liu Song, whose Emperor Wen created him Prince of Yan but sent no real help. By 435 the state was little larger than Helong itself.

In 436 Northern Wei and Goguryeo forces both reached Helong. The Goguryeo troops sacked the city and escorted Feng Hong and his people east after he set fire to the palace. King Jangsu refused to hand him over to Northern Wei and settled his people at Pingguo and then Beifeng, but Feng Hong demanded to be treated as suzerain, ignored Goguryeo's laws and was angered to be called Prince of Longcheng. Jangsu seized Feng Wangren as a hostage, and in 438, when Liu Song sent the general Wang Baiju to fetch Feng Hong, had him and his sons executed, while granting him a posthumous name.
fengxiang: The district lies between 1,000 and 1,600 metres above sea level. Its southern part has deep soils well suited to grain and cotton, while the hilly ground north of the mountains to the river holds more than 1,000 river valleys with silt soil. Wheat is the main food crop, followed by sorghum, corn and beans, with cotton, pepper and tobacco grown as economic crops.

The city of Yong, within the present district, was the capital of the State of Qin during the Zhou dynasty, and as its population grew the surrounding area became Yong County, the ancient name of the district. Under the Tang dynasty the area was known variously as Fufeng Commandery and Qizhou, and it also served as the Western Capital of the empire. From 907 to 924 Fengxiang was the capital of the Qi Kingdom.

In 1062 Su Shi, then a judge in Fengxiang, had a drinking-water pond dredged, creating what is now East Lake Park. The park has a pedestrian causeway like that of West Lake in Hangzhou, which Su Shi also created, and covers 200,000 square metres with several historic buildings and sculptures. The Yin Fung Chi was built under the Song dynasty.

Formerly Fengxiang County, it is now a district administered by Baoji City in the west of Shaanxi province, covering 1,179 square kilometres and divided into 12 towns, with its seat at Chengguan Town. Its heritage sites, all provincial-level key conservation units, include the tomb of Qin Mugong and three sites of the old city of Yong. The district is known for Xifeng Jiu baijiu and for woodcut New Year pictures, clay sculptures and paper cuttings.
feodor-chaliapin: Feodor Chaliapin was born on 1 February 1873 (Old Style) in Kazan and baptised the next day at the Epiphany Cathedral. His father, Ivan Yakovlevich, was a clerk in the district council, and in 1878 the family moved to the village of Ametyevo, now part of Kazan. His vocal teacher was Dmitri Usatov. Chaliapin began his career in Tbilisi and at the Imperial Opera in Saint Petersburg in 1894, and then sang at the Mamontov Private Opera from 1896 to 1899.

At the Mamontov Opera he met Sergei Rachmaninoff, then an assistant conductor, who remained a lifelong friend. Rachmaninoff taught him to analyse a score and insisted that he learn all the roles of an opera, and together they prepared the title role of Modest Mussorgsky's Boris Godunov.

In 1901 he made a debut at La Scala as the devil in Arrigo Boito's Mefistofele under Arturo Toscanini, who later called him the finest talent he had worked with. His first Metropolitan Opera season, in 1907, was disappointing because audiences found the frankness of his acting shocking. He returned in 1921 and sang there for eight seasons. In 1913 the impresario Sergei Diaghilev introduced him to London and Paris, where he also gave recitals of Russian folk songs, among them The Song of the Volga Boatmen.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917 he was at first treated as a revered artist, but the difficulties of life under the new regime and the Civil War, and reportedly the seizure of some of his property, led him to stay outside Russia after 1921. He lived first in Finland and then in France, with Paris as his base. He made one sound film, G. W. Pabst's Don Quixote of 1933, and published the memoir Man and Mask in 1932. His last stage performance was as Boris Godunov at the Monte Carlo Opera in 1937.

He died of leukaemia in Paris and was buried at the Batignolles cemetery until 1984, when his remains were moved to the Novodevichy cemetery in Moscow. Largely through his advocacy, Russian operas such as Khovanshchina, Prince Igor and Sadko became known in the West.
feodor-i-of-russia: Feodor was born in Moscow on 31 May 1557, the third son of Ivan IV by his first wife Anastasia Romanovna. His mother died when he was three, and he grew up in the shadow of a distant father with only one surviving older brother, Ivan Ivanovich. He was sickly and diffident, extremely pious, and fond of visiting churches and having the bells rung, which earned him the name Feodor the Bellringer. In 1575 he married Irina Godunova, sister of the minister Boris Godunov. Ivan Ivanovich died on 9 November 1581, leaving Feodor and the infant Dmitry as the only sons.

Ivan IV died in March 1584, and Feodor was crowned tsar and autocrat of all Russia in the Dormition Cathedral in Moscow on 31 May 1584. Historians have debated whether an assembly, the Zemsky Sobor, elected him; the few contemporary Russian sources say only that he took the throne by his father's blessing. Feodor was the nominal ruler. Boris Godunov acted as de facto regent, and by the end of the 1580s he dealt with foreign powers independently. Irina also took some part in affairs, and three charters to monasteries between 1587 and 1597 are in the names of both tsar and tsaritsa.
