In May 1586 the Shuysky family petitioned in the name of the Zemsky Sobor for Feodor to divorce his childless wife. He refused. The Shuyskys were banished from the capital and Godunov persecuted them heavily the following year. In foreign affairs Feodor declared the country open to all foreigners instead of keeping exclusive trading rights for England, and dismissed the English ambassador Sir Jerome Bowes. Elizabeth I sent Giles Fletcher the Elder to protest, without success.

Irina bore a daughter, Feodosiya, in 1592, after almost twelve years of marriage; the child died in 1594 aged two. Feodor died in Moscow on 17 January 1598 and was buried in the Archangel Cathedral in the Kremlin. After forty days of mourning the Zemsky Sobor elected Godunov tsar. Feodor's death ended the central branch of the Rurik dynasty, and the end of the line was later followed by the Time of Troubles. Contemporaries described his reign as a time of prosperity and stability, though much of the credit went to Godunov. Feodor was venerated soon after his death and is listed in the Great Synaxaristes of the Orthodox Church.
feodor-iii-of-russia: Feodor was born in Moscow on 9 June 1661, the eldest surviving son of Tsar Alexis and Maria Miloslavskaya, and he succeeded his father in 1676 at the age of fifteen. He was educated by Simeon Polotsky, the most learned Slavonic monk of the day, and knew Polish and Latin. He had been disabled from birth, however, and was half paralysed by a mysterious illness, supposedly scurvy. He spent most of his time with young nobles, Ivan Maksimovich Yazykov and Aleksei Timofeievich Likhachov.

On 28 July 1680 Feodor married a noblewoman, Agaphia Simeonovna Grushevskaya, and took up the sceptre. He proved a devoted reformer. The atmosphere of the court became less oppressive and the severity of the penal laws was considerably reduced. He founded an academy in the Zaikonospassky monastery, where professors were to teach everything not expressly forbidden by the Orthodox church, including Slavonic, Greek, Latin and Polish. A household census took place in 1678.

His most notable reform, made at the suggestion of Vasily Galitzine, was the abolition in 1682 of mestnichestvo, or place priority, which had paralysed the civil and military administration of the Tsardom for generations. From then on appointments were to be made by merit and by the will of the sovereign, and the pedigree books were to be destroyed. Agaphia shared his progressive views and was the first to advocate beard-shaving.

On 11 July 1681 Agaphia gave birth to a son, Tsarevich Ilya Fyodorovich, the expected heir. She died three days later, on 14 July, and the child died on 21 July. On 24 February 1682 Feodor married Marfa Apraksina; he was so weak that he could not stand at the wedding. He died on 7 May 1682, three months after it, without surviving issue, and the news of his death sparked the Moscow Uprising of 1682.
feodosia: Greek colonists from Miletos founded Theodosia in the 6th century BCE. Its trade depended on rich agricultural lands, and it was destroyed by the Huns in the 4th century CE. For much of the next nine hundred years it was a minor village, at times within the sphere of influence of the Khazars and of the Byzantine Empire, and it was conquered by the Mongols in the 1230s.

In the late 13th century traders from the Republic of Genoa bought the city from the Golden Horde. Their settlement, Kaffa, virtually monopolised trade in the Black Sea region and housed one of Europe's biggest slave markets. Ibn Battuta described a wonderful harbour with about two hundred vessels, and in 1318 Pope John XXII established a Latin diocese of Kaffa. It is believed that the Black Death entered Europe through Kaffa in 1347, after a siege in which the Mongol army under Jani Beg reportedly catapulted infected corpses over the walls. The plague appears to have spread step by step, and other Crimean ports and overland routes may also have carried it.

In 1475 an Ottoman fleet under Gedik Ahmet Pasha anchored before the city on 1 June, began bombarding it the next day, and received its surrender on 6 June. The Ottomans took the inhabitants' wealth, abducted 1,500 youths for the sultan's palace, and on 8 July ordered all inhabitants of Latin origin to move to Istanbul. In 1616 Zaporozhian Cossacks under Petro Konashevych-Sahaidachny destroyed the Turkish fleet, captured the city and freed the slaves. Russia took over Crimea between 1774 and 1783, and the city became Feodosia.

Feodosia is a resort city on the Black Sea coast of Crimea, with beaches, mineral springs and mud baths. Its Golden Beach, made of small seashells, stretches for some 15 kilometres. The painter Ivan Aivazovsky lived and worked there all his life, and the Aivazovsky National Art Gallery and the Genoese fortress are among its best-known sights.
ferdinand-christian-baur: Ferdinand Christian Baur was born on 21 June 1792 at Schmiden, near Cannstatt. After the theological seminary of Blaubeuren he entered the Tübinger Stift in 1809, where he studied under Ernst Bengel while the philosophers Fichte and Schelling made a deep impression on him. In 1817 he returned to Blaubeuren as a professor, a turning point that began the investigations on which his reputation rests. His first important work, Symbolik und Mythologie oder die Naturreligion des Altertums, appeared in 1824 and 1825 and showed the influence of Schelling and Friedrich Schleiermacher. In 1826 he was called to Tübingen as professor of theology.

At Tübingen Baur wrote on the Manichaean religious system (1831), Apollonius of Tyana (1832), Christian Gnosis (1835) and the Christian element in Platonism (1837). He exchanged Schleiermacher for Hegel and adopted Hegel's philosophy of history, saying that without philosophy history was for him dead and dumb. His essay of 1831 on the Christ party at Corinth argued that Paul was opposed there by a Jewish Christian party.

In 1835 he argued that the Pastoral Epistles were written in the middle of the second century against Gnostics, and in his Paulus of 1845 he held that only Galatians, 1 and 2 Corinthians and Romans were genuinely Pauline, and that the Paul of the Acts of the Apostles differs from the Paul of the letters.

His underlying thesis was that Christianity grew out of Judaism and had to overcome Jewish limits before becoming universal. The antagonism between the Jewish apostles Peter, James and John and Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, lasted, he held, until the middle of the second century, and Catholicism arose from their reconciliation.

In 1847 he applied this to the Gospels, ranking Matthew closest to an original Gospel, then Luke and Mark, and treating John as idealistic and not historical. He also wrote histories of dogma, among them a three-volume history of dogma, Die christliche Lehre von der Dreieinigkeit und Menschwerdung Gottes (1841 to 1843), and a defence of Protestantism against Johann Möhler in 1834.

Baur died at Tübingen aged 68. His Kirchengeschichte appeared in five volumes between 1853 and 1863, partly by himself and partly by his son Ferdinand and his son-in-law Eduard Zeller from his notes and lectures. Otto Pfleiderer called it a classic and the first thorough attempt to explain the rise of Christianity on strictly historical lines.

His school was at its height in the 1840s, with Adolf Hilgenfeld and Albert Schwegler among its members. It then lost ground, as English scholars showed that the late dates it gave the New Testament documents were impossible, and it has been generally abandoned since Adolf von Harnack proposed very early dates for the synoptic Gospels and Acts around 1910.
ferdinand-de-lesseps: Ferdinand de Lesseps was born at Versailles on 19 November 1805 into a family of diplomats; his father Mathieu de Lesseps was in the consular service. Through his father he came to know Muhammad Ali, the ruler of Egypt, and Muhammad Ali's son Sa'id, who became his friend. His own diplomatic career began in Lisbon in 1825 and took him to Tunis, Alexandria, Cairo, Rotterdam, Málaga and Barcelona. In Alexandria he read a memoir on the abandoned ancient canal at Suez, which helped give him the idea of a canal across the isthmus. Recalled in 1849 after a mission to Rome, he left the diplomatic service.

When Sa'id Pasha became viceroy of Egypt in 1854, Lesseps landed at Alexandria on 7 November, and on 30 November the viceroy signed a concession authorizing him to oversee the French portion of the Suez Canal's construction. British opposition, including that of Lord Palmerston, did not deter him. French subscribers supplied more than half of the capital of two hundred million francs, and the Egyptian government took shares worth eighty million francs. The first blow of the pickaxe was struck at Port Said on 25 April 1859, and the canal was opened on 17 November 1869 by the Khedive Ismail Pasha.

A congress of 136 delegates in Paris in May 1879 voted for a Panama canal without locks, like Suez, and Lesseps, aged 74, became president of the company. Work began in 1882 but was dogged by landslides and by deaths from malaria and yellow fever. The Panama Canal Company declared itself bankrupt in December 1888 and entered liquidation in February 1889.

The failure became known as the Panama Canal Scandal after it emerged by 1892 that 150 French deputies had been bribed to vote the company financial aid. In February 1893 Lesseps, his son Charles and others were tried and found guilty. Lesseps was fined and sentenced to prison, but the Court of Cassation overturned the prison sentence because more than three years had passed since the offence. In 1904 the United States bought the company's assets and resumed work on a revised plan. Lesseps died in Indre on 7 December 1894 and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery.
ferdinand-i-holy-roman-emperor: Ferdinand was born on 10 March 1503 at Alcalá de Henares in Castile, the second son of Philip I of Castile and Joanna of Castile. After his father's death in 1506 his maternal grandfather Ferdinand II of Aragon, with whom he shared a name and a birthday, became his guardian, and he was raised in the royal household with an education in literature, the sciences and languages. He grew up as a patron of the arts and of scholars. He did not learn German until he was a young adult.

When Louis II of Hungary and Bohemia was killed at Mohács on 29 August 1526, Ferdinand at once declared himself a candidate. On 24 October 1526 the Bohemian Diet elected him king of Bohemia on condition that he confirm the estates' privileges, but it refused to recognise him as hereditary ruler. In Hungary a Diet of the lesser nobility proclaimed John Zápolya, Voivode of Transylvania, king on 10 November 1526, and Ferdinand, supported by Charles V, held the western part, which became known as Royal Hungary.

In 1547 Ferdinand defeated a Protestant revolt in Bohemia, after which he centralised its administration and revoked many urban privileges. At the Diet of Augsburg of 1555, with authority from Charles to act and settle, he brought the delegates to agree on the principle of cuius regio, eius religio. He rushed one article through the debate and added the Declaratio Ferdinandei at the last minute, and these became flaws in the settlement. Charles abdicated in August 1556, and Ferdinand succeeded him as emperor. He founded the Hofkriegsrat in 1556 to coordinate military affairs in all Habsburg lands, but the governments of Austria, Bohemia and Hungary stayed distinct.

In December 1562 Ferdinand had his eldest son Maximilian elected King of the Romans. Ferdinand died in Vienna in 1564 and was buried in Prague. Historians describe him as a mediocre military commander but an energetic and imaginative administrator, whose framework for his lands endured into the eighteenth century. Some historians hold that he was nearly the closest the Holy Roman Empire came to a Protestant emperor, while others hold that he was as Catholic as his brother but saw religion as outside politics.
ferdinand-i-of-aragon: Ferdinand was born on 27 November 1380 at Medina del Campo, the younger son of King John I of Castile and Eleanor of Aragon. On 15 August 1403 he founded a new order of knighthood, the Order of the Jar. In 1394 he had married Eleanor of Alburquerque, and they had seven children, among them Alfonso V of Aragon, John II of Aragon and Eleanor, who became queen of Portugal. When his elder brother, King Henry III of Castile, died in 1406, Ferdinand declined the Castilian crown and became coregent with Henry's widow, Catherine of Lancaster, during the minority of his nephew John II of Castile, administering domestic affairs prudently.

After the death of his maternal uncle, King Martin I of Aragon, without surviving legitimate issue, Ferdinand was chosen King of Aragon in 1412 through the Compromise of Caspe. He was the first Castilian ruler of the Crown of Aragon, and his titles included king of Valencia, Majorca, Sardinia and Sicily and count of Barcelona. The other candidate, Count James II of Urgell, revolted, and in 1413 Ferdinand dissolved the County of Urgell. On 19 February 1416 he created the title of Prince of Girona for the heir to the Crown of Aragon.

The most notable accomplishment of his short reign was his agreement in 1416 to depose the antipope Benedict XIII, which helped end the Western Schism that had divided the Catholic Church for nearly forty years. Ferdinand died on 2 April 1416 at Igualada. He is buried in the royal pantheon of the Crown of Aragon at the monastery of Poblet, in a tomb that his son Alfonso ordered from Pere Oller in 1417. The Italian humanist Lorenzo Valla wrote his official biography.
ferdinand-i-of-austria: Ferdinand was the eldest son of Francis II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Maria Theresa of Naples and Sicily. His parents were double first cousins, sharing all four grandparents, so that he descended twice from each of his four great-grandparents. Possibly as a result of this closeness, he had hydrocephalus, neurological problems including epilepsy, and a speech impediment. He was educated by Baron Josef Kalasanz von Erberg and his wife, Countess Josephine von Attems. He married Maria Anna of Savoy, the sixth child of Victor Emmanuel I of Sardinia, and the couple had no children.

Ferdinand succeeded his father Francis I on 2 March 1835 as Emperor of Austria, King of Hungary, where he was Ferdinand V, and ruler of the other lands of the Habsburg monarchy. He was also president of the German Confederation until 12 July 1848. Because of severe epilepsy he was thought unable to rule, and his father's will told him to consult his uncle Archduke Louis on internal policy and urged him to be guided by Prince Metternich, the foreign minister. Although he was never declared incapacitated, a Regent's Council of Archduke Louis, Count Kolowrat and Metternich steered the government.

Later accounts have depicted him as feeble-minded, yet he kept a coherent and legible diary and is said to have had a sharp wit. He suffered as many as twenty seizures a day, which severely limited his ability to govern. His good nature earned him the nickname The Benign in Austria and, in Bohemia, the Czech form Ferdinand Dobrotivý. He was the last King of Bohemia to be crowned as such and the last ruler crowned with the Iron Crown of Lombardy as King of Lombardy-Venetia.

When the revolutionaries of 1848 marched on the palace, Ferdinand is supposed to have asked Metternich what was happening and, on hearing that a revolution had begun, to have replied, "But are they allowed to do that?" Prince Felix of Schwarzenberg persuaded him to abdicate in favour of his nephew Franz Joseph. The next in line, his brother Franz Karl, renounced his rights in favour of his son at his wife Sophie's urging. Ferdinand abdicated on 2 December 1848, and Franz Joseph reigned for the next 68 years. In his diary he described the new emperor kneeling for his blessing. He lived in Hradčany Palace in Prague until his death on 29 June 1875, and is buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna.
ferdinand-i-of-bulgaria: Ferdinand was born in Vienna on 26 February 1861, the son of Prince August of Saxe-Coburg and Clémentine of Orléans, a daughter of King Louis Philippe I of France. He was raised a Catholic in the high nobility of Austria-Hungary and served as an officer in the Austro-Hungarian Army. The House of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha held several European thrones in the 19th century, and Ferdinand himself founded the royal dynasty of Bulgaria.

Alexander of Battenberg had abdicated in 1886 after a pro-Russian coup, and the Grand National Assembly elected Ferdinand prince on 7 July 1887. Queen Victoria thought him unfit, but he generally gave a good account of himself in his first two decades. After the fall of the minister Stefan Stambolov in 1894, Ferdinand had his infant son Boris converted to Orthodoxy in 1896, restoring relations with Russia, and was excommunicated by Pope Leo XIII. On 5 October 1908 he proclaimed Bulgaria's independence from the Ottoman Empire and took the title of tsar, at the Church of the Holy Forty Martyrs in Tarnovo.

In 1912 Bulgaria joined Greece, Montenegro and Serbia against the Ottomans, and the Bulgarian army took Adrianople on 13 March 1913. Disputes over the division of Macedonia led to the Second Balkan War, in which Bulgaria was defeated, though the Treaty of Bucharest of 1913 gave it Western Thrace and access to the Aegean. On 11 October 1915 Bulgaria attacked Serbia after a treaty with Austria-Hungary and Germany. After military setbacks in 1918, Ferdinand abdicated in favour of his eldest son, who became Tsar Boris III on 3 October 1918.

Ferdinand married Princess Marie Louise of Bourbon-Parma in 1893; she died in 1899 after the birth of their fourth child, and he married Princess Eleonore Reuss of Köstritz in 1908. After his abdication he lived in Coburg, spending time on gardening, travel and natural history. He lived to see his son Boris III die in 1943, the monarchy end in 1946 and his son Kyril executed. He died in Coburg on 10 September 1948 and was buried in the family crypt there, since the communist authorities would not let him be buried in Bulgaria.
ferdinand-i-of-leon: Ferdinand was a younger son of Sancho III of Pamplona and Muniadona of Castile, and by his father's will recognised the supremacy of his eldest brother, García Sánchez III of Navarre. His uncle García Sánchez, Count of Castile, was assassinated at León by exiled Castilian noblemen as he entered the church to marry Sancha, sister of Bermudo III, King of León. Sancho III nominated Ferdinand as count of Castile, and on 7 July 1029 a council at Burgos recorded him with that title for the first time.

Sancho arranged for him to marry Sancha of León in 1032, and the lands between the Cea and Pisuerga rivers went to Castile as her dowry. After Sancho's death in 1035 Ferdinand continued to rule Castile as count and vassal of the king of León.

In a dispute over the lands between the Cea and Pisuerga, Ferdinand defeated and killed his suzerain Bermudo III at the Battle of Tamarón on 4 September 1037. He was crowned and anointed king in León on 22 June 1038. On 15 September 1054 he defeated his elder brother García at the Battle of Atapuerca and reduced Navarre to a vassal state under García's young son Sancho García IV.

He then turned to al-Andalus. In 1060 he invaded the taifa of Zaragoza, and its emir agreed to pay tribute. In 1062 he besieged Alcalá de Henares in the taifa of Toledo and obtained tribute from its emir. In 1063 he led a great raid into the taifas of Seville and Badajoz. In the west Lamego fell on 29 November 1057, Viseu on 25 July 1058 and Coimbra on 25 July 1064 after a six-month siege. His last campaign, against Valencia in 1065, ended with his victory at the Battle of Paterna.

Ferdinand fell ill in November 1065 and died in León on 24 December, lying on a bier covered with ashes before the altar of the Basilica of San Isidoro. By his will he divided his kingdom among his sons: Sancho received Castile, Alfonso León, and García a separate Galicia. His daughters Elvira and Urraca received Toro and Zamora. Sancho and Alfonso soon turned on García, and Sancho reunited the territories in 1072 before being killed that year, when they passed to Alfonso.

His charters began to style him emperor in 1056, though the notaries of his half-brother Ramiro I of Aragon had used the title earlier. After his death his children called him emperor and the Great. A 14th-century legend, generally regarded as apocryphal, says the pope, the Holy Roman emperor and the king of France demanded tribute from him.
ferdinand-i-of-naples: Ferdinand was the only son, though illegitimate, of Alfonso the Magnanimous. His mother, Gueraldona Carlino, was probably a woman of Neapolitan origin. In 1438 Alfonso called the boy to Naples to prepare him as heir to the kingdom he was conquering, and the party landed at Gaeta on 19 August. Father and son developed a strong bond, and on 9 September 1438 Alfonso made him a knight. In June 1452 he led an army of 6,000 cavalry and 20,000 infantry against Florence, in a war that ended with the Peace of Lodi in April 1454.

Ferdinand succeeded his father in 1458 and had to overcome many rivals. Charles, Prince of Viana, was urged on by some Neapolitans to claim the crown, the barons turned to John of Anjou, son of René, and the pope demanded that the kingdom revert to the Holy See. After the seven years of war of the Angevin-Aragonese conflict, he restored the kingdom by political marriages: his son Alfonso married Ippolita of Milan, his daughter Eleanor married Ercole d'Este of Ferrara and his daughter Beatrice married Matthias Corvinus of Hungary.

In 1478, after the Pazzi conspiracy, he sided against Lorenzo de' Medici and declared war on Florence, reaching an understanding with the Ottoman sultan, whose army pressed Venice. Lorenzo de' Medici then travelled to Naples to deal with him directly. He created the Collateral Council and strengthened the Regia Camera della Sommaria, introduced silk and printing, and drew humanists such as Pontano and Panormita to his court. In 1465 he founded the Order of the Ermine.

Ferdinand kept the peace in his kingdom and in Italy until 1493. Knowing that France was preparing for war, he strengthened the kingdom and recruited armies, but he fell ill with fever and died on 25 January 1494. The historian Jacob Burckhardt wrote that he liked to keep his opponents near him, alive in well-guarded prisons or dead and embalmed in the clothes they had worn in life. Later writers describe a museum of mummies where he took his guests. Ferdinand's sons Alfonso II and Frederick I both reigned in Naples after him.
ferdinand-i-of-romania: Ferdinand was born on 24 August 1865 in Sigmaringen in south-western Germany, the second son of Leopold, Prince of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen, and Infanta Antónia of Portugal. After his father renounced his rights in 1880 and his elder brother in 1886, he became heir presumptive to his childless uncle, King Carol I of Romania. In 1889 the Romanian parliament recognised him as a prince of Romania. He was allowed to remain a Catholic, but his children had to be raised Orthodox, and for agreeing to this he was excommunicated, though the sentence was later lifted. He married Princess Marie of Edinburgh, a granddaughter of Queen Victoria, at Sigmaringen on 10 January 1893.

Ferdinand became king on 10 October 1914 after Carol I died without surviving children. Although he belonged to a cadet branch of the German ruling house, he led Romania into the First World War on the side of the Triple Entente on 27 August 1916, which earned him the nickname the Loyal, for keeping his oath to reign as a good Romanian. Emperor Wilhelm II had his name erased from the Hohenzollern register. After the Central Powers occupied Dobruja and Wallachia, Romania fought on in 1917 and stopped the German advance into Moldavia. When Russia made peace in 1918, Ferdinand refused to sign and ratify the Treaty of Bucharest.

Bessarabia, Bukovina and Transylvania joined the Kingdom of Romania in 1918 to 1920. Ferdinand was crowned king of Greater Romania on 15 October 1922 at Alba Iulia, in the newly consecrated Coronation Cathedral. His reign saw agrarian reform and universal suffrage, and politics were dominated by the National Liberal Party of Ion and Vintilă Brătianu.

In December 1925 his eldest son Carol renounced his rights to the throne, causing a dynastic crisis, because the next in line was Carol's young son Michael. Ferdinand removed Carol's name from the royal house. He died of colon cancer at Sinaia on 20 July 1927 and was succeeded by his grandson Michael under a regency of three. He is known in Romania as the Unifier.
ferdinand-i-of-the-two-sicilies: Ferdinand was born in Naples on 12 January 1751, the third son of King Charles VII and Queen Maria Amalia. When Charles succeeded his half-brother Ferdinand VI as king of Spain in August 1759, treaties forbade him to hold all three crowns.

On 6 October he abdicated the Neapolitan and Sicilian thrones in favour of Ferdinand, since his eldest son Philip had been excluded from the succession because of intellectual disability and his second son Charles was heir to Spain. A regency council was set up under the Tuscan Bernardo Tanucci, who neglected the boy's education and encouraged his love of pleasure and outdoor sports. Ferdinand founded the cadet House of Bourbon-Two Sicilies.

Ferdinand's minority ended in 1767, and his first act was the expulsion of the Jesuits. The following year he married Archduchess Maria Carolina, daughter of Empress Maria Theresa, who used a clause of the marriage contract to gain influence in the council of state.

Tanucci was dismissed in 1777, and the Englishman Sir John Acton, appointed director of marine in 1779, became the leading minister and was largely responsible for reducing the administration to a system of espionage, corruption and cruelty. In 1798, at his wife's urging, Ferdinand went to war with France and entered Rome on 29 November, but the defeat of some columns sent him hurrying back. He fled to Palermo on 23 December 1798 on Nelson's ship HMS Vanguard, and his six-year-old son Prince Alberto died on the stormy voyage.

The French established the Parthenopean Republic in January 1799, and Cardinal Fabrizio Ruffo recovered the mainland that May with British artillery, the Church and the pro-Bourbon aristocracy. Several hundred French collaborators were then executed. After the French victory at Austerlitz Ferdinand fled again on 23 January 1806, and Napoleon proclaimed his brother Joseph king of Naples. Ferdinand kept Sicily under British protection, where Lord William Bentinck insisted on constitutional reform and the queen was exiled to Austria.

After Joachim Murat fell in 1815 Ferdinand returned to Naples, bound by a secret treaty with Austria. In 1816 he abolished the Sicilian constitution, against his oath, and proclaimed the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies on 12 December. The revolt of General Guglielmo Pepe in July 1820 forced him to accept a constitution, but he repudiated it, and an Austrian army defeated the Neapolitans at the Battle of Rieti on 7 March 1821 and occupied Naples. He suppressed the liberals and Carbonari and died in Naples on 4 January 1825.
ferdinand-ii-archduke-of-austria: Ferdinand was the second son of Ferdinand I, Holy Roman Emperor, and Anna of Bohemia and Hungary, and a younger brother of Emperor Maximilian II. He grew up in Innsbruck, where his father governed the Austrian hereditary lands on behalf of Ferdinand's uncle Charles V. He was said to be his father's favourite son, and a visiting dignitary described him as handsome and friendlier than Maximilian. Among his teachers were Kaspar Ursinus Velius and Georg Tannstätter, and other young nobles were invited to court to be educated beside the two archdukes, speaking only Latin, Czech or other foreign languages with them.

At his father's behest Ferdinand took charge of the administration of Bohemia in 1547, and he led the campaign against the Turks in Hungary in 1556. In 1557 he secretly married Philippine Welser, daughter of an Augsburg patrician. Emperor Ferdinand I accepted the marriage only in 1559, on condition of secrecy. Their children were to bear the name of Austria but could inherit only if the House of Habsburg became extinct in the male line, and their sons took the title Margrave of Burgau.

After his father's death in 1564 Ferdinand ruled Tyrol and other Further Austrian possessions under the will, but stayed governor of Bohemia in Prague until 1567 at his brother Maximilian's wish. In his own lands he made sure that the Catholic Counter-Reformation prevailed, and he promoted the Renaissance in central Europe. His collections of art, armour and curiosities were housed at Ambras Castle in a museum built for the purpose. They began in Bohemia, and were so costly that he fell deeply into debt.

Philippine died in 1580, and in 1582 Ferdinand married his niece Anna Caterina Gonzaga, a daughter of William I, Duke of Mantua. He died on 24 January 1595. Because his sons by his first marriage could not inherit and the second marriage produced only daughters, Tyrol was reunited with the other Habsburg lands. His daughter Anna became empress as consort of Matthias, Holy Roman Emperor. The Chamber of Art and Curiosities at Ambras is the only Renaissance Kunstkammer of its kind preserved at its original location, and part of the collections went to the Kunsthistorisches Museum in Vienna.
ferdinand-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Ferdinand was born in the castle at Graz on 9 July 1578, the son of Archduke Charles II and Maria of Bavaria, her husband's niece, whose marriage reconciled the two leading Catholic families of the Holy Roman Empire. His mother managed his education. In early 1590 he was sent to the Jesuit college at Ingolstadt in Bavaria, to keep him away from the Lutheran nobles of Styria. His father died on 10 July 1590, and Ferdinand inherited Inner Austria, with regents appointed by his cousin Emperor Rudolf II. He took over its government in 1596 and 1597.

Ferdinand was charged with defending Croatia, Slavonia and south-eastern Hungary against the Ottoman Empire. He regarded the regulation of religion as a royal prerogative and from 1598 ordered the expulsion of Protestant pastors and teachers and set up commissions to restore Catholic parishes. His attempt to retake the fortress of Nagykanizsa ended in defeat in November 1601. In the Brothers' Quarrel he first backed Matthias against Rudolf II, but Matthias's concessions to Protestants outraged him. In 1617 Philip III of Spain acknowledged his right to succeed Matthias in Bohemia and Hungary in return for territorial concessions.

The Bohemian estates confirmed Ferdinand as successor only after he promised to respect their privileges. Disputes over the Letter of Majesty, which set out the freedoms of Bohemian Protestants, led on 23 May 1618 to an uprising in Prague, when armed nobles threw two royal governors out of a window. After Matthias died on 20 March 1619, Ferdinand was elected Holy Roman Emperor at Frankfurt on 28 August 1619, and the Bohemian estates deposed him as king and offered the crown to the Calvinist Frederick V of the Palatinate.

The Thirty Years' War, which began in 1618, followed from the failures of Rudolf II and Matthias on one account, but Ferdinand's measures against Protestantism spread it through the whole empire. He aimed to make Catholicism the only religion of the empire. The war left the empire devastated, and its population did not recover until 1710.
ferdinand-ii-of-aragon: Ferdinand was born on 10 March 1452 in Sos del Rey Católico in the Kingdom of Aragon, the son of John II of Aragon, of a cadet branch of the House of Trastámara, by his second wife, Juana Enríquez. On 19 October 1469 he married Isabella, the half-sister and heir presumptive of Henry IV of Castile, in Valladolid. The two were second cousins, and they married under a clear prenuptial agreement on sharing power and the joint motto tanto monta, monta tanto. When Isabella succeeded her brother he became king of Castile through his wife, and the two had first to fight a civil war against the supporters of Joanna la Beltraneja, which they won swiftly.

When Ferdinand succeeded his father in 1479, the Crown of Castile and the territories of the Crown of Aragon were united in a personal union, as separate units under the same monarchs. Their early joint rule saw the completion in 1492 of the conquest of the Emirate of Granada. In March of that year they issued the Alhambra Decree, ordering all Jews to convert or leave, and they commissioned Christopher Columbus. The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 divided the world beyond Europe between Portugal and Castile. In 1502 Ferdinand ended the religious freedom guaranteed to Muslims by the Treaty of Granada of 1491 and forced them to convert or leave.

The later part of his life was largely taken up with the Italian Wars against the kings of France. His general Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba won Naples from the French by 1504. After Isabella's death on 26 November 1504 Ferdinand became governor of Castile for their daughter Joanna, but the Castilian nobility rebuffed him and in the Treaty of Villafáfila of 1506 he gave way to her husband Philip. In 1506 he married Germaine of Foix. Philip's death in September 1506 returned him to power, and in 1507 he had Joanna confined and ruled Castile in her name. He took part in the League of Cambrai against Venice and the Holy League against Louis XII, and in 1512 he invaded Navarre.

Ferdinand died on 23 January 1516 at Madrigalejo in Extremadura, and is entombed at the Capilla Real in Granada, beside Isabella, Joanna and Philip. Joanna inherited Aragon and was nominally his successor, but power soon passed to her son Charles, who inherited the Spanish and Italian lands of his maternal grandparents as well as the Austrian and Burgundian lands of his father's family. The Catholic Monarchs centralised the crown's power, at least in name, and laid the groundwork for a formidable military. Legally, Castile and Aragon remained two kingdoms until the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707 to 1716, though Ferdinand is considered the de facto first king of Spain.
ferdinand-ii-of-the-two-sicilies: Ferdinand was born in Palermo to King Francis I of the Two Sicilies and his second wife, Maria Isabella of Spain. His grandparents included King Ferdinand I of the Two Sicilies and Queen Maria Carolina of Austria, and Charles IV of Spain and Maria Luisa of Parma. His sister Teresa Cristina became Empress of Brazil as the wife of Pedro II. In his early years he was fairly popular: progressives credited him with liberal ideas, and his easy manners won over the lazzaroni, the lower classes of Naples.

On succeeding in 1830 Ferdinand promised impartial justice and financial reform. The early years were comparatively peaceful: he cut taxes and expenditure, had the first railway in Italy built between Naples and the royal palace at Portici, and his fleet had the first steamship on the peninsula. Telegraph links were set up between Naples and Palermo. In 1837, however, he violently suppressed Sicilian demonstrators who demanded a constitution, and he kept strict police surveillance of his domains.

A rising in Palermo on 12 January 1848 spread across Sicily and sparked the revolutions of 1848 elsewhere in Europe. On 29 January Ferdinand was forced to grant a constitution modelled on the French Charter of 1830, but a dispute over the deputies' oath led to riots, the army dispersed the crowds, and he dissolved parliament on 13 March 1849 and ruled again as an absolute monarch. Sicily declared independence under Ruggero Settimo, who pronounced the king deposed on 13 April 1848. An army of 20,000 under General Carlo Filangieri was sent, and the bombardment of Messina earned the king the nickname re bomba. Sicily was subdued on 15 May 1849.

Between 1848 and 1851 the king's policies drove many into exile, and an estimated 2,000 suspected revolutionaries or dissidents were jailed. After a visit to Naples in 1850, William Gladstone wrote letters describing the kingdom's conditions, which provoked outrage in much of Europe and contributed to its diplomatic isolation. Britain and France recalled their ambassadors in 1856. A soldier tried to assassinate Ferdinand that year, and many believe the infection from the bayonet led to his death on 22 May 1859. His kingdom was later invaded by Giuseppe Garibaldi and absorbed into a united Italy in 1861.
ferdinand-iii-grand-duke-of-tuscany: Ferdinand was born in Florence on 6 May 1769 into the House of Habsburg-Lorraine, the second son of Leopold, then Grand Duke of Tuscany, and Infanta Maria Luisa of Spain. Because the grand duchy was a secundogeniture, he succeeded his father when Leopold was elected Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, officially taking office on 22 July 1790. In 1790 he also married his double first cousin, Princess Luisa of Naples and Sicily; she died in 1802, and their children included the future Leopold II of Tuscany.

In 1792, during the French Revolution, Ferdinand became the first monarch to recognise the new French First Republic formally. Persuaded by the rulers of Britain and Russia to join the War of the First Coalition, he gave his allies passive support without enthusiasm, and after a year of French victories he became the first member of the coalition to give up, declaring Tuscany's neutrality in a proclamation of 1 March 1795.

By 1799 republicans had set up a provisional government in Florence and he fled to Vienna. The Treaty of Aranjuez of 1801 forced him to renounce Tuscany, which Napoleon turned into the Kingdom of Etruria as compensation for the dispossessed Bourbon Dukes of Parma.

He received the secularised Electorate of Salzburg and the rank of Prince-elector on 26 December 1802. On 25 December 1805 the Treaty of Pressburg gave Salzburg to his older brother, Emperor Francis II, and Ferdinand became Duke of Würzburg, a state created from the old Prince-Bishopric, while remaining an elector. After the Holy Roman Empire's dissolution in 1806 he took the title Grand Duke of Würzburg.

On 30 May 1814, after Napoleon's fall, Ferdinand was restored as Grand Duke of Tuscany. In 1821 he married Princess Maria Ferdinanda of Saxony, a much younger woman, but the marriage produced no children. He died in Florence on 18 June 1824 and was succeeded by his son Leopold.
ferdinand-iii-holy-roman-emperor: Ferdinand was born in Graz on 13 July 1608, the third son of Ferdinand II, Holy Roman Emperor, and Maria Anna of Bavaria, and was baptised Ferdinand Ernst. He grew up in Carinthia and received religious and scholarly training from Jesuits. After the deaths of his brothers Karl in 1603 and Johann Karl in 1619, he was designated his father's successor. He became Archduke of Austria in 1621, King of Hungary on 8 December 1625 and King of Bohemia on 27 November 1627. In 1631 he married his cousin Maria Anna of Spain.

After Albrecht von Wallenstein's assassination, Ferdinand took command of the imperial army on 2 May 1634. He regained Regensburg in July and Donauwörth in August, and in September won the decisive Battle of Nördlingen with Spanish forces under Cardinal Infante Ferdinand, although his personal part in it was limited. He was elected King of the Romans on 22 December 1636 and became emperor on his father's death on 15 February 1637, when much of the empire had been devastated by two decades of war. By 1640 he had permanently lost control of northern Germany.

Peace negotiations began in Münster and Osnabrück in 1644 and lasted until 1648 while fighting went on. He suffered defeat at Jankau on 6 March 1645, after which a Swedish army advanced to Vienna. In the Peace of Linz of 1645 he guaranteed the Hungarian estates freedom of religion for Protestants. Spanish support ceased in 1645, and his instructions to his chief negotiator, Maximilian von Trauttmansdorff, show that he was ready to surrender more than was in the end necessary.

The Peace of Westphalia cost the empire territory: the Three Bishoprics went to France, Sweden received Rügen and Western Pomerania, and the Netherlands and Switzerland gained full independence. The imperial estates won the right to form alliances with foreign powers, and Ferdinand's attempt at absolutist rule of the empire failed. In his own lands his power was greater than his predecessors' before 1618. He restructured the Aulic Council and summoned the last traditional Reichstag in 1652.

Ferdinand died on 2 April 1657 and rests in the Capuchin Crypt in Vienna. His son Leopold I succeeded him after the death of his elder son Ferdinand IV in 1654. He was a patron of music and the first Habsburg monarch recognised as a composer; some of his masses, motets and hymns survive in manuscript.
ferdinand-iii-of-castile: Ferdinand, called the Saint, was the son of Alfonso IX of León and Berengaria of Castile, and was born at the Monastery of Valparaíso, in what is now the Province of Zamora. Pope Innocent III annulled his parents' marriage in 1204 because of consanguinity, though the children were recognised as legitimate, and Berengaria took them to the court of her father, Alfonso VIII of Castile. When her brother Henry I died in 1217 she succeeded him with Ferdinand as heir and quickly crowned him co-ruler. Alfonso of León felt tricked, so the young king began his reign with a war against his father and a faction of Castilian nobles. His mother remained a key influence, even in his choice of wife, Elisabeth of Swabia.

When Alfonso IX died in 1230 his will left León to Ferdinand's older half-sisters Sancha and Dulce. Ferdinand contested it, and the treaty of Benavente, signed on 11 December 1230, gave him León in return for compensation to the sisters. He became the first ruler of both kingdoms since Alfonso VII died in 1157.

A succession crisis in the Almohad Caliphate after 1224 gave Ferdinand his opening. In 1228 the last Almohad forces left Spain for Morocco, and al-Andalus fell into the hands of local strongmen. From then until 1248 he took Úbeda in 1233, Córdoba in 1236, Jaén in 1246 and, on 22 December 1248, Seville, and Murcia came by the pact of Alcaraz in 1243. Only the Emirate of Granada remained unconquered, and in 1238 he extracted a tributary arrangement from it. He divided the conquered land among the military orders, the Church and the nobility, and Pope Gregory IX called him athleta Christi, champion of Christ.

Ferdinand strengthened the University of Salamanca, erected the present Cathedral of Burgos and founded houses of friars of the Dominican, Franciscan, Trinitarian and Mercedarian orders throughout Andalusia. He died on 30 May 1252 after a dropsy contracted in the winter of 1251 and was buried in the Cathedral of Seville. He left his son Alfonso X a greatly enlarged kingdom, whose boundaries stayed nearly unchanged until the late 15th century. Pope Clement X canonised him in 1671.
ferdinand-lassalle: Ferdinand Lassal, who later adopted the French spelling Lassalle, was born in Breslau, now Wrocław, on 11 April 1825. His Jewish family had moved to Prussian Silesia from Poland in the late 18th century, and his father, Heymann Lassal, a prosperous wholesale silk merchant, had trained for a rabbinical career. A diary he kept as a boy shows a quick-witted, ambitious youth, sensitive about his Jewishness and his provincial background. After passing his matriculation examination in 1843 he studied at the universities of Breslau and Berlin, where he discovered Hegel, whose philosophy he later described as a second birth.

In 1846 Lassalle met Countess Sophie von Hatzfeldt, unhappily married to Count Edmund von Hatzfeldt-Kinsweiler, and spent the next eight years almost entirely on her legal claims against her husband. The case brought him public renown and, in 1848, a sentence of two months for criminal libel; arrested for complicity in the theft of documents, he was acquitted at Cologne in August 1848. There he met Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. Engels disliked his ostentation, while Marx was more tolerant, though a report of 1855 left him mistrustful. Lassalle also wrote Heraclitus the Obscure (1857) and The System of Acquired Rights (1861).

In April 1862 he gave two lectures in Berlin arguing that a constitution is the factual power relationship in a society written down, and that the working class should form its own party. In 1863 he founded the General German Workers' Association, whose platform called for socialism through state-aided producers' co-operatives won by universal suffrage. He negotiated secretly with Otto von Bismarck, hoping to ally the workers' movement with the conservative state against the liberal bourgeoisie.

In the summer of 1864 Lassalle became engaged to Helene von Dönniges, daughter of a Bavarian diplomat. Her family opposed the match because of his Jewish origins and political notoriety, and she was pressured into renouncing him for a previous suitor, Yanko von Rakowitza. Lassalle challenged her father to a duel; he declined, and Rakowitza accepted in his place. Lassalle was killed in a duel on 31 August 1864, aged 39.

The association then had only a few thousand members, but under Johann Baptist von Schweitzer it kept Lassalle's centralised organisation and pro-governmental tactics. In 1875 it merged with the Social Democratic Workers' Party at the Gotha Congress to form what became the Social Democratic Party of Germany, whose programme drew on his demand for state-aided co-operatives. Marx thought his state socialism a misunderstanding of his own theories.
ferdinand-magellan: Magellan was born in northern Portugal, possibly around 1480. His father, Pedro de Magalhães, was a minor member of the Portuguese nobility and mayor of the town, and his mother was Alda de Mezquita. He was brought up as a page of Queen Eleanor, consort of King John II, and in 1495 he entered the service of Manuel I.

In March 1505 he enlisted in the fleet sent to host Francisco de Almeida as the first viceroy of Portuguese India, and he remained there eight years. He took part in the battle of Cannanore in 1506, where he was wounded, and the Battle of Diu in 1509. In 1511, under Afonso de Albuquerque, he and his friend Francisco Serrão took part in the conquest of Malacca. Serrão went on to the Moluccas, and his letters to Magellan later gave decisive information about the spice-producing territories.

King Manuel I repeatedly rejected Magellan's proposals for expeditions to the Spice Islands. Magellan then offered the project to Charles I of Spain, who approved it. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 Portugal was to control the eastern routes around the Cape of Good Hope, so Magellan proposed a southwestern passage around South America. He was given command of the five-ship Armada of Molucca and sailed in August 1519 with about 270 men. King Manuel did all he could to disrupt the preparations, and a Portuguese fleet sent after him failed to capture him.

The fleet crossed the Atlantic and went south to Patagonia. Despite storms and mutinies, it passed through the Strait of Magellan into the sea Magellan renamed the Mar Pacifico, landed at Guam and reached the Philippines. Magellan converted as many as 2,200 locals to Christianity, including Rajah Humabon of Cebu, but Lapulapu, the leader of Mactan, resisted. On the morning of 27 April 1521 Magellan sailed to Mactan with a small force and was killed in the battle that followed.

Antonio Pigafetta and Ginés de Mafra left accounts of the death. Lapulapu refused a ransom of copper and iron for the body. Under Juan Sebastián Elcano the expedition reached the Spice Islands, and the ship Elcano commanded returned to Spain in September 1522, completing the first circumnavigation of Earth. In the aftermath Magellan was widely discredited in Spain and Portugal. Some in Portugal regarded him as a traitor for having sailed for Spain.
ferdinand-marcos: Ferdinand Marcos was born in Sarrat, Ilocos Norte, on 11 September 1917. His father, Mariano Marcos, was a lawyer who represented Ilocos Norte in the House of Representatives from 1925 to 1931. Marcos studied law at the University of the Philippines, where he was a national rifle champion. In 1935 Julio Nalundasan, who had defeated Mariano Marcos in two elections, was shot dead at his home. Ferdinand and his uncle were convicted of the murder, but the conviction was overturned on appeal. He fought the Japanese after joining the United States Army in 1941. Researchers later found that most stories about his military service were inaccurate or untrue.

Marcos won his father's former seat in 1949, sat in the House of Representatives until 1959, in the Senate from 1959 to 1965, and was Senate president from 1963 to 1965. He was elected president in 1965 and re-elected in 1969. His early policies centred on massive infrastructure construction, funded by foreign lending. A balance of payments crisis in 1969 and growing Philippine involvement in the Vietnam War then triggered social unrest.

On 23 September 1972 Marcos declared martial law, extending his rule beyond the two-term constitutional limit. A 1973 plebiscite, overseen by the military, ratified his rule; media outlets and opposition politicians were silenced. He lifted martial law on 17 January 1981 and won a third term. The assassination of Ninoy Aquino in 1983 and an economic collapse damaged his standing. He called snap elections in 1986 against Aquino's widow, Corazon Aquino, and allegations of mass electoral fraud led to the People Power Revolution of February 1986.

On 25 February 1986 Marcos and his family left Malacañang by helicopter for Clark Air Base and flew on to Hawaii. He died there on 28 September 1989. The regime committed documented human rights abuses, especially after 1972, against students, farmers, journalists, priests and nuns and political opponents. Estimates generally include about 1,500 to 4,000 extrajudicial killings or disappearances, and tens of thousands imprisoned or tortured. The Marcos family denies responsibility for these violations.
ferdinand-of-brunswick-wolfenbuttel: Ferdinand was born on 12 January 1721, the fourth son of Ferdinand Albert II, Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg. He joined the Prussian army as a colonel in 1740 and fought at Mollwitz and Chotusitz. In 1744 he received command of Frederick the Great's Leibgarde battalion, and at the Battle of Soor in 1745 he distinguished himself in the assault on a steep hill defended by his own elder brother, Louis Ernest. In the ten years of peace that followed he worked closely with Frederick, who made the guard battalion a model for the whole army, and he became one of the king's most intimate friends.

At the start of the Seven Years' War in 1756 Ferdinand led a Prussian column against Dresden and the right wing of the infantry at Lobositz, and in 1757 he distinguished himself at Prague and served in the Rossbach campaign. He then took command of the Hanoverian Army of Observation, raised and paid for by Britain, after the Duke of Cumberland had failed to stop the French invasion of Hanover. He accepted on condition of direct access to George II. Within a week he had taken the offensive, and by spring 1758 he had driven the French out of Hanover; British troops joined his army from June 1758.

After crossing the Rhine he fought an indecisive battle at Rheinberg and won at Krefeld, but fell back to the River Lippe. Defeated at Bergen on 13 April 1759, he retreated and then checked the French advance at Minden, which ended the immediate threat to Hanover. Victories at Villinghausen, Wilhelmsthal and Warburg followed, and his pressure in the west helped Frederick in the east. Frederick made him field marshal, and George II gave him the Order of the Garter.

After the war the Austrians also gave him the rank of field marshal and a regiment, and during the American War of Independence there was a suggestion, which came to nothing, that he command the British forces. An estrangement from Frederick in 1766 led him to leave Prussian service, though he visited the king four times afterwards. He retired to Brunswick and his castle of Vechelde, spent much of his income on those who had suffered in the war and became a patron of learning and a leading Freemason. Unmarried, he died on 3 July 1792; an equestrian statue of him was raised in Berlin in 1863.
ferdinand-of-majorca: Ferdinand was born in 1278 at Perpignan, the third son of King James II of Majorca. Frederick III of Sicily sent him to take command of the Catalan Company in Frederick's name, but Bernat de Rocafort, one of the company's leaders, rebuffed him. On his way back with the chronicler Ramón Muntaner he was captured by the Venetians at Negroponte. He had been freed by 1310, when he distinguished himself at the siege of Almería by killing the son of the King of Guadix, and in 1311 he became Viscount of Aumelas and Lord of Frontignan.

In 1313 he returned to Sicily to fight in the war against the Angevins and was made Lord of Catania. There he met Margaret of Villehardouin, who was pressing her claim to the Principality of Achaea. She gave him her daughter Isabella of Sabran in marriage at Messina and resigned Akova and her claim to the couple. Margaret died in March 1315 in captivity at Chlemoutsi, and Isabella died at Catania on 7 May 1315, shortly after bearing a son, the future James III of Majorca.

Ferdinand then sailed with a small company to the Morea to uphold the claim, now his son's. He seized Clarenza in June 1315 and for a time controlled the Morea, and in the autumn he married Isabella of Ibelin, daughter of Philip of Ibelin, Seneschal of Cyprus.

In the spring of 1316 his rival Matilda of Hainaut and her husband Louis of Burgundy returned with Venetian help. The aid Ferdinand expected from Majorca, Sicily and the Catalan Company in Athens came late, and facing superior numbers he was killed at the Battle of Manolada near Glarentza on 5 July 1316. His elder son became heir presumptive of Majorca, and a posthumous son, also Ferdinand, succeeded him as Viscount of Aumelas.
ferdinand-vii-of-spain: Ferdinand was born on 14 October 1784 at El Escorial, the eldest surviving son of Charles IV and Maria Luisa of Parma. As heir he was excluded from government by his parents and their favourite, the Prime Minister Manuel Godoy. In October 1807 he was arrested for his part in the El Escorial Conspiracy, which sought support from Napoleon, and submitted to his parents. After a popular riot at Aranjuez, Charles IV abdicated in March 1808 and Ferdinand took the throne. He abdicated on 6 May 1808, and Napoleon kept him under guard in France for six years at the Château de Valençay.

The Spanish people rejected Napoleon's choice of Joseph Bonaparte as king, and the Peninsular War began. After the Battle of Bailén the Council of Castile declared the abdications of Bayonne void on 11 August 1808, and Ferdinand was proclaimed king on 24 August. Napoleon recognised him in the Treaty of Valençay of 11 December 1813. Ferdinand returned to a country governed under the liberal Constitution of 1812. On 4 May 1814 he ordered its abolition, and on 10 May he had its liberal authors arrested. He argued that the Cortes had been illegally assembled in his absence, and he never convened a traditional one.

His restored government was guided by a small circle of favourites, and he changed ministers every few months. He reinstated the Inquisition and the Jesuits and suppressed Freemasonry. Several military pronunciamientos followed. The most successful, led by Rafael del Riego in 1820, forced him to accept the constitution and began the Liberal Triennium. In 1823 the Congress of Verona authorised a French intervention that restored him to absolute power, and reprisals followed. Meanwhile wars of independence had broken out in the Americas. After the Treaty of Córdoba of 1821 he refused the Mexican crown and declared the Mexican constitution void.

In May 1830 Ferdinand published the Pragmatic Sanction, which allowed daughters to succeed. His daughter Isabella was born on 10 October 1830 and displaced his brother, Infante Carlos María Isidro, in the line of succession. Ferdinand died in late September 1833. Carlos claimed to be the legitimate king, and Maria Christina, regent for her daughter, turned to the liberals for support, which led to the Carlist Wars. Historians typically criticise his reign. Stanley G. Payne called him in many ways the basest king in Spanish history.
ferdinand-von-hompesch-zu-bolheim: Hompesch was born on 9 November 1744 in the village of Bolheim, now part of Zülpich in the Eifel. He was admitted to the Knights Hospitaller on 10 July 1761, aged 14, with a dispensation from the Holy See, and served as a page to Grand Master Manuel Pinto da Fonseca. He rose to castellan by 1768, became lieutenant in 1770, inspecting the Order's ships and fortifications, and took charge of the island's munitions in 1774.

In late 1775 he was appointed the Order's ambassador at the imperial court in Vienna, a post he held for 25 years, and in 1776 he became a Knight Grand Cross and a member of the Order's Standing Council. He tried without success to reunite the Protestant Bailiwick of Brandenburg with the Order, held a series of commanderies from Rothenburg to Villingen and in 1796 became Grand Bailiff of the German langue. Elected Grand Master on 17 July 1797, he raised Żabbar, Żejtun and Siġġiewi to the status of cities.

Warned in 1798 that the French fleet bound for Egypt meant to attack Malta, he did nothing to strengthen its defences. Napoleon arrived on 9 June with 29,000 men against the Order's 7,000 and demanded entry to the harbour for his whole fleet; when Hompesch allowed only two ships at a time, the French landed on 10 June. A rebellion of Maltese people, the Order's rule against fighting fellow Christians and the reluctance of its French knights weakened resistance, and Hompesch capitulated on 11 June, ceding sovereignty to France the next day in return for promises of a principality and a pension.

He left Malta for Trieste on 18 June 1798 and set up a new headquarters for the Order there, protesting against the French occupation. His abdication of 6 July 1799 took the form of letters to Emperor Francis II and Paul I of Russia; he sent none to the pope, who never accepted it, and from Ljubljana in 1801 he declared that the Austrian government had forced him to sign. He moved to Montpellier in 1804 and died there penniless of asthma on 12 May 1805, and is buried in the Church of Saint Eulalie.
ferdinand-von-zeppelin: Ferdinand von Zeppelin was born on 8 July 1838 into a noble family. He spent his childhood with his sister and brother at the Girsberg manor near Konstanz, educated by private tutors. He became a cadet at the military school at Ludwigsburg in 1855 and began his career as an officer in the Württemberg army.

In 1863 he went to Virginia as an observer for the Union's Army of the Potomac in the American Civil War. At Saint Paul, Minnesota, he made his first aerial ascent with the German-born balloonist John Steiner on 19 August, which he later credited with starting his thinking about dirigibles. A reconnaissance mission behind enemy lines in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 made him known to many Germans.

Zeppelin first set out his idea for a large airship in a diary entry of 25 March 1874: a rigidly framed outer envelope containing a number of separate gasbags. After leaving the army, where his handling of a cavalry brigade at the manoeuvres of 1890 had been severely criticised, he devoted himself to airships. The engineer Theodor Kober refined the design, the Prussian Airship Service rejected it in 1895, and Zeppelin received a patent in August of that year. In 1898 a joint stock company was formed, and he invested 441,000 marks, over half its capital.

On 2 July 1900 the LZ 1 made the first flight over Lake Constance near Friedrichshafen and stayed up for 20 minutes. It was not judged successful enough to justify government investment, and Zeppelin, his funds exhausted, suspended work. The LZ 2 flew only once, in January 1906, and was wrecked by wind. The LZ 3 flew successfully, and the Reichstag voted him 500,000 marks.

The LZ 4 was destroyed by fire at Echterdingen in 1908, but public enthusiasm raised over 6 million marks, which created Luftschiffbau Zeppelin GmbH and the Zeppelin Foundation. The government accepted LZ 3 in November 1908. Until 1914 the German Aviation Association carried 37,250 passengers without incident, and in the First World War the German empire used Zeppelins as long-distance bombers against Belgium, France and the United Kingdom.

Zeppelin died on 8 March 1917, before the end of the First World War. The Treaty of Versailles later halted the Zeppelin project for a time, and his successor Hugo Eckener led its resurgence. The airship LZ 127 Graf Zeppelin, which circled the world, was named after him, as was the unfinished German aircraft carrier Graf Zeppelin.
ferdinando-carlo-gonzaga: Ferdinando Carlo Gonzaga was born at Revere on 31 August 1652, the only child of Duke Charles II of Mantua and Montferrat. At the age of thirteen he received the imperial investiture of the Duchy of Mantua in a coronation at the Cathedral of St. Peter. In 1671 he married Anna Isabella Gonzaga, daughter of Ferrante III Gonzaga, Duke of Guastalla, a match arranged with the help of his aunt, the dowager empress Eleanor Gonzaga. As heir of Guastalla and Luzzara, Anna Isabella brought her rights to these lands, long disputed between two Gonzaga lines, to the Mantua branch.

The young duke's first acts were to curb abuses in the collection of court fees and to reform public order in the duchy. He was intelligent and a lover of music, and in 1700 the composer Tomaso Albinoni dedicated his second opera to him, but he proved more inclined to women and charitable works than to governing. Under his rule Mantua grew more autonomous of the Empire, which roused the suspicion of Spain. Spain suspended its yearly payment of 50,000 crowns towards the garrison of Casale.

Thwarted by the Austrians in his attempt to take Guastalla, he made a pact with Louis XIV of France on 8 December 1678 to sell Casale. His minister Count Ercole Antonio Mattioli, imprisoned at Pinerolo from April 1679 for revealing the pact to France's enemies, may have been the Man in the Iron Mask. The duke denied everything, but a new pact in 1681 brought him a yearly pension of sixty thousand lire, a general's career and a share in future French conquests in Italy. The French occupied Casale on 29 September 1681, and the duke lost respect in Italy.

After his first wife's death in 1703 he courted Louise Bernardine de Durfort, who begged Louis XIV not to make her marry him, and on 8 November 1704 he married Suzanne Henriette de Lorraine in Milan; the marriage was childless. When the French were driven back over the Alps in 1706 he paid heavily for siding with them. The Diet of Regensburg confirmed the imperial ban against him on 30 June 1708 and confiscated all his possessions. He died the same year in Padua, and Mantua ceased its independent existence.
ferdinando-gorges: Ferdinando Gorges was the second son of Edward Gorges of Wraxall, in Somerset, and his wife Cicely Lygon, and was probably born in Clerkenwell, where the family kept its London house, though possibly at Wraxall. His father died young in 1568. Through the male line the family descended from the Russells of Kingston Russell, a Theobald Russell having taken the Gorges name and arms to inherit the estates of the old Anglo-Norman Gorges family. He was brought up at Nailsea Court near Wraxall and had distant family ties to Humphrey Gilbert and Walter Raleigh.

By 1587 Gorges was a captain, one of the commanders of the 800 soldiers sent from Flushing in the attempt by the Earl of Leicester to relieve the Siege of Sluis. By September 1588 he was a prisoner at Lisle. He was wounded at the siege of Paris in 1589 and knighted at the siege of Rouen in 1591, and was rewarded with the governorship of the fort at Plymouth. In 1597 he raised the alarm against a Spanish Armada later scattered by storms. Drawn into the Essex Conspiracy in 1601, he testified against its leader, Robert Devereux, 2nd Earl of Essex.

After the Anglo-Spanish War ended in 1604 Gorges turned to colonisation. His interest was said to have been stirred when Captain George Weymouth brought him three captured American Indians. As a shareholder in the Plymouth Company he helped fund the failed Popham Colony of 1607, and in 1616 he sent Richard Vines to winter at the mouth of the Sago River.

The patent of 10 August 1622 with John Mason covered the land between the Merrimack and Kennebec rivers; in 1629 the two divided it, Mason's part south of the Piscataqua becoming New Hampshire. His son Robert Gorges was Governor-General of New England from 1623 to 1624. In the 1630s Gorges challenged the charter of the Massachusetts Bay Colony before the Privy Council, without success.

Gorges married four times. He died on 24 May 1647 at his wife's home in Long Ashton and was buried there in the Smyth crypt of All Saint's Church, without markings. His eldest son John inherited the Province of Maine. In May 1677 his grandson, also Ferdinando Gorges, sold the family's rights in Maine to Massachusetts for £1,250, ending the hope of an independent proprietary colony. His efforts earned him the title of Father of English Colonization in North America.
ferdinando-i-de-medici: Ferdinando was the fifth son of Cosimo I de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, and Eleanor of Toledo, daughter of the Spanish viceroy of Naples. He was made a cardinal in 1562 at the age of 13 but was never ordained a priest. In Rome he proved an able administrator, founded the Villa Medici and acquired the antiquities collected by Andrea della Valle in 1584, along with other works such as the Medici lions.

Ferdinando succeeded his brother Francesco I in 1587, aged 38, and was in many ways his opposite: approachable and generous, he set out to rule mildly. He re-established the justice system, and Tuscany regained the independence his brother had given up. He founded the Medici Oriental Press, which published many books in Arabic script, and he made Livorno a refuge for Spanish Jews and other persecuted groups. He expanded the harbour built by Cosimo I, rerouted part of the Arno into the Naviglio canal to link Florence and Pisa, and promoted an irrigation project in the Val di Chiana.

He kept his cardinal's position for two years, then gave it up to marry Christina of Lorraine in 1589; her dowry included 600,000 crowns in cash. His foreign policy sought to free Tuscany from Spanish domination. After the assassination of Henry III of France in 1589 he financed Henry IV, urged him to embrace Catholicism and used his influence with Pope Clement VIII to win acknowledgement of the conversion. He also obtained formal investiture of Siena, strengthened the Tuscan fleet, which defeated Barbary pirates in 1607 and a larger Turkish fleet the next year, and in 1608 sent an expedition under Captain Robert Thornton towards northern Brazil and the Amazon.

In 1600 his court staged Jacopo Peri's Euridice to mark the marriage of his niece Marie de' Medici to Henry IV, an early landmark in the emergence of opera. Ferdinando died on 17 February 1609 and was succeeded as grand duke by his son Cosimo II.
ferdinando-ii-de-medici: Ferdinando was born on 14 July 1610, the eldest son of Cosimo II de' Medici and Maria Maddalena of Austria. He was ten years old when his father died, and his mother and his paternal grandmother Christina of Lorraine acted as joint regents. They arranged his marriage to Vittoria della Rovere, a granddaughter of the last Duke of Urbino, hoping to acquire the duchy, but they were too weak politically to secure it, and the Papal States conquered Urbino. In his seventeenth year Ferdinando toured Europe, visiting Rome, Bologna, Ferrara, Venice, Austria and Prague. His personal rule began a year later, though Christina remained the power behind the throne until her death in 1636.

A plague swept through Florence in 1630 and killed a tenth of its people. Unlike the Tuscan nobility, Ferdinando and his brothers stayed in the city and went through it on foot to ease the suffering. Tuscany took part in the Wars of Castro, its last military conflict under the Medici, and defeated the forces of Pope Urban VIII in 1643. The treasury was so empty that the state could not pay interest on its bonds, and the rate was lowered by 0.75 per cent. The economy decayed to the point that barter became common in rural markets, the beginning of a long Tuscan decline.

Ferdinando was fascinated by new instruments and installed hygrometers, barometers, thermometers and telescopes in the Palazzo Pitti. In 1654 he is reported to have invented a sealed-glass spirit thermometer, marked with 360 divisions. His brother Leopoldo established the Accademia del Cimento in 1657 to bring scientists from across Tuscany to Florence, and Ferdinando took an active part in it. Like his father, he was a patron and friend of Galileo, who dedicated his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems to him. He tried to keep the Holy See from holding a full hearing and kept Galileo in Florence until December 1632. In June 1633 the Roman Inquisition convicted Galileo, and after his sentence was commuted to house arrest Ferdinando visited him at his villa.

Ferdinando died on 23 May 1670 of apoplexy and dropsy and was buried in the Basilica of San Lorenzo, the Medici crypt. His marriage to Vittoria was unhappy, but produced two children who reached adulthood: Cosimo, born in 1642, who succeeded him as Cosimo III, and Francesco Maria, born in 1660. He was remembered by his contemporaries as a man of culture and science. His 49-year rule saw the start of the economic decline that his successor Cosimo III made worse.
ferdinando-martini: Martini was born in Florence, in the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, to Marianna and Vincenzo Martini; his father was Secretary General of Finance for Tuscany. His mother died of cholera when he was 14, and his father died in 1862. He did poorly at school and never attended university, though the University of Padua later gave him an honorary degree. He won an award in 1863 for his comedy I nuovi ricchi.

Martini stood for the Chamber of Deputies for Pescia in 1874 and lost in the runoff; the election was annulled, as was his by-election victory of 1875 by 20 votes. He finally won on 30 January 1876 by 16 votes and took almost 90 per cent of the vote in the general election later that year. He was Minister of Public Education from 1892 to 1893, ambassador to Argentina from 1910, Minister of the Colonies from 1915 to 1916 and a senator from 1923.

Before the First Italo-Ethiopian War he warned that Italy lacked the soldiers for the campaign, noting that the British had a large base in Egypt for their war against the Mahdist State. Appointed governor of Italian Eritrea on 30 November 1897, its first civilian governor, he favoured using the colony for raw materials rather than settlement. Because many Italian immigrants were returning home at state expense, an order of 1 December 1898 required newcomers to prove they could support themselves and to pay at least half the cost of their return.

He edited his father's plays in 1876, founded Fanfulla della domenica in 1879 and Domenica letteraria in 1882, and published the memoirs of Giuseppe Giusti in 1890. His own books include Nell'Affrica Italiana (1891), a report on his years in Eritrea (1913) and his autobiography Confessioni e ricordi (1922); his Diario Eritreo appeared in 1942. He supported universal suffrage from 1881 and women's suffrage, Italy's entry into the First World War on the side of the Triple Entente and the Manifesto of the Fascist Intellectuals. He died at Monsummano Terme in 1928, and his manuscripts went to the National Central Library.
ferenc-nagy: Ferenc Nagy was born on 8 October 1903 into a family of middle-level peasants in the small town of Bisse. Self-taught, he began in politics by writing news articles, co-founded the Peasant Union and in October 1930 took part in founding the Independent Smallholders' Party. He entered Parliament in 1939 and opposed the war and the Nazis. The Gestapo arrested him after the German occupation of March 1944, but the government of Géza Lakatos had him released, and after the Arrow Cross coup he went into hiding.

After the war he helped organise the provisional government and became second-in-command of his party after Zoltán Tildy. When the Smallholders won a large majority in November 1945, pressure from the Soviet-dominated Allied Commission forced a coalition with the Communists and Social Democrats, and Nagy became speaker of parliament.

As prime minister Nagy favoured parliamentary democracy over both the prewar aristocratic order and a Communist dictatorship. His government ended a world-record hyperinflation by replacing the pengő with the forint in August 1946, helped by gold reserves that President Harry Truman agreed in June 1946 to return. It signed the Paris Peace Treaties of 1947 and a population exchange with Czechoslovakia.

The Communists used salami tactics against his party, starting with a Left Bloc in March 1946 that demanded the expulsion of 20 Smallholder deputies. Nagy hoped to appease them until a peace treaty brought a Soviet withdrawal. In 1947 the party of Mátyás Rákosi alleged a vast conspiracy, forced the arrest or recall of over 50 Smallholder deputies, and the Soviets abducted the party's general secretary, Béla Kovács. Nagy left for Switzerland on 14 May 1947; with his son held hostage in Budapest, he agreed to resign on 30 May.

Granted asylum in the United States, Nagy wrote The Struggle behind the Iron Curtain (1948) and bought a farm in Herndon, Virginia, with its royalties. He sat on the Hungarian Committee in exile, attended the Bandung Conference of 1955 as an observer for the United States government, and was kept from returning in 1956 by the authorities in Austria. He led the International Peasant Union from 1964 to 1970 and died at Herndon on 12 June 1979. He was Hungary's last non-Communist head of government until 1989–90.
ferenc-szalasi: Ferenc Szálasi was born on 6 January 1897 in Kassa, now Košice in Slovakia, the son of a soldier, and was of mixed Armenian, German, Hungarian, Slovak and Rusyn ancestry. He studied at military academies and served on the front line for 36 months in the Austro-Hungarian Army in the First World War. In 1925 he became a staff officer of the restored Kingdom of Hungary under Regent Miklós Horthy.

He became a fanatical right-wing nationalist and a proponent of Hungarism, which advocated expanding Hungary back to its borders before the Treaty of Trianon. In 1933 he published a pamphlet, a plan for building the Hungarian state, and a military court expelled him from the General Staff. In 1937 he founded the Hungarian National Socialist Party. Imprisoned in 1938, he was proclaimed leader of the Arrow Cross Party by his followers. He was granted amnesty in 1940 but had to run the party clandestinely after Horthy outlawed it.

After the German occupation of March 1944 the Arrow Cross Party was legalised. When Horthy tried to take Hungary out of the war, the Germans kidnapped his son and threatened to kill him unless Horthy abdicated in favour of Szálasi. Horthy signed under duress, and the Government of National Unity was formed on 16 October 1944. On 4 November Szálasi was sworn in as Leader of the Nation.

His regime imposed martial law, took part in Germany's war effort and restarted the Holocaust in Hungary, which Horthy had halted. His militias were responsible for the murder of 10,000 to 15,000 Hungarian Jews and the deportation of a further 650,000 to death camps. His government lasted 163 days and held authority only in Budapest and its surroundings.

Szálasi and his cabinet fled Hungary shortly before the Siege of Budapest began. American troops captured him at Mattsee in Austria on 6 May 1945, and he was returned to Hungary on 3 October. The People's Tribunal in Budapest, in open sessions begun in February 1946, found him guilty of war crimes and high treason. The historian Peter Kenez wrote that he was so out of touch with reality that he could fairly be described as mad. He was executed by hanging on 12 March 1946.
ferentino: Ferentino is a town and comune in the province of Frosinone in Lazio, 65 kilometres south-east of Rome. It lies on a hill 400 metres above sea level, in the Monti Ernici area. In antiquity it was the town of the Hernici of Ferentinum. It stood just above the Via Latina and, being a strong place, served for the detention of hostages.

Ferentinum took no part in the rising of 306 BCE. Its inhabitants became Roman citizens after 195 BCE, and the place later became a municipium. From 1198 to 1557 Ferentino was the seat of the papal rectorate of Campagna and Marittima province. The town was strong in textiles, linen and embroidery, and in handicraft such as clay bricks, and after World War II it saw heavy industrial growth, mainly in pharmaceuticals.

The town keeps remains of ancient fortifications. The lower part of the outer walls is built of roughly hewn blocks of limestone, with rectangular blocks of tuff above in places. Two gates survive, the Porta Maggiore, a double gate built wholly of tuff blocks, and the Porta Sanguinaria. The acropolis, dating from the 2nd to 1st centuries BCE, has massive retaining walls like those of the lower town, and a building of travertine blocks whose cornice carries two inscriptions of the period of Sulla recording its construction by two censors.

The Cathedral of Sts John and Paul stands on part of the ancient acropolis, rebuilt in 1099 to 1118 on the site of an older church. It contains a Cosmatesque ciborium and a 12th-century mosaic pavement. The Gothic church of Santa Maria Maggiore dates from the 13th and 14th centuries. The Romanesque monastery of Sant'Antonio Abate housed the remains of Pope Celestine V until 1327.
fergana-valley: The Fergana Valley is an intermountain depression between the Tien Shan in the north and the Alay in the south. It is about 300 km long and up to 70 km wide, covering about 22,000 square kilometres, and it crosses eastern Uzbekistan, southern Kyrgyzstan and northern Tajikistan. Its fertility comes from the Naryn and the Kara Darya, which join near Namangan to form the Syr Darya. The climate is dry and continental, with hot summers and frost in December and January. The name Fergana is of Persian origin.

As early as 500 BCE the western part of the valley formed part of Sogdiana, which owed allegiance to the Achaemenid Empire under Darius the Great. In 329 BCE Alexander the Great founded Alexandria Eschate, the Furthest, in the south-west of the valley, at the site of the modern city of Khujand. Chinese chroniclers, drawing on the travels of Zhang Qian and published around 126 BCE, present the region as the country of the Dayuan, possibly descendants of Greek colonists, known for its Heavenly Horses. The Chinese waged war against the Dayuan in 104 BCE to obtain them. The Kushan Empire later ruled the area until the 3rd century CE, when the Sassanid Empire invaded.
