fiji: Fiji is an archipelago of 332 islands, of which 106 are inhabited, and 522 smaller islets, in the South Pacific about 2,000 km north-northeast of New Zealand. Only around 10% of its area of some 194,000 square kilometres is land. The two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, account for about three-quarters of the land area. The islands are mountainous, with peaks up to 1,324 metres, and covered with thick tropical forest. Most were formed by volcanic activity beginning around 150 million years ago. The 180° meridian runs through Taveuni, but the International Date Line is bent so that the whole group keeps one time.

Pottery shows that Austronesian peoples had settled Fiji by at least 3500 to 1000 BCE, with Melanesians following about a thousand years later. It is believed that either the Lapita people or the ancestors of the Polynesians settled first, though not much is known of what became of them. Archaeological evidence shows settlement on Moturiki Island from at least 600 BCE and possibly 900 BCE, and some migrants moved on to Samoa, Tonga and even Hawai'i. Trade with neighbouring archipelagos began long before European contact. In the 10th century the Tu'i Tonga Empire was established in Tonga and Fiji came within its sphere of influence, bringing Polynesian customs and language; that empire began to decline in the 13th century.

Europeans first visited in the 17th century. The name Fiji comes from the Tongan pronunciation, Fisi, of the Fijian name Viti, and was first promulgated by Captain James Cook; accounts written until the late 19th century spelled it Feejee. After a brief period as an independent kingdom, the British established the Colony of Fiji in 1874. It was a Crown colony until it gained independence in 1970 as the Dominion of Fiji. After a series of coups, the military government declared a republic in 1987.

Fiji is a parliamentary republic with its capital at Suva on Viti Levu, home to nearly three-quarters of the population. About 54.3% of the people are native Fijians, who are Melanesians with Polynesian ancestry in many cases, and 38.1% are Indo-Fijians, descendants of Indian contract labourers brought by the British in the 19th century. Rotuma, with a culture closer to Tonga and Samoa, has a special administrative status. Rugby sevens is the national sport.
filarete: Antonio di Pietro Averlino was born around 1400 in Florence, where he probably trained as a craftsman. Sources suggest that he worked under Lorenzo Ghiberti, who gave him the name Filarete, meaning a lover of virtue. In the mid 15th century he was expelled from Rome after being accused of attempting to steal the head of John the Baptist, and he moved to Venice and then to Milan, where he became a ducal engineer and worked on architectural projects for about fifteen years. According to Giorgio Vasari, he died in Rome around 1469.

A commission from Pope Eugene IV led Filarete to cast, over twelve years, the central bronze doors of Old St Peter's Basilica in Rome, completed in 1445. Although made in the Renaissance, the doors show distinct Byzantine influences and seem tied to the medieval era. Some critics have described them as showing a mind of medieval complexity crammed full of exciting but not quite assimilated classical learning.

In Milan he built the Ospedale Maggiore around 1456, planned rationally as a cross within a square with the hospital church at the centre. Surviving parts of the much-rebuilt structure show the Gothic detail of Milan's craft traditions, which sit at odds with his design all'antica, after the Antique. He also worked on the Sforza Castle and on Milan Cathedral.

Around 1464 Filarete completed a book of twenty-five volumes that he called his Libro architettonico, usually now called a treatise. It circulated widely in manuscript, and its best-known copy, the illustrated Codex Magliabechiano, is dedicated to Piero de' Medici. Written as a fictional narrative, it treats the technical side of architecture and argues against the Gothic style of northern Italy, which he calls the barbarous modern style, in favour of classical Roman models.

Its most best-known part is the plan for Sforzinda, an ideal city named after Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan, which was never built. Its layout is an eight-point star made by overlaying two squares, inscribed within a circular moat, with towers at the points and gates at the inner angles. Radial avenues led through market squares to a central square, and every other street had a canal. Francesco di Giorgio and Leonardo da Vinci are said to have borrowed ideas from him when planning their own ideal cities.
filipe-de-brito-e-nicote: Born in Lisbon to a French father, de Brito is also recorded under the French spelling Philippe de Brito and as Zwing Gaa Bu. He first travelled to Southeast Asia as a cabin boy and later served as a mercenary under Min Razagyi, King of Arakan, who in 1599 made him governor of Syriam, now Thanlyin, in command of three frigates and 3,000 men.

At Syriam he encouraged more Portuguese to settle and built forts for its defence, and in 1603 he seized control and announced his independence from Arakan. When Toungoo and Arakan attacked in the 1605 Syriam battles he captured Min Khamaung, the crown prince of Arakan, and held him hostage until his independence was granted. He sought official recognition in Goa and received from the Portuguese royal court the titles Commander of Syriam, General of the conquests of Pegu and King of Pegu. By marrying the daughter of Bannya Dala of Martaban he became a subject of the Kingdom of Ayutthaya.

King Ekathotsarot of Ayutthaya sent Bannya Dala and de Brito to help Toungoo against Ava, but Toungoo had submitted to Ava before they arrived. The two men burnt Toungoo and carried its remaining property and people, among them its king Natshinnaung, to Syriam. De Brito is recorded as seizing objects of worship of the Buddha and demolishing Buddha images, shrines and pagodas.

In 1608 his men, using elephants and forced labour, removed the Dhammazedi Bell from the Shwedagon Pagoda and rolled it down Singuttara Hill to a raft on the Pazundaung Creek, intending to melt it down for cannons. Lashed to his flagship, the load proved too heavy: at the confluence of the Pegu and Yangon Rivers, off what is now Monkey Point, the raft broke apart and the bell sank, taking the ship with it.

In 1613 the Burmese forces of King Anaukpetlun besieged Syriam. After the city fell in April 1613, de Brito was executed together with Natshinnaung. He was impaled and took three days to die, and more than 400 Portuguese were taken back to Ava as prisoners of war.
filipp-goloshchekin: Born Shaya Itsikovich Goloshchyokin in Nevel to a family of Jewish contractors, he trained at a dental school in Riga and worked for a time as a dental technician. He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party in 1903, took part in the Revolution of 1905 and led the party's Moscow Committee from 1909. Arrested and exiled to the Narym region, he escaped in 1910. At the Prague conference of 1912 he became a founding member of Lenin's separate Bolshevik Central Committee, taking Filipp as his party name. Deported again to the Turukhansk Territory in 1913, he was freed only after the February Revolution.

In 1917 Yakov Sverdlov sent him to the Urals. He took part in the October Revolution in Petrograd and then became Military Commissar of the Urals in Ekaterinburg, holding overall command over the Ipatiev House, where Yakov Yurovsky was commandant. He carried the Ural Soviet's demand for the tsar's death to Moscow in early July 1918, and on the night of the killings he was at the house, though he does not appear to have fired. Afterwards he announced the tsar's death publicly and oversaw the disposal of the remains.

After a spell in charge of Samara province, he became First Secretary of the party in the Kazakh Autonomous Socialist Soviet Republic on 19 February 1925 and ran it with almost no outside interference. Under Joseph Stalin's collectivisation he ordered the nomads to settle on collective farms, and the famine that followed is usually put at between 1 and 2 million deaths, mainly among Kazakhs; some Kazakh historians give higher figures. Many nomads fled into Xinjiang. Some scholars describe the famine as a genocide of the Kazakhs; others do not accept this view.

After complaints from Uraz Isayev and others, Goloshchyokin was dismissed in January 1933, a few days after boasting at a Central Committee plenum of the enormous successes of the Five year Plan in Kazakhstan. He then served as Chief State Arbiter in Moscow and took part in the repressions of the Great Purge alongside Nikolai Yezhov. After Yezhov's own arrest he was seized on 15 October 1939, accused among other things of Trotskyism and of spying for Nazi Germany. On Lavrentiy Beria's direct orders he was shot near the village of Barbysh on 28 October 1941 with 19 other prisoners and buried in an unmarked grave. He was rehabilitated in 1961.
filippo-brunelleschi: Brunelleschi was born in Florence in 1377, the son of Brunellesco di Lippo Lapi, a notary and civil servant, and Giuliana Spini. He received a literary and mathematical education, but being artistically inclined he was apprenticed at 15 as a goldsmith and sculptor in cast bronze, and in December 1398 he became a master.

In 1401 he was one of seven competitors for the second pair of bronze doors of the Florence Baptistery, each making a panel of the Sacrifice of Isaac. The jury could not choose between his panel and that of Lorenzo Ghiberti and proposed that the two collaborate. Brunelleschi refused to give up total control and preferred that the work go to Ghiberti. He later gave up sculpture for architecture and optics.

His first architectural commission was the Ospedale degli Innocenti, a foundling hospital begun in 1419 and opened on 25 January 1445, whose loggia drew clearly on classical forms and became a model across Europe. He also designed the Old Sacristy and the nave of the Basilica of San Lorenzo for the Medici family.

In 1418 he won the competition to build the dome of Florence Cathedral, helped by a brick model made by his friend Donatello. His later works included the Pazzi Chapel, the Basilica of Santo Spirito and Santa Maria degli Angeli, an octagonal church whose funds the government seized in 1437 for a war against Lucca.

The dome was built from 1420 to 1436 with two shells, one within the other, and more than four million bricks. Brunelleschi left no plans of it, and he invented a new hoisting machine and chains of wood and sandstone that act as tension rings. His early biographer Antonio Manetti says that between 1415 and 1420 he made perspective paintings of the Baptistery and the Palazzo Vecchio, and he is credited as the first to describe a precise system of linear perspective. In 1421 he received what is thought to be one of the first modern patents, for a boat to carry goods on the Arno. He died on 15 April 1446 and was buried in the crypt of the cathedral.
filippo-juvarra: Filippo Juvarra was born in Messina on 7 March 1678 into a family of goldsmiths and engravers and worked in the family shop. He studied for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, while teaching himself architecture from books by Vitruvius and Vignola. He designed festive settings in Messina for the coronation of Philip V in 1701. In 1704 he moved to Rome, where he studied with Carlo and Francesco Fontana. His first independent work was for the stage: he designed sets for operas under the patronage of Cardinal Ottoboni and of the widowed Queen of Poland, Marie Casimire d'Arquien, using scenes drawn at an angle.

In 1706 Juvarra won a contest for the new sacristy of St Peter's, held by Pope Clement XI, and entered the Accademia di San Luca. His Antamoro Chapel of 1708, made with the sculptor Pierre Le Gros, is his only completed architectural work in Rome. In 1714 he was recruited to the Duchy of Savoy by Victor Amadeus II and became chief court architect in Turin. There he built the façade of the Palazzo Madama in 1718–21, a theatrical screen before a grand staircase and a medieval castle. The Basilica of Superga, begun to fulfil a vow Victor Amadeus made during the siege of Turin, took over fourteen years to build and stands on a mountaintop with a dome seventy-five metres high.

He also designed the hunting lodge at Stupinigi (1729–1731), with an oval central pavilion topped by a bronze stag, and worked on the palace of Venaria Reale. In 1719 he went to Portugal, where he planned the palace at Mafra and a palace and cathedral for John V in Lisbon.

After fire destroyed the Royal Alcazar of Madrid on Christmas Eve 1734, Philip V asked Juvarra to supervise a new palace. He moved to Madrid in April 1735 and died suddenly in January 1736, less than nine months after arriving. His pupils, among them Giovanni Battista Sacchetti, carried out his designs. Bernardo Vittone and Benedetto Alfieri followed his manner, and his style fell out of favour with the rise of Neoclassicism. A major exhibition of his designs was held in Genoa and Madrid in 1994.
filippo-maria-visconti: Filippo Maria Visconti was born on 3 September 1392, the son of Gian Galeazzo Visconti and Caterina Visconti. His father died of plague in 1402, and his elder brother Gian Maria became Duke of Milan with their mother's support. Gian Maria came to regard her as a threat and had her imprisoned at Monza on 18 August 1404; she died there on 17 October, and her death was rumoured to have been caused by poison. After Gian Maria was assassinated on 16 May 1412, Filippo Maria allied himself with Beatrice, the widow of the condottiero Facino Cane, gaining access to her late husband's wealth and armies.

Filippo Maria succeeded his brother as Duke of Milan and established his rule over Pavia. His succession was contested by his uncle Estorre Visconti and his cousin Giacomo, who briefly held Milan, but on 16 June 1412 he retook the city. In 1418 he had Beatrice executed at the Castle of Binasco after accusing her of adultery. By employing condottieri such as Francesco Bussone da Carmagnola, Niccolò Piccinino and later Francesco Sforza, he recovered much of the Lombard territory of his father's duchy. His attempt to expand into Romagna in 1423 provoked a war with Florence, which Venice joined in 1425. Venice conquered Brescia, and Filippo Maria was defeated at Maclodio on 12 October 1427. Peace was later signed at Ferrara.

In 1428 he married Marie of Savoy, daughter of his ally Amadeus VIII of Savoy, who later reigned as Antipope Felix V with Visconti's support. Filippo Maria also invited the humanist Gasparino Barzizza to Milan, where he founded a school. The oldest surviving tarot decks, then called carte da trionfi, were likely commissioned by him.

Filippo Maria died on 13 August 1447, the last male of the Visconti line. After a brief republican experiment known as the Ambrosian republic, the duchy passed to Francesco Sforza, who had married Bianca Maria Visconti, Filippo Maria's only child, born to his mistress Agnese del Maino.
fils-river: The Fils rises about two kilometres south-west of Wiesensteig, at a karst spring called the Filsursprung, 624.9 metres above sea level in the Hasental valley, with two smaller springs, the Kleiner Filsursprung and the Hasenquelle, a little further down. It first runs north-east through the Swabian Alb, past Mühlhausen im Täle, where the Bundesautobahn 8 crosses the valley, Gosbach, Bad Ditzenbach, Deggingen, Reichenbach im Täle, Hausen an der Fils and Bad Überkingen, gathering short streams from both slopes.

At Geislingen an der Steige the valley turns through 90 degrees to the left, where the Eyb, swollen by a stream from Amstetten, joins from the north-east and leaves the town in a wide meeting of valleys. The river leaves the Alb for the Swabian Keuper-Lias Plains. Below Kuchen and Gingen the Lauter, its largest tributary, flows in at Süßen. From there the Fils runs roughly west, ever further from the edge of the Alb, past Salach, Eislingen, where the Krumm, its second largest tributary, joins, Göppingen, Faurndau, Uhingen, Ebersbach an der Fils and Reichenbach an der Fils.

The Fils reaches the Neckar at Plochingen, east of Stuttgart, at 248.3 metres, about 377 metres below its source. Its catchment of about 707 square kilometres lies partly in the Swabian Alb and partly, a little larger, in the Alb foothills. Its longer tributaries, besides the Lauter, the Eyb and the Krumm, include the Butzbach, the Marbach, the Pfuhlbach, the Talbach and the Heubach. It is the fifth largest tributary of the Neckar by length and the fourth by catchment area, and thanks to its water the Neckar is navigable from Plochingen downstream.
fin-de-siecle: Fin de siècle is a French term meaning end of century. It covers the sense of the English phrase turn of the century and also the closing of one era and the beginning of another, and without context it usually means the end of the nineteenth century. The period was widely thought to be one of social degeneracy and at the same time of hope for a new beginning. The cultural hallmarks of the 1880s and 1890s included ennui, cynicism, pessimism and a widespread belief that civilisation leads to decadence. The term is commonly applied to French art and artists, since the traits first appeared in France, but the movement affected many European countries.

B. A. Morel's degeneration theory held that societies can regress as well as progress under a flawed environment, with the effects passed from generation to generation. In Degeneration Max Nordau held that the two dominant traits of the degenerate were ego mania and mysticism, and his work brought the concept of genius back into popular thought. Pessimism spread from the work of Arthur Schopenhauer, and R. H. Goodale counted 235 essays by British and American authors on pessimism between 1871 and 1900. Oscar Wilde joked in An Ideal Husband that optimist and pessimist were the only fashionable religions left.

Decadent writers such as Charles Baudelaire and Arthur Rimbaud influenced their English counterparts, the aesthetes, who held that art should evoke an emotional response and show beauty in the unnatural. Holbrook Jackson listed the characteristics of English decadence as perversity, artificiality, egoism and curiosity. Gothic fiction expressed fears of change and decay through the human body, in works such as Robert Louis Stevenson's The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886), Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), H. G. Wells's The Time Machine (1895) and Bram Stoker's Dracula (1897). The age also produced a flood of future war narratives, sold in tens of thousands of copies across Europe, which acted as political advocacy.

The ideas of fin de siècle artists gave the impetus for symbolism and modernism. The political culture of the time was marked by revolt against materialism, rationalism, positivism, bourgeois society and liberal democracy, and favoured emotionalism, irrationalism and vitalism. Its themes were controversial and have been cited as a major influence on fascism and on the beginnings of geopolitics, including the theory of Lebensraum. Michael Heffernan has argued that geopolitics arose in fin de siècle Europe from technological change and the sense that imperialist competition had closed the world's frontiers. Writing of the 1890s, he notes a widespread assumption that the passing of the century would mean a clear break with the past.
final-war-of-the-roman-republic: After Julius Caesar's assassination, Octavian, Mark Antony and Marcus Lepidus formed the Second Triumvirate. They defeated Marcus Junius Brutus and Gaius Cassius Longinus at the Battle of Philippi in 42 BCE, and Lepidus was expelled in 36 BCE. Octavian then held the west, including Hispania, Gaul, Italia and Africa, and Antony the east, including Greece, Asia, Syria and Egypt.

Antony, married since 40 BCE to Octavia, Octavian's sister, took up with Cleopatra, and Octavian had his minister Gaius Maecenas produce a propaganda campaign against him. Antony's Donations of Alexandria gave much of Rome's eastern territory to Cleopatra and her children. Octavian then seized Antony's will from the Temple of Vesta, and its terms, including Antony's wish to be buried at Alexandria, angered the senate. In 32 BCE the senate declared war on Cleopatra. Both consuls and forty percent of the senate left Rome to join Antony.

Both sides raised armies of almost 200,000 men. Octavian's chief adviser Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa commanded his fleet of 350 smaller, more manoeuvrable ships with experienced crews, while Antony brought 290 larger ships with inexperienced crews. Agrippa disrupted Antony's supply lines and took the port of Methone. On 2 September 31 BCE, at the Battle of Actium, Antony's fleet was drawn out from the shore and overcome. Cleopatra's squadron slipped through a gap in the line and Antony followed, but most of the fleet was sunk, and the pair retreated to Alexandria with about 90 ships. Antony's land commanders surrendered their legions after a week.

In early 30 BCE Octavian marched by land through Asia. Lucius Pinarius, whom Antony hoped would supply an army from Cyrenaica, had changed sides. Octavian placed Alexandria under siege, Antony's remaining cavalry and fleet surrendered, and on 1 August 30 BCE Antony fell on his sword. According to the ancient accounts he died in Cleopatra's arms in her mausoleum.

Cleopatra bargained for her children's lives, but Octavian refused to spare Caesarion. According to Strabo she died from a snake bite or a poisonous ointment. Rome annexed Egypt, and Octavian, who executed Antony's supporters, ended a century of civil wars. In 27 BCE the senate named him Augustus and gave him unprecedented powers.

Augustus passed laws that kept the appearance of the republic while making his own position paramount, and ruled as the first Roman emperor. The critical border provinces such as Syria, Egypt and Gaul came under his direct rule. His reign opened a period of internal stability later called the Pax Romana.
finistere: Finistère lies in the extreme west of Brittany. Its prefecture is Quimper, and its largest city is Brest. Other large towns include Concarneau, Morlaix, Carhaix, Quimperlé and Douarnenez, and the department includes the island of Ushant, called Eusa in Breton and Ouessant in French. It is the westernmost department of metropolitan France and has a claim to being the most coastal: 117 of its 277 communes lie on the coast, and its coastline of about 1,250 km makes up almost a quarter of that of Brittany.

The abers, rugged fjord-like inlets, are a notable feature of the north coast. The Pointe de Corsen, at the north-western tip of the department, is the westernmost point of continental France. About 40 kilometres to the south lies the rugged and isolated headland of the Pointe du Raz.

The present department consists of the historical region of Léon and parts of Cornouaille and Trégor, all of them parts of Brittany before the Revolution. Its name comes from the Latin Finis Terræ, meaning the end of the earth. The Breton name, Penn ar Bed, means head or end of the world and resembles the Cornish name of Land's End, Pedn an Wlas. It should not be confused with Fisterra in Galicia, Spain, which has the same origin.

Agriculture, fisheries and food processing occupy an important place in the economy. A military presence, including the Île Longue submarine base and the naval air base at Lanvéoc-Poulmic, together with related industries, employs a significant part of the population. The port of Roscoff has ferry links with Ireland and Great Britain.

Finistère is the area where Breton survives most strongly as a spoken language, and its Breton-speaking schools are called Diwan, Divyezh and Dihun. The Festival de Cornouaille in Quimper celebrates Breton music and traditions. The sculptor Roland Doré made many of the calvaries that stand in the department.
finlaggan: Finlaggan lies on Eilean Mòr in Loch Finlaggan, about 4 km west of the ferry terminal at Port Askaig on Islay. Of the three islands in the loch, two, Eilean Mòr, the Great Isle, and Eilean na Comhairle, the Isle of the Council, together formed the administrative centre of the Lordship of the Isles and the seat of Clan Donald.

In the first half of the 7th century a monastic community was established on Eilean Mòr, dedicated to or perhaps founded by St Findlugan, an Irish monk and a contemporary of St Columba. A building, probably of timber and perhaps on the remains of an Iron Age fort, was raised there in 1138 by Somerled, Lord of Argyll, Kintyre and Lorne. The stone castle whose ruins remain dates from the 13th century and served the Lords of the Isles as a residence, stronghold, principal court and meeting place of their clan chiefs.

Finlaggan remained the centre of the lordship until 1493, when it fell to James IV of Scotland, who governed the territory through a tenant-in-chief. Iain Mòr MacDonald, 3rd of Dunnyveg, and his son Iain Cathanach MacDonald were taken prisoner at the castle through the deception of MacIain of Ardnamurchan and were later tried and hanged on the Burgh Muir of Edinburgh. In 1541 Finlaggan was held from the Crown by Donald MacGilleasbuig, and the castle appears to have been demolished in the 15th or 16th century.

The Finlaggan Trust maintains the site and runs a museum in a converted cottage, which shows finds from the excavations, from a quilted aketon of sheep's wool worn under armour to a cross linked to the lords. The walls of the medieval chapel of St Findlugan have been stabilised, and several 16th-century graves are displayed under glass. In 2019 the University of St Andrews announced a virtual-reality reconstruction of the settlement as it was in the early 15th century.
finland: Finland lies approximately between latitudes 60° and 70° N, and only Reykjavík lies further north among world capitals than Helsinki. Its land is predominantly covered by boreal forest, and it has about 168,000 lakes and 179,000 islands; the largest lake, Saimaa, is the fourth largest in Europe. Much of the landscape is a result of the Ice Age, and the terrain is rising by about 1 centimetre a year around the Gulf of Bothnia because of post-glacial rebound, so that the surface area of the country expands by about 7 square kilometres annually. Halti, at 1,324 metres, is the highest point.

The area was settled around 8500 BCE towards the end of the last glacial period, by hunter-gatherers using stone tools. The first pottery appeared in 5200 BCE with the Comb Ceramic culture, and the Corded Ware culture arrived in the south of coastal Finland between 3000 and 2500 BCE and may have coincided with the start of agriculture. In the Iron Age, Finland Proper was the most densely populated area, and main exports were furs, slaves, castoreum and falcons to European courts. At the end of the ninth century, local artefacts had more common features than ever before, which has been interpreted as expressing a common Finnish identity.

From the middle of the 13th century Finland became part of Sweden during the Northern Crusades. In 1809, as a result of the Finnish War, it was captured from Sweden and became an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire, and an independence movement gradually developed. Finland declared its independence after the Russian Revolution of 1917, and a civil war the following year ended in victory for the anticommunist Whites. During World War II Finland fought the Soviet Union in the Winter War and the Continuation War and Nazi Germany in the Lapland War, losing parts of its territory but retaining its independence and democracy.

Finland has a population of 5.7 million, and Helsinki is the capital and largest city. The official languages are Finnish and Swedish, the mother tongues of 83.5 percent and 5.0 percent of the population. It became the first country in Europe to grant universal suffrage in 1906. A new constitution enacted in 2000 made the presidency primarily a ceremonial office, and Finland is now considered a parliamentary republic. It joined the European Union in 1995 and the Eurozone in 1999, and NATO in 2023. National minorities include the Sámi, Roma, Jews and Tatars.
finlandisation: Finlandization means the process by which a powerful country makes a smaller neighbour refrain from opposing its foreign policy while the smaller state keeps its nominal independence and its own political system. The word arose in the West German political debate of the late 1960s and 1970s. It was coined in scholarly debate and made known by the political scientists Richard Löwenthal, Walter Hallstein and Kurt Birrenbach, who feared the effects of a withdrawal of American troops from Germany. Franz Josef Strauss and others used it in response to Willy Brandt's attempts to normalise relations with East Germany. It is often considered pejorative.

Finland had fought the Winter War against the Soviet Union in 1939, losing 9 per cent of its territory, and re-entered the Second World War in 1941 beside Germany. After the Paris Peace Treaty of 1947 it kept democracy and parliamentary government under heavy Soviet pressure. Its foreign relations followed the doctrine of Juho Kusti Paasikivi, who stressed a trusting relationship with the Soviet Union. In April 1948 Finland signed an Agreement of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance, which obliged it to resist attacks by Germany or its allies but also recognised its wish to stay outside great-power conflicts. Finland stayed out of the Marshall Plan and the Warsaw Pact.

Between 1944 and 1946 the Soviet part of the Allied Control Commission demanded that libraries withdraw more than 1,700 books as anti-Soviet, and Finnish censors banned films such as The Manchurian Candidate. Possession of such books was never banned, and the censorship never took the form of purging; much of it was self-censorship. Finns reacted in varied ways to the term. Many ordinary Finns found it offensive, while the cartoonist Kari Suomalainen defined it as the art of bowing to the East without mooning the West.

After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the treaty of 1948 was replaced by a new treaty with the Russian Federation on a more equal footing, ending the Paasikivi-Kekkonen doctrine. Finland joined the European Union in 1995. After the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Finland applied for NATO membership on 18 May and became a member on 4 April 2023. The word has also been applied to other states near a great power, such as Denmark's attitude toward Germany between 1871 and 1940 and Swiss policy toward Nazi Germany.
finnic-peoples: The Finnic peoples speak languages traditionally classified in the Finnic family and are thought to have originated in the region of the Volga River. The largest of them by population are the Finns, about 6 million, the Estonians, about 1 million, the Mordvins, the Mari, the Udmurts, the Komis and the Sámi. The scope of the term varies. In its narrowest sense it covers only the Baltic Finns of Finland, Scandinavia, Estonia and Northwest Russia.

In Russian academic literature the term usually includes both the Baltic Finns and the Volga Finns, the peoples living near the Volga and Kama rivers, with the Perm Finns sometimes treated as a third group; these eastern peoples include those of the Russian republics of Komi, Mari El, Mordovia and Udmurtia. The broadest present-day usage adds the Sámi of northern Fennoscandia, and older literature sometimes included the Ugrian Finns, the Khanty, Mansi and Hungarians.

From very approximately the Volga area, Finnic peoples migrated westward into northwestern Russia and, first the Sámi and then the Baltic Finns, into Scandinavia, though scholars dispute the timing. The ancestors of the Perm Finns moved north and east to the Kama and Vychegda rivers. Those who stayed in the Volga basin had begun to divide into their present variety by the sixth century and had formed their present nations by the sixteenth.

The name Finn is an ancient exonym that usually referred to the Sámi. Probable cognates such as Fenni, Phinnoi and Skrithfinni appear in a few texts from about two millennia ago in connection with peoples of northern Europe. The first known use of the name for the people of what is now Finland is in the 10th-century Old English poem Widsith, and two 11th-century rune stones in Sweden carry the inscriptions finlont and finlandi.

The name may be of Germanic origin, from an Old Norse word finn for a hunter-gatherer, applied during the first millennium CE to the Sámi and perhaps to other hunter-gatherers of Scandinavia; hence Finnmark in Norway. The Icelandic Eddas and Norse sagas use finnr and finnas inconsistently, mostly for northern dwellers with a mobile way of life.
finnish-civil-war: Finland had been a grand duchy of the Russian Empire since 1809. Its population grew from 860,000 in 1810 to 3,130,000 in 1917, industry and a labour movement developed, and tension rose over the autocratic rule of the tsar and the undemocratic system of estates inherited from Swedish rule. The main cause of the war was the crisis of the First World War. After the February Revolution of 1917 the Russian Provisional Government restored Finland's autonomy, and after the October Revolution both conservatives and socialists came to support independence, though they disagreed about who should lead the nation.

The final escalation began in early January 1918, when each action by one side drew a counteraction from the other. The Red Guards, led by a section of the Social Democratic Party, held the south, including nearly all the major towns and industrial centres. The Whites, led by General Mannerheim and built around the Jägers trained in Germany and volunteer Civil Guards, held the agrarian centre and north. The Reds' general offensive in February failed.

Mannerheim chose to strike first at Tampere, the main industrial town of the south-west, which held nearly 15,000 heavily armed Red Guards. His assault began on 16 March, and the Whites besieged the town. After German troops landed in April, the Reds' leaders withdrew from Helsinki to Viipuri and then to Petrograd. Thousands of Reds tried to flee to Russia, but most were encircled, and those in the Lahti area surrendered on 1 and 2 May. The war ended on 15 May with the capture of Fort Ino. Both sides carried out executions, known as the White Terror and the Red Terror.

The Whites and German troops captured around 80,000 Red prisoners, including 5,000 women and 1,500 children, and held them in camps such as Suomenlinna and Hämeenlinna. Most of the deaths in the war occurred outside the battlefields, in the camps and the terror. Treason courts examined 76,000 cases and convicted 68,000 Reds, and of 555 death sentences 113 were carried out. About 15,000 children were left orphaned, and many moderate Finns came to think of themselves as citizens of two nations.

A plan for a German-led Finnish monarchy collapsed with Germany's surrender in November 1918, and Finland became an independent republic, confirmed by the Constitution Act of 17 July 1919. The war has several names, among them Civil War, Class War, War of Independence and Red Rebellion, each tied to a political viewpoint.
finnish-peoples-delegation: The decision to launch an armed revolution was taken on 23 January 1918 by the Red Guards' leadership and Finland's workers' executive committee, a body split from the party committee of the Social Democratic Party of Finland and drawn from the labour movement's most radical wing. On the night of 27 January the committee ordered the arrest of Pehr Evind Svinhufvud's Senate and other leading bourgeois politicians, including 33 members of Parliament, but a premature public handout warned them and they hid. The Delegation occupied the Senate House in Helsinki on 28 January, and the newspaper Työmies announced its members and aims the next day.

Its members held roles like ministers: Yrjö Sirola for foreign affairs, Otto Wille Kuusinen for education, Jalo Kohonen and later Edvard Gylling for finance, and Oskari Tokoi for supply, among others. It issued 45 statutes in all, about two thirds of them answers to urgent administrative problems and the rest aimed at ideological goals or at winning support, drawing on the Paris Commune of 1871, the October Revolution and above all the earlier programmes of Finland's labour movement. It also drafted a constitution influenced by the American and Swiss constitutions, on which a referendum was planned.

Its first act was to close the capitalist newspapers, and on 2 February the counterrevolutionary press was suspended indefinitely, even the right-wing social democratic Työn Valta; the Whites' Senate closed the social democratic papers in turn. The same day it placed the Red Guards under its authority, but it could barely control them, and many guardsmen saw the delegates as parasites far from the front. Soviet Russia was the only state to recognise the Delegation as Finland's government.

From March, defeats pushed the Reds southeast towards the Karelian Isthmus, and in April the Delegation moved to Viipuri, near the Russian border. With the Whites about to attack, almost all its members fled to Russia on 23 April, which effectively dissolved it; Oskari Tokoi went to the United Kingdom and then the United States. The Red Guards left to defend Viipuri branded them traitors. Excluded from the amnesty of late 1918, the delegates lived in exile and led the underground Communist Party of Finland from Russia, and in the late 1930s many survivors were executed in the Great Purge.
finnish-war: After concluding the Treaty of Tilsit with Napoleon in 1807, Emperor Alexander I of Russia wrote on 24 September 1807 to King Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden that peace between them depended on Sweden accepting the treaty's limits, which in practice meant cutting off trade with Britain. The king, who viewed Napoleon as the Antichrist, secured an alliance with Britain on 8 February 1808. In Saint Petersburg his stubbornness was seen as a convenient pretext for occupying Finland. Swedish plans assumed that war in winter was impossible, while Russian planners chose a winter offensive, when frozen seas would isolate Finland.

On 21 February 1808, 24,000 Russian troops under Friedrich Wilhelm von Buxhoeveden crossed the border and took Loviisa; war was not declared until April. Helsinki fell on 2 March and Turku on 21 March, as the Swedish army under General Wilhelm Mauritz Klingspor withdrew northwards. Sveaborg, with a garrison of 6,000 men and over 700 cannons, surrendered on 6 May 1808 after prolonged negotiations, its commander Admiral Carl Olof Cronstedt believing resistance futile, and the Russians gained most of the Swedish archipelago fleet intact. Swedish counter-attacks at Siikajoki and Revolax halted the offensive for a time, and Finns rose in guerrilla fighting.

Reinforced to 55,000 men against an estimated 36,000, the Russians attacked again in August, and Count Nikolay Kamensky won the most important victory at Oravais on 14 September. By November 1808 Russian forces had overrun all of Finland, and the Convention of Olkijoki of 19 November obliged the Swedish army to leave. In March 1809 Russian columns crossed the frozen Gulf of Bothnia, occupying the Åland Islands and entering Umeå on 24 March. King Gustav IV, blamed for the loss of Finland, was dethroned by a coup in Stockholm on 13 March, and his uncle became Charles XIII of Sweden.

By the Treaty of Fredrikshamn of 17 September 1809 Sweden also gave up its domains east of the Torne river. The Grand Duchy of Finland kept the Gustavian constitution of 1772 with only slight modifications until 1919, and in 1812 Russia attached to it the areas it had gained from Sweden in the 18th century, known as Old Finland. In Sweden the war was followed by a new constitution and, in 1818, by the establishment of the House of Bernadotte. Two studies of 2015 by the political scientists Jan Teorell and Bo Rothstein argue that the defeat moved Swedish elites to reform the bureaucracy.
finno-soviet-treaty-of-1948: The treaty was known in Finland as the YYA Treaty, from the Finnish name Ystävyys-, yhteistyö- ja avunantosopimus, and in Swedish as the VSB-avtalet. It was concluded in the uncertain years after the Continuation War, when relations between Finland and the Soviet Union were still unsettled. The Soviets sought to deter Western or Allied Powers from attacking the Soviet Union through Finnish territory, while the Finns sought greater political independence from their neighbour, which had strategic regions such as the Kola Peninsula and the city of Leningrad close to the border.

Finland was bound to resist armed attacks by Germany or its allies, in practice understood to mean the Western Bloc, against Finland or against the Soviet Union through Finland, and if necessary to ask for Soviet military aid. The pact itself gave the Soviet military no right to enter Finland: any such step had to be agreed separately at Finland's request. Nor did it oblige Finland to act if the Soviet Union were attacked elsewhere. Its recognition of Finland's wish to stay out of great-power conflicts allowed a policy of neutrality in the Cold War.

Because of the treaty's wording and the state of relations, Finland followed the Eastern Bloc and stayed out of the Marshall Plan, which prolonged its post-war hardship and made it more economically dependent on the Soviet Union. It kept its distance from Western military powers, from the proposed Scandinavian Defense Union and from NATO, and so fended off pressure to join the Warsaw Pact. No joint military exercises with the Soviet Union were ever held.

The treaty was the main instrument of the Paasikivi-Kekkonen doctrine, the foreign policy of Paasikivi and of President Urho Kekkonen (1956-1981). It also gave the Soviet Union leverage in Finnish internal affairs, as in the note crisis, an influence called Finlandization; how far Kekkonen used it against his opponents is debated. There was also secret cooperation with the West, from Central Intelligence Agency funding of the Social Democratic Party to the sharing of seismic data on nuclear tests. The Soviet Union made similar agreements with North Korea, India and Vietnam. In 1992 the treaty was replaced by a new one with post-Soviet Russia.
finschhafen: Finschhafen lies 80 kilometres east of Lae. Its name is often misspelt Finschafen or Finschaven, and during World War II some U.S. Navy men logged it as Fitch Haven. The town has a tropical rainforest climate with heavy to very heavy rain all year round.

Unlike many places in Papua New Guinea, Finschhafen and the southern part of the Huon Peninsula receive most of their rain during the south-east monsoon, the low-sun season, because the Huon mountains block the north-westerly winds of the high-sun season. Rainfall varies more over the year than at Lae because of a stronger rain shadow from the north-west monsoon winds.

The area was charted by the British navigator Captain John Moresby in 1873–74. Otto Finsch surveyed it in 1884, and the town built in 1885 as part of the colony of German New Guinea took his name, -hafen meaning harbour. In 1886 Johann Flierl and two other Lutheran missionaries settled in the area and founded a mission station at Simbang.

A malaria epidemic in 1891 led the German plantation owners and government officials to abandon the town. It was resettled afterwards and claimed again by the Germans in 1894, before it was finally abandoned in 1901.

The Imperial Japanese Army occupied Finschhafen on 10 March 1942. Australian forces retook the town on 2 October 1943 during the Huon Peninsula campaign, and the US built Naval Base Finschhafen there in 1943–1944, together with the airfield that became Finschhafen Airport.

On 2 February 2012 the passenger boat MV Rabaul Queen, carrying 350 or more passengers, sank 9 nautical miles from the town. Six people were killed and seven injured, and at least 100, possibly more than 300, were left missing.
fire-arrow: The name translates the Chinese huǒjiàn, literally fire arrow. It is distinct from earlier incendiary arrows: in China the term referred to a bag of gunpowder bound to an arrow shaft and shot from a bow or crossbow. The Wujing Zongyao of 1044 describes wrapping the powder behind the head in two or three layers of soft paper, tying it in a lump shaped like a pomegranate, covering it with hemp cloth sealed with pine resin, lighting the fuse and shooting. Gunpowder's own oxygen made such fires harder to put out than earlier incendiaries. Fire arrows were the predecessors of the fire lance.

Fire arrows are first reported at the siege of Yuzhang in 904. In 975 the state of Wuyue sent the Song a unit skilled in their use, and the Song destroyed the Southern Tang fleet with them that year. In 1083 the Song court produced 350,000 fire arrows for two garrisons. The Jin made them with captured Song artisans by 1127, the Song navy used them to sink a Jin fleet in 1159, and Yu Yunwen used them at the Battle of Caishi in 1161.

The Mongols used fire arrows in their campaigns in Japan, and probably through those campaigns the weapon reached the Middle East, where Al Hasan Al Ramma mentioned it in the late 13th century. Joseon was producing cannons and fire arrows by 1377 and used them against wokou pirates and, in 1592, against the Japanese invasion. The Ming ordered wasp nest rocket launchers in 1380, and Joseon developed the mobile Munjong Hwacha in 1451.

Later the term came to mean the rocket, in which gunpowder drives the arrow, while in Sanskrit the corresponding agni astra came to mean a cannon. When the rocket appeared is disputed. The History of Song credits Yue Yifang and Feng Jisheng in 969 and Tang Fu in 1000, but Joseph Needham argued that rockets could not have existed before the 12th century because the powder formulas of the Wujing Zongyao do not suit a propellant, and Stephen G. Haw finds only slight evidence before 1200.
fire-lance: The fire lance began as a small pyrotechnic device on a polearm, used to gain a shock advantage at the start of a melee. Once lit by its slow match, the gunpowder tube shot a stream of flame towards the spearhead. As the powder improved, iron pellets or pottery shards were packed in with it, so that the weapon worked somewhat like a flamethrower and a shotgun combined, though with a range of only about three metres and usually a single shot.

In 1163 fire lances were fixed to war carts that guarded mobile firebomb trebuchets. By 1232 the Jin had lances with reusable barrels of sixteen layers of paper, which the History of Jin says shot flame more than ten feet. In 1233 Pucha Guannu led 450 Jin fire lancers in small boats against a Mongol camp; by that account 3,500 Mongols drowned in the river, and the Mongols, though disdainful of other Jin weapons, greatly feared the fire lance.

In 1259 a pellet wad that filled the barrel was recorded as a projectile, the first recorded bullet. By 1276 the character for lance was written with the metal radical in place of the wood one, suggesting that barrels were now of metal, and Song cavalrymen carried fire lances. Metal barrels used on their own, called eruptors, became the forerunners of the hand cannon.

The Middle East had fire lances by 1280, European knights took them up as mounted weapons in 1396, and Japanese samurai used them in the 15th century. In Europe versions with wooden tubes, called troncks, fire-trunks or bombas, held fireworks with alternating slow and fast burning sections and were issued to warships; one survived in the wreck of La Trinidad Valencera, and a reconstruction tested in 1988 had several sections ignite at once. The last recorded use in Europe was at the Storming of Bristol in 1643, though the Commonwealth of England still issued them to ships in 1660.
fire-of-moscow-1812: After the Battle of Borodino on 7 September 1812, the Russian army retreated east. On 13 September a military council at Fili agreed to abandon Moscow without fighting. Mikhail Kutuzov pursued a strategy of attrition and scorched earth, with Cossack raids on French supplies and resistance by peasants against French foraging, and he used the Moscow military governor, Count Fyodor Rostopchin, to burn most of the city's resources.

At the start of 1812 Moscow had about 270,184 inhabitants according to a police survey. Between 6,200 and 10,000 civilians stayed after the French arrived, together with 10,000 to 15,000 sick or wounded Russian soldiers.

The Russian army marched through Moscow on 14 September, followed by masses of civilians, and Joachim Murat's corps took the Kremlin that afternoon. The first fires broke out that evening, and on 15 September wind and a series of fires grew into a firestorm that threatened the Kremlin by the early morning of 16 September. Napoleon moved to the Petrovsky Palace, and the French shot people found setting fires. The fire, which destroyed three-quarters of the city, died down when rain began on 18 September, and the last fires subsided on 21 September.

Most buildings were of wood, and the fire brigade's equipment had been removed or destroyed on Rostopchin's orders. Rostopchin has often been held responsible, and Germaine de Staël wrote that he ordered his own mansions burnt. Most historians now blame the first fires on the Russian scorched-earth strategy. A police officer captured at the Kremlin reportedly admitted to being ordered to set the city alight. Leo Tolstoy, in War and Peace, argued that nobody set it deliberately, and that a deserted wooden city in the hands of an invading army was bound to burn.

Of about 4,000 stone structures and 8,000 wooden houses, roughly 200 stone buildings and some 500 wooden houses remained, along with about half of the churches, nearly all of them damaged. The French looted church silver, and a Russian source says they turned churches into stables and killed priests who refused to surrender shrines, while Napoleon personally ensured that food reached the Russians left behind. General Marcellin Marbot doubted that the fire caused the campaign's failure, since enough buildings remained to house the army.

Napoleon proposed peace to the tsar on 20 September and received no agreement. The French army, about 108,000 men, left Moscow on 19 October after 36 days there. Rebuilding under the governors Alexander Tormasov and Dmitry Golitsyn took well over a decade.
fire-temple: Fire rituals are first evident in the 9th century BCE, about the same time as Zoroastrianism itself and the introduction of Atar as a divinity. There is no allusion to a temple of fire in the Avesta proper, nor an Old Persian word for one. Herodotus shows that in the mid-5th century BCE Zoroastrians worshipped to the open sky, ascending mounds to light their fires, so the temple is a later development. The oldest remains identified as a fire temple are on Mount Khajeh, near Lake Hamun in Sistan, tentatively dated to the 3rd or 4th century BCE, rebuilt in the Parthian era and enlarged in Sassanid times.

By the Parthian period there were two kinds of place of worship, the bagin, a sanctuary of a particular divinity with an icon, and the atroshan, a place of burning fire, which became more common as the movement against images gained support. Under the Sassanid dynasty the statues were by law abandoned or replaced by fire altars. There seem to have been virtually only two grades of fire, the Atash-i Vahram, kept continuously burning, and the Atash-i Adaran, a parish fire relit each year. The characteristic Sassanid sanctuary was a domed chamber on a square plan with a pillar at each corner, and Sassanid coins always show a fire altar with flames on the reverse.

Three Great Fires, Adur Burzen-Mihr, Adur Farnbag and Adur Gushnasp, were said to derive from Ahura Mazda and were associated with priests, warriors and farmers; other texts call them symbols of imperial sovereignty. The battles of al-Qādisiyyah in 636 and Nihavānd in 642 were instrumental in the collapse of the Sassanid Empire and of state-sponsored Zoroastrianism, and some fire temples were destroyed or converted into mosques, though others continued. According to Parsi legend, refugees from Khorasan brought the ash of a fire to Gujarat. Its fire was moved from Sanjan to the Bahrot Caves, then to Bansdah and Navsari, and in the 18th century to Udvada.

Fire temples are built to serve the fire within them and are classified by its grade: Atash Dadgah, Atash Adaran and Atash Behram. A Dadgah fire can be consecrated in a few hours by two priests, an Adaran fire requires eight priests and two to three weeks, and a Behram fire gathers sixteen kinds of fire and requires thirty-two priests for a ceremony that can take up to a year. The outer façade of a temple is almost always plain. Only priests may enter the innermost sanctum, which has a double domed roof and no light but the fire's. Worshippers offer dry sandalwood through a priest, who does not preach but tends the fire. Priests hold the ranks of dastur, mobad and herbad.
firestone-tire-and-rubber-company: Harvey S. Firestone founded the company on 3 August 1900 in Akron, Ohio, with 12 employees. It first made solid rubber side-wire tyres for fire apparatus, then pneumatic tyres for wagons, carriages and other vehicles. Akron was also the home of its rival Goodyear and of General Tire and B.F. Goodrich, and Firestone and Goodyear together were the largest suppliers of automotive tyres in North America for over 75 years. In 1906 Henry Ford chose Firestone to supply tyres for his cars, and the close relationship between Harvey Firestone and Ford made the company the original equipment supplier for Ford vehicles.

In 1926 the company opened a rubber plantation of more than a million acres in Liberia, at Harbel, and its first service centre. From then until the outbreak of the First Liberian Civil War in 1990 the Harbel plantation was the largest of its kind in the world. It was planned to employ 350,000 people, more than the number of able-bodied men in the whole country, which created intense pressure for labour. The historian Christine Whyte concluded that the collusion of Firestone and government officials to keep wages low and coerce workers was at best overlooked. In September 1990 rebels under Charles Taylor seized the plantation, and operations fully restarted only in 2003.

The company's first radial tyre, the Firestone 500, began to show tread separation in the 1970s. On 20 October 1978 Firestone recalled over 7 million of them, the largest tyre recall to that date, and in May 1980 the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration fined it $500,000. In late 1979 the company, more than a billion dollars in debt, brought in John Nevin, who closed nine of seventeen plants and moved headquarters to Chicago. In 1988 he negotiated its sale to the Japanese firm Bridgestone.

Firestone is now part of Bridgestone Americas and is based in Nashville, Tennessee. In 2000 a high failure rate of Firestone tyres on Ford Explorers brought lawsuits and a mandatory recall, and in 2001 Bridgestone/Firestone ended its ties to Ford. Its tyres also won every Indianapolis 500 from 1920 to 1966.
firishta: Firishta was born at Astarabad, on the shores of the Caspian Sea, the son of Gholam Ali Hindu Shah. While he was still a child his father was called to Ahmednagar to teach Persian to the young prince Miran Husain Nizam Shah, and Firishta studied with the prince. In 1587 he was captain of the guards of Murtaza Nizam Shah I when Miran overthrew his father. Sunni Deccani Muslims then massacred the foreign population, above all Shias of Iranian origin such as Firishta, but Miran spared his former friend.

In 1589 Firishta entered the service of Ibrahim Adil Shah II at Bijapur. He had held only military posts and did not prosper at first: as a Shia he had little chance of high office in the mostly Sunni courts of the Deccan, and Ibrahim was replacing Shias with Sunni Deccanis. In 1593 the sultan asked him to write a history of India that gave the Deccan dynasties as much weight as the rest of the subcontinent, a balance no earlier work had kept.

The history, also called the Gulshan-i Ibrāhīmī, opens with a summary of Hindustan before the Muslim conquest and the advance of the Arabs through the East. Its books treat in turn the kings of Ghazni and Lahore, of the Deccan in six parts, of Gujarat, Malwa, Khandesh, Bengal and Bihar, Multan, Sind and Kashmir, then the Muslims of Malabar and the Muslim saints of India, and it closes with the geography and climate of India. It was presented to Ibrahim in 1606.

Firishta drew on Nizamuddin's Tabaqāt-i-Akbarī, Mirza Haidar's Tarīkh-i-Rāshidī and Barani. The historian Peter Jackson holds that he cannot be trusted as a first-hand witness, and T. N. Devare regards his account of the Ottoman origin of Yusuf Adil Shah as a fabrication, though it is still widely accepted in Bijapur. His account of north Indian politics under Jahangir is held to be independent. Alexander Dow's English translation of 1768 made the work an authority for the English, and J. Briggs published a fuller version in 1829.
firozkoh: The name Firozkoh means Turquoise Mountain. The city lay in what is now Ghor Province and served the Ghurid dynasty as a summer capital, since the dynasty's leaders were semi-nomadic. Its history, layout and buildings are known chiefly from the Tabaqāt-i Nāsirī of Minhaj al-Siraj Juzjani, who lived in the city in his youth but left in 1215 and wrote the work in Delhi in 1260. He is generally thought a reliable chronicler, though his account is one partial view of the city and its people.

The city was founded in 1146 by Qutb al-Din Muhammad of the Ghurid family. His brother Ala al-Din Husayn overthrew the Ghaznavid dynasty in 1150 and burned their capital, Ghazna, killing up to 60,000 people; according to Juzjani the surviving citizens were made to carry building materials to Firozkoh as prisoners, and their blood was mixed with mud for building. Under the following sultans the city prospered and rivalled Herat as a centre of Ghurid art, literature and theology.

In 1199 Ghiyath al-Din ordered the empire to give up the Karramiyya sect for Shafi'i law, a decision that caused riots in the city. Tombstone inscriptions found in the 1950s, studied by Walter Fischel, point to a Jewish trading community there.

The empire began to break up after the deaths of Ghiyath al-Din in 1203 and Muizz al-Din in 1206, though Juzjani claimed the treasury still held 400 camel loads of gold, a figure that may be unreliable. Muhammad II of Khwarazm took the city in 1215, but it rebelled when the Mongols attacked his empire. The Mongols besieged it in 1220 and withdrew at the onset of winter; returning, they forced its ruler, Malik Mubariz al-Din, to leave for Herat and, according to Juzjani, razed the city.

The site of the city was lost, and it has been proposed that the Minaret of Jam, in Shahrak District, is its only standing remains. After the invasion of Afghanistan in 2001 hundreds of diggers searched the area for rumoured gold; when Rory Stewart visited in 2002 the possible remains had been heavily damaged, and finds had been sold in the markets of Herat, Kabul and Tehran.
firozpur: Firozpur lies on the banks of the Sutlej River in the Firozpur District of Punjab. After the Partition of India in 1947 it became a border town on the India–Pakistan border, and it has memorials to soldiers who died fighting for India. A popular name for the locality is Shaheedon-ki-dharti, 'the land of martyrs'. The name is said to come either from Feroz Shah Tughlaq, sultan of Delhi, or from Feroze Khan, a Manj Rajput chief of the mid-16th century.

The city is said to have been founded by Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who reigned over the Delhi Sultanate from 1351 to 1388, and its fortress is said to date from the 14th century. An epidemic in 1543 sent much of the Bhabra Jain trading community to Kot Ise Khan. Sikh influence was affirmed in 1758, when Adina Beg was defeated, and in 1761 sardars of the Bhangi Misl took hold of Ferozepore, which then held 37 villages.

After the death of the chief Dhanna Singh about 1818–19 his widow Lachhman Kaur ruled it, and in 1823 she enlisted British East India Company help to remove a nephew who had occupied the fort. When she died without issue on 28 September 1835 the territory lapsed to the British, and Henry Lawrence took full charge in 1839.

In 1839 Ferozepur was the British outpost towards Sikh power, and it was the scene of operations in the First Anglo-Sikh War, when the Sikhs crossed the Sutlej in December 1845 and were defeated. It stayed in British hands throughout the Indian Mutiny. Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Orphanage there on 26 October 1877, and the Saragarhi Memorial Gurdwara, opened in 1904, commemorates the 21 Sikh soldiers who died at Saragarhi on 12 September 1897.

On 23 March 1931 the remains of Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev were cremated at Hussainiwala on the Sutlej, a place that passed to Pakistan in 1947 and to India on 17 January 1961 in an exchange of exclaves. Their memorial was begun in 1965 and completed in 1968.

Firozpur Cantonment is a major cantonment of India, and the fort within it, a Sikh Empire-era structure, was reopened to the public on 2 June 2025. The 2011 census counted 110,313 people in the city, 70.5 per cent Hindu and 26.3 per cent Sikh. Moti Bazar and Hira Mandi were once prominent markets for the pearl and diamond trade.
firozpur-district: Firozpur district, also written Ferozepur, is one of the twenty-three districts of the state of Punjab and covers 2,190 square kilometres. Its capital, the city of Firozpur, is described as lying inside ten gates, among them the Amritsari, Zira, Delhi, Multani and Kasuri gates. The district now has three tehsils, Firozpur, Zira and Guru Har Sahai, and six blocks. About 93 per cent of the population spoke Punjabi as a first language at the 2011 census.

In the 18th century Sikh warrior groups called misls united in resisting Mughal rule. In 1763 Hari Singh of the Bhangi Misl sacked Kasur, and his commander Gujjar Singh crossed the Sutlej to take Ferozepur, which he gave to his nephew Gurbakhsh Singh. Around 1792 it passed to Gurbakhsh Singh's son Dhanna Singh, who accepted British protection when Ranjit Singh's favourite, Nihal Singh Atariwala, threatened him; this stopped Ranjit Singh from expanding eastward. Dhanna Singh's widow, Lachhman Kaur, died in 1835 without an heir, and the British then took control of the Ferozepur Jagir.

The First Anglo-Sikh War was fought mainly in the district. The first battle was at Mudki, where the Sikh commander Lal Singh abandoned his troops, and at Ferozeshah another leader, Teja Singh, fled when victory was near. After the Treaty of Lahore of 1846 the British took the land east of the Sutlej and divided it among the districts of Ferozepur, Badhni and Ludhiana. Badhni was dissolved in 1847 and added to Ferozepur. In 1856 the Nawab of Mamdot was removed for the wrongdoings of himself and his son, and his lands joined the district, and in 1884 the western part of Sirsa district, including Fazilka, followed.

After the Partition of Punjab, Firozpur became part of India, and by the 1951 census 349,767 Sikh and Hindu refugees from areas that became Pakistan had settled there. Later changes of boundary reduced its area: in 1972 its Moga and Muktsar tehsils went to a new Faridkot district, and in 2011 Fazilka became a district of its own. Firozpur forms part of the Firozpur division.
first-amendment-to-the-united-states-con: The right to petition for redress of grievances was a principle of the 1215 Magna Carta and of the English Bill of Rights of 1689. In 1776 the Virginia colonial legislature passed a Declaration of Rights that called freedom of the press a bulwark of liberty, and eight other states made similar pledges. After the Constitutional Convention proposed a new constitution on 17 September 1787, George Mason proposed adding a bill of rights. James Madison and other delegates argued that state guarantees were sufficient and that listing rights risked implying that unlisted ones were unprotected, and the proposal was defeated by a unanimous vote of the state delegations. The Bill of Rights was proposed later to answer Anti-Federalist opposition to ratification.

The amendment was adopted on 15 December 1791 as one of the ten amendments of the Bill of Rights. In the original draft it stood third, but the first two articles were not ratified by the states. It prevents Congress from making laws respecting an establishment of religion, prohibiting the free exercise of religion, abridging the freedom of speech or of the press, or limiting the right of peaceable assembly and of petition. Courts have cited Thomas Jefferson's phrase about a wall of separation between church and state in applying the religion clauses, and have held that the amendment also protects freedom of association by implication.

At first the amendment bound only Congress, and many of its provisions were read more narrowly than now. The Supreme Court did not rule on the Alien and Sedition Acts, and punishment for blasphemy was upheld throughout the nineteenth century. During the First World War the Court upheld the conviction of Charles Schenck under the Espionage Act of 1917, with Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr. describing a test of clear and present danger.

Beginning with Gitlow v. New York in 1925 the Court applied the amendment to the states through the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. Near v. Minnesota in 1931 and New York Times Co. v. United States in 1971 limited prior restraint of publication, and New York Times Co. v. Sullivan in 1964 required public officials suing for libel to prove actual malice.
first-anglo-afghan-war: The war was one of the first major conflicts of the Great Game, the nineteenth-century competition between Britain and Russia for influence in Central Asia. In Britain any Russian advance into Central Asia was assumed to be directed at India, although no Russian tsar seriously planned an invasion. Lord Palmerston and John Hobhouse feared the instability of Afghanistan and Sindh and the growing power of the Sikh kingdom. Scholars now also stress the fear that Dost Mohammad Khan and the Qajar ruler of Iran would ally to end Sikh rule in the Punjab. The British decided to replace Dost Mohammad with a more pliant ruler, the former king Shuja Shah Durrani.

The Army of the Indus, some 21,000 British and Indian troops under John Keane, set out from the Punjab with William Hay Macnaghten as Britain's chief representative, followed by 38,000 camp followers and 30,000 camels. The British occupied Kabul in August 1839 and restored Shuja. Most troops then went back to India, leaving 8,000 in Afghanistan, but Shuja's rule could be kept only by a British presence that the Afghans resented, and Macnaghten's decision to let soldiers bring their families seemed to show that the occupation would be permanent.

On 1 January 1842 an agreement allowed the British garrison of Kabul and its dependents to leave Afghanistan, and the withdrawal began five days later. The column numbered about 16,500, of whom about 4,500 were soldiers and over 12,000 camp followers. Almost all of them died in the mountain passes. The garrisons at Kandahar and Jalalabad held out, and Ghazni was stormed. Akbar Khan was defeated near Jalalabad, and relief forces came from India in the spring.

Lord Ellenborough, who replaced Lord Auckland as governor-general, was under instructions to end the war. He ordered the forces at Kandahar and Jalalabad to leave after inflicting reprisals and securing the release of prisoners. Shuja Shah was assassinated and succeeded by his son Fateh Jang, who abdicated for his brother Shahpur Mirza. Their short reign ended with the return of Dost Mohammad Khan from exile in India.

The campaign cost over one million pounds in the year 1840 to 1841. In Britain Lord Aberdeen and Benjamin Disraeli criticised the war as rash, and the army chaplain G. R. Gleig wrote in 1843 that not one benefit was gained from it. In 1878 the British invaded again, beginning the Second Anglo-Afghan War.
first-anglo-burmese-war: Tension between the British and Burmese empires had grown since the British acquisition of Bengal and the Konbaung annexation of Arakan. By the 1820s Burmese expansion into Manipur and Assam, and a forward policy of probing the hill states of Jaintia and Cachar, pressed on British Bengal, because defeated forces from these states often used British territory as a base. In 1822 Calcutta declared Cachar and Jaintia British protectorates and sent troops.

King Bagyidaw and Governor-General Lord Amherst were hesitant but were pushed by war factions, and the Burmese commander-in-chief Maha Bandula argued for an offensive. In September 1823 forces clashed over Shalpuri Island near Chittagong, and war formally broke out on 5 March 1824 after border clashes in Arakan. The British also wanted new markets and feared French influence at the Court of Ava.

Early on, Burmese forces used to the jungles of Manipur and Assam pushed the British back, and a column won the Battle of Ramu on 17 May 1824 and took Cox's Bazar, causing panic in Calcutta. The British then took the fight into Burma. On 11 May 1824 a force of over 10,000 men in 62 ships entered Rangoon, and General Archibald Campbell held the Shwedagon Pagoda compound. Bandula's frontal attack on 30 November failed against British weapons, including Congreve rockets.

Bandula was killed by a mortar shell at Danubyu on 1 April 1825, the day the British took Mrauk-U in Arakan. After an armistice and failed talks, the Burmese threatened Prome in November and were dislodged by 5 December 1825. The Treaty of Yandabo, signed on 24 February 1826, required Burma to cede Assam, Manipur, Arakan and Tenasserim, to stop interfering in Cachar and Jaintia, and to pay an indemnity of one million pounds sterling.

About 40,000 British and Indian troops were involved and 15,000 died, almost 70 per cent of the casualties from tropical disease. The cost to British India, approximately 13 million pounds, contributed to an economic crisis that by 1833 had bankrupted the Bengal agency houses and cost the East India Company its remaining privileges. For the Burmese the treaty was a long financial burden and a humiliation. The British fought two further wars against Burma, in 1852 and 1885, and annexed the whole country by 1885.
first-anglo-dutch-war: In the 16th century England had supported the Dutch Republic against Spain in the Eighty Years' War. The separate peace between England and Spain in 1604 strained the relationship, and the Dutch, having made peace with Spain in 1648, replaced the English as the dominant traders with the Iberian Peninsula, adding to an English resentment of Dutch trade that had grown since 1590. By the middle of the century the Dutch had the largest merchant fleet in Europe, with more ships than all other states combined, and had conquered most of Portugal's territories and trading posts in the East Indies and Brazil.

Tensions rose when the English Parliament passed the Navigation Act 1651, which required cargo to English ports and colonies to be carried in English ships. The Dutch saw acceptance as subordinating their trade to the English system. The more immediate cause was action by the English navy and privateers: 140 Dutch merchantmen were seized in 1651, and another 30 in January 1652 alone. An English embassy under Oliver St John, which reached The Hague on 7 March 1651 proposing a confederation of the two Commonwealths, left on 2 July without an alliance.

Both nations were unready, and war might have been delayed but for an encounter between the fleets of Lieutenant-Admiral Maarten Tromp and General at Sea Robert Blake near Dover on 29 May 1652. Cromwell's ordinance required foreign fleets to dip their flag in salute. The salute was not given promptly, and Blake opened fire in the brief Battle of Dover; Tromp lost two ships but escorted his convoy to safety. The Grand Pensionary Adriaan Pauw went to London in a last attempt to prevent war, but English demands had become extreme. Parliament declared war on 10 July 1652. Despite a series of victories in 1652 and 1653, the Commonwealth could not blockade Dutch trade, although English privateers inflicted serious losses on Dutch merchant shipping.

The economic damage led to the Treaty of Westminster in 1654, in which the Dutch made minor concessions. They accepted the Navigation Act, paid an indemnity of £85,000 for the East India Company's losses and agreed to salute English warships in the Channel. The Dutch realised few of their own aims. Cromwell dropped his aim of a union subordinating the Dutch and asked instead that the House of Orange be excluded from the stadtholdership. In a secret annexe, the States of Holland passed an Act of Seclusion in May 1654. The commercial issues remained unresolved, and in 1665 they led to the Second Anglo-Dutch War.
first-anglo-mysore-war: After the death of Aurangzeb in 1707 the Mughal Empire fractured, and by the Third Carnatic War the British held footholds at Bombay, Madras and Calcutta. Mysore, nominally ruled by the Wodeyar dynasty, had passed in 1761 to the Muslim commander Hyder Ali. Seeking a land link between Madras and Bengal, the East India Company obtained a decree from the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II in August 1765 granting it the Northern Circars. The Nizam, Asaf Jah II, objected but could not afford war, and in November 1766 signed a treaty under which the Company lent him troops.

The war began in January 1767 when the Marathas invaded northern Mysore; Hyder paid them 30 lakh rupees to withdraw. The Nizam then advanced to Bangalore with Company troops under Colonel Joseph Smith, but secretly allied with Hyder. Their combined army attacked a Company post at Changama, and Hyder was decisively repulsed at Tiruvannamalai on 26 September 1767. He besieged Ambur in November until a relief column arrived. Weakened by these failures and by British advances in the Circars, the alliance split, and the Nizam withdrew and later made a new treaty with the Company.

In February 1768 a force from Bombay occupied Mangalore after Hyder's small fleet deserted, but Hyder and his son Tipu retook it and the other ports. Meanwhile the British recovered posts in the Carnatic and joined a Maratha force under Morari Rao. Hyder was repulsed at Ooscota on 22 August and near Mulabagilu in October, where a ruse by Colonel Brooks saved Colonel Wood's detachment, but he then routed Wood near Bagalur. In November 1768 he crossed back into the Carnatic, and at last made a forced march of 130 miles in three days with 6,000 cavalry to the gates of Madras.

With Madras nearly undefended, the Company agreed to the Treaty of Madras on 29 March 1769, though it refused the offensive alliance Hyder wanted. When Hyder went to war with the Marathas in 1770, the British declined to help him. In 1779 the Marathas, Hyder and the Nizam agreed on joint action against the British, which led to the Second Anglo-Mysore War in 1780. The struggle ended only in 1799 with the death of Tipu Sultan and the restoration of the Wodeyars as British clients.
first-anglo-sikh-war: Maharaja Ranjit Singh expanded and consolidated the Sikh kingdom of Punjab in the early nineteenth century, as British-controlled territories advanced to its borders. He kept a policy of wary friendship with the British while building up his army with American and European mercenaries as trainers. After his death in 1839 the kingdom fell into disorder: his successors Kharak Singh and Nau Nihal Singh died within months in suspicious circumstances, and Sher Singh was murdered in September 1843. The army grew from 29,000 men in 1839 to over 80,000 in 1845, and its regimental committees formed an alternative source of power. Jind Kaur became regent for her infant son Duleep Singh, with Lal Singh as vizier and Tej Singh as army commander.

The British East India Company had meanwhile built up its strength near the Punjab, with a cantonment at Firozpur, and annexed Sindh in 1843. Most British accounts say their concern was the Sikh army's threat to the border; Sikh and Indian historians say that preparations such as bridging trains and siege batteries show an intent to conquer.

After diplomatic relations broke, the Sikh army began crossing the Sutlej on 11 December 1845, claiming to enter Sikh possessions; the British saw it as hostile and declared war. They won an untidy battle at Mudki on 18 December. At Ferozeshah on 21 December the Sikh artillery caused heavy British casualties, and Hardinge expected defeat, but the British rallied the next morning. Sikh accounts say that Lal Singh held back the irregular cavalry and that Tej Singh withdrew when victory was near.

On 28 January 1846 Sir Harry Smith won at Aliwal. At Sobraon on 10 February the British broke through the Sikh entrenchments, and the pontoon bridge over the Sutlej broke, trapping nearly 20,000 Sikh troops on the east bank. Sikh accounts say Tej Singh deliberately weakened it; British accounts say it broke under the weight of retreating men. None of the trapped soldiers tried to surrender, and the Sikhs lost between 8,000 and 10,000 men.

By the Treaty of Lahore on 9 March 1846 the Sikhs ceded the Jullundur Doab and owed an indemnity of 15 million rupees. Unable to pay, the Durbar ceded Kashmir, Hazarah and the hill country between the Beas and Indus, and Gulab Singh of Jammu bought Kashmir from the Company for 7.5 million rupees under the Treaty of Amritsar. The Treaty of Bhyroval of 16 December 1846 replaced the regent with a British resident, giving the Company control of the government. Resentment led to the Second Anglo-Sikh War within three years.
first-balkan-war: Serbia and Montenegro had secured their independence by 1867, confirmed by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878. Between 1878 and 1912 Greece, Bulgaria and Serbia sponsored insurgent groups in Ottoman Macedonia that fought the government and each other in the Macedonian Struggle. The Young Turk Revolution of July 1908 revived the question of whether Ottoman rule could last. By 1912 the Ottoman Empire, known as the sick man of Europe, was still fighting Italy in Libya and the Dodecanese, and peace came only on 15 October 1912, days after the Balkan war began. Bulgaria was the strongest of the four states of the Balkan League, with some 600,000 men mobilised, while Greece, thought the weakest, was the only member with a meaningful navy.

Montenegro declared war on 8 October 1912. In Thrace the Ottoman command had wrongly expected the main Bulgarian army to go to Macedonia, and the Bulgarians defeated the Ottoman East Army on the Edirne-Kırklareli line. In Macedonia the Greek Army of Thessaly seized Thessaloniki, and the Serbs and Bulgarians won great victories at Kirkkilise, Lüleburgaz, Kumanovo and Monastir. The Greek fleet took Lemnos and kept the Ottoman fleet in the Dardanelles.

Adrianople fell on 11 March 1913 after a two-week bombardment and a final assault by the Bulgarian Second Army and two Serbian divisions. Ottoman casualties in the whole Adrianople campaign reached 23,000 dead, and the Ottoman command lost all hope of regaining the initiative. On 23 April 1913 the garrison of Shkodër surrendered, starved, to the Montenegrins.
