About 180 survivors were held there, and around 130 died at Wybalenna alone.

After a campaign against the commandant, Henry Jeanneret, that included a petition to Queen Victoria, the remaining 47 people were moved in 1847 to Oyster Cove Station, 56 kilometres south of Hobart. Freehold land was given out from the late 19th century, the Municipality of Flinders Island was set up in 1903, and a proper settlement scheme began only in the 1950s.

The island is part of the Municipality of Flinders Island and is the only island of the Furneaux Group with more than one permanent settlement. Whitemark, which has the main airstrip, and Lady Barron are the largest settlements. Strzelecki National Park covers the area around Mount Strzelecki, and two stretches of the island are recognised as Important Bird Areas. The island is the only remaining habitat of a subspecies of the common wombat.
flint-river-georgia: The Flint River, historically also called the Thronateeska, runs 344 miles (554 km) and drains 8,460 square miles (21,900 km2) of western Georgia. It rises as ground seepage in East Point, in southern Fulton County on the edge of the Atlanta metropolitan area, and passes under the runways of Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport. It then flows south past Sprewell Bluff State Park and within 5 miles of Andersonville, through Albany, the largest city on its banks, to Lake Seminole near Bainbridge, where it meets the Chattahoochee River above the Jim Woodruff Dam.

Geologists divide it into three sections: a deep channel cut into crystalline rocks in the red hills of the Piedmont, a broad forested swampy flood plain below the fall line near Culloden, and a channel in limestone above the Upper Floridan Aquifer south of Lake Blackshear. With the Apalachicola and Chattahoochee it forms the ACF basin.

During the Civil War the Andersonville prison stood close to the river. The Flint has long been prone to floods, with significant ones in 1841 and 1925. In 1994 floods from Tropical Storm Alberto crested at 43 feet in Albany, forcing the evacuation of over 23,000 residents, inundating the town of Montezuma when the river topped its 29-foot levee, and lifting caskets from cemeteries. It was one of the worst natural disasters in the state's history, and Albany and Bainbridge flooded again in 1998.

In the 1970s a plan by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to dam the river at Sprewell Bluff in Upson County was defeated by Jimmy Carter, then Governor of Georgia, whose hometown of Plains lies near the river, and other supporters.

The Flint is one of only 40 rivers in the nation to flow more than 200 miles without dams, and one of four in the southeast with significant populations of the Shoals spider-lily. It is impounded to form Lake Blackshear about 15 miles above Albany. Margaret Mitchell made it the border of the fictional plantation Tara in Gone With the Wind.
flintshire: Flintshire is a maritime county, bounded on the north by the Dee estuary and the Irish Sea, on the east by Cheshire, on the west by Denbighshire and on the south by Wrexham County Borough. The Clwydian Range occupies much of the west, and its highest point, Moel Famau, rises to 554 metres. The main rivers are the Dee and the River Alyn. The county is considered part of the Welsh Marches and belonged to the historic Earldom of Chester and Flint.

At the time of the Roman invasion the area was inhabited by the Deceangli, a Celtic tribe who seem to have submitted with little resistance. Lead and silver were worked there, and several Roman ingots of lead bear the name DECEANGI. The region later formed the Hundred of Englefield, became part of the Kingdom of Mercia by the 8th century, and at the Norman conquest in 1066 was held by Edwin of Tegeingl, from whose lordship the county's coat of arms is derived.

In the 13th century the hundreds of Atiscross and Exestan passed from the Earldom of Chester to the expanding Kingdom of Gwynedd after numerous military campaigns. These lands, with the detached territory of Maelor Saesneg, formed the main areas of the county established by the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284 under Edward I. The Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 to 1542 consolidated it under Henry VIII.

Flintshire was an administrative county from 1889 until 1974, when it was merged with Denbighshire and Edeyrnion Rural District to form Clwyd. The present county was formed in 1996, and its boundaries differ from the historic county: English Maelor went to Wrexham County Borough, and St Asaph, Prestatyn and Rhyl to Denbighshire.

The county covers 169 square miles and had a population of 155,000 in 2021. Connah's Quay is the largest town, followed by Buckley, Flint and Mold. The east is industrial and includes the Deeside conurbation, while the coast further west is developed for tourism, notably at Talacre.

The county held much of the North Wales Coalfield, whose last colliery, at Point of Ayr, closed in 1996. Steelmaking at Shotton ended in 1980, with the loss of 6,500 jobs in one day, though coated steel is still produced there. Airbus makes aircraft wings at Broughton.
flora-tristan: Flora Tristan was born on 7 April 1803. Her father, Mariano Eusebio Antonio Tristán y Moscoso, was a colonel in the Spanish Navy from Arequipa in Peru, and her mother, Anne-Pierre Laisnay, was French. After her father's death in 1807 the family's circumstances changed drastically. In 1821, aged seventeen, she married the engraver and lithographer André Chazal, for whose brother she worked as a colourist. They had three children, and she left the marital home in March 1825. Divorce had been abolished in France in 1816, so she obtained only a separation of property in 1828 and for several years lived under assumed names to escape her husband.

In 1833 Tristan travelled to Arequipa to claim her paternal inheritance, which her uncle held, and stayed in Peru until 16 July 1834. She never secured the inheritance, but her travel diary of post-independence Peru was published in 1838 as Peregrinations of a Pariah. She described Lima's women as freer and more influential than any others she knew. On 20 December 1837 she signed a petition to the Chamber of Deputies for the restoration of divorce, and in 1838 she addressed another against capital punishment. On 10 September 1838 Chazal shot her in the chest; he was sentenced to twenty years' hard labour, later commuted to imprisonment.

Her later works included Promenades in London (1840). In 1843 she left Paris to tour France promoting The Workers' Union, meeting groups of worker activists and urging them to break down occupational, regional and political barriers and to seek national and global working-class solidarity. She held that socialism was possible only with the emancipation of the sexes, drawing on Saint-Simon and Fourier while rejecting the idea that the benevolence of the ruling class would bring socialism.

Tristan died suddenly in 1844; her symptoms in the preceding months match what is now understood as typhoid fever, though the exact cause is not known. After her death her followers tried to carry out her plan for a Workers' Union with little success. According to the historian Maurice Agulhon, her visit to Toulon radicalised its workers and contributed to the 1845 strike at the arsenal. In October 1848 French workers placed a monument on her tomb, and close to eight thousand marched to her grave singing a song from The Workers' Union. She is described as a thinker who joined feminism with socialism, and was the grandmother of the painter Paul Gauguin.
florence: Florence lies about 275 kilometres north-west of Rome, in a basin formed by the hills of Careggi, Fiesole, Settignano, Arcetri, Poggio Imperiale and Bellosguardo. The Arno river flows through it. The name derives from the Latin Florentia, meaning the Flourishing Town, from florēre, to flourish or blossom, and the modern Italian name Firenze descends from it through the older Fiorenza.

Florence was founded as a Roman garrison in 59 BCE in an area previously inhabited by an Etruscan settlement whose name is unknown. After a long period as a flourishing trading and banking medieval commune, it became the birthplace of the Italian Renaissance and was one of the most important cities in Europe from the 14th to the 16th centuries. In 1200 the city had 50,000 people, and by 1300 its population was 120,000, with another 300,000 in the surrounding Contado.

It was the Republic of Florence from 1115 to 1532, then a duchy and, from 1569 to 1801, part of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Its turbulent political history includes periods of rule by the powerful Medici family and numerous religious and republican revolutions. From 1865 to 1871 it was the capital of the Kingdom of Italy.

The language spoken in the city in the 14th century came to be accepted as the model for Italian. The works of the Tuscans Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio led to the Florentine dialect being adopted as the basis of a national literary language. The University of Florence was first founded in 1321 and recognised by Pope Clement VI in 1349.

Florence is the capital and most populous city of the Italian region of Tuscany. UNESCO declared its historic centre a World Heritage Site in 1982. The centre lies within medieval walls built in the 14th century. The domed cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore, known as the Duomo, has a dome built by Filippo Brunelleschi that is still the largest in brick and mortar in the world. The Campanile, partly designed by Giotto, the Baptistery, the Palazzo Vecchio and the Uffizi Gallery are among its landmarks. The city was home to Giotto, Donatello, Masaccio, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, and it is known as the Cradle of the Renaissance.
florence-cathedral: Santa Maria del Fiore was built on the site of Florence's second cathedral, dedicated to Saint Reparata. According to Giovanni Villani's Nuova Cronica, the old building was crumbling and too small for the growing city, and other Tuscan cities, Pisa and Siena among them, were rebuilding their cathedrals. The city council approved Arnolfo di Cambio's design in 1294, and Cardinal Valeriana, the first papal legate ever sent to Florence, laid the first stone on 9 September 1296. The project was to last 140 years.

After Arnolfo died in 1302 work slowed for almost 50 years. The discovery of the relics of Saint Zenobius in 1330 gave it new impetus, and in 1331 the wool merchants' guild, the Arte della Lana, took over its patronage. In 1334 it appointed Giotto, who began the campanile. He died on 8 January 1337, and Andrea Pisano continued until the Black Death halted work in 1348.

The cathedral is a basilica in the shape of a Latin cross, with a wide central nave of four square bays and an aisle on either side. Its trilobate apses were meant to evoke a flower, in homage to Fiorenza, the city of flowers. It is 153 m long and 38 m wide, and its dome rises 114.5 m. The exterior is faced with polychrome marble panels in green, pink and white.

The dome was planned from the start without external buttresses. In 1367 the model of Neri di Fioravanti was chosen over a rival's, a decision described as one of the first events of the Italian Renaissance, since Gothic flying buttresses were thought ugly and were forbidden in Florence. The original façade was dismantled in 1587 and 1588 on the orders of Grand Duke Francesco I de' Medici. The present Gothic Revival façade by Emilio De Fabris was built from 1876 to 1887.

The interior is Late Gothic and bare, which suits the austerity of the mendicant orders. Because public funds paid for the cathedral, its notable works honour Florentine heroes: Dante appears in a fresco of 1465 by Domenico di Michelino, and Paolo Uccello and Andrea del Castagno painted the condottieri Sir John Hawkwood and Niccolò da Tolentino as riders in 1436 and 1456. In 1475 the astronomer Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli pierced a hole in the dome to make a meridian line.

Cracks in the dome were seen even before it was finished. In 1694 two major cracks were measured at up to 29 mm, and a commission proposed iron belts, but after long debate the dome was left as it was. Excavations from 1965 to 1974 uncovered Roman houses and the ruins of Santa Reparata, and Filippo Brunelleschi's simple tomb lies in the crypt.
florentine-camerata: The term camerata was coined by the members of Count Giovanni de' Bardi's circle, apparently from the Italian camera, a room used for important meetings. The name comes from Giulio Caccini's score for Euridice, which remembers the Camerata's good years. The earliest recorded meeting took place on 14 January 1573 at Bardi's house, and the group's activity was at its height between 1577 and 1582. Besides Bardi, known members included Caccini, Pietro Strozzi and Vincenzo Galilei, father of the astronomer Galileo Galilei. Girolamo Mei took part, and the poet Ottavio Rinuccini, probably the first opera librettist, may have as well. The circle of Jacopo Corsi, whose rivalry with Bardi was fierce, is not to be confused with it.

The members shared a belief that music had become corrupt and that a return to the forms and style of the ancient Greeks would improve it and, through it, society. They were influenced by Mei, the foremost scholar of ancient Greece of the time, who held that Greek drama was mostly sung rather than spoken, and by Aristoxenus, who proposed that speech should set the pattern for song. They criticised the overuse of polyphony, which obscured the sung text, and wished to create music for a single line over simple instrumental accompaniment. Gioseffo Zarlino, Galilei's own teacher, replied by asking what the musician had to do with those who recite tragedies and comedies.

Their experiments led to the stile recitativo and to monody. In 1582 Galilei performed his own setting of Ugolino's lament from Dante's Inferno, and Caccini sang songs chanted over chordal accompaniment. In the 1590s Jacopo Peri and Rinuccini developed monody into a vehicle for extended drama. In 1598 they produced Dafne, an entire drama sung in monodic style, regarded as the first opera, though its music is lost; Euridice, Peri's second opera, is usually heralded as the work that made history. Bardi's influence waned after he fell out of favour for publicly endorsing the marriage of Francesco I de' Medici and Bianca Cappello, which Francesco's brother Cardinal Ferdinando opposed.

Bardi wrote the Discorso of 1578, a long letter to Caccini, and Galilei published the Dialogo della musica antica et della moderna in 1581 and 1582. In 1602 Caccini wrote Le nuove musiche. No one named the group until Caccini's label in 1600. By the first decade of the seventeenth century the new music drama was widely composed and performed, and monody and polyphony coexisted before they were synthesised, with Florence, Rome and Venice as the Italian centres. The main innovation to emerge from the Camerata was not a piece of music or an aesthetic ideal but a door opened to further dramatic composition.
florentine-codex: Sahagún called the work La Historia General de las Cosas de Nueva España, the General History of the Things of New Spain; the name Florentine Codex comes from the Laurentian Library in Florence, which holds the best-preserved manuscript in three bound volumes. He worked on the project from 1545 until his death in 1590, with Nahua elders and with authors who had been his students at the Colegio de Santa Cruz de Tlatelolco. A missionary first, he meant it to help friars understand the religion they sought to replace, to give them a rich vocabulary of Nahuatl, and to record the cultural inheritance of the peoples of New Spain.

The pages are generally set in two columns, the Nahuatl written first on the right and a Spanish gloss or translation on the left, with pictures forming a third element. Its twelve books move from the gods, ceremonies, omens, rhetoric and moral philosophy through kings and lords, the long-distance merchants called pochteca and the people, to earthly things, and end with Book 12, the conquest told from the side of the defeated of Tenochtitlan-Tlatelolco. The arrangement follows medieval encyclopedias such as De proprietatibus rerum of the Franciscan Bartholomew the Englishman. Book Eleven, on animals, plants and minerals, holds the most text and about half the drawings, and Books Ten and Eleven record Nahua medicine, dictated by more than a dozen named Aztec doctors.

Sahagún gathered his material in Nahuatl from older people of high standing, used fixed sets of questions and compared different informants. Scholars have identified twenty-two artists, probably native scribe-painters (tlacuilo), whose images blend European and Indigenous styles; some spaces were never filled, suggesting the copies sent to Spain were unfinished.

Copies were sent to the Spanish court and to the Vatican and were then largely forgotten until Angelo Maria Bandini described the Florence manuscript in 1793. Francisco del Paso y Troncoso copied it with Italian permission in 1893. Arthur J. O. Anderson and Charles E. Dibble spent 30 years translating the Nahuatl into English. Mexico published a colour facsimile in 1979, the World Digital Library put scans online in 2012, UNESCO added the work to its Memory of the World register in 2015, and the Getty Research Institute released a Digital Florentine Codex in 2023.
florestan-i-prince-of-monaco: Tancrède Florestan Roger Louis Grimaldi was born in Paris on 10 October 1785, the second son of Prince Honoré IV and Louise d'Aumont Mazarin. Brought up by his mother, he showed an early aptitude for literature. At eleven he enrolled in the school of Fontainebleau but did not stay long. He entered the army, where he struggled and barely reached the rank of corporal, and was taken prisoner during the French invasion of Russia. He was not freed to return to France until 1814.

On 27 November 1816 he married Maria Caroline Gibert de Lametz at Commercy. His family apparently disapproved, so the couple married quietly and modestly. Florestan received only a small income from his family, and the marriage to a member of an upper-bourgeois family of Champagne proved financially favourable. Their children included Charles, born in 1818, who later became Prince Charles III, and Florestine, born in 1833.

Florestan succeeded his brother Honoré V on 2 October 1841, as Prince of Monaco and Duke of Valentinois. The British historian H. Pemberton judged him utterly unsuited for the task, and he had been an actor at the Théâtre de l'Ambigu-Comique. Real power lay with his wife Caroline, who was intelligent and excelled at social skills. Honoré V had handled affairs entirely himself, trusting no one to assist him, and she had to work out the business of the state. For a time her tax reform eased the economic difficulty that came from the Congress of Vienna's assigning Monaco to the protection of the Kingdom of Sardinia rather than France, with the principality surrounded by the Sardinian County of Nice.

His accession was largely welcomed. The historian Gustave Saige recorded a warm reception at Menton, where people were relieved to have a prince who was not invisible, and Florestan founded a school there, though an expensive one.

The prince and princess offered two constitutions in answer to local demands for democratic reform, but the people of Menton rejected them, since King Charles Albert of Sardinia offered something better. When they saw that these efforts were failing, they handed power to their son Charles, but too late. Encouraged by the French Revolution of 1848, Menton and Roquebrune revolted and declared themselves independent free cities. The King of Sardinia garrisoned Menton, and Florestan was dethroned, arrested and imprisoned. He was restored in 1849, but Menton and Roquebrune were lost for good.
Florestan died in Paris on 20 June 1856. Despite his good intentions, Monaco was by then a divided country with few prospects of financial prosperity. His son Charles succeeded him.
floriano-peixoto: Floriano Vieira Peixoto was born on 30 April 1839 in the province of Alagoas and moved to Rio de Janeiro at the age of sixteen to finish his secondary education. In 1858 he entered the Military School of Rio de Janeiro, graduating as a second lieutenant in 1861. During the Paraguayan War he served in the 1st Battalion of Homeland Volunteers, later as its commander, and took part in the battles of Tuyutí, Ytororó, Lomas Valentinas and Angostura.

He returned to the capital in 1870 and took a bachelor's degree in physical and mathematical sciences. Promoted marshal in 1874, he served for just over a year from 1884 as president of the province of Mato Grosso. At the Proclamation of the Republic he refused to lead imperial resistance to the coup, became Minister of War in 1890 and was elected vice president in February 1891.

Peixoto rose to the presidency in November 1891, after Deodoro da Fonseca resigned amid a severe political crisis and an economic crisis worsened by the collapse of the Encilhamento bubble. His policies ended the successive economic crises of the years since 1889, and the economy stabilised and grew again. In 1892 a group of senior officers published the Manifesto of the 13 Generals, arguing that the constitution required him to call new elections rather than finish Deodoro's term.

In 1893 the Second Naval Revolt and the Federalist Revolution broke out, the latter in Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina and Paraná. Peixoto put both down by force, which earned him the nickname Iron Marshal and increased the centralisation of power. His supporters formed the cult known as Florianism, the first significant political movement in Brazil centred on a republican figure. He left the presidency on 15 November 1894.

Peixoto died at Barra Mansa, in the state of Rio de Janeiro, on 29 June 1895, from chronic liver disease, most often identified by historians as cirrhosis. He had been seriously ill for months. He is also called the Consolidator of the Republic. Views of his rule were sharply divided at the time; later generations of Brazilians came to regard it as necessary, and preferable to a continuing cycle of civil war. Nossa Senhora do Desterro, the capital of Santa Catarina, was renamed Florianópolis after the defeat of the federalist rebels there.
florida: About two-thirds of Florida occupies a peninsula between the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic Ocean and the Straits of Florida, and it extends northwest into a panhandle. It is the only state that borders both the Gulf and the Atlantic, and it has the longest coastline in the contiguous United States, about 2,170 kilometres. Its climate varies from subtropical in the north to tropical in the south. Everglades National Park is the largest tropical wilderness in the United States, and the Florida Reef is the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States.

The first inhabitants, the Paleo-Indians, entered Florida at least 14,000 years ago. By the 16th century the major groups included the Apalachee, the Timucua, the Ais, the Mayaimi, the Tequesta and the Calusa. Juan Ponce de León sighted the peninsula on 2 April 1513, and it was the first region of what is now the contiguous United States to be visited and settled by Europeans. The story that he sought the Fountain of Youth is apocryphal and appeared only long after his death. An estimated 700,000 Native Americans lived in Florida in the 1520s, but by 1700 only around 2,000 remained.

Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the United States. Britain held Florida briefly from 1763, and Spain recovered it in 1783. Spain later ceded it to the United States. It was the main location of the Seminole Wars (1816–1858), became the 27th state on 3 March 1845, and seceded on 10 January 1861 as one of the seven original Confederate States, returning to the Union on 25 June 1868.

Florida is a state of the United States, with Tallahassee as its capital and 67 counties. Its most populous city is Jacksonville, and the Miami metropolitan area is the largest in the state. Miami Beach's Art Deco District belongs to the state's large collection of Art Deco and Streamline Moderne buildings, and St. Augustine preserves Spanish revival and other early styles.
florida-keys: The Florida Keys are a coral cay archipelago forming the southernmost part of the continental United States. They begin about 24 kilometres south of Miami and extend in an arc south-southwest and then westward to Key West, the westernmost of the inhabited islands, and on to the uninhabited Dry Tortugas. The islands divide the Atlantic Ocean from the Gulf of Mexico and define one edge of Florida Bay. The southern part of Key West is 150 kilometres from Cuba. The total land area is 356 square kilometres.

The northern and central keys are the exposed portions of an ancient coral reef, the Key Largo Limestone, which formed when sea levels stood about 7.6 metres above the present level, beginning some 130,000 years ago. The islands from Big Pine Key to the Marquesas Keys are exposed Miami Limestone. Just offshore lies the Florida Reef, which extends 270 kilometres. The climate is closer to that of the Caribbean than to the rest of Florida.

The Keys were originally inhabited by the Calusa and Tequesta peoples and were charted by Juan Ponce de León in 1513. He named the islands Los Martires, the Martyrs, because from a distance they looked like suffering men. The word key comes from the Spanish cayo, meaning small island. For many years Key West was the largest town in Florida and grew prosperous on revenue from wrecking. It was well placed for trade with Cuba and the Bahamas and lay on the main trade route from New Orleans. Improved navigation led to fewer shipwrecks, and Key West declined in the late 19th century.

The Keys were long reachable only by water. Henry Flagler's Overseas Railway was completed in the early 1910s after hurricanes disrupted the work in 1906, 1909 and 1910. On Labor Day, 2 September 1935, the strongest hurricane to strike the United States made landfall near Islamorada, with a storm surge more than 5.3 metres high. More than 400 people were killed, including more than 200 First World War veterans working on the roadway, whose evacuation train failed to reach them. The storm ended the railway, and U.S. Highway 1 replaced it.

The Overseas Highway, a 204-kilometre section of U.S. 1, runs over most of the inhabited islands, in places on converted railway bridges. The Seven Mile Bridge, built of concrete on pilings, connects Knight's Key to Little Duck Key. Key West is the county seat of Monroe County, and the major industries are fishing and tourism. Many Cubans settled in the Keys after the Cuban Revolution. The waters around the Keys form the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, and Dry Tortugas National Park lies about 110 kilometres west of Key West.
florida-parishes: The Florida Parishes, also called the Northshore or Northlake region, stretch from the Mississippi state line on their eastern and northern borders to the Mississippi River in the west and Lake Pontchartrain in the south. They cover 4,685.184 square miles (12,134.57 km2), or 10.755% of Louisiana's land area. Unlike most of the state, the region was not part of the 1803 Louisiana Purchase, which applied to territory west of the Mississippi River. Its climate is humid subtropical and prone to hurricanes.

The area was first claimed by French colonists as part of French Louisiana. After the French and Indian War, France ceded the eastern half of Louisiana, excluding New Orleans, to Great Britain in the 1763 Treaty of Paris. Britain divided its new Gulf coast lands at the Apalachicola River into the provinces of East and West Florida. After the American Revolutionary War it ceded them back to Spain, and uncertainty over their borders led to the West Florida Controversy with the United States.

Pinckney's Treaty of 1795 settled the first dispute, but the sale of Louisiana in 1803 raised new questions, since the Third Treaty of San Ildefonso and the Treaty of Aranjuez had not included Spanish West Florida. American and British settlers west of the Pearl River, aggrieved by the provincial Spanish government, elected Fulwar Skipwith governor of their republic. After its annexation four parishes were established in 1810: East Baton Rouge, Feliciana, St. Helena and St. Tammany. Washington Parish followed in 1819, East and West Feliciana in 1824 when Feliciana was divided, Livingston in 1832 and Tangipahoa in 1869, during Reconstruction.

The most populous urban area is the Baton Rouge metropolitan area, and St. Tammany Parish belongs to the New Orleans combined statistical area; the region counted 1,088,014 people in 2020. The Roman Catholic Church is its largest denomination and Baptists the second. In 1990 the legislature named it the Republic of West Florida Historic Region, Interstate 12 has been the Republic of West Florida Parkway since 1993, and the republic's flag flies on many public buildings.
floris-v-count-of-holland: Floris V was born on 24 June 1254, the son of Count William II and Elisabeth of Brunswick-Lüneburg. His father was slain by Frisians in 1256, when Floris was two. Custody passed first to his uncle Floris de Voogd and then to his aunt Adelaide of Holland. At the battle of Reimerswaal on 22 January 1263 Count Otto II of Guelders defeated her and was chosen regent by the nobles who opposed her. Otto remained guardian until 10 July 1266, when Floris was declared old enough to rule.

Floris was backed by the Avesnes count of Hainaut and in 1269 married Beatrix, a daughter of Guy of Dampierre, Count of Flanders. A first attack on the Frisians in 1272 to retrieve his father's body failed at Heiloo. In 1274 nobles led by Gijsbrecht IV of Amstel and Herman VI van Woerden rose against him. He supported the weak Bishop of Utrecht, John I of Nassau, who in 1279 added the rebels' lands to Holland, and gave concessions to the peasants of Kennemerland. He switched allegiance from the Avesnes to the Dampierres.

In 1282 he defeated the Frisians at Vronen and recovered his father's body, and after a campaign in 1287 and 1288 he finally defeated them. In 1290 Guy of Flanders invaded Zeeland-bewester-Schelde, which Floris held as a loan from King Rudolf I, and took him prisoner at Biervliet before releasing him. Edward I of England restrained him from resuming war, and in 1292 Floris claimed the throne of Scotland in the Great Cause without the support he expected.

When Edward I moved his wool trade from Dordrecht to Mechelen, Floris switched sides to France in 1296. Edward then banned English trade with Holland, and some say he conspired with Guy of Flanders to have Floris taken to France. Gijsbrecht of Amstel and Herman of Woerden, with Gerard van Velsen, captured him on a hunting party and took him to Muiderslot. Four days later a crowd of peasants stopped the lords as they left, and in panic Gerard van Velsen killed the count, on 27 June 1296.

His life and death inspired songs, plays and books, the best known being Joost van den Vondel's Gijsbrecht van Aemstel. The nickname God of the Peasants began among the nobility as an insult, for acting as if he were the Good Lord with his peasants, and the peasants remembered him as a saint.
flour-war: In Ancien Régime France bread was the main food of poor peasants, and the king, nicknamed the first baker of the kingdom, was expected to secure his subjects' supply. The royal police checked the purity of flour, forbade exports from regions with bad harvests and could force a merchant to lower his price, while grain merchants were suspected of hoarding or of mixing flour with chalk or crushed bones. Turgot had been shaped by the physiocrats and defended Vincent de Gournay's laissez faire, laissez passer in his Éloge de Gournay, and his opponents saw his edict as an attack on this moral economy.

In the spring of 1775, with the reserves exhausted before the new harvest, prices rose suddenly and unrest broke out at markets and flour depots. Counts vary: 180 conflicts were listed from the Paris Basin over 17 days, Jean Nicolas notes 123 distinct riots and Cynthia Bouton finds 313 occurrences. In exporting regions rioters forced large farmers and landowners to sell at a fair price, in the cities they attacked warehouses and bakeries, and elsewhere they blocked rivers and roads to keep a province's wheat from leaving.

The targets were often millers or, as at Dijon on 18 April, counsellors of parliament. From 27 April the movement spread over the great plains, from West Burgundy to the Beauvaisis, Beauce and Brie, and Parisian bakeries were plundered. The destruction was limited; the main targets were the boats carrying wheat, which were sunk. The historian George Rudé rejected the long-held theory of a plot against Turgot by court factions.

The two rioters hanged as examples on the Place de Grève were a 28-year-old wigmaker and his 16-year-old companion. Food was sent to provinces in need, and the clergy preached the king's messages. Most of the trouble was over by 11 May 1775, though five months passed before it ended. Turgot obtained the resignation of the Lieutenant General of Police, Jean-Charles-Pierre Lenoir, and free trade in grain was discredited.

For the historian Kaplan, the riots marked a growing disenchantment of the people with the king. Rumours of a Pacte de Famine to starve the poor persisted, and such fears fed the Réveillon riots of April 1789, the Great Fear of that summer and the Women's March on Versailles in October 1789.
flower-wars: The flower war, in Nahuatl xōchiyāōyōtl and in Spanish guerra florida, was fought on and off for many years between the Aztec Triple Alliance and its enemies around the capital, Tenochtitlan, probably ending with the arrival of the Spaniards in 1519. The opponents included the city-states of Tlaxcala, Huejotzingo and Cholula in the Tlaxcala-Pueblan Valley. The fullest early account of its origin comes from the Texcocan nobleman Ixtlilxochitl, who tied it to the drought, crop failure and famine that struck the central Mexican highlands from 1450 to 1454.

According to Ixtlilxochitl, the priests of Tenochtitlan declared that the gods were angry and had to be placated with regular sacrifices, so Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlaxcala, Cholula and Huejotzingo agreed to fight such wars to obtain captives. Scholars such as Frederic Hicks doubt this origin story, since Ixtlilxochitl does not name the flower war and is the only source for these events.

Armies met on a preset date at a chosen place, which became a sacred site called cuauhtlalli or yaotlalli, and battle began when a pyre of paper and incense was burned between them. The two sides fielded equal numbers, fewer than in ordinary wars and with more nobles among them. Instead of atlatl darts and stones, warriors fought hand to hand with weapons such as the macuahuitl, which let them display individual skill. Because few farmers were needed, these wars could be fought in any season. A long-running flower war, such as that with the Chalcas, could grow deadlier, as captured commoners and later nobles were killed.

When Andres de Tapia, one of Cortez's captains, asked Moctezuma II why the Aztecs had not conquered Tlaxcala, the emperor answered that the war was a convenient way to gather sacrifices and train soldiers. The Tlaxcalan historian Muñoz Camargo noted that the Aztecs besieged Tlaxcalan towns and cut off their trade, so some scholars think the Aztecs wanted conquest and failed. Hicks holds that Moctezuma's explanation may have been genuine. The historian Hassig sees the wars as a cheap way of wearing down an enemy, holding a threat at bay while the main armies fought elsewhere, and above all as propaganda showing Aztec power to other city-states.
flushing-queens: Flushing lies in the north-central part of the New York City borough of Queens, on the eastern bank of Flushing Creek, now the Flushing River. Before European settlement the area was inhabited by the Lenape. Downtown Flushing is a major commercial and retail area, and the intersection of Main Street and Roosevelt Avenue at its core is among the busiest in the city. The neighbourhood is served by stations on the Long Island Rail Road's Port Washington Branch and by the IRT Flushing Line of the subway, which ends at Main Street.

The settlement was established on 10 October 1645 under a charter of the Dutch West India Company, as part of the colony of New Netherland governed from New Amsterdam. It was named Vlissingen after the Dutch city that served as the company's European base, and the English form Flushing was eventually settled upon.

Many early settlers had come down from the Connecticut Colony. After the English took control of New Amsterdam in 1664, the Town of Flushing became one of the five original towns of Queens County when it was established in 1683. The town was dissolved in 1898, when Queens became a borough of the City of Greater New York.

In the 19th century Flushing's closeness to Manhattan made it a fashionable residential area, and the Village of Flushing was incorporated on 15 April 1837. The Queensboro Bridge, opened in 1909 to midtown Manhattan, and the extension of the Port Washington Branch to Pennsylvania Station the next year brought development.

The Roosevelt Avenue Bridge, carrying the Flushing Line, was the largest trunnion bascule bridge in the world when it was finished in 1927, and the subway terminal on Main Street opened the following year. In the 1970s immigrants from Taiwan settled in what had been a mostly white neighbourhood with a small Japanese community, and a large Korean population also made Flushing its home. Later arrivals came from many provinces of China and from India and other countries.

Flushing Chinatown, centred on Main Street and Roosevelt Avenue, has more than 30,000 residents born in China and is described as the largest Chinatown outside Asia. A Koreatown that began on Union Street has spread east along Northern Boulevard into Murray Hill, Bayside, Douglaston and Little Neck. The neighbourhood includes residential sections such as Broadway-Flushing, whose elegant park-like streets form a state and federal historic district, and Waldheim, an estate subdivision built mainly between 1875 and 1925.
flying-buttress: A flying buttress has two parts: a massive pier, a vertical block of masonry standing away from the building wall, and an arch, the flyer, that bridges the gap between pier and wall. It is called flying because it does not touch the wall at ground level, as an ordinary buttress does. It carries to the ground the lateral forces that arise from stone vaults and from wind on roofs. In Gothic churches two flyers were often set one above the other: the lower, below the springing of the vault, resisted the thrust of the vault, while the upper resisted the wind on the roof. The pier was usually capped with a pinnacle, often ornamented with crockets, whose weight added vertical load.

The system developed in late antiquity and flourished in the Gothic period, from the 12th to the 16th century. Early examples survive on the Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna and the Rotunda of Galerius in Thessaloniki. Byzantine and Romanesque buildings supplied precursors. At Durham Cathedral arches carry the thrust of the aisle vault but are hidden under the gallery roof. By the 1160s architects in the Île-de-France used longer, finer arches running over the roofs of the side aisles from the clerestory wall to a heavy pier, so that they were visible from outside. Saint-Germain-des-Prés, completed in 1163, has them round its apse, and those of Notre Dame de Paris, built in 1180, were among the earliest on a Gothic cathedral.
To build one, carpenters made temporary wooden frames, called centring, on the ground, hoisted them into place and fixed them to the piers; these held the stones until the mortar cured.

The advantage was that outer walls no longer had to be thick and heavy, so that wall surface could be reduced and larger windows, often of stained glass, opened. Early flyers were heavier than needed, as at Chartres Cathedral around 1210, and later builders narrowed them, as at Amiens, Le Mans and Beauvais. Late Gothic flyers carried crockets and sculpted figures in niches. Renaissance architecture preferred thick walls and gave up the form, but in the early 20th century the Canadian engineer William P. Anderson revived it to build lighthouses. It has also been used to prop leaning walls, as at Chaddesley Corbett in Worcestershire.
flying-gang: Piracy in the Bahamas grew after 1696, when Henry Every brought his ship, the Fancy, loaded with loot from Indian trade ships into Nassau harbour and bribed the governor, Nicholas Trott, with gold, silver and the ship itself. A Franco-Spanish fleet attacked Nassau in 1703 and again in 1706, and many settlers left. When the War of the Spanish Succession ended in 1713, many British privateers were slow to accept the peace and slipped into piracy, and large numbers made their way to New Providence. The rival captains Benjamin Hornigold and Henry Jennings dominated the settlement, and the sinking of the Spanish 1715 Treasure Fleet gave them wrecks and salvagers to raid.

The pirates governed themselves by a code that was the basis of their claim to a kind of republic: crews ran their ships by vote, shared plunder equally and chose and deposed their captains. Many were privateers out of work or sailors who had revolted against conditions on merchant and naval ships. Africans could be equal members of a crew, several men of mixed European and African descent became captains, some members were Jacobites hoping to restore the Stuart line, and a few women, among them Anne Bonny and Mary Read, sailed with them. The Governor of Bermuda reported over 1,000 pirates in Nassau, against about a hundred inhabitants.

The gang's raids caused an outcry, and King George I appointed Woodes Rogers, himself a former privateer, as royal governor and offered a pardon to pirates who surrendered. Captain Vincent Pearse of HMS Phoenix brought news of the pardon and listed 209 pirates who said they would take it, but Charles Vane harassed him, and Pearse left Nassau.

Rogers arrived in 1718 with several ships and the authority to grant the pardon. Hornigold accepted it, and Rogers commissioned him to hunt down those who refused. Vane and Blackbeard escaped, but Hornigold took ten pirates prisoner, and nine of them were executed on the morning of 12 December 1718. This ended the pirates' republic in the Bahamas, though those who fled carried on elsewhere in the Caribbean. Jennings lived to enjoy retirement; Vane was hanged on 29 March 1721.
foedus-cassianum: In their first treaty with Carthage the Romans listed the surrounding countryside as their own territory, a claim the Latin League contested. The war that followed ended in a Roman victory at the Battle of Lake Regillus and a conditional surrender soon after. According to Roman tradition the treaty was then made between Rome and thirty Latin cities as two independent powers, placing Rome as equal in power to all the members of the league combined. It took its name from Spurius Cassius Vecellinus, consul at the time, who ratified it in Rome on Rome's behalf.

Besides peace, the treaty joined the Roman and Latin armies for mutual defence against the Italic tribes, divided all spoils of war, provided for joint colonies on captured land, and set up a community of private rights between the citizens of Rome and of any Latin city. A bronze copy survived in the Roman Forum until Cicero's day, but the original is lost.

The version given by Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls for peace as long as the heavens and the earth remain where they are. Neither side was to make war on the other, bring in foreign enemies or grant them passage; each was to help the other with all its forces and take an equal share of booty from common wars. Suits on private contracts were to be settled within ten days, in the nation where the contract was made, and nothing could be changed without the consent of the Romans and of all the Latins.

In 486 BCE Rome, again through Spurius Cassius Vecellinus, made a treaty with the Hernici on apparently similar terms, and the Hernici may have been admitted to the Foedus Cassianum itself, though this is not certain. By adding the military power of the Latins to that of the young republic, the treaty allowed Rome to expand across much of the Italian Peninsula.

It was later regarded as the beginning of the network of socii, Roman protectorates that became a major factor in the Republic's rise, and it served as a model for later treaties with other Italic peoples. The treaty was renewed in 358 BCE, but Rome reneged on it soon after; once Rome had overcome the league's other members in the Latin War, the treaty was void.
foligno: Foligno stands in the province of Perugia in east central Umbria, on the Topino river where it leaves the Apennines and enters the wide plain of the Clitunno river system. It lies 40 kilometres south-east of Perugia and 6 kilometres south of Spello, at an elevation of 235 metres. The town stands along the Via Flaminia, where four major roads converge, matching its four gates. Its name derives from an Umbrian form, Fulginia, which became the Roman Fulginium and is linked to the cult of the goddess Fulginia. Of its Roman past no significant trace remains except the regular street plan of the centre and three Roman bridges on the Topino.

The origins of the town are uncertain. Cicero refers to the municipium and prefecture of Fulginia, and Pliny lists it among the cities of Umbria. Totila seized the city in 546, and Belisarius recovered it for the Empire four years later. When the Lombard king Alboin occupied Umbria in 571 and founded the Duchy of Spoleto, Foligno was included in it. Saracen raids in 840 and Hungarian invasions in 915 and 924 caused further damage. Under Pope Innocent III the town passed with much of Umbria under the authority of the Church.

The Trinci family rose to power in the late Middle Ages. On 30 November 1367 Pope Urban V appointed Trincia II as vicar of Foligno for an annual tribute of a sparrowhawk, and Gregory XI later confirmed him. Trincia II was thrown from the windows of the Palazzo Trinci in 1377. Ugolino Trinci acquired the Palazzo Governativo in 1398, and in 1439 it passed from the Trinci to the municipality. Foligno experienced French rule in 1798 to 1799 and again in 1809 to 1814. After 1816 it was a seat of district government under the papacy until Italian unification.

The first printed edition of Dante's Divina Commedia was produced in the Orfini Palace at Foligno on 5 and 6 April 1472 by Johannes Numeister and Evangelista Angelini, with sheets for 300 copies. Foligno also produced the almanac Barbanera in the 18th century, together with Spello. The Palazzo Trinci, decorated by Gentile da Fabriano, and the cathedral of San Feliciano are among its landmarks, and Raphael's Madonna of Foligno once stood on the high altar of the church of Sant'Anna. Foligno is a rail junction on the line from Rome to Ancona. Allied bombing in the Second World War destroyed about 80 per cent of the city, and an earthquake in 1997 caused serious damage.
folketing: From 1849 to 1953 the Folketing was one of the two houses of the bicameral Rigsdag, the other being the Landsting. The houses differed in their sizes, franchises and electoral systems. The Folketing was elected by common vote among men and consisted mainly of independent farmers, traders and merchants as well as the educated classes. From 1866 to 1915 the right to vote for the Landsting was restricted to the wealthiest, and some of its members were appointed by the king, so that it predominantly represented the landed gentry and other conservatives. From 1915 both men and women could vote for both houses.

In the following decades law-making took place mainly in the Folketing, and the Landsting came to be regarded as a superfluous rubber stamp. In 1953 a revised constitution was adopted by a referendum, which eliminated the Landsting and made the Folketing the sole chamber. Christiansborg Palace, nicknamed Borgen, the castle, has been the seat of parliament since 1849. The office of Speaker was created in 1850, and its first holder was Carl Christoffer Georg Andræ.

No single party has had a majority of 90 seats since the 1903 elections, because a party needs only 2 per cent of the national vote to gain representation. All Danish governments since then have been coalitions or one-party minority governments. A government may take office without a vote of confidence and stay as long as it does not lose a vote of no confidence, so that it must assemble a majority for each piece of legislation.

The Folketing passes all laws, approves the cabinet and supervises the government, and it adopts the state's budgets and approves its accounts. The monarch's role is in practice limited to signing the laws, which must be done within 30 days of their adoption. Of its 179 members, 175 are elected in Denmark proper and two each in Greenland and the Faroe Islands. Of the 175, 135 seats are elected by proportional representation in 10 constituencies by the D'Hondt method and 40 levelling seats make up the difference between constituency and nationwide votes.

Members have immunity from criminal charges unless caught red-handed or unless the Folketing lifts it, which it has almost always done. Debates can be held behind closed doors, though this has not happened since 9 April 1940, the day of the German invasion. The members are allocated into thirty standing committees.
folwark: The word entered Polish in the 14th century from the German Vorwerk, first the fortified outwork in front of a castle and later an outlying manor house that ran a farm estate; the nearest English equivalent is grange. Folwarks were operated in the Crown of Poland from the 14th century, in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania from the 15th and in the joint Commonwealth from the second half of the 16th. The first were created on lands of the Church and the monasteries; the system was then taken up by the nobility and by rich peasants, whose sołtys posts the szlachta eventually took over.

A folwark was land kept by the lord rather than rented out, worked at first by his hired labourers or servants. Peasants farmed lots they rented from him and owed some unpaid labour on the folwark, originally a few days a year. As grain exports to Western Europe grew more profitable, landowners found it paid better to demand labour than to collect money rents.

From the 16th century the labour due rose sharply, and laws sponsored by the szlachta, among them the Statutes of Piotrków of 1496 and the Privilege of Toruń of 1520, forbade peasants to leave their villages. Formerly free peasants fell into what Polish historians call secondary serfdom. In Lithuania serfdom was fully established by the Volok Reform in the mid-16th century.

When farm prices fell at the end of the 17th century the folwark economy entered a crisis, and the nobles' response, taking more peasant land and demanding more labour, deepened it and worsened the peasants' condition. Folwarks nonetheless remained the basis of the szlachta's economic and political power until the late 18th century. After serfdom was abolished they used paid labour, and they survived the Partitions of Poland. The Polish Committee of National Liberation abolished them by its land reform decree of 6 September 1944, and after the Second World War they were nationalised as state farms or divided up, usually with little or no compensation.
fon-people: The Fon are the largest ethnic group in Benin. They speak Fongbe, one of the Gbe languages of the Bight of Benin, and also live in south-west Togo. Their history was kept orally until the late medieval era. According to oral histories, they originated at Tado, an Aja kingdom near the Togo–Benin border. One group moved to Allada with king Lande Ajahouto, and when his sons quarrelled over the succession a group followed his middle son Do-Aklin to the Abomey plateau and founded the kingdom of Dahomey about 1620.

The claim of an origin in Allada is not recorded in contemporary sources before the late 18th century and is probably an attempt by the dynasty at Agbome to legitimise its conquest of Allada in the 1720s.

Dahomey expanded in the early 18th century, particularly under King Agaja until the 1740s, and reached the Atlantic coast from its inland capital Abomey. It became one of the main economic and military powers of the coast, second only to the Oyo Empire. Slavery long predated Dahomey, but its rulers and merchants, established on the coast between 1700 and 1740, entered the Atlantic trade, and Dahomey controlled the port of Ouidah. The Fon were both victims and victimisers. Under Oyo overlordship Dahomey had to supply slaves as annual tribute, many of them Fon men, which led to its reliance on an all-female military unit, the Agoji or Mino, known as the Dahomey Amazons.

After the slave trade was outlawed the king turned to palm oil and leased the ports to the French, who read the agreement as a cession. A French attack in 1890 led to the annexation of Dahomey as a colony in 1892. It gained independence in 1960.

The Fon are traditionally settled farmers, growing cassava, maize and yams, with palm oil as a cash crop. Their culture is patrilineal, and villages are usually headed by a hereditary chief. The traditional religion, Vodun, has public gods, personal gods, ancestral spirits and charms. Fon belief holds a female Supreme Being, Nana Buluku, who gave birth to Mawu-Lisa, the moon and sun, who created the universe with the trickster Legba and the cosmic serpent Aido Hwedo. Many Fon are Christian, but most continue to practise Vodun, which through the slave trade influenced Haitian Vodou and Candomblé.
fondaco-dei-tedeschi: The word fondaco comes from the Arabic funduq, a caravanserai combining warehouse, shop and inn for travelling merchants, a word also used for the lodgings of European merchants in eastern ports; Tedeschi means Germans. The first Fondaco was built in 1228 beside the Rialto Bridge on the Grand Canal. A German friar described it as having two central courtyards facing the canal, and a map by Jacopo de' Barbari shows it as many smaller buildings used for storage and housing. It also appears in the background of Vittore Carpaccio's painting Miracle of the Relic of the Cross at the Ponte di Rialto.

The building raised after the fire of 1505 is much larger, four floors set around one central courtyard, with fifty-six rooms and further storerooms; it could house over one hundred merchants, as many servants and a number of officials. The ground-floor storerooms were reached by water, the upper floors held living quarters and dining rooms, and a five-bay loggia on the canal received goods and merchants from boats. Its stairs resemble those of the Wakala al-Ghauri in Cairo and its arches those of the Great Mosque in Damascus. Of the frescoes only fragments survive, some kept at the Ca' d'Oro and the Gallerie dell'Accademia; others are known from prints in a folio by Antonio Maria Zanetti of the mid-18th century.

The merchants came from cities such as Nuremberg, Judenburg and Augsburg, and on arrival handed over their weapons to the Fontegher, the Venetian official who assigned the rooms. The Republic took a commission on the trade conducted there, which carried goods from the East toward the Alps. Germans occupied the building from shortly after it was built until Napoleon's arrival in 1806. In the 20th century it housed the headquarters of the Poste Italiane for about 70 years. Sold in 2008 to Edizione Property, a company of the Benetton family, for around 55 million euros, it was rebuilt from 2014 amid local protest and served as a luxury department store until the end of April 2025.
fondaco-dei-turchi: Scholars are unsure who commissioned and designed the building, which began as a private palace. As the Palace of the Dukes of Ferrara it lodged ambassadors from Ferrara and, now and then, members of the Este family. When Duke Alfonso II d'Este died without an heir in 1597, his cousin Cesare d'Este inherited his estate, but Alfonso's sisters Anna and Lucrezia contested it. Pope Clement VIII seized Ferrara, and his nephew Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini occupied the palace in 1598. Cesare finally sold it to Antonio Priuli, later Doge of Venice, though some sources date the sale to 1621.

Priuli leased the building to an operator who made it a hospice and trading house. Part of the reason was that through most of the 16th century Ottoman merchants had lodged in many houses, several of them of ill repute. The traders, Jews, Armenians and Greeks among them, brought wheat, cotton, raw silk, leather, spices and the calcined ashes the glassmakers of Murano needed, and took back Venetian textiles made to Ottoman taste. Like the Fondaco dei Tedeschi for German traders, it served as home, warehouse and market, and its residents could enter and leave only at set times. The Turkish traders stayed on after Napoleon abolished the Republic of Venice in 1797.

The rebuilding of 1869 demolished everything behind the canal façade, so the original plan is known chiefly from undated drawings in the Este archives at Modena. Signed by Cesare Torello, known as Franco, a draftsman, stonemason and architect recorded in Venice and Padua between 1578 and 1606, they are thought to date from 1600 or 1601. The building also appears in Jacopo de' Barbari's bird's-eye view of Venice of 1500. Its façade joins classical medallions and columns, a Renaissance arcade and balustrade, and Islamic horseshoe arches and crested merlons, while its axial plan around a central courtyard has roots in the Islamic world.
fontainebleau: Fontainebleau is a commune 55.5 kilometres south-south-east of Paris, in the Seine-et-Marne department, of which it is a sub-prefecture. Its land area is the largest of any commune in the Île-de-France, larger than Paris itself. The Forest of Fontainebleau, a former royal hunting park, surrounds the town and is protected by France's Office National des Forêts. It is popular with hikers, horse riders and climbers.

The name was taken in the sixteenth century from the Fontaine Belle-Eau, a spring in the château garden. Louis VII endowed the hamlet with a royal hunting lodge and chapel in the mid-twelfth century, and Louis IX, who called it his wilderness, built a country house and a hospital. Philip the Fair was born there in 1268 and died there in 1314. Francis I turned the country house into a palace in the largest of his building projects, and from 1528 the court there entertained the new ideas known as the Renaissance. Every monarch from Francis I to Louis XV renovated it.

On 18 October 1685 Louis XIV signed the Edict of Fontainebleau there, revoking the Edict of Nantes and the right of Huguenots to worship publicly. Many Protestants were forced to convert, killed or driven into exile. The Treaty of Fontainebleau of 29 October 1807 allowed French troops to cross Spain to invade Portugal. Pope Pius VII arrived at the château as Napoleon's prisoner on 20 June 1812 and stayed in his apartments until 23 January 1814. On 20 April 1814 Napoleon bade farewell to the Old Guard in the courtyard, now called the Courtyard of Goodbyes, and the Treaty of Fontainebleau of 1814 stripped him of his powers and sent him to Elba.

Until the nineteenth century Fontainebleau was a village and suburb of Avon. In 1946 it hosted the Franco-Vietnamese Conference, which ended in failure, and until 1967 it held Allied land forces headquarters for Central Europe.

About 300,000 people visit the palace each year and more than 13 million the forest. The town is home to the European campus of the INSEAD business school, and the mystic George Gurdjieff and the writer Katherine Mansfield are buried in the cemetery at Avon.
fontana-maggiore: The fountain was designed by Frà Bevignate da Cingoli, who worked with the hydraulic engineer Boninsegna Veneziano. The new aqueduct carried water several kilometres from Mount Pacciano without pumps, and a forced pressure duct let it flow uphill to the city's acropolis in Piazza IV Novembre, formerly Piazza Grande. The fountain, of stone from Assisi, was prepared in a workshop and then assembled in the square.

Nicola Pisano carved the marble reliefs together with his son Giovanni. The bronze upper cup and its group of three female figures holding an amphora, from which the water pours down into the basins, were made by Rosso Padellaio of Perugia. The figures are taken to be the Charites or perhaps nymphs.

The lower basin has 25 sides, each with two relief panels divided by a column. Its annual cycle shows twelve scenes of daily life and farm work for the months, each with its zodiac sign, from a gentleman and his wife at the hearth in January to the slaughter of the pig in December. Manual labour stands beside the liberal arts, from Grammar and Dialectic to Astronomy and Philosophy, scenes from the Bible such as the Original Sin and Samson, the history of Rome with Romulus and Remus, and two fables of Aesop. One of two eagles bears Giovanni Pisano's signature.

At the 24 edges of the upper basin stand figures of saints and of biblical, mythological and civic characters, among them Saint Peter, Saint Lawrence and San Ercolano, the patron saints of the city, Moses, David, Euliste, held to be the founder of Perugia, and the podestà Matteo da Correggio. Augusta Perusia, the Roman name of the city, holds a cornucopia and receives wheat from the lady of Chiusi and fish from the nymph of Lake Trasimeno. Latin verses on the lower frame name the makers and invite the passer-by to look closely.

The earthquake of 1348 damaged the fountain, and the panels were put back in a random order. The architect Giuseppe Sacconi refurbished it in 1948/49, and it was restored again from 1995 to 1999. It inspired Jacopo di Grondalo's Sturinalto Fountain at Fabriano in 1285, and in 1974 Poste italiane issued a 40 lire stamp of it in a series of Italian fountains.
foot-binding: Several stories tell of foot binding before its establishment under the Song dynasty. One concerns Pan Yunu, a consort of the Southern Qi emperor Xiao Baojuan, whose dancing was said to make lotus flowers spring from her steps, though there is no evidence that she bound her feet. Another links the custom to the 10th-century emperor Li Yu of the Southern Tang, who asked his concubine Yao Niang to bind her feet in white silk and dance on a golden lotus; others, it was said, then imitated her.

Admiration for small feet existed earlier: a Tang tale of about 850, that of Ye Xian, contains elements of the Cinderella story. Odoric of Pordenone mentioned foot binding in the 14th century, but Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta did not, which may show that it was not yet widespread. By the Ming period it was a status symbol, and its rise coincided with a decline of women's dance.

Binding began before the arch had fully developed, usually between the ages of four and nine, often in winter, when numb feet made the pain less sharp. The foot was soaked in a mixture of herbs and animal blood, the toenails cut back, and the toes curled under and pressed into the sole until they broke. Long cotton bandages were wound in a figure of eight and tightened with each pass, forcing the arch to break and the heel and ball of the foot together.

Practice varied by region and class. Infection was the commonest problem, and poor circulation left injuries unhealed. It is thought that as many as 10 per cent of girls may have died of gangrene and other infections. Frontier peoples such as the Uyghurs, Manchus, Mongols and Tibetans generally did not practise it.

Interpretations differ. Some see fashion and beauty, since a woman with small lotus feet could marry more prestigiously; others point to the seclusion of women, or to a wish to keep daughters at handwork. Laurel Bossen and Hill Gates reject the idea that it was thought more beautiful or won better marriages.

Some Chinese writers opposed the custom in the 18th century, and the Taiping leaders outlawed it where they ruled. Christian missionaries and Chinese reformers, among them the early feminist Qiu Jin, campaigned against it in the late 19th century. It began to die out in the early 20th century, upper-class and urban women giving it up sooner than poorer rural women.
football-war: The nickname suggests that a football match caused the war, but its causes lay deeper, in land reform in Honduras and in immigration and demographic problems in El Salvador. El Salvador was overpopulated, with too few jobs, and 5 per cent of its farms occupied 70 per cent of the land. Many Salvadorans migrated to Honduras to work on banana plantations, and by 1969 more than 300,000 lived there. A Honduran land reform law, fully enforced by 1967, took land occupied by Salvadoran immigrants and redistributed it to native-born Hondurans, and thousands of Salvadoran labourers were expelled.

In June 1969 the two countries met in a two-leg qualifier for the 1970 FIFA World Cup. Honduras won the first game, at Tegucigalpa on 8 June, and El Salvador the second, at San Salvador on 15 June, each accompanied by harassment and riots. On 26 June El Salvador broke off diplomatic ties, saying that around 12,000 Salvadorans had been forced to flee Honduras.

The war began on 14 July 1969 at about 6 in the evening, when the Salvadoran air force attacked Honduran airfields, mainly Toncontín International Airport, where the Honduran air force kept half of its aircraft. The Salvadoran army then invaded on two fronts, one towards the Sula Valley and the other along the Pan-American Highway towards Tegucigalpa. On 15 July the Honduran air force bombed targets in El Salvador, among them the Ilopango International Airport and oil facilities.

On 16 July, in the only major battle of the war, Salvadoran troops surrounded Nueva Ocotepeque, and Honduran forces retreated with civilians. Both fronts then stalled for want of ammunition and because of growing Honduran resistance. The war was the last conflict in which piston-engined fighters fought each other.

A ceasefire arranged by the Organization of American States took effect at midnight on 18 July and required Salvadoran troops to withdraw within 96 hours. El Salvador delayed until it had guarantees for the Salvadorans still in Honduras, and gave way after the OAS threatened sanctions. Its troops left on 2 August 1969. Most historians agree that civilians accounted for the majority of the losses. Estimates of Salvadorans displaced run from 60,000 to 130,000, and their return to an overpopulated country was one cause of the Salvadoran Civil War about a decade later. Trade between the two countries stopped, and a peace treaty was signed in Lima on 30 October 1980.
forbes-burnham: Burnham was born in Kitty, a suburb of Georgetown, to a schoolmaster, James Ethelbert Burnham, and Rachel Abigail Sampson, in an Afro-Guyanese Methodist household. After returning from his studies in the United Kingdom in 1949 he set up a law practice and became leader of the British Guiana Labour Party. In the election of 27 April 1953, the first with universal suffrage, the People's Progressive Party (PPP) won 18 of 24 seats and Burnham became Minister of Education. On 12 and 13 February 1955 the party split into Burnhamite and Jaganite factions; Jagan favoured a socialist domestic policy, Burnham's faction was more moderate. After the 1957 election Burnham formed the People's National Congress (PNC).

Opposition to the PPP government's budget of 31 January 1962 led to mass demonstrations and the rioting of 16 February 1962, "Black Friday", in which 56 businesses were destroyed; the PNC was accused of leading the mobs. Declassified documents show that the United States government under John F. Kennedy came to regard Jagan as a communist and approved intervention against his government, and that from 1962 to 1968 Burnham received support from the Central Intelligence Agency. A December 1964 election under proportional representation gave the PPP 46% and the PNC 41%; Burnham formed a coalition with Peter D'Aguiar's United Force and became premier on 14 December.

After independence in 1966 he passed a National Security Act allowing detention without trial for up to 90 days. An independent review could verify only 15% of the overseas votes that gave the PNC a majority in 1968. On 23 February 1970 he declared a co-operative republic and nationalised the main foreign-owned industries. A constitution of 1980 created an executive presidency, which Burnham won with 76% of the official vote, though observers protested that Indo-Guyanese voters were prevented from voting in places. In 1978 909 members of Jim Jones's Peoples Temple, which Burnham had allowed to settle in Guyana, died at Jonestown.

Burnham died of heart failure during throat surgery in Georgetown on 6 August 1985, aged 62. His legacy remains disputed. His successor Desmond Hoyte called him a great leader, while the historian Moe Taylor called his premiership a deeply divisive chapter in Guyana's recent history, and John Prados described him as a dictatorial figure. His administration has been accused of discrimination against Indo-Guyanese and of electoral fraud and state violence, including complicity in the car-bomb death of the historian Walter Rodney on 13 June 1980.
forbidden-city: Construction began in 1406, after the Yongle Emperor, the son of the Hongwu Emperor, moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing. The materials included whole logs of precious Phoebe zhennan wood from the jungles of southwestern China, large blocks of marble from quarries near Beijing, and golden bricks, specially baked paving bricks from Suzhou, laid on the floors of the major halls.

The Chinese name Zijincheng means Purple Forbidden City. Zi, purple, refers to the North Star, which in traditional astrology was the heavenly abode of the Jade Emperor; the Forbidden City was its earthly counterpart. The name first formally appeared in 1576.

The complex is a rectangle measuring 961 m from north to south and 753 m from east to west, enclosed by a wall 7.9 m high and a moat 52 m wide. It has 980 surviving buildings with 8,886 bays of rooms; the common claim of 9,999 rooms is a myth not supported by survey evidence. At the heart of the Outer Court a three-tiered white marble terrace carries three halls, the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the Hall of Central Harmony and the Hall of Preserving Harmony. The first is the largest surviving wooden structure in China. Almost all roofs bear yellow glazed tiles, yellow being the emperor's colour.

From 1420 to 1644 the palace was the seat of the Ming dynasty. In April 1644 rebel forces under Li Zicheng captured it, and he soon fled before the armies of the former Ming general Wu Sangui and the Manchus, setting fire to parts of it. By October a ceremony there proclaimed the young Shunzhi Emperor ruler of all China under the Qing. The Qing renamed some principal buildings to stress harmony rather than supremacy and made the nameplates bilingual in Chinese and Manchu. Anglo-French forces occupied it in 1860 during the Second Opium War, and Empress Dowager Cixi fled in 1900 during the Boxer Rebellion.

Under the Qing the emperor lived and worked almost entirely in the Inner Court, using the Outer Court for ceremony. From 1933 the threat of Japanese invasion forced the evacuation of the museum's most important collections.
forcalquier: Forcalquier lies between the Lure Mountain and Luberon ranges, about 30 km south of Sisteron and 10 km west of the Durance river. Its Latin name, Furnus Calcarius, comes from the lime kilns used in Roman times, and a Roman bridge still stands in the valley to the south of the town. The town is built round the slopes of a steep conical hill.

At the end of the 11th century a family of the counts of Provence created the county of Forcalquier. In the Middle Ages the town was the capital of Haute-Provence along the Durance, a territory that included Manosque, Sisteron, Gap and Embrun. It minted its own currency, and its church was raised to the status of a concathedral.

The counts of Forcalquier grew powerful enough to defy the counts of Provence. The rivalry ended in 1195, when Gersende de Sabran, countess of Forcalquier, married Alfonso II, count of Provence, and their son Ramon Bérenger IV inherited both counties.

The hill is crowned by the octagonal chapel of Notre Dame de Provence, built in 1875 where the medieval citadel stood until its destruction in 1601. The oldest part of the town surrounds the Place Saint-Michel, with a Renaissance fountain of 1511 and doorways from the 12th to 16th centuries. The 12th-century concathedral of Notre Dame de l'Assomption stands across from the Place du Bourguet. Franciscans, called cordeliers for their rope belts, built a convent in the 13th century, occupied by monks until the Revolution. The Port de Cordeliers is all that remains of the town walls. The municipal museum holds prehistoric and Gallo-Roman objects, glass and local pottery.
force-publique: Leopold II of Belgium, who held the Congo Free State as his private colony, ordered the Belgian Secretary of the Interior in 1885 to create a military for it. Early in 1886 Captain Léon Roget of the Carabiniers was sent to found the force and on 17 August became its commandant. Its officers were entirely European: Belgian regulars and mercenaries, many from Scandinavia, Italy and Switzerland. The African soldiers were recruited or conscripted in the Upper Congo or hired from Zanzibar and West Africa, until foreign mercenaries were mostly phased out by 1908.

In the Congo Arab war of 1892–1894 the force defeated the African and Arab slavers, at a cost of tens of thousands of casualties, and in 1896 it beat the Rwandan royal army at the Battle of Shangi before withdrawing. It numbered 19,000 men by 1900. After the Belgian state took over the colony in 1908 the force was slowly reorganised. In the First World War Lieutenant-General Charles Tombeur's army took Kigali on 6 May 1916 and Tabora on 19 September 1916, supported by more than 260,000 local bearers.

When Belgium surrendered to Germany on 28 May 1940, Governor-General Pierre Ryckmans kept the colony in the war on the Allied side. The force grew to 40,000 men, fought Italian forces in Abyssinia, which surrendered to General Auguste-Édouard Gilliaert on 7 July 1941, and sent a medical unit as far as Burma.

Most of the force served in small fixed garrisons with a police role. Belgium kept it apart from the people it policed, in tribally mixed units with no more than a quarter of a company from its own province. The chicote was abolished only in 1955, and only about 20 African officer cadets were in training at independence. On the eve of independence it had 22,403 Congolese soldiers and NCOs under 444 European officers. After the mutiny it was renamed the Congolese National Army on 8 July 1960 and its leadership was Africanised; its former sergeant-major Joseph Mobutu later seized power.
former-yan: The Murong were a Xianbei tribe in Tanshihuai's confederation in the late 2nd century. After it broke up, their chief Mohuba led them into the Chinese interior, and they settled in Liaoxi Commandery. They helped the Cao Wei general Sima Yi against the Liaodong warlord Gongsun Yuan in 237 and were allowed to move into northern Liaodong. In 285 Murong Hui became chieftain and in 289 submitted to the Jin, who named him Commander of the Xianbei. He settled his tribes at Jicheng, encouraged agriculture and modelled his government on Chinese bureaucracy. As the Western Jin fell, he welcomed Chinese refugees and recruited scholar-officials among them. In 321 he accepted the title Duke of Liaodong.

Murong Hui had named his eldest son Murong Huang as heir to establish primogeniture, against the Xianbei custom of passing power to the most capable male. After his death in 333 Murong Huang's brothers challenged him. In 337 he claimed the title Prince of Yan, which most historians regard as the start of the dynasty, though he presented himself as a Jin vassal all his life. He conquered the Duan tribe with the Later Zhao the following year, repelled a Zhao invasion, and in 342 moved his capital to Longcheng and sacked the Goguryeo capital at Hwando. In 344 he destroyed the Yuwen, and in 346 he captured the king of the Korean kingdom of Buyeo.

After Murong Huang died in 348, his son Murong Jun invaded the Central Plains while the Later Zhao was torn by civil war. He took Jicheng, modern Beijing, in 350 as his capital. His brother Murong Ke captured Ran Min at the Battle of Liantai in 352, and Ye later surrendered. Murong Jun declared himself emperor and moved the capital to Ye in 357. He died in 360 while planning to conquer the Jin, leaving the child Murong Wei under the regency of Murong Ke, who took Luoyang in 365 and brought the state to its peak. After Murong Ke's death in 367 his uncle Murong Ping proved corrupt, the treasury was exhausted, and nobles hid households on private estates.

In 369 the Jin commander Huan Wen invaded, and Murong Chui, with Former Qin reinforcements, defeated him at the Battle of Fangtou. The Yan then refused to cede the Luoyang region it had promised Qin, and Murong Ping plotted against Murong Chui, who fled to Qin. In 370 Wang Meng crushed the main Yan force at the Battle of Luchuan, Qin entered Ye, and Murong Wei surrendered to Fu Jian. The Murong were treated as honoured prisoners. After the Battle of Fei River in 383 Murong descendants founded the Later Yan, Western Yan and Southern Yan.
formula-of-concord: The work was undertaken at the behest of Elector August of Saxony. A group of seventeen Lutheran theologians and churchmen met at Torgau, the seat of the Saxon government, from 9 April to 7 June 1576. With two earlier texts before them, the Swabian-Saxon Concord that Jakob Andreä had drafted in 1574 and the Maulbron Formula of 1576, they produced the Torgau Book, which Andreä condensed into what became the Epitome.

Over the following eleven months suggested changes were sent to Andreä and Martin Chemnitz. Six of the theologians, Andreä, Chemnitz, Nikolaus Selnecker, David Chytraeus, Andreas Musculus and Christoph Körner, then met at Bergen Abbey near Magdeburg in March and May 1577 and revised the text into its final form, the Bergen Book or Solid Declaration. It was presented to the elector on 28 May 1577. This is why the Formula is also called the Bergic or Bergen Book.

The Formula has two parts. The Epitome sets out its twelve articles briefly; the Solid Declaration, also translated as the Thorough Declaration, explains them in detail. Approved teaching is stated in theses and rejected teaching in antitheses. The articles cover original sin, free will, the righteousness of faith before God, good works, law and gospel, the third use of the law, the Holy Supper of Christ, the person of Christ, Christ's descent into hell, church ceremonies regarded as indifferent things (adiaphora), God's eternal foreknowledge and election, and other heresies and sects. It was written in German, and a Latin translation was made for the Latin edition of the Book of Concord in 1584.
