The Formula was signed by three electors of the Holy Roman Empire, twenty dukes and princes, twenty-four counts, four barons, thirty-five free imperial cities and more than 8,000 pastors, about two-thirds of the Lutheran Church in Germany at the time. In the Electorate of Saxony every clergyman had to sign or set down his objections, and a rhyme of the day ran: Write, dear Sir, write, that you might remain at the parish.

Not all Lutherans accepted it. It was rejected in Hesse, Zweibrücken, Anhalt, Pommerania, Holstein, Denmark-Norway, Sweden, Nuremberg, Strassburg and Magdeburg, and the government of Queen Elizabeth I of England lobbied through its embassies in Germany against its acceptance by the German estates. Where it was received, its promulgation and subscription did much to unify and preserve Lutheranism.
fort-canning-hill: The hill rises about 48 metres (157 ft) beside Singapore's civic district, the highest ground within walking distance of it. The Malay name Bukit Larangan, Forbidden Hill, comes from the belief that the kings of ancient Singapore were laid to rest there, and the hill was thought to be haunted. Around 1330 the Chinese traveller Wang Dayuan described a settlement called Ban Zu on a hill behind Long Ya Men, thought to be this hill, whose people he called honest and who wore turbans of gold-brocaded satin and red clothes.

Historical sources say Singapura was attacked by either the Majapahit or the Siamese, forcing its ruler Parameswara to move to Melaka, and archaeology suggests the hilltop settlement was abandoned then. On 6 February 1819, after the Singapore Treaty, Major William Farquhar climbed the hill and hoisted the Union Jack. Stamford Raffles had a wooden bungalow built there in 1822 and 1823 to a design by George Drumgold Coleman, and set aside 48 acres for Singapore's first botanical garden, abandoned in 1829. Rebuilt in brick, the house served as Government House.

The residence was demolished in 1859 for a fort, completed in 1861 and named after Viscount Charles John Canning, the first Viceroy of India. Its guns were judged a failure, since ships could shell the town from out of their range. The fort was pulled down in 1907, and an underground command bunker of 30 rooms was completed in 1938. There, on 15 February 1942, Lieutenant-General Arthur Ernest Percival surrendered Singapore to the Japanese. The Singapore Armed Forces took over the site in December 1966.

Fort Canning Park was given its name on 1 November 1981 and laid out as a historical park. The bunker reopened on 31 January 1992 as the Battle Box. The fort's gateway, two nine-pound cannons, the Gothic gates of 1846 of the old Christian cemetery and the Keramat Iskandar Shah shrine survive, and excavations begun in 1984 by the archaeologist John Miksic have recovered porcelain, earthenware and glass.
fort-christina: The fort stood about 1.6 km east of present-day downtown Wilmington, at the confluence of the Brandywine River and the Christina River, some 3 km upstream from the Christina's mouth on the Delaware River. The settlers, who arrived on 29 March 1638 aboard the Kalmar Nyckel and Fogel Grip, landed at a stone outcropping that formed a natural wharf, known as the Rocks. Minuit, a former director of New Netherland, chose the site for trade in beaver pelts with the Lenape and because it was easy to defend, and had an earthwork fort built around the Rocks.

The Swedes claimed much of present-day Delaware, and later parts of southeastern Pennsylvania and southern New Jersey, against Dutch claims to the area. Governor Peter Hollander Ridder strengthened the earthworks in 1640, homes and farms spread beyond the fort, and it was rebuilt in 1647. In 1651 Peter Stuyvesant founded Fort Casimir at present-day New Castle, 12 km to the south; the Swedes took it in 1654 under Governor Johan Risingh, who added a wooden palisade to Fort Christina.

In 1655 Stuyvesant returned in force; the fort surrendered after a ten-day siege and was renamed Fort Altena, though most colonists stayed and kept their language and religion. The struggle was seen at the time as one between the Dutch West India Company and the Swedish West India Company rather than a war between the two states. English rule followed in 1664 and the old fortifications vanished; Americans built new works on the site during the Revolutionary period and Fort Union in the War of 1812, and the peninsula was later industrialised.

In 1938, for the 300th anniversary, Delaware created a park containing the Rocks and the site of the forts, dedicated in the presence of President Franklin D. Roosevelt and Crown Prince Gustav Adolf; its monument, topped by a replica of the Kalmar Nyckel, was designed by the Swedish sculptor Carl Milles. In May 2013 King Carl XVI Gustaf and Queen Silvia of Sweden re-enacted the landing there on a replica of the ship. The site became a National Historic Landmark in 1961 and is now part of the First State National Historical Park, authorised in 2014.
fort-dansborg: Fort Dansborg stands on the shore of the Bay of Bengal in the southern part of Tharangambadi, in the Mayiladuthurai District, 283 km from the state capital Chennai. It is the second largest Danish fort after Kronborg. Built of brick in Danish style, with large halls, columned structures and high ceilings, it is trapezoidal, about 60 m long on the side facing the sea and about 11 m wide. The governor's residence, a kitchen and a church room lay in its wings and centre, and four camel-hump domes rest on a central pillar.

The basement served as store room, prison and soldiers' rest room, while the governor and priests lived on the upper level. The citadel around it held the Masilamaninathar Temple of the 13th century, the Zion Church of 1701, the New Jerusalem Church of 1718, the governor's bungalow of 1784 and the town gateway of 1792, laid out like a small European town along King's Street.

The Danish East India Company was founded in Copenhagen in 1616 and sent a mission under Admiral Ove Gjedde, who in November 1620, despite Portuguese resistance, signed a treaty with Raghunatha Nayak of Thanjavur. It ceded an area of 8 km by 4 km for a yearly rent and let the Danes collect taxes from neighbouring villages; the treaty, on a golden leaf manuscript, is kept in the Danish royal archives. A factory set up after the fort minted coins marked TB or DB, and cotton textiles were the colony's main export.

Two Protestant missionaries sent from Denmark by King Frederick IV, Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg and Heinrich Plütschau, arrived on 9 July 1706, founded the Tranquebar Mission and printed the first Tamil New Testament on a press inside the fort. In the middle of the 18th century the town's commercial importance declined as textile production moved to Serampore in Bengal, though Tranquebar remained the colony's headquarters until the sale of 1845.

After India's independence the state government used the fort as an inspection bungalow until 1978, when the Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology took it over; it is now a museum of the fort and the Danish colonial empire in India. The Tranquebar Association, formed in 2001 with the Danish royal family, restored its south end by 2005, and a stone shore defence against erosion was laid in 2007.
fort-de-france: Fort-de-France lies on the west coast of Martinique, at the northern entrance to the large Fort-de-France Bay and at the mouth of the Madame River. The city occupies a narrow plain between the hills and the sea but can be reached by road from all parts of the island. Its climate is tropical rainforest, warm and humid all year, with hurricanes a frequent threat from July to November.

Before French settlement the area was known as Iguanacaera, which in the Kariʼnja language means Iguana Island. In 1638 Jacques Dyel du Parquet, first governor of Martinique, had Fort Saint Louis built to protect against attack. The fort was soon destroyed and was rebuilt in 1669, when Louis XIV appointed the Marquis of Baas governor general, and it was built to a design of Vauban. In the 1680s the area was settled and became the French colonial capital in the Caribbean, governed by the Code Noir, the decree Louis XIV issued in 1685 to regulate slavery in the French colonies.

Called Fort-Royal, the administrative capital was overshadowed by Saint-Pierre, the oldest city on the island, known as the Paris of the Caribbean. A British expedition captured the city in 1762, and the Treaty of Paris returned the island to France. A fire in 1890 razed part of the city, and the town hall was completed in 1901. The eruption of Mount Pelée in 1902 destroyed Saint-Pierre and made Fort-de-France economically important. Until 1918 it had an inadequate water supply and was notorious for yellow fever.

Fort-de-France is the capital of Martinique, an overseas department and region of France. Fort Saint Louis is a French naval base. Its sights include Fort Desaix, the park called La Savane, a botanical garden and the cathedral. Its inhabitants are called Foyalais, after Foyal, the Creole form of the old name Fort-Royal. The psychiatrist and political philosopher Frantz Fanon, born in 1925, is among its notable natives.
fort-duquesne: The forks of the Ohio were considered strategically important for control of the Ohio Country, both for settlement and for trade. The English merchant William Trent had run a successful trading post there from as early as the 1740s, dealing with nearby Native American villages. The French claimed the area as part of the drainage basin of the Mississippi, and in the early 1750s built a line of forts: Fort Presque Isle on Lake Erie, Fort Le Boeuf, and Fort Machault on the Allegheny River.

Robert Dinwiddie, Lieutenant Governor of the Virginia Colony, saw these forts as a threat to the Ohio Company's claims. In late autumn 1753 he sent George Washington to ask the French to leave, and early in 1754 he sent Virginians to build Fort Prince George at the forks. Work began on 17 February; by 18 April a French force of five hundred under Claude-Pierre Pécaudy de Contrecœur had forced the small garrison to surrender. The French pulled down its fort and built Fort Duquesne, named after the Marquis Duquesne, governor-general of New France, on the model of Fort Frontenac.

The site was low, swampy and prone to flooding, and overlooked by highlands across the Monongahela. Contrecœur was preparing to abandon it as General Edward Braddock advanced in 1755, but the British force was destroyed at the Battle of the Monongahela, with Washington serving as one of Braddock's aides. James Grant's attack in September 1758 was repulsed with heavy losses. On 25 November 1758 the Forbes Expedition under General John Forbes took possession of the site, which the French had destroyed and abandoned.

The point where the rivers meet, in Downtown Pittsburgh, has been preserved since the late 20th century as Point State Park, where the outlines of Fort Duquesne and of Fort Pitt, built by the British between 1759 and 1761, are marked on the ground. Excavations in 2007 found a brick drain and a refilled pit that may belong to the fort. The 200th anniversary of its capture was marked on 25 November 1958 with a commemorative stamp.
fort-frontenac: The fort stood at the mouth of the Cataraqui River where the St. Lawrence River leaves Lake Ontario, at a place traditionally known as Cataraqui, now the western end of the La Salle Causeway. René Robert Cavalier de La Salle chose the site on the orders of Governor Daniel de Rémy de Courcelle; it guarded a sheltered bay that could harbour large lake-going boats, which, unlike the canoes of the Ottawa River route, could carry goods cheaply across the lower Great Lakes. First called Fort Cataraqui, the stockade was completed within six days after Frontenac met leaders of the Five Nations of the Haudenosaunee there on 12 July 1673.

La Salle, granted seigneurial privileges, administered the fort, rebuilt it with stone bastions in 1675 and used it as a base for his explorations. In 1687 the intendant de Champigny seized several Haudenosaunee, among them women, children and prominent leaders, as the Marquis de Denonville's army moved against the Seneca; some were sent to France as galley slaves. In retaliation the Haudenosaunee besieged the fort for two months in 1688, and many settlers died, mostly of scurvy. The French abandoned and razed it in 1689, then rebuilt it in 1695 chiefly as a military base.

By the 1750s, overtaken by Fort Niagara, Fort Detroit and Fort Michilimackinac, it served mainly as a supply depot and harbour for French naval vessels, though Montcalm used it in 1756 to attack the British at Oswego. In August 1758 Lieutenant-Colonel John Bradstreet's force of a little over 3,000 men faced a garrison of 110 under Pierre-Jacques Payen de Noyan et de Chavoy, which surrendered and was allowed to leave. Bradstreet took nine French naval vessels. The ruins passed to Britain at the Treaty of Paris of 1763.

In 1783 the British rebuilt the fort for a garrison as Loyalists settled the area, and the community around it became the city of Kingston. Known from 1787 as Tête-de-Pont Barracks, it was the headquarters of the Royal Canadian Horse Artillery from 1905 to 1939, took back the name Fort Frontenac in 1939 and became a National Historic Site of Canada on 25 May 1923; it houses the Canadian Army Command and Staff College. Excavations from 1982 led to a partial reconstruction of the northwest bastion, and in 2020 the east bastion was found with trade beads, beaver jaws and gun flints.
fort-jesus: Fort Jesus stands on Mombasa Island and was built by order of King Felipe II of Spain, who also reigned as Filipe I of Portugal, to guard the Old Port of Mombasa. It was the only fort the Portuguese maintained on the Swahili coast. Its designer, Giovanni Battista Cairati of Milan, was chief architect for the Portuguese possessions in the East, and the master builder was Gaspar Rodrigues; the fort was Cairati's last overseas work.

The design is Renaissance, but the masonry techniques, materials and labour are believed to have come from the local Swahili people. The fort is roughly square with four bulwarks at its corners, and seen from above its plan has the outline of a person lying on the back with the head towards the sea. It was the first European-style fort outside Europe designed to resist cannon fire.

The Portuguese lost the fort in 1631 to Sultan Yusuf ibn al-Hasan of Mombasa and recaptured it in 1632, after which they refurbished it and added fortifications. It was won and lost at least nine times in the following centuries. Omani Arabs under Saif bin Sultan took it in 1698 after a long siege, which ended the Portuguese presence on the coast, although the Portuguese briefly reoccupied it in 1728 and 1729 with the help of the Swahili city-states. The Omanis took it again in 1837 and used it as barracks. The British occupied it in 1895, after the East Africa Protectorate was established, and made it a prison.

The Portuguese walls were 15 metres high, and the Omanis added three more. The Omanis also left inscriptions from the Koran on door posts and ceiling beams and a hall with five stone pillars, while the Portuguese built a cistern for rainwater and the Arabs sank a well too salty for anything but washing.

In 1958 the fort was declared a historic monument and a national museum, and James Kirkman excavated it from 1958 to 1971. UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 2011. It is Mombasa's most visited attraction and houses a museum, a conservation laboratory and an education department.
fort-lovrijenac: According to the Chronicles of Ragusa, early in the 11th century the Venetians tried to build a fort on the very spot where Lovrijenac stands, which would have kept Dubrovnik in their power. The people of the city forestalled them, raising their own fort within three months, and when the Venetian ships arrived laden with building materials they were told to go back to Venice. Chronologists date the fort to 1018 or 1038, but the first record of it is from 1301, when the city council voted on the fort's commander.

Often called Dubrovnik's Gibraltar, Lovrijenac stands outside the western wall of the city and overlooks both of its entrances, from the sea and by land. It was constantly rebuilt after its foundation. The fort is triangular, with three terraces. Its walls facing outwards are up to 12 metres thick, while the walls facing the city itself are only 60 centimetres thick. Two drawbridges lead to the gate with its inscription. The fort is known above all for its part in Dubrovnik's resistance to Venetian rule.

In recent times the fort has also served as a theatre. Performances of Shakespeare's Hamlet there have become the symbol of the Dubrovnik Summer Festival, and A Midsummer Night's Dream was staged at the fort by Midsummer Scene in the summers of 2017 and 2018. In the last week of June 2017 the television series Knightfall, a historical drama about the Knights Templar, began filming around the fort and the bay of Pile, using them to stand for the Siege of Acre of 1291.
fort-mose: From 1689 the authorities of Spanish Florida offered asylum to people escaping slavery from the Virginia Colony, and in 1693 King Charles II of Spain decreed that runaways would be granted asylum in Florida if they converted to Catholicism and served four years in the colonial militia. Governor Manuel de Montiano had the fort built in 1738 about 3 km north of St. Augustine, on a tidal channel whose marshes, mud flats and oyster bars supplied much of the settlers' food. About 100 people lived there within a wall, with a church and an earthen fort.

Its leader, Francisco Menéndez, was a Mandinga from the Gambia region who had been enslaved in Carolina, escaped to Florida and from 1726 captained the free black militia of St. Augustine, distinguishing himself against the British attack led by John Palmer in 1728. Most of the settlers came from West African peoples, chiefly Kongos, Carabalis and Mandinka, and their carpentry, masonry and blacksmithing built the walls and thatched houses. News of Mose drew runaways from South Carolina and Georgia, and it is believed to have helped inspire the Stono Rebellion of September 1739.

The black militia fought beside Spanish troops against James Oglethorpe's attack on St. Augustine in 1740, during the War of Jenkins' Ear. Mose was rebuilt at a slightly different site by 1752, and in 1759 it had twenty-two palm thatched huts housing thirty-seven men, fifteen women, seven boys and eight girls. When East Florida was ceded to the British under the 1763 Treaty of Paris, some 400 black inhabitants left for Cuba with the Spanish. The Spanish returned in 1784 and used the fort again until it was destroyed for the last time in 1812.

The site of the second fort was identified in excavations of 1986 to 1988 led by Kathleen Deagan, Jane Landers and John Marron, though the site of the 1738 fort has never been found. Fort Mose was designated a National Historic Landmark on 12 October 1994 and is protected as Fort Mose Historic State Park, with a visitors' centre, a museum and a replica of the 1738 fort opened in May 2025. The National Park Service treats it as a precursor site of the Underground Railroad.
fort-niagara: The fort stands on the eastern bank of the Niagara River at its mouth, where it controlled access between the river and Lake Ontario; the village of Youngstown later grew nearby. René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle, built the first fortified post, Fort Conti, in 1678. In 1687 the Governor of New France, the Marquis de Denonville, replaced it with Fort Denonville, but winter and disease killed all but twelve of its hundred men, and it was abandoned in 1688.

In 1720 Louis-Thomas Chabert de Joncaire obtained leave from Seneca chiefs to build a trading post, the Magasin Royal or House of Peace. The engineer Gaspard-Joseph Chaussegros de Léry replaced it in 1726 with a two-storey machicolated house, and in 1755 the French enlarged the fort to its present size.

The British took the fort after a nineteen-day siege in July 1759, while the French relief force was ambushed at the Battle of La Belle-Famille. Its commander, Pierre Pouchot, surrendered to Sir William Johnson, who had taken over the expedition after General John Prideaux was killed by a mortar during the siege. In the American Revolutionary War the fort was the base of Colonel John Butler's Loyalist Butler's Rangers. Though ceded to the United States in 1783, it stayed in British hands until the Jay Treaty.

In the War of 1812 British forces captured the fort on the night of 19 December 1813, in retaliation for the American burning of Newark, and returned it under the Treaty of Ghent. A New Fort Niagara was built outside the old walls after the Civil War. It trained troops for the Spanish-American War and officers in 1917, and in World War II held 1,200 German prisoners captured in North Africa.

The US Army deactivated the fort in 1963, though the Coast Guard remains on the site. It was named a National Historic Landmark on 9 October 1960 and is now Old Fort Niagara State Historic Site, run by a non-profit association as a museum and a place for historical re-enactments.
fort-orange: Fort Orange replaced Fort Nassau on nearby Castle Island, a trading post abandoned in 1617 or 1618 because it flooded often. In 1624 a ship brought 30 Protestant Walloons to New Netherland, and 18 of the men built the new fort about 2 miles (3.2 km) north of Fort Nassau and some five miles south of where the Mohawk River meets the North River. Both forts were named for the House of Orange-Nassau. The Dutch built it without the consent of the Mahican and held it through their goodwill and occasional presents.

In 1626 the post traded over 8,000 beaver and other furs, and its commander was killed with two other men when a Dutch party joined the Mohican in their war against the Mohawk. By 1633 an estimated 30,000 pelts a year passed through it. Around 1630 the first farmers settled outside the walls in a village first called the Fuyck and later Beverwyck, within the patroonship of Rensselaerswyck, which Kiliaen van Rensselaer claimed included the fort.

From 1648 Pieter Stuyvesant, Director-General of New Netherland for the Dutch West India Company, quarrelled with the patroon's agent, Commander van Schlechtenhorst, over the fort and the settlement. In 1651 Stuyvesant set the fort's jurisdiction at 600 paces around it, and in 1652 he created a Court of Justice for Beverwyck, the first municipal government of the future Albany. Johannes de Montagne surrendered the fort to the English on 24 September 1664, and it became Fort Albany. The Dutch held it again as Fort Nassau in 1673–74, until the Treaty of Westminster. The English later abandoned it for Fort Frederick, built in 1676, and by 1769 only its ditch could be seen.

Excavations from October 1970 to March 1971, made during the building of Interstate 787, found the south moat, a pebbled path, a brewery of 1647 and houses, with pipes, beads, stoneware and Delftware now at the New York State Museum. The Fort Orange Archeological Site was declared a National Historic Landmark on 4 November 1993.
fort-oranje-sint-eustatius: Fort Oranje stands in Oranjestad, the capital of Sint Eustatius in the Dutch Caribbean, on a cliff overlooking Oranje Bay. It takes its name from the House of Oranje, the royal family of the Netherlands. The site was first fortified by the French, who came to the island from nearby St. Kitts and in 1629 built a wooden fortress there, but they abandoned both fort and island for lack of clean drinking water.

In 1636 settlers from Zeeland took possession of the unoccupied island and, with a commission from the Dutch West India Company, built a new fort where they found the remains of the French one. The original Fort Oranje was square, with four bastions, a courtyard and 16 mounted cannons. Historians presume it was wooden, since the Dutch burned it in 1673 and the English rebuilt it later that year. Like the island, the fort changed hands several times between the Dutch, English and French. The French, who took it in 1689, doubled the palisades and dug a dry moat, and from 1737 the Dutch renovated it with the labour of enslaved Africans.

On 16 November 1776 Governor Johannes de Graaff had the fort's cannons return an 11-shot salute to the Andrew Doria, which flew the Continental Union Flag of the newly independent American colonies. Many took this First Salute as the first recognition of American independence by a foreign power, and it was one of the causes of the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War of 1780 to 1784. In 1939 President Franklin Delano Roosevelt presented a plaque in its memory, placed against the flagpole in the fort square.

The fort served as a garrison for infantry and artillery until 1846 and later, after standing empty, as the seat of the lieutenant governor's office, government services and the prison. Partly destroyed by fire in 1990, it was restored in the late 1990s and houses the public prosecutor's office, the planning department and the tourist office. Between February 2019 and May 2020 the cliff beneath it was stabilised with 2,800 anchors. It is one of the island's protected buildings.
fort-oswego: The original fort stood around the trading post on the lower ground on the north-west side of the mouth of the Oswego River, a place convenient for canoe and bateaux traffic. It was established in 1727 on the orders of the New York governor William Burnet, beside a blockhouse of 1722 that had been a way station for French traders. A stone blockhouse added in 1727 was called Fort Burnet, and a triangular stone wall ten feet (3 m) high, built in 1741, made the whole enclosure Fort Pepperrell. The French called it Fort Chouaguen.

Other forts grew up nearby, and many references to Fort Oswego mean them or the whole complex. Fort Ontario was begun in 1755 as a palisade on the high ground on the north-east side of the river, and Fort George, also called Fort Rascal or the West Fort, stood on a bluff half a mile (800 m) to the south-west.

In August 1756 General Montcalm arrived with 3,000 men, among them three regiments of regulars, companies of Canadian militia and numerous Native American allies. The garrison was made up of British Army troops of the 50th and 51st Foot. Montcalm first captured Fort Ontario, which left the stronger Fort Oswego downhill from 120 cannons in the abandoned fort, and swept it with cannon fire that killed the British commander, Colonel Mercer. After 150 casualties the garrison surrendered on 15 August 1756.

The French took 1,700 soldiers and civilians prisoner. Montcalm gave much of the British supplies to his allies and returned to Quebec in triumph. The victory made a strong impression on the Native American allies of the British, and the Oneida and the Seneca went over to the French side. The site later held shore batteries in the Revolutionary War and the War of 1812, when it was raided by the British, but it was never fortified again.

The site lies within the city of Oswego, New York, and nothing is left of Fort Oswego itself; a marker at West First and Lake Street commemorates it. Fort George stood in what is now Montcalm Park. Fort Ontario, rebuilt several times and given up by the U.S. Army in the 1940s, is cared for by New York State Parks and Historic Preservation and is open to the public.
fort-portal: Fort Portal, formerly called Kabarole, a name that means let them see, lies in Kabarole District in the Western Region of Uganda. It is about 296 kilometres by road west of Kampala, the capital and largest city of Uganda, on an all-tarmac two-lane highway. It stands at an average elevation of 1,523 metres above sea level, at 0°39' north and 30°16' east. The town takes its name from the British diplomat Sir Gerald Portal, whose base was there. It is the seat of Kabarole District and has been the seat of the Tooro Kingdom.

On 1 July 2020 Fort Portal was raised from municipality to a tourism city. In 2019, in preparation for the grant of city status, it annexed several surrounding neighbourhoods and sub-counties, among them Karago, Ibaale Parish, Burungu Parish, Karambi sub-county, Bukuku sub-county and parts of Busoro sub-county. The national census of 2002 counted about 41,000 people, and the census of August 2014 put the population at 54,275. The Uganda Bureau of Statistics estimated 60,800 for mid-2020 and calculated an average annual growth of 2.12 per cent between 2014 and 2020.

The city has three hospitals. Fort Portal Regional Referral Hospital, with 300 beds, is public and administered by the Ministry of Health. Holy Family Virika Hospital, with 155 beds, belongs to the Roman Catholic Diocese of Fort Portal, and Kabarole Missionary Hospital, with 100 beds, is run by the Church of Uganda and was originally founded by John Edward Church of the Church Mission Society.

It has three institutions of higher learning: the main campus of Mountains of the Moon University, once private and now public, in the city centre; the main campus of Uganda Pentecostal University, a private university affiliated with the Pentecostal movement; and the Fins Medical University, founded in 2018. St Mary's Minor Seminary, a Catholic secondary school for prospective priests, is also in the city. Natives of the city include the singer Juliana Kanyomozi, the journalist Andrew Mwenda and the physician Margaret Blick Kigozi, born there in 1950.
fort-prinzenstein: The Dutch West India Company had built Fort Singelenburgh on the same site in 1734 but abandoned it in 1737, probably because the Dutch had sided with the defeated Akwamu in the Akyem-Akwamu conflict. The Danes had a presence at Keta, the commercial capital of the Anlo people. When the Anlo pillaged the local Danish agent in 1783, the Governor of Christiansborg raised an army from peoples with a tradition of hostility to the Anlo, the Ada, Akwapim, Ga and Krobo.

After the Sagbadre War the Danes imposed a treaty in 1784 that allowed them to build the fort and obliged the Anlo to trade only with them. The fort was meant for defence and to keep other colonial powers out of the area. Most of its building stone came from Accra, and it was one of four major structures the Danes built, and one of the few such forts east of the Volta River.

Until 1803 the fort held enslaved people in its dungeon while they awaited transport to the Caribbean. Besides the slave trade it served the exchange of goods such as gold and ivory for muskets, brandy, iron rods, textiles and cowrie shells. In 1850 it passed to Britain with the rest of the Danish Gold Coast, and Keta came under British rule. The fort was afterwards used for a time as a prison.

The sea partly destroyed the fort in 1980. In 1991 ICOMOS Ghana, the Ghana Museum and Monuments Board and the Danish Embassy worked to preserve the remains, but the sea continued to wear them away. Keta remained an open port until Tema Harbour began operating to the west in 1962. Together with other castles and forts of Ghana, the fort is a World Heritage Site for its testimony to the Atlantic slave trade, and its remains draw visitors from many countries, among them the United Kingdom, the United States, Germany, Benin and Denmark.
fort-ross: Fort Ross stands on the northern California coast in what is now Sonoma County. The earliest people known at the site lived there in the Upper Archaic period, and the main occupation began about 1500 CE. The area was a large part of Kashaya Pomo territory, which they called Metini, and archaeological data suggest the Kashaya moved there sometime between 1000 and 500 BCE. The Spanish sometimes called the fort the Presidio Ruso.

Russian hunting parties had reached California aboard American ships in the early nineteenth century. In 1806 Nikolay Rezanov, a director of the Russian-American Company, visited San Francisco to arrange food supplies for the Alaskan colony, and his captain, Lt. Khvostov, charted the coast to the north and found it unoccupied by other European powers. Rezanov recommended a settlement. On 15 March 1812 Ivan Kuskov arrived at Bodega Bay with 25 Russians and 80 Native Alaskans, and on 11 September 1812 the fortress was dedicated on the name-day of Emperor Alexander I. Four ships were later built there.

By 1817 sea otters had been practically eliminated from the area. Between 1824 and 1836 Mexican explorers found Russian farms inland from the fort, and Governor José Figueroa gave land to Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo to counter the encroachment. By 1839 the settlement's agricultural importance had decreased, and after a trade agreement of 1838 with the Hudson's Bay Company it was no longer needed to feed Alaska. It was sold in 1841 to John Sutter for 30,000 dollars. Some Russian historians assert that the sum was never paid, while a Sutter biography reports that his agent paid 19,788 dollars in 1849.

The California Historical Landmarks Commission bought the stockade in 1903, and the state received it in 1906. Fort Ross is part of Fort Ross State Historic Park, a California Historical Landmark and a National Historic Landmark. Excavations in 1990 to 1992 identified 135 graves in its cemetery, with the consent of the Russian Orthodox Church, Kashaya Pomo and Alaskan Native associations. The Rotchev House became a house museum in 2010.
fort-sill: Fort Sill lies north of Lawton, about 85 miles southwest of Oklahoma City. Major General Philip H. Sheridan staked out the site on 8 January 1869, during a winter campaign into Indian Territory to stop raids on the border settlements of Texas and Kansas. The Kiowa, Plains Apache and Comanche, who hunted bison there, were the main peoples of the area. At first called Camp Wichita, and by the Indians the Soldier House at Medicine Bluffs, it was named by Sheridan after his friend Brigadier General Joshua W. Sill, killed in the American Civil War. The 10th Cavalry, African American buffalo soldiers, built many of the stone buildings of the old post quadrangle.

Under President Ulysses Grant's peace policy, Quaker agents oversaw the tribes and the soldiers were barred from punitive action. In 1871 William Tecumseh Sherman ordered the arrest of the Kiowa chiefs Satank, Satanta and Addo-ete on Benjamin Grierson's porch after the Warren Wagon Train Raid; Satank was shot trying to seize a carbine on the way to trial in Texas. In June 1874 the Army launched the Red River War, and the 10th Cavalry marched west from Fort Sill as one of five converging columns.

In 1894 Geronimo and 341 other Chiricahua Apache prisoners of war were brought to the post and lived in villages around it. Geronimo died of pneumonia in 1909. The Apaches stayed until 1913; in 1914 two-thirds of the tribe moved to the Mescalero Apache Reservation and the rest settled near Fletcher and Apache, becoming the Fort Sill Apache Tribe. When the reservation was allotted in 1901, 29,000 homesteaders registered at the fort for the land lottery. Artillery arrived in 1902, the last cavalry left in 1907, the School of Fire for the Field Artillery opened in 1911, and in 1915 the 1st Aero Squadron made its first flights there.

The post covers almost 94,000 acres and is the headquarters of the U.S. Army Fires Center of Excellence. It houses the United States Army Field Artillery School and is a basic combat training centre for field artillery, air defence artillery and electronic warfare, with a Marine Corps detachment that trains Marine artillerymen.
fort-st-george: The East India Company had entered India around 1600 and began licensed trading at Surat. To secure its trade lines in the spice trade, it wanted a port closer to the Straits of Malacca. Negotiations led by Francis Day with the ruler of Chandragiri allowed the English to buy a piece of coastal land, originally called Chennirayarpattinam or Channapatnam, where the Company began to build a harbour and a fort.

The fort was completed on 23 April 1644, at a cost of £3,000, a date that coincided with St George's Day and gave the fort its name. It faced the sea and some fishing villages and soon became the hub of merchant activity. A new settlement, George Town, historically called Black Town, grew up around it and absorbed the villages, leading to the formation of the city of Madras. The fort also helped to establish English influence over the Carnatic region and to keep the kings of Arcot and Srirangapatna, as well as the French at Pondicherry, at bay.

In 1665 the Company heard that a new French East India Company had been formed, and it strengthened and enlarged the fort and increased its garrison. The walls, six metres high, withstood a number of assaults in the 18th century. The French held the fort briefly from 1746 to 1749, and it was restored to Great Britain under the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, which ended the War of the Austrian Succession.

St Mary's Church was built between 1678 and 1680 on the orders of Streynsham Master, then Agent of Madras. Its graveyard holds the oldest English or British tombstones in India, and the church solemnised the marriages of Robert Clive and of Governor Elihu Yale, later the first benefactor of Yale University. The Fort Museum, completed in 1795, first housed the office of the Madras Bank and now displays weapons, coins, medals and uniforms of English and British rule.

The fort stands in Chennai, the city named Madras until July 1996. The Archaeological Survey of India maintains it, with administrative support from the Indian Army. It houses the Tamil Nadu legislative assembly and other official buildings; the legislature and secretariat moved out in 2010 and returned to the fort after the 2011 assembly elections.
fort-william-henry: Sir William Johnson ordered the fort built in September 1755, after the Battle of Lake George, as a base for attacks on the French at Fort St. Frédéric on Lake Champlain; the French answered by building Fort Carillon at the northern end of the lake. It was named for Prince William, Duke of Cumberland, and Prince William Henry, Duke of Gloucester and Edinburgh. The engineer William Eyre of the 44th Foot designed an irregular square with corner bastions and walls 30 feet thick of logs around earth, meant to repel Indian attacks rather than artillery. It held 400 to 500 men and was ready for occupation on 13 November 1755.

In the spring of 1757 command passed to George Monro, and by late July militia and regulars had raised his force to about 2,300, many camped in trenches outside the fort and many sick, some with smallpox. On 3 August 1757 Louis-Joseph de Montcalm arrived with about 8,000 men, including nearly 2,000 Native Americans. General Daniel Webb at Fort Edward, 14 miles south, refused to send help, and with his guns failing Monro surrendered on 8 August on terms that let the garrison march to Fort Edward under French protection with the honours of war.

France's Native allies began plundering the fort and killing the sick and wounded, then attacked the departing column of soldiers and civilians, including about 100 women. The promised protection failed. Estimates of those killed, wounded or captured range from 200 to 1,500; one history puts British losses at upwards of 700. Excavations in the 1990s found remains showing beheadings and mutilation. The French then destroyed the fort and withdrew.

The site lay abandoned for two centuries, though its ruins drew tourists in the 19th century. A replica of the fort was built in the 1950s and is run as a living museum in the village of Lake George. The siege was portrayed in James Fenimore Cooper's novel The Last of the Mohicans.
fort-zeelandia-guyana: Fort Island is a fluvial island of the Essequibo River delta, in the Essequibo Islands-West Demerara region, and the fort stood strategically at the mouth of the river. It is a small structure of 15 by 20 m with ramparts at its four corners, not to be confused with Fort Zeelandia in Paramaribo, Suriname. Its lozenge-shaped design, submitted by Laurens Storm van 's Gravesande, resembles forts built in West Africa in the same period. The lower of its two storeys served as a warehouse and a safe powder house, the upper housed the soldiers, and each storey had twenty gunports for 2- or 3-pounder guns.

From the beginning of the 18th century the commanders of Essequibo recommended moving the colony's administrative centre, as Dutch settlers had moved to the fertile banks of the river. In 1726 it was resolved to build a fort to protect the planters and the interests of the Dutch West India Company, and an engineer, Leslorant, was sent from the Netherlands to build a horn work with a wooden redoubt and a palisade on the northern point of Vlaggeneiland (Flag Island). In 1739 the seat of the colony moved there from Fort Kyk-Over-Al.

In August 1738 Storm van 's Gravesande, then secretary to Commander Gleskerk, reported that the fort was falling to pieces and recommended one of brick. Construction began in 1740 and, with the labour of enslaved Africans, the fort was completed in 1743, though shortages of materials and labour delayed the whole complex until 1749. Brick was baked on the spot, mortar and trass came from Barbados and the Netherlands, and the fort was named after the County of Zeeland, home of many of the first settlers.

By 1781, in the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War, the fort was unfit for use. When six British privateers arrived in late February, the Council instructed its commander, Captain Severyn, to fire a blank shot and then a pro-forma shot and surrender; the privateers seized 16 Dutch vessels, and two sloops sent by Admiral Lord Rodney accepted the colony's surrender. The French occupied the island the next year, the Dutch regained it two years later, and from 1796 the fort declined as attention shifted to Demerara.

The fort is among the oldest structures in Guyana and has been designated a National Monument by the National Trust of Guyana. On 15 November 1995 it was added, with the Court of Policy Building, to the UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in the cultural category.
fort-zeelandia-taiwan: Fort Zeelandia stood on the largest of a line of sandbars at the entrance to the harbour of Tayouan, off present-day Anping District in Tainan, where it controlled the channel into the inner sea known as the Tai-chiang. The site gave direct access to the sea, and with it to supplies and reinforcements from Batavia, but it lacked fresh water, which had to be shipped from the Formosan mainland. The site was later called Fort Orange, Fort Anping and Taiwan City, and its Chinese name today means Anping Old Fort.

The fort had a square three-storey inner fort with an administrative centre, church and garrison on top, and a rectangular outer fort holding houses, a hospital and a commercial plaza. Its bricks came from Java and were laid in Dutch bond with a mortar of sugar, sand, ground seashells and glutinous rice.

Expelled from the Pescadores in August 1624 after failing to force Ming China to trade, the Dutch under Martinus Sonck, the first Dutch governor of Formosa, moved to Tayouan, where some 25,000 Chinese already lived. They first built a temporary fort and later a permanent one, probably named after Sonck's ship, with the smaller Fort Provintia nearby. Formosa's value to the Dutch East India Company lay in its position for harrying Spanish trade between Manila and China and Portuguese trade between Macau and Japan, and the fort became an international business centre. It was built more against the islanders than a major enemy.

On 30 April 1661 the Ming loyalist Koxinga besieged the fort, held by 2,000 Dutch soldiers, with 400 warships and 25,000 men. After nine months and 1,600 Dutch deaths, with no relief coming from Batavia and fresh water running short, the Dutch surrendered. Under the treaty signed with Governor Frederick Coyett on 1 February 1662, they left all goods and company property but were free to depart, and on 9 February Coyett led them back to Batavia, ending 38 years of Dutch rule. Koxinga took Antonius Hambroek's teenage daughter as a concubine, and other Dutch women were sold to Chinese soldiers.
forteviot: Forteviot, in Scottish Gaelic Fothair Tabhaicht, lies on the south bank of the River Earn between Dunning and Perth, in the council area of Perth and Kinross. The early royal site stood on Haly Hill, on the west side of the modern village, overlooking the Water of May. In 1991 the village had a population of 160.

On 11 August 2009 archaeologists announced the discovery at Forteviot of a royal tomb of the early Bronze Age. With the remains of the ancient ruler were a bronze and gold dagger, a wooden bowl and a leather bag, and archaeologists from the universities of Glasgow and Aberdeen continued to study the finds in the Strathearn Environs and Royal Forteviot (SERF) project.

The place is known to have been inhabited in the 9th century, and King Cináed mac Ailpín is said to have died in its palace. The ruins of a castle associated with Máel Coluim III were still visible in the 17th century. The Forteviot Arch, a monolithic sandstone arch of the early 9th century with figural sculpture, was found in an old bed of the Water of May and is now in the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh; it probably adorned a royal chapel.

The present village was rebuilt in the 1920s as a model village designed by the architect James Miller for John Alexander Dewar, 1st Baron Forteviot, of the Dewar's whisky family, under the influence of the Garden City movement. Its village hall, opposite the main square, is a category A listed building. The parish church, dedicated to St Andrew, takes the form of a Georgian box chapel of 1778 and preserves several pieces of early medieval sculpture; its gravestones date from 1690.
fortress-of-luxembourg: In Roman times two roads, from Arlon to Trier and towards Thionville, crossed on the plateau above the Alzette and Pétrusse rivers. Nearby, on the Bock promontory, stood a small fortification called Lucilinburhuc, a name that became Lützelburg and then Luxembourg. In its final form the fortress had three walls covering about 180 ha, when the city itself covered only 120 ha, with 15 forts in the centre, nine outside and a web of casemates cut into the rock. It controlled the Left Bank of the Rhine, the Low Countries and the borderland between France and Germany.

Work on the walls begun under John the Blind in 1320 went on to the end of the 14th century. In 1443 Philip the Good and his Burgundian troops took the city in a surprise attack by night, opening a long period of foreign rule. Around 1545 Italian and Dutch engineers of Emperor Charles V built the first bastions. From 1672 the Spanish engineer Louvigny added towers in front of the glacis, and after Louis XIV's siege of 1683-1684 Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban rebuilt and extended the works with more than 3,000 men.

Austrian troops took the fortress in 1715, and under Charles VI and Maria Theresa the engineer Simon De Bauffe gave it a triple line of defences. French Revolutionary troops took the city by blockade in 1795. From 1815 about 4,000 Prussian soldiers lived among some 10,000 civilians. When King William III agreed in March 1867 to sell Luxembourg to France for 5,000,000 guilder, Prussian objections set off the Luxembourg Crisis, ended by the Second Treaty of London; the Prussians left on 9 September 1867.

The demolition was felt at the time as a liberation, and the city grew beyond its walls for the first time since the 14th century, along the Boulevard Royal and across the Adolphe Bridge. The Bock and Pétrusse casemates, the Vauban towers, the Wenceslas Wall and Fort Thüngen, now the Museum of the Fortress, remain.
forty-years-war: The war grew out of political turmoil in Hanthawaddy, which deepened after King Razadarit took power in 1384 through a rebellion against his ailing father. Governor Smin Sam Lek of Donwun and the viceroys Laukpya of Myaungmya and Byattaba of Martaban refused to recognise him, and Laukpya invited King Swa Saw Ke of Ava to attack from the north so that he could take the throne of Pegu himself. The war, also called the Ava–Pegu War or the Mon–Burmese War, was fought mainly in Lower Burma but also in Upper Burma, Shan State and Rakhine State.

Ava invaded about December 1385 with two armies under the young princes Tarabya and Min Swe. Razadarit retook Fort Pankyaw behind them and slipped back to Pegu, and in a second, larger invasion he recaptured Fort Hmawbi with a decoy detachment and forced Ava to abandon its sieges. While Swa Saw Ke was held up by war with Maw (Mong Mao), Razadarit reunified his kingdom, taking the Martaban province by late 1388 and defeating Laukpya in the Irrawaddy delta. A third invasion failed at Myanaung and Pankyaw, and in 1391 Ava agreed to a truce that lasted until 1401.

The second half began when Razadarit invaded Upper Burma with a large flotilla in 1401, during Ava's succession crisis. Ava's defences held, and Razadarit and Minkhaung I agreed a truce in 1403. Ava then absorbed the Shan states of Kale and Mohnyin and the kingdom of Launggyet (Arakan) between 1404 and 1406, and Pegu renewed the war, driving Avan troops from Arakan in 1408 and allying with the Shan state of Theinni (Hsenwi). Ava's crown prince Minye Kyawswa defeated Theinni and its Chinese allies in 1412, conquered the Irrawaddy delta in 1415 and forced Razadarit to flee to Martaban, but he was killed in battle in March 1415.

After Minye Kyawswa's death enthusiasm for the war faded on both sides, and only three more half-hearted campaigns were fought. Minkhaung I and Razadarit both died in 1421–1422. In November 1423 Ava's new king Thihathu invaded during a succession struggle in Hanthawaddy, and the crown prince Binnya Ran I made peace by giving him his elder sister Shin Sawbu. Ava's forces withdrew early in 1424. The stalemate preserved the independence of Hanthawaddy and effectively ended Ava's efforts to rebuild the former Pagan Kingdom.
forum-hadriani: The town lay in the province of Germania Inferior and appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana, a Roman road map. It stood on the Fossa Corbulonis, the canal dug about 47 CE by the general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo as a shortcut between the Rhine and the Meuse, which largely follows the route of today's Vliet. It formed the centre of the civitas of the Cananefates, who lived west of the Batavians and became loyal allies of the Romans after taking part in the Batavian Revolt.

The town was probably founded in 69 or 70, during or soon after the Batavian Revolt, and was first called Municipium Cananefatium, the Town of the Cananefates. Hadrian probably visited it on his journey along the north-western frontier in 121, and it is thought to have taken his name then. Another name, perhaps the only official one, was Municipium Aelium Cananefatium, after Hadrian's family name. The old name was still in use under Decius (249-251).

About 270, after several plagues, attacks by Saxon pirates and the reconquest of the region from the Gallic Empire, the Romans abandoned the town. In 1771 a bronze right hand dug up in a garden on the Arentsburg estate served Étienne Maurice Falconet as a model for The Bronze Horseman, his statue of Peter the Great. Caspar Reuvens, holder of the world's first professorship of archaeology, excavated the site from 1827 to 1833 but died before the work appeared in print; Jan Hendrik Holwerda dug there from 1908 to 1915 and published both campaigns in 1923.

The Arentsburgh park in modern Voorburg roughly corresponds with the site of the ancient town, whose short official name, MAC, is engraved on a couple of Roman milestones found in the neighbourhood. Because the park is part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, further excavations cannot currently be undertaken there.
fossa-carolina: Near Treuchtlingen and Weißenburg in Bayern the European watershed between the Rhine and Danube basins is very narrow, with only about 2 km of fairly level ground between the Swabian Rezat and the Altmühl. According to Einhard, writing some two decades later, Charlemagne was persuaded by supposed experts that ships could then travel in comfort from the Rhine to the Danube. In the autumn of 793 he assembled a large workforce and supervised in person the digging of a moat 2,000 steps long and 300 feet wide.

The work seems to have been meant to ease the carriage of goods between the Rhineland and Bavaria; another theory holds that its chief purpose was to bring Charlemagne's war vessels back from the Danube to the Rhine. In the 19th century the project inspired King Ludwig I of Bavaria to build the Ludwig Canal, which opened in 1846, and the Rhine–Main–Danube Canal later crossed the same watershed.

A stretch of about 500 m in Graben, part of the municipality of Treuchtlingen, still holds water. Heaps of excavated earth marking the banks run for around 1.2 km in all and rise in places to 10 m, and a waterless section of 700 m to the north remains visible in the landscape, although its earthworks are almost levelled.

Research by Robert Koch in 1992/3 showed that the floor of the canal was not level but rose in steps from the Altmühl towards the north. Geoarchaeological work in 2009 found that a dam at Dettenheim, once thought early medieval, was probably built only in the late Middle Ages and did not serve to dam the Rezat. A research project of the DFG begun in 2012, part of a study of ports from imperial Roman times to the early Middle Ages, examines what the original canal may have looked like.
fossatum-africae: Only one text names the fossatum before the 20th century: a letter of 409 from the co-emperors Honorius and Theodosius II to Gaudentius, the vicarius Africae, preserved in the Codex Theodosianus. It warns the Roman citizens of Africa that if they failed to maintain the limes and fossatum, the work and its land rights would pass to friendly barbarian tribes. Excavated forts and towns along its route give dates from Hadrian in the 2nd century to Constantine in the 4th. Jean Baradez concluded in 1949 that building probably began after Hadrian's first visit to Africa in 122, with a further phase under Gordian III, and that it was abandoned in 430–440 after the Vandal invasion.

Baradez identified at least four sections, near the Hodna Mountains, Tobna, Gemellae and Ad Majores, of about 50 to 100 km each, though a later study found the Ad Majores section is probably a Roman road. The work is usually a ditch with earth banks on both sides, sometimes with dry stone walls, generally 3–6 m wide; near Gemellae the ditch was 2–3 m deep. Small watchtowers and many forts, often within sight of one another, accompany it. The Gemellae section marks the end of the land watered from the Wad Jadi and the start of the Sahara.

Built in a region of strong winds and blowing sand, it soon eroded. The Banu Hilal took a ditch southwest of Biskra for an irrigation canal and said it was built by an Arab queen, Bint al-Khass, to supply pilgrims to Mecca, and 19th-century scholars also thought it a canal until Gsell identified it with the fossatum of the Codex Theodosianus early in the 20th century. Its full extent became known only after World War II, when Baradez surveyed it from the air and on the ground; his book remains the standard reference. He stressed its military role, while later scholars have put more weight on customs and migration control, citing lists of products and tariffs at Zaraï.
fosse-way: The Fosse Way linked Isca Dumnoniorum, the Roman name of Exeter, with Lindum Colonia, now Lincoln, passing through Lindinis (Ilchester), Aquae Sulis (Bath), Corinium (Cirencester) and Ratae Corieltauvorum (Leicester). Because it marked the western frontier of Roman rule in its early decades, it is possible that it began as a defensive ditch that was later filled in and made into a road, or that a defensive ditch ran beside the road for at least part of its length.

The road joined Akeman Street and Ermin Way at Cirencester, crossed Watling Street at Venonis, now High Cross, south of Leicester, and joined Ermine Street at Lincoln. The Antonine Itinerary, a 2nd-century Roman register of roads, includes the section from High Cross to Lincoln and lists stations at Verometo (Willoughby on the Wolds), Margiduno (Castle Hill near Bingham), Ad Pontem (East Stoke) and Crocolana (Brough). Between Lincoln and Ilchester, a distance of 182 miles (293 km), the route never strays more than 6 miles (10 km) from a straight line.

Remains along the way show its use. Near Sharnford a stretch of the raised and slightly domed agger survives with deep ditches on either side, and the remains of a posting station have been found at Nettleton Shrub. At Dinnington the Channel 4 programme Time Team uncovered a mosaic next to the road in 2002. Where the road ended in the south-west is uncertain, since alignments south of Axminster suggest a branch running down the Axe toward Axmouth and Seaton.

Many sections now form parts of modern roads, lanes and parish, district or county boundaries, while some can be reached only on foot. Between Lincoln and Leicester the A46 follows its line, and further south the B4114, B4455, A429, A367 and A37 do so for long stretches. The road also left its mark on place names. Several towns along it end in -cester or -chester, from the Old English word for a Roman camp, while others are named after the road itself, as in Stretton-on-Fosse and Lydford-on-Fosse, or carry forms of street, as in Stratton and Stretford.
fotudeng: Fotudeng, also written Fotu Cheng and possibly Buddhacinga in Sanskrit, studied in Kashmir before he came to the Western Jin capital Luoyang. He was active in spreading Buddhism during the Later Zhao dynasty of the Sixteen Kingdoms period. He is said to have shown many spiritual powers, and he converted the Jie warlord Shi Le, becoming his closest adviser as Shi Le founded the Later Zhao dynasty in 319.

In connection with Shi Le's successful war against Liu Yao of the Han-Zhao dynasty in 328, Fotudeng uttered the only phrase of the Jie language that has come down to us. The Chinese annals record it in Chinese transcription with a translation, and it has been analysed in several publications. Under Shi Hu he became an official of the Later Zhao government, and Shi Hu allowed him to found a great number of Buddhist temples.

Fotudeng is known for his teaching of meditation, above all ānāpānasmṛti, mindfulness of breathing. He taught it through methods of counting breaths, which temper the breathing while the mind is brought into peaceful meditative concentration, samādhi. By teaching methods of meditation as well as doctrine he spread Buddhism quickly. The scholar Nan Huai-Chin argued that Buddhism offered not only theories of emptiness and existence but methods of meditative concentration that could be relied upon, and that this was why it began to grow so vigorously in China with Fotudeng.

His disciples included Dao'an, Zhu Faya, Zhu Fatai, Fa-he and Fa-ch'ang, who had a great influence on Buddhism in China. When the Later Zhao kingdom fell apart in 349, they spread across the north from Shandong to Sichuan and went south as far as Guangdong. Dao'an became a leading translator and organiser of early Chinese Buddhism, and several of his own disciples assisted Kumarajiva, a native of Kuqa, in his translations. The historian John Keay notes that all of them continued to revere Fotudeng's memory, which suggests that he was more than a showman and miracle-worker.
fougeres: Fougères is a commune and sub-prefecture of the department of Ille-et-Vilaine, in Brittany, on the edge of Brittany, Maine and Normandy. It lies 40 kilometres from Rennes, 58 kilometres from Mont-Saint-Michel and 330 kilometres from Paris. Megalithic monuments in the forest of Fougères suggest that the area was inhabited in the Neolithic era. The town stood at the crossing of two Roman roads, one from Chartres to Carhaix and the other from Avranches to Nantes. It is built on rock, and the castle stands not on a height but on a deposit of hard metamorphic rock, which protected it from attack by mining and from underground.

The creation of Fougères dates to the Middle Ages. Its castle was first mentioned around the end of the 10th century as a simple wooden fortification on a rocky ridge dominating the Nançon valley and its marshes. From the 12th century the population moved away from the banks of the Nançon, and the town grew in two parishes, Saint-Sulpice for the lower town and Saint-Léonard for the upper. Tanners, weavers and drapers developed their crafts in the lower town. A belfry, the first built in Brittany, was erected in 1397 with money from local merchants, who modelled it on Flemish examples seen in their travels. The castle formed part of the Duchy of Brittany's ultimately unsuccessful defence against French aggression, together with Vitré.

In the 16th century the town lost its defensive role. During the French Revolution the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the levée en masse triggered the rebellion known as the Chouannerie. In 1793 the Vendéens and Chouans seized the town, and Republicans took it a few weeks later. For eight years the town and its region passed from hand to hand, with massacres and looting, and the Chouan leader in the Fougères area was the young general Aimé du Boisguy. In the 19th century shoemaking replaced older crafts, and the population rose from 9,344 in 1856 to 20,952 in 1901. Workers struck in the shoe factories in the winter of 1906–07, and Jean Jaurès came to support them.

Fougères has been classified as a town of art and history since 1985. Its castle, a medieval stronghold on a granite ledge, is its most visited site. A large section of the town wall survives, and the Notre-Dame Gate of the 15th century, with a double drawbridge, is the only fortified town gate left. The churches of Saint-Sulpice and Saint-Léonard both date from the 15th century, and the town hall was completed in 1535. Shoemaking, once the town's chief industry, has almost disappeared. The Tour de France has started and finished stages in the town.
foulques-de-villaret: Foulques de Villaret, in Occitan Folco del Vilaret, came from Languedoc-Roussillon in France and was born around 1240, the son of Gaucelin de Villaret. He served as commander at Millau between 1259 and 1260. His uncle, Grand Master Guillaume de Villaret, did much to advance his career in the order: Foulques was appointed Admiral in 1299 and Grand Commander two years later, was Lieutenant of the Master by 1303, and became Grand Master himself on his uncle's death.

Under his leadership the Knights Hospitaller took Rhodes and other places, including Kastellórizo and Bodrum, and moved their headquarters to the island. The order also gained greatly from the suppression of the Knights Templar, whose assets the Pope assigned to the Hospitallers in 1312. Even so, Villaret's campaigns of expansion ran the order heavily into debt, which was not paid off until the mid-1330s. He seems to have been a difficult and overbearing man, and allegations spread of arrogant, even tyrannical behaviour, although none of them is specific and one Italian account of the lives of the Grand Masters claimed he was treated unjustly.

In 1317 a group of knights went to kill him at his residence at Rhodini, but his chamberlain helped him escape. He fled to the Hospitaller castle at Lindos, where his own order besieged him. The knights elected Maurice de Pagnac as Grand Master in his place and wrote to Pope John XXII in July to justify what they had done.

The Pope summoned both Grand Masters to Avignon, while Brother Giraud de Pins ran the order in his name. John XXII reappointed Villaret only so that he could formally resign, and Hélion de Villeneuve was named Master on 18 June 1319, the elderly Pagnac having died. Villaret was made Prior of Capua for life on 29 June, then moved to the Priory of Rome in 1325, and after April that year he received only a pension. He lived as a simple brother of the order at his sister's home in Teyran, near Montpellier, died on 1 September 1327 and was buried in the former Templar church at Montpellier.
foumban: Foumban, also spelt Fumban, lies north-east of Bafoussam and is the headquarters of the Noun Division. It had a population of 83,522 at the 2005 census. It is a major town for the Bamoun people and has a museum of traditional arts and culture, a market and a craft centre. The Bamoun trace their origin to the Tikar, and their language was originally related to Tikar before the language of the conquered people, Mben, was adopted.

The Bamoun dynasty was founded in 1394 by Mfon Nshare Yen, the first Mfon, a title now rendered sultan, who founded Foumban as the capital after wars against neighbouring kingdoms between 1394 and 1418. A sultan was beheaded in a war with the Nso people of the North West Province in 1889, and his head was carried off; the skull was returned under German colonial administration before the First World War.

The kingdom's economy was largely agricultural, with slave owning on a small scale. It traded with neighbouring peoples, importing salt, iron, beads, cotton goods and copper objects. At the beginning of the 20th century the Bamun developed an extensive artistic culture in their capital. Under Ibrahim Njoya, who invented the Bamum script and the artificial language Shümom, six dye pits with various colours were maintained, and indigo-dyed raffia-sewn cloth called Ntieya was imported from the Hausa as royal cloth, with Hausa craftsmen kept in palace workshops.

The palace, completed in 1917, resembles a medieval chateau and is the seat of the sultan. Its Sultan's Museum holds royal gowns, arms, musical instruments, statues, jewellery, masks and bead-covered thrones carved in the shapes of the men who sat on them. A few hundred metres south the Musée des Arts et des Traditions Bamoun shows cooking implements, pipes, gongs and an ornately carved xylophone. The Rue des Artisans between them is home to sculptors, basket makers, weavers and embroiderers. Tourism, art and small-scale farming are main activities, with coffee the chief cash crop, along with cattle rearing and palm oil.
four-asian-tigers: Hong Kong was the first of the four to industrialise, developing a textile industry in the 1950s, and by the 1960s its factories in the British colony also made clothing, electronics and plastics for export. After Singapore's independence from Malaysia, its Economic Development Board set up industrial estates and attracted foreign investment with tax incentives. Taiwan and South Korea began to industrialise in the mid-1960s with heavy government involvement. All four were inspired by the Japanese economic miracle and invested in infrastructure and education, and all benefited from economic support from the United States.

By the end of the 1960s the four economies had far more physical and human capital than other countries at similar levels of development. By 1965 all four had achieved universal primary education, and South Korea's secondary enrolment reached 88 percent by 1987. They kept budget deficits within limits, and Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan did not borrow from abroad.

Their export policies differed. Hong Kong and Singapore adopted free-trade regimes, since their domestic markets were small, while South Korea and Taiwan used export incentives, and the governments of Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan promoted particular exporting industries. Together they grew by an average of 7.5 percent a year for three decades. The 1997 Asian financial crisis was a setback: South Korea was hit hardest, its currency falling by between 35 and 50 percent, while Singapore and Taiwan were relatively unscathed.

The causes of the growth are disputed. A World Bank report of 1993, The East Asian Miracle, credited neoliberal policies, including export orientation, low taxes and minimal welfare states. Other analyses argue that state intervention and industrial policy mattered much more, and the economist Dani Rodrik holds that the miracle cannot be understood without the role of government policy.

A cultural explanation points to Confucianism, which is said to have valued stability, hard work, discipline and respect for authority, and Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore advocated Asian values. Critics note that mainland China, the birthplace of Confucianism, did not share the success in the same years, and in 1996 Joseph Stiglitz observed that the Confucian heritage had not long before been cited to explain why these countries had not grown. The four have been proposed as models for other developing countries, especially the Tiger Cub economies of Southeast Asia.
four-books-and-five-classics: The Four Books and Five Classics are traditionally believed to have been written, edited or commented on by Confucius or one of his disciples. Several of the Five Classics were already prominent in the Warring States period. Under the Western Han dynasty, which adopted Confucianism as its official ideology, the texts became part of the state-sponsored curriculum, and it was then that they were first considered together as the Five Classics. The Four Books were selected much later, by the Song dynasty scholar Zhu Xi, as a general introduction to Confucian thought.

The Five Classics are the Classic of Poetry, a collection of 305 poems; the Book of Documents, speeches alleged to come from rulers and officials of the early Zhou period and before; the Book of Rites, on ancient rites and court ceremonies; the I Ching, a divination system; and the Spring and Autumn Annals, a record of the State of Lu for 722–481 BCE. A sixth, the Classic of Music, was lost.

The Four Books are the Great Learning, originally a chapter of the Book of Rites; the Doctrine of the Mean, another chapter of it, attributed to Confucius's grandson Zisi; the Analects, speeches of Confucius and his disciples; and the Mencius, long dialogues between Mencius and the kings of his time.

Traditionally it was thought that Confucius compiled or edited the Five Classics, and that he cut the Classic of Poetry from 3,000 pieces to 305. Many twentieth-century scholars hold that he had nothing to do with editing the classics, while others take the view that he and his followers contributed to their formation. For over 2,000 years he was believed to have written or edited them.

The Han adoption of Confucianism as state orthodoxy led to their preservation, and the Song revival made them the basis of orthodoxy in the examinations. Zhu Xi (1130–1200) fixed the texts of the Four Books and wrote commentaries whose interpretations came to be accepted as those of Confucius himself. In the Ming and Qing dynasties the Four Books formed the core of the civil service examinations.
four-communes: The Four Communes of Saint-Louis, Dakar, Gorée and Rufisque were the four oldest colonial towns of French West Africa. Most of their African inhabitants were originaires, people born in a commune who kept recourse to African or Islamic law, their so-called personal status. The few who gained higher education and were willing to give up those protections could become évolués and were nominally granted full French citizenship, though they still met discrimination in Africa and in France alike.

In 1848 the Second Republic extended full citizenship rights to the inhabitants of the four towns, although legal and social barriers kept most Africans from exercising them. A law of 27 April 1848, passed after the February revolution, let the communes elect a deputy to the French Parliament, and the first election was held from 30 October to 2 November that year. The first deputy was Barthélémy Durand Valantin, of mixed race. Napoleon III abolished the seat on 2 April 1852.

After the fall of the Second Empire a law of 1 February 1871 restored the seat. It was abolished again on 30 December 1875 and reinstated on 8 April 1879, and from then until the fall of the Third Republic in 1940 it was the only parliamentary representation from sub-Saharan Africa in any European legislature. Its deputies were of mixed race or French, among them Alfred Gasconi and François Carpot, until Blaise Diagne became in 1914 the first African deputy elected.

Diagne was the chief advocate of the change of 1916 that granted the originaires citizenship and full voting rights while keeping their legal protections. From then until independence in 1960 the deputies of the Four Communes were always African, among them Galandou Diouf, Amadou Lamine Guèye and Léopold Sédar Senghor, and they stood at the forefront of the struggle for decolonisation.
four-garrisons-of-anxi: The Anxi Protectorate was created at Xi Prefecture (Gaochang) after the Tang dynasty annexed that oasis kingdom in 640. It moved to Qiuci (Kucha) in 648 after the Tang defeated Kucha, but local unrest backed by the Western Turkic Khaganate led to the assassination of the protector general, and the seat went back to Xi Prefecture in 651. Only after the defeat of Ashina Helu and the Western Turks in 658 did the headquarters return to Qiuci, and the full establishment of the four garrisons is dated to that year.

The oasis states of Yutian (Khotan), Shache (Yarkand), Shule (Kashgar), Qiuci and Yanqi (Karasahr) kept their ruling families, but garrisons were placed in their cities and answered to the Protector-General of Anxi. From 679 to 719 Suiye (Suyab), where Wang Fangyi built a city in 679, was listed as a garrison in place of Yanqi. The Buddhist monk Xuanzang, who passed through in the 630s and 640s, described Kucha's orchards, mines, music and about one hundred convents, and Khotan's rugs, fine felt, silk and jade.

After Turkic power declined, the Tibetan Empire became the Tang's main rival and invaded the Tarim Basin in 670, and the region changed hands repeatedly. The Tang gained relative stability after 692 and returned the headquarters to Qiuci. Suiye fell to the Turgesh khagan Suluk; the Tang recaptured it in 748 and destroyed it. In 702 Wu Zetian created the separate Beiting Protectorate further east.

The Tibetans gained a foothold only after the An Lushan Rebellion of 755, when the Tang recalled most of their frontier troops. In 763 a Tibetan army briefly occupied the capital, Chang'an, and in the same year took Yanqi. The Hexi Corridor and Beiting were lost one prefecture after another. Yet in 789 the monk Wukong found Shule, Yutian, Gumo, Qiuci and Yanqi still under Chinese commanders, free of Tibetan or Uyghur control, before the protectorate's end.
four-year-plan: In 1933 Adolf Hitler had named natural antagonism towards the Soviet Union among his foreign policy priorities. When business leaders complained in the autumn of 1935 about the cost of rearmament, Hermann Göring spoke of preparing for the coming war against the Soviet Union, and the outbreak of the Spanish Civil War in July 1936 convinced Hitler that such a war was near. In the economic crisis of 1936 the government split between a free market faction around the Reichsbank President Hjalmar Schacht and the Price Commissioner Carl Friedrich Goerdeler, who wanted lower military spending and less autarky, and a faction around Göring that wanted the opposite.

Hitler wrote the Four-Year Plan Memorandum himself, which historians such as Richard Overy take as a sign of its weight, since he seldom wrote anything down. It foresaw an all-out struggle between what he called Judeo-Bolshevism and National Socialism, held that a showdown with Russia was inevitable, and called for Germany to have the world's first army within four years whatever the economic cost. The economy, it said, existed only to serve the nation's self-assertion and the extension of its Lebensraum. It also asked for a law providing the death penalty for economic sabotage and another making the whole of Jewry liable for damage to the economy.

Beyond rearmament in defiance of the Treaty of Versailles, the plan aimed to reduce unemployment, raise synthetic fibre and automobile production, undertake public works and extend the Autobahn system, while protecting agriculture and promoting autarky.

As Reich Plenipotentiary, Göring could make law by decree and appoint plenipotentiaries over whole industries, and he widened the plan until he was in effect master of the economy; its office and the Luftwaffe became his power base. Under his conglomerate, the Reichswerke, the state built refineries, aluminium plants and factories for synthetic materials. Hitler cited Göring's ignorance of economics as one reason for choosing him, and in the long run the choice proved a disaster. The plan formally expired in 1940 but was extended indefinitely. After Hitler explained the plan to the German Labor Front in September 1936, the correspondent of The New York Times wrote that a thought had been cast into the pool of German mentality whose ripples might spread far.
fourah-bay-college: The college opened on 18 February 1827 as an Anglican missionary school of the Church Missionary Society, with support from Charles MacCarthy, the governor of Sierra Leone. Its first student was Samuel Ajayi Crowther, later Anglican bishop of West Africa. It soon drew Sierra Leone Creoles and other Africans, among them Nigerians, Ghanaians and Ivorians, above all in theology and education. Governor William Fergusson laid the foundation stone of its first building in 1845, and the work was supervised by Edward Jones, an African-American missionary from South Carolina who became the college's first black principal.

The original building stayed in use until World War II, when the college moved for a time outside Freetown; it then housed the headquarters of the Sierra Leone Government Railway and later a magistrate's court, was proclaimed a National Monument in 1955, fell out of use in 1990 and burned in 1999. The college was affiliated with Durham University until 1967. Davidson Nicol became its first Sierra Leonean principal in 1966, the year work began on an Institute of African Studies, half of whose £40,000 cost came from the UK Technical Assistance Programme, with Michael Crowder as its first director.

In 1985 unrest broke out after a purge of those suspected of militancy inspired by Gaddafi's Green Book, and retaliatory violence and arrests followed. By 1998 and 1999 the college had around 2,000 students in four faculties and five institutes.

Its graduates include Lati Hyde-Forster, its first woman graduate; Samuel Lewis, first mayor of Freetown; Africanus Horton, surgeon and political thinker; Christian Frederick Cole, the first black graduate of Oxford; Henry Lightfoot Boston, the first African Governor-General of Sierra Leone; and Kenneth Dike, later vice-chancellor of the University of Ibadan.
fourteen-points: The United States entered the First World War on 6 April 1917, in part because of Germany's resumption of submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram. President Woodrow Wilson wanted to separate American participation from the nationalist disputes of the European powers. The need for moral aims grew when the Bolsheviks disclosed secret treaties made between the Allies, and Wilson was also responding to Vladimir Lenin's Decree on Peace of November 1917. Three days before his speech, the British prime minister David Lloyd George had set out British war aims at Caxton Hall, and Wilson briefly considered abandoning his own, but his adviser Edward M. House persuaded him to go ahead.
