Garnier led a small party out in pursuit, slipped at a dyke and was killed. The French authorities had not approved the conquest, and Paul-Louis-Félix Philastre ordered the conquered cities evacuated. The Treaty of Saigon of 15 March 1874 recognised French sovereignty over Cochinchina and opened the Red River to French trade. In the colonial period Garnier was honoured as a martyr of the conquest of Tonkin, and two gunboats were named after him and Henri Rivière in 1884.
francis-i-duke-of-nevers: François de Clèves was born on 2 September 1516, the only son of Charles II of Nevers, who died in 1521, and Marie d'Albret, Countess of Rethel, and he succeeded his father as Count of Nevers and Eu. He ranked as a prince étranger at the French court. In 1538 he married Marguerite of Bourbon-Vendôme, daughter of Charles de Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme, receiving 100,000 livres of dowry and a royal gift of 20,000 more. Their children were tied by marriage to the leading, largely Protestant, princely families of the northern frontier, the La Marck and the Croÿ.

In 1545 he was named governor of Champagne, where he held much land, and on his mother's death in 1549 he inherited Rethel, Beaufort and other lordships there; his titles were then worth at least 2 million livres. He spent little time in his province, being taken up by the Italian Wars under Henri II. He fought in the defence of Metz in 1552, and in 1554 he led one of the three royal armies that devastated Artois. That July he was with the small force of about 2,000 under François, Duke of Guise, that defeated the army of Charles V at Renty.

After the disaster at Saint-Quentin he was among the commanders who led the remnants of the French army to safety, and he helped in the successful defence of Thionville. In 1557 Protestant pastors counted him among the nobles who might support the worshippers arrested after the rue Saint-Jacques affair. He jousted with the king at the celebrations of the peace that ended the wars.

As Protestants grew bolder in Champagne, he banned Catholic processions in Troyes as unsafe after an attack on a statue of the Virgin Mary. In 1560 he married again, in a double wedding at Saint-Germain-en-Laye. On his deathbed he was allowed to resign the governorship directly to his son, a rare privilege, and he died on 13 February 1561. His campaigns had consumed much of his fortune, and his son was soon forced into bankruptcy. Both his sons died within a few years, and the duchy passed through his daughter Henriette to Louis Gonzaga.
francis-i-holy-roman-emperor: Francis was born on 8 December 1708 in Lunéville, in Lorraine, the fourth and oldest surviving son of Leopold, Duke of Lorraine, and Élisabeth Charlotte d'Orléans. Through his grandmother Eleonore, a daughter of Emperor Ferdinand III, he was connected with the Habsburgs. Emperor Charles VI favoured the family and had meant his daughter Maria Theresa to marry Francis's older brother Léopold Clément. When Léopold Clément died, Charles adopted the younger brother as his future son-in-law, and Francis was brought up in Vienna alongside Maria Theresa, with whom a real affection arose.

At 15 he was established in the Silesian Duchy of Teschen, and he succeeded his father as Duke of Lorraine in 1729. In 1731 he was initiated into freemasonry at a specially convened lodge in The Hague, and in 1732 he became lord lieutenant of Hungary, at Maria Theresa's wish to have him closer.

The War of the Polish Succession began in 1733, and France seized Lorraine, since its chief minister, Cardinal Fleury, feared Austrian power so close to France. Under the peace terms Stanisław Leszczyński, the losing claimant to the Polish throne, received Lorraine, and Francis became heir to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, which he received in 1737. He married Maria Theresa in February 1736, though he had hesitated three times before agreeing, and his mother and his brother Prince Charles Alexander opposed the loss of Lorraine.

After Charles VI died in 1740, Francis and Maria Theresa ruled the Habsburg domains, and she gave him responsibility for finance, which he handled well. In the Treaty of Füssen she secured his election as emperor on 13 September 1745, and he was crowned at Frankfurt am Main on 4 October. He succeeded Charles VII and was the last non-Habsburg monarch of the Empire; she made him co-regent of her hereditary lands.

Francis died suddenly in his carriage on 18 August 1765, while returning from the opera at Innsbruck, and is buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna. He and Maria Theresa had sixteen children, among them Marie Antoinette, the last pre-revolutionary queen consort of France. His eldest son Joseph II succeeded him as emperor, and his younger son Peter Leopold, later Emperor Leopold II, as Grand Duke of Tuscany.
francis-ii-rakoczi: Francis II Rákóczi was born on 27 March 1676 in Borša Castle, the son of Francis I Rákóczi and Ilona Zrínyi, and belonged to a family that had already given Transylvania princes. His father died when he was four months old. The emperor Leopold I kept legal guardianship, while his mother raised him at Munkács. She defended that castle against Antonio Carafa's siege for three years before capitulating in 1688, after which the children were taken to Vienna.

In 1694 he married Princess Charlotte Amalie of Hesse-Wanfried and took over his estates, which made him the richest landlord in Hungary. When remnants of Imre Thököly's army rose in his lands after the Treaty of Karlowitz of 1699, they asked him to lead them, but he declined and returned to Vienna. There he became a friend of Count Miklós Bercsényi.

Rákóczi's contacts with France, which sought allies against Habsburg power, were seized by an Austrian spy. He was arrested and held at Wiener Neustadt, with death the likely sentence, but escaped to Poland with the help of his wife and the prison commander. In 1703, with the War of the Spanish Succession drawing Austrian troops away, the Kuruc forces rose and asked him to lead them. Most nobles held back, but Hajduk soldiers joined, and by late September 1703 he controlled most of Hungary east and north of the Danube.

The Diet at Szécsény in September 1705 elected him ruling prince of the Confederated Estates, and he refused the crown offered to him so that the war would not seem driven by ambition. The victory of Austrian and British forces at Blenheim in 1704 had cut him off from French and Bavarian support, and from 1706 his army was forced back. The Diet of Ónod declared the Habsburgs deposed on 13 June 1707. After a fall from his horse at Trencsén on 3 August 1708 his men fled, and he left for Poland on 21 February 1711.

The Peace of Szatmár, negotiated by Sándor Károlyi, saw 12,000 rebels lay down their arms on 1 May 1711. Rákóczi refused its terms and lost his estates. He then lived in Poland, England and France, and in 1717 accepted an Ottoman invitation, settling at Tekirdağ, where a Hungarian colony grew up around him. He died there on 8 April 1735.

His remains were moved in 1906 to St. Elisabeth Cathedral in Košice. He is regarded in Hungary as a national hero, and an equestrian statue stands before the Hungarian Parliament Building. His memoirs, written in French, and his meditations survive.
francis-iii-duke-of-brittany: Francis was born on 28 February 1518, the first son of King Francis I of France and Duchess Claude of Brittany. His father called him a beautiful dauphin and the easiest child to bring up; he was christened at Amboise on 25 April 1519, with decorations designed by Leonardo da Vinci. He was a marriage pawn from infancy: as a baby he was betrothed to the four-year-old Mary Tudor, later Mary I of England, as a surety for the Anglo-French alliance of October 1518, but the arrangement was abandoned around 1521 when Mary was betrothed to Charles V.

His father was defeated and captured at the Battle of Pavia in 1525 and held by Charles V. To release him, the king signed the Treaty of Madrid in 1526, and Charles demanded the two eldest sons as hostages.

The exchange took place on 15 March 1526 on the border. The king soon repudiated the treaty, and the eight-year-old dauphin and his brother Henry, later Henry II, spent three years as captives, a period that scarred them for life. Francis was subdued, accepted his imprisonment reasonably well, and came to favour black clothes like a Spaniard and a contemplative manner seen as more Spanish than French.

In 1524 the dauphin inherited the Duchy of Brittany on his mother's death and became Duke Francis III, though officials of the French crown actually ruled it. In 1532, after much discussion with Breton deputies, demands were put to the crown: the dauphin was to come to Rennes as duke and owner of the duchy, the king would have the use and management of it, and after union with France the dauphin would swear to respect its rights and privileges. King Francis agreed and issued an edict annexing the duchy to France.

On 14 August 1532 the dauphin was crowned Duke Francis III in Rennes Cathedral. When Henry succeeded to the French throne in 1547, the duchy and the crown were effectively merged, since the Breton estates had already tied the succession of the duchy to the French crown, and the duchy became the Province of Brittany.

Francis died at the Château de Tournon on 10 August 1536, aged eighteen. After a game of tennis he asked for a cup of water, brought by his secretary, Count Montecuccoli, collapsed shortly afterwards and died several days later. Many believed he had been poisoned. Montecuccoli, who had been brought to court by Catherine de' Medici, was accused of being in Charles V's pay, and a book on poisons was found in his quarters. Under torture he confessed and was executed. There is considerable evidence, however, that Francis died of natural causes, possibly tuberculosis.
francis-james-child: Francis James Child was born in Boston on 1 February 1825, the son of a sailmaker. The family was poor, but he was educated in Boston's free public schools, and Epes Sargent Dixwell, principal of the Boston Latin School, saw that he received a scholarship to Harvard. He graduated in 1846 at the top of his class, was chosen class orator and became a tutor in mathematics, then in history, political economy and English literature. In 1848 he published an annotated edition of Four Old Plays, the first of its kind in America, and a loan from Jonathan I. Bowditch let him study English drama and Germanic philology at Göttingen and Berlin, where he heard lectures by the linguists Grimm.

As Boylston Professor he supervised a 130-volume series of the British poets from 1853, editing Edmund Spenser and the English and Scottish Ballads (1857–1858) himself. Finding that no sound early text of Chaucer existed, he wrote Observations on the Language of Chaucer (1863), and his research largely shaped how Chaucer's grammar, pronunciation and scansion are now understood. In the 1860s he campaigned for the Early English Text Society of Frederick James Furnivall to publish Percy's Folio, which appeared in 1868, and with Furnivall founded the Ballad Society.

When Daniel Coit Gilman offered him a research chair at Johns Hopkins in 1876, Harvard's president Charles William Eliot freed him from correcting compositions so that he could research. Child believed the ballads came from a time when society was less divided by class, and by the people he meant all classes. Besides Grundtvig he consulted scholars such as the Sicilian folklorist Giuseppe Pitrè, and his references draw on thirty languages.

He died in Boston on 11 September 1896, his collection complete except for its planned introduction and bibliography. His student and successor George Lyman Kittredge wrote a biographical introduction and saw himself as keeper of Child's legacy. Child left Harvard one of the largest folklore collections in existence. An edition of 2002 printed his rediscovered essay Ballad Poetry of 1874, which answers the charge that his selection was arbitrary. Steve Roud's Roud Folk Song Index later absorbed and extended his sources. He is buried at Stockbridge, Massachusetts.
francis-light: Light was born in Dallinghoo, Suffolk, and baptised on 15 December 1740. Taken in by a relative, William Negus, he was sent to Woodbridge Grammar School in 1747. He joined the Royal Navy in February 1754 as a surgeon's mate on HMS Mars, later served on HMS Captain and HMS Dragon, and was promoted to midshipman on HMS Arrogant in 1761 before leaving the navy in 1763. In the navy he met James Scott, later his business partner.

In 1765 Light sailed for India, where he took command of the Speedwell, a country ship of a Madras trading firm. For about ten years he was based at Thalang in Siam, now Phuket, trading there, in Aceh and on the Malay Peninsula, and learning Malay and Thai. With Martina Rozells he set up a trading post at Kuala Kedah and gained influence with the Sultan of Kedah. In 1785 his warning of a Burmese attack helped the islanders of Thalang, led by Than Phu Ying Chan and her sister Mook, to repel the invasion.

Light had proposed a British settlement at Penang to Warren Hastings as early as 1771. In 1786 he leased the island on behalf of the company for 6,000 Spanish dollars a year and was put in charge as superintendent on 1 July. The island was then described as nearly 107 square miles of jungle with only fifty-eight inhabitants; by 1789 there were about 10,000, and by 1795, 20,000. When the Sultan's lands were invaded and no aid came, the Sultan tried to take back the island in 1790. In 1794 Light recommended a proper system of justice, so that the superintendent would not dispense arbitrary judgement.

Light died of malaria on 21 October 1794 and was buried in the Old Protestant Cemetery in George Town. With Martina Rozells he had three daughters and two sons. The elder son, William Light, became the first Surveyor General of South Australia and chose the site of Adelaide. A bronze statue erected at Fort Cornwallis in 1936, 150 years after George Town's founding, bears Francis Light's name but was modelled on William's features, as there was no portrait of the father.
francis-nicholson: Francis Nicholson was born at Downholme in Yorkshire on 12 November 1655. Little is known of his family. He served as a page to Charles Paulet, later Duke of Bolton, whose patronage advanced his career, and in 1678 Paulet bought him an ensign's commission in the Holland Regiment. In 1680 he joined the 2nd Tangier Regiment, sent to reinforce English Tangier, where he carried dispatches between the Moroccan camp, Tangier and London and came to the notice of the colonial secretary William Blathwayt. In 1686 he went to Boston as a captain with Sir Edmund Andros, who sent him to observe the defences of Port Royal in French Acadia.

As lieutenant governor of the Dominion of New England from 1688 he ruled New York with a council but no assembly, and told colonists they were a conquered people. After the Boston revolt of 1689 he kept the news quiet. A quarrel on 30 May, in which the hot-tempered Nicholson said he would rather see the town on fire than be commanded by a militia officer, set off the rising: the militia took Fort James, Jacob Leisler took command, and on 24 June Nicholson sailed for England.

As lieutenant governor of Virginia until 1692 he helped create the College of William and Mary and was one of its first trustees. Losing the governorship of Virginia to Andros deepened a feud between them; he governed Maryland, then Virginia from 1698 to 1705, and laid out Annapolis and Williamsburg. He proposed uniting the colonies under one viceroy with powers of taxation and a standing army, one of the first such plans, according to the historian John Fiske. In Queen Anne's War he captured Port Royal on 2 October 1710, governed Nova Scotia from 1712 to 1715 and became the first royal governor of South Carolina in 1721.

Nicholson rose to lieutenant-general and died in London unmarried; he was buried in the parish of St George Hanover Square. His temper was notorious, and the historian George Waller wrote that he was subject to fits of passion. His courtship of the young Lucy Burwell, who refused him, contributed to a petition by six Virginia councillors to Queen Anne for his removal. He was a member of the Royal Society and the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts. Nicholson Hall at the College of William and Mary and Francis and Nicholson streets in Colonial Williamsburg bear his name.
francis-william-reitz: Reitz was born in Swellendam on 5 October 1844, the seventh of twelve children of Francis William Reitz, Sr., a model farmer and politician, and Cornelia Magdalena Deneys, and grew up on the family farm Rhenosterfontein by the Breederivier. He studied at the South African College in Cape Town and at the Inner Temple in London, and was called to the bar at Westminster on 11 June 1867. After a hard start as a Cape Town barrister, a few months in Bloemfontein and a failed attempt at diamond prospecting, he sat briefly for Beaufort West in the Cape Parliament in 1873.

President Johannes Brand brought him to Bloemfontein in 1874 to head the new appellate court, and he became the first Chief Justice of the Orange Free State, modernising its courts and publishing the first Ordinance Book of the Orange Free State in 1877. A supporter of Afrikaner nationalism, he wrote a constitution for the Afrikaner Bond and became its chairman. As president he concluded a defence treaty with the South African Republic at Potchefstroom on 4 March 1889 and a customs agreement with the Cape Colony, and in 1890 Indian immigrants were forbidden by law to settle in the Orange Free State.

Hepatitis forced him to resign in 1895, and from June 1898 he was State Secretary of the South African Republic. With Paul Kruger and J.C. Smuts he shaped the policy that led to the joint ultimatum of 9 October 1899 and the Second Anglo-Boer War. After Pretoria fell he moved the government's seat sixty-two times, and he signed the Treaty of Vereeniging on 31 May 1902. Unwilling to swear allegiance to the British, he went into exile in the Netherlands.

Smuts and L. Botha asked him to return in 1907. He was president of the Senate of the Union from 1910 until 1920, when the Smuts government did not reappoint him, and remained a member until 1929. A poet in Afrikaans and a contributor to Die Suid-Afrikaansche Patriot, he belonged to the First Afrikaans Language Movement, while promoting Dutch as the language of government. He died at his house Botuin on 27 March 1934 and received a state funeral. His son Deneys wrote Commando: A Boer Journal of the Boer War.
francis-willoughby-5th-baron-willoughby-: He was the second son of William Willoughby, 3rd Baron Willoughby of Parham, and Frances Manners, daughter of the 4th Earl of Rutland, and was baptised in 1614 at Parham in Suffolk. His father died in 1617 and his elder brother Henry within a year, so Francis inherited the title and the seat in the House of Lords as a small child. In the 1630s he opposed Charles I over ship money and was reluctant to fight the Scots in the Bishops' Wars. In 1628 he married Elizabeth Cecil, daughter of Edward Cecil, 1st Viscount Wimbledon.

In 1642 he refused the king's Commission of Array and took command of a horse regiment under the Earl of Essex, and in January 1643 he became commander-in-chief of Lincolnshire. He seized Gainsborough on 16 July 1643, fought at the Battle of Winceby and took the surrender of Bolingbroke Castle. After quarrels with the Earl of Manchester and the failed assault on Newark in 1644, he led the Presbyterian party in Parliament and was elected speaker of the House of Lords in July 1647. Imprisoned when the army took London, he was released after four months and fled to the Netherlands to join the Royalists, becoming a vice admiral under the Duke of York.

Appointed Governor of Barbados by Charles II, he took up the post in May 1650 and sent a small party under Major Anthony Rowse to Suriname. When Commodore George Ayscue arrived on 25 October 1651 demanding submission to Parliament, Willoughby answered that he knew no supreme authority over Englishmen but the King. After a blockade and the defection of one of his commanders he negotiated; he was replaced, but Barbados was not punished and his English estates were restored. After the Restoration he governed Saint Kitts, Nevis, Montserrat and Antigua, expelled the French from Saint Lucia in 1664 and repelled Michiel de Ruyter's fleet at Barbados in April 1665.

In July 1666, on news that the French had seized Saint Kitts, he sailed from Barbados with a relief force of over 1,000 men. On the night of 2 August most of his ships were destroyed by a hurricane off Guadeloupe, among them his flagship Hope, from which he did not emerge. He left holdings in Barbados, Antigua and Suriname to his children and his nephew, and his title passed to his younger brother William.
francis-xavier: Francis Xavier was born on 7 April 1506 in the Castle of Xavier in the Kingdom of Navarre, the youngest son of an influential noble family. His father, Don Juan de Jasso y Atondo, was president of the Royal Council of Navarre and later finance minister to King John III of Navarre.

On 15 August 1534 he and six other students met in a crypt on Montmartre, Paris: Ignatius of Loyola, Alfonso Salmeron, Diego Laínez, Nicolás Bobadilla, Peter Faber and Simão Rodrigues. They took private vows of poverty, chastity and obedience to the Pope and vowed to go to the Holy Land. Xavier was ordained on 24 June 1537, and Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus in 1540.

King John III of Portugal asked for Jesuit missionaries for his possessions in India, where he believed Christian values were eroding among the Portuguese. Xavier left Lisbon on 7 April 1541 with a papal brief naming him apostolic nuncio to the East, and reached Goa on 6 May 1542. His first task was to restore Christianity among the Portuguese settlers, many of whom, according to recent critical accounts, had been sent out from the jails and lower ranks of Portuguese society.

In 1545 he went to Malacca, and from about January 1546 he preached in the Maluku Islands, including Ambon, Ternate and Morotai. In Malacca in December 1547 he met Anjirō, the first Japanese Christian, who later served as interpreter. Xavier left Goa on 15 April 1549 for Japan with Anjirō, Cosme de Torres and Juan Fernández, carrying gifts for the King of Japan. He set out for China again in April 1552, but was refused recognition of his title in Malacca, and he died on Shangchuan Island on 3 December 1552.

He was first buried on a beach at Shangchuan Island, and in 1553 his body was taken to Malacca and then to Goa, where his relics are kept in the Bom Jesus Basilica. He was beatified by Pope Paul V on 25 October 1619 and canonised by Pope Gregory XV on 12 March 1622, and Pope Pius XI named him co-patron of all foreign missions in 1927. He is also co-patron of Navarre.

Called the Apostle of the Indies, he is said to have converted more people than anyone since Paul the Apostle. His efforts most affected religious practice in India and the East Indies, with less success in Japan and Borneo. In Japan and China Christians later went underground.
francis-younghusband: Francis Edward Younghusband was born on 31 May 1863 at Murree, in the Punjab of British India, into a military family. His uncle Robert Shaw was a noted explorer of Central Asia. He was brought to England as an infant and educated by two aunts at Freshford, near Bath, before entering Clifton College in 1876 and the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, in 1881. He was commissioned in the 1st King's Dragoon Guards in May 1882.

In 1886 and 1887, on leave, Younghusband travelled across Asia from Peking, exploring Manchuria and then crossing the Taklamakan Desert to Chinese Turkestan. He pioneered a route from Kashgar to India through the Mustagh Pass. For this he was elected the youngest member of the Royal Geographical Society and received its Patron's Medal in 1890. In 1889 he was sent with Gurkha soldiers to investigate an uncharted region north of Ladakh, where he dined with his Russian counterpart Captain Bronislav Grombchevsky, and later dealt with Safdar Ali, the ruler of Hunza. He joined the Indian Political Service and spent the winter of 1890 at Kashgar with George Macartney, taking part in the rivalry with Russia known as the Great Game.

In 1903 Lord Curzon appointed him to head the Tibet Frontier Commission, with the stated aim of settling disputes over the Sikkim and Tibet border. The expedition exceeded its instructions and became in effect an invasion. Near Guru, troops with rifles and machine guns routed 600 to 700 Tibetan troops armed with hoes, swords and flintlocks. The expedition lost 202 men in action and 411 to other causes. The Convention of Lhasa that Younghusband signed with Tibetan officials was repudiated by the British government, which feared for its trade and relations with the Qing dynasty. He was made Knight Commander of the Order of the Star of India in December 1904.

Younghusband served as British Resident in Kashmir from 1906 and returned to Britain in 1909. He was president of the Royal Geographical Society from 1919 and chaired the Mount Everest Committee from 1921, which coordinated the early British expeditions. After a mystical experience during his retreat from Tibet he turned to religious writing, advanced ideas of a living universe, and founded the World Congress of Faiths in 1936. He suffered a stroke in July 1942 after addressing one of its meetings and died on 31 July 1942 at Lytchett Minster, Dorset.
franciscans: Francis of Assisi was the son of a rich cloth merchant who gave up his wealth. In 1209 a sermon on Matthew 10:9 made such an impression on him that he decided to devote himself wholly to apostolic poverty, and he began to preach repentance, barefoot and in a rough garment. Bernard of Quintavalle joined him, and within a year he had 11 companions, who lived in the deserted leper colony of Rivo Torto near Assisi and travelled through the mountains of Umbria. The name Ordo Fratrum Minorum, the Order of Lesser Brothers, expresses his rejection of wealth, and he gave his followers the simple tunic of peasants as their habit.

The original Rule approved by Pope Innocent III did not allow the ownership of property, and the friars begged for food while preaching. Clare of Assisi, under Francis's guidance, founded the Poor Clares, and a Third Order was created for men and women who stayed in secular life.

The friars reached the Holy Land in 1217, and in 1219 Francis went to Egypt with the Fifth Crusade and met the Sultan Malik al-Kamil. The extreme poverty required of members was relaxed in the final revision of the Rule in 1223, and how strictly to observe it became a major source of conflict within the order, with numerous secessions. After 1232 Brother Elias gathered money for a great basilica at Assisi, which alienated the zealots, and in the 14th century the quarrels produced a number of separate congregations. In about 1236 Pope Gregory IX appointed the Franciscans, with the Dominicans, as inquisitors, and in 1252 Pope Innocent IV approved their use of torture to extract confessions.

In New Spain the first three Flemish friars arrived in 1523, and in May 1524 the Twelve Apostles of Mexico came, led by Martín de Valencia. They built the Convento Grande de San Francisco, which was the Franciscan headquarters of New Spain for the next three hundred years. Pedro de Gante began the evangelisation and studied Nahuatl through the children of the Indian elite of Tetzcoco.

The First Order comprises three groups, each with its own minister general: the Friars Minor, called the Observants, the Conventuals, formed in 1209, and the Capuchins, founded in 1520. In 1897 Pope Leo XIII combined several smaller orders into the present Order of Friars Minor. Franciscans view creation as good, and Francis expressed affection for animals and natural objects in his Canticle of the Creatures. Among the early members were the scholastics Alexander of Hales, Bonaventure and John Duns Scotus, and the scholar Roger Bacon.
francisco-barreto: Barreto was born in Faro, the second son of Rui Barreto, an influential nobleman, and Branca de Vilhena. He received military training in Morocco and served at Azemmour, near Casablanca. King John III appointed him captain of a large fleet, and he sailed for Portuguese India on 16 November 1547. He was captain of Bassein from 1549 to 1552 and gradually gained influence at the viceregal court.

He took office in Goa in June 1555 after the death of the viceroy Pedro Mascarenhas. A play by Luís de Camões, Auto de Filodemo, was staged at his investiture, but Barreto later exiled Camões to Macau for his satire Disparates da Índia. He held back most of the embassy that arrived for Ethiopia in 1556, letting Bishop André de Oviedo go on with a few companions. He continued his predecessor's support for a usurper against Adel Khan, King of Visapur, and defeated Adel Khan's army at Ponda in 1557. Talks to acquire Daman peacefully failed, but he defeated the Rajah of Calicut and prepared a fleet against the Aceh sultanate.

Succeeded by Constantino de Bragança, he left for Lisbon on 20 January 1559; after a storm, a leak and a voyage back to Goa in which he almost died of thirst, he reached the capital in June 1561, where the regent Queen Catherine of Austria received him well. In 1564 he commanded a Portuguese fleet of a galleon and eight caravels that, with the Spaniard García de Toledo, took the fort of Peñón de Vélez de la Gomera in two days.

King Sebastian named him Conqueror of the Mines and ordered him to act only with the advice of the Jesuit Francisco Monclaros. According to the historian Diogo de Couto, Portuguese mercantilists wanted mines like Spain's in the Americas. Monclaros insisted on the Sena route, and in 1571 the expedition went up the Cuama river and defeated the Mongas with its guns. Recalled to the Island of Mozambique to deal with António Pereira Brandão, Barreto returned to find many men sick, fell ill himself and was later buried in Lisbon's Igreja de São Lourenço. His deputy, Vasco Fernandes Homem, reached the mines of Manica by way of Sofala and found only very small amounts of gold.
francisco-de-almeida: Francisco de Almeida was born at Lisbon, a son of Lopo de Almeida, first Count of Abrantes, and Brites da Silva. As was usual in his social circle he joined the military young. He took part in the Battle of Toro in 1476, fought in several conflicts in Morocco, and in 1492 joined the Castilians in the conquest of Granada. He also served as a counsellor to King John II of Portugal. His brothers included two bishops, an ambassador to the Holy See and the head of the Order of Malta in Portugal.

In 1505 King Manuel I made Almeida, then in his mid-fifties, the first viceroy of Portuguese India. He sailed from Lisbon on 25 March 1505 with 22 ships and about 1,500 soldiers. His orders were to bring the spice trade under Portuguese control, build forts along the East African and Indian coasts, make alliances with local rulers and set up trading posts. In July 1505 his ships attacked Kilwa, where a fort was built, and Mombasa was taken, plundered and burned with the help of its rival, the Sultan of Melinde.

In India he was to build four forts, on Anjediva Island, at Cannanore, Cochin and Quilon, and he began Fort Anjediva and Fort St Angelo at Cannanore in 1505. In March 1506 his son Lourenço de Almeida defeated the fleet of the Zamorin of Calicut at Cannanore, but in March 1508 an Egyptian fleet defeated Lourenço at Chaul, and he was killed. Almeida set out to avenge him. On 3 February 1509 he won the naval Battle of Diu against a joint fleet of the Mamluk Sultanate, the Zamorin and the Sultan of Gujarat, which had support from the Republic of Venice. Afonso de Albuquerque, who bore a commission to replace him, was held under arrest for three months.

The victory at Diu led the Ottomans and Egyptians to leave the Indian Ocean and gave Portugal a trade monopoly there for more than a century, until the Dutch and English ended it. Almeida sailed for Portugal in December 1509. At Table Bay near the Cape of Good Hope, on 1 March 1510, a raid on the cattle of the nearby Khoe-speaking people, the ǃUriǁ'aikua, ended in an attack in which Almeida and 64 of his men died, among them 11 captains. His body was recovered the same afternoon and buried on the shore.
francisco-de-ibarra: Francisco de Ibarra was born in Eibar, in Gipuzkoa in the Basque Country of Spain, and went to Mexico as a young man. On the recommendation of his uncle Diego de Ibarra, a conquistador and wealthy mine owner, who also paid for the venture, he was placed at the head of an expedition to explore north-west from Zacatecas in 1554. The Spanish historian Baltasar Obregón, who travelled with him that year, later wrote an account of the expedition.

On this first journey Ibarra noticed silver near present-day Fresnillo but passed it by. Going further, he founded towns at San Martín and Avino, where the silver mines made him a mine owner in his own right. In 1562 he led another expedition deeper into north-west Mexico, searching in particular for the fabled golden city of Copala. He did not find it, but he explored and conquered what is now the Mexican state of Durango.

Ibarra was appointed governor of the newly formed province of Nueva Vizcaya (New Biscay) in 1562, and the following year he founded the city of Durango as its capital. The province covered parts of present-day Durango and Chihuahua. In 1564, following rumours of rich mineral deposits, he crossed the Sierra Madre Occidental to conquer what is now southern Sinaloa. Prospectors found silver veins there, and in 1565 he founded the towns of Copala and Pánuco.

In 1567 soldiers under his direction explored north from Durango and founded the town of Santa Bárbara, in present-day Chihuahua, to mine the silver they had found there. Ibarra died on 3 June 1575 in Pánuco, Sinaloa, one of the silver-mining towns he had founded.
francisco-de-lima-e-silva: Francisco de Lima e Silva was born on 8 July 1785, the son of Field Marshal José Joaquim de Lima e Silva, a commander of the Order of Aviz, and Joana Maria da Fonseca Costa. Among his brothers were José Joaquim de Lima e Silva, later Viscount of Majé, Manuel da Fonseca Lima e Silva, later Baron of Suruí, and João Manuel de Lima e Silva. Following the family tradition he joined the army at the age of five, and he studied at the Royal Academy of Artillery, Fortification and Design and then at an academy created to train artillery officers.

In 1801 he married Mariana Cândida de Oliveira Belo. Their children were Luís Alves de Lima e Silva, the future Duke of Caxias, José Joaquim de Lima e Silva Sobrinho, the future Count of Tocantins, and Carlota Guilhermina de Lima e Silva, who married her uncle, the Baron of Suruí.

Lima e Silva joined the troops loyal to Prince Pedro, regent at the time of Brazil's independence. In 1824, as a brigadier of the Imperial Army, he commanded a brigade against the Confederation of the Equator, and he disagreed with Emperor Pedro I for having tried to negotiate a surrender with the rebels. After the revolt was put down he became interim president of the province of Pernambuco and headed the military commission that tried the rebels in 1824 and 1825, and he was accused of trying to delay the execution of their sentences. He received no promotion for the campaign.

When Pedro I abdicated on 7 April 1831, the General Assembly elected Lima e Silva to the provisional triumviral regency for the young Pedro II, with José Carneiro de Campos, Marquis of Caravelas, and Nicolau Pereira de Campos Vergueiro. On 17 June 1831 he was elected again, to the permanent triumviral regency, with João Bráulio Muniz and José da Costa Carvalho. On 18 July 1841 he was granted the title of Baron of Barra Grande, after the town on the border of Alagoas and Pernambuco where imperial troops had gathered against the Confederation, but he rejected it. He also received the Grand Cross of the Imperial Order of the Cross.
francisco-de-miranda: Francisco de Miranda was born in Caracas and baptised on 5 April 1750. His father, Sebastián de Miranda Ravelo, was an immigrant from the Canary Islands who had become a wealthy merchant, and his mother came from a wealthy Venezuelan family. His father faced discrimination from rivals because of his Canarian roots, and the white aristocracy, the Mantuanos, resented his appointment as captain of a local militia. Miranda studied at the Royal and Pontifical University of Caracas from 1762 and left La Guaira for Cádiz on 25 January 1771. In Madrid he studied languages and political science, began a personal library and trained as an officer. He saw his first combat in the Siege of Melilla in 1774 and 1775.

In 1781 he was sent secretly to Jamaica to arrange the release of 900 prisoners of war and to carry out espionage. Warned of his coming arrest, he fled to the United States, arriving at New Bern, North Carolina, on 10 July 1783. From 1785 he lived in Europe, travelling through Britain, Prussia, Sweden and Russia, where Catherine the Great protected him from an Inquisition order for his arrest.

From 1791 he served the French Revolution as a maréchal de camp and befriended the Girondins Brissot and Pétion. He served under Dumouriez in the Army of the North and took part in the 1792 campaign, including the Battle of Valmy. In 1806 he raised about 200 volunteers in New York and sailed for Venezuela on 2 February in the Leander. Jefferson and Madison met him but did not involve the United States. He waited in Trinidad for reinforcements that never came.

Venezuela achieved de facto independence on 19 April 1810, when the Supreme Junta of Caracas deposed the colonial administrators. A delegation that included Simón Bolívar and Andrés Bello persuaded Miranda to return, and he was received at La Guaira in 1811. The following year republican forces failed to subdue the royalist provinces, the loss of the Spanish market hit the cocoa trade, and a powerful earthquake struck mostly republican areas. Miranda was forced to sign an armistice with the royalists.

Bolívar and others considered the capitulation treason, arrested him and handed him to the Spanish at La Guaira. He died in the prison at La Carraca, outside Cádiz, on 14 July 1816, aged 66, and was buried in a mass grave, so an empty tomb stands for him in the National Pantheon of Venezuela. He had envisaged an independent empire of all former Spanish and Portuguese territories under a hereditary emperor called the Inca, and the name Colombia was his.
francisco-de-montejo: Francisco de Montejo came from a family of the lesser nobility of Salamanca. He never documented his parentage, but his father was probably Juan de Montejo. In 1513 he joined the expedition of Pedrarias Davila, appointed to govern the new colony of Castilla de Oro in Central America, and was sent ahead to Santo Domingo to recruit men. Disillusioned with his prospects there, he went on to Cuba, where he took part under Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar in the last stage of the island's conquest and was rewarded with encomiendas and extensive grants of land.

In 1518 Montejo helped pay for and captained one of the four ships of Juan de Grijalva's voyage along the coast of Yucatán, and on reaching the Mexican coast he became the first Spaniard to step ashore in the Aztec Empire. He then became one of Hernán Cortés's most important lieutenants, fought in the campaign in Tabasco and chose the site of Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, where he was one of the first alcaldes. In July 1519 Cortés sent him to the Spanish court with treasure and to defend his authority against Velázquez, and in 1524 sent him again. Cortés rewarded him with encomiendas, notably the rich town of Azcapotzalco, and in 1525 he married Beatriz de Herrera in Seville.

His formal petition to Charles V to conquer and settle Yucatán was approved on 8 December 1526. He was made Adelantado, governor and captain general for life, to conquer at his own expense, and raised 28,000 castellanos, four ships and 250 men. The first town, Salamanca, on the mainland opposite Cozumel, was badly placed, and the chronicler Oviedo reported that all the Spaniards fell ill and many died.

Driven back from the east coast at Tulum and Chetumal, Montejo turned west, pacifying Tabasco from 1530, but by 1535 his forces had been expelled from Yucatán. In 1533 he received a decree to conquer Puerto Caballos and Naco in Honduras, which set him against Pedro de Alvarado, and in 1540 the king gave him the governorship of Honduras. His son, El Mozo, founded San Francisco de Campeche in 1540. In 1546 the elder Montejo took the title of Governor and Captain General of Yucatán, but complaints led to his recall to Spain by 1550, and he died there in 1553.
francisco-de-montejo-the-younger: Francisco de Montejo y León, called el Mozo, the Younger, was the son of Francisco de Montejo. Around June 1527 he sailed with his father and his cousin, Francisco de Montejo the Nephew, from Sanlúcar de Barrameda to Cozumel, the voyage that opened the first military campaign of the conquest of Yucatán.

In 1528 he went to Santa María de la Victoria, the first Spanish town in Mexican territory, founded at the mouth of the San Pedro River in present-day Tabasco, with the task of pacifying the region. When his father left for Yucatán in 1530 he took over the campaign. He had subdued almost the whole region of the Grijalva River when the First Court dismissed his father, then in Honduras, and named Baltazar Osorio mayor of Tabasco, forcing el Mozo to leave Santa María de la Victoria and await his father's orders.

After an indigenous uprising against the Spanish in Tabasco in 1535, the Second Court restored the elder Montejo, who sent his son back to pacify the province, a task partly achieved by 1537. In 1539 el Mozo was made captain general and governor of Tabasco, but in 1540 he left to join his father's new attempt on Yucatán. In 1542 he obtained the surrender of the western part of the peninsula and founded Mérida on the former Maya city of Ichkansihóo, or T'Hó, which was then almost abandoned.

After the conquest he lived on in Mérida, which later became the capital of the Mexican state of Yucatán. In his later years he moved to Guatemala, where he died after a long illness on 8 February 1565.
francisco-de-orellana: Orellana was born in Trujillo in western Spain, and biographers still quote various birth dates. He was a close friend of Francisco Pizarro, the conquistador of Peru, also born in Trujillo, and possibly a cousin. He travelled to the New World, probably in 1527, served in Nicaragua, and joined Pizarro's army in Peru in 1533. He supported Pizarro in his conflict with Diego de Almagro in 1538, was appointed governor of La Culata, and re-established the town of Guayaquil.

In 1540 Gonzalo Pizarro arrived in Quito and was charged by his half-brother Francisco with an expedition to find the Land of Cinnamon, thought to lie to the east. Orellana was one of his lieutenants and joined the expedition in March 1541. At the confluence of the Coca and the Napo his men threatened mutiny if they did not go on, and on 26 December 1541 he agreed to be elected chief of a new expedition. He set off with the Dominican Gaspar de Carvajal, who chronicled the voyage, and 50 men, and they built a second brigantine, the Victoria.

They reached the Negro River on 3 June 1542 and entered the Amazon. The name Amazon is said to come from a battle with a tribe whose women fought alongside the men, which Orellana likened to the mythical Amazons of Herodotus. They reached the Atlantic on 26 August 1542 and sailed along the coast to Cubagua Island near Venezuela. Orellana then went to Spain, where Prince Philip appointed him governor of New Andalusia on 13 February 1544, with a charter to explore and settle the Amazonian lands with 300 men and 100 horses.

Orellana sailed from Sanlucar on 11 May 1545 with four ships. An epidemic in the Cape Verde Islands killed 98 of his men, and one ship was lost in the crossing. He reached the coast of Brazil in December 1545, and 57 men died while a riverboat was built. One ship was wrecked on a riverbank. Orellana died on the river in November 1546, according to his wife from illness and grief, and the survivors reached the Spanish base on Margarita Island.

Carvajal's chronicle was long thought a fantasy, but geoglyphs and terra preta have been taken to support its observation of a flourishing civilization along the Amazon. Orellana Province in Ecuador is named after him, and the Amazon was once called the Orellana River.
francisco-de-paula-santander: Francisco José de Paula Santander y Omaña was born on 2 April 1792 in Villa del Rosario, near Cúcuta, in the Viceroyalty of New Granada. His father, Juan Agustín Santander Colmenares, was governor of the rural town of San Faustino de los Ríos and grew cocoa and coffee. Both parents descended from aristocratic Spanish families, and the family owned haciendas and had wide influence in the region. In 1805 he went to Santa Fe de Bogotá to study, and he was a law student at the University of Santo Tomás when the revolt of 20 July 1810 began the process of independence.

At eighteen Santander left his studies and on 26 October 1810 enlisted as a flag-bearer in the National Guard. He served in the civil war between Centralists and Federalists and was wounded and captured in 1813. Released, he served under Manuel del Castillo y Rada and Simón Bolívar in the defence of the Cúcuta Valley. After the Spanish reconquest of New Granada under General Pablo Morillo, he fled to Casanare and joined Venezuelan Patriot forces.

In 1818 Bolívar named him commander of the vanguard of the Liberator Army of New Granada and sent him to raise an army in Casanare. In the campaign of 1819 he led troops at Paya, Gameza, the Vargas Swamp and Boyacá.

Congress at Cúcuta elected him Vice-President of Gran Colombia in 1821, with Bolívar as President, defeating Antonio Nariño by 38 votes to 19. With Bolívar away, Santander governed. The two had been close allies, but they diverged over the rule of law. Santander wished to punish José Antonio Páez and the Venezuelan rebels of 1826, whereas Bolívar granted an amnesty. He also opposed Bolívar's attempt to extend the constitution drafted for Bolivia, with its lifelong presidency, which he thought close to monarchism. In 1828 Bolívar accused him of plotting his assassination. No evidence of guilt was found, yet he was sentenced to death, and the sentence was commuted to four years of exile in Europe and the United States.

Santander returned in 1832 and Congress of the Republic of New Granada elected him President. He sought ties with industrialised nations while avoiding high tariffs, and he ordered Spanish officers still in captivity executed, among them General José Sardá, on 23 July 1833. Later he sat as a representative for Bogotá. He took to his bed in April 1840 and died on 6 May 1840.

He is known in Colombia as the Man of the Laws, with Bolívar as the Liberator. His reputation has been contested because of such acts as the execution of prisoners after Boyacá, and conservatives such as Laureano Gómez vilified him for opposing the Church's influence over public education.
francisco-de-quevedo: Francisco Gómez de Quevedo y Santibáñez Villegas was born in Madrid on 14 September 1580 into a family of hidalgos from Cantabria. His father was secretary to Maria of Spain, and his mother was lady-in-waiting to the queen. Orphaned by six, he attended the Jesuit Imperial School and the university at Alcalá de Henares from 1596 to 1600. He had a club foot and poor sight, and because he wore pince-nez the word quevedos came to mean pince-nez in Spanish. By 1606 he was a well-known man of letters, befriended by Miguel de Cervantes and Lope de Vega.

In 1613 Quevedo went to Italy as secretary to Pedro Téllez-Girón, 3rd Duke of Osuna, and worked at court to win him the viceroyalty of Naples in 1616. He was made a knight of Santiago in 1618. When Osuna fell in 1620 Quevedo was exiled to Torre de Juan Abad, a fiefdom his mother had bought him, whose inhabitants refused to acknowledge him. He wrote some of his best poetry there and studied Seneca, becoming a leading figure of Spanish Neostoicism.

Philip IV's accession in 1621 ended his exile, and under the Count-Duke of Olivares he returned to court, becoming secretary to the king in 1632. A forced marriage in 1634 lasted about three months. He quarrelled with many writers, above all Luis de Góngora, mocking his obscure vocabulary in the sonnet Aguja de navegar cultos and his prominent nose in A una nariz. In 1639 Quevedo was arrested and his books confiscated, and he was taken to the convent of San Marcos in León. He left in 1643, frail and ill, and withdrew to Torre de Juan Abad.

Quevedo wrote in the style called conceptismo, marked by rapid rhythm, simple vocabulary, witty metaphor and wordplay. His vast poetry ranges from satire to love poems and philosophical pieces and was not published in book form in his lifetime. His one novel, the picaresque Vida del Buscón, appeared in 1626, and Los Sueños, five satirical dream-visions, in 1627. He wrote about fifteen theological and ascetic books and political works such as La política de Dios. His writings also include antisemitic attacks on Jews and on Portuguese new Christians. He died at Villanueva de los Infantes on 8 September 1645.
francisco-de-sande: Francisco de Sande Picón was a native of Cáceres and a relative of Álvaro de Sande. He served in Mexico as an attorney, a criminal judge and an auditor before King Philip II appointed him governor-general of the Philippines in 1575. On 25 August 1575 he succeeded Guido de Lavezaris, who had come to the islands with the Ruy López de Villalobos Expedition of 1543, as the third Spanish governor and captain-general.

One of his first acts was to break up the vast encomiendas of wealthy Spaniards: in 1576 he forbade all officials appointed by the Crown to hold encomiendas. He founded the Royal City of Nueva Cáceres, now Naga City, in Camarines Sur on Luzon. The first Augustinian priests reached Manila from Acapulco on 1 July 1577, and the Church of San Agustin was built there the same year. In 1578, besides his attack on Borneo, an expedition he sent saw the Sultan of Jolo become a vassal of Spain by a treaty signed at Río Grande de Mindanao. He was also eager to take the Moluccas from the Portuguese, and China.

In 1579 he sent Captain Gabriel de Ribera to Mindanao and Jolo to secure Moro submission to Spanish authority. Ribera found only abandoned villages on the Rio Grande, built a fortress there and went north against the Butuanons. The same year Sande refused Franciscan friars permission to enter China to preach, though some went to Macao against the orders of the Manila authorities.

Relieved of his post in 1580, he returned to Mexico as a judge of the Real Audiencia of Mexico. In August 1593 he was appointed inspector of the Real Audiencia of Guatemala and then became its president, until a royal decree of 1596 made him president of the Real Audiencia of Santafé and governor and captain general of the New Kingdom of Granada. He died on 12 September 1602.
francisco-de-vitoria: Francisco de Vitoria was born around 1483 in Burgos to noble families of Alava and Burgos, and scholars have proposed years from 1480 to 1492 before settling on 1483. He became a Dominican at the convent of San Pablo in Burgos in 1505. Around 1508 he went to the College Saint-Jacques in Paris, where he studied arts and theology, was influenced by Desiderius Erasmus, and met the Thomist revival led by Peter Crockaert, who taught from Thomas Aquinas's Summa Theologica instead of Peter Lombard's Sentences. In 1523 he returned to Spain to teach theology at the College of San Gregorio in Valladolid, where young Dominicans were trained for missionary work in the New World.

In September 1524 he was elected to the prima chair of theology at the University of Salamanca, the senior chair of theology in Spain, and held it until his death. He made the Summa Theologica the basis of the university's theological teaching, and his students included Domingo de Soto and Melchor Cano. Charles V sought his counsel on the Indies and named him imperial theologian for the Council of Trent in 1545, but illness kept him from travelling.

Vitoria published nothing in his lifetime. His lectures and his annual relectiones, about fifteen between 1528 and 1540 of which thirteen survive, are known from students' notes and were published after his death as the Relectiones Theologicae. In De Indis of 1539 he asked whether the inhabitants of the Indies were true masters of their property and public affairs before the Spaniards came. He rejected four arguments against their rights, mortal sin, lack of belief, madness and irrationality, and denied that they could be understood as slaves by nature in Aristotelian terms. He concluded that neither the pope nor Charles V had a rightful claim over Indian lives or property, and that they should not be forcibly converted.

In De iure belli he held that the conditions for a just war were wholly lacking in the Indies, and he denied the legitimacy of the Requerimiento, the document Spaniards read to Indians before hostilities. He saw justification for intervention only to protect victims seized for human sacrifice. He also asserted the right of the Spaniards to travel and trade freely, and held that unlawful resistance to those rights could justify a just war ending in Spanish rule.

Vitoria died in Salamanca on 12 August 1546 and was buried at the Convento de San Esteban. His influence, for example on Hugo Grotius, was significant, and he has been described as a father of international law along with Alberico Gentili and Grotius. His writings have been read as supporting opposite policies, and Antony Anghie and others argue that his humanitarianism legitimised conquest.
francisco-de-zurbaran: Francisco de Zurbarán was born in 1598 in Fuente de Cantos, Extremadura, and was baptised on 7 November. His father Luis was a haberdasher. In 1614 he was sent to Seville to apprentice for three years with Pedro Díaz de Villanueva, of whom little is known. He married María Paet in 1617 and, after her death in 1624, the wealthy widow Beatriz de Morales in 1625. A contract of 17 January 1626 with the Dominican monastery of San Pablo el Real in Seville for 21 paintings, fourteen of them on the life of Saint Dominic, established him as a painter.

In 1628 the Mercedarians of Seville commissioned 22 paintings for their cloister, and in 1629 the elders of Seville invited him to settle there. In 1631 he painted the altarpiece of The Apotheosis of Saint Thomas Aquinas, his largest composition. Around 1630 he became painter to Philip IV, and in the 1630s he painted the Labours of Hercules for the Hall of Realms in Madrid, his only group of mythological subjects.

After 1640 his austere style was compared unfavourably with Murillo's sentimental religiosity, and his reputation declined. From the late 1630s his workshop exported many paintings to South America. He married a third time in 1644, and in 1658 moved to Madrid in search of work and renewed contact with Velázquez. He died on 27 August 1664. Popular myth has him dying in poverty, but his estate was valued at about 20,000 reales.

Zurbarán was nicknamed the Spanish Caravaggio for his forceful use of chiaroscuro, though it is unknown whether he saw Caravaggio's paintings. Juan Sánchez Cotán and the polychrome sculpture of Seville are thought to have shaped his severe compositions. He painted from nature and used a lay-figure to study drapery, with a special gift for white robes, hence the many Carthusians in his work. His subjects were mostly ascetic religious vigils, often a single figure against a dark, featureless background, and his settings resemble shallow theatre stages. His late works, such as Saint Francis, show Murillo's and Titian's influence in looser brushwork.
francisco-del-rosario-sanchez: Sánchez was born in Santo Domingo on 9 March 1817. His mother, Olaya del Rosario Belén, was a free woman of colour; his father, Narciso Sánchez Ramona, a descendant of slaves, worked in the cattle and meat trade. The parents married only in 1819, which is why he bore his mother's surname before his father's. He was taught first by his mother and then by the Peruvian priest Gaspar Hernández. Juan Pablo Duarte, a classmate, recruited him to La Trinitaria, founded in 1838.

When Duarte and others left the country on 2 August 1843 to escape Haitian persecution, Sánchez, who was ill, stayed behind in hiding and took over the leadership of the movement. On the night of 27 February 1844 his men took the Ozama Fortress, and at the Puerta del Conde, after Matías Ramón Mella fired his blunderbuss, he raised the flag. He presided over the Central Government Board, and assured freed people who had mutinied under Santiago Basora that slavery would not return.

Pedro Santana marched on Santo Domingo and on 12 July 1844 drove the Trinitarios from the board. On 22 August Duarte, Sánchez and Mella were declared traitors and deported for life. He lived as a teacher in Curaçao until an amnesty granted by President Manuel Jimenes in 1848. Back home, he sided with Buenaventura Báez against Santana, was exiled again to Curaçao, returned in August 1856 and became governor of the province of Santo Domingo, and in 1859 was banished a third time, to Saint Thomas.

In 1861 Sánchez formed the Dominican Revolutionary Board and obtained from the Haitian president Fabre Geffrard passage through Haitian territory and weapons for a force of 500 men. He entered through Hondo Valle on 1 June 1861. When Haiti withdrew its support under threat from a Spanish squadron at Port-au-Prince, the expedition turned back. On 20 June Sánchez was ambushed near Hondo Valle by Santiago de Óleo, a former ally, wounded in the leg and groin, and captured.

A war council at San Juan under General Domingo Lazala tried the prisoners; Sánchez, conducting his own defence, asked that he alone be condemned. He was shot at San Juan de la Maguana on 4 July 1861 with some twenty companions, some of whom were finished off with machetes and clubs. Spain withdrew from the country in 1865. Dominicans honour him with Duarte and Mella as a founder of the republic, and the Order of Merit of Duarte, Sánchez and Mella bears his name.
francisco-duenas: Dueñas was born on 3 December 1810 in San Salvador, then part of New Spain, to José Miguel Dueñas and Secundina Díaz, a wealthy family. At 17 he entered the Santo Domingo Seminary to become a priest, but left in 1829 when the Guatemalan government had the seminary dismiss its students. He took a doctorate in law at the University of San Carlos in Guatemala City in 1836, and in 1837 was elected to the Federal Congress of the Federal Republic of Central America.

In 1840 he resigned a post under Francisco Morazán in protest at the invasion of Guatemala. He sat on the Supreme Court of Justice of El Salvador and in 1843 founded the newspaper El Amigo del Pueblo, which criticised President Francisco Malespín. He served as minister under Joaquín Eufrasio Guzmán and Eugenio Aguilar, and was rector of the University of El Salvador from 1850 to 1855.

As first presidential designate he became acting president on 12 January 1851, while Doroteo Vasconcelos invaded Guatemala and was defeated by Rafael Carrera at the Battle of La Arada. Elected unopposed in January 1852, he served until 1 February 1854 and signed a peace treaty with Guatemala. As vice president under Rafael Campo he was acting president twice in 1856 and sent 700 soldiers to fight William Walker's filibusters in Nicaragua.

After Gerardo Barrios took power in 1859, Dueñas went into exile in Guatemala. Proclaimed provisional president on 26 October 1863, he issued a new constitution in March 1864 and won that year's election virtually unopposed. When Barrios rebelled after Carrera's death in 1865 and was captured, Dueñas approved his death sentence, and Barrios was shot. Dueñas changed the flag and coat of arms, founded a military college with French help in 1867, was re-elected in 1869 after the constitution was amended, and opened the National Palace in 1870. Marshal Santiago González overthrew him on 15 April 1871, during a war with Honduras.

Expelled with his family in 1872, he lived in the United States. He tried to return in 1878 and again in 1883, fleeing each time when President Rafael Zaldívar accused him of plotting. He died in San Francisco on 4 March 1884, and his remains were buried in Nueva San Salvador in 1886. He was the last conservative president of El Salvador until Pío Romero Bosque in 1927.
francisco-felix-de-souza: De Souza was born on 5 October 1754 in Salvador, Bahia, then the capital of Portuguese America, and migrated from Brazil to the coast of what is now Benin. His ethnicity is not known for certain, but the few descriptions of him from his time suggest he was white or light-skinned. According to his family he was an eighth-generation descendant of Tomé de Sousa, the first governor-general of Brazil from 1549 to 1553. Alberto Costa e Silva has written at length, in Portuguese, on his early years on the Slave Coast.

He was a major slave trader and merchant, dealing in palm oil, gold and enslaved people. He founded Afro-Brazilian communities in lands now part of Benin, Togo and Nigeria. Jailed by King Adandozan of Dahomey, he helped Ghezo take the throne in a coup d'état. The word chacha has been explained as coming from his saying já, já, a Portuguese phrase for something to be done at once. He went on selling enslaved people after the trade had been abolished in most jurisdictions.

He was known for his extravagance and was reputed to have had at least 80 children with the women of his harem. The people of Dahomey trusted him enough to give him the status of a chieftain. Though a Catholic, he also practised the Vodun religion and kept a family shrine of his own.

De Souza died on 8 May 1849 and was buried in Dahomey. He is regarded as the father of the city of Ouidah, which has a statue of him, a plaza named after him and a museum of the de Souza family. Edna Bay describes him as deeply influential as an intermediary between European and African cultures, and he is remembered as a founding patriarch of the Afro-Brazilian communities of Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria. Bruce Chatwin's 1980 novel The Viceroy of Ouidah was loosely based on his life, and Werner Herzog adapted it as the film Cobra Verde in 1987.
francisco-franco: Francisco Franco Bahamonde was born on 4 December 1892 in Ferrol, Galicia, into a family that had given the Spanish Navy officers for six generations. He would have followed his father into the navy, but after the Spanish-American War the Naval Academy admitted no new entrants from 1906 to 1913. He entered the Infantry Academy at Toledo in 1907 and graduated in July 1910 as a second lieutenant. Serving in Morocco, where officers could win promotion on the battlefield, he became a brigadier general in 1926 at the age of 33.

A conservative and monarchist, Franco regretted the end of the monarchy in 1931 but did not challenge the Second Republic. He led the suppression of the 1934 uprising in Asturias, and after the Popular Front won the 1936 election he was sent to the Canary Islands. He joined the military coup of July 1936 and took command of the 30,000 soldiers of the Army of Africa, securing the Moroccan protectorate in part by the summary execution of some 200 senior officers loyal to the Republic. With aircraft from Italy and Germany he began an air bridge to Seville.

Franco was proclaimed Generalísimo and head of state of the Nationalists in October 1936. On 19 April 1937 he merged the Falange and the Carlist parties into a single party. Barcelona fell in January 1939 and Madrid on 28 March, and he proclaimed victory on 1 April 1939. Repression followed. Paul Preston estimates that Franco's forces killed about 420,000 people in the war and afterwards, while Antony Beevor cites at least 35,000 official executions after 1939, and figures vary widely. Spain stayed non-belligerent in the Second World War though it supported the Axis, and the economy grew rapidly from the late 1950s.

In 1969 Franco named Prince Juan Carlos de Borbón as his heir. He died on 20 November 1975, aged 82, and was entombed in the Valley of the Fallen; in 2018 the government approved legal changes that led to plans to exhume his remains. His legacy remains disputed. Scholars debate whether his regime should be called fascist, a military dictatorship or something between, and Paul Preston and Stanley Payne hold differing views.
francisco-hernandez-de-cordoba-yucatan-c: Little is known of Francisco Hernández de Córdoba before 1517. He was a native of Spain who lived in early colonial Cuba, which suggests that he had taken part in the conquest of the island. He was wealthy enough to own a landed estate, including a native town, and to help finance his expedition. About 110 discontented settlers asked the governor, Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar, for permission to look for new lands and resources. Bernal Díaz del Castillo, a member of the expedition and its fullest chronicler, says he was one of its promoters. His account also suggests that the original aim may have been to capture Indians as slaves for Cuba's farms and mines.

After some haggling over terms, permission was granted, and three ships under Hernández de Córdoba's command sailed on 8 February 1517. The chief pilot was Antón de Alaminos, who had sailed with Christopher Columbus. After two days of storm and 21 days of fair weather, the crew sighted a large town near the coast, bigger than any they had seen in Cuba or Hispaniola. They named it the Great Cairo. The cacique of the town received them peacefully, then prepared an ambush on the following day. In the Battle of Catoche the Spaniards' swords, crossbows and firearms put the more numerous Maya to flight. They took two prisoners, later baptised Julianillo and Melchorejo, who became the first Maya interpreters for the Spanish.

Short of water, the expedition landed at Champotón. By Bernal's account, the Maya outnumbered them and attacked at dawn, and eighty Spaniards were wounded. Hernández de Córdoba was hit by twelve arrows, and two Spaniards were taken alive. Over fifty men had died, so the ships were reduced to two, one being burned at sea. The pilots chose to go by way of Florida, where a landing party found water but fought the local people. The survivors then reached Havana.

Hernández de Córdoba barely reached Cuba. He died within days of landing, of his wounds and the thirst of the voyage, and was reportedly disappointed that Velázquez had given the next expedition to Juan de Grijalva. The Spaniards had met what they regarded as an advanced civilisation, with solidly built buildings and a complex social order that they compared to the Old World's. The gold pieces the chaplain González had taken from a Maya pyramid, and Julianillo's claims that the land held gold, fed the next voyages: Grijalva's in 1518 and that of Hernán Cortés in 1519, which led to the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire.
francisco-i-madero: Francisco Ignacio Madero González was born on 30 October 1873 at the hacienda of El Rosario in Parras de la Fuente, Coahuila, into one of Mexico's wealthiest families. His grandfather Evaristo Madero Elizondo built a large fortune, in part by shipping cotton to Mexican ports during the American Civil War. Between 1886 and 1892 Francisco was educated in France and the United States, at the Lycée Hoche in Versailles, the École des Hautes Études Commerciales in Paris and the University of California, Berkeley. In Paris he took up Spiritism and came to believe he was a medium. Returning in 1893, he managed a family hacienda at San Pedro, where he installed irrigation and built schools, hospitals and a soap factory.

After Bernardo Reyes violently crushed a demonstration on 2 April 1903, Madero, who believed his dead brother's spirit was advising him, decided to enter politics. He founded the Benito Juárez Democratic Club, lost a municipal election in 1904 and started opposition newspapers. His 1908 book The Presidential Succession in 1910 urged voters to stop Díaz's reelection, and he funded the Anti-Reelectionist Party. Díaz had said in 1908 that the 1910 election would be free. The regime arrested Madero on 6 June 1910, and about 5,000 other members of the movement were jailed. A fraudulent election on 21 June gave Díaz a huge majority.

Madero fled to San Antonio, Texas, and issued the Plan of San Luis Potosí, which declared the election void and called for revolt on 20 November 1910. It also promised the return of land to villages and Indian communities. After a defeat at Casas Grandes he gave up military command, and Pancho Villa and Pascual Orozco took Ciudad Juárez against his orders. Díaz resigned on 25 May 1911 under the Treaty of Ciudad Juárez. Madero kept the Federal Army and demobilised the revolutionaries. Elected in a landslide, he was sworn in as president on 6 November 1911.

His slowness on land reform led Emiliano Zapata to proclaim the Plan of Ayala on 25 November 1911, and Orozco rebelled in 1912. Conservatives opposed him, and the press he had freed criticised him. In February 1913 Félix Díaz, Bernardo Reyes and Victoriano Huerta led a coup, supported by the United States, during the Ten Tragic Days of 9 to 19 February. Huerta switched sides, and Madero was arrested and forced to resign. He and Vice President José María Pino Suárez were murdered, and his brother Gustavo A. Madero was kidnapped, tortured and killed.

His death united revolutionaries against Huerta. Venustiano Carranza, governor of Coahuila, led the Constitutionalist Army. He was known as the Apostle of Democracy, and the Monument to the Revolution, completed in 1938, holds his remains.
francisco-jimenez-de-cisneros: He was born Gonzalo Jiménez de Cisneros at Torrelaguna in Castile in 1436, the son of hidalgos. He studied at Alcalá de Henares and Salamanca, took a law degree in 1456 and worked in Rome as a consistorial advocate from 1459. Back in Castile he rose in the secular clergy as vicar general of Cardinal Pedro González de Mendoza's diocese of Sigüenza. In 1484, at forty-eight, he became a Franciscan friar, taking the name Francisco and living an ascetic life that he kept even at the height of his power. In 1492 Mendoza recommended him to Isabella I as her confessor, a post that carried political weight.

After Mendoza died in 1495, Isabella obtained a papal bull naming Cisneros to the Archdiocese of Toledo, the richest in Spain, together with the office of chancellor of Castile. He resisted for six months and accepted only after a second bull. He reformed the Franciscans, requiring celibacy and residence in their parishes, and extended the reforms to other mendicant orders by 1498. Despite opposition from the order's Minister General, he imposed them with the queen's backing.

In 1499 he went with the Inquisition's court to Granada, where he set aside Hernando de Talavera's slow, peaceful conversion of the Muslims, calling it giving pearls to pigs, and ordered forced mass conversion and the burning of Arabic manuscripts, at least 5,000 by the lowest contemporary figure, except those on medicine. The unconverted rose in the First Rebellion of the Alpujarras. It was suppressed, and the Muslims were offered baptism or exile, contrary to the terms of Granada's surrender.

After Isabella's death in 1504 he helped mediate the Treaty of Villafafila, and when Philip I died in 1506 he set up a regent government. Ferdinand II made him Grand Inquisitor for Castile and León in 1507 and obtained a cardinal's hat for him. In 1509 he accompanied the force that took Oran in a single day.

When Ferdinand died on 23 January 1516 Cisneros became regent of Castile for the sixteen-year-old Charles, later Charles V. He fixed the courts at Madrid, established a standing army by drilling townsmen, and ordered most of the fortresses of Navarre demolished. He fell ill in September 1517 on the way to meet Charles at Valladolid and died at Roa on 8 November 1517.

The University of Alcalá, founded in 1500 and opened in 1508 at his expense, held at one time 7,000 students. The Complutensian Polyglot Bible, begun in 1502 and finished in April 1517, set Greek, Latin and Hebrew columns side by side; he died before it was published. He also revived the Mozarabic liturgy. A cause for his beatification was opened in 1669, and he was given the title of Venerable.
francisco-jose-de-caldas: Caldas was born in Popayán to José de Caldas and Vicenta Tenorio, an aunt of the independence leader Camilo Torres Tenorio. He studied at the Seminary of Popayán, where he met Francisco Antonio Zea, and in 1788, pressed by his father, moved to Santafé, now Bogotá, to study law at the Colegio del Rosario, taking a bachelor's degree in 1793. His real interests were mathematics, astronomy and the natural sciences, and his later trading ventures in Popayán were unsuccessful.

On business journeys he carried a barometer, a thermometer and a compass to fix the position and altitude of places, and the accidental breaking of a thermometer led him to the hypsometer. His observations of plants near the equator led José Celestino Mutis to appoint him to the Royal Botanical Expedition to New Granada. On 31 December 1801 he met Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland at Ibarra, gave them altitude data and studied botany with them. Back in Santafé in 1805, he directed the new Astronomic Observatory and in 1808 founded the newspaper El Semanario.

In 1810 Caldas took part in the staged quarrel with the Spaniard José González Llorente on 20 July that led to the Santafé junta, and with Joaquín Camacho he founded the Diario Político de Santafé de Bogotá. As an army engineer he sided with the federalists against Antonio Nariño in 1812, and in Antioquia he built powder mills and gun factories, fortified the Cauca River and taught at the Academy of Engineers in Medellín.

When Pablo Morillo captured Santafé on 6 May 1816, Caldas fled but was arrested at the Paisbamba farm in Sotará and brought back to be shot by a firing squad in the San Francisco Plaza. Morillo answered pleas for his life with the words "Spain does not need savants". The department of Caldas, the Francisco José de Caldas District University in Bogotá and a doctoral scholarship bear his name, and some authors call him the father of Colombian engineering.
francisco-largo-caballero: Francisco Largo Caballero was born in Madrid on 15 October 1869. He left school at the age of seven, was largely self-educated and made his living as a stuccoer of walls. He took part in a construction workers' strike in 1890 and joined the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) in 1894. In his early career he concentrated on municipal politics and burial societies and disapproved of the methods of the anarchist union, the Confederación Nacional del Trabajo (CNT). When the party's founder Pablo Iglesias died in 1925, Largo Caballero became head of the party and of the Workers' General Union (UGT).

He began as a moderate. He advocated a degree of cooperation between the UGT and the military government of General Miguel Primo de Rivera, which let the union go on working, and this began his long conflict with Indalecio Prieto, who opposed any collaboration. From 1931 to 1933 he was Minister of Labour in the first governments of the Second Republic. He tried to improve the lot of landless labourers in the rural south, setting up mixed juries to arbitrate in agrarian disputes and introducing an eight-hour day in the countryside.

After the right-wing CEDA won the elections of 19 November 1933, he turned sharply left. In January 1934 he wrote in El Socialista, Harmony? No! Class war! The historian Angel Smith judges his radicalism almost purely rhetorical. In October 1934 he was one of the leaders of the failed workers' rising, mainly in Asturias, which was put down by the government. It damaged him politically, and Prieto and Manuel Azaña gained the initiative.

After the Popular Front won the elections of February 1936 and the military coup of 17 July began the civil war, President Azaña asked Largo Caballero to form a government on 4 September 1936. He was prime minister and also minister of war, and on 4 November he persuaded the CNT to join the government, with four members in junior ministries. During his term he grew disenchanted with the communists and clashed with the Soviet ambassador Marcel Rosenberg.

The Barcelona May Days of 3 to 8 May 1937 caused a crisis. His attempt to defend the POUM, one of the parties involved, set moderate Socialist ministers such as Prieto and the Communists against him, and he resigned on 17 May 1937; Juan Negrín succeeded him. After the Republic's defeat in 1939 he fled to France, was arrested during the German occupation and held in the Sachsenhausen camp from 1943 to 1945. He died in Paris in 1946, and his remains were returned to Madrid in 1978.
francisco-morazan: José Francisco Morazán Quezada was born on 3 October 1792 in Tegucigalpa, then part of the Captaincy General of Guatemala. His father, Eusebio Morazán, was a criollo from the Antilles whose ancestors were Corsican, and his mother, Guadalupe Quezada, came from a distinguished family of Tegucigalpa. Despite his mixed ancestry he was recorded as Spanish on his baptismal certificate, to avoid discrimination under the colonial casta system. Central America declared independence from Spain on 15 September 1821. Morazán then joined a militia in Tegucigalpa that opposed annexation to the First Mexican Empire, and he rose to prominence at the Battle of La Trinidad on 11 November 1827.

In early 1829 Morazán led an army from Ahuachapán into Guatemala, and after overthrowing President Manuel José Arce he ran the government dictatorially until June 1829. He won the 1830 presidential election against the conservative José Cecilio del Valle and was inaugurated on 16 September. His liberal reforms included freedom of the press, speech and religion, secular marriage, and the abolition of government-aided tithing, which made him powerful enemies. His period of rule was marked by bitter infighting between liberals and conservatives. Del Valle won the next election but died before taking office, and Morazán won the new election and was sworn in on 14 February 1835.

The federation broke apart from 1837, when a cholera epidemic and resistance to the introduction of trial by jury helped ignite revolt. Conservatives rallied around Rafael Carrera and divided Central America into five nations. Elected head of state of El Salvador on 13 July 1839, Morazán faced a war declared by Carrera. On 18 March 1840 he marched on Guatemala City in a last attempt to restore the union, but Carrera's force of about 5,000 men assaulted him from all sides, and he escaped with a small escort.

Morazán went into exile on 8 April 1840, living in Panama and then Peru. He returned to El Salvador in January 1842 and then moved against Costa Rican head of state Braulio Carrillo.
