On 11 September 1842 a popular movement opposed to him rose in San José, and after 88 hours of fighting he tried to break the siege. He was executed on 15 September 1842.

At his death many across Central America saw him as a tyrant, but by the 1880s he was widely revered as a hero. Statues were raised in San Salvador in 1882 and Tegucigalpa in 1883, and the centenary of his birth was marked across the region in 1892. Honduras named him Father of the Nation in 1942.
francisco-pizarro: Francisco Pizarro was born in Trujillo, in the Crown of Castile, probably in the 1470s, the illegitimate son of the infantry colonel Gonzalo Pizarro and Francisca González, a woman of poor means. Little attention was paid to his education, and he grew up and remained illiterate. In 1513 he accompanied Vasco Núñez de Balboa across the Isthmus of Panama to the Pacific. Under the governor Pedro Arias Dávila he was assigned a repartimiento, arrested Balboa on the governor's orders, and served as mayor of Panama City from 1519 to 1523.

In 1524 Pizarro formed a partnership with the priest Hernando de Luque and the soldier Diego de Almagro to explore and conquer the south. His first expedition left Panama in November 1524 and failed, and the second, from March 1526, produced Bartolomé Ruiz's capture of a balsa raft carrying textiles, gold, silver and emeralds. When the new governor refused a third expedition, Pizarro went to Spain, and Queen Isabel signed the Capitulación de Toledo on 6 July 1529, naming him governor of New Castile, a grant that later angered Almagro, who held lesser positions.

The third expedition left with three ships, 180 men and 27 horses. In May 1532 Pizarro founded San Miguel de Piura, the first Spanish settlement in Peru, and on 24 September he advanced inland with 200 men. At Cajamarca in November 1532 he captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa. Atahualpa filled a room with gold as a ransom, but Pizarro charged him with crimes and had him garrotted in July 1533. He entered Cuzco that year and founded Lima in January 1535, and in 1537 he was made 1st Marquess of the Conquest.

On 26 June 1541 about twenty supporters of Diego de Almagro II stormed Pizarro's palace in Lima and killed him, and he reportedly drew a cross in his blood before dying. His remains were buried under the cathedral.

He destroyed the Inca state and ruled the area for almost a decade. The Inca religion was replaced by Christianity, and much of the local population was reduced to effective serfdom under the encomienda system. He is reviled for ordering Atahualpa's death despite the ransom, which he kept after paying the king his due, and some Peruvians, particularly those of indigenous descent, regard him negatively.
francisco-serrano-1st-duke-of-la-torre: Francisco Serrano Domínguez was born on 17 December 1810 on the Isla de León, now San Fernando, in the Bay of Cádiz, the son of a general and Liberal, Francisco Serrano y Cuenca. Following his father into the army, he became a cadet in 1822. In the First Carlist War from 1834 to 1839, as aide-de-camp of Espoz y Mina in the armies of Queen Isabella II, he rose from captain to brigadier-general. He was first elected to the Cortes for Málaga in 1839.

Serrano became one of Spain's chief military politicians. In 1841 he helped Espartero overthrow the regency of Maria Christina, and in 1843 made a pronunciamiento against Espartero at Barcelona. He assisted Marshal Leopoldo O'Donnell in 1854 and 1856, and was captain-general of Cuba from 1859 to 1862, the first viceroy there to advocate political and financial reforms. O'Donnell made him Duke of la Torre.

On 7 July 1868 the government arrested Serrano and other generals and took them to the Canary Islands. Admiral Topete's steamer brought him to Cádiz on 18 September. He signed the manifesto of the revolution with Prim, Topete and others, took command of the revolutionary army and routed Isabella's troops at the bridge of Alcolea. The queen fled to France, and Serrano formed a Provisional Government, becoming regent and prime minister. He accepted the Cortes's choice of Amadeus I of Savoy as king, though he would have preferred Montpensier.

Serrano opposed the federal republic and conspired against it, failed and went into exile in France. General Manuel Pavía sent for him to lead the coup of 3 January 1874, and Serrano again became president of the executive. In his eleven months in office he gave attention to finance, to renewing relations with other powers and to suppressing revolt, but at the end of December 1874 another pronunciamiento restored the Bourbons. He returned to Madrid in 1876 and sat in the senate as a marshal. He died in Madrid in November 1885, a day after Alfonso XII.
francisco-solano-lopez: Francisco Solano López was born in Manorá, a district of Asunción. His father, Carlos Antonio López, became president in 1841 and commissioned him a brigadier general in 1844, at the age of 17. He studied fortifications and artillery in Rio de Janeiro and Asunción and commanded Paraguayan forces on the Argentine frontier during the Platine Wars.

In 1853 he was sent to Europe as minister plenipotentiary to Britain, France and the Kingdom of Sardinia, and spent more than a year and a half there, mostly in Paris. He bought arms and steamers, brought back European military methods, and set up the first electric telegraph in South America. In Paris he met the Irish-born Eliza Lynch, who returned with him and lived with him until his death. Back in Paraguay he became Minister of War and in 1862 Vice President.

When his father died in 1862, Congress proclaimed López president for ten years. He kept the economic protectionism of his predecessors but abandoned strict isolation, hoping to make Paraguay a third force between Argentina and the Empire of Brazil in the Rio de la Plata basin. He allied with Uruguay's government, introduced compulsory military service and built one of the best-trained, though poorly equipped, armies in the region.

When Brazil invaded Uruguay in October 1864, López seized a Brazilian steamer and declared war that December, invading Mato Grosso. After Argentina refused passage across Corrientes, he declared war on Argentina on 13 April 1865. On 1 May 1865 Argentina, Brazil and Uruguay signed the Treaty of the Triple Alliance, aiming to overthrow his government. The destruction of the Paraguayan fleet at Riachuelo on 11 June 1865 gave the Allies control of the rivers. Talks with Bartolomé Mitre in 1866 failed. In 1868, believing in a conspiracy, he had several hundred people executed, among them relatives, ministers, officers, clergy and foreigners.

Allied troops took Asunción on 1 January 1869. López retreated north and made a last stand at Cerro Corá, where Brazilian forces reached his camp on 1 March 1870. Wounded, he refused General José Antônio Correia da Câmara's call to surrender and died in the struggle. His last words are disputed: "I die for my nation" or "I die with my nation".

Paraguay lost between a quarter and a third of its territory, and at least half its people died. Paraguayans still debate whether he was a leader who held on to the end or one who led the country into a war it could not win. Others in Latin America see him as a defender of small nations. 1 March is a national holiday, and he lies in the National Pantheon of the Heroes in Asunción.
franco-dutch-war: France had backed the Dutch Republic during the Eighty Years War against Spain, and the Peace of Münster of 1648 confirmed Dutch independence and closed the Scheldt estuary, which benefited Amsterdam by removing its rival Antwerp. After the death of William II of Orange in 1650, political control passed to the urban patricians, the Regenten, and Johan de Witt was Grand Pensionary from 1653 to 1672. The States of Holland refused to support a division of the Spanish Netherlands, which convinced Louis XIV that his aims could only be reached by force.

The French offensive began on 4 May 1672, with Turenne's main army of 50,000 and a second force under Condé. By 5 June the French had taken Rheinberg, Orsoy and Burick with little resistance, and they crossed the Rhine, fighting the Battle of Tolhuis on 12 June. William of Orange withdrew behind the Holland Water Line, the flooding of which had been ordered only on 8 June. The Dutch remember 1672 as the Rampjaar, the Disaster Year. Rioting in the cities of Holland replaced Regenten with Orangist partisans, and French peace terms of 1 July caused outrage.

The position stabilised by late July. Emperor Leopold I, Spain and Brandenburg-Prussia came to the Dutch side, and England left the war in February 1674. In 1673 the French took Maastricht, which surrendered on 30 June. In 1674 they overran Franche-Comté in under six weeks, and Turenne won a winter campaign in Alsace that ended in January 1675. William was halted by Condé at the Battle of Seneffe. Sweden, France's ally, invaded Brandenburg and was beaten at Fehrbellin.

Neither side won a decisive victory. By 1677 France held Franche-Comté and had made gains in the Spanish Netherlands and Alsace, helped by victory at the Battle of Cassel and by Vauban's line of fortresses. The Peace of Nijmegen of September 1678 returned Charleroi and Ghent to Spain, while France received all of Franche-Comté and towns including Ypres, Valenciennes and Saint-Omer. All but Ypres remain French. The terms were worse than those on offer in July 1672.

Louis came to be called the Sun King in the years after the war. William of Orange became dominant in Dutch domestic politics, and this helped him build the anti-French Grand Alliance of the Nine Years' War (1688-1697) and the War of the Spanish Succession (1701-1714).
franco-flemish-war-1297-1305: From 1285 Philip IV sought to subject his great vassals, and through the Parlement of Paris he backed the towns of Ghent, Bruges and Ypres against their count. The war was bound up with the Gascon War of 1294–1303 and the First War of Scottish Independence. Guy's daughter Philippa was betrothed to the future Edward II, which Philip treated as treason: he imprisoned Guy until February 1295, blocked the English wool trade on which Flanders depended, levied a new war tax and placed royal supervisors in the towns. On 7 January 1297 Guy, allied with Edward I of England, renounced his vassalage.

Edward, faced with opposition at home and the war in Scotland, gave little help. A French army under Charles of Valois besieged Lille, Robert of Artois won the Battle of Furnes on 20 August 1297, and Lille, Kortrijk and Bruges fell. A papal truce on 12 October let Edward withdraw, and the Treaty of Montreuil of 1299 left Guy without allies. When the war resumed in 1300 the French took Damme, Ghent and Ypres, and on 24 May Guy and his sons Robert and William were led into captivity in Paris.

The governor Jacques de Châtillon and the Leliaards, the French king's Flemish supporters, raised new taxes, and the guilds allied with the nobles loyal to the count. The militia of Bruges massacred French troops in the Matins of Bruges, and Guy of Namur and William of Jülich led the revolt. On 11 July 1302 the Flemish militia defeated the French cavalry of Robert II of Artois near Kortrijk in the Battle of the Golden Spurs, and by November the rebels held the whole county. They won again at Arques in April 1303, but in August 1304 a Franco-Hollandic fleet defeated Guy of Namur at Zierikzee, and the two armies met at Mons-en-Pévèle on 18 August.

A truce was made at the abbey of Marquette on 23 September 1304, and the Treaty of Athis-sur-Orge was signed on 23 June 1305. It laid exorbitant fines on the Flemish towns and restored the count as a vassal of the French king. Philip probably restored him because French rule in 1300–1302 had failed and he needed someone able to collect the fines.
franco-hova-war: The United Kingdom and France both sought control of Madagascar, an island of strategic importance on the sea passage to India, but the Merina Kingdom kept its independence through the 19th century, helped by the island's size and terrain, its organised army and government, and tropical diseases deadly to Europeans. British missionaries arrived in Antananarivo in 1820 under Radama I; Queen Ranavalona I, who reigned from 1828, restricted the Christianity they had brought and repelled French attacks on Foulepointe and other coastal towns.

As prince, her son Radama II had granted the Frenchman Joseph-François Lambert large tracts of land in the Lambert Charter, disregarding the significance attached to ancestral land. After Radama was strangled in an 1863 coup, real power passed to the prime minister; Rainilaiarivony held the office for 30 years. The monarchy revoked the charter, holding that the land belonged to the crown and the prince had no right to give it away. The heirs of Jean Laborde, refused the lands and properties promised to their father, pressed their claim with the French government, which rejected Merina offers to negotiate.

France invaded in 1883 seeking to restore the cancelled concessions, and the war ended with the Treaty of Tamatave of 17 December 1885. Madagascar ceded Antsiranana (Diego-Suarez) on the northern coast and paid an indemnity of 10 million francs. An Instructive Letter meant to clarify the treaty was never presented to the French Parliament when it voted to ratify. The treaty gave France control over Malagasy foreign policy, which it used to exert increasing control, but no protectorate was formally declared.

Rainilaiarivony never fully accepted the treaty's terms. In September 1890 the British recognised a French protectorate in return for eventual control of Zanzibar, and on 12 December 1894 French marines took Tamatave. General Duchesne's column marched from Mahajanga to Antananarivo, which fell after a brief shelling; Duchesne entered on 1 October 1895 and Queen Ranavalona III signed a treaty making Madagascar a full protectorate. Twenty French soldiers died in the fighting and 6,000 of malaria and other diseases. After the Menalamba rebellion the French deposed the queen in 1897 and ended the Merina monarchy.
franco-mongol-alliance: Western Europeans had long expected a great Christian ally from the East, the legend of Prester John, and in 1210 rumours made the Naiman leader Kuchlug, at war with Muhammad II of Khwarezm, into that figure. The Mongol court held many influential Nestorian Christians. The first official contacts, between Pope Innocent IV and the Great Khans in 1245-1248, set a lasting pattern: the Europeans asked the Mongols to convert, and the Mongols demanded submission. Some Christian rulers did submit, Queen Rusudan of Georgia in 1243, Hethum I of Cilician Armenia in 1247 and his son-in-law Bohemond VI of Antioch in 1260.

In December 1248 envoys of the Mongol commander Eljigidei met Louis IX of France on Cyprus and proposed that Louis land in Egypt while Eljigidei attacked Baghdad, but the embassy Louis sent to the Great Khan Güyük came back only with a demand for tribute. The Barons of Acre, more wary of the Mongols, let Mamluk forces pass through their territory to defeat them at Ain Jalut in 1260. From the mid-1260s the Ilkhans of Persia, Abaqa, Arghun, Ghazan and Oljeitu, sent repeated embassies, among them that of the cleric Rabban Bar Sauma, and offered to return Jerusalem in exchange for cooperation.

The Mongols invaded Syria several times between 1281 and 1312, sometimes hoping to act with the Franks, but the forces arrived months apart. After the fall of Acre in 1291 the Crusaders withdrew to Cyprus, and a last attempt to hold the island of Ruad in concert with the Mongols ended with its fall in 1302. Contact faded after the Ilkhanate broke up in the 1330s.

Most historians describe the contacts as a series of failed negotiations, though Jean Richard dated an alliance from about 1263, Timothy May placed its peak at the Council of Lyon in 1274 and Alain Demurger held that none was sealed until 1300. Reasons proposed for the failure include strife among the Mongols themselves, European confusion between the Ilkhanate and the Golden Horde, waning interest in crusading, and a Mongol outlook in which outside powers were subjects or enemies rather than allies.
franco-moroccan-war: Soon after the French invasion of Algiers in 1830, Emir Abd al-Kader led the resistance and called on the tribes of eastern Morocco, above all the Beni Znassen confederation, to join him. Sultan Moulay Abd al-Rahman sent him a steady supply of horses, arms and money. After a defeat in October 1842 the emir withdrew into Morocco and used the frontier as a base for raids into Algeria, so the French posted a division under Generals Louis Juchault de Lamoricière and Marie Alphonse Bedeau at Lalla Maghnia.

On 22 May 1844 the commander at Oujda, El-Gennaoui, demanded that the French leave, and on 30 May his troops fired on their camp and were driven back. Marshal Thomas Robert Bugeaud insisted that the border run along the Kiss River and threatened war if Morocco kept sheltering the emir. On 19 June he crossed the frontier and occupied Oujda, while the sultan ordered a general levy.

The war opened on 6 August 1844, when a squadron under François d'Orléans, Prince of Joinville, a son of King Louis Philippe I, shelled the outer batteries of Tangier for about three hours, sparing the town itself. On 14 August, near Oujda, Bugeaud's smaller force defeated a large army led by the sultan's son and heir, Sidi Mohammed, who had advanced against his father's orders.

Mohammed fell back to Taza, and Bugeaud was made Duke of Isly. On 16 August Joinville's ships bombarded Mogador, Morocco's main Atlantic port; some five hundred marines took the island battery and the works were wrecked. Joinville called the shelling much more of a political act than an act of warfare. Britain, with warships at both ports, protested, and together with a dispute over Tahiti the campaign caused a mild war scare.

Under the Treaty of Tangier of 10 September 1844 Morocco recognised Algeria as part of the French Empire, agreed to reduce its garrison at Oujda and to set up a border commission, and declared Abd al-Kader an outlaw to be pursued on both sides of the frontier. He surrendered to Henri d'Orléans on 24 December 1847. The Treaty of Lalla Maghnia of 18 March 1845 fixed the border only from the Mediterranean to Teniet el-Sassi, some seventy miles inland; the French declined to draw a line through the desert south of Figuig.
franco-ottoman-alliance: After Suleiman I extended Ottoman rule to Serbia in 1522, the Holy Roman Empire came into direct conflict with the Ottomans, and Francis I of France looked for an ally against the House of Habsburg, though no French king before him had courted a Muslim power. The first approaches were made while Francis was a prisoner in Madrid after the Battle of Pavia: a mission sent by his mother, Louise de Savoie, was lost in Bosnia, and a second under John Frangipani reached Constantinople in December 1525. Francis told the Venetian ambassador Giorgio Gritti in March 1531 that he wished to see the Turk powerful in order to weaken the emperor.

Ambassadors went both ways: Antonio Rincon met Suleiman at Belgrade in 1532, and Hayreddin Barbarossa led an Ottoman embassy to France in 1533. After the treaty negotiated by Jean de La Forêt in 1536, a Franco-Ottoman fleet raided the Spanish coast and wintered at Marseille, the first Turkish fleet to do so. Under Henry II the allies took Tripoli in 1551, beat Andrea Doria's galleys at the Battle of Ponza on 5 August 1552, and invaded Corsica in 1553, the high point of the military alliance.

Later kings kept the policy. Henry IV signed a Peace Treaty and Capitulation with Ahmed I in 1604, and Mehmed Efendi's embassy to Louis XV in 1720 was the first permanent Ottoman representation abroad. France helped negotiate the Treaty of Belgrade of 1739. The friendship ended with Napoleon's invasion of Egypt in 1798, though France, Britain and the Ottomans allied against Russia in the Crimean War in 1854.

As the first non-ideological alliance between a Christian and a Muslim state, the pact caused a scandal in Christendom. Charles V appealed to Europe against it, Giovanni Botero called it a vile, infamous, diabolical treaty, and the Huguenot Francois de La Noue said it had diminished France. The historian Arthur Hassall judged that it had helped save France from Charles V and aided Protestantism in Germany. It also fed debates over whether reason of state stood above religious unity, and it let the Ottoman Empire take part in European diplomacy.
franco-prussian-war: The war grew out of the unification of the German states under Otto von Bismarck. France had been the dominant power of continental Europe after the Franco-Austrian War of 1859, and the decisive Prussian victory over Austria in 1866 appeared to call that position into question. In 1870 Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was offered the vacant Spanish throne and withdrew his acceptance, but the French ambassador then asked King Wilhelm I at Ems to renounce any future claim. Wilhelm refused, and Bismarck made the report of the exchange public in altered wording. Crowds in Paris demanded war.

France mobilised on 15 July 1870, and its parliament voted for war the next day. The German coalition mobilised more effectively, and its forces were superior in numbers, training and leadership and made better use of railways and artillery.

France invaded German territory on 2 August, and German armies entered north-eastern France on 4 August. French defeats followed at Wissembourg, Spicheren and Wörth, and the largest battle of the war, at Gravelotte on 18 August, drove Marshal Bazaine's Army of the Rhine back into Metz. At the Battle of Sedan on 1 September the Prussians surrounded the Army of Châlons, and on 2 September Napoleon III surrendered with 104,000 of his soldiers.

On 4 September a popular uprising overthrew the Second Empire, and Jules Favre, Léon Gambetta and General Louis-Jules Trochu proclaimed a Government of National Defence and the Third Republic. The Germans began the siege of Paris on 19 September. Bazaine's army at Metz surrendered on 26 October. Paris, starving, fell on 28 January 1871, and an armistice was agreed.

In the last days of the war the German states proclaimed the German Empire under Wilhelm I. By the Treaty of Frankfurt of 10 May 1871, France paid an indemnity of five billion francs and ceded most of Alsace and parts of Lorraine, which became the Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine.

In France the war ended imperial rule and began the first lasting republican government. Resentment at its handling led to the Paris Commune, held from 18 March until the army retook Paris in the Semaine Sanglante of 21 to 28 May. The defeat also produced revanchism in France, a demand for revenge and the return of Alsace and Lorraine. Germany supplanted France as the dominant land power, and other armies adopted the Prussian general staff, universal conscription and detailed mobilisation systems.
franco-savoyard-war-1600-1601: Saluzzo, in the Piedmontese Alps, had been a French enclave since Henry II of France annexed it after the death of its last marquis, Gian Gabriele I, in 1548. France's claim was relatively weak, and Charles Emmanuel I, pursuing the expansion of his duchy, occupied the marquisate in the autumn of 1588, while France was weakened by civil war, on the pretext of keeping it from the Huguenots of Dauphiné.

In 1595 Henry IV offered Saluzzo to one of the duke's sons as a French fief, but Charles Emmanuel wanted it outright. Papal arbitration failed. At Fontainebleau in December 1599 Henry offered two choices: return Saluzzo, or keep it and cede the county of Bresse, the vicarship of Barcelonnette and the Stura, Perosa and Pinerolo valleys. The duke went home to Turin, prepared for war and hoped for Spanish help from the governor of Milan, the Count of Fuentes. After an ultimatum, Henry declared war in August 1600.

Charles de Gontaut, Duke of Biron, took Bourg-en-Bresse, though not its citadel, and occupied most of Bresse, the Bugey and Gex. Charles de Blanchefort, stepson of the Duke of Lesdiguières, took Montmélian; Chambery opened its gates, and Lesdiguières took the fortress of Miolans and Conflans. The French then occupied the Maurienne and Tarentaise valleys, though a move against Nice by Charles, Duke of Guise, was beaten off. In early October Henry entered Annecy.

In November Charles Emmanuel marched from the Aosta Valley with some twenty thousand Piedmontese, Spaniards, Swiss and Savoyards but made no headway. The citadel of Montmélian surrendered in mid-November, and a month later a French and Genevese force took and demolished the fortress of Sainte Catherine, built to threaten Geneva. By the end of the year only the citadel of Bourg still held out.

France had lost little, but the threat of Spanish intervention led Henry to accept peace, and the Treaty of Lyon was signed on 17 January 1601. Besides the lands west of the Rhône, Savoy paid France 300,000 livres, and in exchange France gave up its Italian holdings beyond the Alps. The Spanish Road linking Franche-Comté with Milan was kept open by a new route over the Bridge of Grésin, confined to a single valley, after Geneva objected to a route through the territory of Bern.
franco-spanish-war-1635-1659: In the first stages of the Thirty Years' War France avoided direct involvement, financing Habsburg opponents such as the Dutch Republic and backing the Swedish intervention. After the Imperial-Spanish victory at Nördlingen in September 1634 forced the Swedes out of southern Germany, and most of their German allies made peace at Prague in April 1635, Louis XIII and Richelieu decided on direct intervention. France signed an anti-Spanish alliance with the Dutch and the Treaty of Compiègne with Sweden, and declared war on Spain in May 1635.

A French army of 27,000 defeated the Spanish at Les Avins in May 1635 but lost heavily to disease at Leuven and withdrew. In 1636 a Spanish incursion reached Corbie and caused panic in Paris, but the Cardinal-Infante Ferdinand of Austria retreated for lack of supplies. With the French in Alsace, Spain had to supply Flanders by sea, and in 1639 the Dutch destroyed a large Spanish supply fleet at the Battle of the Downs. Taxes and the cost of the war led to open revolts in Portugal and Catalonia in 1640, which France supported.

On 19 May 1643, five days after the death of Louis XIII, Louis II de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, defeated the Spanish Army of Flanders at Rocroi. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 recognised Dutch independence and, under the Treaty of Münster, gave France strategic places in Alsace and Lorraine and Pinerolo, but left France and Spain at war. Spain backed French rebels in the Fronde, and in 1657 Cardinal Mazarin allied France with the Commonwealth of England.

Under the Treaty of the Pyrenees, signed on 5 November 1659, France gained Artois, Hainaut and Roussillon, which fixed the border along the Pyrenees but divided the historic Principality of Catalonia. Spain recognised the French gains of Westphalia, France withdrew support from Portugal, and Condé regained his titles and possessions. The treaty included the marriage contract of Louis XIV and Maria Theresa of Spain, which he later used to justify the War of Devolution.

Traditional historiography saw the war as the start of France replacing Spain as the predominant European power. Most historians now view it as militarily indecisive, a stalemate from 1637 to 1659, though Spain's economic and military power declined abruptly after 1659 and it became less able to defend territory outside Peninsular Spain without foreign help.
franco-syrian-treaty-of-independence: In 1934 France tried to impose a treaty heavily weighted in its own favour, which promised gradual independence but kept the Syrian Mountains under French control. Syria's head of state, Muhammad 'Ali Bay al-'Abid, was a French puppet. The senior nationalist and parliamentarian Hashim al-Atassi led the opposition and called a sixty-day strike, and his coalition, the National Bloc, won massive popular support: riots and demonstrations spread and the economy came to a standstill.

The new French government led by the Popular Front then recognised the National Bloc as the sole legitimate representative of the Syrian people and invited Atassi to negotiate in Paris. He travelled there on 22 March 1936 at the head of a senior Bloc delegation. The agreement is also known as the Viénot Accords.

The treaty called for immediate recognition of Syria as a sovereign republic, with full emancipation to follow gradually. It guaranteed the incorporation of the formerly autonomous Druze and Alawite regions, but not of Lebanon, with which France signed a similar treaty in November. France promised to curtail its intervention in Syrian domestic affairs and to reduce its troops, personnel and military bases. In return Syria pledged to support France in time of war, including the use of its air space, and to let France keep two military bases on its territory. Further political, economic and cultural provisions were included.

Atassi returned to Syria in triumph on 27 September 1936 and was elected President of the Republic in November. The rising threat of Adolf Hitler made France fear being outflanked by Nazi Germany if it gave up its Middle Eastern territories, and with imperialist leanings in parts of its government this led France to refuse ratification. France also ceded the province of Alexandretta, guaranteed to Syria by the treaty, to Turkey. Riots broke out again, Atassi resigned, and independence waited until after World War II; the last French troops left in 1946.
franco-syrian-war: Edmund Allenby's forces captured Damascus on 30 September 1918, and Faisal, the Hashemite ruler, entered on 3 October during the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans. On 5 October, with Allenby's permission, he announced an Arab constitutional government. The secret Sykes-Picot Agreement of 1916 divided the Ottoman remnants between France and Britain, and General Henri Gouraud became French representative and commander of the Army of the Levant.

The Syrian Congress held its first session on 3 June 1919, with Hashim al-Atassi as president. On 2 July it resolved for a fully independent constitutional monarchy under Faisal and refused French claims. The Anglo-French Agreement of 15 September 1919 withdrew British troops from Syria from 1 November, leaving the French to answer only to themselves. In January 1920 Faisal negotiated with Clemenceau, but his anti-French supporters pressed him to reverse the compromise, and he did.

Attacks on French forces occurred across Syria from January 1920. On 8 March 1920 an independent Arab Kingdom of Syria was proclaimed in Damascus, with Faisal as king and al-Atassi as prime minister; the British and French repudiated it, and the San Remo Conference of April 1920 established the French mandate. Syrian nationalists rejected it. Gouraud issued an ultimatum to disband the Syrian troops, and Faisal surrendered on 14 July, but his defence minister Yusuf al-'Azma, ignoring him, led a small force of disbanded troops and civilians to Maysalun.

At the Battle of Maysalun on 24 July General Mariano Goybet's French forces easily defeated the Syrian forces, and al-'Azma was killed. French forces entered Damascus the same day without resistance, and the next day the kingdom was abolished.

On 25 July a new pro-French government was declared under 'Alaa al-Din al-Darubi. Gouraud established civil administration and divided the mandate into six states: Damascus, Aleppo, the Alawite State, Jabal Druze, the autonomous Sanjak of Alexandretta, now Hatay in Turkey, and the State of Greater Lebanon, which became modern Lebanon. The British, concerned for their position in Iraq, agreed to make the fugitive Faisal king of Iraq.
franco-tahitian-war: Tahiti had been converted to Protestant Christianity by the London Missionary Society in the early 19th century under the patronage of the Pōmare dynasty. In 1836 Queen Pōmare IV, influenced by the British consul and former missionary George Pritchard, expelled two French Catholic missionaries. After a complaint from the French consul Jacques-Antoine Moerenhout, the naval commander Abel Aubert du Petit-Thouars forced the Tahitians in 1838 to pay an indemnity and sign a treaty of friendship, and four years later made the chiefs and the queen sign a request for French protection.

The queen appealed in vain to Queen Victoria and King Louis Philippe I and kept flying the Tahitian flag. In November 1843 Dupetit Thouars deposed her and placed Armand Joseph Bruat in charge as governor. She fled to Raiatea aboard HMS Basilisk, and the imprisonment and deportation of Pritchard, the Pritchard Affair, nearly brought conflict with Britain until France apologised.

Armed resistance began on 13 March 1844, led first by the chief Fanaue and later by Utami and his second-in-command Maiʻo, against French forces that included the pro-French chiefs Paraita, Tati and Hitoti. At the Battle of Mahaena on 17 April 1844, 441 French soldiers defeated a Tahitian force twice their size; 15 French soldiers and 102 Tahitians died. The Tahitians then waged guerrilla war from fortified valleys in the mountainous interior until their defeat at the Battle of Punaruu in May 1846 and the capture of Fort Fautaua on 17 December 1846.

On a second front the French tried to bring the Leeward Islands kingdoms of Raiatea, Huahine and Bora Bora under their rule, but a blockade of Raiatea was lifted after the warriors of Queen Teriitaria II of Huahine defeated the French at the Battle of Maeva, where 18 marines were killed and 43 wounded. Britain stayed officially neutral, though more than a dozen of its warships in the islands were a constant concern to the French.

In February 1847 Pōmare IV returned and agreed to rule under the protectorate. British pressure kept France from annexing Tahiti outright, and in the Jarnac Convention of 1847 the two powers agreed to respect the independence of Huahine, Raiatea and Bora Bora. France formally annexed Tahiti and the Leeward Islands only in the 1880s, through the Leewards War that ended in 1897, forming French Polynesia.
franco-thai-war: The Franco-Siamese Crisis of 1893 and the Franco-Siamese Treaty of 1907 left Siam without the territories of Laos and Cambodia, a loss later seen in Thailand as a national humiliation. Plaek Phibunsongkhram, known as Phibun, became prime minister on 16 December 1938 and had a propaganda campaign run to reclaim lost territories. Siam was renamed Thailand in June 1939. France signed a non-aggression treaty with Thailand on 12 June 1940, days before the fall of France. That defeat left the colonial administration in Indochina cut off from help, and Japan forced the French to allow it military bases. The apparent submissiveness of the French led Phibun to believe France would not resist seriously.

The Vichy French army in Indochina numbered about 50,000 men, 12,000 of them French, with only 20 tanks; the Royal Thai Army had 60,000 men and nearly one hundred armoured vehicles. Border skirmishes along the Mekong began in October 1940, and Thai aircraft bombed Vientiane, Phnom Penh, Sisophon and Battambang. On 5 January 1941, after a reported French attack on Aranyaprathet, two Thai armies attacked Laos and Cambodia. They overran Laos swiftly, while French forces in Cambodia rallied. A French counterattack on 16 January failed in the fiercest fight of the war.

On 17 January a French squadron surprised a Thai detachment at anchor off Ko Chang, sinking two torpedo boats and disabling a coastal defence ship without French casualties. Japan then mediated. A ceasefire took effect on 28 January, and armistice documents were signed aboard the cruiser Natori on 31 January.

A peace treaty signed in Tokyo on 9 May 1941 had France, coerced by Japan, give up the disputed border territories: Battambang and Pailin, Siem Reap, Banteay Meanchey and Oddar Meanchey, Preah Vihear, and Xaignabouli with part of Luang Prabang. Because Japan wished to keep its relationship with Vichy, the Thais accepted only a quarter of the territory they had gained and paid six million piastres to the French. In Thailand the settlement was seen as a personal triumph for Phibun, who erected the Victory Monument in Bangkok. The real beneficiary was Japan, which extended its influence in both countries; it invaded Thailand on 8 December 1941, and Thailand was allied with Japan until 1945.
franco-turkish-war: The Sykes–Picot Agreement of 1916 had envisaged French influence in Ottoman Syria and Cilicia, a region valued for its ports, railways and routes into northern Syria. British troops occupied much of Cilicia after the Armistice of Mudros in 1918, and an Anglo-French agreement of September 1919 provided for their replacement by French forces. These comprised metropolitan and colonial troops and the French Armenian Legion, commanded in Cilicia by General Julien Dufieux under Henri Gouraud, commander of the Army of the Levant.

Many Armenians deported during the Armenian genocide returned after the war, some expecting French protection, and communal tensions mounted. In November 1919 Mustafa Kemal sent Kılıç Ali to the Maraş district to organise armed groups, and Ankara supplied local fighters, many of them former soldiers, whom the French called tchétés.

A siege of Maraş began in January 1920, and the French evacuated the town on the night of 10–11 February, taking several thousand Armenian civilians with them. At Urfa a garrison besieged from February agreed to withdraw in April, and most of its soldiers were killed when the departing column was attacked. A French battalion under Major Mesnil surrendered after an ambush near Karboğazı in May. Up to 12,000 Armenians were killed at Maraş, and nearly 8,000 when Hadjin fell in October 1920.

The French held Adana, defeated nationalist troops in open engagements and took Aintab on 9 February 1921, but lacked the men to guard every road, railway and outpost. Historians such as Andrew Orr and Edward J. Erickson judge that neither side could win outright.

Wishing to cut costs, secure Syria and cultivate Ankara while Britain backed Greece, the French government sent Henry Franklin-Bouillon to negotiate with Mustafa Kemal. Under the Ankara Agreement of 20 October 1921, Ankara accepted French authority over Syria and the Sanjak of Alexandretta. French troops left the main towns by the first week of January 1922, and in December 1921 France organised ships to evacuate tens of thousands of Armenian civilians.

The separate settlement freed Ankara to turn its forces against Greece, and the historian Douglas Dakin called the conduct of France and Italy treachery towards Greece. France also supplied the nationalists with rifles, horses and aircraft. The economic partnership Paris had hoped for did not develop.
francois-charles-de-velbruck: Velbrück was born at Garath Castle near Düsseldorf on 11 June 1719. In 1735, at the age of 16, he received from his brother a prebend of Saint Lambert's Cathedral in Liège, and a year later he was received onto the cathedral chapter by procuration, though he did not live in Liège until 1745. In 1756 he became archdeacon of Hesbaye and, later that year, keeper of the prince-bishop's seal.

In 1757 he led a diplomatic mission to the court at Vienna and was made a canon of Münster Cathedral. Two years later he became grand master of the household and prime minister to Johann Theodor of Bavaria, prince-bishop of Liège. A conduit of French influence, he lost his place after Johann Theodor's death in 1763 and the election of his rival, Charles-Nicolas d'Oultremont. In 1765 Louis XV made him commendatory abbot of Saint-Nicolas at Cheminon in Champagne. On Oultremont's death in 1772 he was elected unanimously to succeed him.

As prince-bishop he tried to bring the ideas of the Enlightenment to the Principality of Liège, though a lack of money and power left many projects unfinished. He set up the Hôpital général Saint-Léonard for the needy and a free course in midwifery, and created free charity schools for poor children. In 1773 he carried out the suppression of the Jesuits in Liège, and he gave more weight in teaching to the physical sciences, mathematics and the human sciences.

He planned a large public library and in 1774 began building a public academy of painting, sculpture and engraving. In 1779 he founded the Société littéraire de Liège and the Société d'Emulation, where the city's scholars met foreign visitors and heard of scientific discoveries and new works of art and poetry. It was later claimed that he was a freemason, but the historian of the Liège lodges found no proof of it.

Velbrück died at Hex Castle, near Tongeren, on 30 April 1784 and was buried in Liège. During the Liège Revolution his remains, unlike those of his predecessors, were not thrown into a ditch, and his mausoleum survived. Restored, it has stood since 15 June 2000 in the cloister of St. Paul's Cathedral, Liège. Its epitaph praises him as both an Augustus and a Maecenas to the people of Liège.
francois-coillard: Coillard was born on 17 July 1834 at Asnières-les-Bourges in the Cher, the youngest of the seven children of François Coillard and his wife Madeleine, both of Huguenot descent. His father died in 1836 and left the family nearly destitute. He entered the Protestant School at Asnières at 15 and later studied at Strasbourg University, offering himself to the Paris Evangelical Missionary Society in 1854.

He trained under Eugène Casalis, a veteran of the southern African mission, and was ordained at the Oratoire in Paris in 1857. He reached Cape Town on 6 November 1857, on the eve of a war between Basutoland and the Orange Free State in which the French stations were destroyed, and his first task was to open a new station at Leribe. On 26 February 1861 he married Christina Mackintosh, daughter of a Scottish Baptist minister, who shared his travels as a co-worker; they had no children.

In the disputes of 1865 Coillard helped negotiations between Basuto chiefs and Theophilus Shepstone of Natal. Boer forces from the Orange Free State forced the evacuation of Leribe in April 1866, and he worked in Natal until Britain proclaimed a protectorate over Basutoland in 1868. Encouraged by Robert Moffat of Kuruman, he led a party with four Basuto evangelists north, reaching Pretoria in May 1877, but the Shona chiefs refused them and King Lobengula of the Ndebele forbade them to preach. Khama III of the Tswana then suggested Barotseland.

Coillard's expedition of 1884 found Barotseland in turmoil, with Lewanika exiled and a usurper on the throne. His early dealings with the usurper cost him credit when Lewanika returned, and he was received at Lealui only in March 1886. Lewanika and Coillard misunderstood the ties between the British crown and the British South Africa Company of Cecil Rhodes, and the Lochner Concession of 27 June 1890 assigned the kingdom to the company, which for seven years paid none of its promised £2000 a year.

Christina Coillard died on 28 October 1891, and the mission suffered high mortality from tropical fevers. After a serious illness in 1895 Coillard spent the period 1896–8 in Europe. In 1903 a breakaway movement of his converts led by Willie Mokalapa shook him further. He died of haematuric fever at Lealui on 27 May 1904 and was buried near his wife at Sefula. His letters, published in 1889 as Sur le Haut-Zambèze and in English in 1897, made him a hero to mission supporters.
francois-de-laval: François de Laval, in full Francis-Xavier de Montmorency-Laval, was born on 30 April 1623 at Montigny-sur-Avre in the old province of Perche. His father, Hugues de Laval, was a member of the House of Laval, and his mother, Michelle de Péricard, came from a family of hereditary royal officers in Normandy. He received the tonsure at eight and entered the College of La Flèche in 1631, where reports of the Jesuit missions to the Huron in Canada made him want to be a missionary. When his two oldest brothers were killed in battle he became head of the family, but he renounced his rights of primogeniture and was ordained a priest on 1 May 1647.

As archdeacon of Évreux he oversaw 155 parishes, and he later spent three years at the Hermitage near Caen. New France had then had no bishop for fifty years. The Jesuits backed Laval against the Sulpician candidate, but Rome made him vicar apostolic and titular bishop of Petra rather than bishop of a French diocese. He reached Quebec on 16 June 1659 and spent nearly two years contesting the authority of the Sulpician Gabriel Thubières de Levy de Queylus.

Laval clashed with Governor d'Argenson over protocol and threatened excommunication against those who sold alcohol to indigenous people. In 1662 he sailed to consult Louis XIV, secured Governor d'Avaugour's recall and returned with greater powers, choosing the next governor, Mézy, and sitting on the Sovereign Council from its first session on 18 September 1663. After Intendant Jean Talon joined the council he withdrew somewhat from state affairs. He opened a minor seminary in 1668 with eight French and six Huron students, gave most of his fortune to the seminary and founded a school of arts and crafts at Saint-Joachim.

Named first bishop when the Diocese of Quebec was established on 1 October 1674, he obtained a royal decree against the alcohol trade on 24 May 1679 and drew up parish boundaries in 1681. Failing health led him to hand his diocese, which reached from Acadia to Lake Michigan, to Jean-Baptiste de La Croix de Chevrières de Saint-Vallier in 1688. He died of an ulcer on 6 May 1708. His remains lie in the Cathedral-Basilica of Notre-Dame de Québec, and Pope John Paul II beatified him in 1980. The city of Laval, north of Montreal, is named after him.
francois-duvalier: François Duvalier was born in Port-au-Prince on 14 April 1907, the son of Duval Duvalier, a justice of the peace, teacher and journalist whose family came from Martinique, and Ulyssia Abraham, a baker. He completed a degree in medicine at the University of Haiti in 1934 and spent a year at the University of Michigan studying public health. From 1943 he took part in a campaign to control typhus, yaws, malaria and other tropical diseases, and his patients called him Papa Doc. The racism and violence of the United States occupation of Haiti, which began in 1915, inspired a black nationalism in him, and in 1938 he co-founded the journal Les Griots.

Duvalier became Director General of the National Public Health Service in 1946 and Minister of Health and Labor in 1949 under President Dumarsais Estimé. He left the government after Paul Magloire's coup of 1950 and went into hiding in the countryside in 1954. In the 1957 campaign he stood against the mulatto landowner Louis Déjoie, appealing to the black majority's resentment of the small mulatto elite. He was elected president on 22 September 1957 with 679,884 votes to Déjoie's 266,992, although there are accounts of fraud and intimidation.

After an attempted coup in July 1958 he dismissed the general staff and turned the Presidential Guard into an elite corps. In 1959 he created the militia known as the Tonton Macoute, which by 1961 was twice as big as the army. A sole-candidate election in 1961 extended his term, and a referendum on 14 June 1964 made him president for life, with ballots reportedly premarked yes. His government is estimated to have killed between 30,000 and 60,000 people, and many educated professionals fled to New York, Miami, Montreal, Paris and African states.

He cultivated a personality cult that drew on Vodou, modelling his image on the lwa Baron Samedi, and he expelled foreign bishops, which brought his excommunication. A concordat of 15 August 1966 lifted it and let him nominate Haitian bishops.

Duvalier died of heart disease and diabetes on 21 April 1971, aged 64, and his 19-year-old son Jean-Claude, called Baby Doc, succeeded him. He had suffered a heart attack in 1959, and he had been a diabetic since early adulthood. The regime fell on 8 February 1986, when a crowd attacked his mausoleum. Many books treat the Duvalier era, the best known being Graham Greene's novel The Comedians.
francois-fenelon: François de Salignac de la Mothe-Fénelon was born on 6 August 1651 at the Château de Fénelon in Sainte-Mondane, Périgord, into an old noble family reduced to modest means, in which fifteen generations had held the bishopric of nearby Sarlat. Private tutors taught him the Greek and Latin classics, and his uncle arranged his studies in Paris, where he preached a public sermon at 15. He was ordained about 1675.

In 1679 the Archbishop of Paris made him director of the Nouvelles-Catholiques, a community for young Huguenot girls about to join the Catholic Church, and in 1687 he published his Treatise on the Education of Girls. After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, he preached to Protestants in Saintonge at Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet's suggestion.

In 1689 he became tutor to the seven-year-old Duke of Burgundy, second in line to the throne. For his pupil he wrote Fables, Dialogues of the Dead and, in 1693 and 1694, The Adventures of Telemachus, a novel about the son of Ulysses that also attacks the divine-right absolute monarchy of Louis XIV's France. It contains the line that good kings are rare and most monarchs bad.

Published in 1699, it was a best seller across Europe and supplied the plot of Mozart's opera Idomeneo. It is read as the programme of the circle of the Duc de Beauvilliers and the Duc de Chevreuse, who hoped for a less centralised monarchy after the king's death. Fénelon also argued that all wars are civil wars, since each person owes more to humanity than to a single country.

Fénelon defended the Quietism of his cousin Madame Guyon. He refused to sign Bossuet's Instructions on the states of prayer and set out his own view in the Maxims of the Saints. Louis XIV removed him as tutor and confined him to the archdiocese of Cambrai, and on 12 March 1699 the Inquisition condemned the book, Pope Innocent XII listing 23 propositions. Fénelon at once submitted. Telemachus angered the king the same year, so the confinement stayed. He sheltered refugees from the War of the Spanish Succession in his palace, wrote against the Jansenist party and died on 7 January 1715.
francois-grimaldi: Francesco Grimaldi, called François in French, was the son of Guglielmo Grimaldi and his wife Giacobina or Giacoba, a Genoese noblewoman. His family descended from Grimaldo Canella, a twelfth-century Genoese statesman who served several times as Consul of Genoa. In the 13th and 14th centuries the cities of northern Italy were torn by the conflict between Guelphs, who were allied to the Pope, and Ghibellines, who supported the Holy Roman Emperor. The Grimaldi were among the most influential families of Genoa and held to the Guelph side.

In 1295 Guelph forces from Liguria under Francesco Grimaldi were routed by a Ghibelline advance and had to take refuge on the Rock of Monaco. In the same year he married Aurelia del Carretto, the widow of his cousin Lanfranco Grimaldi. On 8 January 1297 he dressed as a Franciscan friar and led a small band of followers to the gates of Monaco's castle, where they were let in, and seized it together with his cousin Rainier I, Lord of Cagnes. The coat of arms of Monaco recalls the event with two friars holding swords. The citadel was held for four years, until the Ghibelline stronghold was worn down by prolonged Genoese attack.

Francesco failed to establish Grimaldi rule over Monaco, though this was the family's first attempt. The Grimaldi later resolved to regain the territory because of its value as a base for the maritime trade that was the source of the family's wealth. His marriage was childless, so the modern Grimaldi are not his descendants. After his death in 1309 he was succeeded by his cousin and stepson Rainier I of Monaco, Lord of Cagnes, from whom the later rulers descend. In 1419, more than a century after the coup, three Grimaldi brothers, Ambroise, Antoine and Jean, bought Monaco from Queen Yolande of Aragon in the name of the family, which became the undisputed ruler of the Rock.
francois-guizot: François Guizot was born on 4 October 1787 at Nîmes into a bourgeois Protestant family. His father was executed on the scaffold there on 8 April 1794, during the Reign of Terror, when François was six. His mother took him to Geneva, where he was educated, and in 1805 he arrived in Paris as a tutor. He began writing for the journal Publiciste and in 1812 married Pauline de Meulan, a fellow contributor. Under the Restoration he was one of the leaders of the Doctrinaires, a small party attached to the charter and the crown that favoured the juste milieu, a middle path between absolutism and popular government. In 1822 his lectures were banned.

After the July Revolution of 1830 he supported the constitutional monarchy of Louis Philippe I. In 1832 he became minister of public instruction and carried the law of 28 June 1833, which established primary education in France. He also revived the Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques and founded the Société de l'histoire de France, which published medieval chronicles at the state's expense. He went to London as ambassador in the spring of 1840. From 29 October 1840 he led the government for nearly eight years, as foreign minister and, after Marshal Soult retired, as prime minister from September 1847.

With Lord Aberdeen he built an understanding between France and Britain, and Napoleon's ashes were brought from St Helena. Opponents called his foreign policy subservient to England, and he answered that they would never reach the height of his disdain. He was unpopular with the more advanced liberals for restricting the vote to propertied men. When he banned the reform banquets in January 1848, the opposition grew, and on 23 February 1848 the king told him he doubted he could keep him as prime minister. Guizot resigned and escaped to London, where he arrived on 3 March.

He never returned to public life and spent most of each year at Val Richer in Normandy, supporting himself by writing. His works include histories of England under Cromwell, the Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire de mon temps, and a history of France told to his grandchildren. He was elected to the Académie Française in 1836. He died in 1874, after reciting verses of Pierre Corneille and texts from the Bible, according to report.

In the 1820s his Histoire générale de la civilisation en Europe was admired by John Stuart Mill, Goethe and Alexis de Tocqueville. His critics call him a conservative or reactionary for resisting universal suffrage, but he defended representative government against both absolutism and the excesses of democracy, and he called for the abolition of capital punishment.
francois-mackandal: Where Mackandal came from is not known for certain. Early sources place his origin in the Atlas Mountains of the Maghreb, while the scholar Sylviane Diouf has suggested Senegal, Mali or Guinea. The Haitian historian Thomas Madiou wrote that he was educated and knew Arabic well, and contemporary accounts say he recited the Shahada, the Muslim testimony of faith, during his interrogation and translated it for his captors. Tracing the etymology of his name, the historian Kathryn de Luna suggests a region near the coast of Cameroon. François was the name given him in slavery. Some historians call him a houngan, others a bokor.

Sent to work at a remote location, he escaped and lived as a maroon. The protective bags he made and distributed, and the rituals he held to create and maintain them, drew a large religious community among the enslaved. C. L. R. James compared his eloquence to that of a European orator. His association with black magic rests on these Congo-inspired practices and on his reputation as a poisoner.

His arrest came amid a panic among enslavers that the enslaved were poisoning whites to take over Saint-Domingue, fed by the confessions of an enslaved man named Médor and of an enslaved woman named Assam, who under torture named dozens of supposed accomplices. At the time poison was a word Africans used for any powerful substance charged with magic. Later doctors suggested the deaths were more likely caused by anthrax in animals that people had eaten. At a plantation celebration someone told French observers that a poisoner was present, and Mackandal was seized.

He was executed on 20 January 1758 after a trial of only a few days. Some reports say he briefly escaped from the fire before being recaptured; many of the enslaved believed he had risen from the flames as a winged creature or slipped away. After his death his case was publicised as proof of unrest, and unverifiable stories made him the leader of a great maroon band planning to kill all whites. His figure appears on Haitian currency and in novels such as Alejo Carpentier's The Kingdom of this World.
francois-michel-le-tellier-marquis-de-lo: Louvois was born in Paris on 18 January 1641, the son of Michel Le Tellier and Élisabeth Turpin. His father instructed him in the management of state affairs, and the young man won the king's confidence; in 1666 he succeeded his father as war minister. In the War of Devolution (1667 to 1668) Turenne noticed his talents and taught him the art of supplying armies. After the peace of Aix-la-Chapelle he devoted himself to organising the French army. The years from 1668 to 1672 were, in the words of Camille Rousset, years of preparation, when Lionne laboured to find allies, Colbert money and Louvois soldiers for Louis XIV.

With his father, Louvois oversaw an increase in the French Army to 340,000 soldiers, which fought four wars between 1667 and 1713. According to Cathal Nolan he created the Régiment du Roi in 1663 and founded the Royal-Artillerie regiment in 1673. He reorganised the army and exercised strict control over officers, which slowed tactical and operational responses. His logistics were more successful: he improved the magazine system left by his father and built up enough grain and wagons to supply his armies with 200,000 rations a day for up to six months in the Franco-Dutch War (1672 to 1678). He also founded the Hôtel des Invalides and reorganised the military orders of merit.

Louvois had a prominent part in the capture of Strasbourg in 1681 and in the revocation of the Edict of Nantes. He annulled a clause of the revocation allowing some liberty of conscience, with the phrase that the king wished the worst harshness on those who would not share his religion, and he claimed credit for inventing the dragonnades. After Colbert died in 1683 he took over the ministry of public buildings, and in 1688 he began the collection of plans-reliefs of French strongholds, now the Musée des Plans-Reliefs.

Louvois died suddenly of apoplexy on 16 July 1691 after leaving the king's cabinet, although Voltaire claimed he died while taking the waters at Balaruc, and the suddenness of his death caused suspicion of poison. Historians credit him with creating the civilian role of minister of war. French writers have compared him with Carnot, since both reorganised armies with existing resources and new systems, though his methods were unscrupulous in his private life and his work, including harsh measures against Huguenots.
francois-mitterrand: François Mitterrand was born on 26 October 1916 in Jarnac, Charente, into a devoutly Catholic and conservative family; his father was a stationmaster. He studied at the École Libre des Sciences Politiques in Paris. Called up in 1938, he was wounded by shrapnel on 14 June 1940 and captured by the Germans on 21 June. He escaped from a prisoner-of-war camp on 28 November 1941 with forged papers, and then worked as a mid-level official of the Vichy government looking after prisoners of war. In 1943 he built up a resistance network of former prisoners. His wartime conduct caused much controversy in France in the 1980s and 1990s.

Under the Fourth Republic Mitterrand held ministerial office several times, among them Minister of the Interior in the cabinet of Pierre Mendès-France in 1954–1955, when he had to direct the response to the Algerian War of Independence. In 1958 he was one of the few who opposed Charles de Gaulle's plan for a Fifth Republic, and his book Le Coup d'État permanent (1964) criticised de Gaulle's personal power. In 1971 he became first secretary of the Socialist Party, arguing that an alliance with the Communists was necessary to win power. He was the left's standard bearer in 1965 and 1974.

On 10 May 1981 Mitterrand became the first socialist President of the Fifth Republic. His first term began with nationalisation of key firms and a 39-hour work week, alongside the abolition of the death penalty, but facing economic tensions he soon turned to austerity and market liberalisation. In July 1985 French intelligence agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland, killing a photographer.

He was re-elected in 1988, and twice governed in cohabitation with conservative cabinets led by Jacques Chirac and Édouard Balladur. With the German chancellor Helmut Kohl he advanced European integration through the Maastricht Treaty. He left office in 1995 and died in Paris on 8 January 1996 of prostate cancer, which had been concealed for most of his presidency.
francois-ravaillac: Ravaillac was born in 1578 at Angoulême into an educated family. His grandfather François Ravaillac was the prosecutor in Angoulême, and two of his maternal uncles were canons of Angoulême Cathedral. His father, Jean Ravaillac, was a violent man whose misdeeds caused a public scandal and legal difficulties, while his mother, Françoise Dubreuil, was known for her Catholic piety. He worked first as a servant and later as a school teacher. Obsessed with religion, he sought admission to the ascetic Feuillants order but was dismissed after a short probation for being prey to visions. An application to the Society of Jesus in 1606 was also unsuccessful.

In 1609 Ravaillac claimed a vision instructing him to convince King Henry IV of France to convert the Huguenots to Catholicism. Between Pentecost 1609 and May 1610 he made three trips to Paris to tell the king, lodging with Charlotte du Tillet, mistress of the duc d'Épernon. Unable to meet him, he interpreted Henry's decision to invade the Spanish Netherlands as the start of a war against the Pope, and resolved to kill the king.

On 14 May 1610 he waited in the Rue de la Ferronnerie. The king's coach was halted by a blockage in the street, and Ravaillac climbed onto the wheel and stabbed Henry to death. The Duke of Montbazon, riding with the king, was wounded. Ravaillac was seized and taken to the Hôtel de Retz to avoid a lynching, then to the Conciergerie.

He was frequently tortured to make him name accomplices, but denied he had any and said he had acted alone. The king had been on his way to visit Maximilien de Béthune at the Arsenal to make final preparations for intervention in the War of the Jülich Succession. According to the account, Ravaillac had seen that the king wanted to make war on the Pope, in order to transfer the Holy See to Paris.

On 27 May 1610 Ravaillac was taken to the Place de Grève in Paris, tortured a last time and pulled apart by four horses, a method reserved for regicides. His parents were forced into exile, and the rest of his family was ordered never to use the name Ravaillac again. In January 1611 Jacqueline d'Escoman denounced the duc d'Épernon as responsible for the king's death and was jailed for life. Philippe Erlanger concluded that Ravaillac, the king's mistress Henriette d'Entragues and Charlotte du Tillet planned the assassination, while Roland Mousnier held that he had no accomplices but his confessors. Later ages saw Ravaillac as an evil figure, though a few Catholics viewed him as a hero.
francois-timoleon-de-choisy: Choisy was born on 16 August 1644. His father served in the household of the Duke of Orléans, and his mother, who was on close terms with Anne of Austria, was often invited to amuse the young Louis XIV. According to his own memoirs, his mother dressed him in girls' clothing until he was eighteen; he briefly wore men's clothes and then returned to women's dress, reportedly on the advice of Madame de La Fayette.

An inheritance after his mother's death allowed him to live without regular employment. He wrote that he wore elaborate women's clothing until he was publicly criticised by the duc de Montausier, after which he withdrew to the provinces. The historian Paul Scott has pointed to implausibilities, contradictions and anachronisms in these accounts, and to the lack of any contemporary corroboration.

Money troubles later led him to live at his benefice of Sainte-Seine in Burgundy, where he came to know Bussy-Rabutin. After his journey to Rome in 1676 he wrote that a serious illness had led to a religious conversion. With the Abbé Dangeau he wrote the Quatre dialogues sur l'immortalité de l'âme (1684), which explained their conversion. He was admitted to the Académie Française on 24 July 1687, and his Histoire de l'Eglise appeared between 1703 and 1723.

Choisy died on 2 October 1724. His Mémoires, with their detailed portraits of his contemporaries, passed through many editions and were edited in 1868 by M. de Lescure. Some of his letters survive in the correspondence of Bussy-Rabutin. He is said to have burnt some of his more indiscreet writings, but he left many unpublished manuscripts.

Part of this material was used without acknowledgement in an anonymous Histoire de madame la comtesse de Barres (Antwerp, 1735) and, heavily edited, in the Vie de M. l'abbé de Choisy (Lausanne and Geneva, 1742), which Paul Lacroix attributed to Lenglet Dufresnoy. Lacroix finally edited the text in 1870 as Aventures de l'abbé de Choisy. His autobiographical writings, describing his frequent use of women's clothing in private and public life, have been a subject of scholarly debate.
francois-tomb: The tomb lies in the Ponte Rotto Necropolis of Vulci, in Lazio, and dates to the last quarter of the 4th century BCE. It seems to have belonged to the Etruscan family of the Saties, or Seties, and one of its chief occupants was Vel Saties. Alessandro François found it in 1857 together with Adolphe Noël des Vergers. Some pottery vessels from the tomb are now in the British Museum.

The frescoes of the central T-shaped chamber set scenes of myth beside Etruscan history. They show Cassandra dragged from the altar by Ajax, son of Oileus; Nestor and Phoenix before palm trees; the duel of Eteocles and Polynices; and the torment of Sisyphus in the presence of Amphiaraus. In the scene from the Iliad, Achilles, Agamemnon and Ajax, son of Telamon, kill Trojan prisoners in honour of Patroclus, watched by the Etruscan figures Vanth and Charun.

Vel Saties himself appears in the toga picta with his wife and his dwarf servant Arnza, whose name means little Arnth. Arnza holds a woodpecker on a string, the bird of the god Laran, which may show the watching of a bird's flight for divination.

The cycle of Mastarna is the best known. Caelius Vibenna was believed by the Romans to have given his name to the Caelian Hill, and the Emperor Claudius identified Mastarna with the Roman king Servius Tullius. Another scene shows Marce Camitlas, in Latin Marcus Camillus, about to draw his sword on a crouching Cneve Tarchunies Rumach, Gnaeus Tarquinius of Rome, though no ancient history of Rome mentions a Tarquinius named Gnaeus.

Prince Torlonia had the frescoes removed in 1862 and kept them in the Torlonia Museum in Rome; from 1946 they were stored at the private Villa Albani in Rome as part of the Torlonia collection. They are valued both for their imagery and for what they say about Etruscan history and identity.
francois-tombalbaye: François Tombalbaye was born on 15 June 1918 in the village of Bessada in southern Chad, near Koumra. His father was a prominent trader and he belonged to the Sara, the main ethnic group of the five southern prefectures. He attended a primary school run by Protestant missionaries in Sarh and studied to become a teacher in Brazzaville, since Chad had no such schools. During the Second World War he fought for Free France. In 1946 or 1947 he formed a chapter of the Chadian Progressive Party in Sarh, and in 1949 the French authorities revoked his teaching post as punishment for his political activism.

Tombalbaye won a seat in the colonial territorial assembly in 1952, succeeded Gabriel Lisette as leader of the party in March 1959 and led the independent state from 11 August 1960. He banned the other parties, dissolved the National Assembly in 1963 after rioting and began replacing French administrators with local staff. A programme of Africanization largely ignored the Muslim north and centre. On 1 November 1965 riots over taxes and corruption in Guéra Prefecture caused 500 deaths and spread, and the rebel FROLINAT, based in Sudan, took up arms. Tombalbaye called on France, which agreed to help on condition of reforms; he accepted in 1969, and prisoners were released.

In 1971 an attempted coup with links to Muammar al-Gaddafi was uncovered, and he cut relations with Libya. Drought gripped the country, and by the end of 1972 over 1,000 political prisoners had been arrested. In August 1973 he replaced his party with the National Movement for the Cultural and Social Revolution, renamed Fort-Lamy as N'Djamena and took the name N'Garta. Under authenticité, missionaries were expelled and non-Muslim men in the south had to undergo yondo initiation rites, including floggings and scarification, to gain promotion. These rites were native only to a subgroup of the Sara.

His support in the south dwindled, and he made arbitrary promotions and demotions in the army. On 13 April 1975, after some leading officers had been arrested over an alleged coup, he was reportedly shot in his palace and died of his wounds. His body was buried in secret at Faya. The military installed Félix Malloum, by then a general, as head of state.
francois-xavier-donzelot: Donzelot was born at Mamirolle on 7 January 1764, the son of François Donzelot and Jeanne–Baptiste Maire. He entered the army in 1785 as a private in the Régiment Royal-La Marine, became a second lieutenant in the 12th Regiment of Cavalry in 1792 and an adjudant-general in 1793, and served in the campaigns of the Army of the Rhine under Pichegru and Moreau.

In Egypt he distinguished himself at Cairo and in the Battle of Heliopolis. Made general of brigade, temporarily in 1799 and permanently in 1801, he signed the surrender of Egypt to British forces. He then served on the staff of the minister of war Louis-Alexandre Berthier, in the Army of Italy and under André Masséna at the Siege of Gaeta, and was promoted general of division on 6 December 1807.

Replacing César Berthier on Corfu, Donzelot strengthened its fortifications on Napoleon's orders and led a garrison of about 20,000 men; he was named Baron of the Empire in 1808. When the British captain Richard Hussey Moubray captured a ship carrying Donzelot's library, he returned it, and Donzelot thereafter received captured British officers at his table. In 1809 he offered Theodoros Kolokotronis help against Ali Pasha, which allowed Kolokotronis to raise 3,000 men. After Napoleon's fall he held Corfu until Louis XVIII ordered him to leave.

At Waterloo his division suffered heavy losses from British heavy cavalry, but at 16:00 he regrouped and, with the 1st Division, took La Haye Sainte. Made Inspector General of the Infantry on 18 August 1816 and a count in 1819, he governed Martinique until 1826. There a plan to bring poor white settlers from France failed against the Creole elite, and he backed a steamship company whose boat, the Comte Donzelot, entered service on 1 March 1823.

He retired to Mamirolle and to his château of Ville-Évrard at Neuilly-sur-Marne, where he lived as a patron of the arts among artists and writers and served as a model for Alfred de Vigny's Servitude and Military Grandeur. Recalled in 1831 to train troops for the security of Paris, he died at Ville-Évrard in 1843. His tomb in the town cemetery is a mastaba decorated with the disc and winged serpents of Edfu, and his name is inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe de l'Étoile.
franconia: Franconia is not a political entity with a fixed area, and it is debated whether some districts belong to it. It is defined by its history, its culture and especially the East Franconian dialect, and in part by the territory of the former Duchy of Franconia and the Franconian Circle. Most of it lies north and south of the River Main and its tributary the Regnitz, in the three Bavarian districts of Lower, Middle and Upper Franconia. Upland ranges such as the Franconian Jura, the Fichtel Mountains, the Rhön and the Spessart surround it. Its highest mountain is the Schneeberg in the Fichtel Mountains, at 1,051 metres.

Fossil finds show people were living in the region about 600,000 years ago. In the Iron Age, from about 800 BCE, the Celts were the first people discernible there, and they built hill forts and settlements such as the one Ptolemy called oppidum Menosgada on the Staffelberg. As Rome expanded in the first century BCE and Germanic tribes advanced from the north, Celtic culture declined. The southern parts came under Roman control, but most of the region stayed in free Germania.

The Franks gained the region through victories over the Alamanni and Thuringians in the 6th century. Its name does not mean it was the homeland of the Franks, since it was only partly settled by Franks from the Rhineland. After the Frankish Empire was divided, East Francia was formed from the territories of the dioceses of Mainz, Worms, Würzburg and Speyer, and Bamberg was added later. Slavs began to settle the north-east from the 7th century. Irish and Anglo-Saxon monks first spread Christianity strongly there, and Saint Kilian was martyred at Würzburg in the late 7th century. Saint Boniface probably carried the mission to the ordinary people.

On 2 July 1500, under Emperor Maximilian I, the Empire was divided into Imperial Circles, and the Franconian Circle was formed in 1512. The region was severely affected by Kleinstaaterei, a patchwork of tiny states, and the bishops of Würzburg used the nominal title of Duke of Franconia. In 1559 the circle was given jurisdiction over coinage. After the Holy Roman Empire ended, Napoleon's restructuring of the south German states gave most of Franconia to Bavaria.

Franconia is divided among Bavaria, Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg and Hesse, and its largest part belongs to Bavaria. Its largest city is Nuremberg, followed by Fürth, Würzburg and Erlangen, and the region has roughly five million inhabitants. Franconians count as one of the four tribes of Bavaria. Large areas of Middle and Upper Franconia are Protestant, while Lower Franconia and western Upper Franconia are mostly Catholic, reflecting the territories of the Franconian Circle.
franconian-circle: Franconia, which included the former Duchy of Franconia, lay between the Rhenish territories of the empire and the Kingdom of Bohemia, and since the Middle Ages it had had very close links to king and empire. By order of Emperor Louis of Bavaria, Bamberg, Würzburg, Eichstätt and Fulda joined the Hohenzollern Burgraves of Nuremberg, the Counts of Henneberg, Castell and Hohenlohe, the three episcopal cities and the imperial cities of Nuremberg and Rothenburg in a Landfrieden union, the first time they had united. This Franconian Landfrieden did not last long: it broke apart in the face of opposition from cities and princes.

On 2 July 1500, at the Reichstag of Augsburg, the empire was divided into six imperial circles, which were at first numbered. Franconia's was the first, made up of the Bishops of Bamberg, Würzburg and Eichstätt, the Margrave of Brandenburg as Burgrave of Nuremberg, and the counts and free and imperial cities of the region. The circles were later named after their location, and the name Franconian Circle first appeared in 1522. In the late Middle Ages Franconia had meant the land between the Spessart and the Steigerwald, mainly the estates of the Bishopric of Würzburg, whose bishops claimed the title Duke of Franconia.

The circle stretched from the Franconian Saale river to the Altmühl and covered most of the upper and middle Main, roughly the present-day Bavarian Regierungsbezirke of Upper, Middle and Lower Franconia, but without the Electoral Mainz estates of the Upper Stift around Aschaffenburg. It held only the eastern part of the old Franconian stem duchy, as western Rhenish Franconia belonged to the Upper Rhenish Circle. The shared name fostered among its members a sense of unity and solidarity that did not exist in political or sovereign matters.
francysk-skaryna: Francysk Skaryna was born into a wealthy family of Polotsk, then a major trade and manufacturing centre of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. His father, Luka Skaryna, and his older brother Ivan were merchants. The date of his birth is unknown. In 1504 he is recorded as a student at Jagiellonian University, where he graduated Bachelor of Arts in 1506, and in 1512 he received a doctorate in medicine at the University of Padua, having asked to take the examination there without, it seems, studying in the city. Whether he was Catholic or Orthodox is not known for certain.

By 1517 Skaryna was in Prague, where he rented a printing house from a merchant named Severin and began publishing a new translation of the Bible with his own prefaces. His Psalter appeared on 6 August 1517, and on 10 August 1518 he issued four books at once. The Bible of twenty-three books printed from 1517 to 1519 under the name Biblia Ruska was the second printed Bible of the Slavic world, after a Czech edition. All were in quarto, in a Church Slavonic with many Ruthenian words and some Polish and Czech influence.

Skaryna added his own comments, forewords, afterwords and prints with his image, which no other Bible of Eastern Europe has. In his prefaces he said that he wanted ordinary people to become acquainted with wisdom and science. In 1522 he opened the first printing house in Vilnius and published The Little Travel Book, followed by the Apostol in 1525. He tried to sell his books in Moscow in the late 1520s or early 1530s without success.

After his brother's death in 1529 Skaryna went to Poznań for a share of Ivan's property. In 1532 he served as doctor and secretary to John, Bishop of Vilnius, and when Ivan's creditors had him imprisoned in Poznań for several months, royal certificates of 21 and 25 November 1532 exempted him from every jurisdiction but the King's.

The last record of him dates from 1534, when he moved to Prague. He is presumed to have died between 1551 and 29 January 1552. Some Belarusian scholars see him as a Renaissance figure comparable to Copernicus and Erasmus, though the Oktoikh of Schweipolt Fiol, printed in 1491, was an earlier Cyrillic book.
frank-swettenham: Frank Athelstane Swettenham was born on 28 March 1850 in Belper, Derbyshire, the son of the attorney James Oldham Swettenham and Charlotte Elizabeth Carr, and was educated at the Dollar Academy in Scotland and St Peter's School, York.
