His elder brother, Sir James Alexander Swettenham, was also a colonial administrator. In 1871 he went to Singapore as a cadet in the civil service of the Straits Settlements, where he learned Malay.

He played a major role as an intermediary between the British and the Malays in the British intervention in the peninsular states in the 1870s. After the Pangkor Treaty of 1874 he sat on the Commission for the Pacification of Larut with John Frederick Adolphus McNair and the Chinese Kapitan Chung Keng Quee and Chin Seng Yam, which freed many women taken captive in the Larut Wars, had stockades dismantled and restarted tin mining. As Resident of Selangor from 1882 he promoted coffee and tobacco estates and built a railway from Kuala Lumpur to the port of Klang, later named Port Swettenham after him.

As Resident of Perak he secured the agreement of Perak, Selangor, Negri Sembilan and Pahang to federation in 1895, and he served as Resident-General from 1 July 1896. As Governor of the Straits Settlements he pressed Siam for British influence in Kelantan and Trengganu, which sent Siam a golden flower every three years; Siam agreed to British advisers only if Bangkok appointed them, and his hope of bringing Patani under British control failed. He later chaired a royal commission on Mauritius in 1909.

With Hugh Clifford he compiled A Dictionary of the Malay Language, abandoned after the letter G, and he wrote books including Malay Sketches and British Malaya. His first marriage, to Constance Sydney Holmes in 1878, ended in divorce in 1938, and in 1939 he married Vera Seton Guthrie. He was one of close to forty former officials who opposed the Malayan Union, and he died on 11 June 1946. Mount Swettenham in the Cameron Highlands and Swettenham Pier in George Town bear his name.
frankenstein: Mary Shelley's mother, Mary Wollstonecraft, died of infection eleven days after her birth, and she grew up among the writers and political figures who gathered at the home of her father, William Godwin. She met Percy Bysshe Shelley at sixteen, and in the summer of 1816 she, Percy and Claire Clairmont visited Lord Byron at the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva. It was the rainy summer known as the Year Without a Summer, after the eruption of Mount Tambora in 1815, and the party stayed indoors reading German ghost stories. Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story.

Shelley could think of nothing for days. After a night of talk about the principle of life and galvanism, she imagined a pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together. She finished writing in April or May 1817.

Victor Frankenstein, born in Naples to an upper-class Genevese family, is obsessed with alchemy in youth and then turns to chemistry and electricity. At the University of Ingolstadt he finds a way to create life and assembles a large humanoid creature from body parts. Repelled when it awakens, he flees. In Shelley's text Victor discovers an unknown principle of life and does not say how it works; the electric jolt and the stitched-together image come from James Whale's 1931 film.

The creature teaches himself to speak and read, learns his origin from papers in his clothes, and is driven away by a family he has watched. Embittered, he travels to Geneva, kills Victor's younger brother William and frames the servant Justine, who is executed. He then asks Victor to make him a female companion. He compares himself to Adam and to the fallen angel of Milton, and the subtitle The Modern Prometheus alludes to the Titan who gave fire to humans.

Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus appeared anonymously on 1 January 1818 in three volumes, in an edition of 500 copies, with a preface by Percy Shelley and a dedication to Godwin. The second English edition, of 11 August 1823, named Mary Shelley as author after the success of Richard Brinsley Peake's stage play Presumption, which she attended on 29 August 1823.

The revised one-volume edition of 31 October 1831 added a new introduction and a more moral tone, and it is the one most widely read. The novel has influenced literature and popular culture and produced a genre of horror stories, films and plays, and the name Frankenstein is often wrongly given to the creature.
frankenthal: Frankenthal was first mentioned in 772. An Augustinian monastery was built there in 1119, and its ruins, known after the founder as the Erkenbertruine, still stand in the town centre. In the second half of the 16th century people from Flanders, persecuted for their religious beliefs, settled in the town. They were industrious and artistic, brought economic prosperity and included important carpet weavers, jewellers and artists, whose Frankenthaler Malerschule, or Frankenthal school of painting, acquired some fame. In 1577 Count Palatine Johann Casimir raised the settlement to the status of a city.

In 1600 Frankenthal was converted into a fortress. In 1621 English soldiers under Sir Horace Vere garrisoned it and the Spanish besieged it during the Thirty Years' War, after which troops of the opposing sides occupied it in turn. Trade and industry were ruined, and the town was not rebuilt until 1682. French troops burnt it to the ground in 1689 in the War of the Grand Alliance, and it did not fully recover for more than fifty years.

In 1750 Elector Charles Theodore made Frankenthal a centre of industry. A port was built between 1772 and 1781, factories were opened and mulberry trees were planted for silk production. The porcelain factory opened in 1755 and remained in production until 1800. The town came under French occupation in 1797 and passed to Bavaria in 1816, and modern industrialisation began around 1859. The synagogue built in 1884 was burnt to the ground on Kristallnacht in 1938, and a bombing raid in 1943 almost destroyed the town centre. Since 1946 Frankenthal has been part of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate, and it had 49,051 inhabitants in 2022 and some medium-sized industries.
frankfurt: Frankfurt lies on both sides of the river Main, south-east of the Taunus mountain range, in the western part of Germany. Its downtown is north of the Main in the Altstadt, the historical centre. The southern part of the city holds the Frankfurt City Forest, Germany's largest forest within a city. A ring-shaped Green Belt, formally created in 1991, covers a third of the administrative area.

The name derives from Franconofurd, from the Germanic tribe of the Franks and furt, a ford where the river was shallow enough to cross on foot. The first written records of 794 give Frankonovurd in Old High German and Vadum Francorum in Latin.

The first traces of Roman settlement along the river Nidda date to the reign of Emperor Vespasian, from 69 to 79 CE, and Nida was a Roman civitas capital. Alemanni and Franks later lived in the area, and in 794 Charlemagne presided over an imperial assembly and church synod at which Franconofurd was first mentioned. It was one of the two capitals of his grandson Louis the German, together with Regensburg, and Louis founded the collegiate church, rededicated in 1239 to Bartholomew the Apostle and now Frankfurt Cathedral.

Frankfurt has been an imperial city since 1372. As the Free City of Frankfurt it was a city state for nearly five centuries and one of the most important cities of the Holy Roman Empire, as a site of imperial coronations. It lost its sovereignty when the empire collapsed in 1806, regained it in 1815 and lost it again in 1866, when the Kingdom of Prussia annexed it after the Austro-Prussian War. It has been part of the state of Hesse since 1945.

Frankfurt am Main is the most populous city in the German state of Hesse, with 778,589 inhabitants. It is a financial centre, home to the European Central Bank, the Deutsche Bundesbank and the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, and Frankfurt Airport is the busiest in Germany.

The Römer, a complex of nine houses that the city council acquired in 1405 from a wealthy merchant family, is the city hall. Its Kaisersaal, the Emperor's Hall, is where newly crowned emperors held their banquets. The Römer was partly destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt, and the Goethe House, where Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was born in 1749, was destroyed and rebuilt in 1947.
frankfurt-parliament: The assembly was part of the outcome of the March Revolution in the states of the German Confederation. Opposition politicians demanded basic and civic rights, liberal governments in the states and above all a German nation-state with a pan-German constitution and a popular assembly. On 5 March 1848 they met at the Heidelberg Assembly and resolved to form a pre-parliament, which sat in St Paul's Church in Frankfurt from 31 March to 3 April. It decided to cooperate with the Confederate Diet in forming a national constitutional assembly, with one deputy for every 50,000 inhabitants.

The assembly was elected on 1 May 1848 and opened on 18 May in the Paulskirche, with 379 deputies present. Heinrich von Gagern was elected president. Because it had not been created by the German Confederation, it had no head of state, no government and no legal legitimation, and powers such as France and Russia declined to recognise it. On 28 June it voted for a Provisional Central Power and the next day chose Archduke John of Austria as Regent of the Empire. In November 1848 the Austrian army executed the deputy Robert Blum in Vienna, despite his parliamentary immunity, which showed how dependent the assembly was on the goodwill of the states.

The deputies began drafting the constitution on 19 October 1848. It passed on 27 March 1849 by 267 votes to 263, with a hereditary emperor, a directly elected lower house and a House of the States. On 28 March the assembly chose the Prussian king as emperor.

Frederick William IV refused the crown, on the grounds that the constitution and the offer abridged the rights of the princes, and Prussia rejected the constitution on 21 April 1849. The Austrian deputies had left Frankfurt on 5 April, and Gagern resigned on 10 May. Revolts followed in Dresden, the Palatinate and Baden. On 31 May the remaining deputies decided to move to Stuttgart, and from 6 June a rump parliament of 154 deputies met there. On 18 June the Württemberg army occupied the chamber and expelled the deputies from other states. In the 20th century major elements of the Frankfurt constitution became models for the Weimar Constitution of 1919 and the Basic Law of 1949.
frankfurt-rhine-main: The Rhine-Main Metropolitan Region lies in the central-western part of Germany and stretches over parts of three states: Hesse, Rhineland-Palatinate and Bavaria. It is named after its core city, Frankfurt, and the two rivers Rhine and Main. Its largest cities are Frankfurt am Main, Wiesbaden, Mainz, Darmstadt, Offenbach, Worms, Hanau and Aschaffenburg. The German Federal Ministry of Transport, Building and Urban Affairs designates it a European Metropolitan Region, and it covers roughly 13,000 square kilometres with a population above 5.9 million. It is the third-largest metropolitan region in Germany after Rhine-Ruhr and Berlin-Brandenburg.

The region is polycentric, but Frankfurt's economic size and political weight give it a monocentric relation with its commuter belt. Since the early 1970s the Frankfurt am Main metropolitan area has been defined as the cities of Frankfurt and Offenbach and their neighbouring districts. The Regierungsbezirk Darmstadt of Hesse lies entirely inside the region and adds Darmstadt and Wiesbaden, and a wider ring takes in Mainz in Rhineland-Palatinate and Aschaffenburg in Bavaria.

Its central position in south-western Germany made it an important industrial and transport centre once industrialisation began in the middle of the nineteenth century, and the area's growth is traced chiefly to favourable communications that promoted early industrialisation.

Banking, trade and logistics have largely replaced heavy industry. The European Central Bank is headquartered in Frankfurt am Main. The chemical industry has a long presence, notably in the Industriepark Höchst on the south-western edge of Frankfurt, which hosts over 90 chemical, pharmaceutical and healthcare firms. Insurers have offices in Darmstadt and Wiesbaden. Frankfurt Airport is the busiest in Germany by passenger numbers, and the Frankfurt am Main Hauptbahnhof and the Frankfurter Kreuz are among Europe's busiest rail and road interchanges. An S-Bahn network runs from Wiesbaden and Mainz in the west to Hanau in the east.

The region has five universities and over 20 colleges, with more than 200,000 students. Three public research universities, Goethe University Frankfurt, Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz and TU Darmstadt, form the Rhine Main Universities alliance.
franklin-d-roosevelt: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on 30 January 1882 in Hyde Park, New York, to James Roosevelt I and his second wife, Sara Ann Delano, who were sixth cousins from wealthy families. Apart from a stint in public school in Germany at nine, he was educated by tutors until 14, when he entered Groton School, whose headmaster Endicott Peabody urged students into public service. He graduated from Harvard University and married Eleanor Roosevelt, a niece of Theodore Roosevelt, on 17 March 1905.

In the Democratic landslide of 1910 Roosevelt won a surprising victory for a strongly Republican seat in the New York State Senate. In August 1921, at Campobello Island, he fell ill with what was diagnosed as polio, which left him permanently paralyzed from the waist down. He taught himself to walk short distances with iron braces and in 1926 established a rehabilitation centre at Warm Springs, Georgia.

He was elected governor of New York in 1928 by less than one percent. After winning the Democratic nomination on the fourth ballot in 1932, he pledged a new deal for the American people and defeated President Herbert Hoover.

Roosevelt had declined in health since at least 1940. On 12 April 1945, at the Little White House in Warm Springs, he said he had a terrific headache, slumped forward while sitting for a portrait, and was pronounced dead of a massive intracerebral hemorrhage, aged 63. The expansion of government programmes under Roosevelt redefined the role of government in the United States and permanently increased the power of the president at the expense of Congress. Surviving programmes include the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Labor Relations Act and Social Security.
frankokratia: Frankokratia, also called Latinokratia, and for the Venetian domains the Venetian Occupation, names the collection of primarily French and Italian states, fiefs and colonies established on the territory of the partitioned Byzantine Empire after the Sack of Constantinople in 1204 during the Fourth Crusade. The terms come from Franks, the name the Orthodox Greeks gave to Western French and Italians whose homelands had once belonged to the Frankish Empire. The period's span differs by region, because the situation was volatile: Frankish states fragmented and changed hands, and Greek successor states reconquered many areas.

The Latin Empire (1204 to 1261), centred on Constantinople and covering Thrace and Bithynia, claimed nominal suzerainty over the other crusader states. It shrank to little more than its capital, which Michael VIII Palaiologos of the Empire of Nicaea captured in 1261. Among the other Latin states, the Kingdom of Thessalonica (1205 to 1224) fell to the Despotate of Epirus, and the Principality of Achaea (1205 to 1432) in the Peloponnese became the strongest, until the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea conquered it. The Duchy of Athens (1205 to 1458) passed to the Catalan Company in 1311 and to the Acciaiuoli family in 1388. The Duchy of the Archipelago, founded by the Sanudo family in 1207, lasted until 1579.

Genoese families such as the Gattilusi held Lesbos and other north-eastern Aegean islands, and the Maona company held Chios until 1566. The Republic of Venice built the most durable holdings: the Kingdom of Candia on Crete (1211 to 1715), Corfu for most of the period from 1386 to 1797, the coastal fortresses of Modon and Coron, held until 1500, and the whole island of Negroponte from 1390 to 1470. The Knights Hospitaller held Rhodes from 1310 until the Ottomans ousted them in 1522. Many areas were captured by the Ottomans between the 14th and 17th centuries, and the Ionian Islands and some islands and forts stayed Venetian until the turn of the 19th century, though the Byzantine Empire itself was restored in 1261.

The Franks left a mark on the Greek language. The fragmentation of the Byzantine world caused communication problems and divided the common language into dialects, and since the Franks used the speech of ordinary people for administration, the prestige of the literary language declined. Latin loanwords, mostly Italian and including Venetian, then French, entered Greek. The vocabulary of feudal law and property was mainly French, while that of trade and shipping was Italian. Frankish place names are the most significant influence, and a number of Greek given names are of Frankish origin.
frankopan-family: The first known member of the line was Dujam I Krčki, lord of Krk, whom Domenico Michieli, Doge of Venice from 1118 to 1130, allowed to rule the island as a vassal of the Republic of Venice. His origin is unknown, and his descendants appear in the documents as the Counts of Krk. In 1428 Nikola IV Krčki, Ban of Croatia and Dalmatia, was the first to call himself Frankapan, and in 1430 Pope Martin V recognised the family as descendants of the Roman patrician Frangipani, a link that modern reference works such as the Croatian Encyclopedia strongly question.

In 1221 King Andrew II of Hungary gave the brothers Henry and Servidon the islands of Brač, Hvar, Korčula and Lastovo. When the Mongol Empire advanced on Hungary in 1240–1241, the family sheltered King Béla IV and supplied him with arms and money, and he rewarded them with the county of Senj and the castle of Modruš. In 1294 Nikola Frankopan rebuilt the Holy House of Our Lady at Trsat. In 1425 Emperor Sigismund confirmed the noble status of Nikola Frankopan as Count of Krk, Senj and Modruš and granted the family the right to seal in red wax.

Over the following centuries the Frankopans and the Zrinski family, joined by many marriages, led the defence of Croatia against the Ottoman Empire and opposed Habsburg absolutism. Several Frankopans served as bans of Croatia, among them Krsto Frankopan and Franjo Frankopan. Fran Krsto Frankopan took part in the conspiracy against King Leopold I and was executed with his brother-in-law Petar Zrinski at Wiener Neustadt. With him the Trsat branch died out in 1671, the other branches having ended in the 16th century.

Many Frankopan castles survive in Croatia, mostly in the Gorski kotar region and on Krk, at places such as Bosiljevo, Severin na Kupi, Novi Vinodolski, Ogulin, Slunj, Ozalj and Trsat; the castle in the town of Krk serves for open-air performances in summer. In 1991 Louis Doimi de Lupis, a British citizen, adopted the names Frankopan, Šubić and Zrinski, which a cousin publicly disputed.
frans-hals: Hals was born in 1582 or 1583 in Antwerp, the son of the cloth merchant Franchois Fransz Hals van Mechelen. His parents fled to Haarlem in the new Dutch Republic during the Fall of Antwerp in 1584 and 1585, and he lived there for the rest of his life. He studied under the Flemish émigré Karel van Mander, whose Mannerist influence is barely noticeable in his work. In 1610 he joined the Haarlem Guild of Saint Luke and began to earn money restoring pictures for the town council, which had confiscated Catholic religious art. With the market for religious themes gone, he turned to portraiture.

His earliest known work is the portrait of Jacobus Zaffius of 1611, and his breakthrough came in 1616 with the life-sized group portrait The Banquet of the Officers of the St George Militia Company. His best-known sitter was René Descartes, painted in 1649. He married Anneke Harmensdochter around 1610, and after her death in 1615 he married Lysbeth Reyniers in 1617, and they had eight children.

Hals painted wealthy citizens, civic guards and the regents of local hospitals, and also itinerant players, fishwives and tavern figures. In his group portraits each sitter is shown differently, with unidealised faces and a variety of poses. Between 1620 and 1640 he painted many married couples as pairs of panels, and only once on a single canvas. He worked with visible brushstrokes, which earlier painters had treated as a flaw, though most of his works were built up in layers rather than thrown onto the canvas in one go.

His palette darkened over his life, probably because of the sober dress of his Protestant sitters. Unlike Rembrandt, he refused to travel to his clients, and when he began a militia portrait in Amsterdam it was finished by Pieter Codde because he insisted that the sitters come to Haarlem. Five of his sons became painters, as did his brother Dirck Hals.

Hals lived so long that he went out of fashion and fell into financial difficulty. In 1652 he sold his belongings to settle a debt with a baker, and in 1664 the city gave him an annuity of 200 florins. He died in Haarlem on 26 August 1666 and was buried in the Grote Kerk. His reputation waned, and for two centuries some of his paintings sold for a few pounds or shillings. From the 1860s the critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger restored his standing. His technique influenced Édouard Manet, Claude Monet, Gustave Courbet and others, and Vincent van Gogh wrote to his brother of the joy of seeing a Frans Hals. Several of his main works hang in the Frans Hals Museum in Haarlem.
frans-post: Frans Janszoon Post was born in Haarlem, the son of Jan Janszoon Post, a glass painter trained in Leiden, and Francijntje Verbraken. His elder brother was Pieter Post, one of the leading architects of Dutch classicism. Little is known of his life before Brazil. He most likely trained first with his father and brother, and probably also with a Dutch master; the Post scholar Erik Larsen believes this was the landscape painter Pieter de Molijn, though not everyone accepts it. Frans Hals painted his portrait.

Post probably won a place at court through his brother's connections, and was encouraged to travel by Johan Maurits van Nassau-Siegen, the governor of Dutch Brazil, at a time when plague had broken out in Haarlem. In Brazil he made many sketches and etchings but finished only six paintings, dated 1637 to 1640, which Maurits later presented to Louis XIV in 1679. They show recognisable places, most with water, Brazilian plants and sometimes animals in the foreground, perhaps inspired by his travelling companion, the naturalist Georg Marcgraf, under grey skies that fill half the canvas. Another of Maurits's artists, Albert Eckhout, recorded the native people.

Back in the Netherlands, Post joined the Haarlem Guild of St. Luke in 1646 and served as an officer in 1656–7 and 1658. In 1650 he married Jannetje Bogaert, daughter of Professor Salomon Bogaert. His Brazilian scenes painted in Haarlem grew more imaginary the further he was from Brazil, with brighter colours, dark framing foliage and idealised baroque compositions. Nearly all include groups of people dancing or working in sugar mills, typically enslaved, who become part of the landscape rather than its subject.

Post produced about 140 paintings, nearly half of them dated, and the last dated work is from 1669. Since no dated paintings survive from the 1670s, he seems to have stopped about ten years before his death; Whitehead and Boeseman claim he developed an alcohol problem. His two sons died before him and his daughter shortly after. He died in Haarlem and was buried in the St. Bavochurch on 17 February 1680. His works were widely collected in the Netherlands, Europe and Brazil and present an idealised vision of Dutch colonial rule.
frantisek-palacky: František Palacký was born on 14 June 1798 at Hodslavice, a village in north-eastern Moravia. His ancestors had belonged to the Bohemian Brethren and had kept their Protestant faith in secret through the years of persecution. His father was a schoolmaster. In 1812 he was sent to the Evangelic Lutheran Lyceum at Bratislava, where he met the philologist Pavel J. Šafařík and became a zealous student of Slavic languages; he mastered 11 languages.

He settled in Prague in 1823 and found a friend in Josef Dobrovský, who introduced him to Count Sternberg and his brother Francis, founder of the Society of the Bohemian Museum. The society collected documents on Bohemian history in order to reawaken national sentiment. In 1825 Palacký became the first editor of its journal, Časopis Českého musea.

His principal work was Dějiny národu českého v Čechách a v Moravě, the History of the Czech Nation in Bohemia and Moravia, which runs to 1526 and the end of Czech independence. He said that in writing of the later period he would have to lie. It rested on research in the archives of Bohemia and the libraries of the chief cities of Europe, and the first volume appeared in German in 1836. Police censorship hindered it, especially over his account of the Hussite movement: he had to cut passages and accept others interpolated by the censors. After censorship ended in 1848 he published a new edition, completed in 1876, which restored the original form.

The Revolution of 1848 drew him into politics. In his Letter to Frankfurt he declined to join the preliminary parliament, since as a Czech he had no interest in German affairs. In June he presided over the Slavic Congress at Prague, and he sat in the Reichstag at Kroměříž from October 1848 to March 1849. He favoured a strong Austrian empire, a federation of southern German and Slavonic states retaining their rights, a view called Austroslavism, and was offered a post in the Pillersdorf cabinet. The collapse of the federal idea in 1852 led him to retire from politics.

After the concessions of 1860 and 1861 he became a life member of the Austrian senate, and in the Bohemian Diet he led the nationalist-federal party. He sought a Czech kingdom of Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia, and attended the Panslavist congress in Moscow in 1867. He died in Prague on 26 May 1876. He is counted as one of the three Fathers of the nation, with Charles IV and Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk.
frantz-fanon: Frantz Fanon was born on 20 July 1925 in Fort-de-France, Martinique, then part of the French colonial empire, into a middle-class family. His father was a customs officer and his mother a shopkeeper. After the fall of France in June 1940, Martinique came under the control of naval elements loyal to the Vichy regime, whose rule Fanon later described as that of authentic racists. In January 1943 he left for the British colony of Dominica to join Allied sympathisers, and after a local uprising overthrew the regime in June 1943 he returned and enlisted in the 5th Antillean Marching Battalion of the Free French Forces. He later studied at the University of Lyon, including literature, drama and philosophy, and qualified as a psychiatrist in 1951.

Fanon did his residency at Saint-Alban-sur-Limagnole under François Tosquelles, who emphasised the role of culture in psychopathology. While finishing his residency in Lyon he published Black Skin, White Masks in 1952, an analysis of the psychological effects of colonial subjugation on black people. The book began as a doctoral dissertation that Lyon rejected. From 1953 he worked in Algeria as head of a service at the Blida-Joinville Psychiatric Hospital. He developed sociotherapy and trained nurses and interns.

After the Algerian revolution began in November 1954, Fanon joined the Front de Libération Nationale (FLN). He treated both French soldiers who had carried out torture and Algerian victims of it. In November 1956 he submitted a letter of resignation to the Resident Minister, and he was expelled from Algeria in January 1957. He then moved to Tunis, wrote for the FLN newspaper Al Moudjahid and served as ambassador to Ghana for the Provisional Algerian Government.

A Dying Colonialism, published in 1959, recounts how Algerians changed old cultural patterns during the revolution. In The Wretched of the Earth, published shortly before his death, Fanon defends the right of a colonised people to use violence to gain independence. He also describes the forces leading either to national independence or to neocolonialism, and the French government censored the book. He was influenced by Jean-Paul Sartre, Jacques Lacan, Marxism and the Négritude of Aimé Césaire. Fanon died on 6 December 1961, having gone to the United States for leukaemia treatment in October. His work influenced Steve Biko in South Africa, Amílcar Cabral in Guinea-Bissau and the Black Power movement in the United States.
franz-anton-von-kolowrat-liebsteinsky: Kolowrat was the only son of Count Franz Josef von Kolowrat-Liebsteinsky and Countess Maria Katharina von Kolowrat-Krakowsky, a scion of the Liebsteinsky branch of the House of Kolowrat, an ancient Bohemian family of high nobility whose ancestors had served the emperor Charles IV. Raised in Prague, he studied at Charles University and entered the Austrian civil service at the Beroun district administration in January 1799. During the Napoleonic Wars he became stadtholder of Emperor Francis I of Austria at Prague, and in 1810 Oberstburggraf of the Bohemian kingdom.

A moderate liberal, Kolowrat encouraged Czech cultural and civic-national movements, as in the founding of the Prague National Museum in 1818, where State Chancellor Prince Klemens von Metternich did not. Their rivalry grew after the emperor called him to Vienna in 1826 to lead the Austrian State Council for the Interior and Finances: while Metternich favoured a strong army, Kolowrat cut the military budget.

After Ferdinand I came to the throne in 1835, the two men led the Secret State Conference, the de facto government of the empire from 1836 to 1848. Their constant disagreement paralysed Austrian politics and contributed to the collapse of the Metternich system. When the Revolutions of 1848 forced Metternich to resign, a ministers' conference was set up and Kolowrat took the new office of Austrian minister-president, the first constitutional holder of the post, but he gave it up after one month, between 3 and 5 April, officially for health reasons.

On 8 June 1801 Kolowrat had married Countess Maria Rosa Johanna Kinsky von Wchinitz und Tettau, daughter of Prince Joseph Ernst Kinsky von Wchinitz und Tettau; the marriage was childless, and she died in 1842. He died in Vienna on 4 April 1861 at the age of 83, outliving his wife and sisters, and with him the Liebsteinsky branch of the family became extinct. He was buried in the Holy Trinity Church at the family's ancestral castle in Rychnov nad Kněžnou. Among his decorations was the Order of the Golden Fleece.
franz-conrad-von-hotzendorf: Franz Xaver Josef Conrad von Hötzendorf was born on 11 November 1852 in Penzing, a suburb of Vienna, into an Austrian officers' family. His father, a retired colonel of hussars, had fought at Leipzig. He was educated at the Theresian Military Academy in Wiener Neustadt, took an interest in natural science and in Darwin's theory of evolution, and was commissioned in 1871. After the Kriegsschule he joined the General Staff in 1876, served in Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Treaty of Berlin and became a popular professor of tactics in Vienna in 1888. His books on infantry tactics sold well.

At the suggestion of Archduke Franz Ferdinand he became Chief of the General Staff in November 1906. He saw conflict as always inevitable and held that the fate of nations was decided on the battlefield rather than at diplomatic conferences. He proposed preventive war against Serbia in 1906, in 1908 to 1909, in 1912 to 1913 and in May 1914, and Hew Strachan counts twenty-five such proposals between 1 January 1913 and 1 January 1914. His differences with Foreign Minister Aehrenthal, who rejected his plan for preventive war against Italy, led to his dismissal in 1911, and he returned in December 1912.

His war plans assumed more soldiers than were available, with better training than they had, and relied on railway timetables of the 1870s. In August 1914 an army of 460,000 men sent into Serbia was defeated, and the offensive against Russia through Galicia brought the loss of Lemberg, though Conrad's forces won at Limanowa in December 1914. Austria-Hungary suffered nearly a million casualties, many in efforts to relieve Przemyśl, which surrendered in April 1915.

From 1915 his troops depended increasingly on German support and command. Emperor Charles I made him a field marshal in November 1916 but dismissed him as Chief of Staff in March 1917, after the failure of his Trentino Offensive. He then commanded an army group on the Italian front until he retired in the summer of 1918. He married Virginia von Reininghaus in 1915 after a long affair, and after his death in 1925 a journal was found that held more than 3,000 letters to her which he had never sent. The historian John Leslie describes him as a loner who was politically inept.
franz-grillparzer: Franz Grillparzer was born in Vienna on 15 January 1791. His father, a lawyer ruined by Napoleon's invasion, wanted him to follow the same profession, and Franz entered the University of Vienna in 1807 as a student of jurisprudence, and his father died two years later. After his degree in 1811 he tutored privately, and in 1813 he became a clerk at the Imperial Hofkammer. In 1832 he became director of its archives and held the post until he retired in 1856. He regarded his official career merely as a means of independence, and he never married. From early youth he had a strong literary impulse, and he studied Spanish drama, especially Pedro Calderón de la Barca.

The Ancestress, published in 1816, was a gruesome fate-tragedy, and its first performances in 1817 brought him wide recognition. Sappho followed in 1818, and in 1821 he completed the trilogy The Golden Fleece. Some critics consider its last part, Medea, his highest achievement. He wrote King Ottokar's Fortune and Rise in 1823, but difficulties with the censor delayed its performance until 19 February 1825.

His only comedy, Woe to Him Who Lies, failed at its premiere on 6 March 1838, and he turned his back on the theatre. After that he published only the fragment Esther, but three finished tragedies were found among his papers, among them The Jewess of Toledo and Libussa. He also wrote the novella The Poor Musician in 1848.

After 1840 he almost passed from the memory of his contemporaries. Heinrich Laube became artistic director of Vienna's court theatre in 1849 and staged his forgotten works, and Grillparzer became the most popular author of the day, ranked with Goethe and Schiller. He was made a member of the Academy of Sciences and in 1861 was elected to the Austrian Herrenhaus. His eightieth birthday was marked by all classes from the court downwards.

He died in Vienna on 21 January 1872. He was buried first in the Währinger Cemetery, now Schubertpark, and now lies at Hietzing Cemetery. He is regarded as the national poet of Austria, and the Grillparzer Prize and Grillparzer Ring are named after him. He wrote the oration for Ludwig van Beethoven's funeral and the epitaph for Franz Schubert.
franz-joseph-i: Franz Joseph was born on 18 August 1830 at Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna, the eldest son of Archduke Franz Karl and Sophie, Princess of Bavaria. His uncle Ferdinand, emperor from 1835, was disabled by seizures and his father was unambitious, so his politically ambitious mother raised him as a future emperor, stressing devotion, responsibility and diligence. During the Revolutions of 1848 he joined Field Marshal Radetzky's campaign in Italy and received his baptism of fire at Santa Lucia on 5 May. In December 1848 Ferdinand abdicated at Olomouc as part of Felix zu Schwarzenberg's plan to end the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, and Franz Joseph took the throne at eighteen.

Largely considered a reactionary, he spent his early reign resisting constitutionalism. After Schwarzenberg's death in 1852 the emperor effectively became his own prime minister, and he was forced to issue the February Patent of 1861 to borrow money abroad. Austria lost influence in Italy after the Second Italian War of Independence in 1859 and the war of 1866. The Austro-Prussian War of 1866 ended in the Peace of Prague, which settled the German Question in favour of Prussia, though he ceded no territory to it. His main foreign-policy goal had been unification of Germany under the Habsburgs. In 1854 he married his cousin Elisabeth of Bavaria, whom he had chosen in place of the bride his mother favoured.

In the Compromise of 1867 he granted Hungary greater autonomy and created the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary, which he then ruled peacefully for 45 years. In 1873 he joined the League of Three Emperors with Wilhelm I of Germany and Alexander II of Russia. His troops occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and in 1908 he annexed it, causing the Bosnian Crisis. In 1903 he used the last veto by a Catholic ruler on a papal election, against Cardinal Rampolla.

He suffered personal tragedies: the execution of his brother Maximilian of Mexico in 1867, the suicide of his son Rudolf in 1889, and the assassinations of his wife Elisabeth in 1898 and of his nephew and heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia then began the First World War. Told of the killing, he said that a superior power had restored the order he had been unable to maintain.

Franz Joseph died at Schönbrunn on the evening of 21 November 1916, at the age of 86, of pneumonia caught after a walk with King Ludwig III of Bavaria. After almost 68 years on the throne he was succeeded by his grandnephew Charles I, and he is buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna. Franz Josef Land in the Arctic was named for him in 1873.
franz-joseph-ii-prince-of-liechtenstein: Franz Joseph was born on 16 August 1906 at Schloss Frauenthal in Austria-Hungary, the first child of Prince Alois of Liechtenstein and Archduchess Elisabeth Amalie of Austria. Emperor Franz Joseph I was his godfather. He spent his youth on family estates, notably the castle of Groß Ullersdorf in Moravia, attended the Schottengymnasium in Vienna and took a diploma in forestry engineering in 1930. On 26 February 1923 his father renounced the succession in his favour, worried about his own age, and in 1930 he was appointed deputy of his childless grand-uncle, Prince Franz I.

On 31 March 1938, after the Anschluss of Austria, Franz I made him regent. It was speculated that Franz I did not wish to remain in control if Nazi Germany invaded, because his wife, Elisabeth von Gutmann, was of Jewish relation. Franz I died on 25 July 1938, and Franz Joseph became prince and settled permanently in the principality. Liechtenstein stayed neutral in World War II. He supported Prime Minister Josef Hoop's policy of non-provocative diplomacy towards Germany and tied the country as closely as possible to Switzerland. He met Hitler in Berlin in March 1939, a visit he later said was made to flatter Hitler's ego, while a small German National Movement staged a failed coup at home.

Near the end of the war he granted asylum to Russian emigrés of the First Russian National Army, and the principality refused Soviet demands for their repatriation in August 1945; about a hundred later moved to Argentina. In 1945 the family lost its estates in Czechoslovakia and Poland without compensation, and it later sold artworks, among them Leonardo da Vinci's Ginevra de' Benci in 1967. The family bank and the principality's role as a tax haven brought rapid economic growth from a poor agricultural state.

Women received the vote after a referendum among men only in 1984. In the same year Franz Joseph handed most day-to-day decisions to his son Hans-Adam on 26 August, while remaining sovereign. He used his veto once, in 1985, against a hunting law he called silly. His wife, Countess Georgina von Wilczek, whom he married in 1943, died on 18 October 1989, and he died on 13 November 1989 after a long period of poor health. He had ruled for 51 years, and was succeeded by Hans-Adam II.
franz-joseph-spiegler: Spiegler was born on 5 April 1691 in the Free Imperial City of Wangen im Allgäu, the son of a district court attorney. After his father's death in 1692 his mother married the painter Adam Joseph Dollmann, a member of an old patrician family of Wangen, and through him the boy was introduced to the arts. Around 1710 he began training as a painter in Munich under his great-uncle, the Bavarian court painter Johann Kaspar Sing, and came to know the history painting then in vogue among Dutch painters.

Among his early works are the frescoes of the parish church of Maria Thann at Hergatz, painted in 1722–1723. From 1723 to 1725 he painted frescoes in the corridors, stairways and theatre of Ottobeuren Abbey, among them a ceiling of Comedy and Tragedy, in a manner that shows the strong influence of the Italian painter Jacopo Amigoni. He went on to create frescoes and oil paintings for monasteries, churches and castles across Upper Swabia, Lake Constance, the Black Forest and the Upper Rhine, beginning with Schloss Bonndorf in 1726 and the Cistercian abbey church of Salem in 1730.

In the following decades he painted the castle chapels of Mochental in 1734 and Mainau in 1737–1738, Lindau Cathedral in 1736, the parish church of St. Remigius at Merdingen in 1739–1741, the Augustinian Church of the Holy Trinity at Konstanz in 1740 and the parish church of St. Martin at Altheim in 1747, and he supplied altar paintings for the Benedictine Abbey of Muri in Switzerland in 1746. His frescoes in Zwiefalten Münster are considered his masterpiece, and among his last works were those of the convent church of St. Fridolin at Bad Säckingen in 1753–1754. He died at Konstanz on 15 April 1757.
franz-liszt: Liszt was born on 22 October 1811 in the village of Doborján (now Raiding, Austria), in the Kingdom of Hungary. His father, Adam Liszt, was a land steward in the service of Prince Nikolaus II Esterházy and an amateur musician who knew Joseph Haydn. Franz improvised at the piano before the age of five and gave his first public concert at Sopron in 1820, aged nine. In 1823 the family moved to Paris. The Conservatoire refused him entry because it did not accept foreigners, so he studied under Anton Reicha and Ferdinando Paer. He gave concerts from 8 March 1824 and toured France and England, where he played for King George IV.

In 1833 Liszt began a relationship with Countess Marie d'Agoult. They lived together for four years and travelled in Switzerland and Italy; the journeys later inspired Années de pèlerinage. They had three children, among them Cosima, who married Hans von Bülow and later Richard Wagner. Liszt's tours in the 1830s and 1840s produced what was called Lisztomania, a popularity that earlier virtuosos had not known. He is credited as the first pianist to give solo recitals in the modern sense, the term first applying to his concert at the Hanover Square Rooms in London on 9 June 1840.

In July 1848 he settled in Weimar, where he arranged festivals of the music of Hector Berlioz and Wagner and gave the premiere of Lohengrin. His planned marriage to Princess Carolyne was stopped by a Vatican official in Rome in October 1861. In January 1869 he agreed to give masterclasses in Weimar, and from 1872 he travelled regularly among Rome, Weimar and Budapest, a life he called his vie trifurquée. He taught, by some estimates, over 400 pupils.

Most of Liszt's music is for the piano, and it is often marked by difficulty. Weimar saw the first fifteen Hungarian Rhapsodies, shaped by the Romani bands he had heard in Hungary, and the Grandes Études de Paganini, published in 1851, which include La campanella. He also wrote 137 secular vocal pieces, now relatively obscure. In an essay of 1855 on Berlioz's Harold in Italy he coined the term program music and argued that it was artistically superior to absolute music. His late works, from about 1869, push the limits of tonality. Romantic music fell out of favour in the early twentieth century, and only a few of his pieces, such as the Liebesträume and the Hungarian Rhapsodies, stayed in print.
franz-marc: Franz Marc was born in Munich on 8 February 1880. His father, Wilhelm Marc, was a landscape painter, and his mother was a devout Calvinist. At 17 he wanted to study theology, as his older brother Paul had, but two years later he enrolled in an arts programme. After a year of military service he began studies at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich in 1900. He spent time in Paris in 1903 and 1907, copying paintings in museums, and found a strong affinity with the work of Vincent van Gogh. He married twice, first Marie Schnür and then Maria Franck, and both were artists.

In 1906 Marc travelled with his brother, a Byzantine expert, to Thessaloniki and Mount Athos. In 1910 he became a friend of the artist August Macke. A critic, Morgan Meis, writes that Marc became an artist in the winter of 1910 to 1911, when his animals began to emerge on the canvas with color as the main thing. In 1911 he founded the journal Der Blaue Reiter with Macke, Wassily Kandinsky and others who had split from the Neue Künstlervereinigung. The first Blue Rider exhibition was held at the Thannhauser Galleries in Munich between December 1911 and January 1912, and travelled to Berlin, Cologne, Hagen and Frankfurt.

In 1912 Marc met Robert Delaunay, whose use of color and the Cubist method influenced him. He painted The Tiger and Red Deer in 1912, and The Tower of Blue Horses, The Foxes and Fate of the Animals in 1913. His work is characterised by bright primary color and a near-cubist treatment of animals. Marc gave colors a meaning, using blue for masculinity and spirituality, yellow for feminine joy and red for violence. He made some sixty prints in woodcut and lithography. He wrote to his wife that Fate of the Animals was like a premonition of the war.

Marc was drafted into the Imperial German Army as a cavalryman in 1914. By 1916 he was a lieutenant, had been awarded the Iron Cross, and had turned to camouflage, painting canvas covers to hide artillery from aerial observation. The government had listed notable artists to be withdrawn from combat for their own safety, but he was killed instantly by a shell splinter at the Battle of Verdun before orders reached him. In 1936 and 1937 the Nazis condemned him as a degenerate artist and ordered about 130 of his works removed from German museums. The Blue Horses was auctioned in Lucerne in 1939. Most of his work survived the war, and the Franz Marc Museum at Kochel am See opened in 1986.
franz-schubert: Franz Schubert was born in Himmelpfortgrund, now part of Alsergrund in Vienna, on 31 January 1797, the twelfth child of the parish schoolmaster Franz Theodor Florian Schubert and Maria Elisabeth Katharina Vietz. His father gave him lessons from the age of five, and his brother Ignaz taught him the piano, though Schubert surpassed him within a few months. In 1808, aged eleven, he entered the Stadtkonvikt school, where he came to know the orchestral music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. He left in November 1813 for teacher training and in 1814 taught the youngest pupils at his father's school, while continuing private lessons in composition with Antonio Salieri until 1817.

Schubert was immensely prolific. In 1815 he composed over 20,000 bars of music, including about 140 Lieder. In 1816 Franz von Schober invited him to lodge at his mother's house, and Schubert gave up teaching to devote himself to composition. In 1817 he met the baritone Johann Michael Vogl, who sang many of his songs. In March 1821 Vogl sang Erlkönig at a concert that was extremely well received. Publishers remained distant, and Anton Diabelli agreed to print the first seven opus numbers only on commission.

In 1822 he began the Symphony in B minor, known as the Unfinished Symphony, with two movements and sketches of a third; why he left it unfinished is still discussed. In 1823 he wrote his first large-scale song cycle, Die schöne Müllerin, and the later cycle Winterreise, of 1827, is widely considered one of the pinnacles of Lieder. In his career he wrote roughly 630 songs, seven complete symphonies, seven masses and a large body of piano and chamber music. In March 1828 he gave a concert of his works to critical acclaim, the only one of his career.

Schubert's health deteriorated in the late 1820s, and symptoms of syphilis had first appeared in 1823. At the beginning of November 1828 he fell ill with headaches, fever, swollen joints and vomiting, and he died on 19 November 1828. The cause was officially attributed to typhoid fever, but some historians believe it was syphilis. During his lifetime his appreciation was limited to a small circle of admirers in Vienna, and about 100 opus numbers were published, mainly songs, chamber music and small piano pieces. Many larger works stayed hidden in cabinets and file boxes until George Grove and Arthur Sullivan travelled to Vienna in October 1867 and found manuscripts of six of the symphonies. Mendelssohn, Schumann, Liszt and Brahms discovered and championed his works.
franz-von-papen: Franz von Papen was born on 29 October 1879 in Werl, Westphalia, into a wealthy noble Catholic family. His father was a Prussian cavalry officer. Papen entered a cadet school at the age of 11 and trained for the German General Staff, which he joined as a captain in March 1913. He became a military attaché in the United States in December 1913 and also observed the Mexican Revolution, where he was involved in selling arms to the government of General Victoriano Huerta.

He later commanded a battalion on the Western Front, fighting on the Somme and at Vimy Ridge, and ended the war on the General Staff in the Middle East as a lieutenant colonel. After 1920 he entered politics as a monarchist on the national conservative wing of the Centre Party.

President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Papen chancellor on 1 June 1932, on the advice of General Kurt von Schleicher. His cabinet was nicknamed the cabinet of barons, and he had little support in the Reichstag. He governed by presidential decree, launched the Preußenschlag against the government of Prussia led by the Social Democratic Party, and dissolved the Reichstag twice. Hindenburg removed him in favour of Schleicher.

Papen met Adolf Hitler secretly in Cologne on 4 January 1933 and on 22 January agreed to support him as chancellor with himself as vice-chancellor. Hindenburg appointed Hitler on 30 January. Papen believed Hitler could be contained, but Hitler and his allies quickly marginalised him. On 17 June 1934 he gave a speech at the University of Marburg calling for an end to SA terror. During the Night of the Long Knives his office was ransacked and associates including Herbert von Bose, Erich Klausener and Edgar Julius Jung were shot. Papen resigned, then served as ambassador in Vienna from 1934 to 1938 and in Ankara from 1939 to 1944. He joined the Nazi Party in 1938.

Papen was captured on 14 April 1945 and was one of the defendants at the main Nuremberg trial. The tribunal found no solid evidence that he had been involved in the annexation of Austria. It acquitted him, saying that his actions were political immoralities that were not punishable under the charge of conspiracy to commit crimes against peace. A West German denazification court later sentenced him to eight years of hard labour, but he was released on appeal in 1949. His memoirs of 1952 downplayed his involvement and portrayed him as a tragic patriot. He died on 2 May 1969. He is largely remembered for his role in Hitler's rise to power.
franz-von-waldeck: Franz was the third and last son among the six children of Count Philip II of Waldeck-Eisenberg, governor of the County of Ravensberg, and Countess Catherine von Solms-Lich, who died a year after his birth. His father, once destined for the ministry himself, intended him for a place in an aristocratic cathedral chapter. Since chapter members needed a secular law degree, Franz studied at Erfurt from 1506 and at Leipzig from 1510.

Without taking holy orders he gathered many canons' benefices, becoming a canon of Cologne, Trier, Mainz and Paderborn and dean of St. Alexander's Foundation in Einbeck. In Einbeck he met Anna Polmann, daughter of the linen weaver Barthold Polmann. They lived together as a married couple and had eight children, four sons and four daughters, though whether they were ever properly married is unclear.

His attitude to the Reformation was ambiguous. Münster embraced it in the early 1530s and soon fell under the control of the radical Bernhard Rothmann. Waldeck moved against the city, seizing goods of its merchants, until the Treaty of Dülmen of February 1533 granted it full religious freedom. When the Anabaptists won the council election of 23 February 1534, he laid siege to the city. On Easter Sunday 1534 the Anabaptist leader Jan Matthys led a small band out and was killed, and John of Leiden then made himself king of Münster as the New Jerusalem.

With help from the Holy Roman Empire and a traitor inside the walls, Waldeck's troops retook the city on 24 June 1535. Münster was made Catholic again, yet Waldeck used his influence to further Luther's teachings. His efforts at reform in 1541 met united resistance in the bishopric of Münster; in 1543 he planned with the Lübeck superintendent Herman Bonnus to introduce the Reformation in Osnabrück, and in Minden, where Lutheran doctrine was already widely held, he sought support beyond the cathedral chapter. These efforts were closely tied to his wish to have his union with Anna Polmann made lawful and to secularise the three dioceses into a territory for his heirs. He died on 15 July 1553.
frascati: Frascati is a city in the Metropolitan City of Rome Capital, in Lazio, on the Alban Hills 20 kilometres south-east of Rome and close to the ancient city of Tusculum. The most important archaeological find nearby is a patrician Roman villa of the late Republic, probably belonging to Lucullus. In the first century CE its owner was Gaius Sallustius Crispus Passienus, who married Agrippina the Younger, mother of Nero.

According to the Liber Pontificalis Frascati was a little village in the ninth century. Its name probably comes from a local tradition of collecting firewood, called frasche in Italian. After the destruction of Tusculum in 1191 the population increased and the bishopric moved to Frascati. Raids impoverished it, and baronial families such as the Colonna held it until Pope Pius II fortified it with walls in 1460. In 1538 Pope Paul III conferred the title of civitas on it, with the name Tusculum Novum, and building of the cathedral began in 1598.

On 1 May 1527 a Landsknecht company that had sacked Rome approached the town but turned aside at a shrine of the Virgin Mary, and a church commemorates the event. On 15 September 1616 the first public and free school in Europe was established on the initiative of Saint Joseph Calasanz. Frascati was annexed to the French Empire in 1809, and in 1837 it was the only town to open its doors to 5,000 people fleeing plague in Rome. In 1943 it held the German general headquarters for the Mediterranean zone and was heavily bombed, and about half its buildings were destroyed. It was liberated on 4 June 1944.

From the sixteenth century popes, cardinals and Roman nobles built villas on the slopes as status symbols, designed for social life rather than farming, among them Villa Aldobrandini, Villa Falconieri and Villa Mondragone. The cathedral, rebuilt after the bombing, holds the tombstone of Charles Edward Stuart. The town produces a white wine of its name and hosts scientific laboratories, among them the Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati, where the first Italian particle accelerator was developed in the late 1950s.
fraser-river: The Fraser rises at Fraser Pass in the Canadian Rocky Mountains, near the border with Alberta, and flows for 1,375 kilometres into the Strait of Georgia just south of Vancouver. It drains 220,000 square kilometres and discharges about 20 million tons of sediment into the ocean each year. It turns sharply south at Giscome Portage and meets the Nechako River at Prince George. South of Williams Lake it cuts the Fraser Canyon. At Hell's Gate the walls force the whole river through a gap only 35 metres wide. Yale is the head of navigation, and below it the river crosses the Fraser Valley and splits around Lulu Island and Sea Island before reaching the sea.

The river is named after Simon Fraser, who led a North West Company expedition in 1808 from the site of present-day Prince George almost to its mouth. On 14 June 1792 the Spanish explorers Dionisio Alcalá Galiano and Cayetano Valdés anchored in the North Arm, the first Europeans officially to enter it. Alexander Mackenzie explored the upper reaches in 1793, and Fraser traced the river in 1808 and confirmed it was not connected to the Columbia.

The Hudson's Bay Company built the original Fort Langley in 1827, the first settlement of mixed European and Indigenous ancestry in southern British Columbia. In 1828 George Simpson went down the canyon and wrote that the passage would be certain death in nine attempts out of ten, so Fort Vancouver stayed the company's main Pacific depot. After the Oregon Treaty of 1846 the Fraser was the essential route between the Interior and the Lower Coast, and in 1858 the Fraser Canyon Gold Rush brought prospectors. The worst floods came in 1894 and 1948. In 1998 it was designated a Canadian Heritage River.

The Fraser is the largest producer of salmon in Canada, and holds white sturgeon, steelhead trout and all five Pacific salmon species. Its banks are rich farmland, its water serves pulp mills, and a few dams on its tributaries make electric power, but the main flow has never been dammed. The estuary is a site of hemispheric importance in the Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network.
frauenfeld: Frauenfeld is the capital of the canton of Thurgau in Switzerland and lies along both banks of the Murg river. The earliest traces of human settlement are La Tène graves east of Langdorf, and a Roman road from Oberwinterthur to Pfyn ran through what is now the Allmend. Two Roman villas have been found, at Thalbach and Oberkirch, and by the 9th century a church stood at Oberkirch. By the end of the 1220s a fortified tower with a mill and chapel had been built, and a village grew around it on land owned by Reichenau Abbey. The tower grew into Frauenfeld Castle.

Frauenfeld is first mentioned in 1246 as Vrowinvelt, and in 1286 as a city. By then it had been integrated into the Habsburg territories, and it belonged to the Habsburg district of Kyburg. How the city came into being is not clear. In 1374 the Habsburgs gave the right of judgment for all Thurgau to the Duke of Frauenfeld, and the castle became the centre of the Habsburg district of Frauenfeld. The Landsberger family held it until 1534. In 1460 the Swiss Confederation captured Thurgau, including Frauenfeld.

Under the Confederation Frauenfeld became the centre from which the Confederates managed Thurgau. After 1499 it was the home of a Confederation court, and after 1504 the Thurgau governor lived there, after 1532 in the castle. The Reformation affected the city, and Catholic and Protestant councils shared its government. Protestants had no church of their own until 1645. The assembly of the Confederacy, the Tagsatzung, met at Frauenfeld in the 18th century, and the fall of the old Confederacy in 1798 ended those gatherings. Fires in 1771 and 1788 destroyed nearly all the houses, so the present old city dates from the end of the 18th century.

The constitution of 1798, under the Helvetic Republic, made Frauenfeld the capital of the new canton of Thurgau, although Weinfelden, geographically central, was the main alternative. Since 1832 the cantonal parliament has met twice a year alternately in Frauenfeld and Weinfelden. On 25 May 1799 French and Austrian forces fought a battle in the city, and the Austrians were victorious. The city walls were demolished between 1808 and 1834. The old city is included in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and the castle, which holds the Historical Museum, and the town hall are among ten buildings of national significance. The Thurgauer Zeitung, founded in 1798 as a weekly journal, is still published.
frauenkirche-munich: A late Romanesque church stood beside the town's first ring of walls from the 12th century and served as the second city parish after the older Alter Peter. The late Gothic cathedral that replaced it was commissioned by Duke Sigismund and the people of Munich in the 15th century and raised in about twenty years by Jörg von Halsbach. Because no stone quarry lay nearby, and for financial reasons, brick was chosen. Construction began in 1468, and when the money ran out in 1479 Pope Sixtus IV granted an indulgence. The church was consecrated in 1494. Its size was striking: it could hold 20,000 standing people in a city of about 13,000 inhabitants.

The church is of red brick, designed very plainly, with its buttresses moved into the interior. It is 109 metres long, 40 metres wide and 37 metres high, a hall church whose nave and two aisles are of equal height and are divided by a double row of 22 pillars. Heinrich von Straubing designed the arches. The twin towers stand just over 98 metres high; the north tower is 98.57 metres and the south 98.45, though a legend says they differ by one metre. Plans for tall open-work spires were never carried out for lack of money, and in 1525 the towers received domes in a cheaper design, possibly modelled on the Dome of the Rock.

Inside are the tomb monument of Emperor Louis IV, Gothic stained glass and choir stalls carved by Erasmus Grasser between 1495 and 1502. The stalls burned in the Second World War, but their figures had been moved and survive. The crypt holds the tombs of the Archbishops of Munich and Freising and of members of the Wittelsbach dynasty. A black mark at the entrance, the Devil's Footstep, is linked by legend to the devil, who stood there and mocked the church for seeming to have no windows.

In 1919 Eugen Leviné, leader of a short-lived Bavarian Socialist Republic, had the church declared a revolutionary temple. In the later stages of the Second World War air raids collapsed the roof, badly damaged a tower and destroyed or lost most of its historical contents. A restoration in several stages began soon after the war and was completed in 1994. Its domed towers have made it a symbol of Munich.
fraumunster: The Fraumünster, whose name means Women's Minster, began as a Benedictine convent for aristocratic women. Louis the German endowed it with the lands of Zurich, Uri and the Albis forest, granted it immunity and placed it under his direct authority. His daughter Hildegard was its first abbess and another daughter, Bertha, followed her. Richardis, wife of Emperor Charles the Fat, was abbess from 878 to 893. The foundations of the crypt under the choir date back to the 9th century.

In 1045 King Henry III granted the convent the right to hold markets, collect tolls and mint coins, which effectively made the abbess the ruler of the city. Emperor Frederick II gave the abbey Reichsunmittelbarkeit in 1218, making it independent of every authority except the emperor. The abbess appointed the mayor and often delegated the minting of coins to citizens. Elisabeth von Wetzikon, abbess from 1270 to 1298, held office at the height of this power.

The convent's political power waned in the 14th century, beginning with the guild laws, the Zunftordnung, introduced in 1336 by Rudolf Brun, who became the first mayor not appointed by the abbess. At least 29 abbesses led the house. The last, Katharina von Zimmern, abbess from 1496, supported the Reformation of Huldrych Zwingli, and the abbey was dissolved on 30 November 1524. The crypt had kept the abbey's relics until the Reformation banned the veneration of saints.

The monastery buildings were pulled down in 1898 to make room for the new Stadthaus, while the church is now a parish church of the Evangelical Reformed Church of the canton of Zurich and one of the city's four main churches. Its choir holds five stained glass windows by Marc Chagall installed in 1970, and the north transept a window by Augusto Giacometti of 1940. The crypt opened to the public on 19 June 2016. The Münsterhof, the main square of the medieval city, is named after the abbey.
fraxinetum: The fort stood on the Mont des Maures above present-day La Garde-Freinet, near Saint-Tropez, and had existed since Roman times; its name, from the Latin fraxinus, probably refers to the ash forest covering the hill. The Muslim geographers al-Iṣṭakhrī and Ibn Ḥawqal called it Jabal al-Qilāl, the mount of timber, and described the enclave as vast and fertile, two days across. Most of its history comes from Latin writers, above all Liudprand of Cremona, with Flodoard, Ekkehard and the lives of saints, and only a little from Arabic and Persian geographers.

Muslim raiders had attacked Marseille in 838 and Arles in 842 and 869. According to Liudprand, about twenty Andalusī sailors landed near Saint-Tropez, seized the fort and called in about 100 more warriors from Spain and the Balearics. Exploiting the quarrels of the Provençal lords after the collapse of Carolingian authority, they held the Mont Cenis pass by 906 and all the western Alpine passes by 911, taking tolls from traders and pilgrims. In 939 they attacked the Abbey of Saint Gall and razed Saint-Maurice d'Agaune.

Around 942 King Hugh of Italy, allied with the Byzantine emperor Romanos Lekapenos, attacked the base while Byzantine ships burned the Muslim fleet with Greek fire, but Hugh broke off the siege to meet a rival, Berengar of Ivrea, and let the Muslims keep the passes. After a raid into the Upper Rhine Valley in 956, Otto I sent embassies to the Umayyad court, and aid from Spain declined. The capture of Abbot Maiolus of Cluny led to the Christian victory at Tourtour in the summer of 972.

Ibn Ḥawqal says the settlement depended on the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba, and historians describe its people as Andalusīs, probably a mix of Arabs, Berbers and muwalladūn; Manfred Wenner thinks most of its soldiers were Berbers. Rule was indirect: Christians kept their religion and towns their self-government by paying the jizya. Its main business was capturing Europeans for the slave markets of the Islamic world. After its fall, Muslims who did not leave were killed or enslaved, and many converted and stayed as serfs.
fred-rwigyema: He was born Emmanuel Gisa on 10 April 1957 in Gitarama, in southern Rwanda. Considered a Tutsi, he fled with his family to Uganda in 1960, after the Rwandan Revolution of 1959 and the ousting of King Kigeli V, and grew up in a refugee camp at Nshungerezi in Ankole. After finishing high school in 1976 he went to Tanzania and joined the Front for National Salvation (FRONASA), a rebel group headed by Yoweri Museveni, brother of his friend Salim Saleh. From then on he called himself Fred Rwigema. Later that year he joined the FRELIMO rebels fighting Portugal's colonial rule in Mozambique.

In 1979 he joined the Uganda National Liberation Army, which with Tanzanian forces took Kampala in April 1979 and drove Idi Amin into exile. In 1981 he was among the first 27 armed men who followed Museveni into the bush after the disputed elections of 1980, beginning the Ugandan Bush War against Milton Obote's government. In the National Resistance Army he fought beside future leaders of the Rwandan Patriotic Front, among them Paul Kagame, James Kabarebe, Patrick Karegeya and Kayumba Nyamwasa.

When the NRA took power in 1986, he was one of three former rebel leaders commissioned as major generals, with Salim Saleh Akandwanaho and Elly Tumwine, and became Deputy Minister of Defence. He went on directing operations in northern Uganda against remnants of the ousted army and other rebel groups, where he earned the Swahili nickname Mungu wa vita, god of war.

On 1 October 1990 he led a splinter group of 10,000 NRA troops into northern Rwanda, starting the Rwandan Civil War; the date, close to Uganda's independence day on 9 October, let the movement pass as preparation for a parade. He was shot in the head on Nyabwenshogozi Hill, and his death was kept secret for a month to protect morale. Kagame's government held that a stray bullet killed him; the historian Gérard Prunier states that he was killed by his subcommander Peter Bayingana after an argument over tactics. He is considered one of Rwanda's national heroes and is buried at the Remera Heroes Cemetery in Kigali.
fredegund: Fredegund was born into a low-ranking family around 543 and gained power through her association with King Chilperic I. She was originally a servant of Chilperic's first wife Audovera, and she won the king's affection and persuaded him to put Audovera in a convent and divorce her. Chilperic then put Fredegund aside and married Galswintha, daughter of the Visigothic king Athanagild, after his half-brother and rival Sigibert I of Austrasia had married Galswintha's younger sister Brunhilda. The marriage deteriorated, and Galswintha died, probably strangled on the orders of Chilperic or Fredegund, who succeeded her as queen. Brunhilda began a feud with Fredegund that lasted more than 40 years.

Gregory of Tours, the main source, records that an epidemic of dysentery in 580 struck Chilperic and their sons Chlodobert and Dagobert. Fredegund burned tax records she feared were unjust and urged Chilperic to do the same, but the two sons died, and she then made large donations to churches and the poor. Gregory also reports that she quarrelled with her daughter Rigunth, and that Rigunth's journey to her Visigothic fiancé in Spain ended in robbery and the loss of most of her treasure.

Fredegund is said to have ordered the assassination of Sigibert in 575 and to have made attempts on the lives of Sigibert's son Childebert II, King Guntram of Burgundy and Brunhilda. Gregory suggests she drove the persecution of Bishop Praetextatus, who was stabbed during Easter Mass in 586. After Chilperic was murdered in 584 she took refuge in the cathedral in Paris and became regent for her infant son Chlothar II, protected by Guntram until his death in 592. She commanded the Neustrian armies, and in 593 she led troops to a victory over Brunhilda's at the Battle of Droizy. She kept the support of the clergy and gave land to the Bishop of Le Mans.

Fredegund died of natural causes on 8 December 597 in Paris. Her tomb, a mosaic of marble and copper, stands in Saint Denis Basilica. Her reputation has been poor, mostly because of Gregory of Tours, who calls her murderous and cruel. Historians note that he was a Gallo-Roman bishop appointed through Sigibert and Brunhilda, who receive almost no criticism from him, so his account may be exaggerated. Bishop Leudovald, said to have been a target of her plots, was still favoured by the Neustrian monarchy after her death. Composers later dramatised her story, among them Camille Saint-Saëns and Paul Dukas, who completed Ernest Guiraud's opera Frédégonde in 1895.
frederic-cesar-de-la-harpe: La Harpe was born on 6 April 1754 in Rolle, Vaud, to Sigismond de la Harpe and Sophie Dorothée Crinsoz de Colombier. Vaud had been a subject land of Bern since the 16th century, in a confederacy of largely self-governing cantons with no central government. He took a doctorate in law at the University of Tübingen in 1774 and then went to Russia, where in 1783 he became tutor to Konstantin and Alexander, the two eldest heirs of Paul I, and educated Alexander in the ideas of the Lumières.

A republican idealist, La Harpe saw Bernese rule as an oligarchy that violated the natural rights of the people of Vaud. Bern denounced him in 1791 for approving revolutionary banquets in Vaud, one organised by his cousin Amédée de la Harpe. He returned to Switzerland in 1794 and went on to Paris, where he published an Essay on the Constitution of the Vaud and on 10 December 1797 told the French Directory that the Duke of Savoy's treaty commitments to Bern, made at Lausanne in 1564, gave France the right to help the Vaudois.

When French troops entered Vaud in late January 1798, the people had already expelled the Bernese bailiffs and proclaimed the Lemanic Republic. La Harpe and Peter Ochs then led the movement that created the centralised Helvetic Republic, and La Harpe joined its Directory on 29 June 1798. The new state was unpopular, burdened by French pillaging of state funds, limits on worship and the harsh crushing of resistance in Nidwalden. In 1799 La Harpe deposed Ochs, and in 1800 he was himself overthrown by a coup and fled.

He lived near Paris until 1814, visiting Alexander in Saint Petersburg in 1801 and 1802. He criticised Napoleon's Act of Mediation of 1803 to the tsar, though it kept the former subject lands as cantons. In 1813 he and Henri Monod persuaded Alexander, and through him the other Allied powers, to recognise Vaudois and Argovian independence, and he represented several cantons at the Congress of Vienna while opposing the Federal Treaty of 1815. He settled in Lausanne in 1816, sat as a liberal in the Grand Council of Vaud from 1817 to 1826 and died there on 30 March 1838. The Helvetic Directory's model of a small collective executive survives in the Swiss Federal Council.
frederic-chopin: Frédéric François Chopin was born in Żelazowa Wola, 46 kilometres west of Warsaw, in the Duchy of Warsaw. The baptismal record gives his birthday as 22 February 1810, but the composer and his family used 1 March, now generally accepted. His father, Nicolas Chopin, was a Frenchman from Lorraine who had emigrated to Poland in 1787 and insisted on Polish at home; his mother was Justyna Krzyżanowska. In October 1810 the family moved to Warsaw, where his father taught French at the Warsaw Lyceum. His first professional tutor, from 1816 to 1821, was the pianist Wojciech Żywny. A child prodigy, Chopin gave public concerts by the age of seven.

Chopin wrote his early works in Warsaw, among them six works for piano and orchestra, including two piano concertos. He left Poland at 20, less than a month before the November 1830 Uprising, and at 21 settled in Paris. He gave only about thirty public performances, preferring the salon, and lived by selling compositions and giving piano lessons, for which he was in high demand. He befriended Franz Liszt and was admired by Robert Schumann. After a failed engagement to Maria Wodzińska in 1836 to 1837 he kept up an often troubled relationship with the writer George Sand. Their brief and unhappy visit to Mallorca in 1838 to 1839 proved one of his most productive periods of composition.

More than 230 of Chopin's works survive, all involving the piano. His influences included Bach and Mozart, Polish folk music and the Paris salons. He took the nocturne, invented by John Field, to a deeper level of sophistication, was the first to write ballades and scherzi as individual concert pieces, and established the free-standing prelude with his Op. 28, published in 1839. His mazurkas were written for the concert hall rather than the dance hall, and his waltzes for the salon.

In his last years Jane Stirling supported him financially. He died in Paris on 17 October 1849 at the age of 39. Debussy dedicated his 1915 piano Études to Chopin's memory, and the Fryderyk Chopin Institute, created by the Polish parliament, hosts the International Chopin Piano Competition.
frederic-maurice-de-la-tour-dauvergne: Born in Sedan, Frédéric Maurice was the son of Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Duke of Bouillon, and Elisabeth of Orange-Nassau. Raised a Protestant, he received a military education in Holland under his uncles Maurice of Nassau-Orange and Frederick Henry, Prince of Orange. On his father's death in 1623 he became Duke of Bouillon and Prince of Sedan, Jametz and Raucourt, and in 1629 governor of Maastricht in the United Provinces. In 1634 he married Countess Eleonora van Berg's-Heerenberg, under whose influence he converted to Catholicism.

He entered the service of King Louis XIII in 1635 as maréchal de camp, and in 1637 lost his offices in the United Provinces after negotiating with Spain. With Louis de Bourbon, comte de Soissons, he conspired against Cardinal Richelieu, and with Spanish troops they defeated the royal army sent against them at the Battle of La Marfée outside Sedan in 1641. He then submitted to the king and Richelieu, and in 1642 he was made lieutenant general in command of the French army of Italy, but after conspiring again with Cinq-Mars he was arrested at Casale.

He was freed only when his wife threatened to open Sedan to the Spaniards, and he promised to cede Sedan and Raucourt to France. In 1650 he joined the Fronde and was one of its leaders with his brother Turenne, until Cardinal Mazarin won him over that same year with the promise of high office and compensation. In 1651 Sedan and Raucourt were exchanged for the duchies of Albret and Château-Thierry, the counties of Auvergne and Évreux and several other lands.

He died at Pontoise in 1652 and was buried at Évreux; his and his wife's bodies were moved to Cluny, arriving in 1692. Between 1697 and 1707 his son Émmanuel-Théodose, Cardinal de Bouillon, abbot of Cluny, commissioned Pierre Le Gros the Younger to sculpt a family monument for the abbey. The sculptures reached Cluny in 1709 but were not unpacked for nearly a century, because the cardinal had defied Louis XIV and been declared an enemy of the state; they are now in the Hôtel-Dieu at Cluny. Of his nine children, Godefroy Maurice became the 3rd duc de Bouillon.
frederic-thesiger-2nd-baron-chelmsford: Frederic Augustus Thesiger was born on 31 May 1827, the eldest child of the lawyer Frederic Thesiger, later Lord Chancellor and the first Baron Chelmsford, and was educated at Eton College. In 1844 he bought a commission in the Rifle Brigade and the next year moved into the Grenadier Guards. He served in the Crimean War as an aide-de-camp and staff officer, then with the 95th (Derbyshire) Regiment of Foot at the end of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. In Bombay he befriended the governor, Sir Henry Bartle Frere, and he was deputy adjutant general in the 1868 Expedition to Abyssinia and Adjutant-General in India from 1869 to 1874.

Sent to command in the Cape Colony in 1878, he ended the Ninth Cape Frontier War that July and succeeded his father as baron in October. His fighting against the Xhosa left him with a low opinion of African soldiers. When Frere's ultimatum to King Cetshwayo expired on 11 January 1879, Chelmsford invaded the Zulu Kingdom in three columns aimed at Ulundi. At Isandlwana the Zulus destroyed the part of the central column left under Lieutenant Colonel Pulleine, and more than 1,300 men on the British side were killed. Chelmsford's own detachment returned after dark and the next day found that the garrison at Rorke's Drift had held out.

Ordered to be replaced by Sir Garnet Wolseley, Chelmsford ignored Cetshwayo's overtures and pressed on to Ulundi before his successor arrived.
