The ideological basis of French colonialism was the civilising mission, which aimed to spread French language, institutions and values; some French politicians contested it. Colonial subjects lived under unequal legal systems and rarely received full citizenship. France sent few settlers to most colonies, Algeria being the main exception. Remaining possessions were integrated into France as overseas departments and territories, and links with former colonies persist through La Francophonie and the CFA franc.
french-committee-of-national-liberation: After the defeat of France in 1940, Marshal Philippe Pétain took full power, signed an armistice with Nazi Germany and set up the Vichy regime, which governed unoccupied southern and central France and most of the overseas territories. Free France, under Charles de Gaulle in London, became a government in exile, but neither the United States nor Britain officially recognised it.

In November 1942 the Allies invaded French North Africa. Vichy forces resisted until Admiral François Darlan ordered them to join the Allies, who recognised him as ruler of the region; Darlan named General Henri Giraud commander-in-chief of the army. Free France had not been told of the invasion or of this Darlan deal. After Darlan was assassinated in December, Giraud ruled with the Vichy officials in place and resisted de Gaulle's call for a purge of collaborators, though he grew more critical of Vichy, notably in a speech written by his adviser Jean Monnet.

The committee was founded in Algiers on 3 June 1943 with Giraud and de Gaulle as co-presidents. Its charter promised to re-establish all French liberties, the laws of the Republic and the republican regime, and it declared the Vichy regime illegitimate for its collaboration with Germany. It governed Algeria, then counted part of metropolitan France, and the liberated parts of the colonial empire.

The United States and Britain at first treated it as a wartime body with limited functions rather than a future government of France. It expanded its membership, built its own administration and set up the Provisional Consultative Assembly. De Gaulle outmanoeuvred Giraud politically, and on 9 November 1943 the committee came under his sole chairmanship.

After the Allied landings in Normandy the committee moved its headquarters to London, and in August 1944, after the liberation of the city, to Paris. In September the Allies recognised it as the legitimate provisional government of France. Reorganised under de Gaulle, it took in representatives of the Socialists, the Communists and other parties and began work on the constitution of the French Fourth Republic. De Gaulle resigned in 1946 over the provisional legislature's refusal to give more powers to the President and over quarrels between the factions.
french-community: The French Union of 1946 had held that there were no French colonies, only metropolitan France, the overseas departments and the overseas territories forming one France, but in practice power stayed centralised in the French Parliament. An enabling law of 31 January 1956 abandoned assimilation in favour of autonomy, to quiet concern over Algeria.

The one million French settlers in Algeria demonstrated in Algiers on 13 May 1958, the crisis ended the Fourth Republic, and General Charles de Gaulle was recalled to write a new constitution. It gave overseas territories the right to request independence. A referendum on 28 September 1958 approved it everywhere except French Guinea, which chose complete independence and became independent on 2 October 1958.

The territorial assemblies had until 4 February 1959 to choose between keeping overseas territory status, becoming a state of the Community or becoming an overseas department. Twelve African territories chose to be states of the Community: Chad, Dahomey, French Sudan, Ivory Coast, Madagascar, Mauritania, Middle Congo, Niger, Senegal, Ubangi-Shari and Upper Volta.

The Community did not fully function until 1959, and its executive council held six sessions that year. Foreign affairs, defence, the currency, economic policy and control of raw materials were common matters, so that, under an appearance of equality, the states' sovereignty was restricted and the precedence of France reaffirmed. The Senate of the Community had little power and was abolished in March 1961.

The constitutional act of 4 June 1960 allowed states to become independent and still remain members. In 1960 the Mali Federation and the Malagasy Republic became independent within the Community in June, and Dahomey, Niger, Upper Volta and Ivory Coast became independent and left it in August. Chad, the Central African Republic, Congo and Gabon became independent within it, and Mauritania left it in November. By 1961 only six states still belonged, and the Community had ceased to function in practice. Its provisions stayed in the constitution until Constitutional Act 95-880 of 4 August 1995 repealed them.

The President of the French Republic was President of the Community and was represented in each member state by a High Commissioner. The Community also had an Executive Council of the heads of government and ministers for common affairs, and a Court of Arbitration of seven judges nominated by the President. The French government remained responsible for security. Africans in the Community did not form a majority voting bloc, since France did not wish to become a colony of its colonies.
french-conquest-of-algeria: The coastal and mountainous parts of Algeria were controlled by the Regency of Algiers, which was nominally part of the Ottoman Empire but acted independently of the Sultan. The dey exercised direct control only in and around Algiers, with governorates called Beyliks in the west, centre and east. Much of the interior was effectively under local Berber and Arab leaders, and the inner Sahara was only claimed by the dey. In 1827 an argument between Hussein Dey and the French consul over debts, and over French attempts to fortify storehouses at Bône and La Calle, escalated into a naval blockade.

Admiral Duperré took an armada of 635 ships from Toulon, and General de Bourmont landed 34,000 soldiers at Sidi Ferruch on 14 June 1830. The French defeated the dey's army at Staouéli on 19 June and entered Algiers on 5 July. The dey accepted capitulation and went into exile in Naples, and the Janissaries left for Turkey, ending 313 years of Ottoman rule there. Governor Clauzel then introduced a civil administration, recruited zouaves and helped form a company to settle European farmers on the land, which set off a land rush.

Resistance centred on Ahmed Bey at Constantine and on Emir Abdelkader in the west. In May 1837 General Bugeaud signed the Treaty of Tafna with Abdelkader, which effectively recognised his control of much of the interior. French forces took Constantine later in 1837, after Clauzel's attack had failed in November 1836; the commander Damrémont was killed in the siege. Abdelkader renewed the jihad in 1839 and waged guerrilla war through 1840. Driven into Morocco in 1842, he fought on until the Moroccan government, pressed by France after the Franco-Moroccan War, attacked him, and he surrendered in 1847.

The conquest of the Sahara began in March 1844 at Biskra under Louis-Philippe, duc d'Aumale, a twenty-two-year-old general, and proceeded partly through agreements with local tribes. The Mokrani Revolt of 1871 in Kabylia spread widely, and by April 250 tribes, nearly a third of Algeria's population, had risen. France secured its Saharan borders only in 1903.

According to several historians, the French methods reached genocidal proportions, and war, famine and disease killed between 500,000 and 1 million Algerians in the first three decades, out of an estimated 3 million. French losses from 1831 to 1851 were 3,336 killed in battle and 92,329 dead of disease in hospital. Various governments and scholars have considered the conquest a genocide. The colonists numbered roughly 130,000 in 1871 and controlled most of the arable land; the number grew to over a million before the century ended.
french-conquest-of-corsica: The Republic of Genoa had ruled Corsica since 1284. In 1729 the Corsican Revolution for independence began, led first by Luiggi Giafferi and Giacinto Paoli and later by Giacinto's son Pasquale Paoli. After a short-lived attempt in 1736 to proclaim a Kingdom of Corsica under the German adventurer Theodor von Neuhoff, the independent Corsican Republic was proclaimed in 1755. Paoli wrote its constitution in Italian, the language of culture on the island, but the republic never managed to drive the Genoese from the coastal fortresses of Calvi and Bonifacio.

After the Corsicans took Capraia, a small island of the Tuscan Archipelago, in 1767, Genoa, exhausted by decades of fighting, decided to sell the island to France, which after its defeat in the Seven Years' War was trying to strengthen its position in the Mediterranean.

King Louis XV sent an expedition in May 1768 to secure French rule. The first, rather small expeditionary force marched inland and suffered an unexpected and significant defeat at the Battle of Borgo in October 1768. France then sent large reinforcements, raising its army on the island to 24,000 men, and under the Comte de Vaux, a veteran of the Seven Years' War, it decisively defeated the Corsican army at the Battle of Ponte Novu. Many Corsicans took to the hills and fought on as guerrillas, so that consolidating French control took about a year, with sporadic rebellions after that.

The invasion set off the Corsican Crisis in British politics: the British government sent secret aid to the Corsicans but chose not to prevent the occupation. Paoli lived in exile in Britain, where he was very popular and joined Samuel Johnson's dining club, until the French Revolution allowed him to return. In 1794 an Anglo-Corsican expedition took the island and set up the Anglo-Corsican Kingdom, but the French reconquered Corsica on 19 October 1796, and it became a French département. Italian remained the official language until 1859.

Napoleon Bonaparte, born on the island in 1769, was a French citizen from birth, although his parents, Carlo Maria Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino, had fought in the resistance against the French while Maria was pregnant with him. Raised as a Corsican nationalist, he gradually turned his loyalty to France and went on to rule it.
french-directory: The Directory grew out of the Constitution of the Year III, which the National Convention debated from 4 July to 17 August 1795 and adopted on 22 August. It was a long document of 377 articles, against 124 in the constitution of 1793. Of five million eligible voters, 1,057,390 approved it in a referendum and 49,978 opposed it. The Convention required that five hundred of its own members remain in the new legislature.

In October 1795 royalists and constitutional monarchists, hostile to that rule, tried to seize power in Paris and were put down. The elections that followed returned 379 members of the old Convention, and the Convention required that every Director be a former member who had voted for the execution of Louis XVI.

The Directory began with an empty treasury and almost worthless assignats. It stopped printing them in 1796, replaced them with the mandats territoriaux, which also collapsed, and then returned to silver and gold coin, which brought falling prices and wages. Bread shortages in Paris in 1796 fed the Conspiracy of the Equals of François-Noël Babeuf, which the government crushed.

The main task was the war against Britain and Austria. The Directory annexed Belgium and the left bank of the Rhine, and set up twenty-nine short-lived sister republics in Italy, Switzerland and the Netherlands, which sent France money and art treasures. By the Treaty of Campoformio of 17 October 1797 France received the Ionian Islands, Belgium and the left bank of the Rhine as far south as Andernach.

The royalists triumphed in the elections of 1797 and were then put down by a coup, and in 1798 the Directors disqualified Jacobin candidates. In 1799 Britain, Austria and Russia formed a Second Coalition. Bonaparte returned from Egypt and, with Abbé Sieyès and others, overthrew the Directory on 9 November 1799.

Five Directors held executive power. The presidency was an entirely ceremonial post, held first by Jean-François Rewbell, chosen by lot on 2 November 1795, and passed on every three months. Louis Gohier was the last president.

Under the Directory the middle and upper classes replaced the nobility at the top of Paris society, and enormous fortunes were made by army suppliers and property speculators. Young Parisians known as Incroyables and Merveilleuses dressed in extravagant costumes and attended the Bals des victimes. The Goncourt brothers reported 640 balls in Paris in 1797 alone. Crime and highway robbery increased, and the death penalty was applied to robberies on the main roads.
french-equatorial-africa: French Equatorial Africa accounted for a little less than an eighth of Africa, across the present-day Central African Republic, Chad, the Republic of the Congo, Gabon and most of Cameroon. The greater part of it extended over a granite plateau framed by the Tibesti, Ouadaï and Fertit massifs, with two basins, that of Chad and that of the Congo. The highest point was Mount Emi Koussi, at 3,415 metres, in Tibesti. The climate ran from arid Saharan in the north to humid tropical in the south, with savannahs in the centre where millet, peanuts and cassava were grown, and tropical forests in the south that supplied ebony and okoumé.

The federation was established in 1910 with four colonial possessions: French Gabon, French Congo, Ubangi-Shari and French Chad. The Governor-General was based in Brazzaville with deputies in each territory. In 1911 France ceded parts of the territory to German Kamerun after the Agadir Crisis, and it was returned after Germany's defeat in World War I.

France granted private companies contracts to exploit ivory and rubber, and Ubangi-Shari had a concession system like that of the Congo Free State, with similar atrocities. The writer André Gide travelled there and was told of mutilations, executions and the burning of children, and his Travels in the Congo, published in 1927, was fiercely critical of the concession companies. The number of victims remains unknown. The French authorities long tolerated indigenous slavery, but acted against the slave trade of the Sultan of Dar Kuti in 1908 and 1911, and annexed his territory in 1912.

Until 1934 the AEF was a federation of colonies, and in that year it became a unitary entity with a single budget. In August 1940 the whole federation except Gabon rallied to the Free French Forces, and Gabon followed after the Battle of Gabon on 12 November 1940. Félix Eboué was installed as Governor-General, and the federation became the strategic centre of Free French activities in Africa. In the September 1958 referendum the territories voted to become autonomous within the French Community and the federation was dissolved. They formed an interim Union of Central African Republics in 1959 and became fully independent in August 1960.
french-first-republic: Under the Legislative Assembly, France was already at war with Prussia and Austria. In July 1792 the Duke of Brunswick, commanding the Austro-Prussian army, issued the Brunswick Manifesto, threatening the destruction of Paris if the royal family were harmed. On 10 August 1792 citizens stormed the Tuileries Palace, killing six hundred of the king's Swiss guards. In the first week of September mobs broke into the city's prisons and killed over half of the prisoners in the September Massacres.

The Convention met for the first time on 21 September 1792 and unanimously abolished the monarchy. The Republic was never formally proclaimed, but acts were dated from the year I of the Republic, and on 25 September it was declared one and indivisible. From 1792 to 1802 France was at war with the rest of Europe, and it also fought internal conflicts such as the wars in Vendée.

Louis XVI was tried for treason from December 1792, convicted on 16 January 1793 and executed on 21 January. Food riots and hunger continued, and on 6 April 1793 the Convention created the Committee of Public Safety, which adopted a policy of terror under which perceived enemies were guillotined at an increasing rate. The Constitution of 1793 was ratified in early August, but the rights it guaranteed were suspended under the committee.

After Robespierre was executed on 28 July 1794, the Jacobin club was closed. The Constitution of the Year III restored freedom of worship, and on 3 November 1795 the Directory was established, with a Council of Elders of 250 members, a Council of Five Hundred and an executive of five directors. Hyperinflation of the paper assignats and military disasters in 1798 and 1799 brought it down after four years.

The Consulate began with the coup of 18 Brumaire, on 9 November 1799, planned by members of the Directory itself, with Napoleon Bonaparte as a co-conspirator and then First Consul. It had four bodies: a Council of State that prepared draft laws, a Tribunate that debated them, a Legislative Body of three hundred that voted on them without debate or amendment, and a Conservative Senate of sixty irremovable members appointed by Bonaparte. On 18 May 1804 the Senate proclaimed Napoleon Emperor of the French, which ended the Republic.
french-flanders: French Flanders lies in the northernmost part of France, in the Nord department of the Hauts-de-France region, and roughly corresponds to the arrondissements of Lille, Douai and Dunkirk on the border with Belgium. With French Hainaut and Cambrésis it makes up the department. The landscape is flat and low-lying, with fertile plains where wheat, sugar beet and chicory are grown. Maritime Flanders, or the Westhoek, runs along the North Sea coast and includes Dunkirk, while inland Flanders is rural, with towns such as Cassel, Hazebrouck and Bailleul and the hills around Cassel. The Lys and the Yser cross the region.

The region was once part of the feudal County of Flanders and later of the Southern Netherlands. It came under English and then Spanish control, became part of the Spanish Netherlands, and was retained by Spain at the end of the Eighty Years' War. It was separated from the county in 1659 by the Peace of the Pyrenees, which ended the French-Spanish conflict, and further parts were added by treaties in 1668 and 1678 under Louis XIV. It then became part of the province of Flanders and Hainaut, and most of it later fell within the department of Nord.

Some western parts had separated in 1237 and formed the County of Artois, which France gained in 1659; they now lie in Pas-de-Calais. Rich in coal and facing the North Sea, French Flanders was fought over many times between the Middle Ages and World War II, when the name was applied to all of Nord-Pas de Calais under German occupation.

French is the main language, but about 20,000 people speak French Flemish, a West Flemish dialect of Dutch, and the traditional language of Walloon Flanders is Picard. Many local schools teach Flemish, partly to revive it, though it has no official recognition as a regional language. The region is known for red-brick architecture, stepped gables and belfries, for the Carnival of Dunkirk and the giant puppet parades of the north, and for dishes such as carbonade flamande, potjevleesch and Maroilles cheese. Its flag and arms follow those of the County of Flanders, a black lion on gold.
french-foreign-legion: Louis Philippe, King of the French, created the Foreign Legion on 10 March 1831 to bring foreign nationals into the French Army from the foreign regiments of the old kingdom. Its recruits included soldiers from the recently disbanded Swiss and German regiments of the Bourbon monarchy. The royal ordinance allowed the foreigners to serve only outside France. The French expeditionary force that had occupied Algiers in 1830 needed reinforcements, so the Legion was sent by sea from Toulon to Algeria. It was first divided into six national battalions: Swiss, Poles, Germans, Italians, Spanish and Dutch-Belgian.

The Legion was initially stationed only in Algeria, where it took part in the conquest, described as a genocide, and in the drying of marshes near Algiers. It served in the First Carlist War in Spain from 1835, the Crimean War in 1854 and the Italian campaign of 1859. It was part of the French intervention in Mexico from 1863 to 1867 and the Tonkin campaign and Sino-French War of the 1880s. French law kept it out of metropolitan France except in an invasion, so it was not in the army that capitulated at Sedan in 1870.

It helped extend the French colonial empire in Africa. After 1871 volunteers from Alsace and Lorraine joined it, and it fought in many critical battles on the Western Front in the First World War. Its numbers swelled in the First Indochina War, and it suffered heavy losses at Dien Bien Phu, which fell on 7 May 1954.

In the Algerian War its parachute regiments fought the National Liberation Front. By the mid-1960s the Legion had lost its home in French Algeria, and Charles de Gaulle, who considered disbanding it, cut it from 40,000 to 8,000 men and moved it to metropolitan France. Over its history it has lost nearly 40,000 men.

The Legion is the only unit of the French Army open to people of any nationality, and most of its commissioned officers are French, with about 10 per cent promoted from the ranks. Legionnaires may apply for French citizenship after three years' service, or at once if wounded in the line of duty, a provision known as Français par le sang versé. Its flags bear the motto Honneur et Fidélité rather than Honneur et Patrie. It marches at 88 steps a minute, against 116 for other French units, and always comes last in a parade. Its marching song is Le Boudin.
french-invasion-of-russia: Napoleon began the campaign to force the Russian Empire to comply with the continental blockade of the United Kingdom. France had been at war with the major European powers since 1792, and Napoleon had won the War of the Third Coalition, the War of the Fourth Coalition and the War of the Fifth Coalition. Russia had learned from earlier defeats at Austerlitz and Friedland. Between 1810 and 1812 it built and rebuilt fortresses, created military intelligence offices and formally established the corps system. In April 1812 Alexander I issued an ultimatum demanding that French troops leave Prussia and the Grand Duchy of Warsaw. Napoleon chose war, and called it the Second Polish War to win support from Polish nationalists.

The multinational Grande Armée crossed the Neman River on 24 June 1812. Estimates of its size vary, with figures of 400,000 to 500,000 men commonly given, and only about half the soldiers were French. The Russian armies under Barclay de Tolly and Pyotr Bagration, together about 180,000 to 220,000 men, retreated eastward and used scorched earth tactics. Heat, disease, desertion and supply failures cost the French heavily before they took Smolensk in August. Mikhail Kutuzov then became commander-in-chief.

At the Battle of Borodino on 7 September, more than 250,000 troops fought and at least 70,000 were killed or wounded. The French took the main positions but failed to destroy the Russian army. Kutuzov decided at the council at Fili to abandon Moscow, and Napoleon entered it on 14 September to find it deserted and set ablaze by its military governor Fyodor Rostopchin. He waited five weeks for a peace offer that never came and left on 19 October. After losing the Battle of Maloyaroslavets he had to retrace his earlier route. Snow, frost, hunger, typhus and attacks by peasants and Cossacks followed. Napoleon left the army at Smorgonie on 5 December and returned to Paris.

Estimates of the losses differ. Richard K. Riehn gives 685,000 men entering Russia and fewer than 70,000 known survivors, while Adam Zamoyski estimates that as many as 400,000 of the 550,000 to 600,000 who crossed the Neman died, counting prisoners who died in captivity. About 100,000 prisoners were taken, and more than 50,000 died. The campaign is also said to have claimed around a million soldiers and civilians. The saying that General Winter defeated Napoleon is disputed, since Minard's map shows the French losses were highest in summer and autumn, owing to inadequate logistics and disease. The campaign remains present in Russian culture through Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace and Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture.
french-invasion-of-switzerland: Vaud was then a subject territory of Bern, and many of its Francophone people felt oppressed by German-speaking Bern; the patriot Frédéric-César de La Harpe called a rising in 1795 and had to flee to France. In late 1797 Napoleon Bonaparte, fresh from founding the Cisalpine Republic, pressed the French Directory to occupy Switzerland, chiefly to secure the Alpine passes into northern Italy. Valtellina, Chiavenna and Bormio seceded to the Cisalpine Republic on 10 October 1797, and the southern Prince-Bishopric of Basel was annexed to France in December.

The Helvetic Revolution began with a patriot rising at Liestal on 17 January 1798. On 24 January the urban elite of Vaud proclaimed the Lemanic Republic at Lausanne, and more than 40 other short-lived republics followed by April.

Invited by the Lemanic Republic, and citing the killing of two French hussars at Thierrens, 12,000 French troops under General Philippe Romain Ménard occupied Vaud from 28 January without resistance. A second army under General Balthazar Alexis Henri Schauenburg advanced on Bern. Fighting began on 1 March, Solothurn surrendered, and Bern's government resigned on 4 March. The next day the Bernese lost at Fraubrunnen and Grauholz; their victory at Neuenegg changed nothing, and their commander Karl Ludwig von Erlach was murdered by his own soldiers. Bern lost 700 killed.

On 12 April 1798, 121 cantonal deputies proclaimed the Helvetic Republic under a constitution drafted in Paris by Peter Ochs. Schwyz, Nidwalden and Uri rejected it and raised about 10,000 men under Alois von Reding, but after Schauenburg's counterattack, the fall of Zug and Lucerne and a defeat at Schindellegi, the Landsgemeinde of Schwyz gave up on 4 May. The French, impressed by their resistance, let them keep their arms. A revolt of the Upper Valais was put down in late May.

In September 1798 the French under Schauenburg crushed the Nidwalden uprising, leaving some 100 dead on both sides and 300 civilians massacred. The conquest of a country neutral since the Revolution strained the Treaty of Campo Formio, helped bring about the Second Coalition, and led to the Austro-Russian campaign in Italy and Switzerland of 1799.
french-revolution: Between 1715 and 1789 the French population grew from 21 to 28 million, and the middle class tripled in size. The benefits of rising prosperity were largely restricted to the rentier and mercantile classes, while living standards fell for wage labourers and peasant farmers who rented their land. An economic recession from 1785 and bad harvests in 1787 and 1788 led to high unemployment and food prices.

The state's finances were in crisis. The nobility and the Church benefited from exemptions, so the tax burden fell mainly on the lower classes, and the parlements could block new tax laws. By 1788 half of state revenue went on servicing the debt. Reforms proposed by the finance minister Calonne in 1786 were rejected, and the notables and parlements argued that new taxes could be approved only by an Estates-General, last held in 1614.

The Estates General met in May 1789, and in June the representatives of the Third Estate re-constituted themselves as a National Assembly. On 14 July a crowd, joined by soldiers, attacked the Bastille, a royal fortress with large stores of arms. Its governor surrendered after fighting that cost the lives of 83 attackers. The Bastille held only seven prisoners but was a potent symbol of the Ancien Régime. The Assembly then abolished feudalism, placed the Catholic Church under state control and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

Military defeats after the outbreak of war in April 1792 led to the insurrection of 10 August 1792. The monarchy was replaced by the First Republic in September, and Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. Political power then passed to the Committee of Public Safety, dominated by Jacobins led by Maximilien Robespierre. About 16,000 people were sentenced by the Revolutionary Tribunal and executed in the Reign of Terror, which ended in July 1794.

The Directory replaced the Committee in November 1795 but faced internal unrest, a weak economy and an expensive war. It ended with the coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799 and the Consulate, with Napoleon Bonaparte as First Consul. The Revolution also began the French Revolutionary Wars, which lasted until Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo in 1815, involved every major European power and redrew the map of Europe.

Historians disagree about the role of ideology: Jonathan Israel holds that the radical Enlightenment was the primary driving force, while Cobban argues that the revolutionaries mostly sought practical solutions to immediate problems.
french-revolutionary-wars: As early as 1791 the other monarchies of Europe looked with outrage on the French Revolution and considered whether to intervene in support of King Louis XVI or to profit from the chaos. On 27 August 1791 Emperor Leopold II and King Frederick William II of Prussia issued the Declaration of Pillnitz, threatening vague but severe consequences if anything befell the king and his family. Leopold meant it as a non-committal gesture, but it was seen in France as a serious threat. France declared war on Austria and Prussia in the spring of 1792, and their coordinated invasion was turned back at the Battle of Valmy in September.

The wars fall into the War of the First Coalition, from 1792 to 1797, and the War of the Second Coalition, from 1798 to 1802. In 1793 France declared war on Great Britain and the Dutch Republic, and drafted hundreds of thousands of men by mass conscription. After reverses, the French regained the initiative at Fleurus in June 1794 and occupied Belgium, the Rhineland and the south of the Netherlands. In 1795 the Batavian Republic was founded, and Prussia signed the Peace of Basel on 6 April, ceding the west bank of the Rhine to France. In Italy in 1796 and 1797 Napoleon Bonaparte drove the Habsburg forces out of the peninsula, and Austria agreed to the Treaty of Campo Formio on 17 October 1797.

In 1798 Napoleon invaded Egypt and won at the Battle of the Pyramids, but Nelson sank his fleet at the Battle of the Nile. The allies gradually pushed the French out of Italy until the French victory at Zurich in September 1799 made Russia drop out of the war. Napoleon failed at the siege of Acre in 1799 and returned to France. Austria signed the Treaty of Lunéville on 9 February 1801. Britain and France signed the Treaty of Amiens in 1802, which is generally taken as the transition to the Napoleonic Wars.

France had conquered territories in Italy, the Low Countries and the Rhineland. The wars spread revolutionary principles over much of Europe, and French armies, mobilized by mass conscription, replaced eighteenth-century armies with their rigid protocols and aristocratic officer classes. Scholars identify the era as the beginning of modern war. The peace with Britain lasted less than a year, though it was the longest period of peace between the two countries between 1793 and 1815.
french-union: The first official use of the term Union française came in the Declaration on Indochina of 24 March 1945. The Union was established by the constitution of the Fourth Republic of 27 October 1946, which held that there were no French colonies and that metropolitan France, the overseas departments and the overseas territories together formed a single France. Its stated goal was the assimilation of the overseas territories into a greater France inhabited by French citizens. It ended the indigène status of colonial subjects.

It had five components: metropolitan France, including the four departments of Algeria; the old colonies that became overseas departments in 1946, Guadeloupe, Guiana, Martinique and Réunion; the new colonies, renamed overseas territories; the associated states, namely Cambodia, Laos, the State of Vietnam, Morocco and Tunisia; and United Nations trust territories such as French Cameroons and French Togoland.

The Union had a President, who was the President of the Republic, a High Council and an Assembly. The Assembly had members from the Council of the Republic, the National Assembly and the regional assemblies of the overseas territories, but ultimately had no power. The High Council met only three times, first in 1951. In practice colonial areas were represented, but all power remained in the French Parliament, and local assemblies had limited authority. Some African leaders, among them Félix Houphouet-Boigny and Leopold Senghor, supported the Union and its investment. African students educated in France came to see a contradiction between the claim of equality and reality, and resistance grew.

The associated states of Indochina moved toward independence between 1949 and 1954, and all three withdrew from the Union in 1954: Vietnam on 20 July, Cambodia in 1955 and Laos in 1957. On 31 January 1956, in response to the Algerian War, the system changed from assimilation to autonomy, allowing territories to develop local government and eventually independence.

In 1958 Charles de Gaulle's Fifth Republic replaced the Union with the French Community, in a constitutional referendum held on 28 September. More than 95% of voters in Guinea, with a turnout of 85.5%, rejected the constitution and so chose independence. French officials there destroyed furniture, lightbulbs and windows, and over 3,000 civil servants and army health officials left. In most other territories upward of 90% approved. The Community did not last long, as most African states left it by 1962, and mentions of it were removed from the French constitution in the 1990s.
french-wars-of-religion: Tensions between Catholics and Protestants had been building since the 1530s. After the Affair of the Placards in October 1534, when Protestant radicals put up posters rejecting the Catholic doctrine of the real presence, Protestantism was clearly defined as heresy. The accidental death of Henry II in July 1559 left a political vacuum and a struggle for power between his widow Catherine de' Medici and powerful nobles: a Catholic faction led by the Guise and Montmorency families and Protestants headed by the House of Condé and Jeanne d'Albret, queen of Navarre. Spain and Savoy supported the Catholics, and England and the Dutch Republic the Protestants.

Catherine, ruling as regent for her son Charles IX, at first backed the moderates known as Politiques. Her Edict of Saint-Germain of January 1562 was opposed by the Guise, and fighting broke out in March after the massacre of Vassy. Condé seized Orléans on 2 April 1562, and the Huguenots took towns along the Loire. In 1572 Catherine backed the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in Paris, in which Catholic mobs killed between 5,000 and 30,000 Protestants throughout France. The wars were commonly counted in eight numbered phases, ended by edicts and peaces such as Amboise and Longjumeau.

The Catholic League, formed by Henri, Duke of Guise, opposed concessions. When the Duke of Anjou died in 1584 the Calvinist Henry of Navarre became heir to Henry III, and the League allied with Philip II of Spain. On 23 December 1588 Henry III had the Duke of Guise killed at Blois, and in July 1589 a Dominican friar, Jacques Clément, stabbed the king to death. Navarre, now Henry IV, abjured Protestantism on 25 July 1593 and was crowned at Chartres on 27 February 1594.

Between two and four million people died from violence, famine or disease directly caused by the conflict, and the power of the monarchy was severely damaged. The Peace of Vervins with Spain was signed in May 1598. The Edict of Nantes granted the Huguenots substantial rights, but it was less a sign of genuine toleration than a grudging truce with guarantees for both sides.

Henry IV was assassinated in 1610, and the political freedoms of the Huguenots, which detractors called a state within the state, caused trouble in the 17th century. Their revolts ended with the Siege of La Rochelle and the Peace of La Rochelle in 1629. Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685.
french-west-india-company: The company was created by the Conseil du Roi on 28 May 1664 as part of Jean-Baptiste Colbert's strategy to compete with the colonial ventures of the Dutch Republic. It received a monopoly of trade between France and all French lands in North and South America and the islands of America, and over the French posts on the coast of Africa from Cape Verde to the Cape of Good Hope. Its purpose was to win back the profits of long-distance trade for France and to build up shipbuilding and the French ports.

The state carried much of the venture. Louis XIV subscribed two million livres of the initial capital against 1.3 million from private investors, and the crown promised to cover the company's losses for its first four years. From its base at Le Havre, 45 vessels were equipped and sent out in less than six months.

In Canada the company brought in the Carignan-Salières Regiment in 1665 against Iroquois attacks, together with 1200 settlers. Jean Talon's first census of 1666 counted 3215 inhabitants, and the colony had grown to 6700 by 1672. In 1665 the company acquired Saint Croix from the Knights of Malta.

It held a monopoly on the slave trade from Senegal and in 1666 set up two trading posts in Dahomey, at Savi and Ouidah. In the Caribbean it clashed with French settlers who smuggled with the Dutch: its monopoly made French sugar dear beside that of Barbados and Jamaica, and planters accused it of delivering too few enslaved people. A secret plan of 1669 to seize Dutch posts on the Gold Coast came to nothing.

By 1670 Colbert claimed the company had succeeded in stimulating private French shipping to French America. The Franco-Dutch War brought it into financial hardship: it borrowed heavily and gave up its exclusive privilege on the coasts of Guinea. Liquidation began in January 1672, and when its monopoly was revoked in December 1674 the French state took direct control of its American possessions. It was succeeded in Africa by the Compagnie du Sénégal and in America by private traders.
frere-jacques: The earliest known version of the melody is in a French manuscript, titled Recueil de Timbres de Vaudevilles and held by the Bibliothèque Nationale, which the library dates between 1775 and 1785. There the tune is labelled Frère Blaise. A publication of 1825 printed the words with a description of the melody in solfège but without musical notation. The words and music appear together in Charles Lebouc's popular collection of children's rounds, Récréations de l'enfance, issued by Rouart, Lerolle in Paris. The musicologist Sylvie Bouissou has found some evidence that Jean-Philippe Rameau wrote the music, since a manuscript at the French National Library lists him as author of this piece among 86 canons.

The French song asks a friar, Frère Jacques, whether he is sleeping and tells him to sound the bell for matins, the midnight or very early morning prayers. The usual English version, Brother John, keeps the rhythm but reverses the sense, so that the bells wake the sleeper. English friar comes from the Old French frere, which comes in turn from the Latin frater.

Several origins have been proposed. A link with the 17th-century surgeon Frère Jacques Beaulieu was explored without evidence, and Martine David and A. Marie Delrieu suggest the song mocked the Dominican friars, known in France as the Jacobin order, for sloth. Resemblances exist with a piece by Girolamo Frescobaldi first published around 1615, with a French song of 1650 and with a Hungarian folk tune.

The tune is one of the simplest repeating canons, like Three Blind Mice, and it has spread easily. In 1926 officers of the Whampoa Military Academy used it for the patriotic song Revolution of the Citizens, and in China it is also widely thought of as a folk song called Two Tigers. Gustav Mahler set it in a minor key in the third movement of his Symphony No. 1, calling it by its German name, Bruder Martin. Leonard Bernstein used it to explain counterpoint in his Young People's Concerts. The Beatles' Paperback Writer has the title sung beneath its last verse, and the French group Les Frères Jacques took its name from the song's friar.
fretilin: Fretilin was founded on 20 May 1974 as the Timorese Social Democratic Association (ASDT). It renamed itself Fretilin on 11 September 1974 and took a more radical stance, proclaiming itself the sole legitimate representative of the East Timorese people. After a coup by the Timorese Democratic Union (UDT) on 11 August 1975, Fretilin hastily formed an armed wing, Falintil, which emerged victorious after a three-week civil war.

Fretilin declared East Timor's independence from Portugal on 28 November 1975 and inaugurated an 18-member cabinet drawn from its Central Committee, with Francisco Xavier do Amaral as president and Nicolau dos Reis Lobato as vice president and prime minister. Falintil fought the Indonesian armed forces during their invasion on 7 December 1975 and the occupation that followed. The two leaders fell out under the pressure of the occupation, and in September 1977 Lobato had do Amaral arrested for high treason. Lobato, as president, was killed by Indonesian forces on 31 December 1978, and his successor, António Duarte Carvarino, was tracked down and executed on 2 February 1979. From September 1977 to February 1979 only three of the 52 members of the Central Committee survived.

Fretilin survived the military collapse and was slowly rebuilt under the relatively moderate and nationalist leadership of Xanana Gusmão. Between March 1981 and April 1984 it was known as the Partido Marxista–Leninista Fretilin and Marxism-Leninism was its declared ideology; in 1984 the old name returned and revolutionary politics was dropped to further national unity and win the support of the UDT and the Catholic Church.

In the first elections, in 2001, Fretilin polled 57.4% of the vote and took 55 of the 88 seats in the Assembly, a working majority short of the two-thirds it had hoped for to draft the constitution. It formed the government until independence in 2002. In June 2007 it again came first, but with 29% of the vote and 21 seats, and its secretary-general, Mari Alkatiri, spoke of a minority government. On 6 August José Ramos-Horta announced that a coalition led by the CNRT of Xanana Gusmão would govern instead. Fretilin denounced the decision as unconstitutional, and its supporters in Dili held violent protests.

The CNRT was in power from 2007 to 2017. After the July 2017 election Alkatiri formed a coalition government, but his minority government soon fell, and a second general election in May 2018 was won by the CNRT as part of the Alliance for Change and Progress. Francisco Guterres of Fretilin was president from 2017 to 2022, and lost his bid for a second term to José Ramos-Horta.
friday-mosque-of-herat: The mosque stands on ground where religious buildings had been located for many centuries. The first known building was a Zoroastrian temple converted into a mosque in the 7th century; it was later enlarged by the Ghaznavids, and in the second half of the 11th century a smaller mosque with a wooden roof was founded under the Khwarazmian dynasty. An earthquake in 1102 almost destroyed it, and a later fire ruined the rebuilt mosque. The Ghurids seized Herat in 1175, and at the end of the 12th century Sultan Ghiyath al-Din Muhammad chose the plot of the burned mosque and additional land in the elevated north-eastern quarter, which had a direct water supply for its fountain.
When he died in 1203 he was buried in a mausoleum in the mosque. His son Sultan Ghayath-ul-din Mahmood continued the work, which was completed in 1210 with a madrasa added.

The Ghurids built the original mosque entirely of brick on a four-iwan plan around a courtyard with a water basin, now disappeared. The qibla faces west, about 20 degrees off the true direction of Mecca. The present complex is 180 metres long and 120 metres wide, with 460 domes, 444 pillars and 12 minarets, grouped around a courtyard 82 by 60 metres. At the south-east corner stands the Ghurid portal, which has not served as an entrance since unknown times; its brick mosaic and terracotta Kufic inscriptions, glazed blue on the front, survive. Stucco ornament of the Ghurid period has been uncovered in the southern and western iwans.

After the Mongols conquered Herat in 1221 the mosque fell into ruin, and rebuilding began only after 1245 under Shams al-Din Kart. An earthquake in 1364 nearly destroyed it again. The last Kart ruler commissioned a bronze basin in 1375 that is still in the mosque.

Under the Timurid Shah Rukh (1405 to 1444) the courtyard facades received glazed tile mosaic and a marble mihrab, and Mir Ali-Shir Nava'i, adviser to Sultan Husayn Bayqara, remodelled it with a marble minbar and more tilework. The Timurid period corresponds to the time of its highest magnificence.

A major renovation took place in 1942 and 1943, with a tile studio established by UNESCO, and a fuller reconstruction followed from 1951 to 1973 that left little of the original Ghurid plasterwork or Timurid decoration visible. In the Soviet-Afghan War a rocket brought down a minaret in 1986, killing many people, and repairs were not finished until 1995. During the Taliban's rule in Herat from 1996 to 2001 the mosque was closed to non-Muslims. The roofs were renovated in 2002, and parts of old Ghurid decoration were found in 2004.
fridtjof-nansen: Fridtjof Wedel-Jarlsberg Nansen was born on 10 October 1861. The family originated in Denmark, where the trader Hans Nansen, an early explorer of the White Sea region, became borgmester of Copenhagen in 1654. In 1880 Nansen passed his university entrance examination and chose to study zoology at the Royal Frederick University in Christiania, saying later that he thought it offered a life in the open air. He later worked as a curator at the University Museum of Bergen, where his research on the nervous system of lower marine creatures earned him a doctorate and helped establish the neuron doctrine.

Earlier attempts on the Greenland interior, by Adolf Erik Nordenskiöld in 1883 and Robert Peary in 1886, had set out from Disko Bay and turned back after about 160 kilometres. Nansen proposed to travel from east to west, so that his party would have no line of retreat. The sealer Jason picked up his party at Ísafjörður on 3 June 1888, and after weeks of drifting along the coast they crossed the interior on skis. Between thirty and forty thousand people crowded the streets of Christiania to welcome the party in 1889.

He then planned to reach the North Pole by drifting with the current. The naval engineer Colin Archer built the ship Fram, with a rounded hull designed to be pushed upwards by pack ice, and it left Christiania on 24 June 1893. On 14 March 1895 Nansen and Hjalmar Johansen left the ship to dash for the pole, reaching 86°14′ N before turning back. They met the British explorer Frederick Jackson at Cape Flora on 17 June. After 1896 Nansen turned chiefly to oceanography, and in 1905 he spoke out for ending the union with Sweden.

In 1921 Nansen became High Commissioner for Refugees at the League of Nations, with the task of resettling about two million Russian refugees. He introduced the Nansen passport for stateless people, recognised by more than 50 countries, and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922. He died of a heart attack on 13 May 1930, and his ashes were laid under a tree at Polhøgda. The Nansen International Office for Refugees, set up afterwards, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1938.
friedberg-hesse: Friedberg is the capital of the Wetteraukreis district, about 30 kilometres north of Frankfurt am Main in the Wetterau region. It stands on the river Usa just before it flows into the Wetter, on a basalt plateau, and extends west into the Taunus up to the 518-metre Steinkopf. It has been populated at least since Roman times: relics of a Mesolithic settlement have been found in the suburb of Bruchenbrücken, and Castle Hill was the site of a Roman military camp on the limes, presumably the castellum in monte tauno of Roman records of the 1st century, though this is still discussed. The remains of Roman baths survive. The Roman settlement was abandoned in the retreat from the Rhine frontier by 260 CE.

The Hohenstaufen dynasty of the Holy Roman Empire refounded the old city at a point convenient for important trade routes. It at first rivalled Frankfurt with an important annual trading fair and rapid growth, but its fortunes soon dwindled. Friedberg consisted of two entities, the city and the castle, which were politically independent and in permanent, often malicious competition, and which once ended with angry citizens ransacking and destroying the castle. The city became a Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire by a charter of 1211.

From the 14th to the 15th century the castle was a noble republic in which twelve noble families shared a single castle. Between 1337 and 1498 its constitution developed, with knightly families holding the right to elect a burgrave, two Baumeister and twelve Regimentsburgmannen, who represented the community, kept up the buildings and governed its affairs. The arrangement was unusual in being sustained by many families under a formal constitution. Under Napoleon Friedberg was incorporated in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, or Hesse-Darmstadt.

Friedberg's old town once housed a prosperous Jewish community. Many Jews fled to Palestine and the United States before the Holocaust, and all who remained were deported to Treblinka in 1942. The medieval Jewish ceremonial bath, the Judenbad, a memorial to the old synagogue burned down, and a plaque at a school remain. From about 1956 to 2007 the town was the home of a United States Army installation, Ray Barracks.

Friedberg has seven districts: Bruchenbrücken, Friedberg, Dorheim, Ockstadt, Bauernheim, Fauerbach and Ossenheim. Its most prominent feature is the castle's Adolfsturm, whose crown was restored in the 1980s. The main station lies on the Main-Weser Railway and is the northern terminus of Frankfurt's S-Bahn line S6.
friedenstein-palace: The site was first occupied by Grimmenstein Castle, mentioned in 1316. After the Ernestine branch of the House of Wettin lost the Battle of Mühlberg in 1547, imperial forces blew up its fortifications, and in 1567 the fortress was almost completely razed after John Frederick II tried to regain the electoral title by force. In 1640 Ernest I, first ruler of the new Duchy of Saxe-Gotha, chose Gotha, the duchy's largest town, as his residence. By naming the palace Friedenstein he set it apart from its warlike predecessor. Andreas Rudolph built it to plans by Casper Vogell, and Ernest justified its size by the need to house the new duchy's administration.

The palace follows a form favoured by Protestant rulers of the time, with one dominant wing: the four-storey north wing, 100 metres long, faces the town, and the two side wings are 140 metres long. Its plain exterior was chosen to contrast with the ornate palaces of Catholic princes, and statues of Moses, Elijah, John the Baptist and Martin Luther once stood at its corners. The ground floors held an armoury, a stable, a mint and a smithy, the first floor the ducal offices and the second the state rooms. After lightning burned the east pavilion in 1677, Frederick I rebuilt the interior.

In the west pavilion, Caspar Lindemann and Hans Hoffmann built the Schlosstheater in 1681-87. It is named after Conrad Ekhof, called the father of German acting, who directed it from 1774 until his death in 1778, and its scenery machinery is largely unchanged since 1683. The English landscape garden to the south, laid out after 1769 to designs by John Haverfield, is one of the oldest in continental Europe.

From 1826 Gotha passed to the House of Saxe-Coburg, which lived mainly at Coburg, and Charles Edward abdicated on 23 November 1918, after which the palace became a museum. Much of its art went to the Soviet Union as war reparations after World War II and was mostly returned in the late 1950s. Five paintings stolen on the night of 13-14 December 1979 were recovered only after 40 years. Today it holds the Schlossmuseum, the Museum der Natur, the Historical Museum Gotha and the Forschungsbibliothek Gotha.
friedrich-durrenmatt: Friedrich Reinhold Dürrenmatt was born on 5 January 1921 in Konolfingen, in the canton of Bern, the son of a Protestant pastor. His grandfather Ulrich Dürrenmatt was a conservative politician. The family moved to Bern in 1935. In 1941 he began studying philosophy and literature at the University of Zürich but moved to Bern after one semester and also studied natural science. As a student he was briefly a member of the Fröntler, a far-right movement, an activity he later attributed to a wish to rebel against his father. In 1943 he decided to become an author and left academic life.

Like Bertolt Brecht, Dürrenmatt explored epic theatre, and he has been called its most original theorist after Brecht. His first play, It Is Written, premiered in April 1947 amid fights and protests in the audience. It sets a sensation-craving cynic against a religious fanatic in a city under siege. From 1948 to 1949 he wrote sketches for the anti-Nazi Cabaret Cornichon in Zürich. His first major success was Romulus the Great, set in 476 CE during the last days of the Roman Empire.

The Visit (1956) is his most widely performed and translated play, a grotesque mixture of comedy and tragedy about a wealthy woman who offers her hometown a fortune if its people avenge the wrongs done to her. The Physicists (1962) is a satire on the responsibility of science for dangerous changes to the world. He also wrote radio plays and detective novels, among them The Judge and His Hangman (1950) and Suspicion (1951). In 1970 he announced his intention to abandon literature and adapt established works for the theatre instead.

Dürrenmatt married the actress Lotti Geißler in 1946, and they had three children. After her death in 1983 he married Charlotte Kerr in 1984. In 1990 he gave a speech for Václav Havel, Switzerland, a Prison, after learning that he and 800,000 other left-leaning Swiss had been spied on for five decades by the Swiss secret service. He died of heart failure on 14 December 1990 in Neuchâtel. Over 1,000 of his paintings and drawings have been exhibited since 2000 in the Centre Dürrenmatt Neuchâtel, designed by Mario Botta around his former home.
friedrich-ebert: Friedrich Ebert was born in Heidelberg on 4 February 1871, the seventh of nine children of a tailor. His family could not afford university, so he trained as a saddle-maker from 1885 to 1888 and then travelled as a journeyman. He joined the Social Democratic Party in Mannheim in 1889. He read Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels but cared more for practical and organisational questions that would improve workers' lives.

After settling in Bremen in 1891 he worked on a socialist newspaper, ran a pub that became a centre of socialist and union activity, and was elected to the Bremen assembly in 1900. In 1905 he became Secretary-General of the party and moved to Berlin, and in 1913, after August Bebel's death, he was elected party leader.

In August 1914 Ebert led the party's Reichstag members to vote almost unanimously for war loans, regarding the war as a defensive measure against the autocratic regime of the Tsar. He backed the Burgfrieden, the truce among parties for the duration of the war, a stance that contributed to a split in 1917 when opponents of the war formed the Independent Social Democratic Party. Two of his four sons were killed in the war. In October 1918 he persuaded his party to join the government of Prince Maximilian of Baden, arguing that it was a duty. He did not favour a republic, and told the prince that he hated social revolution like sin.

After the revolution reached Berlin on 9 November 1918, Ebert and the party leadership sided with the civil service, army, police and judiciary against those who wanted a more radical revolution. He and General Wilhelm Groener planned the return of army units to Berlin in December. On 11 February 1919 the National Assembly, meeting at Weimar, elected him provisional president, and he was sworn in under the new constitution on 21 August 1919. He denounced the Treaty of Versailles as unbearable but accepted it after Hindenburg concluded the army could not resume the war.

Ebert suffered from gallstones. A Magdeburg court in December 1924 fined a journalist who had called him a traitor, yet said that, in strict legal terms, he had committed treason by his role in the January 1918 strike. He gave evidence and delayed medical help. In February 1925 he underwent an emergency appendectomy and died of septic shock on 28 February, aged 54. Paul von Hindenburg succeeded him on 12 May. Historians remain divided. Some defend his actions as the price of preventing a socialist state on the model promoted by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, while leftist critics call him a traitor who paved the way for the far right.
friedrich-engels: Friedrich Engels was born on 28 November 1820 in Barmen, in Prussia, now part of Wuppertal. He was the eldest of nine children of Friedrich Engels Sr., a prosperous cotton mill owner, in a devout Pietist Protestant family. He grew up in the Wupper valley, an early industrial centre known as the German Manchester, and saw polluted rivers, dangerous working conditions and the contrast between the merchant elite's houses and the poverty of the workers.

In September 1841 he began a year of military service in Berlin, where he attended the University of Berlin as a non-matriculated student and joined the Young Hegelian circle known as Die Freien. In 1842 his father sent him to Manchester to work in a cotton mill in which the family had an investment, and his experience of the industrial working class led to The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845).

In August 1844 Engels met Karl Marx for the second time in Paris, and over ten days they found their complete agreement in all theoretical fields. Their first joint work was The Holy Family (1845). After moving to Brussels they wrote The German Ideology, which argued that social structures, politics and ideas are determined by the economic base; it was never published in their lifetimes. The Communist League commissioned them to write the Manifesto of 1848, and Engels fought in the Revolutions of 1848 before exile in England.

In November 1850 he returned to Manchester and the firm of Ermen & Engels to support Marx financially. He led a double life as a respectable cotton merchant and a clandestine communist, became a partner in 1864, and over twenty years sent the Marx family between 3,000 and 4,000 pounds, which effectively funded Das Kapital. He retired in 1870 and moved to London, where he joined the General Council of the International Working Men's Association.

Anti-Dühring (1878) explained their shared scientific socialism in response to Eugen Dühring's influence in Germany, and a section of it appeared separately as Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880). After Marx's death in 1883 Engels devoted his life to editing his writings, completing the second and third volumes of Das Kapital. His application of dialectics to science, in works such as Dialectics of Nature, was later controversially developed into the state ideology of the Soviet Union. He died of cancer in London on 5 August 1895, and his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head.
friedrich-hayek: Friedrich August von Hayek was born in Vienna on 8 May 1899 to August von Hayek, a medical doctor and part-time botany lecturer at the University of Vienna, and Felicitas Hayek, née von Juraschek. In his teens Hayek fought in the First World War, and he said later that this experience, together with a wish to help avoid the mistakes that led to the war, drew him into economics. At the University of Vienna he first studied philosophy, psychology and economics, and he earned doctorates in law in 1921 and in political science in 1923.

With the help of Ludwig von Mises, Hayek directed the Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research in the late 1920s. He joined the London School of Economics in 1931 at the invitation of Lionel Robbins. In Prices and Production (1931) he argued that the business cycle resulted from a central bank's credit expansion, which, by holding interest rates artificially low, caused capital to be misallocated. Building on Mises, he argued that central planners could never have enough information to allocate resources reliably.

The Road to Serfdom (1944) grew from his concern at the view in British academia that fascism was a capitalist reaction to socialism; Hayek argued that fascism, Nazism and state socialism shared roots in central economic planning. In 1950 he left London for the University of Chicago's Committee on Social Thought, and from 1962 until 1968 he taught at the University of Freiburg, where he worked on Law, Legislation and Liberty. On 9 October 1974 it was announced that he would share the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics with Gunnar Myrdal.

Hayek also wrote on psychology. The Sensory Order (1952) set out a learning and memory model close to what became known as Hebbian learning. In social and political philosophy he based his views on the limits of human knowledge and on spontaneous order, favouring a market order in which the state mostly enforces abstract legal rules. In 1975 Margaret Thatcher, newly elected leader of the Conservative Party, held up his book The Constitution of Liberty at a meeting and said that this was what the party believed. He received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1991 and died on 23 March 1992.
friedrich-hecker: Hecker was born at Eichtersheim, now Angelbachtal, the son of a revenue official, and studied law at the University of Heidelberg. In 1838 he was an advocate before the Supreme Court in Mannheim. Elected to the Second Chamber of Baden in 1842, he joined the opposition at once and helped to oust the Blittersdorf ministry. A speech of 6 February 1845 against the incorporation of Schleswig and Holstein with Denmark made him known beyond Baden, and a democratic campaign with Johann Adam von Itzstein led to his expulsion from Prussia.

With Gustav von Struve he drew up the radical programme adopted at Offenburg on 12 September 1847. In the preliminary Frankfurt Parliament he moved that Germany be declared a republic, without success. After the arrest of a friend, the editor of the Constanzer Seeblatt, on 8 April 1848, he and Struve summoned armed men to Donaueschingen for 14 April; they expected 70,000 but only a few thousand came. Troops of Baden and Hesse under General Friedrich von Gagern defeated them near Kandern on 20 April, though Gagern was killed.

From the Canton of Basel he published a radical newspaper and wrote Die Volkserhebung in Baden. Refused admission to the Frankfurt Parliament though twice elected for Thiengen, he emigrated in September 1848 and bought a farm near Belleville, Illinois. In 1856 he and Abraham Lincoln were chosen as Illinois Republican electors-at-large. In the Civil War he commanded the 24th Illinois Infantry Regiment until December 1861 and from October 1862 the 82nd Illinois, and was badly wounded at Chancellorsville on 2 May 1863.

In 1864 Hecker led a faction of Frémont supporters against Lincoln's renomination. After the war he returned to his farm, wrote for the German-language press and in 1873 visited Germany, where he criticised the new state's lack of individual rights. He died at his farm in Summerfield, Illinois, on 24 March 1881. The Heckerlied and the Hecker hat, a broad slouch hat with a feather, became symbols of middle-class political activism, and a monument to him was installed in Benton Park, St. Louis, on 1 October 1882.
friedrich-hildebrandt: Hildebrandt was born on 19 September 1898 at Kiekindemark, now part of Parchim, the son of a farm worker. He volunteered for the Imperial German Army in April 1916, was badly gassed in Flanders in 1917 and won the Iron Cross. In 1919 he fought with the Freikorps von Brandis in Upper Silesia and the Baltic until the Red Army captured him at Riga. In 1920 he joined the security police in Halle and took part in putting down the Kapp-Putsch; tried for brutality against captured Spartakists, he was acquitted but dismissed. In 1924 he entered the Landtag of Mecklenburg-Schwerin for the German Völkisch Freedom Party.

He joined the refounded Nazi Party in February 1925 and was named Gauleiter of Mecklenburg-Lübeck on 27 March 1925. He founded the Niederdeutscher Beobachter in 1927 and entered the Reichstag in September 1930. Suspended by Rudolf Hess in July 1930 for criticising Adolf Hitler's alliance with industry, he was reinstated in January 1931 after declaring his loyalty. In 1933 he also became governor of the Free City of Lübeck, and he joined the SS that December, rising to SS-Obergruppenführer in 1942. He later commanded the Volkssturm in his Gau.

Hildebrandt took part in the murders of Aktion T4: in April 1941 he had the deaconess house at Lübtheen seized, and the mentally handicapped children living there were taken to Schwerin and later murdered. In the winter of 1941 to 1942 several thousand Soviet prisoners of war starved to death in Mecklenburg, and by the end of 1943 there were 152,148 foreign workers there, most held against their will as slave labourers.

Arrested by the British after the war, he was handed to the Americans in 1946 for his part in orders to execute downed Allied airmen in 1944. The British and Americans refused repeated Soviet demands for his extradition over the euthanasia murders at Sachsenberg. At the Dachau trials in 1947 he and five others were sentenced to death for the killing of American airmen. Appeals for clemency failed, and he was hanged at Landsberg Prison on 5 November 1948, blaming Communists for his fate in his last statement.
friedrich-joachim-stengel: Friedrich Joachim Michael Stengel was born on 29 September 1694 to a Protestant family in Zerbst. At 14 he moved to Berlin into the care of his mother's brother and studied at the Prussian Academy of Arts, learning fortification engineering, civil architecture, artillery and geometry. In 1712 he entered the military service of Saxe-Gotha as a cadet and spent several months in northern Italy during the War of the Spanish Succession.

From 1715 to 1719 Stengel worked as a state surveyor for the duchies of Saxe-Gotha and Saxe-Eisenach. A survey in Saxe-Eisenach brought him into contact with Adolphus von Dalberg, and he went to Fulda as surveyor and building inspector until 1729. In 1733 he became court architect to Prince Charles of Nassau-Usingen, for whom he converted the Prinzenpalais and built the east and west wings of Biebrich Palace in Wiesbaden.

In 1735 William Henry, Prince of Nassau-Saarbrücken, asked him to report on the condition of Saarbrücken Castle, his intended residence. Stengel found it structurally unsound and in 1738 was commissioned to plan its rebuilding, completed in 1748. He moved to Saarbrücken in 1740, and with the prince turned the town into a Baroque residence, drawing up building codes and planning new urban spaces, commercial buildings and houses across the principality. His works there include the Friedenskirche (1743–1751), the Basilica of St. John the Baptist (1754–1758) and the Ludwigskirche (1762–1775), and nearby Schloss Jägersberg in Neunkirchen. He also rebuilt Dornburg Castle for Joanna Elisabeth of Holstein-Gottorp between 1751 and 1758.

In 1761 Stengel became General Building Director and Real Chamber Councilor of Nassau-Saarbrücken; he also presided over the Forest Chamber and directed the Saarbrücken orphanage, poorhouse and penitentiary until he retired in 1775. He married Katharina Hoffmann in 1720; she died in 1741, and a year later he married Klara Storch, first maid to Princess Charlotte Amalie of Nassau-Dillenburg. Their sons Johann Friedrich and Balthasar Wilhelm both became master builders like their father. Stengel died on 10 January 1787 at the age of 92 and was buried in Saarbrücken two days later.
friedrich-ludwig-weidig: Weidig was born on 15 February 1791 in Oberkleen, in Langgöns north-west of the Wetterau, the son of a chief forester and his wife, born Liebknecht. He went to school in Butzbach from 1803 and studied theology at the Ludoviciana in Giessen, where he belonged to the fränkische Landsmannschaft. In 1812 he became headmaster of the boys' school in Butzbach. Following the example of Friedrich Ludwig Jahn, he taught his pupils drill and gymnastics, and in 1814 he laid out an exercise ground on the Schrenzer, a foothill of the Taunus; later writers called him the father of Hessian drill.

From 1818 the authorities watched his teaching, preaching and private life, for he was one of the liberal democrats who wanted Germany to become a unified democratic nation state. In 1832 he travelled to south-west Germany to help prepare the Hambach Festival. First arrested in 1833, he still published four illegal issues of Leuchter und Beleuchter für Hessen in 1834. That year he met Georg Büchner and worked with him on the manuscript he then published, against Büchner's wishes, as Der Hessische Landbote, while he and his students organised the printing and distribution of illegal pamphlets.

On 5 April 1834 he was suspended from teaching and sent as pastor to the small village of Ober-Gleen in the Vogelsberg. When the Landbote was betrayed that summer Büchner fled to Straßburg, but Weidig refused to emigrate to Switzerland with his family.

He was soon arrested in the Klosterkaserne barracks in Friedberg and in June 1835 taken to Darmstadt. There, after two years of questioning and physical abuse by state investigators, among them Konrad Georgi, a known alcoholic, he took his own life on 23 February 1837. His letters to his wife from prison were held back for many years for reasons of state. His friends called him a freedom fighter on his gravestone, but the authorities had the words bricked over. The Weidigschule in Butzbach bears his name.
friedrich-schiller: Johann Christoph Friedrich Schiller was born on 10 November 1759 in Marbach, in the Duchy of Württemberg, the only son of the military doctor Johann Kaspar Schiller and Elisabetha Dorothea Schiller. He grew up in a devoutly Lutheran family and spent much of his youth studying the Bible. His parents wanted him to become a priest, and the village priest taught him Latin and Greek. In 1773 he entered the Karlsschule Stuttgart, an elite military academy founded by Karl Eugen, Duke of Württemberg, and graduated as a doctor of medicine in 1780.

At the school he read Rousseau and Goethe and wrote The Robbers, a play about two aristocratic brothers, one of whom leads rebellious students into the Bohemian forest as Robin Hood-like bandits. Its critique of social corruption astounded its first audience and made him an overnight sensation.

In 1780 Schiller became a regimental doctor in Stuttgart, a post he disliked. He left his regiment without permission to see the first performance of The Robbers in Mannheim, was arrested, sentenced to 14 days of imprisonment and forbidden by the duke to publish further works. In 1782 he fled Stuttgart and went by way of Frankfurt, Mannheim, Leipzig and Dresden to Weimar. On 26 May 1789 he gave his inaugural lecture as professor of History and Philosophy at the University of Jena and wrote historical works there. On 22 February 1790 he married Charlotte von Lengefeld.

From 1788 until his death he kept a productive but complicated friendship with Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who convinced him to return to playwriting. Together they founded the Weimar Theater and wrote the Xenien, satirical short poems aimed at their opponents. The Duke of Saxe-Weimar ennobled him in 1802.

Schiller's philosophical work was concerned above all with human freedom, a theme that runs through his histories and plays: the Wallenstein trilogy concerns the Thirty Years' War, and Don Carlos the revolt of the Netherlands against Spain. His On the Aesthetic Education of Man, first published in 1794, was prompted by his disillusion with the French Revolution and its descent into violence, and argues that a people's moral character can be raised by first touching their souls with beauty. He died of tuberculosis in Weimar in 1805, aged 45. A skull long believed to be his was shown by DNA tests in 2008 not to be.
friedrich-schlegel: Friedrich Schlegel was born on 10 March 1772 at Hanover, where his father, Johann Adolf Schlegel, was pastor at the Lutheran Market Church. The family was fervently Protestant, but as a young man he rejected religion in favour of atheism and individualism. He studied law for two years at Göttingen and Leipzig and met Friedrich Schiller, then in 1793 devoted himself entirely to literary work. In 1796 he moved to Jena, where his brother August Wilhelm lived, and collaborated with Novalis, Ludwig Tieck, Fichte and Caroline Schelling. In 1797 he quarrelled with Schiller, who disliked his polemical work.

Schlegel published Die Griechen und Römer in 1797 and a history of Greek and Roman poetry in 1798, then turned to Dante, Goethe and Shakespeare. With his brother he founded the journal Athenaeum, in which fragments, aphorisms and essays set out the principles of the Romantic school. They are generally recognised as deep and significant expressions of the subjective idealism of the early Romanticists. In 1799 he published the first part of the novel Lucinde, seen as an account of his affair with Dorothea Veit, which caused a scandal in German literary circles. It contributed to the failure of his academic career in Jena.

In Paris from 1802 he studied Sanskrit and Persian. In 1808 he published Über die Sprache und Weisheit der Indier, arguing that a people originating from India founded the first European civilizations. He compared Sanskrit with Latin, Greek, Persian and German and noted many similarities in vocabulary and grammar. The common features he asserted are now generally accepted with significant revisions, while the Out-of-India model has been discredited. He was the first to notice what became known as Grimm's law, and he was a pioneer of comparative linguistics.

Schlegel married Dorothea Veit in Paris in April 1804, and in 1808 the couple joined the Catholic Church in Cologne Cathedral. From then on he increasingly opposed political and religious liberalism. In 1809 he moved to Vienna and was appointed imperial court secretary at the military headquarters, editing the army newspaper and issuing proclamations against Napoleon. After the Congress of Vienna he was councillor of legation at the Austrian embassy in Frankfurt, and in 1820 he started a conservative Catholic magazine, Concordia. He died on 12 January 1829 at Dresden while preparing a series of lectures.
friedrich-von-gartner: Gärtner was born in Koblenz on 10 December 1791. His father, also an architect, moved to Munich in 1804, and there the son received his first training. To complete it he went to Paris in 1812 to study under Percier, and in 1814 to Italy, where he spent four years studying antiquities. The result appeared in 1819 as a set of views, with descriptions, of the best-preserved monuments of Sicily.

After a visit to England he was appointed professor of architecture at the Academy of Munich in 1820, which began his practical work, and in 1822 artistic director of the Nymphenburg Porcelain Manufactory. He became head government surveyor of buildings and, from 1842, director of the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. With Leo von Klenze he is the best known architect of Bavaria under Ludwig I, and his generally Romanesque style was much to the king's taste.

His Ludwigskirche strongly influenced church architecture elsewhere, especially in North America. Besides his buildings on the Ludwigstrasse he designed the Wittelsbacher Palais in Munich, since destroyed, the Pompejanum at Aschaffenburg and the Kursaal and arcades at Bad Kissingen. He began the Befreiungshalle at Kelheim, which Klenze redesigned and completed. His palace in Athens is now the seat of the Hellenic Parliament. Gärtner died in Munich on 21 April 1847 and is buried in the Alter Südfriedhof there. His son, also named Friedrich Gärtner, became a noted architectural painter.
friedrich-wilhelm-von-haugwitz: Haugwitz was born in Saxony on 11 December 1702, the son of a general in Saxon service. As a young man he went to Rome and then entered the civil service in Silesia, a post that ended when Frederick II invaded the province and Haugwitz escaped to Vienna. Maria Theresa sent him to the part of Silesia still under her rule to put its finances in order. A student of the Austrian cameralist Wilhelm von Schröder, he had learned hostility towards the wealthy estates, and he admired the new Prussian administration of Silesia.

He aimed to change the monarchy's institutions by dividing government functions, centralising the economy and supplying the crown with economic information. He separated justice from political and fiscal affairs through a new High Court, the Oberste Justizstelle. The Directorium in publicis et cameralibus, which he headed, supervised the lands of the monarchy, and its local offices, the Representationen und Cammern, collected taxes so that most of each levy reached the crown. Through the Theresianum he brought Johann Heinrich Gottlob Justi to Vienna to teach cameralism and modern economics, though Justi, a Protestant and former Prussian soldier, was distrusted there.

To support a standing army of 108,000 he sought 14 million gulden from the estates and, against their resistance, secured a guarantee of payment for ten years, the Ten Years' Recess. He also introduced something close to conscription, uniform dress, Prussian tactics and a school to train officers in them. His reforms did not reach Hungary, Transylvania, the Netherlands or Lombardy, and the Seven Years' War thwarted many of them. The Directorium lost its military and financial functions and became the Bohemian and Austrian Court Chancellery, while his old rival Wenzel Anton Graf Kaunitz rose in influence.

In her testament Maria Theresa wrote that he was truly sent to her by Providence. The young Joseph Haydn briefly played the organ in his chapel. In the summer of 1765 Haugwitz moved to his castle at Miroslavské Knínice, where he died of dysentery on 30 August 1765, and he was buried at Náměšť nad Oslavou.
friedrichstadt: Friedrichstadt was founded in 1621 by Dutch settlers. Duke Friedrich III of Holstein-Gottorp persuaded them to bring capital and knowledge to the region in return for freedom to practise their Mennonite and Remonstrant faiths, and for the chance to reclaim fen and marsh land around the town.
