One of the settlers was Johannes Narssius. Dutch became an official language, and the town took its name from the duke.

By 1630 many of the Arminians had already returned to the Netherlands. Between 1633 and 1637 the duke sent an embassy to Tsar Michael I of Russia and to Shah Safi of Persia, hoping to make Friedrichstadt a European trade terminus. The delegation was led by the jurist Philip Crusius and the merchant Otto Brugman; their secretary, the scholar Adam Olearius, later wrote a book about the journey. The aim of a regular trade route that avoided the passage round Africa was not achieved, and the town did not prosper as expected.

The town lies in the district of Nordfriesland, on the river Eider, about 12 km south of Husum. Besides Remonstrants and Mennonites, Unitarians, Quakers, Catholics and Jews also settled there. Natives include Johannes Thedens, governor-general of the Dutch East Indies in 1741–1743, and the folklorist Wilhelm Mannhardt. The painter Jürgen Ovens, a pupil of Rembrandt, lived in the town and is buried in St. Christophorus Church.
frisia: Frisia is a cross-border cultural region in northwestern Europe along the Wadden Sea, taking in the north of the Netherlands and parts of northwestern Germany. It is commonly divided into West Frisia, roughly the Dutch province of Friesland, East Frisia in Lower Saxony, and North Frisia, between the Eider River and the Danish border, which belonged to the Danish Duchy of Schleswig until 1864. The name comes from the Latin Frisii, possibly from a Proto-Germanic word meaning curly or crisp, presumably referring to the hair of the tribesmen.

The people later known as Frisii began settling in the 6th century BCE, and in Roman times lived, according to Pliny the Elder, on terps, man-made hills. The Frisians of the early Middle Ages were, according to archaeology, descendants of Anglo-Saxon immigrants from the German Bight. The Frisian Realm of 650 to 734 had its centre in Utrecht and its law written down as the Lex Frisionum. It ended at the Battle of the Boarn in 734, when the Franks conquered the western part up to the Lauwers; they took the area east of it in 785. From the 7th to the 10th centuries Frisian merchants took a large part in the luxury trade, with districts in cities such as Hedeby, York and Cologne.

In the 12th century Frisian noblemen and the city of Groningen founded the Upstalsboom League under the slogan of Frisian freedom, to counter feudalising tendencies; it collapsed after 1337. In 1464 a nobleman of the Cirksena family became count of East Frisia, with the help of the Hanseatic League, and Friesland was conquered in 1498 by Duke Albert of Saxony-Meissen. West Friesland had fallen to the count of Holland in 1289. Friesland joined the nascent Dutch Republic in 1577 and Groningen was conquered by the Dutch in 1594.

About half a million Frisians in the province of Friesland speak West Frisian, several thousand people in Nordfriesland and Heligoland speak North Frisian dialects, and a small number in four villages speak Saterland Frisian. Friesland has been called Fryslân since 1996. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries Frisian freedom became the slogan of a regionalist movement demanding equal rights for the Frisian language and culture within the Netherlands.
fritigern: Fritigern was a Thervingian Gothic chieftain whose name is reconstructed as Frithugairns, desiring peace. The earliest references concern the years between an attack on the Thervingi by the emperor Valens and the Hunnic raids of about 376. Socrates Scholasticus, Sozomen and Zosimus report a civil war between Fritigern and Athanaric, another prominent Thervingian ruler; Ammianus Marcellinus and Philostorgius do not mention it. According to Socrates, Fritigern asked for Roman aid and, with Valens, defeated Athanaric. Before or during this conflict he became an Arian Christian. Athanaric seems to have prevailed, since he later led the Thervingi against the Huns.

In 376 the Thervingi, pressed by the Huns who had already conquered their kinsmen the Greuthungi, were allowed by Valens to cross the Danube. In the winter of 376-377 famine struck them. The Roman governors Lupicinus and Maximus sold them food at extreme prices, so that many Goths sold their children into slavery, and invited several leaders to a feast where some were killed and others taken hostage.

Fritigern escaped, became leader of the Thervingi and declared war. His forces beat Lupicinus at the Battle of Marcianople, and by 377 they held most of Thracia. He held a wagon fort through the winter and won Hunnic and Alanic cavalry to his side.

On the night of 8 August he sent envoys proposing peace and an alliance in exchange for territory in Thrace, with a private letter to Valens. Valens refused and marched. At the Battle of Adrianople the Goths won a decisive victory, the Roman army was routed and Valens was killed. Fritigern besieged Adrianople without success. Theodosius I succeeded Valens in January 379, and peace was declared on 3 October 382.
fritigil: Fritigil, also spelled Fritigils, ruled the Marcomanni, a Germanic people historically centred in Bohemia who had by then settled in Pannonia, probably including the Vienna Basin, in what is now eastern Austria and western Hungary. She is believed to have governed from a royal seat in present-day Burgenland and is the last documented ruler of her people. Her reign followed the Roman defeat at the Battle of Adrianople in 378, which weakened the empire's defences as migrations of Goths, Alans and Huns along the Danube frontier grew.

According to the 5th-century Life of Ambrose by Paulinus of Milan, Fritigil heard from travellers from Italy of the holiness of Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, sent gifts to his church and asked him for a statement of faith to guide her. Ambrose answered with a catechetical letter explaining the articles of faith and urging her to persuade her husband to make peace with the Romans. He died on 4 April 397, before any visit she might have made to Milan.

Fritigil worked to convert her husband and brought him or the tribal leadership to submit to Rome. The treaty, probably made in the 390s, placed the Marcomanni under the oversight of a Roman tribune, as the Notitia Dignitatum records. It is the last documented agreement between Rome and the Marcomanni, who then fade from the records.

Pope John Paul II recalled Fritigil in his apostolic letter Operosam Diem of 1 December 1996, written for the 1600th anniversary of the death of Ambrose. A tradition at Žarošice in South Moravia holds that she founded a chapel there and was later buried in it, a story shown in sgraffiti on the church complex. By the 14th century the site had become a significant religious centre, and in 1322 Queen Eliška Rejčka of Bohemia acquired Žarošice for a Cistercian convent in Old Brno.
fritz-steinbach: Fritz Steinbach was born in Grünsfeld on 17 June 1855, the brother of the conductor Emil Steinbach. He studied at the Leipzig Conservatory and in Vienna, where his teachers included Martin Gustav Nottebohm and Anton Door. He met Johannes Brahms in 1875, and the two kept up a relationship until the composer's death. Steinbach's performances of Brahms's music repeatedly won the composer's praise.

In 1886 Steinbach succeeded Richard Strauss as conductor of the Meiningen Court Orchestra. In those years he often worked with Brahms and gave frequent guest performances at the court of Georg II, Duke of Saxe-Meiningen, and from 1898 to 1901 he was president of the Allgemeiner Deutscher Musikverein. He then became music director of the Gürzenich Orchestra in Cologne, a post he held until 1914, and directed the Lower Rhenish Music Festival in 1904, 1907, 1910 and 1913.

At the Cologne Conservatory he taught conducting. His pupils included Fritz Busch, Karl Elmendorff, Hans Knappertsbusch, Allard de Ridder, Franz Mittler, Albert van Raalte, Karl Aagard Østvig and Erwin Schulhoff, while Adolf Busch studied composition with him. Another pupil, Walter Blume, continued his research into Brahms.

Steinbach also performed Bach, Beethoven, Mahler and Reger, but he was most closely associated with Brahms, and his Brahms performances influenced younger conductors such as Arturo Toscanini and Adrian Boult. His conducting generally followed the Classical, rhythm-focused style of Hans Richter rather than the Romantic, lyrical style of conductors such as Arthur Nikisch, although his flexible tempos also won admirers. He died in Munich on 13 August 1916. The conductor Peter Maag was his great-nephew.
fritzlar: Fritzlar lies mainly on the north bank of the Eder river in the Schwalm-Eder district of northern Hesse, about 160 kilometres north of Frankfurt. The surrounding country is fertile farmland with wooded basalt peaks, many of them topped by medieval castles or castle ruins. The town stood at the crossroads of several important trade routes, and an imperial residence stood there from the time of Charlemagne. This made it a frequent place for royal visits and for assemblies and synods of German princes and church leaders in the early Middle Ages.

Saint Boniface established a church and monastery dedicated to Saint Peter at Fritzlar. Under its first abbot, Saint Wigbert, the Benedictine monastery became a centre of religious and worldly learning, and Wigbert built a stone basilica in 732. Across the Eder, on the Büraburg, Boniface also set up Germany's first bishopric outside the old Roman frontiers, which was absorbed into the diocese of Mainz after its only bishop, Witta, died in 747. In 774 the Saxons destroyed Fritzlar but spared the basilica, which gave rise to a legend that two angels had driven off the invaders. In 782 Charlemagne granted the monastery imperial protection and substantial territory.

In 919 an assembly at Fritzlar proclaimed Henry I, duke of Saxony, king of the Germans. King Conrad I of Germany had died in December 918 without a son and urged his brother Eberhard to nominate Henry. Henry was proclaimed by the leaders of the Franks and Saxons, and Burchard I, Duke of Swabia, soon swore allegiance, although Duke Arnulf of Bavaria did not submit until Henry marched into Bavaria in 921.

In 1079 Emperor Henry IV gave Fritzlar to the archbishop of Mainz, and that year Saxon partisans of the rival king Rudolf of Swabia attacked Henry there, sacking the town and church. A Thuringian landgrave sacked it again in 1232, when much of the population was killed. After the Reformation it remained a Catholic enclave of Mainz within Protestant Hesse. The Thirty Years' War and an outbreak of plague cut its population from about 2,000 to 600. In 1803 it passed to Hesse-Kassel, which Prussia annexed in 1866.

Fritzlar is a small town of about 15,000 people with a medieval centre ringed by a wall and watch towers. The Grey Tower, at thirty-eight metres, is the highest surviving urban defence tower in Germany, and the city hall, first documented in 1109, is described as the oldest in Germany still used for its original purpose. The Romanesque-Gothic Church of St. Peter dominates the town.
friuli: Friuli covers about 8,240 square kilometres between the Livenza river in the west, the Carnic Alps in the north, the Julian Alps and the Timavo river in the east and the Adriatic Sea in the south. The Tagliamento crosses its hills and flows into a large flood plain, and the lagoons of Marano and Grado lie to the south. The historical capital and most important city is Udine, which was also the capital of the medieval Patria del Friuli.

In prehistory the area belonged to the Castellieri culture and the Raeti, and in the 4th century BCE the Carni settled there. From the 2nd century BCE the Romans colonised it. Aquileia became the fourth largest city of Italy under the empire, a river port that dominated trade between the Adriatic and northern Europe. In 452 Attila razed it to the ground. The Patriarchate of Aquileia ranked among the highest ecclesiastical authorities in Italy from the mid-6th century.

In 568 the Lombards took the region, and King Alboin established the Duchy of Friuli, the first Lombard duchy, which he gave to his relative Gisulf I, with its capital at Forum Iulii. The historian Paul the Deacon was born in Friuli. After the Frankish conquest the region became the March of Friuli in 846. On 3 April 1077 Emperor Henry IV granted the county of Friuli to Sigaerd, Patriarch of Aquileia, and the patriarchal state became one of the best organised polities of medieval Italy. It had a parliament from the 12th century, which met for the last time in 1805, when Napoleon Bonaparte abolished it.

Venice conquered the patriarchate in 1420 but left Friuli its own parliament. On 27 February 1511 starving citizens of Udine began a revolt known as Joibe Grasse, which spread through the whole territory and was put down by 1 March, when Venice sent about a hundred cavalry. From 1516 the Habsburg Empire controlled eastern Friuli. In 1866 central and western Friuli were annexed by Italy with the Veneto, while the east stayed under Austria until the First World War.

Friuli forms the major part of the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia, with the provinces of Udine, Pordenone and Gorizia. Its people, the Friulians, speak the Friulian language, which around 350,000 people claim as their native language. Slovene, German and Venetian dialects are also spoken in parts of the region.
frog-lake-massacre: Chief Big Bear had signed Treaty 6 in 1882 and settled with his band near Frog Lake late in 1884, without yet choosing a reserve. Angered by a treaty he saw as unfair and by the starvation that followed the decline of the buffalo, he began organising the Cree for resistance. On 28 March 1885 news reached Frog Lake of the Métis victory at the Battle of Duck Lake and of Poundmaker's looting of Battleford. Wandering Spirit became war chief and sought arms and food, and the Indian agent Thomas Quinn, who controlled the meagre rations, stood in his way.

Early on 2 April armed Cree men took Quinn hostage and seized the settlement, looting its stores. After mass at the Catholic church, at about 11:00, Wandering Spirit ordered the white settlers to move to a camp a few kilometres away. When Quinn refused, Wandering Spirit shot him, and despite Big Bear's efforts to stop it his men killed eight more unarmed people, among them the priests Leon Fafard and Felix Marchand. The clerk William Bleasdell Cameron escaped with help from sympathetic Cree. About 70 survivors were taken captive, including the widows Theresa Gowanlock and Theresa Delaney.

On 4 April the church and every building of the settlement were burned. Troops of the Alberta Field Force arrived on 14 June, buried the dead and pursued Big Bear's band to Frenchman's Butte. Wandering Spirit surrendered at Fort Pitt. He and seven others, tried for murders at Frog Lake and Battleford without legal counsel, were sentenced by Judge Charles Rouleau and hanged on 27 November 1885, the largest mass hanging in Canada's history. Big Bear, who had opposed the killings, was convicted of treason and died in 1888. The site became a National Historic Site in 1923.
frombork: Frombork lies on the Vistula Lagoon in Braniewo County, in the historical region of Warmia. The town was founded as a defensive stronghold on an Old Prussian site, after the Teutonic Knights, granted control of the region by the imperial Golden Bull of Rimini, conquered it. According to a local legend, its name, Frauenburg in German, honours Gertruda, the widow of the stronghold's lord, who offered the settlement to the bishop. The name is a common one, since it usually marks a fortified chapel, church or monastery dedicated to the Virgin Mary.

The village is first mentioned in a document of 1278 signed by Bishop Heinrich Fleming, and on 8 July 1310 Bishop Eberhard of Neisse granted the town Lübeck city rights. The Brick Gothic cathedral was built between 1329 and 1388. The town was plundered and burned in 1414 during the Hunger War, joined the anti-Teutonic Prussian Confederation in 1440, and was recognised as part of the Polish Kingdom by the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. It was devastated again in 1520, in the Polish–Teutonic War.

Nicolaus Copernicus lived and worked there as a canon in 1512–16 and from 1522 until his death. In 1519 he wrote to the King of Poland asking for help against the Teutonic Knights; the letter was intercepted, and the Knights took and burned the town after Copernicus and other canons had left. He wrote De revolutionibus orbium cœlestium in Frombork, and after its publication in 1543 he died there and was buried in the cathedral. Between 1626 and 1635 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden occupied the town and sent many cultural treasures, including Copernicus's manuscripts, to Sweden. Prussia took the town in 1772 and it became part of the German Empire in 1871.

Heavily damaged in the Second World War, the town passed to Poland in 1945, regained its city rights in 1959, and was rebuilt in 1966–1973 by Polish Boy Scouts and others, in time for the 500th anniversary of Copernicus's birth. The fortified Cathedral Hill holds the cathedral, the Copernicus Tower and the Old Bishop's Palace, which houses the Nicolaus Copernicus Museum, listed as a Historic Monument of Poland. The cathedral is the seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Warmia. Archaeologists found a grave believed to be Copernicus's in 2005; DNA tests confirmed it in 2008, and he was reburied in the cathedral in 2010.
front-de-liberation-du-quebec: The Front de libération du Québec aimed to establish an independent and socialist Quebec. Its ideology combined an extreme form of Quebec nationalism, which denounced Anglo exploitation and control of Quebec, with Marxist–Leninist ideas. The first FLQ drew on members of the Rassemblement pour l'Indépendance Nationale who wanted faster action, and its attacks began on 7 March 1963 with Molotov cocktails planted at three armouries. Members were called Felquistes, and the group was a loose association of clandestine cells. In 1966 it prepared a text setting out a plan of successive waves of robberies, bombings and kidnappings culminating in revolution.

The history of the FLQ is often told as a series of waves. In 1963 a bomb at the Canadian Army Recruiting Centre in Montreal killed a furnaceman, William Vincent O'Neill. In July 1965 Charles Gagnon and Pierre Vallières merged their Popular Liberation Movement with the FLQ and published the revolutionary paper La Cognée. A bomb at the Montreal Stock Exchange on 13 February 1969 seriously injured 27 people.

On 5 October 1970 the Liberation Cell kidnapped the British Trade Commissioner James Cross, and on 10 October the Chénier Cell kidnapped Pierre Laporte, Quebec's Minister of Labour and Vice-Premier. The FLQ demanded the release of 23 so-called political prisoners, 500,000 dollars in gold, publication of its manifesto and a flight to Cuba or Algeria. Laporte was killed, and his body was found after a radio call on 17 October. Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau invoked the War Measures Act, for the first time in peacetime, and 453 people were arrested, 435 of them released without charge. Cross was freed in December, and five of his captors were flown to Cuba on 3 December.

Public support collapsed after the murder of Laporte, and by 1971 police informants had penetrated the group. The events of October 1970 reduced support for violent means and increased support for the Parti Québécois, which won the most votes in 1976. In December 1971 Vallières announced that he was joining that party. Exiles returned from late 1971 to 1982 and mostly received light sentences. According to the Mitrokhin archive, the KGB likely made contact with the FLQ and later forged documents portraying it as a CIA false-flag operation.
front-for-the-liberation-of-occupied-sou: FLOSY was the creation of Abdullah al Asnag, a labour leader of the Aden Trade Union Congress. In the late 1950s Gamal Abdel Nasser's Pan-Arabism spread to the region, and Britain persuaded the feuding emirs to merge into the Federation of South Arabia. The Colony of Aden joined it in 1962, so that Aden's pro-British members could counter the union's influence in the assembly. The next day Muhammad al-Badr was overthrown in Yemen, and the civil war that followed spread into the Aden Emergency, declared on 10 December 1963.

In 1965 Britain suspended the Federation's government and imposed direct colonial rule. Asnag, seeing that he would not be given power, left the country and joined the National Liberation Front, but as elements of the NLF became more radically Marxist and broke with Egypt, he formed FLOSY to counter them.

The NLF denounced FLOSY as an imperialist force controlled by Nasser and fought it as well as the British. In February 1967 Britain, no longer able to protect its bases in Aden, announced its departure. Nasser backed FLOSY and arrested the NLF's leader, who was living in Egypt. Both fronts publicly refused to deal with the British, but secret talks between the British and the NLF aimed at FLOSY's defeat. The last governor, Sir Humphrey Trevelyan, left with no clear successor.

Egypt's defeat in the Six-Day War of 1967 forced Nasser to withdraw his troops from Yemen, leaving FLOSY without military support. The NLF allied with the Federal army, and on 7 November 1967 FLOSY suffered heavy losses in an attack on a federal army base, after which its forces ceased to exist. The Federation ended on 30 November 1967 with the creation of the People's Republic of South Yemen, and some FLOSY cadres and leaders remained abroad.
front-for-the-restoration-of-unity-and-d: FRUD came into being in 1991 through the merger of three Afar groups: Action for the Revision of Order in Djibouti, the Front for the Restoration of Right and Equality, and the Djibouti Patriotic Resistance Front. Late in 1991 it took up arms against the Issa-dominated government, and nearly 1,000 people died in the conflict up to 1994. The movement speaks for the interests of the Afar of Djibouti, but it has also drawn supporters living outside the country.

In 1994 the movement split in two. A moderate wing under Ali Mohamed Daoud signed a peace agreement with the government at Aba'a on 26 December 1994. A second wing under Ahmed Dini Ahmed rejected the accord. Its supporters had already held a six-day congress in northern Djibouti in late September, announcing on 30 September that the delegates were resolved to pursue armed struggle until their political goals were met, and electing Dini to head their executive committee.

The radicals, known as FRUD-C (Combatant) or the Ahmed Dini faction, fought on with arms and probably logistical help from Eritrea, trying to cut Djibouti's supply routes to landlocked Ethiopia during the Eritrean–Ethiopian War. Attacks under the FRUD-C name did not cease entirely: a policeman was killed in January 2021, and on 7 October 2022 an assault on the barracks at Garabtisan killed seven soldiers. The moderate faction joined the government in condemning it as unjustifiable in a time of political pluralism.

Under the 1994 agreement the moderate faction received two ministries on 8 June 1995: Daoud became Minister of Health and Social Affairs and the secretary-general Ougoure Kifle Ahmed Minister of Agriculture and Water Resources. The party was legalised in March 1996. At its first congress, on 15–16 April 1997, it elected a 153-member National Council and a 21-member Executive Committee that included Issa, Gadabursi, Arab and Isaaq members, among them the Issa Djama Djellai as First Vice-President.

FRUD then allied with the ruling People's Rally for Progress. Their joint list won all 65 seats of the National Assembly in December 1997, and in April 1999 the party backed Ismail Omar Guelleh, who took 74.02% of the presidential vote. In the elections of 2003 and 2008 it stood within the Union for the Presidential Majority, while the radical faction ran with the opposition in 2003. Daoud was re-elected party president in 2002 and again in 2007.
front-palace: The office of uparat, a viceroy, came to Siam from Greater India, and in the 15th century its holders, with few exceptions, were also kings of Sukhothai, seated at Phitsanulok. After the first fall of Ayutthaya in 1569, Maha Thammaracha made his son Naresuan uparat and king of Sukhothai, and built a palace in front of his own royal palace for Naresuan to live in when he came to Ayutthaya. From this building the office took the name Front Palace.

Naresuan, once crowned, named his brother Ekathotsarot uparat and declared that his brother in the Front Palace had equal status to the king. In 1688 Phetracha appointed his son Luang Sorasak and first used the formal style Krom Phra Ratchawang Bowon Sathan Mongkhon. The uparat, usually the king's brother, was heir presumptive rather than heir apparent, which left the succession uncertain; keeping him in the palace was also a way of watching him. When he died before the king, the post often stayed empty for years.

When he founded the Chakri dynasty in 1782, Phutthayotfa Chulalok made his younger brother Bunma, as Maha Sura Singhanat, the Front Palace, and Bunma oversaw the building of the palace in Bangkok, which later holders enlarged. Only Prince Itsarasunthon lived elsewhere, at the Thonburi Palace, and he alone of the Rattanakosin holders came to the throne, as Phutthaloetla Naphalai. The viceroys of this period commanded a private army and even a navy.

In 1851 King Mongkut made his brother Pinklao the Front Palace and crowned him a king of equal rank, with all the royal styles; to Europeans Pinklao called himself the Second King. In 1868, after the young Chulalongkorn's coronation, the regent Sri Suriwongse had the title given to Pinklao's son, Prince Yingyot, as Wichaichan.

The conflict between the reforming Chulalongkorn and the conservative viceroy broke out after a fire in the Grand Palace was blamed on Wichaichan, who sought protection in the British consulate, and the reforms stalled for several years. In 1886 Chulalongkorn named his son Prince Maha Vajirunhis Crown Prince of Siam, replacing the heir presumptive with the Western concept of a crown prince as heir apparent. The palace's main building now belongs to the Bangkok National Museum, and Mahidol Adulyadej was later given an equivalent rank after his death.
frostating: The Frostating, in Old Norse Frostuþing, was one of the four lagting, the regional law assemblies of medieval Norway, beside the Gulating, the Eidsivating and the Borgarting. Its seat was Tinghaugen, the assembly hill, close to the medieval church at Logtun in what is now Frosta Municipality, where the Frostatinget bautasten marks the site. It is arguably the oldest court in Norway, older than the Viking Age.

The assembly had authority over the eight districts of Trøndelag, among them Norðmørafylki, covering Nordmøre and Fosen, and Naumdølafylki, covering Namdalen; later Hålogaland came under it as well. It acted both as a court, settling disputes, and as a lawmaking body. When Norway was united as a kingdom, the existing lagting became superior regional assemblies, to which delegates from the districts of each region came to give judgments and pass laws.

In 1274, with the consent of all four lagting, King Magnus the Lawmender promulgated a national law, the landslov, a single code for the whole kingdom. Until then only the Kingdom of Sicily, with the Liber Augustalis of Frederick II in 1231, and Castile, with the Fuero Real of Alfonso X, had such codes. The new law replaced the Frostating Law, greatly reduced the assembly's power to legislate and drew authority to the crown. It remained in force until Frederik III of Denmark–Norway declared absolute monarchy in 1660, set down in the King Act of 1665.

The Frostating seal shows Magnus enthroned, crowned and holding a sceptre, with the Norwegian lion under his foot, handing the new law to the lawman while the representatives of the assembly stand three deep at his side; below, two bowmen aim at a squirrel and a bird in trees. The seal survives on a document of 1 June 1453 in the Diplomatarium Norvegicum, and a version of it lives on in the coat of arms of Frosta.
fructuoso-rivera: Rivera was a rancher who joined the army of José Gervasio Artigas in 1810 and eventually rose to the rank of general. When the Banda Oriental was occupied by the United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves and Artigas was forced into exile in 1820, Rivera stayed in the newly created Cisplatina province and briefly served in the Imperial Brazilian Army, reaching the rank of brigadier.

He first met Juan Antonio Lavalleja in 1825, in an event known as the Abrazo del Monzón. In the same year the Thirty-Three Orientals led by Lavalleja and their Argentine supporters began their fight against the Empire of Brazil, and Rivera joined them, though it is unclear whether he did so voluntarily. He became an important commander in the Cisplatine War and took part in the Battle of Rincón and the Battle of Sarandí.

After Uruguayan independence was proclaimed in 1828 through the Treaty of Montevideo, arguments between Rivera and Lavalleja turned into fighting, and José Rondeau became the first provisional governor. Rivera held the presidency from 6 November 1830 until 24 October 1834 and survived an unsuccessful assassination attempt and coup by Lavalleja's supporters in 1832. On 11 April 1831 he organised the Salsipuedes Massacre: Charrúa leaders and warriors were lured to a meeting and killed by the military, and surviving women and children were marched to Montevideo and held in household servitude.

Rivera backed Manuel Oribe as his successor but came into conflict with him. In October 1838 he defeated Oribe, who fled to Buenos Aires. Rivera's supporters wore red armbands and Oribe's white, the origin of the division between Colorados and Blancos. Rivera held the presidency again from 1 March 1839 to 1 March 1843. Oribe, backed by Juan Manuel de Rosas, invaded Uruguay, and in December 1842 he defeated Rivera at the Battle of Arroyo Grande and began the Great Siege of Montevideo.

Rivera's power was limited to the capital until he was forced into exile in Brazil in 1847; he stayed there until 1853. A triumvirate of Venancio Flores, Lavalleja and Rivera was created on 25 September 1853. Lavalleja died on 22 October, and Rivera died on 13 January 1854 on his way to Montevideo. He is regarded as the founder of the Colorado Party, which ruled Uruguay without interruption from 1865 until 1958, and a Riverista tendency within it remains a counterpoint to the Batllista and other factions.
fructuosus-of-tarragona: Fructuosus, known in Spanish as San Fructuoso and in Catalan as Sant Fructuós, holds an important place in the early history of Christianity in Hispania: the historical list of the bishops of Tarragona begins with him. He was arrested during the persecution of Christians under the Roman Emperor Valerian, who reigned from 253 to 260, together with his deacons Augurius and Eulogius. According to the account of their martyrdom, they were just going to bed when they were taken, and when examined by the praeses Aemilianus they affirmed their faith. Asked whether he was the bishop, Fructuosus said that he was, and the examiner replied, Fuisti, You were.

The three were sentenced to be burnt. The 18th-century hagiographer Alban Butler wrote that on the way to his execution, on a Friday morning, Fructuosus refused a drink because the hour for breaking the day's fast had not come. Officers had been posted to prevent a disturbance, but near the gate of the amphitheatre some Christians reached him and one asked for his prayers. He answered aloud that he was bound to bear in mind the whole universal Church from east to west, and spoke words of consolation. As the flames rose, the martyrs stretched out their arms and prayed until they died.

The Acta of Fructuosus and his deacons are the earliest Hispanic Acta and have been praised for a realistic simplicity that contrasts with many accounts of Diocletian's persecution. The poet Prudentius refers to them in a hymn, and Augustine of Hippo praised and quoted them at length. His feast day is 21 January, and the abbey of San Fruttuoso on the Italian Riviera is dedicated to him.
fruela-ii-of-asturias: Fruela was a son of Alfonso III of Asturias and his wife Jimena. In 910 he and two of his brothers deposed their father and divided the kingdom among themselves. Fruela, the youngest brother, took the original portion, Asturias; Ordoño took Galicia; and García, the eldest, took León. Although Fruela called himself king of a much-diminished Asturias, evidence suggests that his role was subordinate to the king of León. As king of Asturias he had the task of consolidating the region later called Castile and keeping its counts in check.

Fruela married twice, first in 910 to Nunilo Jimena, daughter of the Navarrese king, and by 917 to Urraca, daughter of the Banu Qasi governor of Tudela. He had at least three sons, Alfonso, Ramiro and Ordoño, none of whom inherited the throne. Bishop Pelayo gives all three to Nunila, while Ibn Khaldun gives Ordoño and Ramiro to Urraca.

Fruela kept good relations with his brother Ordoño, who held the hegemony. They cooperated in the Reconquista, and Fruela signed Ordoño's diplomas as Froila frater confirmat, 'Fruela the brother confirms'. When Ordoño died in 924 the magnates ignored his heirs and elected Fruela king. He had never been popular with the nobles and his subjects, and some doubt that his election was regular and see it as a likely usurpation.

He had Gebuldo and Aresindo, sons of Olmundo, who claimed descent from King Witiza, assassinated, which alienated the nobility further. One chronicler relates that for this he was condemned to a reign of only fourteen months. According to Ramón Menéndez Pidal, he also exiled Frunimio, bishop of León and a relation of Olmundo. He reigned for fourteen months and died of leprosy in August 925.

After Fruela's death several claimants competed for his lands. They included Ramiro, who appears to have married the widowed queen Urraca and used the royal title but was eventually unsuccessful, the sons of Ordoño II and Fruela's own young sons. There is some debate about the immediate succession.
fruitbearing-society: The society, also called Societas Fructifera, set out to standardise vernacular German and to promote it as a language of scholarship and literature, after the pattern of the Accademia della Crusca in Florence and similar groups then thriving in Italy; comparable academies followed later in France, in 1635, and in Britain. Its founding father was Caspar von Teutleben (1576-1629), Hofmarschall at the court of Weimar, who had been inspired by the Italian language academies while travelling in Italy as a young man.

Teutleben made his proposal in August 1617, during the funeral celebrations of Duchess Dorothea Maria, which several princes attended. Prince Ludwig von Anhalt-Köthen, who had himself joined the Accademia della Crusca in 1600, took up the idea and became the society's first president.

Because its emblem was the fruit-bearing date palm, then an exotic tree, the society was also known as the Palmenorden, the Palm Order. Each member took a fruitbearing name of his own within the society. Over its life it had 890 members, among them a king, Charles X Gustav of Sweden, 153 German princes and more than 60 barons, nobles and distinguished scholars. Axel Oxenstierna, Johan Banér, Ottavio Piccolomini and Frederick William of Brandenburg were members, as were many princes of the houses of Anhalt, Saxony and Brunswick-Lüneburg.

Among its literary members were Martin Opitz, Andreas Gryphius, Georg Philipp Harsdörffer, Philipp von Zesen, Friedrich von Logau, Johann Rist, Georg Neumark, Johann Michael Moscherosch and Sigmund von Birken, as well as the scholar and traveller Adam Olearius, the theologian Johann Valentin Andreae and the painter Joachim von Sandrart. The first book about the society, Der Teutsche Palmbaum by Carl Gustav von Hille, was published in Nuremberg in 1647.
frumentius: According to the fourth-century historian Tyrannius Rufinus, who cites Frumentius' brother Edesius as his authority, the two were born in Tyre, in present-day Lebanon. As children, about 316, they accompanied their uncle Meropius on a voyage to 'India'. On the return voyage their ship stopped at a harbour on the Red Sea, where local people massacred the whole crew but spared the two boys, who were taken as slaves to the King of Axum. Edesius became the king's cupbearer and Frumentius his secretary and treasurer. Shortly before his death the king freed them, but the widowed queen persuaded them to stay and help her educate the young heir, Ezana, and administer the kingdom during his minority.

Frumentius, especially, used his influence to spread Christianity. He first encouraged Christian merchants in the country to practise their faith openly and helped them find places for prayer, and later he converted some of the local people. When Ezana came of age Edesius went back to Tyre, where he was ordained a priest, while Frumentius travelled as far as Alexandria and asked Athanasius, Patriarch of Alexandria, to send a bishop and priests as missionaries to Ethiopia. By Athanasius' own account he judged Frumentius the most suitable person, and consecrated him bishop, traditionally in 328, or according to others between 340 and 346.

Frumentius returned and set up his see at Axum, where he converted and baptised Ezana, who built many churches and spread Christianity through the country. Frumentius founded the first monastery of Ethiopia, Dabba Selama in Dogu'a Tembien. Around 356 the Roman emperor Constantius II wrote to Ezana and his brother Saizana asking them to replace Frumentius with Theophilos the Indian, who supported Arianism, as the emperor did. Athanasius, a leading opponent of Arianism, had appointed Frumentius, and the king refused the request.

Frumentius died about 383. He was called Kesate Birhan, meaning Revealer of Light, and Abba Salama, meaning Father of Peace, and was the first Abuna, the title of the head of the Oriental Orthodox Churches in Ethiopia. His appointment began the tradition that the Patriarch of Alexandria appointed the bishops of Ethiopia. Ethiopian traditions credit him with the first Geʽez translation of the New Testament and with a part in developing the Geʽez script from an abjad into an abugida. The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Churches celebrate his consecration on 18 Taḫśaś, the Coptic Orthodox Church keeps his feast on 18 December, the Eastern Orthodox Church on 30 November and the Catholic Church on 20 July.
fruto-chamorro: Chamorro was born illegitimate on 20 October 1804 and was at first known as Fruto Pérez. His father, Pedro José Chamorro Argüello, had gone from Nicaragua to Guatemala for graduate studies, and Fruto grew up and went to school there. His father acknowledged him shortly before dying in 1824, and his stepmother had him use the name Fruto Chamorro Pérez. He then left his studies for Nicaragua to manage the family's large inheritance and to act as guardian of his half-siblings, among them Pedro Joaquín, Dionisio and Fernando.

Like his father, one of the founders of the Conservative Party centred on Granada, he became a party activist. He was elected to the State Assembly in 1836 and sat as a senator of the State of Nicaragua from 1839 to 1842. When the Pact of Chinandega of 1842 tried to revive a union of El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua, he was named supreme director of the Confederation's junta in 1843 and lived in San Miguel, El Salvador. Guatemala withdrew, and he helped prevent a war over it, but the union collapsed in 1844. He then served as prefect and military governor of Granada and treasury minister, and in November 1851, under Supreme Director Laureano Pineda, became commander-in-chief of the army.

Chamorro became supreme director on 1 April 1853 and moved the seat of government to Granada, the Conservative stronghold. On 20 January 1854 he convened a Constituent Assembly while most of the western Liberal deputies were absent, and with its consent he gave up the title of supreme director and named himself president.

Liberals saw this as the return of the provincial oligarchy to power. In May 1854 they set up their own government in León with the backing of Honduras and El Salvador and sent General Máximo Jerez to besiege Granada. Chamorro took command of the army, leaving executive power to his deputy, José María Estrada, and the city held. He died of dysentery at his hacienda outside Granada. He was married to Mercedes Avilés and had no children.
fruttuaria-abbey: Fruttuaria lies about twenty kilometres north of Turin. Guglielmo da Volpiano donated the land, and the first stone of a large Romanesque church was laid on 23 February 1003. Ottobiano, bishop of Ivrea, consecrated it in the presence of Arduin, marchese of Ivrea and King of Italy, and his consort Berta. The monastery was completed in 1006 or 1007 and followed the Benedictine rule as reformed at Cluny. In 1027 a bull of Pope John XIX placed the abbey and all its lands under direct papal supervision.

Empress Agnes was a patron and retired there in 1065 before moving to Rome; she helped bring Fruttuaria's customs to Saint Blaise Abbey. The abbey was at its height in the 12th and 13th centuries, when it minted its own coin. In 1265 it held eighty-five churches in Italy, four comuni, San Benigno Canavese, Montanaro, Lombardore and Foglizzo, and lands in France and Austria, and some 1,200 monks lived there.

Decline began in the 14th century. In 1477 the monks lost the right to name their abbot, which passed to the pope, and in 1585 Pope Sixtus V suppressed the monastery and put a college of secular priests in its buildings; the last monk died in 1634. Troops of Victor Amadeus II, Duke of Savoy, occupied the abbey's lands from 1710 until 1741, when the papacy gave up all territorial control.

From 1770 the abbot in commendam Carlo Vittorio Amedeo delle Lanze razed the Romanesque church and monastery, keeping the campanile and parts of the apse, and raised the present late-baroque church, designed by Bernardo Antonio Vittone and completed by Mario Quarini. In 1979 work on heating uncovered an 11th-century mosaic of two griffons, and excavations have revealed the foundations of the Romanesque church, which had three naves and a large transept. Restoration ended in May 2004.
fu-deng: Fu Deng, courtesy name Wengao, was born in 343 under Later Zhao rule, the son of Fu Chang, a distant grandnephew of the Former Qin founder Fu Jiàn. His father served as a general and commandery governor but was executed under the emperor Fu Sheng, and was honoured after Fu Jiān overthrew Fu Sheng. Fu Jiān, impressed by Fu Deng's abilities, made him magistrate of the capital Chang'an, but he was later demoted to Didao for unspecified faults.

As Former Qin collapsed, Fu Deng served the general Mao Xing in the west. In 386 the soldiers killed Mao Xing, set up the aged Wei Ping and then replaced him with Fu Deng, whom Fu Pi made a provincial governor and Prince of Nan'an. During droughts and famines in his wars with Yao Chang, Fu Deng called the enemy dead cooked food, and his soldiers ate the corpses. When Fu Pi died later in 386 and his territory fell to Western Yan, Fu Deng's officers urged him to take the throne himself.

He kept a shrine to Fu Jiān in his army, reported his key decisions to it, and was described as a master of square and circular formations. He won a number of early battles, and Yao Chang set up a shrine of his own before beheading his effigy of Fu Jiān and sending the head to Fu Deng. In 387 the Western Qin ruler Qifu Guoren accepted the title Prince of Wanchuan from him. But Fu Deng failed to strike decisively, and Yao Chang destroyed the other semi-independent generals of the Guanzhong region one by one.

In summer 389, while Fu Deng took Pingliang, Yao Chang surprised his base at Dajie, killing Empress Mao and his sons Fu Bian and Fu Shang and capturing some 50,000 of his people. After that Fu Deng could no longer mount major attacks, though neither side could destroy the other. When Yao Chang fell ill in 392, Fu Deng attacked Anding, but the sick Yao Chang faced him and drew off unexpectedly.

When Yao Chang died around the new year of 394, Fu Deng launched a major assault without securing water. Yao Xing camped at Mawei to keep him from the river, and his army collapsed from thirst. Fu Deng fled to the mountains and sought help from Qifu Gangui, but Yao Xing ambushed and executed him as he came out to join the relief force.
fu-hao: Fu Hao, whose posthumous temple name was Mu Xin, was one of the many wives of King Wu Ding of the Shang dynasty, believed to have numbered 64. Her life and achievements are known almost entirely from the contents of her tomb and from oracle-bone inscriptions, not from literary records.

Wu Ding cultivated relations with neighbouring tribes by marrying a woman from each, and Fu Hao may have entered the household in this way; the weapons in her tomb suggest she came from the border or the Steppe. She became one of three queens, the secondary queen after Fu Jing, and bore Prince Zu Ji. Oracle-bone divinations by Nan show concern for her at the birth.

Fu Hao owned land and, according to the oracle bones, several times offered the king valuable tribute. Wu Ding repeatedly told her to conduct the most special rituals and sacrifices to the ancestors, and she is described as a high priestess. Since the character for wife can have varied meanings, some scholars suggest that women such as Fu Hao were first priestesses and married the king later.

She was also a general. She defeated the Tufang, who had fought the Shang for generations, in a single decisive battle, and campaigned against the Yi, Qiang and Ba. The campaign against the Ba is remembered as the earliest recorded large-scale ambush in Chinese history. She commanded up to 13,000 soldiers, with the generals Zhi and Hou Gao under her.

She died well before Wu Ding, who built her tomb at his capital Yin, on her own land across the river from the royal cemetery. For that reason it is the only royal Shang tomb found unlooted. Archaeologist Zheng Zhenxiang unearthed it in 1976 at Yinxu.

Besides the remains of a wooden chamber and a coffin that had disintegrated, it held 775 jade objects, 564 bone objects, 468 bronze objects including 130 weapons, over 6,880 cowry shells, 16 human sacrifices and 6 dogs. After her death the king offered sacrifices there, hoping for her spiritual help against the Gong. She has been called the Chinese Tutankhamun, since the two were close contemporaries whose tombs were found generally intact.
fu-jian-337-385: Fu Jian was born in 337 to Fu Xiong and Lady Gou, when the family name was still Pu. His grandfather Pu Hong, a Di chieftain and general of Later Zhao, took the name Fu, and his uncle Fu Jian (317–355) founded Former Qin in 351. Under his cousin Fu Sheng, whose rule was violent and capricious, he helped defeat the Qiang chief Yao Xiang in 357 and persuaded the commander to spare Yao's brother Yao Chang. Warned that Fu Sheng meant to kill him, he attacked the palace with his brother Fu Fa, put Fu Sheng to death and took the title Heavenly King rather than emperor.

With Wang Meng as his chief minister, Fu Jian established the rule of law, encouraged officials to recommend able men and held them responsible for those they named. He repeatedly spared rebels and defeated enemies. In 369 his troops helped Former Yan defeat the Jin general Huan Wen, and when Yan withheld the Luoyang region it had promised, Wang Meng led 60,000 men against it and destroyed it in 370. Fu Jian pardoned its emperor Murong Wei and moved many Xianbei to the Guanzhong region. In 373 he took the Jin lands of modern Sichuan, Chongqing and southern Shaanxi.

Wang Meng died in 375, advising him on his deathbed to stop the wars against Jin and to trust the Xianbei and Qiang officials less; Fu Jian followed neither counsel. His later campaigns drained the empire. In 380 he spread his Di people, a small minority, across the provinces, leaving Guanzhong full of Xianbei and Qiang. Against most of his officials he invaded Jin in 383, boasting that his soldiers' whips could stop the Yangtze.

After the defeat at the Fei River, Murong Chui escorted the wounded Fu Jian back to Luoyang but then founded Later Yan, and Murong Hong began Western Yan in Guanzhong. When Fu Jian killed Yao Chang's messengers, Yao fled and founded Later Qin. Besieged and starving in Chang'an, Fu Jian led an army out to find food, and the city fell behind him. Captured near Wujiang Mountain and held at Xinping, he refused to pass the throne to Yao and killed his own daughters Fu Bao and Fu Jin to spare them humiliation, before Yao's soldiers strangled him. Traditional histories judged him virtuous and just, but held that sparing too many enemies brought about his downfall.
fu-youde: Fu Youde was born in Suzhou, in northern Anhui, under the Yuan dynasty; the date of his birth is unknown. His family fled the Yellow River floods and the unrest that followed them, settling first in Dangshan and later in Yingzhou. Of humble rural origins and without formal education, he made his name locally as a young man for leadership and martial skill. When the Red Turban Rebellion broke out in 1351 he joined a rebel band in Xuzhou.

He served the Song regime of Han Lin'er under Li Xixi, one of the generals of Liu Futong, until defeats drove that army into Sichuan in 1358. He then followed Ming Yuzhen, a general of Xu Shouhui, and after Chen Youliang killed Xu in 1360 he passed to Chen's state of Han. Unrewarded there, he went over with his troops to Zhu Yuanzhang, the future Hongwu Emperor, in September 1361.

Under Zhu, Fu was valued as a tactician who led from the front. Serving under Xu Da and Chang Yuchun, he fought in the victories over Chen Han in 1363–64, over Zhang Shicheng's state of Wu in 1366–67 and in the conquest of northern China from the Mongols in 1368–1370. In November 1370 he was made Marquis of Yingchuan. In January 1371, with Tang He's army and Liao Yongzhong's fleet, he struck Sichuan from the north while the main attack was expected along the Yangtze.

Between campaigns he built fortifications on the northern frontier and in Gansu and taught the emperor's sons the art of war. In 1381 he led 300,000 soldiers into Yunnan, with Lan Yu and Mu Ying as deputies, taking Kunming by January 1382 and Dali in April. He set up a provincial administration and returned only in April 1384. He later served in Beijing, fought rebels in Yunnan again and was Feng Sheng's deputy in the Liaodong campaign of 1387 against the Mongol chieftain Naghachu.

In March 1392 the emperor angrily refused his request for nearly 1,000 mu of land, the only recorded rebuke of his career. After Lan Yu was executed for treason in March 1393 and thousands of his associates purged, Fu died by suicide on 20 December 1394, and the generals Wang Bi and Feng Sheng died within two months. Historians see the three deaths as the emperor's work. In 1645 the Hongguang Emperor of the Southern Ming gave Fu the posthumous name Wujing.
fuad-i-of-egypt: Fuad was born in Giza Palace in Cairo, the youngest son of Isma'il Pasha, and spent his childhood with his exiled father in Naples. He was educated at the military academy in Turin. Before becoming sultan he played a major role in the establishment of Egyptian University, now called Cairo University, and was its first rector from 1908 until his resignation in 1913.

In 1911, after the Italian invasion of Tripoli and Cyrenaica, he sought to establish himself as Arab Muslim ruler of Libya under the Italian crown, but the Italian government preferred direct colonial administration. In 1913 Azzam Pasha suggested him for the throne of Albania, but the European Allied powers chose a German prince in March 1914. He was president of the Egyptian Geographic Society from 1915 until 1918.

Fuad succeeded his elder brother Hussein Kamel as Sultan of Egypt in 1917. After the Egyptian Revolution of 1919 the United Kingdom ended its protectorate and recognised Egypt as a sovereign state on 28 February 1922, and on 15 March 1922 Fuad issued a decree changing his title from Sultan to King of Egypt. The 1923 Constitution granted him vast powers. He made frequent use of his right to dissolve parliament, cabinets were dismissed at royal will, and parliaments never lasted their full four-year term. In 1930 he abrogated the constitution and replaced it with one that limited the role of parliament to advice only, but large-scale public dissatisfaction compelled him to restore the earlier constitution in 1935.

Fuad had eighty-seven volumes of correspondence of his ancestors copied, translated and arranged from European archives, and later gathered old documents from Egyptian archives into what became the Royal Archives in the 1930s. His effort to portray his great-grandfather Muhammad Ali, his grandfather Ibrahim and his father as nationalists and benevolent monarchs became an enduring influence on Egyptian historiography.

Fuad married first Princess Shivakiar in 1895, a marriage that ended in divorce in 1898, and second Nazli Sabri on 24 May 1919. His second marriage produced five children, among them the future King Farouk and Princess Fawzia, who became queen consort of Iran. Fuad died on 28 April 1936 at the Koubbeh Palace in Cairo, reportedly of heart failure, and was buried at the Khedival mausoleum in the al-Rifa'i Mosque. He was succeeded by Farouk I, who was 16 years old and studying in England.
fuad-stephens: Stephens was born Donald Aloysius Marmaduke Stephens at Kudat on 14 September 1920. His father, Jules Stephens, was half Kadazan and half British and had dropped the surname Pavitt of his own father, who came from New Zealand. His mother, Edith Cope, was of mixed Japanese, British and Dusun ancestry from Kinabatangan. His younger brother Leo Benedict later became President of the Dewan Negara.

Stephens founded the United National Kadazan Organisation in August 1961. At first he opposed Sabah's joining a federation, but he came round to it and negotiated the formation of Malaysia with Tun Mustapha of the United Sabah National Organisation, Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore and Tunku Abdul Rahman of Malaya. He saw Malaysia as a federation of four equal partners, wanted English as Sabah's official language and promoted a united Kadazan-Dusun identity, without success.

He was chief minister from 16 September 1963, at the head of the Sabah Alliance. Relations with the federal government soured when he pressed Sabah's rights under the 20-point agreement and sought to replace British officials with local men as fast as they could be trained, while the federal government preferred officials from Peninsular Malaysia. Forced to resign on 31 December 1964, he became the first federal cabinet member from Sabah. After Singapore left Malaysia in 1965 he sought a review of Sabah's place in the federation, which the federal government rejected. He was High Commissioner to Australia from 1968 to 1973 and governor of Sabah from 1973 to 1975.

On 7 January 1971 he converted to Islam with his wife and five children at Tun Mustapha's residence and took the name Muhammad Fuad. In 1975, with Harris Salleh, he founded the Sabah People's United Front (BERJAYA), which defeated Mustapha's party in the 1976 state election.

On 6 June 1976 his plane from Labuan crashed about 2 kilometres from Kota Kinabalu International Airport, killing everyone on board, among them his son Johari and several cabinet members. The disaster is known as the Double Six Crash, and the Double Six Monument marks the site. He was buried at the State Mausoleum near the Sabah State Mosque and was given the title Bapa Malaysia Dari Sabah, Father of Malaysia from Sabah.
fubing-system: The fubing militia was first employed by the Western Wei under the administration of the regent Yuwen Tai, and was adopted in turn by the Northern Zhou, Sui and Tang dynasties as the basis of their armies from the 6th to the 8th centuries. It supplemented the equal-field system, which assigned every household a share of land to farm. The Sui placed the militia units under local civil administration, while the Tang brought them under metropolitan control through the Ministry of the Army. The name is written fǔbīng zhì in pinyin and fu-ping chih in Wade–Giles.

Militiamen farmed their land when off duty and were mobilised again whenever a war occurred, and as reserves they could also be called up quickly in times of political instability; those living more than 2000 li away served for two months every 18 months. The units became hereditary military families and gave rise to large militarised settlements and communities. The Tang fielded 634 militia units, later called Zhechongfu, with every six families expected to provide one man. A unit had 800 to 1200 men, divided into tuan of 300, dui of 50 and huo of 10.

The units were concentrated in the north: Guanzhong alone fielded 261, Shanxi 164, and Henan and Shandong 74, together about 80 percent of fubing conscripts. Because the militiamen supported themselves by farming, the system cost the government little. It provided, however, only for peacetime and brief campaigns, since prolonged warfare kept the men from their fields, and it was gradually abandoned in favour of full-time army units known as jian'er.
fucine-lake: The Fucine Lake was an endorheic karst lake between 650 and 680 metres above sea level in western Abruzzo, ringed by the Sirente and Velino ranges, Mount Salviano and the Vallelonga, with Avezzano to its north-west. Once the third largest lake in Italy after Garda and Maggiore, it lay in a tectonic depression formed between the Pliocene and the Quaternary. Its only real tributary was the Giovenco, and with no outlet but karst sinkholes its level rose and fell sharply, flooding farmland. The Romans called it Fucinus Lacus, founded Marruvium on its shore and believed it harboured malaria.

Julius Caesar wished to drain the lake but was killed first. According to Suetonius, the emperor Claudius employed 30,000 workers for eleven years, from 41 to 52, on a tunnel 5.6 km long under Mount Salviano to carry the water to the Liri. At the opening, marked by a naval battle staged on the lake, a landslide blocked the flow, and a later one sent a wave over the imperial banquet; the freedmen Tiberius Claudius Narcissus and Pallante, prefects of the works, were blamed. The scheme reduced the lake from about 140 to perhaps 90 square kilometres, and Hadrian's deeper canal shrank it to about 57.

When the empire fell, maintenance stopped. Sediment choked the collecting canal, and an earthquake, probably shortly before 508, lowered the lake side of a fault across it. By the end of the 5th century, and certainly by the end of the 6th, the lake had returned to its old size. Attempts to restore the Roman scheme in the 13th and 15th centuries failed.

Prince Alessandro Torlonia commissioned the Swiss engineer Jean François Mayor de Montricher, who began a larger canal along the Roman route in 1862, and the lake was drained by 1878. The plain is one of Italy's most fertile vegetable-growing areas, known for the Fucino potato and carrot, and Avezzano is its largest town. It also holds the Fucino Space Centre, begun by Telespazio in 1963. Roman antiquities found there entered the Torlonia Collection.
fuhrer: Führer has been used as a military title in Germany since at least the 18th century. A company's temporary or less qualified commander, for example, was a Kompanieführer, while a fully qualified commanding officer was a Kompaniechef. The first political use of the word was for Georg Ritter von Schönerer (1842–1921), the pan-German Austrian nationalist, whose followers called him the Führer. According to the historian Richard J. Evans, this probably introduced the term to the German far right, though the Nazis may also have been influenced by Benito Mussolini's informal title of Duce, which likewise means leader.

Adolf Hitler took the title to denote his function as head of the Nazi Party. He received it in 1921, when he resigned in anger at party founder Anton Drexler's plan to merge with another party and returned only on condition that he be made chairman with dictatorial powers. After he became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, a law of 1934 merged the offices of president and chancellor on the death of President Paul von Hindenburg. Hitler then became Führer und Reichskanzler, although Reichskanzler was quietly dropped from everyday use. Soldiers swore allegiance to him as Führer of the German Reich and Nation, and on 23 June 1941 he declared himself Germanic Führer, to assert leadership over peoples the Nazis counted as Nordic-Germanic.

The slogan Ein Volk, ein Reich, ein Führer, meaning One People, One Empire, One Leader, was among the most repeated of the Nazis and appeared on countless posters. It stressed the leader's absolute control over almost every part of German society, with the churches formally the main exception. The term spread from the party to the state, the armed forces, the nation and finally all Germanic peoples. Hitler kept up a pretence of legality, issuing thousands of decrees based on the Reichstag Fire Decree, and his vague orders set subordinates against one another. Lower ranks also used the word: Gauleiter led Nazi regions, and the SS and SA used Führer in their rank titles.

In German the word remains common in compounds such as Reiseführer, travel guide, and Führerschein, driving licence. Because of its link with Hitler, the isolated word usually has negative connotations when it means a political leader.
fuhrerprinzip: The political-science term Führerprinzip was coined by Hermann von Keyserling, a Baltic German philosopher. As an ideology it sees an organisation as a hierarchy of leaders, each with absolute responsibility in his own area, owed absolute obedience and personal loyalty by those below and answerable to those above. Rudolf Hess described it as unconditional authority downwards and responsibility upwards. Adolf Hitler proclaimed it the law of the Nazi Party as early as July 1921, when he left the party in a quarrel with its founder Anton Drexler and returned only when the committee accepted his demand to replace Drexler as chairman.

The Nazi Party split into a northern faction led by Otto and Gregor Strasser, which disagreed about whether the principle was essential, and a southern faction led by Hitler. At the Bamberg Conference on 14 February 1926 Hitler defeated the opposition and made it the managing principle of the party. In 1934 he imposed it on the government and civil society, and organisations in schools, sports associations and factories were led by appointed leaders rather than elected committees. The armed forces swore a Führer Oath to Hitler personally from 1934. The legal theorist Carl Schmitt defended it as the foundation of the total state.

Propaganda supported the idea in films such as Der Herrscher and Kolberg, and appealed to the memory of Frederick the Great and Otto von Bismarck. Hermann Göring told the British ambassador that none of the leadership counted for more than the stones they stood on, and that the Führer alone decided.

After the Second World War, defendants at the Nuremberg trials of 1945 and 1946 and at the Eichmann trial in 1961 argued that the Führerprinzip voided their responsibility, since they were officers following superior orders. In Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963) Hannah Arendt described Eichmann as an ordinary administrator who denied personal responsibility, the figure she called the banality of evil. Eichmann said he had been doing his job and had tried to act in accordance with Immanuel Kant's categorical imperative.
fujian: Fujian is bordered by Zhejiang to the north, Jiangxi to the west, Guangdong to the south and the Taiwan Strait to the east. The province is mostly mountainous, traditionally described as eight parts mountain, one part water and one part farmland, and its highest point is Mount Huanggang, at 2,157 metres. The name Fujian, 'happy establishment', combines the names of Fuzhou and Jianzhou, which is now Nanping. Because of the mountains and successive waves of migration, it is one of China's most culturally and linguistically diverse provinces.

Excavations at Keqiutou on Pingtan Island show that Fujian had entered the Neolithic by the middle of the sixth millennium BCE. The kingdom of Minyue was located there; its name joins Min, perhaps an ethnic name and also that of the main river, with Yue, after the State of Yue in Zhejiang, whose royal family fled to Fujian after Chu annexed that kingdom in 306 BCE. King Wuzhu built a fortified city at Fuzhou, and his kingdom reached into eastern Guangdong, eastern Jiangxi and southern Zhejiang.

A first wave of settlers from the north arrived in the early fourth century, mainly from eight families of central China, among them Chen, Lin, Huang and Zheng, which remain the commonest surnames in the province. In the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period a second wave came with the brothers Wang Chao, Wang Shengui and Wang Shenzhi, who set up a Kingdom of Min with its capital at Fuzhou. The name Fujian was first used for an administrative region in 985.

From 1357 to 1366 Muslims of Quanzhou took part in the Ispah Rebellion before the Yuan crushed it, and the city then lost its foreign trade. Under the Ming, Fujian became a province, and Changle served as the base for Zheng He's expeditions. A sea trade ban hampered it, and the Qing imposed another ban of about twenty years against Koxinga's Ming loyalists on Taiwan.

Fujian has a population of about 41.5 million, with Fuzhou as its capital. Quanzhou is its largest prefecture-level city by population, and Xiamen was one of China's first special economic zones. Southern Min, or Hokkien, is spoken by much of the ethnic Chinese population of Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, because of emigration. The province has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Fujian Tulou, earth buildings of the Hakka, listed in 2008.
fujiwara-clan: The clan descended from the Nakatomi clan and, as legend held, through them from the ancestral god Ame-no-Koyane. Its founder, Nakatomi no Kamatari (614–669), was rewarded by Emperor Tenji with the honorific Fujiwara, after the wisteria field on Mount Tono where Kamatari and the then Prince Naka, whom he had befriended in a game of kemari, conspired against the Soga clan. Kamatari led a coup against the Soga in 645 and began the sweeping reforms known as the Taika Reform.

The surname passed to the descendants of his second son Fujiwara no Fuhito (659–720), who married his daughter Kōmyōshi to Emperor Shōmu, the first empress consort of Japan who was not herself of the imperial family. Fuhito's four sons founded four branches, of which the Hokke, or Northern branch, came to lead the whole clan.

During the Heian period the Hokke built a hereditary claim to the posts of regent for a minor emperor (sesshō) and for an adult one (kampaku). The clan's strategy was to marry its daughters to emperors, so that its male heads were often the emperor's father-in-law, uncle or maternal grandfather. Fujiwara no Yoshifusa was the first non-imperial person to become regent for a minor emperor, in 858, when his grandson was enthroned as Emperor Seiwa, and his adopted son Mototsune became the first kampaku.

The family reached its peak under Fujiwara no Michinaga (966–1027), grandfather of three emperors and father of six empresses or consorts; he never took the title of kampaku, as he held more power than the office gave. Under the Fujiwara the court produced kana scripts, the Pillow Book of Sei Shōnagon and the Tale of Genji by Murasaki Shikibu, herself a Fujiwara.

Their control weakened with Emperor Go-Sanjō (reigned 1068–73), the first emperor since Uda whose mother was not a Fujiwara, and with the cloistered rule begun in 1087. The Hōgen Disturbance of 1156 and the Heiji Disturbance of 1160 brought the Taira to power and ended Fujiwara dominance, and the Kamakura shogunate was founded in 1192.

A northern branch, the Northern Fujiwara, ruled the Tōhoku region in the 12th century. In the 13th century the Hokke split into five regent houses: Konoe, Takatsukasa, Kujō, Nijō and Ichijō, which kept a monopoly on the offices of sesshō and kampaku until they were abolished in the Meiji era. Younger branches turned to the arts and produced scholars such as Fujiwara no Shunzei and Fujiwara no Teika. Emperors and crown princes often took their principal consorts from the Fujiwara until the marriage of the Crown Prince Hirohito in January 1924, and Fumimaro Konoe and Morihiro Hosokawa, both descended from the clan, became prime ministers.
fujiwara-no-kiyohira: Kiyohira was a samurai of mixed Japanese and Emishi descent, born in 1056 somewhere in the Kitakami Basin. His father, Fujiwara no Tsunekiyo, came from the Hidesato branch of the Fujiwara, known for its fighting men, and had been a mid-level official at Fort Taga, in present-day Sendai, before he married a daughter of Abe no Yoritoki, left his post and went to live with her family. The boy was thus born in an Emishi household to a father the Japanese authorities regarded as a traitor.

The wars of his youth cost him his family. His grandfather Abe no Yoritoki fell in battle in 1057, his uncle Sadato in 1062, and in the same year his mother's brothers were deported to Kyūshū. Minamoto no Yoriyoshi beheaded his father with a blunt sword. His mother then became the concubine of Kiyohara no Takehira, who had fought on Yoriyoshi's side, and Kiyohira grew up as Kiyohara no Kiyohira beside his elder stepbrother Sanehira and younger half-brother Iehira.

The Later Three Years' War grew out of the rivalry between the three brothers. Kiyohira won it in 1087 with the help of Minamoto no Yoshiie, the son of Yoriyoshi, though Iehira killed his wife and son during the fighting. He went back to Fort Toyota, in present-day Ōshū, and some time between about 1090 and 1100 moved to Mount Kanzan in what is now Hiraizumi. The site lay on the Frontier Way, the main road south to the capital, at the centre of his realm, and on the south bank of the Koromo River, in traditionally Japanese territory where Emishi forts had never stood.

He seems to have used the name Kiyohara until 1117, when he was over sixty, and then took the name Fujiwara and passed it to his children. He had several wives, among them a Taira wife from Kyōto who left the frontier for the capital, and two Emishi wives, a Kiyohara and an Abe. His eldest son Koretsune was the rightful heir, but his successor was his second son Motohira, born about 1105. Kiyohira died on 10 August 1128. The temple complex of Chūson-ji on Mount Kanzan, with its pagodas, repositories and gardens, was meant as the lasting expression of his vision for his family and domain, which his dynasty ruled until 1189.
fujiwara-no-michinaga: Michinaga was born in Kyōto in 966, the son of Kaneie, who became regent in 986 and held the position until his death in 990. Under the hereditary principle of the Fujiwara regents, Michinaga stood in line after his elder brothers Michitaka and Michikane. Michitaka was regent from 990 until his death in 995, and Michikane succeeded him but ruled for only seven days before he too died of disease.

With both brothers dead, Michinaga struggled against Fujiwara no Korechika, Michitaka's eldest son. Fujiwara no Senshi, mother of Emperor Ichijō, coerced Ichijō into granting Michinaga the title of Nairan in 995. Korechika was ruined the next year by a scandal likely arranged by Michinaga: believing that the retired Emperor Kazan was visiting his mistress, he and his brother ambushed Kazan and shot an arrow through his sleeve. Michinaga's supporters pressed charges of lèse-majesté. He became Minister of the Right in 995 and Minister of the Left in 996.

He was known as the Mido Kampaku, after his residence, Mido, and because he was regent in all but name; he never formally took the title of Kampaku. He made his first daughter, Shoshi, Ichijō's Chūgū empress, though the emperor already had an empress, Teishi. His second daughter, Kenshi, married the future Emperor Sanjō, and his third and fourth daughters, Ishi and Kishi, married Ichijō's sons Go-Ichijō and Go-Suzaku. Minamoto no Yorimitsu and Minamoto no Yorinobu were his two principal commanders.

Michinaga and Sanjō often came into conflict, and in 1016 Michinaga pressured Sanjō into retirement. Because Go-Ichijō was young, he ruled as Sesshō, and a month after resigning as Chancellor he gave the office to his eldest son Yorimichi. In 1019 he became a monk at the Hōjō-ji, which he had built.

Michinaga died on 3 January 1028 aged sixty-two. He is said to have called out to Amida on his deathbed, asking for entry to Paradise. His diary, the Midō Kanpakuki, records the Heian court at the height of Fujiwara power. The character Genji in the Tale of Genji is believed to be based in part on Michinaga as well as on Korechika.
fujiwara-no-mototsune: Mototsune was the son of Fujiwara no Nagara, one of the brothers of Fujiwara no Yoshifusa, and Yoshifusa adopted him as his son and heir. His rise through the offices of the court followed in his adoptive father's footsteps. He was named Sangi in 864, in the era Jōgan, Chūnagon in 866 and Dainagon in the first month of 870. In 872 he became Udaijin, and four years later, in 876, he was named Sesshō.

From the regency he rose to the highest offices of state. In 880, in the era Gangyō, he was named Daijō Daijin, and in 884 he received the new title of Kampaku, which let him keep his hold on the court after an emperor came of age. He held it for six years and retired as Kampaku on the 14th day of the 12th month of 890, in the era Kanpyō, shortly before his death.

Mototsune died on 25 February 891, the 13th day of the 1st month of Kampyō 3, at the age of 56. He was known as Horikawa Daijin, and as Daijō Daijin he received the posthumous name Shōsen Kō. He married a daughter of Imperial Prince Saneyasu, son of Emperor Ninmyō, and also Princess Sōshi, a daughter of Imperial Prince Tadara and granddaughter of Emperor Saga.

His sons carried the family's power into the next generation. Tokihira and Nakahira both became Sadaijin, and Tadahira became Daijō Daijin and regent. Several of his daughters married into the imperial house: Yoriko and Kazuko became consorts of Emperor Seiwa, Kamiko of Emperor Kōkō, the elder Onshi of Emperor Uda, and the younger Onshi of Emperor Daigo, whose sons became Emperor Suzaku and Emperor Murakami.
fukui-prefecture: Fukui Prefecture lies in the Chūbu region of Honshū and borders Ishikawa Prefecture to the north, Gifu Prefecture to the east, Shiga Prefecture to the south and Kyoto Prefecture to the southwest. It covers about 4,190 square kilometres and faces the Sea of Japan, within the historic Hokuriku region. The western part, formerly Wakasa, is a narrow plain between the mountains and the sea. The larger eastern part, formerly Echizen, has wider plains and holds the capital and most of the population. The area lies within Japan's snow country, and parts of it are protected as Hakusan National Park and the Echizen-Kaga Kaigan and Wakasa Wan Quasi-National Parks.

The Kitadani Dinosaur Quarry on the Sugiyama River, in the city of Katsuyama, has yielded dinosaurs such as Fukuiraptor, Fukuisaurus, Koshisaurus, Fukuivenator, Fukuititan and Tambatitanis, and fossils from the prefecture are shown at the Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum.

Fukui originally consisted of the old provinces of Wakasa and Echizen before the prefecture was formed in 1871. During the Edo period the daimyō of the region bore the surname Matsudaira and descended from Tokugawa Ieyasu. The Matsudaira clan was headquartered at Fukui Castle, which stood on the site of the modern prefectural offices. Fukui was heavily bombed in World War II, and the castle, surrounded by a moat, was demolished; the prefectural government buildings were built on its site.

Fukui is the capital and largest city, and other major cities include Sakai, Echizen and Sabae. Sabae produces 90 per cent of Japan's domestically made glasses, and Fukui has long been a centre of papermaking, with makers of traditional Echizen paper. The prefecture is also known for sake, rice and soba noodles, and its people speak a distinctive accent, Fukui-ben.

Among its historic sites are Eihei-ji, a Buddhist training temple founded by Dōgen in 1244 on about 33 hectares; the Ichijōdani Asakura Family Historic Ruins; the National Treasures of Myōtsū-ji, its three-storied pagoda and main hall; and Maruoka Castle, built in 1576 and the oldest standing castle in Japan. Nuclear power stations stand along Wakasa Bay.
fukuoka: Fukuoka is built along Hakata Bay, bordered by mountains on three sides and open to the Genkai Sea on the north. It is the point of Japan's main islands nearest to the Asian mainland, and Busan in South Korea lies about 180 kilometres away. People have lived in the area since the Jomon period, and settlers of the Yayoi period were among the earliest to arrive. Distance from Kyoto, Osaka and later Edo gave the city a distinctive local culture and dialect.

The Book of the Later Han records that an envoy from the region visited the court of Emperor Guangwu in 57 CE and received a gold seal, which was found in the 17th century. By the end of the Asuka period the port, sometimes called the Port of Dazaifu, had grown into the regional government headquarters for Kyushu and a trade centre with Tang China. Trade continued to grow after the Kōrokan declined at the end of the Heian period, and monks who had studied in China founded temples there. Eisai founded Shōfuku-ji, described as the oldest Zen temple in Japan, and is credited with bringing tea to Japan; Enni, who built Joten-ji, is credited with bringing udon from China.

From 1268 Kublai Khan sent envoys to make the Kamakura shogunate acknowledge his suzerainty, and the shogunate refused. During the Muromachi period Hakata was the first free city in Japanese history, governed by a council of 12 wealthy merchants called Tongyoji, and it remained Japan's main port for trade with mainland Asia, particularly with the Song and Yuan dynasties of China and with Korea. The name Fukuoka, combining the characters for good fortune and hill, was given by the daimyō Kuroda Nagamasa to his new castle town after the Fukuoka district of Bizen Province, the ancestral home of his clan.

In the early 20th century the city gained the Fukuoka Medical College in 1903 and a streetcar service in 1910. In World War II it was a regional military centre, and it was firebombed on 19 June 1945, an attack that destroyed 21.5 per cent of its urban area.

Fukuoka is the capital of Fukuoka Prefecture and the most populous city on Kyushu, with a population of over a million and a half in seven wards. It was designated a city by government ordinance on 1 April 1972. Its oldest festival, Hakata Gion Yamakasa, is held for two weeks each July and is said to date from 1241. The city museum displays the gold seal of 57 CE.
