fukuoka-prefecture: Fukuoka Prefecture lies at the northernmost point of Kyūshū, on the Kanmon Straits, which connect the Tsushima Strait and the Seto Inland Sea across from Yamaguchi Prefecture on the island of Honshu. It extends south towards the Ariake Sea and borders Saga, Kumamoto and Ōita prefectures. The prefecture faces the sea on three sides, and it includes a number of small islands off the north coast. Fukuoka is the capital and the largest city on Kyūshū, and other major cities include Kitakyushu, Kurume and Ōmuta. The prefecture includes the former provinces of Chikugo, Chikuzen and Buzen.

The prefecture's religious history is old. Kōra taisha, Sumiyoshi-jinja and Hakozaki-gū are its chief Shinto shrines. The oldest of its Buddhist temples, Kanzeon-ji at Dazaifu, was founded in the 7th century by the emperor to honour his mother, and together with its Kaidan-in it was one of three places in Japan where Buddhist monks could be ordained.

Monks who had studied in China sailed back and founded temples in the heart of Hakata, now Fukuoka City. Eisai founded Shōfuku-ji, known as the oldest Zen temple in Japan, and Kūkai established Tocho-ji. Enni built Jōten-ji, and he is also credited with first bringing udon noodles to Japan. During the Tokugawa shogunate the daimyo Arima Toyōji was relocated to the region and moved his family temple to Kurume, where it became the Zen temple Bairin-ji.

The prefecture contains much of Kyūshū's industry, with automobiles, semiconductors and steel among its major products; the tire maker Bridgestone was founded there. Kyushu University is in Fukuoka. The Kyushu National Museum at Dazaifu covers the history of Kyūshū from prehistory to the Meiji era, with emphasis on its cultural exchange with China and Korea. The Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival is held each July, and the Genko Historical Museum displays arms and armour of the 13th-century Mongol invasions.
fukushima-masanori: Fukushima Masanori, first called Ichimatsu, was born in 1561 at Futatsudera in Owari Province, the eldest son of the barrel merchant Fukushima Masanobu, though some sources suggest his real father was Hoshino Narimasa, a cooper from Kiyosu. His mother was the younger sister of the mother of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who was thus his first cousin, and as a young man he served Hideyoshi as a page. He first saw battle in the assault on Miki Castle in Harima Province from 1578 to 1580.

At the Battle of Shizugatake in 1583 Masanori took the first head, that of the enemy general Ogasato Ieyoshi, and became known as one of the Seven Spears of Shizugatake, alongside Katō Kiyomasa. After the Kyūshū Expedition of 1587 he was made a daimyō with the fief of Imabari in Iyo Province, rated at 110,000 koku. In the Korean campaign he captured Ch'ongju in 1592, and in 1595 he led 10,000 men to surround Seiganji Temple on Mount Kōya until Toyotomi Hidetsugu had killed himself, after which he received Hidetsugu's former fief of Kiyosu.

After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 Masanori was one of seven generals who moved against Ishida Mitsunari, who had underreported their achievements in Korea. Popular accounts call it a plot to kill him, while the historian Watanabe Daimon sees a legal dispute that Tokugawa Ieyasu mediated. In the campaign of 1600 Masanori helped take Takegahana Castle and Gifu Castle, and at Sekigahara he led the Eastern Army's advance guard, opening the battle with a charge against Ukita Hideie's army in one of its bloodiest clashes, which turned his way when Kobayakawa Hideaki changed sides.

The charge against him was that, by repairing part of Hiroshima Castle damaged by a typhoon flood, he had broken the Buke Shohatto. He had applied for permission two months earlier without receiving it. The matter was first settled on condition that he apologise and remove the repairs, but the bakufu then held the removal insufficient and confiscated his lands in Aki and Bingo, worth 500,000 koku. He was given instead the Takaino Domain, worth 45,000 koku, in Shinano and Echigo. He died on 26 August 1624. His descendants became hatamoto in the service of the Tokugawa shōgun.
fulbert-youlou: Youlou, whose last name means grape in Lari, was born in Madibou, a younger child in a family of three boys. He was baptised at nine, received the Christian name Fulbert, and entered the Petit Séminaire of Brazzaville in 1929. He completed his studies in Cameroon and Libreville, and at Yaoundé met Barthélemy Boganda and André-Marie Mbida, later nationalist leaders. He served as a priest in the parish of Saint-François de Brazzaville, directing youth organisations and Catholic groups.

In the territorial elections of 1947 he stood for the African college in the district of Pool and was heavily defeated. In 1955 a Kongo council chose him as its candidate for the legislative elections, and his bishop tried to dissuade him. He was banned from wearing the cassock and celebrating Mass. Some supporters regarded him as the reincarnation of Jesus-Matswa, and he became a symbol of resistance to colonial rule.

On 17 May 1956 Youlou founded the Union démocratique de défense des intérêts africains, an anti-communist party of Liberal Christian persuasion whose symbol was the crocodile. In September 1957 it won a majority in the Assembly with 23 seats, and rivalry with Jacques Opangault's African Socialist Movement turned violent. In the referendum of 28 September 1958 he supported the Yes vote on the French Community. On 28 November 1958 the socialist deputies left the Assembly, and Youlou proclaimed the Republic, was named head of the provisional government and became prime minister on 8 December.

In August 1960 he led the country into independence. He favoured economic liberalism, pursued a pro-Western policy he called moderate and in December 1960 held a conference in Brazzaville that created the anti-communist groupe de Brazzaville. In August 1962 he announced a one-party state, and in August 1963 the unions refused his proposed system. Union leaders were imprisoned, and the revolution of the Trois Glorieuses followed. Charles de Gaulle despised him, France refused to assist him, and he resigned in the face of overwhelming opposition.

Youlou was imprisoned after his resignation and on 25 March 1965 fled to Léopoldville with the help of his successor, Alphonse Massamba-Débat. A popular tribunal in Congo-Brazzaville tried him in absence from 8 June 1965 on charges including misappropriation of public funds, and sentenced him to death. He answered with a book, J'accuse la Chine, in 1966. Later regimes held him responsible for the country's problems, and his name was struck from public discourse. He died of hepatitis in Madrid in 1972, and was buried in Madibou without official ceremony. The National Conference of 1991, which restored multi-party democracy, rehabilitated his memory.
fulda: Fulda lies on the river Fulda in the German state of Hesse and is the administrative seat of the Fulda district. Since 1974 it has been included in the district as a city with special status. Its station is an interchange between local and long-distance services on the Hanover to Würzburg high-speed line, and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Fulda has its seat in the cathedral.

In 744 Saint Sturm, a disciple of Saint Boniface, founded the Benedictine monastery of Fulda as one of Boniface's outposts in the reorganisation of the church in Germany. Carolingian rulers and leading families supported it with large donations, and in 751 it was placed directly under the Papal See. Boniface was killed by the Frisians in 754 and his relics were brought to Fulda. Between 790 and 819 the abbey church was rebuilt on the model of Old St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. Rabanus Maurus was abbot from 822 to 842, and the abbey owned the Codex Fuldensis and works by Cicero and Bede. Its school became a centre of learning.

On Christmas day 1235 five boys died in a house fire, and local people accused the Jewish community of killing them for ritual purposes. Jews were tortured and 34 were killed after two confessed. Emperor Frederick II investigated and found them innocent. In the Counter-Reformation Prince-abbot Balthasar von Dernbach called in the Jesuits in 1571 and ordered his subjects, most of them Lutheran, to return to the Catholic faith or leave. He also ordered the Fulda witch trials, in which hundreds were arrested.

Fulda became a bishopric in 1752 and the prince-bishops ruled until Napoleon I dissolved the bishopric in 1802. The cathedral was remodelled in 1704–12 and the Stadtschloss in 1707–12 by Johann Dientzenhofer, which give the city its title of Baroque City. After 1814–15 most of the territory went to the Electorate of Hesse, which Prussia annexed in 1866.

From 1938 to 1943 a Nazi forced labour camp for Romani people stood at Fulda. In the Cold War the Fulda Gap, an old east-west invasion route, was presumed to be where a conventional war between NATO and Soviet forces would begin, and American cavalry regiments were stationed in the city until 1993. The crypt of the abbey church still holds the relics of Boniface.
fulda-abbey: Saint Boniface commissioned Sturm to build a larger church than any other Boniface had founded. In January 744 Sturm chose an unpopulated plot along the Fulda River, and the monastery's foundation dates to 12 March 744. Sturm visited monasteries in Italy, among them Monte Cassino, for models, and became the first abbot. In 751 Boniface had the house placed directly under the Holy See by Pope Zachary, freeing it from the local bishops. His tomb at Fulda made it a place of pilgrimage.

The monks practised many trades, copied manuscripts and made goods that made the house wealthy, and some settled villages in the surrounding land. Under Abbot Baugulf the school had an inner school for Christian studies and an outer school for secular pupils, and in 787 Charlemagne praised it as a model. The monks' own account, the Supplex Libellus, tells how Abbot Ratgar's harsh rule and costly building led Louis the Pious to exile him in 817. Rabanus Maurus, abbot from 822, gave the school separate departments for the sciences, theology and the arts and gathered relics and manuscripts.

The library held about 2,000 manuscripts and preserved works such as the Annales of Tacitus and the Res gestae of Ammianus Marcellinus. An Italian book-hunter probably found there in 1417 the last surviving manuscript of De rerum natura by Lucretius. The monks also kept the Annales necrologici, a list of the dead of the house for whom they prayed, which later took in patrons and nobles.

After the decline of Carolingian rule the abbey relied on other patrons. Its abbot was for several centuries primate of the Benedictine monasteries in Germany, and in 1221 Emperor Frederick II made the abbots princes of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1356 Emperor Charles IV gave the prince-abbot the title of Archchancellor of the Empress. Nobles came to fill the abbey, and in the 14th century Count Johann of Ziegenhain led a rising against Prince-Abbot Heinrich VI. Much of the collection of Rabanus was lost when the Hessians looted Fulda in the Thirty Years' War.

The monastery was dissolved in 1802 and the principality secularised in 1803, though the diocese of Fulda continued. The territory passed through the Principality of Nassau-Orange-Fulda, French rule, the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt, occupation by Austria and then Prussia, and in 1815 the Electorate of Hesse.
fulgencio-batista: Fulgencio Batista y Zaldívar was born on 16 January 1901 in Veguita, in the municipality of Banes, Cuba, to parents who had fought in the Cuban War of Independence. He was of Spanish, African and Chinese descent, and possibly of some Taíno descent. His mother named him Rubén and gave him her surname, and he was legally Rubén Zaldívar until 1939. When he then tried to register as a presidential candidate, no birth certificate existed for Fulgencio Batista, and he had to pay the local judge 15,000 pesos.

Batista joined the Sergeants' Revolt of 1933, which overthrew Gerardo Machado. Contemporaries claimed he was drawn in mainly because he was the only sergeant with a car. He then became army chief of staff with the rank of colonel and controlled the armed forces behind a short-lived five-member presidency. In January 1934 he, conspiring with the United States envoy Sumner Welles, forced President Ramón Grau San Martín to resign, and he ruled through puppet presidents until he was elected president in 1940. He carried out social reforms and pro-union policies, and Cuba entered the Second World War on the side of the Allies on 9 December 1941.

After four years in the United States he returned, and on 10 March 1952, three months before an election in which he stood a distant third, he seized power with army backing and cancelled the vote. He suspended the 1940 constitution and revoked most political liberties, including the right to strike. Havana became a centre of gambling and prostitution run for the American Mafia, and United States companies owned large shares of Cuba's sugar lands, mines and utilities. After Fidel Castro's attack on the Moncada Barracks on 26 July 1953, Batista relied increasingly on police violence. Estimates of those killed range from hundreds to 20,000, a figure that is disputed.

From December 1956 to December 1958 Castro's 26th of July Movement waged guerrilla war against the government. Rebels under Che Guevara defeated Batista's forces at Santa Clara on New Year's Eve 1958, and on 1 January 1959 Batista fled to the Dominican Republic under Rafael Trujillo's protection. He later found asylum in Portugal, living on Madeira and in Estoril, and died of a heart attack in Marbella, Spain, on 6 August 1973.
fulk-king-of-jerusalem: Fulk was born in late 1089 or 1090, the son of Count Fulk IV of Anjou and Bertrada of Montfort. He became sole count of Anjou when his father died on 14 April 1109, and count of Maine in 1110 through his marriage to Eremburga, daughter of Elias of Maine. He subdued rebellious castellans and clashed with King Henry I of England over Maine, for which he did homage to Henry in 1113. In 1120 he became a major sponsor of the Knights Templar and made an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

In 1128 his son Geoffrey married Empress Matilda, and in 1129 Fulk left Anjou to Geoffrey and went to Jerusalem to marry Melisende, daughter of King Baldwin II. As her dowry the couple received Acre and Tyre.

Baldwin II died on 21 August 1131, and Fulk and Melisende were crowned on 14 September in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, the first monarchs crowned there. In Antioch, Princess Alice seized power, and in 1132 Fulk marched north, fought Count Pons of Tripoli and won the regency for the young Princess Constance.

At home he appointed Angevins to key offices and tried to exclude Melisende from power. In 1134 Hugh II of Jaffa, her cousin, was accused of plotting to murder the king. Hugh allied with the Muslims of Ascalon and lost the support of the other lords. Fulk besieged Jaffa until Patriarch William of Malines negotiated peace, with three years of exile for Hugh. Melisende then forced Fulk to share rule, and William of Tyre wrote that he did nothing without her consent.

Fulk and Melisende made little attempt to expand by conquest. They blockaded Fatimid-ruled Ascalon and guarded the borders against Imad al-Din Zengi. In 1137 Zengi defeated Fulk's army near Montferrand, and Fulk gave up the fortress in return for his freedom. That year Emperor John II Komnenos demanded the submission of Antioch, and Fulk affirmed the Byzantine claim. In 1142 he avoided a confrontation with John by saying that the kingdom could not support so large an army.

On 7 November 1143 Fulk rode out with Melisende for a picnic near Acre. They flushed a hare, he spurred his horse after it, and the horse stumbled and threw him. The saddle struck his head, and he died on 10 November. He was buried beside the gate on the right side of the Holy Sepulchre. Melisende promptly made herself sole ruler, despite the coronation of their son Baldwin III on 25 December. The Arab chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi judged Fulk an unsound and unsuccessful successor to Baldwin II, while William of Tyre described him as faithful, gentle and an experienced warrior.
fulk-nerra: Fulk III, known as Fulk the Black or Fulk Nerra, was born around 970, the son of Geoffrey I of Anjou, also called Geoffrey Grisegonelle, and Adele of Meaux. He was a natural horseman and fearsome warrior with a keen sense of strategy, and he sided with the Capetians against the Carolingians. His county seat was Angers, and his bitter enemy was Odo II of Blois, his neighbour to the east along the Loire; the two traded towns, followers and insults throughout their lives.

Fulk is regarded as one of the first great builders of medieval castles, and is estimated to have constructed about a hundred, as well as abbeys, in the Loire valley. His first castle, at Langeais, began as a wooden tower and was later replaced in stone with a donjon. It stood in the territory of Odo I of Blois, and they fought over it in 994, but Odo I died suddenly and his son did not manage to evict Fulk. He went on building in a slow encirclement of Tours: Montbazon, Montrésor, Mirebeau, Montrichard, Loches and in 1016 Montboyau.

In June 992 he won his first victory, at Conquereuil, over Conan I, Duke of Brittany, who was killed. The biggest battle against Odo II was fought at Pontlevoy in July 1016. Fulk's smaller force attacked Odo's 10,000 men from behind and was routed, but Odo, thinking the battle won, went swimming in the Cher, and reinforcements led by Count Herbert Wake-Dog of Maine arrived and routed his surprised men.

Fulk made four pilgrimages to Jerusalem. The first, in 1003, was penitential, and the second, in 1008, was imposed by the king as punishment after Fulk ordered the murder of an enemy. For the third, in 1035 with Robert I, Duke of Normandy, and the fourth, in 1038, he felt a duty to protect pilgrims and provided armed security along the route. He died at Metz in 1040 on his return and was buried at his monastery at Beaulieu.

Some sources call him devout, noting that he built or endowed abbeys; others see this as an anxious effort to ensure his salvation after a life of ruthless violence against enemies and his own family. His wife Elisabeth died by burning on a charge of adultery, which one account says he trumped up. His son Geoffrey Martel, by his second wife Hildegarde, succeeded him.
funcinpec: Norodom Sihanouk founded FUNCINPEC on 21 March 1981 in Pyongyang, North Korea, as a royalist resistance movement against the People's Republic of Kampuchea. He had long resisted Chinese pressure to ally with the Khmer Rouge, whom he accused of killing members of his family during the Cambodian genocide, but he reconsidered, since both sought to oust the government under Vietnam's influence. After meeting Son Sann of the Khmer People's National Liberation Front and Khieu Samphan of the Khmer Rouge, he became president of the Coalition Government of Democratic Kampuchea formed on 22 June 1982.

The movement's army, the Armee Nationale Sihanoukiste, formed on 4 September 1982 from groups such as MOULINAKA, had some 7,000 troops under In Tam, a former Prime Minister of the Khmer Republic. Ranariddh became party president in February 1992 and registered FUNCINPEC as a party under UNTAC that August. Between November 1992 and January 1993, 18 of its officials were killed in attacks attributed to the State of Cambodia's police and intelligence services. After the 1993 election it shared the cabinet equally with the Cambodian People's Party, though officials observed that Hun Sen held more sway than Ranariddh.

On 5 July 1997 troops aligned with the two parties fought in Phnom Penh, and FUNCINPEC's forces were defeated the next day. Ung Huot replaced Ranariddh as First Prime Minister, and splinter parties broke away. After the 1998 election FUNCINPEC returned as the junior partner of the CPP, and Ranariddh became President of the National Assembly. In 2006 the former secretary-general Nhek Bun Chhay ousted him and sued him for pocketing $3.6 million from the sale of the party's headquarters; a court in Phnom Penh sentenced Ranariddh to 18 months.

The party's vote fell at the elections of 2003, 2008 and 2013, and in 2013 it won no seat in the National Assembly. Ranariddh returned and was reappointed president at a party congress on 19 January 2015, prevailing over Nhek Bun Chhay in a dispute over the party stamp. The name is the French acronym for Front uni national pour un Cambodge indépendant, neutre, pacifique, et coopératif.
fundamental-orders-of-connecticut: In 1634 a group of Puritans and others, dissatisfied with the pace of Anglican reform and wanting a wider suffrage than the Massachusetts Bay government allowed, sought to found a society under their own rules; the fertility of Connecticut also drew them. The Massachusetts General Court let them settle Windsor, Wethersfield and Hartford, and set up the March Commission under Roger Ludlow to deal with the claims of the holders of the Warwick Patent of 1631. When the commission expired in March 1636, the settlers went on governing themselves.

On 31 May 1638 the Reverend Thomas Hooker preached that the choice of magistrates belongs to the people by God's allowance, and that those who appoint officers may also set bounds to their powers. Magistrates and committeemen, among them Ludlow, John Haynes, John Mason and Thomas Welles, met at Hartford to draft the Orders. No record of their debates survives, and the colony's secretary Welles copied the text into the official records.

The Orders set up a government of three parts, the electorate, the officers and the General Court, which held supreme authority; they made no mention of the Crown or any outside power. Officers such as the governor were chosen by secret paper ballot, and there were no property, tax or military qualifications for voting. The vote was not confined to church members.

Their democracy had limits. Ordinary inhabitants could vote in town meetings and hold town office, but only freemen, a status granted by the General Court or the magistrates, could vote for governor. The government rested on Puritan principles, punishing profanity and adultery, and an oath of fidelity would have kept non-Puritans from office.

In 1662 the colony obtained a royal charter from Charles II, written largely in Connecticut and keeping the Orders' form of government, which colonists saw as a continuation of them. The historian John Fiske first called the Orders the first written constitution, a claim some modern historians dispute, and the Mayflower Compact is older. Connecticut is known as the Constitution State, and the first article of its present constitution, adopted in 1965, is a Declaration of Rights that keeps the rights of the Orders.
funiculi-funicula: The song was composed in 1880 by Luigi Denza in his hometown of Castellammare di Stabia, with lyrics by the journalist Peppino Turco, to commemorate the opening of the first funicular railway on Mount Vesuvius. It was first sung at the Quisisana Hotel in Castellammare di Stabia and was presented by Turco and Denza at the Piedigrotta festival the same year. The publisher Casa Ricordi sold over a million copies of the sheet music within a year, and the song became immensely popular in Italy and abroad.

In Turco's Neapolitan lyrics a young man compares his sweetheart to a volcano and invites her to a romantic trip to the summit. The singer says that from the top one can see France, Procida and Spain, and ends by hoping to marry her. The chorus repeats the word funiculì, funiculà, which gives the song its name. Edward Oxenford wrote English lyrics with scant relationship to the original, which became traditional in English-speaking countries and often appear under the title A Merry Life.

Some composers who borrowed the tune took it for a traditional Neapolitan folk song. Richard Strauss heard it on a tour of Italy six years after it was written and used it in his tone poem Aus Italien; Denza sued and won, and Strauss had to pay him a royalty. Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov likewise used it in his Neapolitan Song of 1907. In New York in 1884 the publishers Spear and Dehnhoff issued the melody as Tra-la-la-lee without crediting Denza. Arnold Schoenberg arranged a version for ensemble in 1921.

Denza died in 1922, and the song has been in the public domain since 1 January 1993. It has been recorded by many artists, among them Beniamino Gigli, Mario Lanza, the Mills Brothers, Connie Francis, Luciano Pavarotti and Andrea Bocelli, and sung in Japanese and German versions. It has been parodied and used in films, television, games and advertising, and in 1991 a parody, Pizza Song, probably helped associate it with pizza.
funj-sultanate-of-sennar: The Christian kingdoms of Makuria and Alodia in Nubia began to decline from the 12th century. By the 13th century central Sudan seemed to have broken into petty states, and between the 14th and 15th centuries many Bedouin moved in, bringing Islam and Arabic. Tradition names one of them, Abdallah Jammah of the Abdallabi, who created a tribal federation and destroyed what was left of Alodia. In the early 16th century the federation was attacked from the south by the Funj, nomadic pastoralists who followed their own religion. The Funj founded their capital Sennar on the Blue Nile and ruled a population that included Nubians, Beja, Bedouin and Hamaj.

In 1525 the Ottoman admiral Selman Reis called the kingdom weak and easily conquerable, and noted a yearly tribute of 9,000 camels paid to Ethiopia. The Funj exported horses to Ethiopia, and in 1618 and 1619 war with the Ethiopian emperor Susenyos devastated many eastern provinces. The state reached its peak in the late 17th century, when it stretched from the Third Cataract to the edge of the Ethiopian Highlands, east to the Red Sea and west to Kordofan. Under Badi III, Sennar was a prosperous and cosmopolitan trading city.

In the 18th century the monarchy lost power to merchants, scholars and discontented nobles. About 1718 Unsa III was overthrown by the Funj aristocracy, and the Hamaj seized power in a coup in 1762. From the late 18th century the sultanate broke up in civil wars. In 1821 the last sultan, greatly weakened, surrendered to the Turco-Egyptian conquest.

The sultan, called mek, was chosen by the royal court from the sons of earlier rulers and Funj noblewomen, and a council of 20 elders had a say in decisions. Provinces were governed by a manjil, subdivided among makks, and each manjil had to travel to Sennar yearly to pay tribute. The army was feudal, and most warriors were slaves taken in annual raids on the Nuba mountains. The Funj adopted Islam, but its observance among the populace remained thin until the 18th century. Trade in gold, caravans and slaves to Egypt supplied the sultans' wealth.
fur-trade: The fur trade is a worldwide industry dealing in the acquisition and sale of animal fur. Since the establishment of a world fur market in the early modern period, the furs of boreal, polar and cold temperate mammals have been the most valued. Historically the trade stimulated the exploration and colonisation of Siberia, northern North America, and the South Shetland and South Sandwich Islands. Fur was relied on to make warm clothing, a critical consideration before coal was distributed for heating.

Before the European colonisation of the Americas, Russia was a major supplier of fur pelts to Western Europe and parts of Asia. Its trade developed in the early Middle Ages through exchanges at posts around the Baltic and Black seas, with Leipzig the main market, and Kievan Rus' was the first supplier. Russians settled in Siberia, rich in Arctic fox, lynx, sable, sea otter and ermine, and in a search for sea otter pelts, first used in China, and later the northern fur seal, the Russian Empire expanded into Alaska. From the 17th to the second half of the 19th century Russia was the world's largest supplier of fur.

European contact with North America made it a major supplier in the 17th century. The trade began as early as the 1500s between Europeans and First Nations. In 1578 there were 350 European fishing vessels at Newfoundland, and sailors traded metal implements, particularly knives, for the natives' well-worn beaver pelts, which the new felt-hat industry found especially useful. By the 1580s beaver wool was the major material of the French felt-hatters. In 1599 Captain Chauvin obtained a monopoly from Henry IV and tried to found a colony at Tadoussac.

The maritime fur trade was ship-based and sought sea otter furs from the peoples of the Pacific Northwest Coast and Alaska, mostly to be traded in China for tea, silks and porcelain. Russians pioneered it, and the British and Americans entered in the 1780s. It boomed around the turn of the 19th century and declined from the 1810s.

Beaver felt hats were an expensive status symbol in Europe, and the demand was such that the beaver in Europe and European Russia had largely disappeared through exploitation. Today the trade has diminished and rests on pelts from fur farms and regulated trapping, and it is controversial: animal rights organisations oppose it, citing the way animals are killed. Fur has been replaced in some clothing by synthetic imitations.
furstenwalde: Fürstenwalde, called Pśibor pśi Sprjewje in Lower Sorbian, is the most populous town in the Oder-Spree District of Brandenburg. It lies in the glacial valley of the Spree river north of the Rauen Hills, about 60 kilometres east of Berlin and 30 kilometres west of Frankfurt (Oder). It stands on the western part of the historic Lubusz Land, and its station is a stop on the railway line from Berlin to Frankfurt (Oder).

The settlement was first mentioned in a deed of 1272 and was founded in the course of the German Ostsiedlung migration at a ford across the Spree, probably near the site of a former Slavic settlement. The Margraves of Brandenburg of the Ascanian line had acquired the Lebus Land from Poland in 1248 or 1249. The town's importance rose as a staple port and terminal for the transport of goods on the river.

In 1373 Emperor Charles IV enforced the renunciation of the Wittelsbach margrave Otto VII of Brandenburg by the Treaty of Fürstenwalde, and from 1373 to 1415 the town was part of the Bohemian Crown. The collegiate church in Lebus had been destroyed, and Bishop Wenceslaus moved the seat of the Bishopric of Lebus to Fürstenwalde, where St Mary's Church was raised to a cathedral. The last Catholic bishop, Georg von Blumenthal, was besieged in his palace by Lutheran robbers led by Nickel von Minckwitz and had to escape through a window in disguise. The bishopric was secularized during the Reformation in 1555 and was completely disbanded when Joachim Frederick became Margrave of Brandenburg in 1598.

From the 18th century Fürstenwalde was part of the Kingdom of Prussia, and from 1815 to 1947 it lay in the Province of Brandenburg. A community of French Huguenots was established there in the early 18th century. During the World War II it was the location of a subcamp of the Sachsenhausen concentration camp. From 1952 to 1990 it belonged to the Bezirk Frankfurt of East Germany, and since 1990 it has again been part of Brandenburg.
furth: Fürth lies in the Middle Franconia region of Bavaria. Its centre is only seven km from that of Nuremberg, and it forms a continuous conurbation with Nuremberg, Erlangen and Schwabach. The historic centre stands to the east and south of the Rednitz and Pegnitz rivers, which join to form the Regnitz northwest of the Old Town. To the north lies the fertile market-gardening area called the Knoblauchsland, the garlic country. The name comes from the German word for ford, because the first settlements grew up around one.

Founded as a Franconian settlement in the mid-8th century, Fürth is first mentioned in a document of 1 November 1007, in which Emperor Heinrich II gave his property there to the newly created Bishopric of Bamberg. Market privileges were granted but later lost to Nuremberg under Heinrich III, and restored from 1062, by which time Nuremberg was already the more important town. In 1524, as part of the Reformation, Fürth became a Protestant town like Nuremberg, though ties with Bamberg meant there were always some Catholics.

In the Thirty Years War the town lost about half its population. When Croatian soldiers set fire to it in 1634 it burned for several days and was almost completely destroyed, and at the end of the war only 800 people lived there. Huguenots from France settled in 1685, and by 1700 restoration was complete and the population had risen to about 6,000. Until the end of the 18th century a representative of the Diocese of Bamberg administered it. Fürth passed to Bavaria in 1806 and from 1818 was a city responsible for its own administration.

Jews are mentioned in Fürth as early as 1440. In 1528 the Margrave of Ansbach, George the Pious, allowed two Jews, Perman and Uriel, to settle in return for high taxes, and the community grew. By the 17th century there was a Talmudic academy of considerable repute, a synagogue was built in 1617, and in 1653 the first Jewish hospital in Germany was founded. The position of Jews in Fürth earned it the name Franconian Jerusalem, a phrase based on an older reference meant as an insult. The Jewish Museum in Franconia, opened in 1999, occupies a house that goes back to the 17th century.

Fürth survived the Second World War with less damage than most German cities and has many historic buildings. The Protestant Church of St Michael, dating from about 1100, is the oldest, and the Rathaus, built in 1840–50, has a tower modelled on the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence. The toy industry remains a major employer, and the football club SpVgg Fürth has won the German championship three times.
further-pomerania: Farther Pomerania, also called Hinder Pomerania, Rear Pomerania or Eastern Pomerania, is a subregion of historic Pomerania in north-western Poland. It lies mostly within the West Pomeranian Voivodeship, with its easternmost parts in the Pomeranian Voivodeship. It stretches roughly from the Oder in the west to Pomerelia in the east, and Polish historiography takes the river Łeba as the eastern limit. Its four cities are Kołobrzeg, Koszalin, Stargard and Słupsk. The name Pomerania comes from the Slavic po more, land at the sea. By the 16th century the name had come to cover the areas east of Szczecin.

In the 960s Pomerania became part of the emerging Polish state under Mieszko I, and around 1000 Bolesław I the Brave founded the Diocese of Kołobrzeg. Farther Pomerania emerged as a subdivision of the Duchy of Pomerania in the partition of 1532, as Pomerania-Stettin. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 and the Treaty of Stettin of 1653 divided the duchy between the Swedish Empire and Brandenburg-Prussia, and Farther Pomerania became the Brandenburg-Prussian Province of Pomerania. After the reorganisation of the Prussian Province of Pomerania in 1815 it was administered as the Regierungsbezirk Köslin, and in 1938 the northern part of the dissolved Grenzmark Posen-West Prussia was merged into it.

The Treaty of Versailles in 1919 awarded the bulk of Pomerelia, with minor parts of the Stolp, Lauenburg and Bütow districts, to Poland, while most of Farther Pomerania stayed in Germany. Nazi Germany set up the Stalag II-D prisoner-of-war camp at Stargard in 1939 and a camp for kidnapped Polish children at Połczyn-Zdrój. In 1945 death marches of prisoners from the Stutthof concentration camp and from prisoner-of-war camps passed through the region.

After Germany's defeat in 1945 the region was returned to Poland under the border decisions confirmed at the Potsdam Conference. German civilians left or were removed from the territories east of the Oder-Neisse line, and many new inhabitants came from central Poland and from eastern borderlands incorporated into the Soviet Union. Before 1999 the area was administered as the Szczecin, Koszalin and Słupsk Voivodeships. Under the reform effective 1 January 1999 it was divided between the West Pomeranian Voivodeship, which took about two thirds, and the Pomeranian Voivodeship. The main regional museums stand in Słupsk, Stargard, Koszalin and Darłowo.
fusagasuga: Fusagasugá, often shortened to Fusa, lies in the warm valley between the rivers Cuja and Panches, in a central region of the Andes, about 56 kilometres from Bogotá. It stands 1,728 metres above sea level, with an average temperature of about 20 °C, and the municipality covers roughly 194 square kilometres. The name is said to come from a Cariban word meaning woman who becomes invisible; Spanish interpretations range from the woman who becomes invisible to the woman who hides herself behind the mountain. The city has been called Tierra Grata for its country houses, and the Garden City of Colombia for its production of orchids.

The Sutagao people lived in the region until the Oídor Bernardino Albornoz founded the town between 5 and 13 February 1592. Not much is known about its earlier indigenous residents. At the visit of the Oídor Ibarra 759 indigenous people lived in Fusagasugá, but when the Oídor Aróstequi arrived in February 1760 only 85 remained, alongside 644 new settlers in 109 families. In 1776 two officials, Moreno and Escandón, decreed that the native villages of Pandi and Tibacuy no longer existed, and merged them into Pasca. The town became part of the province of Tequendama in 1852 and in 1895 was made capital of the new Sumapaz Province.

Roads shaped its growth. A directive of 7 August 1846 recognised the road from Fusagasugá to the southern provinces nationally, and an iron and wood bridge over the Sumapaz River at Boquerón was finished in 1907. A highway from Sibaté, begun in 1905 and interrupted until 1913, reached Fusagasugá in 1930. On 9 February 1877 government forces fought rebels at the hacienda El Novillero, and the first hospital was built in 1893. The main church has been rebuilt several times, from the first church of June 1658 to the fourth, begun in June 1909 and consecrated on 15 August 1926. During the Second World War a hotel in the city held citizens of Axis countries as an internment camp.

The municipality had a population of 138,498 at the 2018 census, of whom 114,722 lived in the urban centre. Its economy rests mainly on agriculture and construction, with a growing service sector in education, health, recreation and tourism. Several universities have campuses there, including the Universidad de Cundinamarca. The Pan-American highway passes through the municipality, and travellers from the north bound for Ibagué, Neiva or Cali must pass through it.
fussen: Füssen lies in the district of Ostallgäu, one kilometre from the Austrian border, on the banks of the Lech River at 808 m above sea level. The mountains of the Ammergau Alps surround it, and at the 47th parallel north it is one of the southernmost towns in Germany. The Lech flows into the Forggensee, a man-made lake built to prevent flooding. The town is known for violin making and is the nearest transport hub for the castles of Neuschwanstein and Hohenschwangau.

The town was settled in Roman times on the Via Claudia Augusta, the road from northern Italy to Augusta Vindelicum, now Augsburg, the capital of the province of Raetia. Its first name, Foetes, comes from the Latin word for a gorge, probably the gorge of the Lech. In Late Antiquity a part of the Legio III Italica was stationed there to guard the trade route over the Alps.

Below the High Castle stands the Baroque complex of the former Benedictine monastery of St Mang, whose history goes back to the 9th century. Saint Mang, Magnus of Füssen, is the town's patron saint; he and his brother monk Theodor, from the Abbey of Saint Gall, are considered its founders. His bones were moved to the crypt of a church built in 850, and around 950 they all disappeared. The coat of arms, a triskeles alluding to the German word for feet, is based on a seal of the early 14th century.

The Treaty of Füssen, signed in 1745 between the Electorate of Bavaria and Habsburg Austria, ended Bavaria's part in the War of the Austrian Succession. In the 19th century the composer Richard Wagner came to Füssen by railway to visit King Ludwig II of Bavaria. Since the 1950s the town has been the southern end of the Romantic Road.

The High Castle houses a branch gallery of the Bavarian State Collections of Paintings, with late Gothic and Renaissance works. The crypt of St Mang's Basilica holds the oldest fresco in Germany, from about 980. The saint's feast day, 6 September, is marked by a Mass and a torchlight procession through the old town.
fustat: Fustat lay on the eastern bank of the Nile, just north of the Roman fortress of Babylon, beside what is now Old Cairo. According to legend a dove laid an egg in the tent of Amr ibn al-As just before he marched on Alexandria in 641. He took it as a sign, left the tent untouched, and on his return had his soldiers pitch their tents around it. The name Misr al-Fustat is popularly translated as city of the tents, though this is not an exact translation. The Mosque of Amr was later built on the site of his tent, and was the first mosque in Egypt.

Egypt's capital had been Alexandria for nearly a thousand years. After Alexandria fell in September 641, Amr founded the new city. Its early population was almost entirely soldiers and their families, and it was laid out like a garrison, serving as a base for conquering North Africa until Qayrawan was founded in 670. Fustat grew as a series of tribal areas, khittas, around the mosque, with most settlers coming from Yemen. Under the Abbasids the seat of government moved to al-Askar, and later, under Tulunid rule, to al-Qatta'i, but Fustat regained its place in 905.

Under the Fatimids it prospered, and the geographer Ibn Hawkal wrote in 987 that it was about a third the size of Baghdad. It had shaded streets, gardens and markets, and tall residential buildings, some reported at seven storeys. From 975 to 1075 it was a major centre of Islamic art and ceramics. In 1168, with the Crusader king Amalric I of Jerusalem approaching, the vizier Shawar ordered the city burned. The historian al-Maqrizi wrote that the blaze lasted 54 days. The philosopher Maimonides settled in Fustat in 1166 and wrote his Mishneh Torah there in 1180.

After the fire Fustat declined, and under the Mamluks it was used as a rubbish dump. Its remains were absorbed into the growing city of Cairo, and it is now part of the district of Old Cairo. Few buildings from its time survive, and the Mosque of Amr has been so extensively rebuilt that nothing of the original remains. Excavations have found trade goods from as far away as Spain, China and Vietnam, and finds are shown in Cairo's Museum of Islamic Art.
futa-toro: Futa Toro is a semidesert region stretching about 400 kilometres along the middle course of the Senegal River, but only a band of up to 20 kilometres on either side of the river is well watered and fertile; the interior is dry and porous. Its provinces were fertile pockets of the waalo flood plain, controlled by kin groups, and disputes over inherited land rights fed many family quarrels and political crises. Futa was the general name the Fulbe gave to any land they lived in, while Toro, like the name Toucouleur, is thought to derive from the ancient kingdom of Takrur. Its people speak Pulaar and call themselves Haalpulaar'en, those who speak Pulaar.

The Fula first arrived in the time of the Wagadu Empire, fleeing the drying Adrar and Hodh regions, and mixed with earlier proto-Serer and Wolof fishing and farming peoples. Known then as Takrur, the region was one of the first in West Africa to become Muslim, by the 11th century, and grew rich on the trans-Saharan trade, especially after the Almoravid capture of Aoudaghost. It was conquered or made a vassal in turn by Wagadu, the Sosso Empire, the Mali Empire and the Jolof Empire, until Koli Tenguella founded the Denanke state in the early 16th century.

From the 17th century the region shrank as the Sahara dried and Berber and Hassani raids grew. The Almamyate founded in 1776 by the Torodbe, educated Fula Muslims, inspired Islamic reform movements and jihads across the region, though in the 1780s the forces of the almaami Abdul Kader could not impose control on neighbouring states. Futa Toro later supplied recruits for the jihads of al-Hajj Umar Tall and the anti-colonial rising of al-Hajj Mahmadu Lamine.

The southern bank of the river, where most of Futa Toro lies, remained in Senegal at independence. The north bank along the border, called Chemama, is part of Mauritania. The region is also remembered as a source of migrants to the Fouta Djallon.
futuna-wallis-and-futuna: Futuna is the largest island of the Hoorn Islands, or Îles Horne, in the Pacific Ocean. Futuna and Alofi are remnants of the same extinct volcano and are bordered by a fringing reef. Mont Puke, at 524 metres, is the highest point of Futuna. The island is separated from Wallis Island to the north by water deeper than 4,500 metres in the Vitiaz Trench. It has a tropical rainforest climate, with an average annual rainfall of about 3,300 millimetres, and the 2009 Samoa earthquake and tsunami reached it with a run-up height of 4.4 metres.

The first Europeans to map Futuna and Alofi were Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire in 1616, during their circumnavigation of the globe in the ship Eendracht. They named the islands Hoorn Eylanden after Schouten's birthplace, the city of Hoorn, a name that became Horne in French and English, and called a natural harbour on the south-west coast Eendrachts baai. On landing they made a show of force, which opened the way to peaceful barter: the islanders offered coconuts, yams and hogs for iron nails, beads and knives.

The king of Futuna told his subjects not to disturb the visitors, and a few days later the king of Alofi arrived with 300 men. A feast followed, with a kava ceremony and an ʻumu, which Schouten and Le Maire were probably the first Europeans to witness.

In the 19th century whaling ships from the United States and elsewhere called at Futuna for water, wood and food, the first known being the Independence in 1827. Pierre Chanel was martyred on the island in 1841 and became Polynesia's only Catholic saint. The cathedral of Poi now stands on the site.

The 2018 census counted 3,225 people on Futuna, 1,950 in the district of Alo and 1,275 in Sigave, about 27.9 per cent of the population of Wallis and Futuna. Futunan is spoken by 94.5 per cent, and about 99 per cent of the population of Wallis and Futuna is Catholic. Two kings, elected from the local nobility every few years, rule alongside the French authorities: the king of Sigave in the west and the king of Alo in the east, a province that includes Alofi. Villages lie along the south-west coast, with Leava as the capital and wharf. The vernacular and culture are more Samoan than those of Wallis.
futurism: Futurism was founded in Milan in 1909 by the poet and art theorist Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, who first published his Manifesto of Futurism on 5 February 1909 in La gazzetta dell'Emilia; Le Figaro reproduced it on 20 February. He was soon joined by the painters Umberto Boccioni, Carlo Carrà, Giacomo Balla and Gino Severini and by the composer Luigi Russolo. Marinetti expressed a passionate loathing of everything old, especially political and artistic traditions. The Futurists admired speed, technology, youth, violence, the car, the airplane and the industrial city, and they were passionate Italian nationalists. They praised originality and dismissed art critics as useless.

The movement worked in every medium, including painting, sculpture, theatre, film, music, architecture, fashion and cuisine. Boccioni's sculpture Unique Forms of Continuity in Space (1913) and Russolo's The Art of Noises (1913) are among its works.

In architecture Antonio Sant'Elia drew La Città Nuova (1912 to 1914), a city meant to be an efficient, fast-paced machine, never built; he was killed in the First World War. Francesco Balilla Pratella joined in 1910 and wrote a Manifesto of Futurist Musicians. In literature the Futurists called their poetry parole in libertà, rejecting meter and syntax. Italian Futurist cinema affected the film industry from 1916 to 1919, and only 35 minutes of Anton Giulio Bragaglia's Thaïs (1917) survive.

Many Italian Futurists supported Fascism in the hope of modernising Italy. Marinetti founded the Futurist Political Party in early 1918, which was absorbed into Benito Mussolini's Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in 1919. He walked out of the 1920 Fascist congress, calling its later exaltation of existing institutions reactionary, but supported Italian Fascism until his death in 1944. After Fascism's triumph in 1922 the Futurists gained official acceptance and could carry out important work, especially in architecture. A second generation took up aeropittura, aeropainting, from 1926, launched by the 1929 manifesto Perspectives of Flight.

Parallel movements appeared in the Russian Empire, where Vladimir Mayakovsky, Velimir Khlebnikov and Kazimir Malevich took part; their Cubo-Futurism combined Cubism's forms with Futurist movement, but many Russian Futurists were ideological opposites of the Italian movement, embracing the emerging communist movement.

Futurism influenced Art Deco, Vorticism, Constructivism, Surrealism and Dada. As an organised movement it is regarded as extinct, having died out in 1944 with Marinetti's death. After the Second World War many Futurist artists struggled in their careers because of their association with a defeated regime. Marinetti's manifesto also declared contempt for women, though he later called Luisa, Marchesa Casati a Futurist.
fuvahmulah: Fuvahmulah lies 494.2 km south of the capital, Malé, and is the third largest island of the Maldives, about 4.5 by 1.2 km, with a submerged reef, Rashikedefaro, running some 3 km to the south-east. It was once a small coral atoll whose southern end lay open at Diyarehifaando, enclosing a saltwater lagoon that formed a natural harbour. Two freshwater lakes, Dhadimagi Kilhi and Bandaara Kilhi, lie inland. At the northern tip, the beach of Thūndu is made of small, smooth white pebbles found nowhere else in the country.

The name joins fuvah, the local word for the areca nut, to Mulah, probably the island's original name. Admiralty charts called it Fua Mulaku and old French maps Poue Molluque. Its people speak a distinctive dialect of Dhivehi, known locally as Fuvahmulaki baha.

The island's oldest remains date from before its conversion to Islam. The ruin of a Buddhist stupa, the Fua Mulaku Havitta, stands about 40 feet high, though its shape was altered after excavation, and Thor Heyerdahl visited the island and wrote a book about it, titled Fua Mulaku in its German edition. The Vasho-Veyo, a circular bath with stone steps, shows skilled cutting of Porites coral stone. Gemmiskiy, the oldest building, was part of a Buddhist monastery and became the first mosque after the islanders converted. The Hukuru Miskiy was long the only Friday mosque, and its cemetery holds princes of the Dhiyamigilee and Huraage dynasties.

Fuvahmulah has produced many scholars, among them the cleric and poet Mohammad Jamaaluddeen, known as Naibu-Thutthu, who wrote raivaru couplets and served as chief justice. Former President Ibrahim Nasir was born on the island and spent his early childhood there before his family moved to Malé.

Fuvahmulah forms the administrative atoll of Gnaviyani and has city status, with a council of seven members elected by its wards. The 2022 census counted 9,166 residents. A hospital has served the island since 2001, and an airstrip on its south-eastern side has operated since 11 November 2011.
fuzhou: Fuzhou lies between the Min River estuary to the south and the city of Ningde to the north; together the two make up the Mindong linguistic and cultural region. According to a geographical treatise published in the 9th century under the Tang dynasty, the Yuanhe Maps and Records of Prefectures and Counties, its name comes from Mount Fu, a mountain said to lie northwest of the city, combined with zhou, meaning settlement or prefecture. Fuzhou has a humid subtropical climate, with long, hot summers, short mild winters, and typhoons in late summer and early autumn.

Archaeology shows long settlement. Bone analysis links the ancient inhabitants of Xiying (7300–6500 BCE) to Austronesian peoples, and the Keqiutou culture (6500–5000 BCE) is the oldest known site of rice cultivation in Fujian. During the Warring States period the Chinese called the area Minyue. According to the historian Sima Qian, the surviving members of the royal family of Yue fled south after Yue fell to Chu in 306 BCE and settled among the local Yue people. In 282 CE, under the Jin dynasty, two artificial lakes and a canal system were built in Ye, and the core of modern Fuzhou grew around these water systems. The first large-scale migration of Chinese settlers to the south and southeast began in 308.

In 893 the warlord brothers Wang Chao and Wang Shenzhi captured Fuzhou in a rebellion against the Tang and took control of Fujian, and in 909 they proclaimed the Min Kingdom. Under the Song dynasty Fuzhou produced ten zhuangyuan, scholars who placed first in the imperial examinations, a large number for any city of the time. Between 1405 and 1433 Admiral Zheng He's fleets visited en route to the Indian Ocean, and at Changle he built a shrine to Tian-Fei and in 1431 erected a stele.

Lin Zexu, a native of Fuzhou, was appointed in 1839 to enforce the ban on the opium trade; the First Opium War followed, and the Treaty of Nanjing of 1842 made Fuzhou, then known to Westerners as Foochow, one of five treaty ports. Japanese forces took the city in 1938, and the People's Liberation Army occupied it with little resistance on 17 August 1949.

Fuzhou is the capital of Fujian. Besides Mandarin, most of its people speak Fuzhounese, the prestige form of Eastern Min. Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism are its traditional religions, and its cuisine is one of the four traditional styles of Fujian cuisine. Its arts include bodiless lacquerware, paper umbrellas and horn combs, called the Three Treasures. The Sanfang Qixiang, the Three Lanes and Seven Alleys, preserves ancient residential buildings from the late Jin dynasty, and Hualin Temple, built in 964, has a main hall known as the oldest surviving wooden building in south China.
fyodor-dostoevsky: Fyodor Dostoevsky was born in Moscow on 11 November (Old Style 30 October) 1821, the second child of Dr Mikhail Dostoevsky and Maria Nechayeva. He grew up in the grounds of the Mariinsky Hospital for the Poor, where his father worked, and met patients from the lower end of Russian society when playing in the hospital gardens. His nanny read him sagas, fairy tales and legends, and his mother taught him to read from the Bible. His parents also introduced him to Pushkin, Schiller, Goethe, Cervantes, Walter Scott and Homer.

Dostoevsky completed his first novel, Poor Folk, in May 1845. His friend Dmitry Grigorovich took the manuscript to the poet Nikolay Nekrasov, who showed it to the critic Vissarion Belinsky, and Belinsky called it Russia's first social novel. It appeared on 15 January 1846 and sold well. He soon wrote The Double. He also read the French socialists Fourier, Cabet, Proudhon and Saint-Simon, but his Russian Orthodox faith could not accord with Belinsky's atheism and scientific materialism, and he parted from Belinsky and his circle.

In 1849 he was arrested for belonging to the Petrashevsky Circle, which discussed banned books critical of Tsarist Russia. He was sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted at the last moment. He spent four years in a Siberian hard labour camp, which inspired The House of the Dead, and then six years of compulsory military service in exile. Later he edited magazines of his own and wrote A Writer's Diary, travelled in Western Europe and developed a gambling addiction that brought financial hardship.

His major novels include Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot (1869), Demons (1872), The Adolescent (1875) and The Brothers Karamazov (1880). Notes from Underground, a novella of 1864, is considered one of the first works of existentialist literature. After his release from prison he put religious themes, especially those of Russian Orthodoxy, into his writing. His fiction takes up suicide, poverty, human manipulation and morality, and depicts the chaotic sociopolitical order of contemporary Russia.

Mikhail Bakhtin saw polyphony, the simultaneous presence of several narrative voices and perspectives, as an important element of his style and a major advance in the novel. Friedrich Nietzsche called him the only psychologist from whom he had something to learn, and Sigmund Freud ranked him second only to William Shakespeare among creative writers. He died on 9 February (Old Style 28 January) 1881 after a series of pulmonary hemorrhages, and asked that the parable of the Prodigal Son be read to his children.
fyodor-sergeyev: Fyodor Andreyevich Sergeyev was born on 19 March 1883 to a peasant family in the village of Glebovo in the Kursk Governorate, near Fatezh. In 1888 his father, a building contractor, moved the family to Yekaterinoslav, where Fyodor finished the realschule in 1901 before entering the Imperial Moscow Technical College. Arrested that year for joining a student demonstration, he spent four months in Voronezh prison and then went to Paris to study at the Russian Higher Free School. He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party and its Bolshevik faction, taking the name Artyom.

Back in Russia from 1903, he agitated in the factories of Yekaterinoslav while working as a stoker. In Kharkov he headed the Bolshevik organisation and in December 1905 led an armed rising of factory workers. He escaped from Kharkov prison in 1906, was arrested again in Perm and, after nearly three years in prison, was deported to Siberia. In 1910 he escaped through Korea and Japan to Brisbane, where he organised the Union of Russian emigrants, edited Echo of Australia from 1912 and, known as Big Tom, joined the Australian Socialist Party and union opposition to the First World War.

Returning after the February Revolution of 1917, he organised the Bolshevik seizure of power in Kharkov and the Donets basin in October. Under German occupation in 1918 he chaired the Sovnarkom of the Donetsk-Krivoy Rog Soviet Republic, secured the nationalisation of its industry and on 27 March formed the Donetsk Army, which was merged into Kliment Voroshilov's 5th Army by the end of April. In 1919 Vladimir Lenin made him People's Commissar for Agitation and Propaganda in Ukraine, and he later led the Society for Aid to Bashkiria. He sat on the Central Committee of the Russian Communist Party from 1920 and chaired the All-Russian Union of Miners.

Sergeyev was killed on 24 July 1921 during a test of the Aerowagon and was buried in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis. Joseph Stalin adopted his infant son Artyom. Bakhmut was renamed Artemovsk after him in 1924 and took back its old name in February 2016 under Ukraine's decommunisation law of 2015. Thomas Keneally's novel The People's Train has a hero loosely based on his life.
fyodor-the-black: Fyodor was a son of Prince Rostislav Mstislavovich of Smolensk, who died in 1240, and from birth he held the title of Duke of Mozhaysk. His nickname is also read as Theodore the Beautiful. In 1260 he married Maria Vasilievna, daughter of Prince Vasily of Yaroslavl; recent research holds that her real name was Anastasia. The marriage made him prince of Yaroslavl, but real power lay with Maria's mother, Princess Xenia. The couple had two daughters and a son, Michael.

Around 1266 Fyodor left his family and went on his own initiative to Sarai, the capital of the Golden Horde, where he became a loyal servant and military commander of Khan Mengu-Timur. He took part in the khan's invasion of Ossetia, and in 1277–1278 led a punitive campaign in Volga Bulgaria in which, according to the documents, his troops sacked 40 cities and 600 villages. Mengu-Timur made him his butler. When news came of Maria's death, Fyodor tried to return to Yaroslavl, but Xenia and the boyars refused to let him into the city.

Back at the Horde he married a daughter of Mengu-Timur, who was baptised as Anna; the chronicles credit her dowry with 36 towns, and they had two sons, David and Constantine. After his brothers died in 1278–1279 he inherited the Principality of Smolensk and probably lived there in 1279–1281. When his son Michael died in 1290, he returned to rule Yaroslavl with a yarlik from the Mongols. He fought in the war between the sons of Alexander Nevsky, and in 1293 joined Dyuden's punitive campaign in north-eastern Rus', in which 14 towns were sacked.

In his last years Fyodor became a monk, and he died in Yaroslavl. Known in Russian also as Fyodor Chermny, he was canonised by the Russian Orthodox Church for the depth of his repentance on his deathbed, and he is venerated as a saint.
fyodor-ushakov: Fyodor Fyodorovich Ushakov was born on 24 February 1745 in the village of Burnakovo in Yaroslavl province, into a modest family of the minor nobility. His father was a retired sergeant of the Preobrazhensky Regiment of the imperial guards. The family had not been officially confirmed as nobles and Ushakov himself could not prove nobility.

In 1798, as vice-admiral of the Black Sea Fleet, he asked for official nobility and arms, his coat of arms was entered in the General all-Russian book of heraldry in 1807, and in 1815 he and his family were added to the Yaroslavl genealogical book. He signed up for the Imperial Russian Navy in Saint Petersburg on 15 February 1761.

After training he served on a galley in the Baltic Fleet, and in 1768 he moved to the Don Flotilla at Taganrog for the Russo-Turkish War (1768–74). He commanded Catherine II's own yacht and protected Russian merchant ships in the Mediterranean. After Russia conquered the Crimean Khanate in 1783 he supervised the building of the naval base at Sevastopol and of docks at Kherson. In the war of 1787–92 he defeated the Ottomans at Fidonisi, the Kerch Strait, Tendra and Cape Kaliakra, showing the ingenuity of his naval tactics.

In 1798 he was promoted to full admiral and sailed to the Mediterranean through Constantinople, where an Ottoman squadron joined his under his command in the War of the Second Coalition. The fleet took the Ionian islands, which France had acquired from Venice in the Treaty of Campo Formio, and the siege of Corfu led to the creation of the Septinsular Republic. His squadron blockaded Genoa and Ancona, and landing parties took Naples and Rome, where Italians greeted the Russians as liberators. Tsar Paul ordered him to Malta, but he was recalled to Russia in 1800, and Alexander I failed to appreciate his victories.

Ushakov resigned command in 1807 and withdrew to the Sanaksar Monastery in Mordovia. He declined to command the local militia in 1812 because of ill health but gave his savings. He died on 14 October 1817. In 43 naval battles under his command he is said never to have lost a ship or a battle.

He used unified marching and fighting orders, closed resolutely with the enemy, concentrated on flagships, kept a reserve and chased the enemy to destruction or capture, and valued sea and fire training in the manner of Suvorov. His innovations were among the first successful steps from line tactics to manoeuvre. The Soviet Union established the Order of Ushakov in 1944, and the Russian Orthodox Church glorified him as a saint on 7 August 2001. His relics are at Sanaksar.
fyrkat: The fortress stands near Hobro, some distance from the present end of the Mariager Fjord, on a narrow strip of land between a stream and a swampy area. It may have served as barracks or as a defensive stronghold, and would have helped to control traffic on the main land route between Aalborg and Aarhus. Tree-ring dating places the very similar Trelleborg near Slagelse in the spring of 981, and Fyrkat might be a year or two older. The forts are so alike that a single mind most probably conceived them.

Like Aggersborg and Trelleborg, Fyrkat is an exact circle with four gates opposite each other, joined by two wooden roads crossing at right angles in the middle. The rampart, 12 to 13 metres wide at the base, was built of three rows of wooden posts with some 10000 cubic metres of turf between them, and its outer wall probably stood about four metres high. A ditch guarded the north-east quarter, while a river and swampy ground protected the other sides.

The longhouses were 28.5 metres long, with slightly curved long walls, a large middle room with a hearth and sleeping benches, and a small room at each end. At least two held smithies, gold was worked in two others, and about a quarter seem to have been warehouses. A cemetery of about 30 graves of men, women and children lay to the north-west; the richest, grave 4, held a woman buried with much jewellery and foreign objects.

The fort seems to have been lived in only briefly, perhaps a decade or less; by 1000 it was deserted, and soon after it burned to the ground with no evidence of fighting. C.G. Schultz excavated the site between 1950 and 1958, piling up the ploughed-down ramparts again and filling the postholes with concrete. A longhouse was reconstructed beside the ramparts in 1985, and the Viking Center Fyrkat, a reconstructed farm, opened about a kilometre away in 1993. Most finds are in the museum at Hobro.
